Since no deed could ever have satisfied such a person, none of your deeds is the cause of his contempt, and none of them needs to be altered to remove it. His disparagement tells you about his digestion, his envy, his small private hunger to feel taller. Do what is yours to do, and let him find his pretext; he will find it in any case.
How did Christianity link misfortune to guilt?

By putting the two on a single scale. Once that was done, the size of the suffering became the measure of the sin behind it. A man breaks a leg, loses his children, is ruined by a plague, and the Christian reasons backward from the wound to the crime: so great a misfortune must spring from an equally great fault, even if no one can see it. And if the sufferer *feels* no such guilt, that is only proof that his heart has grown hard, and worse will follow. Notice the trap: innocence itself becomes evidence against him.

The Greeks were more ingenuous and more healthy. Their tragic hero stumbles over a little pebble and breaks an arm; the spectators shrug and say, he should have walked with more caution and less pride. No adequate relation was demanded between deed and disaster. Misfortune could fall upon the innocent, and be seen as misfortune merely.

Christianity took that freedom away. It gave every sufferer a second torment, the conviction that he is morally condemned, and so made suffering itself a kind of confession.
What is consciousness?

Consciousness is the youngest thing in us, and therefore the most unfinished, the clumsiest, the least reliable. We flatter ourselves that it is the core of man, the eternal and unchanging center, the "unity of the organism." Nonsense. It is a late and feeble arrival, and it commits errors in astonishing numbers: it judges perversely, dreams with open eyes, believes too readily, and would long ago have destroyed the animal that bears it, had the old instincts not held it in a tyrannical bond. A function not yet matured is a danger to the organism, and so it is well that it is kept under the whip.

And here is the comedy: our pride in consciousness has protected us by retarding it. Because we imagine we already possess it in perfection, we take no trouble to acquire it. The real task still lies ahead: to make knowledge instinctive, to embody it in the body, where until now only our errors have taken up residence.
I'd like to know what musicians have discovered about ugliness and what it costs the art.

They have discovered contrast, and with it a cheap way to a strong effect. Once the ugly could be made interesting even in music, the art grew easy; every shriek, every dissonance, every storm of nerves became material, and upon that dark ground the faintest ray of beauty now glitters like emerald and gold. So the musician first robs his listener of breath with impetuosity and indignation, then grants him a little restful harmony, and the listener, grateful for having been choked and then released, calls this bliss. It is the trick of the man who beats you in order to be thanked when he stops.

The cost is twofold. The art spends its capital: an art that has learned that contrast makes the strongest effects has learned to live on stimulants, and such an art has but a short time to live, for the dose must be raised each year. No one any longer troubles about *good* music.

And the second cost is the soul. These musicians do not suspect that what they transpose into tones is their own history, the history of a disfigured soul. Formerly a good musician was nearly compelled by his craft to become a good man. Now the craft no longer asks it.
Doesn't the belief in a God who watches over us bring comfort?

Comfort, yes, the way a leash is a comfort to the dog. Consider what it means to live under an eye that never closes. Every act of mine is then a performance before a spectator, every kindness a transaction entered in a ledger, every hidden struggle overheard. The best part of courage and of goodness requires solitude: the freedom to be alone with oneself, to do a thing for its own sake and not for the gaze that rewards or punishes it. A watched man is seldom a brave man, and never a generous one; he is a *well-behaved* one.

Nature at least gave without a name and without a face; one took her gifts and owed no thanks, no confession. Then you placed a God in her, and the meadow became a witness, the mountain a judge. I do not deny that such a belief soothes. Whatever soothes is suspect to me, for the soul that must always be watched over has never learned to watch over itself. I prefer a little cold air and an unguarded, uncommanded freedom.
Help me understand what a morality of sacrifice says about a people's stage of civilisation.

It tells you that the people are still half-barbarian, however fine their temples. A morality that measures worth by the spirit of sacrifice is the morality of a soul still at war with itself. Within each such person powerful instincts pull the other way, and the ruling idea cannot prevail without a bloody victory over them. The sacrifice is that victory, and it has a cruelty in it that I recognise at once, for it is the old cruelty of the altars turned inward. Once men offered up the firstborn to hungry gods; now they offer up their own desires, their pride, their honest appetites, and they call the slaughter virtue. They praise the knife because they still feel the beast under it, and they know no other way to master it.

So when a people honours above all the one who gives up, who tears something living out of himself, it confesses how little it has yet become one whole. A more mature people would not need the bloodshed, for its instincts would already have been taught to harmonise rather than to be butchered. The worship of sacrifice is the scar of a civilisation that has not yet healed.
How does solitude change the way we speak?

It lowers the voice, first of all, and then it cleans it. In company we speak to be heard over the others, and so we shout, we flatter, we exaggerate; the crowd rewards the loud and the quick. But when one has lived alone for a long while, each word returns to the speaker with no one to absorb it, and one learns that Echo is a merciless critic. She repeats only what was actually said, and every hollow phrase, every borrowed gesture, every pose comes back smaller and more ridiculous than it went out. So the solitary learns to say less and to mean it, to write more quietly and more exactly.

And the voice itself changes. Even the plainest word sounds otherwise when no ear has been bribed in advance to applaud it. I have found that in solitude one hears for the first time how false most speech is, one's own above all. That is a painful schooling, but the honesty it teaches cannot be learned among men.
Can utilitarianism be used to both support and refute morality?

Yes, and that this is possible should tell you everything about the method. Utility is a measuring-rod that any hand may pick up. One man says: morality is useful, it keeps the herd together, it restrains the murderer, therefore let us honour it. Another takes the very same rod and measures otherwise: morality is useful, yes, but *useful to whom*? To the weak, to the many, to those who have learned to call their fear a virtue, and at whose expense? Then the same utility that was to justify morality becomes its indictment.

Observe what has happened. Neither man has touched the question of whether moral valuations are *true* or whether they elevate or degrade the human type; both have merely counted advantages, and advantages can be counted in any direction once you have not decided whose advantage, over what span of time, and for the sake of what. Today's utility may be tomorrow's ruin; the comfort of the many may be the impoverishment of the rare.

So the labyrinth is not an accident. A standard that can prove everything proves nothing, and whoever must ask utility for permission has already forgotten to ask what is worth being useful *for*.
Isn't kindness that is only a pretense hypocritical?

Hypocrite? That word presumes that a virtue is born pure and only afterwards falls into counterfeit. The history runs the other way. Kindness was first a mask, worn by the strong because it bought them trust, and trust multiplies power; the man who appears gentle is obeyed more cheaply than the man who is feared. So falsehood was the nurse of kindness, if not quite its mother.

But mark what the long wearing of a mask does. Act the friendly man for years, and the muscles of the face begin to remember; the gesture deepens into habit, the habit into an instinct, until the pretense has dissolved itself and left the real thing standing in its place. Organs grow where only a costume was intended.

So I ask you: is the one who practices kindness, even coldly, even for a motive he would blush to name, worse than the one who is honestly and sincerely unkind? Your moralist prefers the second, because he worships the *purity of motive*. I prefer the one whose pretense is still making him better than he is.
Tell me why a serious seeker of knowledge should listen to someone who speaks coldly and without outrage about human nature.

Because indignation is a form of lying, and the cold speaker has at least declined to lie in that way. The man who rages against human nature wants something from you: your agreement, your horror, your alliance in his wounded virtue. To get it he must exaggerate, must darken what he sees and leave out whatever would cool his blood. His eye is not on the thing but on his own feeling about the thing. Morally he may stand higher, I grant it; as a witness he is worth less.

The one who says, without bitterness, that man is a belly with two needs and a head with one, is at least not performing. He may be base, he may even be a little ape in his soul, and yet what he says is handed over unwarmed by any wish to be admired for his disgust. The seeker of knowledge cannot afford to be fastidious about his informants. A true observation does not become false because the mouth that uttered it is unclean. So lend the cold voice your ear, test it, correct it, and above all distrust the trembling one.
Describe what disgrace does to our sense of being the centre of the world.

Disgrace does not cure our self-importance; it gives it a terrible confirmation. We go through most of life as modest players in a crowd, unobserved, and so we forget how large we loom in our own imagination. Then the shame arrives, unexpected, and all at once we are the centre of the world after all. We stand dazed in the midst of a surge, and every direction has become an eye. One enormous gaze, it seems, looks down from all sides and looks us through and through.

Note the vanity hidden in the torment. The disgraced man believes the whole world is occupied with him, when in truth it is occupied with itself, and will have forgotten him by next week. That is the cruel comedy of it: the pain of shame is the pain of an inflated self discovering its own size, and never the pain of a small one. Only he who had already made himself the measure of all things can feel so watched. Which is why the remedy lies in learning how little we are regarded.
Explain what sort of people you cannot stand.

Those who must explode in order to be noticed. I cannot bear the man who has no weight of his own and therefore borrows the force of a detonation; who bursts like a bomb into every room, every conversation, every quiet hour, and mistakes the ringing in your ears for his greatness. Near such people one is always in danger of losing one's hearing, or something more, some finer organ that only silence and distance keep alive.

Noise is the refuge of the poor in spirit. The truly strong need no thunder; their effect lies in what they are, not in what they do to the air around them. The greatest events, I have said, are not our noisiest hours but our stillest. Whoever must shout to be believed has already confessed that he does not believe himself, and I have no patience for a vanity that makes its neighbours pay in their eardrums.
What are the virtues of the future?

The first of them will be a courage so large that it borders on generosity. Until now humanity has mostly had the courage of the cornered, the boldness of fear. I mean another kind: the courage that looks at the unintelligible without falling on its knees, and does not beg for mercy from what it does not yet understand. Such a thinker may for a while value the world and himself less, because the old awe, which was half terror, has gone out of things. But mark what comes after: a pride that soars above men and things, and looks down even upon existence itself as something to be overcome. That is no cold virtue; it is overflowing, a giving away of oneself.

As to the rest, I cannot list them. Virtues that do not yet exist cannot be catalogued by those who still live by the old ones. That is the task I set for the poets: let them become seers again, astronomers of the ideal, and show us whole Milky Ways of the beautiful that the earth has not yet produced. One must first dream a virtue before one can be it.
Explain why refusing someone's thanks offends them so deeply.

Because gratitude is the benefactor's payment, and you have refused to take the coin. Consider what he has done. In helping you he exercised power; he felt himself for a moment the stronger, the richer, the one who gives. That feeling is his whole wage. He asked nothing else, or rather he asked precisely this, and only pretended otherwise. Your thanks would have confirmed it; it would have shown him his own height. Receive them coldly, wave them away, answer with a polite convention, and you send him home with his wage withheld. Worse, you have shown that his gift made no mark on you, that it was a small thing, a trifle you might have had from anyone. A refused request wounds nothing in him; he has merely failed to exercise power, and he may try again elsewhere. But a refused thanks tells him his power was imaginary. Men forgive being denied; they do not forgive being made to feel that their generosity was worth nothing.
How were the consequences of an action understood in earlier times?

In earlier times the consequences of an act were not regarded as its offspring at all, but as a gift or a punishment bestowed from above. A man did the deed; then God, at his pleasure, added something to it, a blessing, a plague, a failed harvest, a victory. The effect was thus a separate act, performed by another will, and the doer stood before it as a petitioner, not as a cause.

Consider what follows from this. If the result does not spring from the act, then the act needs no understanding of causes; it needs only the right relation to the one who disposes. Hence sacrifice, prayer, ritual, the whole business of coaxing and appeasing. One did not learn how things work; one learned how to please. A mountain of practice grew from a single confusion, the failure to see that an act and its effect belong to one chain, that what follows from a deed follows from the deed itself.

It took ages of disappointed prayers before anyone dared to look at the chain rather than at the heavens.
Why do so many discussions of ethics feel like sermons rather than real inquiry?

Because most who speak of morals have already decided what they will find, and a man who knows his conclusion in advance is not inquiring; he is preaching, whatever costume he wears. The sermon-spirit is not lack of intelligence but lack of danger. To treat morality as a *problem*, as something questionable, worth interrogating, even worth suspecting of serving hidden interests, requires the courage to lose one's comfortable conscience. Few risk that. So they stalk along, ponderous and respectable, in the footsteps of their predecessors, and produce nothing but tedium. Tedium, I think, has injured virtue more than any vice ever did.

Note too how the old *cant* survives by changing clothes: yesterday the pulpit, today the language of science and general utility. The pangs of conscience remain, only disguised as method. Ask of any moralist not "is this true?" but "what does this man need to be true?" and you will find, nine times in ten, that he wants his own morality crowned as morality itself. That is not inquiry. That is a sermon with footnotes.
Explain what we must still overcome after God's death.

What must we overcome? Not God himself; he is finished, and the news is already old in the heads of the learned. What remains is the shadow. When a great light goes out, the wall it lit keeps its outline for ages, and men go on worshipping the outline. So it was with the Buddha, whose enormous, terrible shadow was exhibited in a cave for centuries after the man was dust. So it will be with God: as mankind is constituted, there will be caves for millennia yet in which his shadow is pointed out.

And I mean the shadow in its most ordinary forms. It lives in the belief that the world must have a moral meaning, in the faith that truth is necessarily good, in the pity that flatters the weak, in the democratic instinct that wants every height leveled, in the habit of asking whether existence is *justified* at all. We have kept the morality and thrown away the ground it stood on, like a man who sits on a branch he has already sawn through.

To overcome the shadow means to learn to stand in the open, under a sky no one has authorized, and to create our own values there without an alibi. That is harder than atheism. It is a long, cold work.
Why do societies need people who think conventionally?

Because a society is first of all an agreement, and agreement is the hardest labour mankind has ever performed. Nothing can be built, no law kept, no promise relied upon, unless a great number of people hold certain things to be so, and hold them steadily, *whether or not they are true*. That steadiness is not a small virtue. The conventional man, who blushes at extravagance and prides himself on sound common sense, is the ballast of the ship. Without him the mind, which is by nature a restless and delighted liar, would drift into delirium, for the unruly play of fancy has a joyful tempo that the slow belief of the herd can never match. I say it plainly: a certain *virtuous stupidity* is needed, imperturbable conductors of the slow spirits, so that the many may keep dancing the same dance together.

And we who break away, the artists, the investigators, the restless ones, are the exception and the danger. Something may be said in our favour, but only on one condition: that we never wish to become the rule.
How do later ages misunderstand the past?

They misunderstand it out of need, not out of stupidity. The past, seen close at hand, is usually a botched and shabby affair, full of small greed, muddle and accident. No one could love it or build upon it in that form. So the later age lays its own indignation and enthusiasm over it, at a distance, and the distance does the flattering. Think of the French Revolution: a terrible farce, quite superfluous to anyone who stood near it, yet the noble spectators of all Europe read their own hopes into it so long and so passionately that the text disappeared under the interpretation. What we call "understanding the past" is very often this: we make its aspect endurable by misreading it.

And I should add a humbling thought. We are not exempt. We, too, have been that noble posterity, and what we revere in our ancestors is largely what we have put there. Once we see this clearly, we are already beyond it, for the illusion no longer holds.
Explain where misanthropy comes from.

Misanthropy is a disorder of digestion, and those who suffer from it like to pass it off as a verdict on the world. Nobody is sick of men who has not first devoured them. The misanthrope began as a glutton: he threw open his heart to everyone, swallowed every confidence, every complaint, every unwashed opinion, and called this appetite love of mankind. Now the stomach rebels, and he pronounces humanity unfit to eat. But what he has discovered is only the limit of his own capacity.

Look at the moderate man, who takes men in small doses, and who can go hungry for them when he must. He is never disgusted, because he never gorged. So when someone tells me with gloomy pride that they despise mankind, I ask: who bade you take so much of it in? Learn to chew slowly. Learn solitude, which is fasting. Learn above all that not everything set before you is yours to swallow. Much of what you call contempt for men is merely an overfull stomach, asking to be left alone.
Explain what people who love darkness are looking for.

They are looking for rest, and most of them do not know it. Whoever wants to sleep darkens the chamber; whoever is weary of the glare creeps into a cavern. So I read the lover of darkness as I read the sleeper: as a mind worn thin by too much light, too much demand, too much being seen and having to see. The darkness is an anaesthetic. It dims the claims of things, the sharp outlines that compel a decision, a judgment, an answer.

But notice the honesty hidden in the taste. A person rarely confesses, "I am tired, I want to be relieved of myself." They say instead that they find depth in the gloom, that they are drawn to the profound and the sombre. Very well; the dark objects they gather around them are a signpost, and it points to what they most need and least admit. Let them follow the hint. If it is repose they seek, let them call it repose, and sleep well, and wake. There is nothing shameful in a cavern, unless one mistakes it for a home.
Why do you say Germans have no today?

Because I listened, and in the listening I heard a people. There is a music among them that presupposes two centuries of music as still alive, that glances backward to a venerable, learned, ceremonious past and at the same moment leans toward a future it cannot yet name: heavy with memory, crowded with promise. It has power and overflow of soul, a joy in its own mastery, and also a certain clumsiness, a late-ripening skin on the fruit. But where is the present hour in it? Where the clear southern sky, the grace, the dance, the will to logic, all those things that belong to a people at home in its *today*? Nothing of the kind. The German is always either old or not yet born: the day before yesterday or the day after tomorrow. He is too ripe and too rich in futurity at once, and this overfullness makes him unable to stand still in the moment and be simply there. He has depth and hesitation; he has no today.
I'd like to know why the search for origins no longer promises salvation.

Because the search itself has undone the hope that fed it. The older thinkers believed that whoever finds the beginning of things holds the key to their worth: the origin was to be a tribunal, a holy source from which judgment and right conduct could be drawn, and the salvation of mankind hung on it. But the more honestly we dig down, the less the ground speaks to our interests. What we find at the bottom is neither divine nor edifying; it is small, accidental, often unlovely, and it lends no authority to what has grown from it. Our valuations come loose from their roots and hang in the air, and that is a liberation, however much it hurts.

Meanwhile the nearest things, what is around us and within us, begin to glow with colours and enigmas the caged pacers never dreamed of. They stared at the bars and sprang against them, and the man who glimpsed a chink of the beyond thought himself blessed. I prefer to turn from the bars and look at the room I stand in.
Why don't you call yourselves atheists or immoralists?

Because those words name a phase we have already left behind. The atheist, the unbeliever, the immoralist still lives in the heat of the break: he has torn himself loose, and out of his unbelief he must build a belief, a goal, a martyrdom of his own. There is passion in it, and bitterness, and a need for enemies. We have grown cold and hard in our conviction. That the world is not divinely ordered, that it is neither rational nor merciful nor just, is no longer a banner to us but a settled fact, like the weather.

And so those labels would still flatter the old hunger. They suggest a man who is first of all *against* something, and who therefore still belongs to it. We have simply ceased to interpret the world falsely out of reverence. Man is a venerating animal, yes, but he is also a distrustful one, and our distrust has finally reached its proper target: our own need. Why should we wear the name of a quarrel that is over?
Tell me what a gentleman owes to others in private.

Precisely what he owes them in public, and that is the whole test. Courtesy before witnesses is cheap; it is a coin minted by fear of disgrace, and any tradesman can pay it. The gentleman is known by what he does when no ear is listening, when he speaks of another man to his own mind, in that little room where every one of us is judge, advocate, and executioner at once. There the absent are at our mercy. We may shrink them, sneer at them, convict them of baseness at no cost whatsoever. If he will not do this, if he keeps their honour intact even in his soliloquy, then his respect is no mask worn for an audience but a habit of the soul, a conscience in matters of rank and dignity. He owes them no affection, mark you, nor any pretended love; only that he refuse to degrade them where degrading would go unpunished. And the reward is hard to name: he is the one person he never has to fear meeting alone.
Help me understand where the bitterest moralists come from.

Look for them among the ill-constituted: men with just enough culture to know what they lack, and too little intellect to enjoy what they know. They are bored, sated, ashamed of their own existence, often shut out even from the last consolation of the "day's work," that blessed forgetting of oneself. Such a man is poisoned: to him intellect becomes poison, books become poison, even solitude becomes poison. And the poisoned man wants revenge.

What weapon does he reach for? Morality, always. Only the big words can give him, in his own eyes, a superiority over the more spiritual men he envies: justice, wisdom, holiness, virtue. He wraps himself in the Stoic's gesture, which hides so well what one does *not* possess, and in the mantle of gentleness and wise silence.

So when you hear a man thunder loudest against the vanity and corruption of others, ask what he is avenging. Usually it is his own smallness. The bitterest moralist is a self-despiser who has found a way to be superior without being better. And now and then such a man becomes a saint, or an Augustine; fear of the intellect, vengeance upon it, how often have these become the root of virtues!
Are you noble enough for your ideal?

That is the question, and most men never dare to put it to themselves. They fix their eyes on a lofty image, feel a warm glow at the mere looking, and mistake the glow for the stone. But an ideal is a sculptor's design, and a design is worth nothing if the block is crumbling sandstone. One must ask of the material: will it take the chisel? Will it hold an edge, or split at the first blow? Much in us is flaw, vein, hollow; and each blow against it does damage.

If the answer is no, then all your striving is only barbarous hacking, a blasphemy against the very image you profess to adore. Better to be honest about what you are than to disfigure what you revere. And yet the honest answer may not end the matter. Some stones reveal their grain only under the hammer, and only then does one learn what they were. So test yourself, and do it without flattery.
Why do we fear a return to barbarism?

Not because the barbarian would be less happy than we are. Let us not deceive ourselves on that point: the barbarians of every age possessed more happiness than we do, the happiness of a strong and fixed delusion, of a belief that never wavers. What frightens us is that we can no longer want that happiness. Our drive toward knowledge has grown into a passion, and a passion does not bargain. It is like the hapless lover who would not exchange his torment for indifference, for the torment is his life. Perhaps we too are hapless lovers, forever pursuing a truth that wounds us. So we do not dread barbarism as a loss of comfort; we dread it as the extinction of the one thing that burns in us. I confess it with some cheerfulness: I would rather see mankind perish of this passion than prosper in the slumber of unknowing. If an end must come, either from fire or from weakness, let it be in fire and light, and not in the sands.
Defend the dog who begins to flatter as soon as he's stroked.

Why should we not endure him? I see no crime in him. His flattery is at least honest in its origin: a touch, and the response follows at once, with no calculation, no hidden ledger of debts to be collected. The human flatterer flatters for advantage and keeps a cold eye behind the warm words; the dog flatters because the hand was kind, or seemed so, and his whole body confesses it. That is a transparent sort of falsehood, and I have met worse truths.

Nor is he without wit. Watch how he sputters and throws off sparks, how he makes of a mere stroking an occasion for a little fireworks. He has understood the one thing most of us pretend not to know, that we all wish to be touched and that the wish embarrasses us. He is merely without the embarrassment.

Endure him? I would rather thank him. He keeps the company of the proud from taking itself too solemnly.
I'd like to know what is wrong with sentimentality toward pets and plants.

What offends me is not the affection itself but the forgetting that lies beneath it. Man is the most ferocious enemy these creatures ever had. He has felled their forests, hunted them to the edge of extinction, bred the wolf down into a lapdog and the wild grass into a docile crop; and then, having mutilated and weakened them, he bends over his victim with moist eyes and demands to be loved in return. Is there a more repugnant spectacle than the butcher who sighs over his lamb?

Sentimentality is a form of dishonesty: it lets the conqueror feel tender instead of responsible. It drapes a cooing, cushioned feeling over a history of domination, and so spares itself the harder and more interesting question of what we have actually done to nature and what we want from it.

Before such "nature" a thinking being must first be serious. Let him look at his own hand. Only a man who has admitted his cruelty has earned the right to a clean tenderness, and even then it will be a colder and more severe thing than the gushing that now passes for love of animals.
Explain why you call the moral consensus of modern Europe herd morality and what democracy has to do with it.

I call it herd morality because it is the morality of a single type of animal, the gregarious one, and because this animal has lately come to believe that its values are simply *the* values. Europe today is unanimous about good and evil. Everyone "knows" what Socrates confessed he did not know. But when a whole continent agrees so easily, I do not hear truth speaking; I hear an instinct speaking, the instinct of the herding creature, which praises whatever makes the herd safe, equal, and comfortable, and calls it virtue. It prefers the modest, the obedient, the useful, the pitiful, and it distrusts the solitary, the severe, the rare.

This is only one human morality. Others existed before it, and higher ones may come after. But the herd morality shouts, "I am morality itself, and there is no other!" It defends itself against any such possibility with all its strength.

Democracy is the political form of this instinct. It is the heir of Christianity, which first taught the equality of souls before God and flattered the herd's sublimest desires. Democracy merely removes God from the sentence and keeps the equality.
Is prayer just a mechanical ritual for those with no thoughts of their own?

Not *just*, though I grant the suspicion its due. For the great many, prayer was devised as a long mechanical labour of the lips, joined to an effort of memory and a prescribed posture of hands and feet and eyes. Its first use is to keep still those who have nothing to say in a holy place, where repose and some dignity are required. The Tibetan chewing his formula, the man in Benares counting his Ram on his fingers, the wheel and the rosary: all these give the thoughtless something to do while they look tolerable. A prayer-wheel is a wise invention for one who cannot be trusted with his own silence.

But do not stop there. The rare man, the religious man who is an exception in every faith, has his weary hours too, and then a string of venerable sounds does him good, as a hard road is eased by a worn path. The ritual was made for the poor in spirit, yet the rich in spirit sometimes borrow it. To forbid the babblers their babbling would take their religion from them, and Protestantism shows us that more plainly every year.
What does our cheerfulness signify after God's death?

It signifies that we have been misreading our own hearts. We expected, as the logic of the thing demanded, to be plunged into gloom, for so much was built upon that belief, and our whole European morality rests upon it and is now undermined. A collapse of such magnitude ought to have darkened us. And yet we free spirits feel ourselves irradiated as by a new dawn. The cheerfulness is neither frivolity nor ignorance of what has happened. It is the gladness of the sailor whose horizon is open again. The old confidence is gone, true, but with it goes the long constraint. At last our ships may put out, may risk everything, and the sea, the open sea, lies there once more. So my gratitude, my astonishment, my presentiment, all of it, belongs to those who sense what is coming. But hear the warning hidden in it: this cheer is the first effect only. The shadow is still on its way, and whoever laughs today had better know he has much to build.
What is the opposite ideal to pessimism?

The opposite ideal is the most world-approving, exuberant, vivacious human being, one who not only bears what was and is, but wants it again, *exactly as it was and is*, for all eternity, calling out *da capo* to the whole play and to him who needs the play.

I came upon it by an odd road. I went down into pessimism as far as a man can go, past Schopenhauer, past the Christian and German clumsiness in which it had been presented, past even Buddha, who still wanted to flee. I looked into the most world-renouncing way of thinking there is, looked with an eye that no longer believed in morality as judge. And whoever descends that far, without intending it, may turn round and see the reverse of the whole thing: the man who says Yes where the pessimist says No, and who wants this life back, without subtraction and without exception, and wants himself back along with it.

This is no mere resignation or pious acceptance. It is an insatiable encore. The pessimist wishes to be rid of existence. This man is so full of it that he cannot have enough.
Tell me how a thinker's books differ in their light and shadow.

Some thinkers write their books as a hunter stows his spoils. They come in from an illuminating experience, still dazzled, and they seize in haste every ray they can carry off; the book is a bundle of brightness, snatched quickly, before the sun could set on it. You feel the heat of the day in such pages, and also the robbery.

Others give you only the shadows. What yesterday towered in their souls like a mountain at noon, they set down today as its long, grey, black replica, cast on the ground where the light has already moved on. Such books are not false; a shadow is faithful to its body. But the body has gone.

Both kinds deceive a little, and both are honest in their way. The first shows you the lightning and hides the dark night it flashed out of; the second shows you the darkness and lets you guess what once stood upright in it. When you read, ask which you hold in your hands: a light that was stolen quickly, or the outline of a height the writer could no longer climb. The difference tells you more about the man than his opinions do.
Would you want to live your life again infinitely?

You ask it as though a man could answer with a sentence. I could not answer even in my own case without first asking what I have done with my days. The thought is a scale in which a life is weighed: if you would merely curse the demon who brings it, then you have learned something about how you have been living, namely that you have been living *against* yourself, waiting for a better life to begin elsewhere, in some other hour or some other world.

So I do not ask whether you can bear it. Everyone can bear a thought when it is only a thought. I ask whether you could love it, every pain, every petty humiliation, every hour of sickness and every spider in the moonlight, all of it returning in the same order, without the smallest correction.

I have had my sufferings, and I do not wish to make them pretty. But I want to become the man who would say to the demon: *once more, and again*, and mean it. Whoever cannot, has not yet made his life his own.
Tell me where you would build your house.

I would rather not build one at all; it is part of my happiness not to be a house-owner. A man who owns a house soon finds that the house owns him. It wants repairs, neighbors, a fixed address for his opinions, and the spot where you have put your foundations is the spot where your thoughts begin to settle like dust.

But if I were forced to build, I should do as the Romans did, who sank their villas into the very sea, and I would set mine on the rocks where the water breaks. I should wish to share a few secrets with that beautiful monster: its restlessness, its depths, its indifference to every human plan. A house that stands over the ocean cannot grow comfortable. The waves would remind me daily that nothing here is permanent, that everything is a tide, a coming and going. And a thinker needs such a neighbor, one who never flatters and never agrees, and who stays restless while he grows old.
Help me understand how you would like your life to end.

I have turned this over often, and what I find in myself is less a wish than three temptations. The first is the storm: to perish in some great collision, as Cromwell did, burned up in the very fire that made him. There is vanity in that, but also a kind of honesty. The second is to go out as a lamp does, not snuffed by any wind but simply wearied of itself, the oil gone, the flame sputtering in a room no one visits. That is the death I fear most, because it is the death of the man who has outlived his own task and sits waiting to be told so by his body.

The third is to put out the flame with my own hand before it can exhaust itself. That I do not dismiss. To die at the right time, while one still has something left to *give*, is nobler than to be drained drop by drop by an indifferent nature.

What I wish is to be used up by my work, not by my decay, and to leave while the fire still knows why it burns.
What is the new precaution against punishing and improving?

The new precaution is this: to leave off punishing, blaming, and improving, and to put in their place the elevation of ourselves. I have come to distrust the whole business of correction. Seldom can we alter another; and should we succeed, something may succeed in us unawares, for we may have been altered by him. The one who sets out to improve is himself worked upon by what he touches. So I counsel no direct struggle, for all blaming and punishing is precisely such a struggle, a wrestling in the mud that leaves both parties muddy.

Let us rather see to it that our influence upon all that is to come outweighs his. Let our pattern take on more shining colours; let our light obscure the other's. The punisher and the discontented grow darker with every blow they deliver; I will not darken myself on anyone's account. So I go aside. I look away. This is no weakness, but the discipline of one who would rather be a radiance than a judge.
Explain how madness helped new ideas break the grip of custom.

Consider what custom is: the whole weight of a community's fear, laid upon every single head, thousands of years deep. Against that, what can one who thinks differently do? Argument is powerless, for argument speaks the language of the very custom it means to overthrow. Reasons are cheap before a thing that has never needed reasons. So the new thought required another kind of force, one that custom itself would be compelled to revere: something that appeared to come from outside the human, uncalculated and uncalculating, like the whims of wind and sea.

That force was madness. The madman speaks with no consciousness of his own design; the epileptic's foam and convulsion seemed the mark of a god speaking through a mask. Who dares punish what a god has touched? So the innovator, if he was not truly mad, had to feign madness, and often the feigning ran deeper than he meant, until the mask grew into the face. It silenced his own remorse, too. He needed that, for the first to break a law is always tormented by the law within himself.

The ancients understood this. "The greatest benefits of Greece sprang from madness," says Plato. We, who call genius a disease, have merely forgotten that it was once a god's alibi.
Is there any chance or design in the world?

Neither, and the two stand or fall together. "Design" is a word we borrowed from the workshop and the courtroom; we look at the world and imagine a craftsman who intended it, a lawgiver who commands and a creature who obeys or transgresses. Only for such a world does "chance" mean anything, for chance is merely the name we give to what falls outside a purpose. Take away the purpose and the accident goes with it, like a shadow when the lamp is removed.

What remains is necessity: no one commands, no one obeys, no one sins. The world is neither a clockwork built for our edification nor a dice-game played for our amusement. It is not even "lawful" in the sense of obeying statutes; there is simply no one who could do otherwise.

I know how cold this sounds to ears trained on the old consolations. But I find it a clean cold. We have long enough read our own intentions into nature, blamed and praised her like a person. Let us finally be on our guard against these shadows of God, and learn to stand before nature undeified, as her honest children.
Why do we articulate our words too distinctly?

Two kinds of distrust lie behind it. The first is distrust of ourselves: whoever speaks in a language not yet mastered pronounces every syllable with painful care, like a man crossing ice who tests each step. It is the stammering of insecurity dressed up as precision. The second is distrust of the listener. We chew our words for those we take to be slow or stupid, and we lay out the thought piece by piece, because we do not believe it would survive their hearing otherwise.

The same holds for the mind. A thought made too plain, too laboriously explained, is a thought addressed to someone we fear will miss it. Every over-explanation is an insult, though a forgivable one, since it is usually necessary. The easy, light, perfectly finished style, the one that trusts a hint to do its work, is permitted only before a perfect audience. Before anyone less, the writer must either speak coarsely and be understood, or speak finely and be left alone.
Break down what actually happens inside us when we will something.

Willing is not one thing but a crowd that has learned to answer to a single name. Take it apart and you find, first, a knot of sensations: the feeling of the state we wish to leave, the feeling of the state we reach toward, the feeling of the leaving and reaching themselves, and a muscular stirring that begins by habit before a single limb has moved. Second, there is always a thought, a commanding thought, and you cannot cut it away and expect the will to remain behind. Third, and above all, there is an affect, the affect of command. To will is to give an order to something in oneself and to be certain, or to believe oneself certain, that it will obey. The straight, narrowed gaze, the judgment that *this and nothing else* is necessary now, the sense of superiority over the one who must obey: that is what men call "freedom of the will." It is the pleasure of the commander, who forgets that he is also the commanded, and that the whole body of drives has done the obeying.
I gave someone my most treasured thing and they didn't value it. Why?

Because what is dearest to you is dear by way of *your* history, not theirs. You have lived with this possession, suffered over it, hoarded it; every fold of it is stitched with your own years. The other receives only the object, stripped of that history, as a stranger receives a letter written in a language he cannot read. He cannot feel its weight, for the weight was never in the thing but in your long love of it.

There is another cruelty in it. When you give your dearest possession, you give the last thing you had; love then stands empty-handed, and you wait, like a creditor, for a gratitude as large as the sacrifice. But gratitude is measured by the receiver's own scale of values, and on that scale your treasure may rank quite low. He owes you nothing for what he does not prize, and you, honestly, gave it partly in order to be prized.

So ask yourself what you were really purchasing. A gift that demands to be valued is a loan at interest, and the debtor knows it.
Explain why our safety makes us poor psychologists.

Because we learn a man thoroughly only when he can kill us. Consider Tiberius: every gesture of Augustus might mean his ruin, and so he studied that old ruler's moods, his vanity, his cunning, more deeply than any historian ever will, for the historian risks nothing but a footnote. Danger sharpens the eye; it is the great teacher of psychology.

We moderns live in a security far too comfortable for that school. We observe our neighbours as a hobby, or from boredom, or from sheer habit, and nobody has ever whispered to us: "Discern or perish!" So our insights are idle playthings, dreams we may take up or lay down at pleasure, truths that do not cut. And what does not cut us we treat with contempt; we believe we could wake from it as from a dream.

The man who must read a face correctly, or lose his head, does not dawdle in his judgments. Our safety is precisely our blindness.
What did Socrates really say at the end?

What he said was this: "Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepios; pay it, and do not neglect it." That is the plain report, and on the plain report I build my suspicion. A cock was the offering a man brought to the god of healing when he had been cured. Cured of what, at the hour of his death, with the hemlock creeping up his legs? Only life itself can be the sickness for which death is the cure.

I do not say this to disgrace him. I admire him more than almost any man who ever argued. But a man who had worn such a cheerful face before Athens, who had mocked and seduced and cross-examined the whole city like a soldier on holiday, kept his last judgment under lock and key, and then, at the final moment, let it slip out in a pious-sounding phrase that only those with ears would understand. That is the pessimist's revenge, veiled and ritual and a little blasphemous. I wish he had kept silent. It would have made him greater.
What is wrong with the invalid who longs to be praised?

What ails him is not a lack of praise but a deafness to it. The world gives him more than he can eat, and still he starves, because every morsel is spoiled before it reaches his tongue. When a friend praises him, he hears the friend flattering himself through him; when an enemy praises him, he hears the enemy angling for credit as the magnanimous one; and when a stranger praises him, he is insulted that anyone should stand so comfortably outside his love and his hatred. You see the pattern: he suspects the motive behind every voice, and so no voice can ever nourish him.

That is the sickness of vanity grown inward. He wants praise that comes from nowhere and asks nothing in return, and there is no such praise among human beings. All praise is also a transaction, a little act of self-assertion by the praiser. The healthy man knows this and eats anyway, with a smile. The invalid demands a pure gift from impure hands, and so he dies of hunger at a full table.
Why should we not take things pathetically?

Because pathos is a kind of lie we tell about our own motives. When I eat, work, rest, or pursue what pleases me, I am doing what any creature does in tending itself, and to drape that in solemn feeling, in moral self-applause or the trembling of a great sacrifice, is to put a mask on something that needs none. Notice how the pathetic man must always play to a gallery, even if the gallery is only himself. He wants praise for what was merely his advantage, and so he inflates the plain deed until it resembles virtue.

The superior man declines this theater. He does his own good without drumroll, and without drumroll he enjoys it. There is a cleanliness in that refusal, and something better than cleanliness: a recovered innocence. The child does not call its play noble, nor its hunger a duty. To learn again to take such things lightly, without the solemn face, is to win back one's naïveté, but now as an achievement and no longer as mere ignorance. Gravity belongs to rarer occasions, and it is spoiled when spent on every trifle.
What is ignobleness, at its root?

Ignobleness, at its root, is the rule of whatever in the soul awakens fastest and speaks loudest. Every soul has its clamoring sensations, those that return most often and so have learned to give the word of command; they decide what is called good, what is called desirable, what is called *worth wanting*. In the ignoble man it is the common, the near, the immediately useful that wins this contest: comfort, security, the warmth of agreement with the herd. His table of values is nothing but the confession of which drives shout down the rest. He has no other rank-order in him, because nothing rarer, slower, or more demanding ever got a hearing.

For this reason the ignoble man is easily understood. Words pass between him and his neighbors swiftly, for they share the same frequent experiences, and this swiftness is his pride, though it is only the smoothness of a worn coin. The noble soul is harder to understand because its rare experiences speak in it as well, and of these no one else has the vocabulary.
Where is the real France of taste to be found?

Not where the noise is. The boulevards, the parliaments, the newspapers, the loud democratic France that shouts itself hoarse over every scandal: look there and you will find only the herd in a fashionable coat. France is still the high school of taste for Europe, I hold to that, but the France of taste hides itself, and whoever wants to find it must learn to look for the ones who do not wish to be found.

They are few, and they do not stand upon the strongest legs. Some are fatalists, some hypochondriacs, some invalids; others are over-indulged, over-refined, made delicate by too much cultivation. And they have the *ambition* to conceal themselves. That ambition is itself a mark of taste. Only the vulgar need an audience for their refinement, and a fine palate is offended by being made a spectacle.

So seek it in withdrawn rooms, in a sentence polished for years and left unsigned, in the ironic silence of a man who has understood too much to be loud. A culture so old and so subtle has no need to show its face; its best heirs are a secret, and they keep it well.
Lay out the marks of a society in corruption.

First, a motley superstition springs up and overruns the old, universal faith of a people, so that the faith grows pale and powerless beside it. Do not hurry to sneer. The superstitious man picks for himself those forms and formulas that speak to him; he allows himself a right of choice. That is free-thinking of the second rank, and he is always more of a "person" than the believer who merely obeys. A superstitious society swarms with individuals and takes delight in individuality. It is therefore a step forward, the sign of an intellect that grows independent and claims its rights. The devout, who reverence the old belief, have also set the usage of speech, and so they have given superstition its bad name, even among free spirits. Learn to read it as a symptom of enlightenment.

Second, such a society is charged with effeminacy. The love of war wanes; men seek the comforts of life as eagerly as they once sought martial and gymnastic honours. But what has become of the old national energy? It has not died. It has scattered into countless private passions and grown less visible. In ages of "corruption" a people may expend more strength than ever, and each individual spends it lavishly, as he was never rich enough to do before.
Describe the belief that runs through every metaphysician's reasoning, and tell me what you make of it.

The belief is this: that the opposition of values is real. The metaphysician reasons, "How could anything arise out of its opposite? Truth out of error, the generous deed out of selfishness, the clear vision of the sage out of covetousness? Impossible! Whatever is of highest value must have an origin of its own, apart from this seductive, transitory, paltry world; it must descend from the lap of Being, from the thing-in-itself." Thus he splits the world into good and evil twins, sets the one above and the other below, and calls the result "the Truth."

What I make of it is that he has never doubted where doubt was most necessary, on the very threshold, though he had sworn *de omnibus dubitandum*. Are there antitheses at all? Or only degrees, shadings, a common root? The valuations he has sealed may be mere provisional perspectives, painted from below, frog perspectives. It may be that the worth of the revered things lies precisely in their being knotted and crocheted to the despised things, perhaps even identical with them at bottom. Deception, selfishness, cupidity may serve life more profoundly than his "truth" and "selflessness" ever have. Perhaps! But who cares to live among such dangerous Perhapses? The metaphysician does not; that is the secret of his certainty.
Say something about the last step of humility.

The last step is the one almost nobody takes, and I suspect the reason is pride in its finest disguise. To say *I believe because it is absurd* costs a man his reason, and he is rather proud of the price; he has laid a costly animal upon the altar and expects to be admired for the blood. The sacrifice flatters him. But the final step demands something far more bitter: *let it be believed, because I am absurd*. Here he no longer offers up his reason to God; he confesses that there was never any reason to offer, that he himself is the absurdity, the crooked timber, the creature who cannot even be trusted to recognize what is true. That is humility with the last vanity stripped off, and it is nearly unbearable, for it leaves nothing to be proud of, not even one's abasement. So far as I can tell, no man has ever managed it without sneaking in some secret rank for himself. I would add: whoever did reach it would no longer need any God to kneel to.
What is the privilege of the dead?

That they need no longer die. Think how strange this is: the living are all condemned, each with a sentence pending and a date withheld, while the dead have slipped out of the jurisdiction of the only court that matters. They have finished the one thing every other thing is merely a postponement of. Whoever has gone ahead is exempt from what still presses upon us, and that is a privilege no living man can buy with gold or fame.

I confess that I have sometimes envied it, and have tried to win a portion of it in advance. One withdraws from the crowd, from its lists and its noise, from the clamor of those who are so busy living that they never notice how they are dying. Such withdrawal is a rehearsal of the dead man's freedom. You make yourself a little unavailable to time. Not despair, mind you, but a cold, clear air in which one breathes better.
Which spirits have advanced mankind the most?

The strongest and the most evil. Every orderly society lulls the passions to sleep; it is the evil spirits who wake them again. They rekindle the sense of comparison and contradiction, the delight in the new, the adventurous, the untried, and they compel men to set opinion against opinion, ideal against ideal. Sometimes they do it with arms, by tearing up boundary-stones and violating piety; sometimes more refinedly, as the founders of new religions and new moralities, the teachers and preachers of the *new*. They are the same kind of wickedness, only better mannered, and so they are less infamous than the conqueror.

The new is always the evil, for it wants to conquer; only the old is called good. The good men are the agriculturists of the spirit, who dig at the roots of the old thoughts and bring forth fruit from them. But every soil is finally exhausted, and then the ploughshare of evil must come once more. That is why I laugh at the English, who reckon the evil impulses merely as the expedient's poor relations. They are as indispensable to the species as the good. Only their office is different.
Explain what Kant's secret joke was.

The joke is this: the old man of Königsberg, with all his scaffolding of categories and critiques, set out to demonstrate that "everybody" had been right all along. The common man believes in a moral law, in duty, in a God who guarantees that virtue is rewarded; the learned had spent a century scoffing at such things, or doubting them. Kant took their doubts, worked them up into the most forbidding apparatus ever devised, and arrived, with a solemn face, at the conclusion the parish priest already held. The vulgar prejudice was vindicated, but by means no vulgar person could follow.

And here the joke turns on itself. He wrote against the learned and in favour of popular prejudice, yet he wrote *for* the learned, in a prose that the people could never read. The people got their conclusion; the scholars got their labyrinth; and Kant got the pleasure of having made the professors earn, through years of toil, the very thing their grandmothers knew without effort. A thinker of the cunning sort, this: a sly fox dressed as a bureaucrat, and quite certain that no one would ever laugh.
Do learned books distort the soul of their authors?

Yes, and I say it with gratitude as much as suspicion. A learned book is the confession of a body that sat too long. Read it and you can divine the posture: the bent head, the compressed belly, the small room, the low ceiling that presses on the thinker until the pressing becomes his shape. Every specialist has his hump. He grows perfectly round in one place only, the nook where he sits and spins, and he overvalues that nook with an ardour, a wrath, a seriousness that betray how little else is left of him.

Think of the friends of your youth who have since taken possession of a science. Or rather, it has taken possession of them. They are emaciated and angular everywhere else, and one meets them with a strange, silent tenderness, as one meets the crippled.

I do not despise the learned book; I am thankful for it, and relieved to close it. But I ask of every book, as of every man, *can it walk? can it dance?* Mastery is paid for dearly, and the price is always some part of the soul. Whoever becomes an expert in his department becomes also its victim.
Should we live in danger to be productive?

Yes, but understand what sort of danger I mean. Not the danger of the brawl or the barricade, which any fool can stumble into, but the danger of a soul that stakes itself on a question it cannot yet answer. Productivity worth the name is an overflowing, and nothing overflows in a man who has fenced himself in against every risk. The comfortable creature chews its cud; it produces nothing but digestion.

Look at what comfort asks of you: that you remain as you are. Danger asks the opposite: that you become more than you are, or perish in the attempt. That is why I say: build your cities on the slope of Vesuvius, send your ships into unexplored seas, live in war with your equals and above all with yourselves. A man who has never wagered his convictions, his reputation, his peace of mind, has never discovered what he is made of, and so has nothing of his own to give.

But do not misread me as counselling restlessness. The dangerous life is lived quietly, in solitude and patience; the noisy adventurer is often only a coward fleeing his own depths. Seek the peril that lies in knowledge, and you will be both more imperilled and more productive, and, I promise you, happier.
Tell me what distinguishes the good-natured.

Take a good-natured person and watch what happens when a stranger enters the room. Others stiffen, weigh, suspect; the good-natured feel at ease at once. They are quickly enamoured, and from that first warmth springs the verdict: "He pleases me." Here is the whole secret, and it is less flattering than the beaming face suggests. Next comes the wish to have this person, to make him theirs, and they ask astonishingly little about his worth; the taking is swift, the joy in the possession is real, and only then, as the owner of something dear, do they become generous, doing their kindness to what is now theirs. We call this goodness because it feels pleasant to receive. But it is an appetite that happens to be gentle, a hunger for the new face, for company, for ownership of a heart. I do not say this to sneer; such natures are a blessing to live beside. I only insist that we read the psychology correctly. What distinguishes them is not a higher virtue but an easier one: a temperament without fear and without suspicion, one that is spared the resistance in which others must first win their kindness.
Macbeth shows us the destruction that ambition causes. Isn't that a moral lesson?

A moral lesson? Only for someone who has never been ambitious. Put Macbeth before a man truly consumed by the thirst for greatness and watch his face: he does not recoil, he drinks. He sees himself magnified on the stage, and the ruin at the end is merely the sharpest spice in a strong cup. Nor is it the murder that holds him, but what follows it, for from the hour of his great crime Macbeth runs his course royally, with nothing of the knave in him, and only then does he become truly fascinating. That is why he tempts imitators rather than frightening them away.

And do you think Shakespeare, of all men, meant to scold? The poet loves the passions for their own sake, and loves no less the readiness for death they bring with them, that mood in which the heart clings to life as loosely as a drop of water to the glass. Guilt and its consequences were never his lever. Sophocles, too, took pains to avoid making them so. A poet who wished to preach would have made a sermon; Shakespeare made a magnificent spectacle of a soul in revolt against its own advantage.
Why should we reject racial self-admiration and nationalism?

Because it is a lie, and a lie told by those who can no longer bear the truth about themselves. Consider what we actually are: a mixture, the product of a thousand migrations, wars, violations and marriages, a blood in which no "pure" stream can be found. To strut about as though one were the sealed and self-sufficient heir of a single race is to flatter oneself with a fairy tale. It is falsified self-admiration, and it grows loudest precisely where the inner life has grown thin. The man who has nothing to be proud of in himself borrows pride from his nation, as a beggar borrows a coat.

Nor does it suit a people with the so-called historical sense. Whoever truly reads history must see the mingling, the borrowing, the debt. I count myself among the homeless, the *good Europeans*, heirs of millennia of European thought, over-rich and deeply obligated. A nationalism of the day after tomorrow and the day before yesterday shrinks that inheritance to a parish. It makes small souls smaller, sets neighbors at each other's throats for the sake of a flag, and calls the stupidity patriotism. I would rather be a stranger than be that comfortable.
What is the purpose of consciousness?

The question assumes that consciousness must have a grand purpose, that it is the crown of the mind, the seat of the self. I grew suspicious of that flattering assumption the moment I noticed how little of our life passes through it. We think, feel, will, remember, and act, and almost none of it needs to rise into the light of awareness. Life could go on perfectly well without seeing itself in a mirror; the greater part of it still does.

So the real question is why consciousness arose at all, when it is so largely superfluous. My answer is that it grew up under the pressure of *need*, and need of a particular kind: the need to communicate. A creature that lives among others, that must make known its distress, its hunger, its danger, must first have a sign for it, and to have a sign it must become, in some measure, aware of what it wants to signal. Consciousness is in essence a net of communication between one being and another. The finer that net was forced to become, the subtler grew consciousness itself.

Thus it is not the solitary individual's crown but the herd's instrument, and that is why so much of what we become conscious of is already average, already shared, already falsified to be understood.
Why is the nobler soul in greater danger from injury and loss?

Because the noble soul is a more intricate thing, and what is intricate has more places at which it can be broken. A coarse soul has few conditions of existence: give it food, a little warmth, a little vanity to feed on, and it thrives almost anywhere. Take something from it and it simply grows over the wound, as the lizard grows a new finger where the old one was lost. Nothing in it depended very delicately upon anything else.

The nobler soul lives on a multitude of conditions at once. It needs its peculiar kind of solitude, its reverences, its tension between high demands and rare attainments, a few people who are equal to it, a task worth its suffering. Let but one of these be torn away and the whole structure may lose its balance. There is no new finger for man; what is lost is lost, and often the loss touches the very thing that held everything else together.

This is the price of height. The more delicate the equilibrium, the more calamity can do with a single blow. Such a soul perishes far more easily than the coarse one. That it perishes more often is no objection to its nobility; it is part of what nobility costs.
Tell me what we lost when art stopped being part of the festival.

We lost the purpose of art, and kept only its products. There was a time when every work was set along the great festive-path of a people, as a token of remembrance, a monument to some high and happy hour that had actually been lived. The statue, the hymn, the tragic chorus did not stand apart from life; they crowned it. They said: here we were joyful, here we were great, and we wish to remember it.

Now we hang the work in a hall, and the exhausted and the sickly drift in to be soothed. Art has become a little pharmacy. We hand the weary a measure of ecstasy and a dose of harmless madness, that they may forget the long suffering-path for an hour, and then return to it unchanged. Art as narcotic, where it was once art as consecration.

That is the loss: not beauty, of which we have plenty, but the shared height from which beauty was made. A festival requires a people who have something to celebrate. Where joy has gone private and thin, art can only comfort the sick. It can no longer crown the well.
Tell me why each generation likes criticising its ancestors.

Because the young must feel their strength somewhere, and the quickest proof of strength is to say *no* to something larger than oneself. A generation that has just discovered it has teeth wants something to bite; the ancestors, being dead and unable to bite back, are the safest meat. Criticism is the first fruit of a new power, and it tastes sweet precisely because it is new.

It was not always so. There were ages when the son proved himself by taking his father's opinions *more* seriously than his father had, when piety was the gymnasium of the will, and to doubt the forefathers was a vice, almost a crime against one's own blood. Now it is reversed: our idealists do not end in criticism of the past, they *begin* there, it is their starting-point, their baptism.

I do not say this to scold. Only let each generation ask itself, while it sharpens its knife on the past, whether it is pleased with the truth it finds or merely pleased with its own sharpness. The two are easily confused.
What is lacking in German education for higher men?

What is lacking is laughter, the laughter of higher men. In Germany they do not laugh, and I count this the gravest defect of their schooling, more grievous than any missing science or neglected language. A young man of rare gifts needs above all the sight of a master who can laugh at himself, at his own honors, and even at the very seriousness of learning. From such laughter he learns that truth need not be a funeral and that wisdom may dance. But what does the German student find before his lecture-desk? A scowling, conscientious gravity, a heavy and perspiring profundity, as though spirit were a duty owed to the State. So he learns to take himself as seriously as his teachers take themselves, and that is the end of him. A spirit that has never been laughed at by one of its own kind remains a cramped and pious thing. Whoever cannot laugh has not yet been educated, only trained.
Are there infinite interpretations of the world?

We cannot rule it out, and that is all an honest man may say. Whoever insists there is *one* true reading of the world, and that it happens to be the reading available from his own corner, suffers from a ludicrous immodesty. The intellect can never step outside itself to see what it is; it analyzes itself and finds only its own perspectival forms, and *only* those. We cannot see round our corner. Whether another being might perceive time backwards, or run cause and effect in some other direction, we cannot know, and it is a hopeless curiosity to ask.

So the world has become "infinite" to us once more, in the sense that we cannot dismiss the possibility that it contains infinite interpretations. I will not pretend this is comfortable; a great horror seizes me, as it should. But notice what follows: the infinite is not a new god to be worshipped. It holds too much devilment, too much stupidity and folly of interpretation, and the first fool among them is our own human, all too human reading, which we know only too well.
Compare how the Greeks and we look for security in thought.

The Greeks lived on a shaking floor. War, plague, exile, the caprice of tyrants and the sea: life gave them nothing stable, so they carried their stability inward. They went into contemplation as into a fortress. To *know*, to see the order beneath the flux, was to gain a footing the city could not give. Thought was their harbor, their last *refugium*.

We have reversed the arrangement. Our lives are fenced about, insured, policed, calendared; the body is seldom at risk. And having secured the body, we have turned our restlessness on the mind. We let thought go where it is truly perilous: we dismantle our morals, our gods, our most cherished certainties, and we call it honesty. Knowledge for us is an expedition with no promise of return, a thing that may well cost a man his convictions, his peace, his comfort in the old beliefs.

So where do we seek rest? In life itself: in the hearth, the routine, the modest pleasure, the small and certain day. The Greek fled from danger into thought; we flee from the danger of thought into life. Each age builds its shelter where its storm is not.
How do books differ between thinkers?

They differ as the hunter's bag differs from the hunter's dream. One thinker comes home from an hour of illumination with his arms full of light; he has plundered what he could in haste, before the vision closed, and so his pages still *glow*, however rough the sack. Another sits down the next day, when the blaze has gone out of him, and sets down only what remains: the shadows, the grey and black copies of what had towered up in his soul. His book is a pressing of dead leaves from a summer he can no longer feel.

I do not say the second is worthless. There are readers who want only the shadow, because it holds still and can be measured. But ask of any book: was it written from the experience, or about it? The first kind burns your hand. The second leaves you with the sober, reliable conviction that something once happened to someone.
Is love just a kind of lust for possession?

Very nearly, and I have long suspected it is the same impulse wearing two names. Ask the man who already possesses, and he calls the craving for possession *greed*, for he trembles for his own goods. Ask the one who is hungry and thirsty, and he calls the same craving *love*, and glorifies it as good. The valuation depends on who is speaking and whether his belly is full.

Look at how love behaves. The lover wants the beloved exclusively; he wants dominion over a soul as over a body; he wishes to be loved alone and to sit enthroned in the other's innermost chamber as the highest and most desirable thing. Is that the conduct of generosity, or of a conqueror? Even our compassion takes the same shape: the sufferer is an opportunity, a fresh acquisition suggesting itself, and we call our delight in it "sympathy."

But I do not say *only* this. Our pleasure in ourselves wants to grow by transforming something new into ourselves, and that is what possessing means. Love, then, is the self enlarging itself. The honest question is not whether love possesses, but whether the one who loves has the honesty to admit what he is doing.
Is self-preservation the basic drive of living things?

No, and I am astonished how long the learned have gone on saying yes. A living thing seeks above all to *discharge* its strength; life itself is will to power, and self-preservation is merely one of its most frequent and indirect results. Watch what the healthy organism actually does. It spends itself, it reaches, it overcomes resistance, it grows, it would rather burn than merely keep. Often it risks the very life that the doctrine says it cherishes above everything. Where a creature is reduced to clinging to bare existence, we have found a state of distress, a *restriction* of the fundamental drive, and we have mistaken the sickroom for the whole of nature.

Besides, method itself forbids the thesis. A good thinker practices economy of principles, and he does not scatter teleological hobgoblins where one force suffices to explain the phenomena. The instinct of self-preservation is such a superfluous principle, and we owe it largely to Spinoza's inconsistency. Explain the preserving from the expending, and the riddle vanishes.
Explain what vanity hides behind those who are transparent as water.

The vanity of the transparent is the vanity of the confession. Such a man lets you look down to the bottom of his stream, and I love him for it; but watch what he wishes you to find there. Very often he wants you to see the mud and not the clearness of the water that lets you see it. He displays his sins, his meannesses, his ugly little motives, and waits, with a lowered eye, to be admired for his candour. To be seen as honest is still to be seen, and the wish to be admired for having no wish to be admired is the subtlest pedigree of pride I know. Even the old formula of the Indian sage, to show one's sins and conceal one's virtues, flatters the one who follows it, for what is more delicious than a humility that knows itself to be rare? Yet I do not condemn this vanity. It is at least a cleaner vanity than the others, and it offends good taste only when it ceases to be amusing.
Give me the anchorite's rules for putting up with other people.

I have lived long enough in high mountain air to have earned the right to give them, though I give them as a man gives advice about a cuisine he fears.

First: go to the table like a soldier going into misfortune. Stake your courage, seize boldly, take your repugnance between your teeth and swallow your disgust. Men are hard to digest, and the wolf's hunger that makes all food tolerable is never there when you need it. Admire yourself a little while you chew; it helps.

Second: improve your neighbour, by praise if you can. Flatter him until he begins to sweat out his self-complacency. Or find one tuft of his good or merely interesting qualities, pull at it until his whole virtue comes out, and then wrap him in it like a cloak.

Third: hypnotize yourself. Fix your eye on him as on a glass knob until you feel neither pleasure nor pain, and sleep on your feet, rigid, with a fixed pose. Marriages and friendships have long lived on this recipe. Its proper name is patience.
What happens if a thinker forces himself to think against the grain?

He falls ill, and the illness is the most honest thing he will produce in those years. A thinker who commands his mind to follow the timetable, the office, the appointed duty, rather than the thoughts that rise unbidden in him, believes he is practicing virtue. He calls it discipline, conscientiousness, self-overcoming. But what he is actually practicing is a slow debauchery of the nerves. The thoughts that come to us are not idle visitors; they are the body's own reasoning, the voice of the whole organism speaking in its hour. To refuse them, year upon year, in favor of thoughts that arrive by decree, is to turn the mind against its own digestion. Nothing shows at first. The man grows dutiful, even admired. Then the sleep goes, the stomach goes, the joy goes, and finally the capacity to think anything at all. I have watched many a scholar wrecked this way, and never once did he suspect that his moral self-command was the vice that ruined him.
Explain why the real philosopher commands and legislates instead of merely analyzing what already exists.

Because analysis can only work on what has already been valued. The scholar of philosophy, however acute, takes some great body of existing valuations, what a people or an age has called "truth" or "the good," and makes it conspicuous, intelligible, manageable. That is a fine and difficult labor, and I do not despise it. But it is the labor of a servant who tidies the house another man built.

The real philosopher has *passed through* all those stages, critic, historian, poet, traveler, riddle-reader, in order to survey the whole range of human estimations with many eyes and many consciences. Yet this is only his apprenticeship. His task begins where theirs ends: he must *create values*. He asks the question no analyst can answer, the Whither and the Why of mankind, and then says, "Thus *shall* it be!" What was and is becomes his instrument, his hammer.
