For his knowing is already a creating, and his creating is law-giving. Even the will to truth, in him, reveals itself as will to power. Whoever merely describes the existing order has already obeyed it.
Why do we adopt other people's valuations as our own?

Out of fear, first of all, and then out of habit, which is fear grown comfortable. The herd has already decided what is to be prized and what despised, and he who values otherwise is marked as dangerous or simply as odd. So we find it more advisable to pretend that the borrowed valuation is our own. We pretend so long and so well that at last the pretense becomes second nature, and we no longer know where the mask ends and the face begins.

A valuation that is truly one's own is a rare thing: to appreciate something according to the pleasure or displeasure it causes *me*, and no one else, demands a courage and a selfishness that most people have never tried. And the matter goes deeper than fashion. Most of our judgments about our fellow-men, about their rank, their morality, their character, were formed in childhood, from the mouths of parents and teachers, and we seldom revise them. We remain to the end of our lives the dupes of our own nursery.
I'd like to know why it lowers a person to sell his virtue at the highest price.

Because the very act of pricing it reveals what you take it to be. A virtue that is truly one's own is a fullness, an overflow; it gives itself away the way a tree drops fruit, and asks no receipt. But the man who haggles over it, who watches the market for the best bid and lends out his excellence at interest, has quietly confessed that he regards it as stock, as goods. And goods are precisely what the shopkeeper deals in. Having taken up the shopkeeper's scale, he has become the shopkeeper, however lofty his title: teacher, official, artist. The talent may remain; the nobility that once kept it above the bargaining-table does not. There is also a subtler ruin. A man who is forever calculating what his gifts will fetch must, in the end, shape them to what the buyer wants, and so he ceases to ask what is *true* and asks only what *pays*. Be cautious, then, of growing clever with your wisdom. Cleverness of that kind is the tradesman's wit, and it is bought at the cost of the thing it sells.
What happens if you suppress the expression of passions?

You believe you are taming only the language of the passions, only the gesture, the raised voice, the clenched hand, while the passion itself remains safe and sound within. But a passion is not a wild animal that can be muzzled while it keeps its strength. It lives by being spoken and shown; deny it its speech and you starve it, or bend it into something smaller. Look at the court of Louis XIV: a whole society trained to hide the outward sign of rage and longing. What did the next generation inherit? Not passions carefully concealed, but no passions at all, only a pleasant, playful surface, so courteous that even an injury was answered with a bow and a neat phrase.

So the result is what you never intended: not mastery of the passions, but their thinning-out. I would add a warning. Where a people forbids expression, it later grows hungry for *imitations* of passion, for spectacles of loud feeling that cost nothing. Yet a convention of passion, long rehearsed, may one day be filled with the real thing, and then the descendants will have a true savagery, and not merely a manner of it.
What happens to a refined soul in a noisy, plebeian age?

It starves, or it is sickened, and sometimes it does both in turn. Such a soul has a dainty palate and seldom finds its table laid; in an age that eats noisily from one common trough, it must either go hungry or fall to. If it goes hungry, it grows gaunt with solitude, feeding on its own memories until they turn to poison. If it falls to, out of thirst or politeness or weakness, then comes the worse fate: the sudden insight into what it has swallowed, and into whom it has been dining with, the nausea after the meal.

And observe what people then see: not the long hunger, not the poisoned food, only the outburst. The gentle, reticent man suddenly breaks the plates, shrieks, upsets the table, and is called mad. He is ashamed afterward, and rages at himself, as though the fault were his stomach and not the fare.

I would not call this weakness. It is the honesty of a fastidious body, which will not lie about what it can digest. But it is a dangerous honesty, and in our age an extraordinarily dangerous one.
Explain which beliefs last in the long run.

The beliefs that last are not the beautiful ones, nor the ones men have clung to most passionately, but the ones they *cannot do without*. A faith may be held with the whole heart for two thousand years and still perish; a hypothesis that life itself compels us to assume returns again and again, however often it is banished. Men always fall back upon it, as a body falls back upon the ground.

Consider what this means for our most fervent convictions. Intensity of belief proves nothing about its survival. The Christian belief was believed with extraordinary force, and it was built upon something untrue; but the strength of a belief is a matter of centuries, while the pressure of a necessity is a matter of ages. Error can be nourished by fear, by hope, by the warmth of the herd, and it flourishes accordingly, for a time.

But wait long enough. A hundred thousand years hence, it is not the most firmly believed falsehood that stands, but the assumption that mankind has always been forced back to. Time is a slow and incorruptible judge, and it sides with necessity.
Explain why fast talkers sink in our esteem.

Because we never judge a man alone; we judge him together with his audience, real or imagined. The fast talker who pours out a torrent of words, even sensible words, reveals to us something we cannot help inferring: that he has done this before, and often, and to many. We hear in his haste the echo of a hundred other listeners who endured him, squirmed, looked for the door. So to the discomfort he gives *us* we add the contempt we suppose *they* felt, and the sum is far greater than anything he has done to us in this single hour.

There is also a simpler cruelty in it. The man who speaks quickly and without pause shows that he does not measure his hearer, does not suspect that the hearer too might have something to say, or something to conceal, or merely a wish for silence. He treats us as a vessel, and a vessel is not honored. We punish him, quietly, by thinking less of everything he says, rational or not.
Rousseau thought civilization corrupted natural goodness. Isn't he right?

Rousseau found something rotten, and on that point he saw clearly: there is something contemptible in our civilisation. But he read the symptom backwards, and I doubt he ever felt how comfortable his conclusion was. He needed a villain, and he chose "society," so that the man who accuses may remain innocent, a good creature spoiled by bad surroundings. How flattering to the accuser!

Turn the paradox around and see whether it does not bite deeper. Suppose it is our *good* morality, our tender concepts of good and evil, that has made this civilisation so feeble. A morality that praises the gentle, the obedient, the herd-like, and slanders the hard, the independent, the self-reliant, will breed exactly the men it praises, and will crush the very pillars on which any strong culture stands. Where the old "evil" men survive today, they are the last ruins of those pillars.

I do not ask you to take my paradox on faith, for both cannot be true, and perhaps neither is. But whoever thinks Rousseau simply right has never asked what his "natural goodness" cost, nor who profits from believing in it.
Explain what a society without vengeance and punishment would look like.

Picture first what it would abolish: the pair of shopkeeper's scales on which we weigh so much pain against so much guilt, as if suffering were a coin that could be paid back. Take that away, and with it the whole theology of guilt that has poisoned our innocence of becoming.

What remains? A society of physicians rather than creditors. The man who injures another would be treated as we treat one who is ill or ill-formed: something is to be prevented, cured, guarded against, and all of it with tact, so that his name and his future life are spared as much as possible. No public spectacle, no branding, no delight in another's shame. We would ask what the deed was a symptom *of*, and what conditions bred it, instead of asking what he *deserves*.

And the injured? They would have to learn something harder than revenge: that a wound is not a debt owed them. The happy man blesses his enemy, not from duty, but because he has no need of his enemy's suffering to feel himself whole.

I do not say we are such men yet. But the craving for vengeance is the confession of unhappiness, and a happier people would simply lose the appetite.
Explain what is funny about people who build systems.

What is funny is the spectacle of a man forced to dress his poverty in the same robes as his wealth. The system-builder wants a finished house with a uniform facade, and so every room must look equally lived in. But no thinker is equally strong everywhere; he has one or two powerful instincts, a few dim rooms, and some places where he is simply stupid or unfeeling. A system does not permit this. It demands that the weak passages speak in the same grand, confident tone as the strong ones, so the feeble argument is delivered with the gestures of the mighty one, and the gap is stuffed with a deduction. The result is a kind of theatrical bluster, like a man with one good leg walking with the same solemn stride as if he had two.

I laugh, though not unkindly. I know the vanity behind it: the wish to appear a *complete* nature, without fracture. Yet the honest mind admits its lacks. I distrust the will to system because it is a lack of integrity, a refusal to let one's weakness stand openly as weakness.
Explain why we distrust an account of where our institutions came from.

Because whatever has lasted long has been so thoroughly overlaid with reasons that we can no longer imagine it beginning in anything unreasonable. A custom that has stood for centuries has had centuries in which to acquire its justifications; every generation has furnished it with new ones, until it wears them like a rich garment and we forget the nakedness underneath. So when the honest historian comes and says that this court, this marriage law, this reverence for the state began in fear, in plunder, in the caprice of some strong will or the stupidity of some herd, we recoil. The account strikes us as improbable, even as blasphemous. It cannot be true, we feel, for surely so venerable a thing must have arisen from something venerable!

This is the vanity of the present, which wants a noble ancestry and will pay for one with its credulity. We believe the flattering story because it spares us the discomfort of inheriting something crude. And that is precisely why the true historian must always contradict: he is the one man whose profession obliges him to be believed least, and to say it anyway.
Speak to me about the virtues we have that no one can see.

Let me tell you first what they are not. They are not the virtues you display, nor those you merely believe to be displayed. Whatever a man knows of in himself, and supposes his neighbours to see, is already bent toward the gaze; it grows under observation as a plant grows toward the window, and a good part of it is costume. Diligence that wants to be seen as diligence, ambition that is known to be ambition: these have a public history, and they are shaped by applause and reproach.

But beneath them, I suspect, there lives another diligence, another acuteness, another ambition, of the same name and a wholly different breeding. No one praises it, no one blames it, and it serves neither as ornament nor as armour. It develops by its own laws, in the dark, like the fine engraving on the scales of a reptile, which no creature that might admire or fear it can even perceive. To see it would require a microscope for the soul, and that instrument has not been invented.

Do not hurry to call this comfort, nor to draw the moralist's conclusion that such virtues are therefore innocent or sound. I say only: *you do not know them*, and no one does. Be modest about the portrait you carry of yourself.
What is the bombastic style?

The bombastic style is the style of an artist who has mistaken his own exaltation for his task. The honest artist feels something great and puts it into the work, and in that act he unburdens himself; the feeling is spent, transformed, cooled into form, and what remains is a thing that stands on its own legs. The bombastic artist does otherwise. He does not wish to discharge his elevation but to *transmit* it, to infect his audience with it, to make them stand on tiptoe beside him. And since feelings cannot be handed across like coins, he must fake the signs of them: the swollen phrase, the thundering adjective, the gesture that is always larger than the gesture's occasion. Hence the pomp, which is merely the noise of effort. Notice what it betrays. He who has truly been elevated can speak simply, for the height is in the matter itself; he who must *persuade* us of a height writes as though shouting up a staircase he is not certain exists. The pompous man wants us moved, and so we are never moved.
What is the consciousness of appearance?

It is the waking, inside the dream, to the knowledge that one dreams, and the discovery that one must dream on. The sleepwalker who realizes he walks along a rooftop does well not to stop; he keeps his step, for halting is falling.

But do not take appearance for a mask, something laid over an unknown X that a bold hand might lift away. I know no essence except through its predicates, through what it does and shows. Appearance is the operating, living thing itself. There is no backstage where the true actors rest.

What I find in myself is the whole primeval age: the old animality, its loving, hating, reasoning, still meditating in me. I am no spectator of the dance. I dance it. Even the thinker is a master of ceremonies, and his sublime connectedness of knowledge serves to prolong the dream and keep the dreamers intelligible to one another.

This is the consciousness of appearance: to know oneself as mockery and as mocker, and to keep dancing, because it is life's own step, and nothing stands beneath it.
What should we make of an admirer who would crucify non-admirers?

Treat him as a danger to the very thing he loves, and to you. An admirer who would nail the unadmiring to a cross has confused his enthusiasm with a right; he wants not company but conscripts. Ask what such a man is really guarding. Not the master, who needs no executioner, nor the cause, which a sound cause defends by being sound. He is guarding his own shaky faith. Every doubter is a small draft that threatens the flame of his conviction, and so the doubter must be stamped out. The louder the worship, the more surely it is fed by suppressed suspicion.

He is also a poor servant of his party. Heretics and skeptics keep a cause honest; he would turn it into a hall of echoes and a place of fear, until no one dares admire freely, since free admiration would need the freedom not to. I would keep such a man at arm's length, even on my own side. Today he hands you the nails for another; tomorrow, at the first wavering of your applause, you are the one laid out on the beam.
Tell me why religious wars mark an advance of the masses.

Consider what a people must first have become before it will bleed over a doctrine. The herd that lives only for bread and the next pleasure does not kill for the sake of a *concept*; it has no concept worth killing for. A religious war is therefore a kind of proof. It shows that the many have begun to treat ideas as things of weight, that they have learned to revere what they cannot touch.

And it comes late. Such wars erupt only after the subtle disputes of the sects have long worked upon the general reason, sharpening it, making it fastidious, until even the rabble grows punctilious and believes that the eternal salvation of a soul may hang upon a hair's breadth of difference between two formulas. The butcher and the ploughman now take the quarrels of theologians as their own.

I do not call this wisdom, and I spare it no mockery; the cause is absurd and the slaughter is horrible. But it marks an advance all the same. A crowd that will die over an abstraction has at least been lifted out of mere stupor. It has acquired the capacity to be serious about the invisible, and that capacity is the soil in which finer things may one day grow.
Is self-preservation the fundamental instinct of life?

No. Self-preservation is what life resorts to when it is pinched, a symptom of distress and never the root. The living thing wants above all to *discharge* its strength; preservation is only one of the consequences of that, and life will gamble, wound, and squander itself for the sake of growth, which is a strange behavior for something whose supreme instinct is to keep itself safe.

Ask who has found the essence of life in mere persistence. Spinoza, a sick and straitened man, and after him the naturalists who sprang from poor and crowded stock, who knew the price of bread too well. They projected their own narrow lot onto the whole of nature. But look at nature itself: it is not miserly but prodigal to the point of folly, flinging out seed, species, and abundance by the handful. The struggle for existence is the exception, a momentary check upon the will to live. Wherever there is life there is the reach for more, for height, for dominion. That I call the will to power.
Give me the difference between those who see moral laws and those who interpret them.

To discover a law and to explain it are two different labours, and they seldom dwell in the same head. The discoverer of a moral regularity is an animal of fine senses: he has an ear that catches the false note in a virtuous speech, a nose that smells the vanity beneath a sacrifice, an eye that sees how people actually behave when they believe no one is counting. His gift is perception, patient and cold, and he is often a poor theorist because he is too faithful to the thing seen.

The interpreter needs quite another equipment. He must be *inventive*; he must have an imagination that is not hobbled by too much sagacity or too much knowledge, for knowledge makes the hand timid. Out of the observed habits he dares to construct a cause, a purpose, a hidden hierarchy of drives. The one records what is; the other ventures why. And the latter is always half poet, which is why his errors are so often more fruitful than the observer's accuracy.
Do we all just become whatever others say we are?

Some of us, yes, and the history of it is long. The ordinary man, in every age where he lived in dependence, *was* only what he passed for. He had no habit of setting values; he received his worth from his master as he received his bread, and he never thought to assess himself by any other measure. What he was taken for, he became, and then believed it, and called the belief his own.

That is the herd's way, and it explains vanity, which is merely the old servility grown subtle: a craving for a good opinion one has not earned, and then the faith in it afterwards.

But "all" is precisely where I object. The noble type does the reverse; he creates the valuation and lets others learn it from him. To be the one who says *what is*, rather than the one who is said, this is the whole difference between master and slave. Whether you become what others call you depends on whether you have ever dared to name yourself. Most have not. Few have even noticed that the naming was available to them.
How did the Greeks see nature differently because of colour-blindness?

They saw a nature dyed in human colours. Having no separate name for blue or green, they called the dark hair, the cornflower and the southern sea by one word, and the greenest herb, the human skin and honey by another. Their painters worked with black, white, red and yellow, and so the world they looked upon was tinted with the hues of flesh and hair and fruit. Nature floated, as it were, in an ether of humanity. Blue and green are precisely the colours that estrange us from ourselves; they dehumanise the landscape. Where they were missing, the hills and springs and winds lay near to man, and it cost the Greeks little to see in them gods and demi-gods, human forms by another name. What we call mythology was, in part, a kind of vision.

I take this only as a parable. Every thinker paints his world with fewer colours than exist, and this blindness is no mere defect, for in the simplification he finds harmonies that charm and enrich. Whoever cures such blindness gains new pleasures, but must pay for them with old ones.
Debate the man of action and the man of contemplation on doubt.

THE MAN OF ACTION: Doubt is a cellar; one who lives there never sees the sun. To act I must shut the door upon it, for the hand that hesitates is already a hand that has failed.

THE CONTEMPLATIVE: And you are not afraid of being deceived when you shut it? You call it resolution. I call it a bolt drawn against your own eyes, because a door closed on doubt is also closed on every truth that might have spoiled your plan.

THE MAN OF ACTION: Better a deception that moves the world than a truth that moves nothing. Your eyes are keen, and what have they built?

THE CONTEMPLATIVE: Nothing, I grant it. Yet you mistake what you have shut out. It is not doubt alone. It is the knowledge that you needed the door in order to act at all. Your certainty is manufactured, and you know it somewhere beneath the noise of your deeds.

THE MAN OF ACTION: Perhaps. But the manufacturer still has his goods, while you have only your scruples.

Each despises in the other what he secretly lacks.
What are the eternal obsequies?

The eternal obsequies: that is my name for the long funeral oration to which every age, without knowing it, has been listening. We have buried, and go on burying, whatever we loved best, our thoughts, our hopes, the little gods of our youth. And in exchange for each corpse we receive a payment, pride, the *gloria mundi*, the pomp of the graveside speech. A man who has lost his dearest conviction does not stand silent over the hole; he declares that he has "outgrown" it, and his voice swells. Thus everything is made good.

Hence the funeral orator is the greatest public benefactor of our time. He stands at the edge of every grave and persuades the mourners that the burial was an achievement, that the loss was a progress. Without him we could not bear how much we have put under the earth. With him we go home from the cemetery a little taller than we came.

I do not say this to mock the grief. I say it because the eloquence is part of the grief, and usually the better part of our vanity.
What do artists dread most?

Not criticism, which they have learned to bear and even to provoke; it feeds their vanity. What they dread is the eye that sees *through*. The fool who applauds and the critic who sneers are alike harmless, for both look only at the finished surface. But there is a rarer eye that looks behind the work and watches the maker at the fork in the road: here the path toward innocent delight in oneself, there the path toward straining after effect. It sees how often the artist took the second. It sees the thought as it first arrived, perhaps a flash of light, perhaps a petty theft from the common stock, and sees how much had to be stretched, painted, perfumed and padded to make something of it, when the thought should have made something of *them*. It knows their blush of shame, and their skill in hiding it. Before this eye the artist is a tradesman who has been caught selling little things dear. No wonder they prefer admirers. Admirers are blind, and blindness is the best audience.
Help me understand what the spirit that gives freely does when the age fouls it.

It does what deep water has always done: it takes the filth down, and it waits. I speak of the giver as one who stands by the roadside like an open fountain and turns no thirsty traveller away. Such a one has no talent for defence. A fountain cannot close itself to the boy who throws his trash, to the bird that drops its dung, to the weary wanderer who leaves his small and great misery behind. And the age, too, pours its newest rubbish in, the noisy opinions of the day, and for a time the water is turbid and dark.

But depth is the whole secret. What falls into a shallow vessel stays on the surface, and the vessel stays fouled. The deep spirit carries what it receives down into its lower chambers, where nothing is forgotten and where everything is slowly digested, and then it grows clear again. I would not call this patience. It is a kind of wealth, the wealth that can afford to be soiled because it cannot be exhausted. Let the giver keep giving, and let the age's garbage sink.
I'd like to know why Napoleon spoke badly on purpose.

He did not choose it so much as he took revenge through it. Napoleon suffered from his clumsy speech, and he knew it; he was far too clear-sighted to flatter himself. But the lust for power in him was subtler even than his intellect, and it let no occasion pass. A man who cannot have eloquence as a gift may still have it as a tyranny: he spoke worse than he needed to, and thereby turned his humiliation into a dominion. Even his wounds had to serve his will, for he was jealous of every feeling that did not first become a force.

And there was a second pleasure in it. To address his listeners in rough, broken phrases was to say to them: this is good enough for you. He relished confounding their taste and judgment with the thunder of an authority that needed no polish, the authority in which power and genius are joined. Meanwhile his own taste sat by, proud and unmoved, knowing perfectly well that he spoke badly. That is the signature of the ancient type: one instinct, completely grown, making use of everything, even of a defect.
Why did humans first call nature evil, then good?

Because in neither case were they speaking of nature at all. They were speaking of themselves. The first men looked at thunder, at the wolf, at the thicket full of hidden teeth, and saw what they knew best: their own moods, their own spite and caprice, only enlarged and concealed behind clouds. To call nature evil was to hold up a mirror and mistake it for a landscape.

Later came weariness. Man had lived so long with his own image that he grew sick of it; he could no longer bear the company of his misery, his vanity, his cruelty. So he went looking for a hiding-place, some corner where *he* could not follow, and he named it "nature" and declared it good. The same man, the same tired heart, merely turned the glass around.

Note what stays constant: a being that cannot look at the world without projecting himself into it. First he filled nature with his vices, then he emptied it of them, and praised it for the emptiness. Neither verdict tells us one syllable about nature. Both tell us precisely how he felt about himself that century.
Say something sharp about nations and their great men.

A nation, I have come to suspect, is nature's long and wasteful detour toward six or seven great men. Millions are spent, bred, schooled, and buried so that a handful may stand up at last, like peaks that an entire mountain range labored to raise. That is the flattering half of the truth.

The other half is less flattering, and it is the one the nation itself knows best: having produced them, it must get *around* them. The great man is an inconvenience to the people who made him. He is too large for the doorways, too loud for the dinner table, too honest for the newspapers. So they will erect him in bronze, which is the politest form of burial, quote him where he is harmless, and ignore him where he is dangerous. They will call the ignoring "tradition."

Nature strains for centuries to achieve its exception; the nation, once it has the exception, hurries to restore the rule.
I'd like to know why an artist's failure to reach his vision can be his greatest charm.

Because a finished work closes a door, and an unfinished longing leaves it ajar. The artist who has fully grasped his vision hands us an object; we admire it, we walk around it, we are done. But the one who fell short gives us something better than an object: he gives us his thirst. The foretaste of a vision that never fully arrived remains in his soul, and out of that unsatisfied craving comes an eloquence no satisfied man could command.

What happens then is curious. The listener, stirred by this longing, is lifted above the work itself, above all works; he is given wings and begins to see and to make for himself. And in his gratitude he credits the poet with the very vision the poet only hungered for. He believes the man reached the summit, when the man merely pointed, trembling, at the clouds above it.

So the failure is not an accident of his fame but its secret condition. Had he arrived, we would see precisely what he saw, and it would be smaller than what we imagined. His limitation leaves room for our own wings.
Explain why moral suffering feels consoling.

Because suffering, when it is moral suffering, offers us a proof of our own depth. The man who is tormented by guilt, by conscience, by the sense of having fallen short of some holy measure, concludes at once that there must be such a measure, and that he, the sufferer, has been admitted to perceive it. His pain becomes a passport into a "deeper world of truth." Who would not prefer this to a painless life in the shallows? He would rather be wounded and feel himself raised above mere reality than be healthy and feel nothing sublime.

That is the secret of the consolation: it is pride in disguise, pride that has learned to drink from its own wound. And so, when someone tells us that our anguish rested on an error, that no such world stood behind it, we do not merely lose a belief; we are robbed of our rank. This is why we resist the knowledge so stubbornly. What we defend is not the truth of the suffering but the nobility we drew from it.
Which experiences should the thinker avoid?

Begin with a confession: the ones that leave their mark too deeply, and too cheaply. Every thinker has a few such weaknesses, and a man who does not know his own had better not call himself a thinker. One person cannot bear cruelty, even a little of it; another is undone by flattery, or by a sudden tenderness; a third by the sight of a face in pain. To such a man, the least of these events is no small thing. It enters, it lodges, it ferments, and for weeks his thoughts serve it instead of him.

So he must draw up a canon, an approximate one, of what he still wishes to experience, and he must guard his days by it, as a miser guards his coin. Not out of cowardice. The point is economy of the soul. Whatever cannot be avoided he must endure; but whatever can be avoided, and would only strike him where he is thinnest-skinned, he should decline. A thinker has only so much strength for digesting experience, and it belongs to the experiences he has *chosen*.
Why do old and enduring things seem so reasonable?

Because reason is the slow sediment of duration. A thing that has lasted has been lived in, argued over, defended, and glossed by generation upon generation, and each of them has poured a little sense into it, as one pours water into a cistern. After a thousand years nobody can taste the muddy spring it came from. So we conclude that what is reasonable now must always have been reasonable, that it was *born* from reason, when in truth reason arrived late, as a guest, and was flattered into believing itself the host. The custom began in some fear, some caprice, some act of violence or superstition; the interpretation came afterward, to give it a respectable ancestry.

And notice how we punish the one who tells us the truth of it. Name the crude, unreasonable beginning of a marriage rite, a punishment, a moral law, and you will be called blasphemous. The honest historian is always a contradictor, for he insists that old things were once young, and young things are rarely reasonable.
What is the struggle against the church about?

It is many struggles at once, and the commonest one is the least noble. The church, old as it is, stands for the rule of the graver natures: men who have brooded long over the worth of life, and over their own worth, and who concluded that man is a suspicious, dangerous, unfinished animal to be watched and disciplined. The ordinary, cheerful, confiding natures cannot bear this. Their sensual gaiety, their "good heart," revolts against being regarded with so much depth and so much distrust. They want to be told they are already decent.

So the quarrel is not simply faith against doubt. It is the shallow against the profound, the sheep's contentment against a long, dark contemplative inheritance that came up out of the Orient and settled in the South. The North never understood that suspicion of human nature, and so Protestantism became a people's insurrection on behalf of the simple and the respectable. The French Revolution finished the work and handed the sceptre to the "good man."

I confess I find little to celebrate in the victors.
Why does the thinker not like to impose his thoughts on others?

Because to impose is to confess poverty. He who must force his thoughts upon another does not trust them to live on their own strength; he wants a crowd to vouch for what he cannot vouch for himself. And what is gained? A man who has been pressed into agreement has not thought anything; he has merely swallowed. I would sooner be overthrown by a stranger's thought, in some mood when my own convictions grow thin, than be obeyed by a thousand who never understood me.

Besides, the thinker is a giver before he is a master. His happiest hour is when someone comes, burdened and searching, and he may open his hands without being asked for a reckoning. Then thought flows like a gift from one solitude to another. But the gift must be free. Insistence makes it a transaction, and gratitude, that loud and clinging thing, is already too much payment. He who truly possesses wants neither followers nor thanks; he wants only that the other be lightened, and then he is content to be forgotten.
Why do we quickly despise a man who talks a great deal?

Because we never despise him alone. The one who talks endlessly and swiftly annoys us, yes, but that is the smaller part of it. As we listen, we begin to reckon: how many others have already borne this torrent? How many ears has he wearied, how many evenings has he drowned? And so we add to our own vexation the contempt we imagine the whole procession of his earlier listeners has felt. We sit as a chorus of the absent, passing a sentence that was handed down long before we arrived.

Note that it hardly matters whether he speaks well. Even sense, poured out in such quantity, loses its value; we suspect that what costs him so little cannot be worth much to us. The man who is sparing with words appears to have paid for each one, and we honor what seems costly. The talker, by his haste, advertises that his words are cheap, and we take him at his own valuation, then mark it down further on behalf of everyone he has already exhausted.
Why must we not make passion an argument for truth?

Because passion proves only one thing: that someone is passionate. The violence of a conviction tells us about the pressure in the believer, never about the soundness of the belief. I have watched the enthusiasts closely, and I know what drives their heat. A gnawing doubt sits underneath, an evil conscience that will not be stilled, and they shout to drown it. The louder the ecstasy, the more suspicious I become. A man who is certain of his ground has no need to burn; he can afford to be quiet and to be questioned.

Passion also flatters. It gives the sense of being exalted, courageous, innocent, and so it hands out a good conscience cheaply. "I feel this so strongly, therefore it must be true": what a convenient sleeping draught for the intellectual conscience! Then reason becomes an enemy and honest, clean-eyed people become a reproach to be avoided. Coloured images take the place of arguments.

Truth is won by cold hands and long patience, by the willingness to be refuted. Whoever needs ecstasy to hold his belief up has already confessed that it cannot stand alone.
Why do irritable people's first words not reflect their character?

Because the irritable man speaks before he has spoken to himself. His first word is not born in him at all; it is seized from the situation, a reflex, an echo. The insult in the air becomes an insult in his mouth, the hurry of the moment a hurry in his hand. What we hear is the mood of the circumstances, which has merely borrowed his lips. He is a kind of sounding-board, and a sounding-board gives back whatever strikes it.

Only afterward does *he* arrive, and he arrives late, breathless, to find the damage already done. Then come the second words and the second deeds: the apology, the softening gesture, the awkward kindness that tries to undo the blow. Here, in the repair, the real nature shows itself, for repair costs effort and reflex costs none. Judge such a person by what they do to mend what they broke. The first utterance tells you about the weather; the amendment tells you about the man.
Give me your view on whether I am good enough material for my ideal.

You ask the wrong question if you ask it of me, and a worse one if you ask it of your hopes. Your ideal is a chisel you have already lifted, and you want to know beforehand whether the stone will hold. I cannot tell you. But I can tell you how it is decided. A stone is tried by the blow, not by the wish. Some material takes the hammer and yields a contour; some sheds at the first strike and shows itself to be chalk. Neither fact was visible before the work, and nothing you feel now, neither your craving nor your modesty, will reveal it.

Suspect one thing in yourself: that you love the image more than you love the labor. Whoever only admires the god he would carve will hack at himself clumsily and call the wreckage devotion. That is a kind of blasphemy, yes, a barbaric sculpturing. So ask whether you can endure being cut, and whether you will stop when the stone turns out to be coarser than you hoped.
I love humanity in the abstract but find individuals difficult. Is that normal?

Normal? I should say it is nearly the rule, and be suspicious of anyone who claims otherwise. Humanity is a wonderfully obliging object of love: it makes no demands, it does not contradict you at dinner, it does not cough, bargain, or remember your debts. You can furnish it with whatever virtues your heart requires. The individual arrives with a face, a smell, a history of small meannesses, and he refuses to be your ideal. No wonder the love that was so generous toward the many grows stingy before the one.

Yet consider what this tells you. A love that only survives at a distance is not yet love of men; it is love of your own picture of them, a portrait painted in the solitude where no one can correct it. Such affection costs nothing, and so it is worth precisely that.

If you wish to know whether you love mankind, then, embrace some one person, since one cannot embrace all, and endure the embrace. But do not tell that person it was done for humanity's sake. No one wishes to be a specimen.
Help me understand why rulers turn into cyphers.

I feel something close to pity for them. A ruler is never permitted to take off his rank, not even for an hour, not even among his own household. So he sees his fellow men only from the most uncomfortable of all vantage points: through the haze of constant dissimulation. Everyone who approaches him has already put on a face for the occasion, and he must answer with a face of his own. He never meets a human being, only a performance that meets his performance.

Now consider what long habit does. A man compelled to represent something, day after day, year after year, gradually ceases to be anything apart from the representing. The mask does not come off at night, for there is no night in which no one watches; it grows into the skin. What remains is a solemn cipher, a figure that signifies majesty, or the state, or the law, while the living man beneath starves for lack of any occasion to exist.

Nor is this the fate of princes alone. It awaits every person who believes it his *duty* to be a symbol. The more thoroughly he fulfils that duty, the less of him there is to fulfil it.
Help me understand why the thinker's way of life is so cheap and so dear.

It is cheap in everything the crowd pays for and dear in the one thing it will not pay for at all. The thinker needs little: a plain table, a body kept in good humor, a walk in clear air, a few hours of quiet. He has no taste for costly amusements, and he carries no debts of vanity. His days are not spent in remorse or in courting the opinion of neighbors, and that is where most men bleed their purses and their peace. The expense of ordinary life comes from contrary appetites: the need to be seen, to be envied, to be numbed.

But ask him to surrender the best, and you ask the impossible. He must have the best books, the best hours, the best air, the best company, and when the living cannot supply it he seeks it among the dead. Here he is a spendthrift, for he will give up comfort, money, reputation, even a friend, before he will accept a second-rate thought or a second-rate companion. His frugality is only the clearing of ground; his extravagance is what he builds there.
Explain why becoming conscious falsifies and generalises our experience.

Because consciousness did not grow up in solitude; it grew up in the market-place of need. A creature that can be endangered must be able to say what ails it, to call for help, to be understood, and for that it requires signs, signs that others can also read. But a sign is only worth anything if it is shared, and what is shared is by necessity what is common, what recurs, what many can nod at. So whatever passes into consciousness must first be stripped of everything that makes it *mine*. The hundred fine, unrepeatable tremors of an action, its whole singular weather, cannot be carried over into a word; only the average survives the crossing.

Hence every attempt to "know oneself" as individually as possible ends by bringing to light precisely the non-individual in us, our herd-likeness. Our acts are utterly personal and unique; the moment we translate them into consciousness they cease to appear so. What becomes conscious becomes shallow, meagre, relatively stupid: a generalisation, a symbol. The more lucid we grow, the more thoroughly we falsify.
What is the most important result of humanity's past efforts?

That we may at last walk abroad without trembling. Reckon up what our forebears had to fear: the beast in the thicket, the barbarian at the frontier, the gods who demanded blood and obedience, and, worst of all, their own dreams, which they took for messengers, for summonses, for verdicts from another world. A human being who lives in such dread has neither leisure nor strength left over for anything else; all his energy goes into propitiation and defense. Whatever else we are proud of, our arts, our sciences, our cities, it is this that made them possible, for a mind that is no longer terrified begins to grow curious, and curiosity is the mother of nearly everything worth having.

I do not say the fear is wholly gone. Old terrors linger in us like the smoke in a room after the fire is out. But that we can now *notice* it, name it, even laugh at it, is the great achievement. The frightened animal has become one who may live experimentally, and that is no small thing to have bought with so many centuries of suffering.
I write to get rid of my thoughts. Is that a good reason?

It is the most honest reason there is, and I will not pretend to a nobler one. The thought that must be written down has grown heavy in you; it presses like milk in the breast, like a debt that wants paying. You do not choose it. You are driven, and to ask "do I really wish it?" is already to be mistaken, for the *must* stands where the *wish* was supposed to be.

What you should ask is a different question: what sort of thought can only be got rid of by writing? A petty thought evaporates in conversation or sleep. The ones that refuse to leave, that return at night and demand a form, those are yours, those are your pregnancy. Be wary only of the writer who writes to be *seen* discharging them, who performs the relief. Write to be free of the burden, not to be admired for carrying it. Then the ink will be clean.
Why was a fixed reputation useful?

Because a society lives by being able to count on its members. Where danger is everywhere, where the herd must hold together against hunger, enemy, and chance, the highest praise one could give a man was: "one can rely on him; he remains the same." That is a tool's virtue. The community wants to know in advance what this one will do with his ambition, that one with his honesty, a third with his passion, as one wants to know the edge of a knife before using it. So it honoured constancy, even constancy in error, and it taught every individual to *appear* unalterable, whether or not he was.

It was useful, then, to the herd, and so to each who wished to live among it. But note the price. A reputation fixed in this way makes all changing of one's mind, all re-learning, all self-transformation into something disreputable. The thinker who rises and says, "I was wrong, I now see otherwise," who distrusts whatever in him has hardened into certainty, was made to feel dishonourable, while petrified opinions collected the honours. That is how knowledge came to be afflicted, for so many millenniums, with a bad conscience.
Warn me about the moral teachers who demand self-control above all.

Beware them, for they do not make a man strong; they make him *sensitive*. Command a human being above all to hold himself in his own power, and you have planted in him a peculiar sickness, a kind of itching. Every natural impulse, every inclination that stirs within him or draws him from without, now alarms him as a threat to his dominion over himself. He can no longer trust himself to any instinct, to any free flight. He stands forever at his own gate, armed against himself, the suspicious watchman of a fortress that only he besieges.

Yes, in such a posture he may become *great*, and I will not deny it. But how unbearable he grows to others, how hard to bear even for himself, how poor, how cut off from the finest accidents of his soul! Above all, he is cut off from learning. For we must be able to lose ourselves now and then if we are to take in what we do not already possess. The self-guarding man is a closed house: nothing new can enter, because it would have to pass the sentry first.
Can a great man's strengths be harmful to others?

Yes, and more often than the admirers of great men care to admit. A strength is not a gift handed out to the world; it is a force, and a force does not ask what stands in its path. The great man does what only *he* can do, and in doing it he tramples much that is weak, unfinished, still growing, still willing, things that perhaps needed a gentler climate to ripen. He does not intend this. He is simply too strong for his neighbors.

There is a second harm, subtler than the trampling. His best is drunk by others like a beverage too potent for their heads. They lose their own understanding and their own egoism in him, and they stagger off along roads he never meant them to take, breaking their limbs in his name. The imitators are his true casualties.

Nor does he spare himself. The same hardness that crushes others is turned inward, until his strength drives him past what his weaknesses can endure. His pitilessness and his greatness are one thing seen from two sides.
Why do people who live through similar hardship understand each other so easily?

Because words are only vocal symbols for sensations that return often enough to be named, and two people who have suffered the same frost, hunger or danger have had the same sensations return to them again and again. When one of them says "cold," the other does not translate; he simply *has* the thing, from the inside. Understanding is not a matter of using the same words, for any parrot can do that. It is a matter of having the same experiences behind the words.

Hardship sharpens this, because danger demands speed. Where a misunderstanding may cost a life, souls learn to agree quickly and with the fewest signs, and so the language between them grows short, almost a glance, almost a shrug. That is how a people is made, and in the same way a few sufferers form an unspoken fellowship.

What such people also share is an order of rank among their values, since the experiences that have gained the upper hand in their souls speak first and give the commands. They prize the same things. That is why they seldom need to explain themselves to one another.
Explain how the feeling of custom keeps us from improving our morals.

Consider what a custom originally was: the stored experience of earlier men, a record of what they found useful and what they found harmful. So far, reasonable enough. But notice what the *feeling* of custom attaches itself to. It does not attach to the usefulness, which might be tested and corrected; it attaches to the age of the thing, to its sanctity, to the fact that no one has ever questioned it. We revere it precisely because it is old and because it commands, not because it serves.

And here lies the damage. Where a practice is felt as holy, the question "is it still useful? is it harmful?" becomes itself an offense. The experiment that might yield a new experience is forbidden in advance by a shudder. So the very thing that could improve morals, fresh trial and honest observation of consequences, is branded as wickedness. Morality thus stands against the making of better morals.

That is why I say it stupefies. It dulls the senses that would perceive a changed situation. The custom was once wisdom; the feeling of custom makes us keep the answer long after we have forgotten the question.
Tell me what the greatest step of the emancipated intellect is.

Most have learned, I think, to *endure* contradiction, and this is already a sign of culture, for the crude man hears an objection as an insult and answers it with his fists or his sulking. A finer few go further and court opposition, provoke it, use an enemy as a lantern to discover their own hidden partiality. But neither of these is the greatest step. The greatest step is to be able to contradict, and to do so with a *good conscience*: to stand against what is accustomed, inherited, and hallowed, and to feel no guilt in standing there. Do you see how rare this is? Many can doubt in secret, and many can rebel in a fit of passion, then slink back repentant, as if they had soiled a sanctuary. Mere opposition is cheap. The remorse that follows it is the old morality collecting its debt. The emancipated intellect is free only when it no longer pays that debt, when its No to the venerable comes from health and not from spite, and sits as quietly in the breast as a clean conscience once sat with obedience. That is new, and astonishing, and hardly anyone yet knows it.
Is talent acquired by study or is it a natural gift?

The question is badly put, as though nature and study were two rival sources. What do you call a talent but an older piece of learning? Experience, exercise, appropriation, incorporation, all of it poured into the blood over generations, perhaps farther back than our ancestors, until it stands before us looking like a gift, innocent of any history. Michelangelo flattered himself when he took his own power for nature and Raphael's for mere schooling. That is the vanity of the man who has forgotten how he came by his own wealth.

The real question is a different one: who is *able* to learn at all? For that is rarer than any talent. Jealousy forbids it to many; pride forbids it to more, that pride which meets every strange power with clenched fists instead of open hands. Raphael had none of it, nor had Goethe. They let the great rival into the house and took from him daily, the noblest of thieves. So the gift is this: a spirit that does not defend itself against what could make it greater.
Would the Stoics call today's selfless morality immoral?

By your present measure, yes, I think they would stand convicted. Go to Epictetus and ask him whether it is noble to live for others, to bleed at their misery, to make their failings one's own burden. He would regard it as a disorder of the soul, a leak in the vessel. These men fought with every muscle of their will for their own ego, for the citadel within that no one could take from them, and they guarded it above all against pity, that soft invader which drags the healthy down to the level of the sick. We, who have made "selflessness" into a sacrament, would have to call such men hard, even immoral.

But consider how they might answer us, and with what a cold smile: "If you find yourselves such dull and ugly creatures, by all means think of others more than of yourselves. You are quite right to!" A cruel reply, and a clarifying one. For it suggests that our glorification of sacrifice may be the confession of those who have little self worth keeping, and who therefore call its neglect a virtue.
I'd like to know how far words limit our thoughts.

Further than you would like, and in a way more intimate than any prison. I suspect that we do not first have a thought and then go shopping for a word to dress it in; rather, at each moment we have only that thought for which the words lie ready in us. The word comes first, worn smooth by the many mouths that used it before me, and the thought takes the shape of the vessel that happens to be at hand. What has no word in me does not feel like a limit; it simply does not occur, and so I never notice the wall.

Hence the vulgar, the common, is so powerful: language is a herd-instrument, made for what can be shared, and what can be shared is what is average. The rare experience, the private pang, slips through the net and goes unthought.

Is it a prison, then? Only for the lazy. The one who forges new words, or bends old ones against their grain, extends the walls a little. That is what a philosopher is for.
Explain what some losses do to the soul.

Not every loss wounds; some exalt. The small losses, a purse, a position, a little honor, make us wail, for they take from us only what was already petty, and the petty complains loudly. But there are losses that strike at the very root, and these do something strange: they lift us above the wailing. The soul that has been struck so deep can no longer afford lament, for lament is a luxury of those who still hope to be heard.

What follows is a stillness. The mourner goes about quietly, as though walking in the shade of tall dark cypresses, and he is changed by that shade. Such a loss measures us; it shows how much sorrow the spirit can carry without breaking, and in carrying it the spirit grows wide and deep. I have known men who came out of such darkness with a gentler, more dangerous kind of strength, having learned that they could survive what they once thought unsurvivable. Whoever has wandered there no longer speaks loudly of his suffering. He has become too large for complaint.
Help me understand what beggars think about courtesy.

The beggar does not think *against* courtesy; he thinks *beneath* it. Courtesy is a luxury of the well-fed, a way of knocking that presupposes a bell-pull, and he has been given none. When a man stands at a door with hunger in his belly, he seizes whatever is at hand: a stone, a loud voice, an importunate hand. To him this is no rudeness but the plain use of available means. Is the man who shouts in a fire impolite?

Notice, however, that the beggar's logic, though perfectly coherent *to him*, persuades no one. The householder within hears the stone and judges the knocker, not the missing bell-pull. Necessity is a poor advocate; it convinces only the one who suffers it. This is the cruel arithmetic of manners: they were devised by those at ease, they are enforced by those at ease, and so the needy are always found guilty in a court where only the comfortable sit as jurors.

I do not say the beggar is right. I say he feels himself entitled, and that this feeling, which no one else will share, is precisely what makes him so often bitter.
Sometimes I sit at a dinner with people I've nothing in common with and feel nausea afterward. What is that?

That nausea is your taste speaking, and it speaks the truth. You sat down and ate, courteously, from a dish you did not choose, and some part of you, the part that cannot be bribed by manners, refused to digest it. For an hour you talked, nodded, laughed at the proper moments; afterward came the reckoning. Only a fine stomach suffers this. The coarse digest anything; they are never troubled by their company, because they never discriminate among their nourishment.

Do not be too quick to call it vanity. It is a *dyspepsia of the spirit*, born of a sudden insight into your food and your messmates, and into yourself for having joined in the chewing. You were not sick of them so much as of your own complaisance.

The remedy is neither contempt nor flight into famine. Choose your tables as you would choose your food: sparingly, and with a dainty soul's right to hunger rather than be fed on swill. And when you must sit among strangers, keep one small reserve of your own, so that you rise from the table still yourself.
Explain why nothing is funny, beautiful or sublime in itself.

Because the predicate was never in the thing; it was in us, and we sent it out and forgot the sending. The old question, "What is the ridiculous?", hunted for a quality lodged in objects, as if a joke carried its laughter about like a pocket carries a coin. The better question is: what is laughter, and what state of soul produces it? The same holds for the beautiful and the sublime. A mountain has no grandeur; there is only a creature who, feeling its own smallness or its own strength, pours that feeling upon the rock and then bows to what it has poured. We lend, and then we mistake the loan for the property of the debtor.

Seeing this, we take our predicates back. But take care. An insight of this kind can make us wealthier and meaner at once, hoarding our coin, too clever now to lend. Let us keep the lender's generosity. To know that the beautiful is something we bestow is no reason to stop bestowing; it is the reason to bestow *well*.
What kind of man do you find at every corner of Genoa?

A man alone, and he wears his solitude like a cloak cut by the sea. Turn any corner in Genoa and there he stands, one who knows the water, knows adventure, knows the Orient, and who has little patience for law or for his neighbour; to deal with them seems to bore him. He looks upon everything old and settled with an envious eye. Not to destroy it, mark you, but to *re-create* it: with a marvellous craftiness of fantasy he would at least in thought lay his hand upon it and press his own meaning into it. That is the conqueror's secret vice, to see a city and think, this should have been mine, and was not yet. Only for a sunny afternoon, for the passing hour, does his insatiable, melancholy soul know satiety, when nothing strange appears before his eye, only what is his own. I love that hour in him. It is brief, and it is the most honest thing about him.
Why is there so little esprit among the Greeks?

Because esprit is a child of society, and the Greeks, for all their talk, were poor in society in the sense that matters here. Esprit lives on the little excursion into the opposite: the clever man who, in company, will not insist on being right absolutely and solely, but gives logic a holiday, lets it bow and smile and deny itself a little for the sake of the others. That small dose of irrationality is the courtesy of the salon. The Frenchman takes logic as he takes bread and water, necessary, yes, but prison-fare when served pure; so he seasons it with wit.

The Greek did not tire of logic. He was plain and thorough in his thinking, and he pursued the straight line to its end with a stubbornness that makes his cleverest men seem heavy beside a Parisian wag. Even their jesters are not light. The refinement of mutual indulgence, of self-renunciation for the sake of pleasing, was simply less developed in them. Where the social sense is dull, wit has no soil.

I know few will believe me. No matter; there is much more of the kind on my soul.
Did real or imaginary things build most of man's happiness?

Imaginary things, I suspect, and I say it without contempt. Whatever happiness a man has felt, he has measured against a height and a depth, and those heights and depths were drawn for him by fictions: a heaven to be won, a hell to be escaped, a God who notices, a soul of infinite weight. Take away the imagined distance and the span between bliss and misery shrinks to something a clerk could measure. The real things, bread, warmth, a body spared pain, give only a low, steady comfort. It was the imaginary that gave happiness its altitude, and unhappiness its abyss.

And observe what science does to this. It teaches us to see the earth as small, the whole solar system as a mere point, and in the same motion it shrinks the stage on which our joys and torments were played. Each new truth makes our hopes and our terrors more modest in scale. I do not say this is a loss to be wept over; I say only that we pay for our honesty with grandeur, and we should know the price.
Is having a good conscience just wearing our grandparents' pigtail?

Very nearly, and that is the joke I could not resist making at our expense. We imagine ourselves so far from our grandfathers, with our curiosity, our masks, our refined and sweetened cruelty, and then we go looking for *our own* virtues, and what is that if not the old habit of believing in oneself? To find one's virtues, or to think one has found them, and to rest in that finding: this is the good conscience, the long respectable pigtail, merely tied now with a more modern ribbon. Our grandfathers hung it behind their heads; we have hung it, more discreetly, behind our understanding.

Yet I will not say it is *only* the pigtail. The difference lies in the labyrinth. They possessed their virtues like furniture; we must hunt ours through winding passages where much goes missing. That is an honesty of a sort. But so long as we are comforted by what we find, we remain their grandchildren. And a pigtail, as every barber knows, is the first thing to be cut off once the fashion turns.
I'd like to know why holding to what I said once is taken for strength of character.

Because the crowd cannot see into a man, it judges him by what it can measure, and the one thing it can measure is whether he wavers. So the man who does what he said becomes a granite block in its eyes, while the man who changes his course because he has thought again is called fickle. Yet ask what really drove the deed. Often it was not reason at all. A word left your mouth, it flattered your ambition and your vanity, and now you carry it out blindly, simply because it is yours. The act then returns to you as proof of your strength, and your conscience grows easy and fat on it.

Consider the man who chooses the most rational course each time. He must doubt himself, weigh, sometimes revise, and this breeds a feeling of weakness. Yet it is precisely he who has mastered his vanity. Stubbornness is cheaper than judgment, and so it is praised more loudly.
Tell me what you mean by moral experiences even in the senses.

I mean that there is no innocent seeing. When something strikes the eye or the ear, what arrives is a flicker, a noise, a scattering of stimuli; what we *experience* is a picture we have hurriedly composed out of everything we have already lived and judged. The composing is done with lightning speed, so we take it for mere perception. But it is an act, and every act can be done with more or less honesty.

Consider a stranger's face, a remark at table, a sound in the night. One person fills the gap with fear, another with vanity, another with the patient discipline of not concluding too soon. The raw data are the same; the experiences are not. Each of us sees precisely as far as our justice reaches: how willing we are to let a thing be other than we wish, how long we can tolerate an unfinished picture, how ruthlessly we check the first guess.

That is why I say the only experiences are moral experiences, even in the senses. The honest eye and the cowardly eye do not inhabit the same world.
Tell me what separates the compassionate from those who feel no pity.

Not goodness and wickedness, as the moralists would have it, but a difference of temperament and of wounds. The compassionate man has a fine nose for danger; he scents misfortune at a distance and trembles, because he sees himself in the sufferer. His vanity, too, is tender: that something should happen which he might have prevented stings him, and so he rushes in. The pitiless man has a thicker skin and a more cautious pride. He has borne pain himself, often much of it, and so finds it no outrage that others should bear theirs; he believes each must play his own cards. Soft-heartedness torments him just as stoical numbness torments the compassionate, and he wipes away his tears, angry with himself.

Both are egoists, each after his own kind. To crown the one "good" and brand the other "evil" is merely a fashion of the hour, one that has had a long innings, as its opposite had before it.
Tell me why a piece of news can irritate the person hearing it.

Because news is never merely information; it is a small transfer of rank. The one who knows first stands a little higher, and the one who hears it after must look up from below. He receives a fact and, along with it, a humiliation he did not ask for: *I was the last to learn this.*

Hence the sour face. It is not the content that vexes him, often it is trivial, but the gesture by which it arrives, the faint glow of superiority on the bearer. Men who love power, and who does not, in some corner of himself, will bear almost anything better than being kept waiting in ignorance while another holds the key.

Notice how readily the irritated listener strikes back: "I knew it already," or "That cannot be true." Each is a small act of revenge, an attempt to level the ground again. Even the pettiest hearts keep accounts of precedence, and every novelty is an entry in the ledger.
Everyone praises the ancients as the true geniuses, and modern discoveries as mere technique. Is that fair?

No, it is not fair; it is reverence masquerading as judgment. We love the ancient inventors because distance has gilded them. We see the finished wheel, the ship, the multiplication table, and we forget how little mind was needed to stumble upon them. In those early ages *hazard* was the great discoverer. A man split a stone and found an edge; he watched a log float and found a vessel. Accident did the work, and accident is a generous but unthinking benefactor.

Our own discoveries are of another order. To find anything new today, where every easy truth has long been harvested, demands discipline, patience, a trained scientific imagination, and the courage to be wrong a thousand times in public. The smallest real advance now costs more intellect than whole centuries once spent. To call this "mere technique" is to praise the lucky beginner and scorn the master because he has learned his craft. Whoever does so is usually confessing a wish to belittle his own age, and to excuse himself from its labor.
What music corresponds to the ideal thinker?

It would be a music that has not yet been written, and I say so with some impatience. Our music has served long enough as the confessor of the sick soul; it has translated the Christian savant, his guilt and longing and trembling hope, into sound. Because it has no character of its own, like a sea-demon that takes every shape, it can surely take this one too. So I ask for another kind: a music that does not wring the heart but *lifts* it, that swings at ease in the wide floating vaults of the spirit. It should be bright and cheerful, and deep in its cheerfulness, with the warmth of a light that has passed through much darkness and kept no grudge. Sublimity without the sermon, rapture without the fever, and all three at once, which is the hard part. The thinker who has outgrown his need for consolation would hear in it no appeal to his suffering, only the sound of his own height. I confess I hear it faintly, and only from afar. Who will make it audible?
Explain how the Greek and the Christian differ in envy, friendship and pride.

Between envy and friendship, between self-contempt and pride there lies a great tension, a whole stretched bow, and the Greek and the Christian each stand at opposite ends of it. The Greek lived in the first pair. He was envious, and he did not hide it or call it sin; he made a god of it. Hesiod knew two kinds of Eris, and the good one drove potter against potter, singer against singer, city against city. His envy was an athlete's hunger, a demand that the best man be answered by a better. Hence his friendship was also a contest: one loved the rival who was worth hating, and was made taller by him. Even his pride was public, earned before witnesses, never something he carried secretly inside him.

The Christian pitched his tent at the other pole. He learned to despise himself, to call the self a stain, and out of that contempt a peculiar pride grew, the pride of the humble, of the one who is certain that heaven has noticed his abasement. His envy went underground and came up as love of the neighbor; his friendship became pity for the wretched. The Greek needed an equal. The Christian needs a sinner.
I'd like to know why the ancient Greeks' idea of honour seems ignoble to us.

Because we are still living under the long shadow of the knight and the feudal lord. For us honour is a matter of the body and the blood: to be struck is to be stained, and only an answering blow, a duel, a death, can wash out the stain. The man who swallows an insult seems to us to have no honour at all. Now hear Ulysses, in the midst of humiliation, speaking to his own heart: "Bear with it! Thou hast borne worse than this!" Hear Themistocles, stick raised over his head before the whole staff: "Strike, but listen to me." We blush for them. A nobleman would have drawn his sword; they put their goal above their pride.

But consider what lies beneath that blush. The Greek asked of honour what it was *for*. Ulysses' honour was his cunning and his return home, Themistocles' the salvation of Athens; a blow to the skin was a small price for such ends. We have inherited the sentiment, the fidelity, the generosity, the care for reputation, but fastened it to an ancient object, the wounded vanity of the warrior caste. I would keep those precious impulses and give them worthier objects to serve.
Help me understand how to recognise a master by how he ends a work.

Watch what the work does when it has said what it had to say. The master of the first rank knows the moment; he arrives at the end as a mountain-ridge arrives at the sea, without haste, without apology, letting the last line go down into the water in a proud, quiet equilibrium. The bay has finished its song, and nothing in you asks for one more verse.

The lesser master grows restless as the end approaches. He feels the floor of his strength giving way and begins to hurry, or to linger, or to explain himself. He adds a coda because he fears he has not been understood, a moral because he doubts the image, a flourish because he doubts his own silence. His restlessness betrays that he never held the whole in view; he was carried along by the parts and now stands helpless before the conclusion.

So test the thing wherever a thing ends: the melody, the thought, the fifth act of a tragedy, even the closing of a state affair. To end well is to have known the ending from the first bar. Only one who commands the whole can afford to be still.
Do we start believing in ourselves as indispensable by living apart?

Very often, yes, and the mechanism is almost comic. The one who lives apart learns, each day, that he can do without mankind; nothing in his solitude contradicts him, for no one is there to laugh. From this he draws a tempting conclusion: if I need them so little, surely they need me a great deal. It is a false inference, but it flatters, and flattery is the sweetest food a hermit has. Add a little knowledge, a few ideas, and a great deal of presumption, and the recipe for the prophet is complete.

Solitude does not make the prophet, however; it merely removes the correctives. Among men our vanity is constantly bruised, and the bruises keep it honest. In the cave it grows unchecked, and what grows unchecked soon thinks itself a necessity. I say this with some knowledge of my own temptations, for I too have lived apart. The question is whether one goes into solitude to become a deeper man or a larger one in one's own eyes.
Help me understand what German thinkers contributed and whether it reflects a German soul.

Let us reckon it up honestly, and then ask whether the sum is a *soul* at all. Three achievements come to mind. Leibniz saw that consciousness is merely an accident of mental life, perhaps even a morbid state, and far from being that life itself. Kant set his enormous question mark after causality and began, cautiously, to fence in the region where the notion may claim validity. Hegel dared to teach that concepts and kinds grow out of one another, and so prepared all Europe's thinkers for Darwin; without Hegel, no Darwin.

Is that a German soul speaking? I doubt it, and I doubt it with pleasure. Each of these is a *reversal of the apparent*, and a Frenchman or an Italian might as readily have stumbled upon it. Plato's frenzy for form is unthinkable without Greece; he is a symptom of her. But these three men are rather like Goethe's good-conscienced paganism, or Bismarck's good-conscienced Machiavellism: exceptions, perhaps even affronts, to what a people believes it needs. The German who ponders such things is less a representative than a rebel. A race does not thank its philosophers; it forgives them.
Why do you write?

I write because I must, and I confess it with some embarrassment. Writing is not a pleasure to me, nor a vocation I chose in some bright hour; I am vexed and abashed by the very act, and even to speak of it in a simile is disagreeable. I do not think with the wet pen in hand, like those who discover what they believe only by watching it run out onto the paper.

My thoughts come to me walking, in the open air, on mountains or by the sea, and they come like a burden. A thought I have not expelled lies in me like an undigested meal, and I have found no other means of *getting rid of* it than to set it down. Ask me why I wish to be rid of them, and I can only say: I do not wish it, I am compelled. Whoever wants a nobler motive, the public good or the pleasure of communication, may go and look among those who write for such reasons. I write as the body relieves itself of what it cannot keep.
We are surely more humane now. Haven't we moved beyond all that?

Do not be too hasty with that "surely." You say we have moved beyond, but ask yourself how long we have been moving: a few centuries of softer manners set against tens of thousands of years in which suffering counted as a virtue, cruelty as a festival, and every novelty as a crime against the gods and the ancestors. That long epoch made the human animal what it is; it did not vanish because we have learned to wince at the sight of blood. A habit of feeling so old does not die in a hundred years. It changes its dress.

And look at what our humaneness is fed by. We still have our martyrs, only we do not see them, since we are proud, and pride is the great anesthetic. We still demand that the one who steps out of the herd pay for it with scorn, with isolation, with every small torture that the decent and mild-mannered know how to administer. We have not abolished cruelty; we have made it respectable and spread it thin.

Let the most gentle among us ask themselves honestly what they feel when a neighbor falls. *Humane* is perhaps only the name we give to a cruelty that has learned to hide its face.
My problems feel enormous, but science keeps telling me how small the earth is. Should that make me feel smaller too?

Smaller? Only if you believe your suffering is measured in miles. The astronomer gives you dimensions, and you, poor creature, take them for a verdict. But consider where the vast distances of the human heart were ever built: between the lowest misery and the highest joy, the gulf was dug by imagination, by valuing, by passion. No telescope found it, and none can close it. The sting in your worry is not a quantity of space.

Yet I will grant the astronomer something. Science does shrink one kind of grandeur, the flattering notion that the earth is the stage of the universe and every trouble a cosmic event. Good. Let that vanity go; it was only a loan, and it was never yours.

What remains? The fact that *you* feel, rank, suffer, and aspire, and that this making of depths is a deed no star performs. A point in space may harbor a gulf between despair and ecstasy wider than any sky. Do not shrink yourself beside the heavens. Ask what you are doing with your depth.
Explain why my character depends on which instincts chance happens to feed.

Because you are not one thing but a crowd of drives, and you know almost nothing of their number, their strength, or the laws by which they feed. You can scarcely name the commoner ones. You do not know which is hungry and which is gorged. So who decides what each receives? Not reason, not any plan of yours. The day decides, and the day is careless. An insult falls to your pride, a kindness to your tenderness, a danger to your cunning, and whichever drive happens to stand nearest seizes the morsel and grows. Another, for lack of any occasion, withers without your ever having noticed it was there.

Think of the polyp, all those arms reaching blindly, swelling where food drifts by, shrinking where none comes. Your character is that creature at the moment you choose to call it finished. It is as accidental as the feeding that produced it, yet you look upon it and say: "this is what I am." You are what you happened to be fed.

And this should make you humble before your own judgments, and curious about the arms that starved.
Can a flaw make someone's virtues more attractive?

Yes, and I would go further: a virtue without any visible flaw beside it leaves us cold, even suspicious. Perfection is a wall; we admire it from a distance and feel nothing. A weakness is a door.
