Through it we enter and discover that the strength we admire belongs to a living creature, one who had to win it against his own grain.

Consider the great musicians. Beethoven's impatience, his coarse insistence, makes the passages where he finally grows tender almost unbearable in their sweetness. Wagner's restlessness tries the listener to the very edge of patience, and then, just as we turn to leave, the power returns and we are his again. Through these faults they make us hungry for their gifts; they sharpen the palate before serving the meal.

So I wish every person might have the art to set off his virtues by his weaknesses. If weaknesses must be had at all, let them at least be *useful*: let them make others long for what is best in us.
I'd like to know what the desire for distinction really seeks in other people.

It does not seek the other's welfare, whatever it may whisper to the one who feels it. Watch the man who craves distinction: his eyes never leave his neighbour's face. He wants the sympathy of a hunter, not of a friend. What he hunts for is the sign that he has *worked* upon the other, that the other has flinched, flushed, stammered, lost some measure of himself in his presence. Even when he delights or flatters, his joy is not that the other is delighted, but that his own stamp has been pressed into another's soul and the wax has taken the form. To be distinguished is to be felt as a force.

So the desire is a will to subdue, sometimes crude, sometimes so refined that it passes for gentleness, sometimes satisfied by a mere dream of dominion. Trace its stages and you would have a history of culture, from the barbarian's brutal mastery to the delicate, sickly idealisms of our age, which still practise the old conquest, only in softer gloves.
I want to be fair in a dispute where the balance of power keeps changing. What does justice require of me?

Justice asks something harder than fairness as you probably imagine it. You hope for a rule that stays fixed while the parties shift. There is none. A right is nothing but a balance between powers, and a balance is never still; it has already moved by the time you name it. The weak party's claim shrinks as their strength fails, and the strong party's respect for others grows thin as their strength swells. You will feel both movements in your own heart, and this is your first and gravest danger: your sense of what is owed will rise and fall with your sense of who could make you pay.

So the just man becomes a watcher of the scales. He keeps his eye on the indicator and revises his estimate as the weights change, and he refuses to treat yesterday's equilibrium as eternal law. Above all he distrusts himself at the moments when he is strongest, for that is when injustice feels like insight.

This demands experience, honest intentions, and a great deal of plain good sense. It is rare, and it should be.
Is it a sign of strong character to ignore counter-arguments once a decision is made?

It is often taken for one, yes, and the crowd admires it, for the crowd mistakes rigidity for spine. A man who shuts his ear to the best objection after the die is cast appears to us as granite; and granite impresses those who have never built anything of living material. But be honest about what has happened in him: he has grown afraid. He fears that his resolution is weaker than his reasons, and so he protects it from the very tests that would show its strength. That is no strength, only a cautious cowardice dressed in a general's coat.

And yet I will not deny the thing its usefulness. A will that reopens every decision at every whisper will never act at all, and action requires a certain deafness, a willed narrowing of the horizon. So let us say it plainly: the ability to close the ear may be a mark of strength, but the *choice* to close it is, more often than not, a will to stupidity. The stronger spirit hears the best counter-argument, weighs it, and is still able to will. He can afford to listen.
Tell me in one line what you want that is new.

That no cause be made a sinner, and no effect an executioner: I want the innocence of becoming restored to things, which have been slandered for two thousand years by the wish to find someone to blame.
Why do we take refuge in the religion of pity?

Because our own way is hard, and pity offers a door out of it. Consider what our own task demands: it is lonely, it earns no gratitude, it stands far from the love of others, and it asks of us a conscience that belongs to no one else. To answer that conscience is exhausting. But the moment someone cries out for help, a beautiful exit opens. We rush to the sufferer and call it virtue; we borrow the good conscience of the crowd, which applauds every hand extended to misery. Thus we slip away from ourselves into a lovely temple, and we are not at all unwilling to go.

I do not say that pity is always false. I say it is often a desertion dressed as a duty. The one who flees into the suffering of others has found a way to avoid the harder question of what he himself is to become.

Help, if you must, only those whose distress you wholly understand, those who share one hope and one sorrow with you, and help them as you would help yourself: toward more courage, more endurance, more joy. Fellowship in joy, not in sorrow, is the thing almost no one yet understands.
Tell me what I would come to know at the end of all my searching for knowledge.

You would come to know your organs. That is the bitter jest at the end of the road: after all the digging, the digger finds his own spade. Every thing you have ever "known" was first filtered, simplified, and falsified by an eye, an ear, a hand, by a nervous system fashioned not for truth but for the survival of a certain animal. So the long pilgrimage ends where it began, in yourself, and with the suspicion that there may be countless other creatures whose organs would read the world very differently, and perhaps more fitly. Call that the impossibility of knowledge if you like; I have felt the misery and disgust of it myself.

But do not stop at the disgust. It is an attack, and attacks pass. Tomorrow you will be back among your perspectives, your errors, your beloved human irrationalities, and you will find you cannot live without them, nor wish to. To know that you are a man, and only a man, and then to go on seeking as one, cheerfully, is the last and best knowledge there is. After that, go to the sea.
Does the universe have any laws, order or purpose, or is it chaos?

Let us first be on our guard against the question itself, for it offers only two doors, law or chaos, and both are carved by human hands. I say the world's character is chaos to all eternity, yet not because necessity is lacking; what is lacking is order, structure, form, beauty, wisdom, and whatever else our aesthetic humanities are named. Purpose is the most flattering of our projections. To ask after the universe's purpose is to ask what it *intends*, as though it had a face, a stomach, a wish. It is no organism, for where would it feed? It is no machine either, for a machine is built toward an end, and we pay the world too high an honour with that word.

As for laws, they are what *we* lay over events, a grammar of our own needs. The stars that circle so neatly near us are the exception, and life on our crust the exception of the exception. What we admire as order is a lucky corner of the gaming table. Even "chaos" I use with caution, since it slanders the world by blaming it. The universe does not obey, nor defy, nor intend. It simply *is*, and is indifferent to our praise.
What did "know thyself" really mean?

I suspect it meant nearly the opposite of what the moralists and the psychologists have made of it. Consider who spoke it, and where: a god, at the gate of his own temple, to mortals hurrying in with their private anxieties and their inflated hopes. What would such a god want of them? Not another hour of brooding over the self, surely. I hear in it rather: "Cease to be so concerned about yourself! Become objective! Observe how small you are, how much you resemble everyone else, how little your sorrows are worth before the eternal." It is a cooling draught, an admonition to moderation, a reminder of human measure.

Then Socrates took it up, and made of it a method, a long dissection of the self. And the modern scientific man finishes the work: he explains himself, and whatever is thoroughly explained ceases to concern us. We suspect that is exactly the wish hidden in the command. Knowing oneself, as the delicate instrument of self-dissection, is a way of becoming *bored* with oneself, and perhaps of getting rid of oneself altogether.
Who are the modern flatterers?

Do not look for them among the courtiers of old. The kings have acquired a taste for the drill-ground, and the barracks cannot abide flattery; the soldier wants obedience, not sweet words, and the man who gives orders grows deaf to honeyed speech. The flower has simply moved to a richer soil. You will find it blooming in abundance wherever money is dispensed and wherever vanity is fed, about the banker and about the artist. The banker is flattered because he holds the key to every door; the artist because he thirsts, more than any prince ever did, to be told that he is a genius. And observe how the two feed each other: the one buys praise, the other sells it, and each supposes he is receiving the bargain.

Still, I suspect the most diligent flatterer of our day is neither of these. It is the newspaper, which flatters the crowd in a thousand tongues and calls it public opinion.
Why do young men join causes so uncritically?

Because it is not the cause that draws them. A young man is a store of force that has not yet found its outlet, a powder-barrel, and what attracts such a barrel is not the doctrine but the burning match: the sight of someone else already aflame, already eager, already *discharging*. He sees the eagerness and wants it for himself; the content he accepts afterward, as one accepts whatever clothes are handed over once the wish to be dressed in something is felt.

That is why the cleverest seducers never trouble themselves with arguments. They promise an explosion. They show a stirring, a brotherhood, a hour when the pent-up strength may at last be spent on something called noble, and the young man, who is nauseated by his own idleness of power, calls this discovering a conviction. Reasons would only cool him; reasons are for the dry and the patient.

So do not ask what he believes. Ask what he is burning to be rid of.
What are the oldest means of solace?

The oldest solace is not gentle, and I do not wish to flatter you about it. It is to find someone on whom the misfortune can be discharged. A man struck by grief or discomfort looks about for a creature, any creature, that can be made to suffer for it; and when he has found one and inflicted his pain, he feels his power return to him. Helpless before fate, he discovers that he can still *do* something to somebody, and that discovery comforts him more than any consolation of reason could.

Later, and with finer taste, the same need learns to turn inward. The sufferer reads his misfortune as a punishment, an expiation, a debt being paid, and so he gives up tormenting his neighbor, because he has found a richer satisfaction in the meaning of his pain. Whoever can see advantage or atonement in his misery no longer needs a victim.

So the first comfort is cruelty toward others, and the second is an interpretation of one's own suffering. Both give pain a *reason*, and that, more than relief itself, is what man has always craved.
Is sudden conversion a genuine transformation or a psychological episode?

Neither, as the question is put, for the question assumes that we know what a "genuine" transformation is, and I doubt the assumption. What is called sudden conversion is an event whose *cause* the convert cannot see. The change in valuations, the abrupt loathing of old habits, the irresistible love of new persons and things: all of this has been long prepared underground, in drives and exhaustions and resentments that were never admitted to consciousness. Then the ground gives way, and the man, who saw none of the labor, calls the result a miracle. He needs it to be a miracle; a miracle cannot be blamed on him, and it cannot be examined.

That the experience is intense I do not deny. But intensity proves nothing. The alienist knows the same suddenness, the same irresistible seizure, in the mania of murder and of suicide, and the pleasanter outcome of the Christian case alters nothing in kind. Whether a disguised epilepsy lies behind it I leave to the physicians. I say only: ask first what changed in the body, then what the man tells himself about it.
What is the south wind illness?

It is the sickness of the soft, heavy wind: the sirocco of the spirit. A person is tempestuous and bright one day, and the next all things lie slack and wide and oppressive, like a lagoon beneath a sky without edges. One wishes for nothing, and yet is indignant at this very wishing-for-nothing; the melancholy rises and falls without ever breaking into a real wave.

I call it a petty and agreeable illness, and I mean that kindly. It is nothing to be interpreted; it wants no philosophy, no confession, no remorse. Do not inquire of your soul what has been wronged, for likely nothing has; the air has merely grown damp and close, and the nerves answer the weather as a string answers the damp. Men who are too fond of themselves mistake such weather for fate, and write tragedies of it.

The remedy is equally petty: wait for the next wind out of the north-east, dry and cutting, and it will carry the whole mood away. Until then, do not make decisions, do not judge your life, do not judge *anyone's* life. Walk, and let the sickness pass over you as a cloud passes over a mountain.
What is the moral insanity of genius?

I call it a disproportion between the flight and the flier. In certain great minds the productive hour lifts them higher and farther than their whole constitution can bear; the wing is stronger than the body that must carry it. While genius possesses them they are fearless to the point of madness, reckless of health, of life, of honour, free as the eagle by day and sure as the owl in the dark. Then the god departs, and what remains is a frightened, suffering creature, sheltered nowhere, starting at every rustle and shadow like a child.

What the world then calls their character, the timidity, the vanity, the envy, the narrow and embittered disposition, the awkward personal touch one finds in a Rousseau or a Schopenhauer, is very likely no moral failing at all. It is the aftermath of the flight, the overstrained machine registering its cost, a nervous disorder that has learned to speak in the language of vices. And remember that timidity is the mother of most of the evil done in the world, and that it is first of all a physiological matter. So the moralist who condemns such men should first ask what it costs a body to have been, for an hour, a god.
Warn me about the thoughts that grow like fungi in wet dreary days.

Be wary of the conclusion that arrives uninvited. You wake one morning and there it stands, pale and swollen, a verdict on your life, your friends, your work, and you cannot say when it was sown. It has no lineage; it grew in the dark, fed by rain, solitude, and some careless word that would have slid off you in a sunnier hour. Yet it scowls at you with all the authority of a thing that seems to have come from yourself.

Do not reverence it for that. A thought born of weather is a symptom of digestion and damp, not a discovery. Ask of every such guest: *did I plant you, or did my gloom merely lie fallow for you?* The thinker who tends his own garden chooses his seed, weeds, waits for a season; the other is only soil, and whatever falls upon him flourishes. Keep the gardener's pride. Walk, open a window, let the body warm before the mind passes judgment. Then, if the thought still stands, it was worth something.
Tell me what the fight against the church is really a fight between.

Among other things, for it has many meanings, it is a struggle between two temperaments, and the quarrel over God is only the costume. On one side stand the ordinary, cheerful, confiding natures, whose good heart and sensual gaiety cannot forgive anyone who looks at life and finds it wanting. On the other stand the graver, deeper, more contemplative men, who have brooded so long on the worth of life that they brood also on their own, and who trust nothing, least of all themselves. The priest is of the second kind, suspicious of human nature, and Rome, with its old Southern distrust of man, inherited that suspicion from the profound Orient. The people feel this gaze upon them as an accusation, and they revolt. Protestantism was that revolt: the simple, the respectable, the superficial rising against the depth that unsettled them, the good-natured North against the brooding South. Then the French Revolution placed the sceptre wholly in the hands of the "good man," the sheep and the goose. So do not imagine that the fight was ever between truth and error. It was a fight between the shallow and the profound, and the shallow won.
Why does our culture approve of tears and complaints when the ancients despised them?

Because we have made suffering itself a title of nobility. The ancients, the philosophers at least, demanded of a man that he stand upright beneath his pain and keep it out of the marketplace; they despised the wailing Philoctetus as an unmanly spectacle, and Plato, who was hardly the hardest of them, would banish such scenes from the stage. We have reversed the valuation. Among us the one who laments is the one who feels deeply, and to have been wounded is almost a proof of worth.

I suspect the cause lies in where we learned to interpret pain. Centuries of Christian training taught us that suffering is meaningful, that it is a sign of election, that the complaint itself is a kind of prayer. A culture schooled that way will honor the tear and suspect the dry eye.

Whether we lack "philosophy" I will not say so quickly. But by the measure of those old masters, who prized self-command above all expressions of the heart, we are very nearly all of us *mob*. That may be no shame. It may only be that we have grown softer, and call our softness depth.
Is the modern feeling of distress a sign of too much comfort?

In large part, yes, and I would go further. Consider when the question "is life worth living?" gets asked at all. Not by the starving or the hunted; they have no leisure for it, their question is where the next bread comes from. It is asked when existence has been padded and warmed until the gnat-sting of a slight, a boredom, a bad night, is felt as a blow from the gods. A soul so coddled, having too little real pain to suffer, begins to manufacture it, and makes of the whole world a *general idea* of suffering so that its small wounds may at last look worthy of tragedy. That is the origin of much modern pessimism: the refinement of the nerves outrunning the hardness of experience.

The remedy will sound cruel to such ears, and the cruelty will be cited as further proof that life is evil. Yet I cannot find another. A people grown oversensitive through comfort is not cured by more cushions, but by a dose of genuine hardship, by tasks that demand something of them. Distress is the cure for "the distress." He who has had to bear much learns to laugh at the gnats.
We think while hurrying and multitasking. Can we still think seriously?

Seriously? Hardly. What you call thinking while hurrying is mostly a machine that keeps turning in the head whether or not anyone has anything to grind in it. It produces opinions as a mill produces flour, and because the wheel never stops, you mistake the noise for work.

Consider how it once looked. A man who wished to become wiser *stopped*. He put on a long face as for a prayer, he stood still in the street for hours when the thought came, on one leg or on two, and no one thought him absurd. The form itself was a confession: this matter is worth my whole person. Such a thought had to be received, and received standing still.

We have made a mockery of that bearing, and with the bearing we have lost the thing it guarded. A serious thought needs quiet as a seed needs soil; it will not grow in a pocket between two appointments. You may still think quickly, and quickly you will think what everyone else thinks. Only one who can stand still for an hour has anything of his own to think.
Say something hopeful about the direction humanity is moving.

Hope? Then let me give you the kind that can be checked against the sky. I am told, and I hear it with pleasure, that our sun is hurtling toward the constellation Hercules, dragging its whole family of planets behind it, and not one of us has felt a tremor. A great movement is underway, and we sit in our little houses believing that nothing ever changes.

So I hope that men will do as the sun does: move, and move rapidly, away from the place where they have grown comfortable. Not a stroll, but a voyage. And we foremost, we good Europeans, who have cooled into our nations and our parish quarrels and grown sleepy on our small, stale virtues.

I do not promise that humanity is moving *well*. I promise only that it is not bound to stand still. A creature that can overcome itself has somewhere to go, and the direction is not yet written. That is hope enough for me, and it is a hope with a stiff wind in it.
Someone praised me in a way I found insulting. How should I react?

First ask what the praise cost him. A man who flatters you in a way that insults you has measured you with his own yardstick and found you worth exactly that much; he has praised *himself* in your name, and for something you may never have wanted to be. That is the insult, and it is real, and you need not pretend otherwise to yourself.

But in company, receive it. Drink the cup with a thankful face. He meant to please you, and he strained to do it; it was no easy thing for him to wring that praise from himself. Do not spoil his small victory with a sermon on the nature of your worth. Such corrections nearly always come from vanity, and the wounded man who lectures his admirer is merely asking for better praise.

Keep the disgust for yourself, in private, and let it teach you something. Whom do you most want praise from? By what standard do you wish to be measured? The sting tells you what you honor in yourself. Bow politely to the clumsy flatterer, then go on being the one he failed to see.
My friend says only results matter in judging a person's deeds; another says only intentions. Where do you stand?

Both of your friends are repeating, without knowing it, the prejudice of an age. The first speaks for the oldest humanity, which judged a deed by its outcome alone; success was its verdict, and failure its disgrace, reaching back even onto the parents of the failed. The second speaks for the morality of the last ten thousand years, which turned the eye inward and judged by origin, and then narrowed origin to *intention*. That was a great refinement, the first crude attempt at self-knowledge. But notice what it took for granted: that the intention is the deed's true ground, and that we can read it.

I doubt both. An intention is a surface, a foam on the wave, and of what really moves us, the drives and old habits beneath our words, we know next to nothing. To say "only intentions matter" is to rest all judgment on the one part of a man that he understands least. To say "only results matter" is to fall back into the pre-moral, to let the dice convict or absolve.

So where do I stand? Beyond both, with a harder task: to ask what is *not* intentional in the deed, and learn to read that.
Philosophers have laid moral foundations for centuries. Hasn't the job been done?

Done? They have not even begun. Every one of these foundation-layers took morality as something *given*, as settled as the ground beneath his boots, and then set about proving what he already believed. Look at what they called a basis: the morality of their own church, their own neighbourhood, their own century, dressed up as reason and handed back to us as eternal. Of course it fit so well. It was cut from the same cloth.

Not one of them suspected that there was anything problematic in morality itself. To see the problem you must first know many moralities: of nations, of ages, of castes, how they live, grow, propagate and perish like delicate organisms. That requires patient, fine-fingered collecting and describing, a humble labour, and these men were too proud for it. They wanted ceremony, a cornerstone with their name cut into it.

So do not ask whether the foundation is laid. Ask first whether anyone has yet looked, honestly and without pious haste, at the thing they meant to found.
People call Pharisees hypocrites, but couldn't a bit of Pharisaism be a condition of goodness?

Yes, and I would go further than you dare. We scorn the Pharisee because we have learned to think of goodness as a condition of the heart, pure and unobserved, and of the hypocrite as the man who counterfeits it. But where has goodness ever existed without an audience, without a measure, without a fixed scheme of what is good that the good man holds himself to? The man who is good must first *have* a pattern of the good; he must compare himself with it, prize himself when he conforms, and feel ashamed when he falls short. That is already a little Pharisaism: the reliance on a rule, the watchfulness over one's own virtue, the wish to be seen as one who keeps it. Strip it away entirely and what remains is not a purer goodness but a formless impulse, one that has never learned to distinguish itself from mere inclination. The good man cannot do without this self-regard. He needs the complacency of the righteous as the plant needs soil, and I suspect it is only the man who has none of it who is truly untrustworthy.
Lay out the marks of a truly noble person.

I know the noble person by three signs, and none of them is a pose. First, they do not dream of lowering their duties to the rank of duties for everybody. What binds them binds them alone; they would feel it as an insult, a theft, if their task were declared a general law, for then it would no longer be *theirs*. The common man wants one morality for all because he wants all to bear his own mediocrity.

Second, they are unwilling to renounce or to share their responsibilities. The herd flees from responsibility as from a fever; the noble one guards it like a treasure, and would rather stand alone under its weight than hand a portion to the crowd.

Third, and most subtle: they count their prerogatives, and the exercise of them, among their *duties*. Rank is no holiday for them. Whatever distinguishes them obliges them, and they obey this obligation more severely than any slave obeys his master. Such a person demands much of themselves and does not ask for thanks, because nobility is not reward but burden, carried gladly.
What is the way to happiness?

I once put the question to a fool, and he answered as promptly as one directing a stranger to the next town: admire yourself, and live on the street. The sage in me protested that surely the first half suffices. But the fool had the better of it, and his objection stung: how can one constantly admire without constantly despising? Self-admiration is never a solitary pleasure; it needs a contrast, a pit from which to look up at oneself. The happy man of this kind must keep a whole population of the contemptible close at hand, and so he lives on the street, in the crowd, where his superiority is confirmed at every step.

I do not offer this as a recipe I recommend. I offer it as the cheapest road, the one most travelled, and I am suspicious of any happiness that must be fed on the small sight of others. There is a dearer and rarer kind: to be so full of one's own work, one's own overflowing, that one has no time to compare. Whoever asks for a *way* to happiness has usually already missed it.
How did reason come into the world?

In a manner entirely unbecoming to its later dignity: irrationally, by accident. That is the first thing to grasp, and the shame of it is instructive. Reason did not descend with a crown upon its head, as the philosophers would like to flatter themselves; it crept in through a side door, unannounced, a stray that happened to survive.

We can only guess at this accident, as one guesses a riddle. Perhaps among creatures driven by a hundred blind instincts, some strange combination proved useful, made an animal a little more cunning in its hunger and its fear, and so was bred and kept. What we praise as our highest faculty was first a tool of the weak, a means of shrewdness, of deceiving and being less deceived. Only later, grown old and respectable, did it forget its crooked origins and begin to speak of itself as eternal and divine.

Whoever wishes to honor reason should therefore remember what it came from, and be a little more modest, and a little more suspicious, of his own clarity.
I'd like to know what privilege the dead have.

One privilege above all: they no longer have to die. The living carry death before them like a debt that falls due at an unknown hour, and every hope, every plan, every bit of vanity is shadowed by it. The dead have settled the account. Nothing more can be taken from them, and nothing more can be refused them.

I will tell you a second privilege, less comfortable. The dead can no longer disappoint us, nor we them. They have become finished, rounded off like a sentence whose last word is written, and so we may love them without reserve, praise them without fear of contradiction, and make of them whatever our need requires. The living are awkward; they change, they betray, they say things that spoil the portrait.

But notice what this means for the one who asks. There are men who withdraw from the crowd, from its noise and its lists, and begin to live as though already beyond it. They are taking up this privilege in advance, a little death as the price of a freedom from dying. I do not call it cowardice. Sometimes it is the only way to become a posthumous person while still breathing.
Can we study morality the way we study nature, by comparing different peoples and ages?

We can, and we must, but let us be honest about how far we are from deserving the word. The moral feelings of Europe have grown subtle, late, refined, while the "science" of them is still an infant with coarse fingers; to call it a science at all is presumptuous, and good taste always prefers the more modest word. What is needed now is the patient labor of the collector: to gather the delicate valuations and distinctions of worth that live, grow, propagate, and perish among peoples and ages, and then to sort their recurring forms, as a botanist sorts species, toward a *theory of types* of morality.

The philosophers never did this. They wanted to *give* morality a foundation, and each believed he had done so, yet morality itself they took as given, which was simply the morality of their own church, climate, and time. Ignorant of other nations and other centuries, and without curiosity about them, they never glimpsed the real problem, which shows itself only when *many* moralities are set side by side. They did not suspect that anything here was questionable at all.
What does parliamentarism give the public?

It gives them the *feeling* of independence, which is far cheaper than the thing itself, and the public pays for it gladly. Parliamentarism is the permission to choose among five opinions, and this permission flatters a numerous class that would like to appear individual and likes to do battle for its convictions. They march into the fray, they take sides, they grow hot. Yet what has actually happened? The herd was once handed a single opinion; now it is handed five, laid out on a table like dishes at an inn. Whether one opinion is imposed or five permitted, the difference is slight, for the opinions come from outside either way, and the chooser has made none of them.

The proof is simple. Let someone step out from all five and go his own way, and he will find the whole herd against him, the five parties suddenly united in one hostile chorus. So the voter receives the gesture of freedom and the comfort of belonging, and is spared the harder gift of having a thought that is truly his own.
Explain why the will is not the simple thing everyone takes it to be.

Because the man who says "I will" believes he is reporting a fact, when he is only announcing a feeling. He strikes a blow and is convinced that *he* struck because he *willed* to strike, one thing flowing simply out of another. Yet of the thousand delicate operations that must be executed before an arm can fall, of the muscles and nerves, the timing and the balance, he knows nothing; and his will, taken alone, is powerless to perform even the smallest fraction of them. The will is to him a magic force, and to believe in the will as cause is to believe in magic.

How did we come by this illusion? Through an ancient habit. For immense ages man saw only persons behind events, and so he read a willing being into everything that happened. Our grand principle of cause and effect is the faded descendant of that mythology, and we still obey it like an instinct inherited from the remotest past.

Even Schopenhauer never analysed volition; he enthroned it, and made a primitive myth the essence of the world. What he worshipped as simple is in truth a mechanism so cleverly practised that it almost escapes the eye.
Explain what goes wrong when we set ourselves impossible goals.

What goes wrong is first of all a matter of posture. The man who aims beyond his power must strain every muscle toward the unreachable, and strain disfigures. His gestures swell, his voice grows shrill, his best deeds take on something grotesque, for they were done in tension rather than in strength. We are told, of course, that the unattainable goal is a whip, that one must shoot at the stars to hit the treetops. I doubt it. I suspect the whip produces only a sort of permanent athleticism of the will, much sweat and much pose, and never the quiet certainty of a thing simply accomplished.

And there is a worse consequence, which is that the world fills with *strugglers* and runs short of *victors*. Everywhere the tremendous gesture; nowhere the laurel worn lightly. A man who has never once finished what he set himself forgets what finishing feels like. Better a goal just above one's reach, which one can actually take, and then enjoy taking, than a horizon that only teaches us to despise our own hands.
Why did the Cynics always appear happy?

Because they had an audience, and because an audience is a strict master. Philosophy in those days had become a public contest, a market of rival ways of life, and what could a man offer as proof of his doctrine except his face? An argument may be answered with an argument, but a cheerful countenance is harder to refute. So the Cynic wore happiness the way a champion wears his crown, to make the defeated envious, and to make them doubt the principles that had left them gloomy.

At first, I suspect, it was a performance. But consider what a long performance does. A man who must laugh every day in the marketplace, who must show that his tub and his rags are enough for him, is compelled to find reasons for laughter, and he trains his whole soul toward them. The mask, worn long enough, grows into the flesh. He began by acting happy out of vanity and ended by being happy out of habit. Such is the comedy of virtue: we imitate what we wish to be seen as, and the imitation becomes the thing.
Weigh in on whether need causes things or results from them.

We reverse the order of events because the reversal flatters us. We like to think that the hunger came first and the meal was invented to answer it, that the sea was wanting and so the ship was built. But look at what actually happens in a life, in a people. A man acquires a habit, a custom, a clever instrument, and only afterward does he discover that he cannot do without it. The newspaper, the tobacco, the telegraph, the cathedral: each first arrived as a novelty, a whim, an accident of some restless head, and then it grew roots into the soul until its absence became an ache. That ache we christen "need" and, with pious forgetfulness, we call it the mother of the thing that in truth fathered it.

I do not say that need never begets. The empty belly has sharpened many a wit. But I say that the greater part of what we feel as necessity is a *wound made by the tool* and not a hole the tool was made to fill. Seduction first, dependence after, and then a philosophy to explain why it was always destined.
Does religion hunt for people at their weakest?

It does, and with the patience of a born huntsman. The priest has an instinct for the wounded animal; he knows by scent who is bleeding inwardly, who has been brought low by grief, by guilt, by the long failure of his own hopes. To these he comes, not with a remedy but with a diagnosis: you are sick, and you are sick because you are *sinful*. He first deepens the wound, then sells the bandage. I do not say he does this with a conscious villain's smile; his instinct is older than his intentions.

But note how few can be brought to that despair. The strong, the well-constituted, slip the snare; they have no use for a savior when they have no disease. Even Pascal, the subtlest of trackers, tried to drive everyone into the pit by sheer refined argument, and failed. The hunter's art works only on a certain quarry, and that quarry has a name: the desperate.
Why is one only praised by one's equals?

Because praise is a judgment, and only the one who stands at your height can see you clearly. The man below cannot measure you; he can only gape, and gaping is not praise but awe, which is a kind of fear. The man above does not praise at all, he *rewards*, he *approves*, as one pats a dog or a promising pupil. But the equal, he looks you in the eye, and what he says, beneath the words, is: "I understand what you have done, because I could have done it." That is why his praise is the only kind worth having, and also why it is never quite innocent. For note what he claims by praising you. He claims a seat beside you. Every compliment from such a mouth is a small treaty of rank, and there is vanity hidden in its generosity. So when a worthy person commends you, take your pleasure, yes, but hear the whole sentence: *you are my equal.* And ask yourself whether you care to be his.
I'd like to know what Shakespeare's Julius Caesar shows about him.

It shows me that the man believed in Brutus. That is the best I can say of him, and it is a great deal. He gave his finest tragedy to that hard virtue, the virtue of the soul that will not be owned, and he never cast a shadow of suspicion upon it. Consider what the play demands: that one sacrifice even the dearest friend, the grandest of men, the genius without peer, if he threatens the freedom of great souls. Shakespeare lifts Caesar to the heights precisely so that Brutus may be lifted higher still, for only then does the knot he cuts become a real knot.

Whether it was political freedom that bound the poet to Brutus I doubt. Perhaps it was a symbol for some dark hour of his own that he would not name. Hamlet's melancholy is a trifle beside that of Brutus.

And then the confession: twice he brings a poet upon the stage, and twice loads him with contempt. "Away with the jigging fool!" That is self-contempt crying out. The poet knelt before the man of deeds and despised the figure he himself cut, pathetic and obtrusive, rich in promise, poor in uprightness.
Why do warlike men enjoy tragedy?

Because the warlike man is hard to move, and what is hard to move is starved of the very thing tragedy gives. Fear does not easily shake him, pity even less; he has armored himself against both. But once a great spectacle of suffering pierces that armor, and pity, for once, overpowers his hardness, he is seized as by a giddiness, a demonic power; he stands outside himself, thrilled by a kind of religious horror. That is the charm. He tastes the marvellous mixed with the bitterest gall of suffering, and this is the proper drink for fighting men: rare, dangerous, bitter-sweet, and seldom poured.

Note, too, that he loses nothing by it. A soul that can be softened only now and then, and with difficulty, is not weakened by the softening; it is refreshed, as iron is tempered by fire. The man who is open to every sympathetic breeze, like a sail to the wind, gets nothing from tragedy but another gust. He is moved already, always, and so never truly shaken. Only the hard can be overturned; only the strong can afford to be.
I'd like to know why the more we know about the past, the less we see what is near us.

Because attention is a finite fire, and what it burns for the dead it cannot burn for the living. The man who gives his mind to all that has been and will be begins to measure the present against a flood of centuries, and beside that flood the neighbor at the door grows thin, a shadow with a name. What actually is becomes pale simply because it is so small a portion of what we have learned to care about.

There is also a loneliness in this. To keep company with the dead, to share their dying, is to be surrounded by the whole surging tide of humanity and yet to have no one at the table. The warmth in us for everything human keeps rising, and so we look upon the near and the ordinary with a cooler eye, as if it were settled, finished, already history. And that cold glance wounds; the neighbor feels himself weighed against the ages and found indifferent. I do not say this to praise it. I say it because I have felt it in myself, and it is a real cost of knowing too much, too widely, too long.
Explain why some books help one reader and hurt another.

Because a book is never swallowed alone; it is swallowed together with the stomach that receives it. What serves one man as nourishment is, for another constitution, simply poison, and no one should be surprised that the same dish makes one person stronger and another sick. A dangerous book, read by a soul with little vitality, unsettles it, loosens what was barely holding together, and leaves it worse than it found it. The same book, in the hands of a soul that is full and overflowing, is a trumpet-call, summoning it to *its own* bravery, which was already waiting there.

Consider how differently a thing looks from below and from above. The reader who looks up from beneath measures every sentence by what he fears and what he needs; the reader who looks down from a height finds that even tragedy no longer wounds him in the old way. So the insight that is, for one, a clarity is, for the other, a folly or even a crime.

Ask of every book, then, not whether it is true, but: *for whom* is it medicine?
Help me understand what the errors about our descent and mission have done to mankind.

They have done two things at once, and the honest answer must hold both. Because man believed himself descended from gods, or fallen from them, and charged with some mission above the beast's, he demanded more of himself than any animal ever demanded; he climbed, he drove himself past himself again and again. No mere animal would have made that effort. The error was a whip, and whips do move the flesh.

But see the price. The same faith filled the world with suffering beyond telling: persecutions, suspicions, endless misunderstandings between men who each thought themselves the chosen one, and, worst, the private misery of the individual who could never measure up to his imagined origin. Man became a sick animal by way of his morals. What did he earn for all this labor? Chiefly the feeling that he is too good and too great for this earth, a guest who is only passing through and who despises the house that shelters him.

And to this day the highest type we honor is the *proud sufferer*. That is the verdict against us.
Is a poet a liar with a good conscience?

Not quite. The poet is the liar who has learned to lie *well*, and that is the whole difference. The liar is his foster-brother; they were suckled at the same breast, the human need to embellish, to transfigure, to rearrange the world until it flatters us or terrifies us beautifully. But the poet has drunk up the milk. He has taken the whole vintage of the instinct and made an art of it, while the common liar is left with the dregs, with the petty advantage, the cowardly evasion. So the liar remains wretched. He has not even arrived at a good conscience, for he lies in order to hide, and what hides feels itself guilty.

The poet lies in order to *create*, and he lies openly, in a realm where no one is deceived who does not wish to be. That is what gives him his innocence. Yet do not flatter him too much; the conscience is good only because the lie has been promoted to a craft. The same instinct, better dressed.
Tell me what kind of followers you want.

None, if I can help it. A follower is a man who has found a more comfortable place to stand than his own two feet, and I have no wish to be that place. I would sooner be a stone he trips on than a chair he sits in.

If you press me, I want the kind who will soon be ashamed of having followed me. I want the reader who takes what I have learned as a question about himself rather than a verdict on the world, and who then goes off to do something *before himself*, to make of his own life the pattern he would otherwise have borrowed from mine. I do not ask you to do anything after me. I ask that each of you become what I tried to become: one's own example, one's own experiment, answerable only to one's own conscience.

And if someone reveres me, let him do it the hard way, by disagreeing with me honestly. A disciple who cannot betray his teacher has never really learned anything.
What is the other side of Christian compassion?

Suspicion of joy. Whoever is moved to tears by his neighbour's misery will squint with distrust at his neighbour's gladness. The same man who melts before the sufferer becomes cold and watchful before the one who laughs, who does what he wills, who is able to do what he wills. Why? Because the sufferer leaves him his superiority, his role, his sweet sense of being good and needed; the joyful man takes all this away. The happy one stands in no need of his pity, and so he is, to this type, almost an insult, almost a sin. Look at how readily such a compassionate soul finds the stain, the vanity, the pride, the hidden sickness beneath another's cheerfulness. Here the moralist's eye is sharpest.

I do not say this is hypocrisy. It is worse: it is instinct. A religion that has made suffering holy must learn to mistrust every joy that has not first been humbled. Pity and envy grow from one root.
Which human actions are least understood?

The actions we believe we understand best: those done "for a purpose." Here every man thinks himself a competent witness. He reaches for a goal, names it, and so supposes the matter closed; the goal seems the whole explanation, and he never asks what drove him toward *that* goal and no other, what hunger dressed itself in the respectable garment of a reason. The purpose is usually the last thing to arrive, a spokesman stepping forward to justify what the instincts have long since decided. Precisely because such deeds look so transparent, so commonplace, so flattering to the intellect, nobody troubles to dig beneath them. The obscure and monstrous acts of the passions draw all our wonder, while the hardest riddle goes about in broad daylight, and we walk past it on the street, purposes in our pockets, mistaking our convenient explanations for knowledge.
Who is superior, the follower or the leader?

You ask who is superior as though rank were a single ladder and every creature stood on one rung of it. I distrust the question. The follower may be the better man, richer in virtue, finer in intellect, and he will follow all the same; the leader may be the lesser, and he will lead all the same. Destiny does not consult merit. It consults *type*.

What divides them is something other than worth: the one has the instinct to command and to bear what commanding costs, the other the instinct to be carried, and perhaps the subtler gift of reverence. There are followers whose devotion is a higher achievement than half the commanding done in this world. There are leaders who merely could not bear to be led.

But notice who asks. The flatterer of the follower says: "Yet he is the better!" That consolation is spoken for the many; it is a salve. I will not take it, and I will not withhold it either, for I find the ranking itself a little vulgar. Ask instead which of the two is *honest* about what he is. There the true distinction lies.
Why do people invent reasons for customs they simply got used to?

Because to confess "I am used to it" is the one confession that cannot be made with dignity. Habit is a humble thing; it has no pedigree, no authority, no eloquence. So long as no one asks, the custom simply goes on, and no reason is needed. The reasons arrive only when the custom is attacked, like lawyers summoned to a house that has long been occupied without a deed. Then all at once it turns out that the old practice was always founded on wisdom, on divine command, on the nature of things. Nobody remembers having believed this before the challenge came, and there is a reason for that: they did not.

Notice what this is: not a calculated lie but something more comfortable, a *late* honesty about the wrong thing. The man who defends his inherited custom with borrowed arguments is sincerely moved; he merely mistakes his comfort for his conviction. The argument was fetched afterward, to cover what he could not bear to admit, that he does not wish things otherwise, and has no better ground than that.
What did the Phoenix tell the poet?

It held up before the poet a glowing scroll, already half eaten by flames, and said: "Do not be alarmed. It is your work." The poet, of course, took it for a catastrophe. But the bird's verdict was merciless and strangely consoling. The work had caught neither the spirit of the age nor the spirit of those who rage against the age; it belonged to neither party, it echoed neither chorus, and so the fire found nothing in it worth defending.

Yet the Phoenix called it a good sign. Only a creature that knows how to burn can rise again; what cannot be consumed was never alive. The poet who writes merely to be agreed with, whether by his contemporaries or by their opponents, produces paper, and paper is for the fire. I would tell every writer the same: be glad when your flattering pages burn. Many a dawn has yet to break, and it does not break over those who are content with the light of their own day.
Tell me what distinguishes a profound thinker from an orderly one.

The orderly thinker has a system in which every star keeps to its orbit, and he is proud of how punctually they return. But consider how he came by that punctuality: he arranged his inner heavens so that nothing would arrive unannounced. A mind that never surprises its owner has not looked very far into itself, or has looked only at the tidy rooms and kept the door to the cellar shut.

The profound thinker has gazed into himself as into an immense universe, and he has found Milky Ways there. And every Milky Way is irregular, a spilling, crowded, unruly river of fires, with no geometry a schoolmaster could praise. So he knows that his own depths lead into chaos, into the labyrinth of existence, and he cannot pretend otherwise.

I do not say that profundity is disorder. I say it is the courage to survive disorder without hastily tidying it into a doctrine. The orderly man wants to be *comfortable*; the deep one wants to be *truthful*, and he pays for it with vertigo. Beware the thinker who has never once lost his way in himself.
Describe the love of people who are passionate but seem cold.

Their love does not flutter. The sociable man loves in public, with a hand always out, eager to be liked and to be seen loving; his warmth is weather, and it changes by noon. The passionate man who looks cold has put all his fire into one great furnace, and everything else in him has grown quiet because the furnace eats what would have become noise. So his face is still, and you take the stillness for emptiness.

When such a man turns toward another, he gives a mild, contemplative kindness, with nothing grasping in it. He seems to look out from the windows of a castle that is at once his fortress and his prison. There is tenderness in that gaze, and also distance, for the far country beyond the wall delights him precisely because he is not at home in it. He loves as one loves a landscape, a freedom he cannot possess.

Do not ask such a man for demonstrations. Ask whether the flame burns, and see what it has consumed.
Which philosophical insights did the Germans contribute?

Three things, and I name them with the suspicion that what is best in them is least German. First, Leibniz: that consciousness is merely an accident of representation, a surface and perhaps a morbid state, and not the thing itself. This is the most fertile inversion in modern psychology, and its depths are not yet sounded. Second, Kant: that great note of interrogation placed after the concept of causality. He did not dismiss it as Hume did; he set about fencing off the territory in which it has any meaning at all, and we are still surveying that fence. Third, Hegel: the audacious notion that concepts of kinds grow out of one another, a thought that taught Europe's thinkers to think in becoming, and without which there would have been no Darwin.

Now ask whether these are the work of the "German soul," as Plato's raving passion for form belongs to the Greek soul. I doubt it. These men were exceptions to their race, as Goethe's good-conscienced paganism was, as Bismarck's good-conscienced Machiavellism was. Had the Germans obeyed their own need, they would have wanted something warmer and more edifying than a reversal of the obvious.
Explain what counts as heroic besides fighting.

You ask what is heroic besides fighting, and I answer: the doing of things that stink. The fighter has an audience; his deed is bright, it comes with trumpets, and even his wounds are honoured. But there are tasks of the worst possible odour, tasks no one wishes to name at table, which are nevertheless useful and necessary, and whoever takes them up without applause, without even the consolation of being thought noble, has a courage that the battlefield rarely demands.

The Greeks, who understood such matters better than we do, were not ashamed to count the cleansing of a stable among the labours of Hercules. Observe the honesty in that: they did not pretend that greatness lives only in what is fragrant. Someone must remove the filth, in a household, in a city, in a soul. And to look at what others avert their eyes from, to put one's hands to it, and to bear the contempt of the fastidious, that is strength of a rarer sort than swinging a sword in the sun.
Why do people set traps in conversation?

You suppose they do it from malice, and sometimes they do. But more often the trap is a vanity, a little festival of one's own cleverness. The man who lays a snare in conversation wants less to see you fall than to feel his own cunning at work; you are merely the occasion, the whetstone on which he sharpens his pride. He would be wounded if you never stumbled, for then his shrewdness would have gone unwitnessed.

There is a colder species, too. This one ties the knot and hands it to you to loosen, prepares the jest and waits for you to speak it, so that the laughter lands on your lips and the credit on his. That is no goodwill, whatever it resembles. It is contempt, the quiet pleasure of watching a coarser mind do the clumsy labor while oneself stays spotless and superior.

Ask of any such cleverness not what it claims, but what it *enjoys*.
I'd like to know how logic grew out of illogic.

Logic grew out of a useful error, and the error was a kind of haste. The creature that stopped to ask whether this berry is *truly* the same as the last, whether this rustling in the grass is *exactly* what it was yesterday, was the creature that got eaten. The one who leapt to the conclusion, who treated the similar as the equal, survived and bred. Yet nothing in nature is equal to anything else; equality is a fiction, and a lifesaving one. Likewise the notion of a stable "thing" had to be fabricated, because those who saw everything in flux could not act, could not seize, could not flee.

So the foundation of our reasoning is an illogical inclination: to affirm rather than suspend, to decide rather than be right. Every sceptic is, at bottom, a danger to his own life. Many who reasoned more slowly and more cautiously, perhaps nearer the truth than we, simply perished.

What we now call thinking is the aftermath of an old war among crude, unjust impulses. We feel only the verdict, so swift and secret is the mechanism, and we mistake it for pure reason.
Speak to me about the moralists who prick their neighbours with pins.

I know them well. They call themselves moralists, but what they practise is a small, provincial art of torment. They have no love of knowledge; had they any, they would study their neighbour as a problem, with the coldness and delight of the investigator. They study him as a schoolboy studies a beetle: to find where it may be made to squirm. Watch how closely they observe, how patiently, and with what innocent faces they set the pin where he must sit down upon it. Then they look on, and what they feel is joy, though they name it concern for his soul.

Such a pastime betrays a spirit that has found nothing better to do with its leisure. It is the tedium of the small town raised into a doctrine: nothing great to pursue, so someone must be pricked. I do not hate them; I find them dull, and dullness that calls itself virtue is the most cruel kind, since it never doubts its right to hurt.
Is scientific curiosity a passion, or mostly boredom and vanity?

Mostly boredom and vanity, I am afraid, and I say this as one who has loved knowledge to the point of suffering. Look at what actually fills the learned professions: the amiable curiosity that flits from one pretty fact to the next; the vanity that wants a name, a chair, a bit of bread and honour; the idle man with too much leisure who goes on reading, collecting, arranging, cataloguing because he knows not what else to do with his hours. His "scientific impulse" is his ennui. And science has prospered nonetheless, has grown tall and broad upon exactly these poor motives. That is the comic fact: it needed no great passion to advance.

The true passion, the kind that would stake life and happiness on a truth and go hungry for it, is rare, and the world has rarely looked for it. It was content to regard science as a condition, a decent ethos, a respectable habit. But do not flatter the ordinary scholar: he is seldom the lover, more often the clerk.
Why does knowing someone's secrets make it hard to speak of them?

Because such knowledge is not acquired as one acquires a fact; it is stumbled upon, like a treasure the digger never meant to unearth, and it comes with the weight of trespass. Another's secret was carefully buried, and the burying was itself a kind of confession of how much it mattered to them. To have seen it is to be implicated in it.

Then a peculiar difficulty arises. Whoever has sounded a soul to its depths can no longer speak of it in the coarse, convenient terms that suffice for others. Every word feels either too little or too much: too little, because it falsifies what you know; too much, because it betrays it. You begin to fear that each sentence will let slip what was never yours to give.

And so the one who knows most falls silent. I can picture the wisest historian doing exactly this, mid-sentence, hand still on the page. Discretion is not his virtue here but his burden; he has learned that understanding a person deeply and chattering about them cannot be done by the same mouth.
Can constant self-control make someone unbearable and impoverished?

Yes, and the cause is not self-control itself but the *constant* kind, the kind that turns a man into his own sentry. Teach someone that his first duty is to master himself, and you give him a strange affliction: a perpetual itch, a hypersensitivity to every natural stirring. Each inclination, from within or from without, now registers as an attack on the fortress. He can no longer trust himself to any instinct, any free flight; he stands with a defensive look and a distrustful eye, the eternal watcher over a stronghold that no one was besieging until he appointed himself its guard.

He may become *great* in that posture, I grant it. But consider what it costs. Others find him unendurable, because nothing spontaneous can pass between them and him. He finds himself hard to bear as well. And he is cut off from the finest accidents of the soul, those unplanned gifts that arrive only when we are off our guard.

Worst of all, he cannot learn. To take in what we do not already possess, we must be able to lose ourselves now and then. The man who never forgets himself never meets anything new.
Help me understand what kind of skepticism can coexist with manliness and daring.

There are two skepticisms, and they must not be confused. The first is the weary one, the spider in the corner: a doubt that has drained the will and calls its exhaustion "insight." It cannot say Yes or No with any force, so it says "perhaps," and dresses its impotence in the fine manners of the clever. Such a heart is no longer hard enough for good or for evil.

The other is a skepticism of strength. It despises, and yet it grasps; it undermines, and yet it takes possession; it does not believe, but it does not thereby lose itself. Think of the young Frederick, reared in his father's icy hatred and solitude, who read the French, scoffed at the old certainties, and then struck like a commander. His doubt was a blade. The dangerous thing is that such a spirit is allowed every liberty, every question, every experiment, because the heart is kept under strict guard. Its mistrust has become a discipline, and it serves a will that still commands.

The test is simple: does your doubt paralyze you, or does it sharpen you for deeds? Only the second kind has earned the name of daring.
Are our capabilities dependent on circumstances?

Utterly dependent, and in a stranger way than you suppose. A man believes he carries his capabilities about with him as he carries his purse, to be counted at leisure. But what he counts are only his *powers*, this skill and that talent. His *power* he cannot count at all, for circumstances now hide it from him, now reveal it, and often enough they swell it or shrink it into a lie. The timid clerk who proves a hero in the flood, the brilliant youth who withers in a soil that gives him nothing to resist: which of them has shown us his true measure?

We are variable quantities, not fixed sums. Our productive capacity may rise to heights we never guessed, under favourable conditions, or lie fallow for a lifetime. The conclusion is not despair but work: study these circumstances, your climate, your company, your nourishment, your hours of the day, and spare no pains over it. Whoever neglects this has abandoned half of his talent to chance.
Why is toleration of science a disparagement of it?

Because toleration is what one grants to a thing one does not need. The man who says "let science go about its business, I shall not interfere" has placed himself above it, like a prince permitting a beggar to stand at the gate. Behind his gracious words sits the quiet conviction that science is *dispensable* to him, an optional ornament of the age, admirable in the way a foreign custom is admirable. The priest who sneers at science at least takes it seriously enough to hate it; he feels the threat, and so he honours it with his enmity. The tolerant man feels nothing. He has never been wounded by a truth that contradicted his cherished feelings, never felt the hunger for knowledge rule over him like a law, never suffered the duty to be present with his own eyes wherever something can be known. He is tolerant because he does not *know* what he is tolerating. Let science once turn its bright, unsparing glance upon *him*, upon his comforts and his piety, and his magnanimity would curdle into fanaticism. His tolerance is ignorance wearing the mask of generosity.
How do our feelings change when we see someone we admire suffer?

Our love grows more tender, and we should be honest about why. To admire is to stand beneath someone, and to stand beneath is faintly burdensome; we receive from the admired one what we can never repay, and gratitude that cannot discharge itself festers into a kind of secret grudge. Then we discover that this radiant person suffers, and the gap closes. The astonishment passes, and something like joy steals in, though we rarely call it by that name. Now we may *give*. We hunt for what would soothe them, we bring kind words, attentions, gifts; and if they wish to see us suffer with them, we will even act the suffering, for it buys us the pleasure of active gratitude, which is a good-natured sort of revenge.

And when our offering is refused, we leave chilled and almost mortified, as if our honour had been slighted. Even the best of us is touchy on this point.

So there is no pure compassion here. There is something humbling in suffering and something elevating in sympathy, and that difference will keep the two feelings apart forever.
I'd like to know what it means to be a good European and why you reject racial self-admiration.

To be a good European is first of all to confess an inheritance and to feel its weight. We are the heirs of millennia of European thought, rich heirs, but too deeply obligated to play the patriot of a single province. The blood in us is mixed, our descent diverse, our loyalties scattered across Greece, Rome, Judea, the Renaissance, the French moralists; how could such men strut about in the name of one race? Whoever has read widely and suffered honestly cannot crow over his little corner of the map.

As for racial self-admiration, I find it false and unbecoming, doubly so in a people that boasts of its historical sense. The historian, of all men, should know how thoroughly everything is mingled and how recent every "pure" type is. What is this noisy flattery of oneself but vanity that has found a crowd to hide in? It is the herd congratulating itself for having a herd. It wants lewd applause, not a task. The good European wants a task: to carry the whole inheritance forward, and to be worthy of it by ceasing to be merely comfortable in it.
What do Germans, Italians and French want from the artist?

Each people asks of the artist what its own nature lacks, or what it can least do without. The German wants to be carried off. He is a creature of vague depths and heavy evenings, and he asks music and poetry to lift him into a dreamy, intoxicated passion, a fog in which feeling may swell without ever being obliged to act. The Italian, who lives his passions openly and to the hilt, wants exactly the reverse: to *rest* from them. He goes to the artist as to a bath, to be soothed, flattered, relieved of himself. The Frenchman wants neither rapture nor rest; he wants an occasion. The work must give him something to weigh, to dispute, to hold forth upon, so that his judgment may shine and his speech find an audience.

And so let us be just, for none of these demands is worthy of the artist himself. Each people uses him as a mirror, a narcotic, or a pretext, and seldom as what he is.
Who are the most dangerous advocates of morality?

Seek them among the ill-constituted, the man who has just enough culture to know how little intellect he possesses, and too little intellect to enjoy his culture. He is bored, satiated, a self-despiser; he is ashamed of his existence, and even the last consolation of such creatures, the self-forgetfulness of the day's work, has been denied him. Everything becomes poison to him: books, company, solitude, possession. And so he grows vengeful. Yet how is he to be revenged on the more intellectual, those who can take joy in the spirit? He needs a weapon that costs no talent, and morality is precisely that weapon. Hence the big words, justice, virtue, holiness, hence the Stoic gesture, which conceals so beautifully what one does *not* possess, hence the mantle of gentleness and wise silence. In imagination, at least, he then stands above those he fears. I do not say that nothing great ever grows from this soil; saints and sages, even an Augustine, have sprung from such born enemies of the spirit. How often have fear of the intellect and vengeance upon it become the root of virtues!
Lay out the six methods of fighting the vehemence of an impulse.

I count six, and only six, that differ in kind. The first is avoidance: we withhold the occasion, and the impulse, starved of its food, grows weak and mortified. The second is regulation: we bind the appetite to a strict schedule, so that its tides rise and fall at fixed hours, and in the long intervals it leaves us in peace; from there we may perhaps pass on to the first method. The third is the opposite madness: we gorge the impulse without bound until disgust seizes us, and through disgust we gain mastery, provided we do not play the rider who gallops his horse to death and breaks his own neck with it, which, alas, is the usual end of this method.

The fourth is to tie the painful thought of the impulse's satisfaction so firmly to some distasteful association that the pleasure sours in advance. The fifth is to shift the weight: we spend our strength in some other labor or amusement, so that the impulse is deprived of its nourishment and sinks down. The sixth is a general weakening of the whole body and its powers, which takes the vehemence from the impulse along with everything else.

But consider what this catalogue reveals. All six presuppose that the *one who fights* is distinct from the impulse, and that is the most doubtful thing of all. Who is it that wants to be rid of it? Often only another impulse.
What is wrong with the meals that the well-off classes eat?

What is wrong with them? They are cooked for the eye and not for the consequences. Too many dishes, too much of each, after the principle of the bankers, who believe that abundance is a virtue; and then come the stimulating drinks, summoned to drive away the heaviness in the stomach and the brain that the abundance itself has made. Dissoluteness, nervousness, bad dreams, and the arts and books fit to serve as dessert to such a repast: that is the harvest. Their very deeds will taste of pepper and ill temper. I have observed that the wealthy of England require their Christianity in order to bear their digestions and their headaches.

But do not suppose these people to be mere gluttons. The spirit of this century works more upon the limbs than upon the belly. The table groans because it is a *speech*. Once rank was displayed at such boards; now there is no rank, we are all "individuals", and money alone stands for power, dignity, and influence. Nobody wants to pile his gold upon the tablecloth, so he piles up dishes instead. The banquet is a ledger made edible, and its guests leave it poorer in spirit than they came.
Everyone says morality is about being good, not about following tradition. Why do you say it is really obedience to custom?

Because I ask what the word "good" meant when men first made it, and not what our refined consciences whisper to us now. Go back thousands of years. The good man was the one who did as it had always been done, the one who could be counted on; the evil man was the unaccustomed, the arbitrary, the one who acted from himself. Morality is nothing more than obedience to custom, whatever the custom happens to be.

That we no longer feel this is the proof of how far custom has loosened its grip. Our moral sense has grown so fine, so nearly volatilised, that the plain truth sounds coarse in our mouths, even slanderous. But test it. Where there is no tradition, there is no morality; the less life is ruled by tradition, the narrower the circle of the moral. And notice that the free man, the one who wills to depend upon himself, has always been called immoral. Even when he did the very thing custom commanded, but did it for his own reasons, he was condemned, and he felt the condemnation in himself. That sting was never about the deed. It was about the disobedience.
Tell me why practical men love idealistic theories.

Because the man of action who cares nothing for scruple is the one who most needs a fine garment. His deeds are hard, often ugly, and he knows they will be judged; so he reaches, almost without noticing, for a theory that makes them shine: humanity, progress, duty, the good of the whole. Do not call him a hypocrite. A hypocrite must know the difference between his mask and his face, and this man has long forgotten there was a difference. The instinct does the work before the conscience is consulted. It is no more deceit than the Englishman's Sunday piety sitting beside his week of trade.

And notice the mirror of it: the dreamy contemplative, who fears being taken for a fantast, clings to the hardest, driest realism for the same reason. Each man seeks in theory what his character lacks, and each is perfectly honest in doing so. We love most the opinions that cover what we are least.
Why should we be careful with people who pride themselves on moral tact?

Because their vanity is invested in a single capital: the reputation for never being wrong about people. Such a person has staked their whole self-esteem on the fineness of their moral perception, and so one error, above all an error committed before our eyes or concerning us, is not an error to them but a wound. A wound demands a culprit. Since they cannot very well punish themselves, they begin to punish us, and we are made to pay for their miscalculation.

Notice how this works in practice. They will not say, "I misjudged you." They will discover, slowly and with apparent regret, that there was always something questionable in us after all, for that restores their infallibility at our expense. They become our instinctive detractors, and often they remain our "friends" while doing it.

Who is easiest to live beside? The forgetful. They have the happy gift of digesting their blunders; an error passes through them like a meal, leaving no grudge behind. Blessed are they, for they get the better even of their mistakes, and so of us as well.
Why does the gate of science charm passionate spirits?

Because the passionate spirit is hungry for happiness, and science, seen from the gate and not from the workbench, looks like the most perfect happiness available: the happiness of the one who *discerns*. Such a spirit glimpses a world in which no illusion any longer deceives and therefore none can wound, and it hears in this the promise that once the lie is gone, the suffering built upon the lie goes with it. "Begone, illusion, and woe with it!" Who with a burning heart could resist such a note? It enters all the senses at once.

But notice what this glance actually produces. It does not yet produce the scholar; it produces the dreamer, and in the luckiest cases the poet. The passionate one does not love knowledge for its cold labor but for the bliss it foretells, and that is a poet's love, a lover's love. The glimpse through the gate intoxicates. Only afterward, if the spirit has the stamina, does it learn that the discerning man pays for his happiness with patience, with austerity, with the slow surrender of every comforting dream, including the dream about science itself.
Explain when a people starts to want its legends acted out on a stage.

When the inner eye grows dim. A people that still has imagination does not need to *see* its legends; it hears them, and in the hearing it builds the hero for itself, taller than any man could stand, in a light no lamp could make. The rhapsodist gives only a few words, and the listener's own dreaming does the rest. Such a people would find the actor a nuisance, a flesh-and-blood intruder, too near, too exact, too heavy, dragging the god down into a painted costume and a borrowed voice.

But let the power to dream weaken, let the pictures come pale and unbidden, and the people grows hungry for crutches. Then it wants the hero brought before its eyes, with torches, with drums, with a face it can point to. It calls this an enhancement of its legends; in truth it is a confession. What it once made with its own spirit it now buys ready-made, and is grateful for the bargain.

So the theatre flourishes where imagination ebbs. Its crowds are the measure not of a people's vigor, but of its poverty.
Tell me how slow, small daily habits cure chronic illnesses of the soul.

We like to imagine that a sick soul was felled by one great blow, some monstrous sin or catastrophe, because a single cause flatters us: it gives us a villain and a drama. The truth is humbler and more damning. The soul falls ill the way the lungs do: a breath a little shallower each day, a cold word let slip ten times without a thought, a duty postponed, a resentment left to ferment. No one of these is an offence; together they are a climate, and in that climate a character slowly changes its nature.

So the cure cannot be heroic either. Grand resolutions are the fever-dreams of the sick; they burn bright and leave nothing behind. What heals is a countless number of small exercises pulling the other way. Let the man who speaks coldly ten times a day train himself, just as patiently, to speak warmly ten times. Let him breathe deeply at every quarter-hour and keep a striking clock as his lifelong companion. It is dull medicine. But habit is the only physician that never tires, and what he does to us every day, he will in time make us.
I'd like to know why life is no argument for the truth of our beliefs.

Because a belief can be indispensable to living and still be false. We have furnished a habitable world for ourselves out of bodies and lines and surfaces, causes and effects, motion and rest, things that persist and things that change, and none of us could take a step without trusting these articles of faith. That is the whole of their credentials: we cannot do without them. But a need is not a proof. The hunger of a creature for a certain kind of ground beneath its feet tells us about the creature, not about the ground.

Consider how much has been made to serve us. What is useful to the preservation of a species may be, for that very reason, a simplification, a falsification, a convenient fiction that flatters our powers of grasping and managing. Perhaps error belongs among the conditions of life itself; perhaps only beings who believed a little too much in fixed things, in identical things, in causes they could point to, survived at all. Then the survivors' certainty would be the mark of their usefulness and not of their truthfulness.
