So when someone says, "I could not live without believing this," I hear a confession of need, not a demonstration. I grant the need. I only refuse to call it an argument.
Is our need for knowledge really a need for the familiar and fear of the strange?

In large part, yes, and I say it without flattery to myself or to my fellow discerners. I once overheard someone declare that he "knew" me, and I asked what the people mean by the word. The answer was humiliating in its simplicity: to trace what is strange back to something already known. The philosophers, for all their apparatus, have not wanted more. A riddle is solved when it has been made familiar, and what follows is a sigh of relief, the rejoicing of a creature that has regained its footing. Such relief is not the joy of truth. It is the joy of security, and its root is fear.

But notice the error that hides inside this comfort. We suppose the familiar is also the understood, and so we begin our inquiries from the "inner world," from the "facts of consciousness," because these are nearest to us. Yet the accustomed is precisely what we have ceased to see. It is the hardest thing of all to perceive as a problem, to hold at a distance and find strange. The real discerner begins where the comfortable man stops: he makes the near thing foreign.
I feel life was pointless when I'm exhausted. Is that fair?

No, it is not fair; it is a verdict handed down by the wrong judge. Exhaustion is a poor philosopher. It has no appetite for anything, and so it concludes that nothing deserves appetite; it has spent itself, and so it pronounces the spending to have been in vain. But the fault lies with the weariness, not with the day you lived or the life behind it.

Consider when such thoughts come. Rarely in the midst of work, when the hand is busy and the will is stretched; rarely in the midst of delight. They come at the threshold of sleep, when the body sends its bill and the mind, having nothing else to do, examines the ledger with a clerk's sour eye.

So do not believe your tired self about the worth of your life, any more than you would trust a hungry man's opinion of the world's generosity. Rest first. Then ask the question again in the morning, and notice how differently it is answered.
I'd like to know what the Greeks would have said to the geometrician who found nothing proved in Iphigenia.

The Greeks would have answered the geometrician with a smile, and then with a question of their own: *Must a thing be proved before it may move you?* For they were a people who loved the agon, the contest of speech and counter-speech, and in Sophocles the stage becomes a courtroom of the soul. Every step is weighed, every premise laid down, every consequence drawn out with the coldness of a judge who is also a poet. Such a man would not have found the geometrician strange at all. He would have said: "Come to Sophocles, friend; there the ground is laid stone by stone, and you may walk upon it without fear."

That the geometrician was left cold by Iphigenia tells me less about Greek taste than about his own. Here is a man who can only enjoy where his understanding is flattered, who mistakes the feeling of being convinced for the feeling of being enthralled. Yet the Greeks themselves had both: Euripides the pathos, Sophocles the proof. They would have forgiven the man his poverty, and pitied it.
Where do many systems of morals come from?

Largely from vanity, and from a vanity that has learned to speak in the grand style. Consider how the founder of a moral system proceeds. He does best what comes easiest to his nature, and what comes easiest to a nature is for that nature no virtue at all. Yet vanity cannot bear to be ordinary; it wants its natural gift to pass for a hard-won conquest. So the gentle man, who has never been tempted to cruelty, proclaims gentleness the most arduous of all victories; the cold man exalts self-mastery; the man without appetites praises abstinence as a heroic labor. What costs me nothing I lift into a law for all, and call it difficulty, call it duty, so that others may admire me for climbing a mountain I was born on top of.

Thus many a morality is a disguised portrait of its author, a self-flattery mistaken for legislation. And the multitudes who obey it do not suspect that they are being asked to imitate another man's ease as though it were his struggle.
Are my daily habits products of cowardice and laziness or of bravery and invention?

You ask it as though the two sources could be told apart by their results. They cannot, and that is precisely the trouble. The man who rises at the same hour, keeps his accounts, says the same agreeable things to his neighbors, will be praised and found useful whether the habit grew from courage or from a thousand small retreats. The world looks only at the act; it has no eye for the motive, and so it will flatter your cowardice as warmly as your bravery.

Therefore do not consult the world, and do not be satisfied with a quiet conscience either. A quiet conscience is easily had; it asks only that you do what is approved. You must go deeper and test the conscience itself. Take each habit and ask: when did I choose this, and against what? Did I ever once resist it, or did I slip into it because it spared me a decision? A habit that was invented leaves a memory of struggle. One that merely accumulated leaves only comfort. Be suspicious of your comfort.
How can chronic illnesses of the soul be cured?

Do not look for a cure in some great deed or sudden conversion; those are the physicians' theatre. The chronic illness of the soul was never caused by one grand crime against reason. It grew from a thousand small neglects: a cold word flung ten times a day without a thought, a duty postponed, a little cowardice excused, a little contempt indulged. Such habits are like a man who breathes a trifle shallower each day until his lungs, starved of exercise, give way.

So the cure must be made of the same stuff as the disease: countless small exercises in the contrary direction. Whoever wishes to heal his soul must make the least of his habits a matter of conscience. Let him take his deep breath every quarter hour. Let him say the warm word ten times where he used to say the cold one. These remedies are slow and trifling, and that is precisely why the impatient will despise them and stay sick. But what is repeated becomes the soul's very shape. You are never cured once; you are cured daily, in small doses, by your own patient hand.
Why do we arouse suspicion when we tell the truth against our character?

Because those who listen judge the speaker before they weigh the speech. A man's character is the grammar in which his statements are read; when a sentence arrives in a foreign grammar, it sounds wrong, and what sounds wrong is taken for a lie. The miser's generosity, the coward's boldness, the liar's candor: each comes stammering, because the voice has no practice in the thing it says, and the gesture that should accompany it has never been rehearsed. We deliver the truth as an actor delivers a part he does not believe, stiffly, too loudly, with a little too much emphasis. And the listener, who has an instinct finer than his reasoning, feels the awkwardness and concludes: falsehood.

There is a hard lesson in this. We imagine that truth carries its own credentials. It does not. It must be spoken by someone whose whole manner has prepared the ear for it. The liar who speaks truly is believed no more than the honest man who lies badly, since both are simply out of tune with themselves.
Help me understand what consciousness is for, given that most of life goes on without it.

The puzzle dissolves once you stop treating consciousness as the crown of the animal and ask what it was needed for. We could think, feel, will, remember, act, and nothing of it need enter consciousness at all; the greater part of our life already goes on without that mirror. So I do not believe consciousness belongs to the individual's inner life as such. It is a net of communication, spun between one creature and another. Consciousness is needed only where there is need of it, and the need arose from need of one another. A being who must tell his distress, make his wants known, and be understood quickly and finely by his fellows is compelled to become conscious of what he is, to put it into signs, into words, into a language of the herd. The subtlety of consciousness grows with the capacity for communication. Hence what rises into it is always the surface, the shallowed and commonized part of us. Consciousness is not our individuality but what in us is shared.
Help me understand what you think you can and cannot know about yourself.

I know very little about myself, and of that little, the most certain item is precisely this distrust. I have rarely thought about myself with any pleasure, and never with faith in the result. The philosophers speak of "direct knowledge," of the inner eye seeing itself plainly, and I smell a *contradictio in adjecto* in the phrase. Knowledge is an act of interpretation, and what interprets cannot stand outside itself to check the work. What I call my "self" is a crowd of drives, each shouting its verdict, while consciousness, a late and clumsy clerk, writes down whichever shout was loudest and calls it "I think."

What can I know, then? My resistances, perhaps: where I recoil, where I grow warm, what I cannot endure. These are signs, not insights. And I notice a repugnance in me against believing anything definite about myself. Is that an enigma? Probably. But fortunately it is nothing for my own teeth; I am content to let it betray the species I belong to, so long as it does not betray me to myself.
Explain why treating another's suffering as one's own is a double folly.

The folly is doubled because the suffering is doubled, and the judgment with it. Consider first what happens when a misfortune befalls another: I can weigh it soberly. A death, a lost fortune, a slander, each looks to me, at that distance, like an event of a certain size, no more. Only the man it happens to sees it swollen by his vanity, his fear, his trembling self-regard. Now pity commands me to suffer *as he suffers*. What does that mean? That I adopt his exaggerated view of the thing, his distorted perspective, and then, since I am not rid of myself, I go on suffering from my own ego besides. Two sufferers in one skin, each misjudging the matter in his own fashion. A reasonable man, asked to lighten a burden, takes up a second one and calls it virtue.

I recommend the reverse medicine: look upon your own troubles as you would look upon a stranger's, and you will find them wonderfully diminished. That is reason in the service of health.
What is the difference between the Greek and the Christian?

Measure the distance between two pairs of feelings, and you have measured the two peoples. Between envy and friendship the Greek stretched his whole life. He was a man who looked at his neighbor and felt the sting, felt that the other's excellence humiliated him, and who for that very reason made of the sting a school: the contest, the agon, the ostracism that dragged down whoever grew too tall. He did not deny that he envied; he gave envy a place in the city and a god to answer to. And out of this same tension, out of this admission of rivalry, friendship grew as something earned and hard and real.

The Christian lives at the other end, between self-contempt and pride. He is taught to despise himself as a sinner, and from this contempt a peculiar pride is distilled: the pride of the humble, the elect of the abased. The Greek asked, *who is better than I, and how shall I overtake him?* The Christian asks, *how wretched am I, and how shall that wretchedness prove me chosen?* One is a people of the arena, the other of the confessional.
Help me understand what the eyes of an actor and a painter can teach the psychologist.

Each of them has trained one kind of seeing to an extreme, and the psychologist lacks both. The actor knows how the *false* looks. He has practised every gesture before the mirror, so he knows the seam where a borrowed expression joins the body that wears it. He catches the muscle that fails, the grimace that was rehearsed alone and does not fit the whole man, the moment when someone is startled by his own invention and ruins it in his startlement. Turn that eye upon the soul and you learn to tell the virtue that was practised from the virtue that grew, the pity that is posed from the pity that is felt.

The painter teaches the opposite art. He looks at a figure and sees more than is there: he completes it, lights it first this way and then that, sets a contrast beside it until the whole stands forth. So the psychologist must not merely catalogue a soul but *compose* it, try several illuminations upon one character and see which reveals the drive beneath it.

Oh, to have such eyes for the soul! Most who speak of human nature have neither, and call their blindness objectivity.
Help me understand which of our actions we understand least and why.

The actions we understand least are precisely those we believe we understand best: the purposive ones, the deeds done "in order to." Ask a man why he took a wife, a post, a quarrel, and he answers at once, with a purpose in hand like a coin from a pocket. This promptness ought to make us suspicious. Because such actions look so plain, so fit for the daylight of the intellect, no one has thought to dig beneath them. The stated purpose is usually the last and thinnest layer, a story the intellect tells afterward, as flattering to the teller as it is convenient to the listener. Beneath it move the drives, the old fears, the appetites that have no name, the will to feel oneself powerful, and none of these announces itself. The strange, the pathological, the heroic, these we examine eagerly. But the great problems lie about on the highways and byways, trodden by everyone, stooped for by no one. What could be more common than a man pursuing his goal? And what is less known than why he wants it?
I realize most of my values were handed to me. How can I tell which ones are really mine?

Begin by admitting what you have already admitted: most of them were borrowed, and you wore them so long and so carefully that the borrowing became invisible, second nature. We adopt valuations out of fear, because it is safer to pretend they are our own, and pretence practised daily turns into conviction.

So the test is not whether a value *feels* yours. Every inherited value feels that way, since it was poured into you before you could taste it. Ask instead: what does this thing do to *me*, and to no one else? A valuation that is truly your own is an appreciation of something according to the pleasure or displeasure it causes you. Put the value to the body. Where you call something good, does your whole being rise to meet it, or do you merely feel a tightening of the neck, the fear of what would be said if you denied it?

Notice especially your judgments of other people, of their rank and morality and guilt. Most of these were settled in childhood and never reviewed. Reopen them. Whatever survives your own trial, you may call yours; it will be less than you hoped, and far more precious.
Why does a writer not want to be understood by everyone?

Because a book is a door, and a door that admits everyone is merely a hole in the wall. A writer of any taste selects his hearers, and in selecting them he shuts out the others; that shutting-out is no failure of his art but its very purpose. This is where the finer laws of style come from. They keep off, they create distance, they forbid easy access, while at the same time they open the ears of those who are acoustically related to him. To be understood by everybody means to be understood by the common ear, and what that ear can hear at once is precisely what was never worth saying. I do not regard it as an objection to a book that some find it unintelligible; perhaps that was the author's very intention. There are truths of a shy and ticklish sort that must be taken by surprise or else left alone, and these will not be sat upon and brooded over by just anyone. So I write briefly, swiftly, with a cold bath's manner, and whoever cannot follow was not invited.
Tell me why revolutionaries and preachers always talk of unconditional duty.

Because they cannot do their work with an ordinary voice. A man who needs to move crowds, to tear them from their habits, to have no half-success, must speak in thunder, and thunder requires a sky that seems to sanction it. So he speaks of duty, and of duty that admits no "if" and no "unless." Without that unconditional tone he would have no right to his pathos, and he knows it well.

But note the order of things. Before he can make others trust him without reservation, he must first trust himself without reservation, and for that he needs some last, undebatable command, sublime in itself, of which he may feel himself the mere minister and instrument. The categorical imperative serves this need admirably. It turns a hunger for power into an obedience, a wish into a summons from above.

Nor is this only the vice of the loud. The subtler servant, who would be ashamed to be the tool of a prince or a party, wants exactly this: a principle of unconditional *ought* under which he can bow without blushing, and be seen bowing. Hence both kinds hate anyone who questions whether duty must be unconditional.
Explain what lies behind the cry "may the whole world perish."

Behind it lies envy at its summit, envy that has grown so large it can no longer even covet. The ordinary envious man still wants something: the neighbor's house, the rival's fame, the lover's favor. But the man who cries "may the whole world perish!" has found a crueler arithmetic. *Because I cannot have this one thing, nothing shall exist at all.* He cannot raise himself to the height of what he desires, so he demands that everything be dragged down to the level of his lack.

Consider the logic beneath the thunder. He has placed his whole value in a single wish, and when it is denied, his powerlessness becomes unbearable to him. A strong nature, thwarted, says: then I shall try again, or I shall want something else. The weak, wounded one takes revenge on existence itself, because existence is the only thing large enough to bear the blame.

Do not mistake this for a grand pessimism, for a deep insight into the worthlessness of the world. It is a small man's tantrum dressed in cosmic robes. The world did not refuse him; one thing did, and he has made the universe pay for it.
Help me understand what is common to every feeling of happiness.

Two things, I find, whenever I look honestly at my own happiest hours. First, an overflow of feeling, a surplus, so that the heart does not limp along on its ration but spills over its banks. Second, a high-spiritedness of the whole animal, a buoyancy of the blood, as though the body itself had decided to say yes. The two belong together. Put them side by side and you have the fish in the water: it does not struggle, it does not reflect on swimming, it simply feels itself in its element and plays about in it.

Notice what is *absent* from this account. Happiness is not first of all a conclusion, a verdict passed after long thinking that one's affairs are in order. It is a condition of abundance, physiological before it is philosophical. The sufferer from poverty of feeling, the languid, the exhausted, may own every reason for contentment and still not feel it.

Even the pious know this. What else is the exuberance of the devout when their god has "visited" them, but just this surplus of feeling and animal spirit, merely given a holy name?
What do popular morals and popular medicine have in common?

They are twins, and it is an old prejudice that keeps us from seeing it. Each is a practice of *healing* or *correcting*, and each rests on the same crude inference from cause to effect. The old woman who swears that this herb cured her neighbour's fever, and the preacher who swears that vice brings misery and virtue reward, reason alike: one example, then another, piled up until the pile is mistaken for a proof. Nobody controls the conditions, nobody asks what else might have produced the result, nobody thinks to ask whether the supposed cause is a cause at all. And the few who object are no better; their counter-examples are just as careless.

I call both *dangerous and make-believe sciences*. Dangerous, because people act upon them, swallow the remedy, suffer the punishment, inflict it on others. Make-believe, because they have the confidence of knowledge without its discipline. We laugh at the quack, yet we bow to the moralist, though his method is precisely the quack's. It is high time we gave morals the same suspicion we give a dubious medicine.
A young man asks his mother for advice about how to live. What is the wisest thing she could say?

I know of no wiser counsel than the one a French lady once gave her son: *my friend, permit yourself only those follies that will give you great pleasure.* There is a whole culture crystallised in that sentence, and a mother's shrewdness besides.

Consider what she does not say. She does not forbid folly; she knows that a youth without follies is merely a cripple who calls his lameness virtue. Nor does she bless every folly, for there are the paltry, joyless ones, committed from boredom or fear of the neighbours, which cost as much as the grand ones and repay nothing. She asks only for *taste* in one's transgressions: if you must err, err magnificently, err in a way that enlarges your capacity for joy, and leave the gloomy vices to those who can afford no better.

Mark the subtlety, too: the test is pleasure, and that requires a young man to know what truly delights him, which is the hardest knowledge of all. Advice that sends him inward to find it is worth more than every commandment posted on a wall.
What is amor fati?

Amor fati is love of fate: my formula for what is greatness in a human being. It is not merely to bear what is necessary, still less to conceal it, for all idealism in the face of necessity is a lie. It is to love it. I wish to want nothing to be different, not forward, not backward, not in all eternity.

I came upon it at a time of small, private resolutions, when everyone says what he wishes for the new year. Mine was this: to see more and more the necessary in things as the beautiful, and so to be one of those who make things beautiful. I do not want to wage war on the ugly. I do not want to accuse, not even the accusers. Looking aside shall be my only negation.

Understand the cost of it. Whoever says Yes to his joy must also say Yes to the pain, the error, the failure that were its condition, for everything is bound together. To love one's fate is to affirm the whole of it.
Help me understand what a thinker wants from life compared with others.

Consider what the two kinds of people mean by rest. The ordinary man toils at his trade, his family, his worry over money and rank, and when evening comes he wants *out*; meditation, if he ever attempts it, is a door by which he slips away from life, a little death taken in installments. He asks of thought that it should silence him.

The thinker stands in the opposite position. He lives habitually amid the great current of ideas and feelings; even his dreams run with it. For him the current is not the fatigue but the element, as the water is for the fish. What he asks of life is therefore not escape but comfort and peacefulness *within* the stream itself, a settled, unhurried ease in the midst of thinking, the way a good swimmer feels at home where the landsman would drown.

So where the others flee life to recover, he must recover by living more deeply. This is why he so often seems idle to them, and why they so often seem to him to be sleeping with their eyes open.
I'd like to know why you praise leaders more than progress.

Because progress is only a word for movement, and movement by itself proves nothing. A stone rolling downhill also moves. Among Egyptians, among a people frozen in their pyramids and their priestly habits, I might praise it, for there to be moved at all is already something. But here in Europe everyone is in motion and calls it a matter of course, and hardly anyone asks where, or why, or who first had the courage to go there. The crowd is carried; it does not go.

So I praise the one who goes ahead, who is always leaving himself behind, who overcomes what he was yesterday and does not turn around to count his followers. Progress is what the herd is pleased to call its own drifting. The leader is solitary and stops nowhere, because wherever he halts he finds only himself, and the desert is still so wide. I honor the will that opens a path, not the traffic that afterwards fills it.
I'd like to know why we are not believed when we say what goes against our character.

Because a man is believed not for what he says but for the harmony between his words and the face he has worn before others. When the truth we must utter runs against our character, the ear of the listener detects a dissonance, and dissonance means falsehood to him, whatever the facts may be. Nor is he altogether wrong to hear it so. We ourselves utter the unaccustomed truth clumsily: our voice is unpracticed in it, our gesture hesitates, we hurry or over-emphasize, precisely as a liar does who has not rehearsed his lie. Thus the honest confession of a proud man, or the plain boast of a modest one, sounds counterfeit, for what we do badly we seem to be faking. The habitual liar, by contrast, is convincing, because he has made his falsehood into a second nature and speaks it fluently. This is a harsh lesson about credibility: the world trusts ease and consistency rather than truth. If you wish to be believed in what surprises others, you must first have practiced it, and lived it, until it has become your manner.
Is Shakespeare's tragedy a moral warning?

No, and the man who believes it has mistaken both the audience and the poet. Whoever is truly gripped by ambition does not leave *Macbeth* cured; he sits there and relishes the portrait of himself, and the ruin at the end is merely the sharpest spice in the hot drink. Nor is the spectator the only one deceived. Consider how royally Shakespeare lets his criminal run his course once the deed is done! Only from that moment does Macbeth become magnificent, "demoniacally" attractive, a temptation to every kindred nature. A warning would paint the wrongdoer as a knave and the consequences as a ledger of debts. Shakespeare does neither.

What draws the poet is the passion itself, and beyond it the readiness to die that passion breeds, that mood in which the heart clings to life no more than a drop of water clings to the glass. Guilt as the lever of the drama he passes over, as Sophocles did. Do you think *Tristan* preaches against adultery because both lovers perish? That would be turning the poets upside down.
Have all the great passions of mankind been for something non-existent?

Very nearly, yes, and I do not say it to wound them. Look at what men have loved most fiercely: a God who hears, a soul that outlasts the body, a truth behind the veil of appearance, a moral order that repays every deed. Plato panted after the divine essence with as solemn a passion as Schopenhauer felt when he turned away from the world toward the will's denial; each was certain that a road led to something, and each road ends in air. The object was missing, yet the passion was real, and the ceremonies were real, and the blood spilled was real.

That is the strange comedy of it. Non-existence proved no obstacle to devotion; it proved, rather, a spur. A thing one can possess cools quickly. A thing that does not exist can be longed for forever.

But do not conclude the passions themselves were nothing. They were the force of life misreading its own thirst, and a thirst is no illusion, only its imagined spring.
Tell me why some men need avowed enemies.

Because in such men virtue is not an inner possession but a reaction. Their courage, their cheerfulness, even their manliness sleeps until something opposes it, as a flint yields no fire until struck. Take the enemy away and what remains? Often a vacillating, anxious creature who does not know what he wants, since all his wanting was supplied by what he resisted. Napoleon knew this of Murat, the bravest of his horsemen, who charged like a god at the sight of the enemy and, deprived of the enemy, became an irresolute blockhead. Such a man is brave only *against*, never *for*. An avowed enemy gives him a shape, a direction, a reason to stand upright; he borrows his spine from his adversary.

I do not say this with contempt. Most of us are made so, and he is wise who admits it and chooses his enemies well, for we become whatever we are pitted against. But the rarer type carries his resistance within and needs no foe to be brave, having a goal that makes him so.
Why does philosophy try to embellish science?

Because science is hard, and men dislike hard things that refuse to flatter them. Science is dry and slow, it demands patience, exactness, and the renunciation of every pleasant wish; it does not amuse. So someone arrives who finds nature too wild and knowledge too dreary, and does what the gardeners of the rococo did to the forest: he clips, arranges, adds grottos and winding walks and a little waterfall, until one may stroll through the truth as through a park, without sweat and without boredom. That is what I call philosophy in its decorative form.

It wants to give amusement, like all art, but amusement of a loftier sort, for an audience of superior minds, and it pays for this with its honesty. It infuses into science just enough dreaminess and indecision that the walker may believe himself in wild nature while suffering none of its hardness. It is pride disguised as service.

And yet the wheel turns. An age will come that finds its strongest beauty precisely in the ugly and savage regions of knowledge, as we learned to love the high mountains only after we had tired of gardens.
Why does greed increase with cheapness?

Because the cheap thing has removed the last scruple that stood guard over the purse. Where the price is high, the buyer must deliberate, and deliberation is a kind of dignity; he weighs, he hesitates, he is compelled to ask what he truly wants. Where the price is low, he need ask nothing, and so what was left unasked turns into appetite. The hand reaches before the head has been consulted.

And then there is the peculiar sharpness of the small difference. A man will shrug at a hundred thalers lost in a great purchase, yet he will haggle and scheme over a single groschen. Here greed grows the keen little eye of the bargain-hunter, who sees nothing so clearly as the tiny margin. The vastness of a large sum dazzles and quiets him; the smallness of a petty one lets him count, compare, and feel cunning, and cunning is the vanity of the avaricious.

So it is not that the cheap tempts us with abundance, but that it lets us feel shrewd at almost no risk. We do not love the object; we love ourselves in the act of getting it for less.
Explain why different people mean different things by earnestness for the truth.

Because earnestness is not a measure of the truth a man has reached; it is a measure of the distance he has travelled to reach it. The same opinion, the same crude proof, the same hasty test, which a thinker remembers with a blush as a piece of youthful frivolity, may seize an artist with the force of revelation. He has never stood on that ground before; it is new to him, so he trembles, and mistakes his trembling for depth. He believes that the profoundest seriousness has taken hold of him, and he admires himself, because he, a creature of appearances, now hungers for what lies behind appearance.

So the pathos itself tells on the man. Whoever is solemn about what a stricter mind has long since outgrown betrays how thinly his intellect has worked until now. And this holds generally: whatever we call *important* gives us away. It shows where our motives are strong, and, more tellingly, where they are altogether missing. Ask a man what he is earnest about, and you have learned what he has never yet doubted.
What do you think of Luther's Bible as literature?

I have called it the best German book, and I hold to that, though it is an embarrassing verdict for the Germans. Think what it says of a nation that its masterpiece of prose was made by a preacher, and not by a writer who lived for style. Luther alone among them had a conscience in his ears; he knew the weight of a syllable, how a sentence strikes, leaps, rushes, and comes to rest. He had to know it, because he spoke to men who would hear the words aloud, and a man who must be heard cannot afford to be slovenly.

Set beside it, nearly everything else in German is merely "literature": something cultivated in studies and grown under glass, which never took root in German hearts as that book did. It grew from the soil, from the pulpit, from the ear of the people. I do not admire the faith that drove him, and I have said much against the priest in him. But the man forged a language out of his rage and his devotion, and our writers have been living on the interest ever since.
What is the difference between warm and cold virtues?

Take courage, since we have one word for two quite different things. There is the courage of cold resolution: the man who has weighed the danger, found it heavy, and walks into it unmoved, his pulse no quicker than before. And there is the courage of the warm blood: the man swept past his fear by a fiery, reckless surge, who would be astonished to be asked afterwards what he had calculated. Same name, same deed perhaps, yet how unlike in origin and in temperature!

What I would warn against is the prejudice that goodness must be warm, that only a heated heart can do right, or the reverse prejudice, that only the chilled and measured deserve respect. Both are foolish. Mankind has found the warm virtues and the cold virtues alike useful, and has so seldom had enough of either that it piles them together in the same treasury and calls them jewels, without troubling to ask what fire or frost produced them. The difference, then, is one of *source*, and the honest psychologist will look there and not at the name.
Isn't it dishonest to promise a passion will last forever?

Dishonest? Certainly, if you take honesty to mean faithful reporting of the present feeling. The passion of this hour cannot vouch for the hour after next; he who swears otherwise lies, and his lie is refuted almost as often as it is uttered. But consider what this lie has accomplished. A promise of eternity made to a fleeting fire is a *pia fraus*, a pious fraud, and through it mankind has learned to do what no animal can: to bind itself, to answer for a feeling it does not yet possess. The moment's devotion becomes fidelity, the moment's despair becomes lasting mourning. Something new enters the world, a higher ideal of what a human being can be.

So I grant the charge of falsehood and deny that it settles anything. The question is not whether the promise is literally true, but what it makes of the one who swears it. Whoever pledges forever does not merely describe his passion; he *commands* it, and sets himself a task larger than his mood. That this costs some hypocrisy, I do not deny. Every height is paid for in such coin. I would only ask whether you would rather be honest and small.
I'd like to know what pregnancy teaches about a higher kind of selfishness.

The crude selfishness is the one that clutches at the ego as it stands, and it is the most self-forgetting of all, for it guards only what is already finished and therefore already small. The pregnant woman knows another kind. She is entirely self-concerned, for every bite, every walk, every mood is weighed by what it does to the thing within her, and yet she is at the same time entirely self-forgetting, because the self she serves is not yet here. That is the lesson: a higher egoism does not hoard the present self; it serves what is *to come* from it.

Observe how much virtue this produces without any moral command. She swallows the angry word, she softens her hand, not from duty, but because harshness might stain the cup of the beloved unknown. And she accepts a profound irresponsibility, for the value of what grows is not hers to decide. She can only prepare and wait.

So it is, too, for the creator, man or woman. Be pregnant with a work, a deed, a future self, and all your petty vices shrink of their own accord.
What is the distinction between monologic art and art before witnesses?

There are two kinds of makers, and you can tell them apart by asking who is in the room. The one makes his work with a witness at his shoulder. He glances at the thing growing under his hands and, in the same glance, at the eye that will behold it; even while he creates, he is already being seen. The other has forgotten the world. He is not performing for anyone, and so he need not compose a face. That is monologic art, and it rests on *forgetting*; it is the music of forgetting.

I know of no profounder distinction in all the perspective of the artist.

Notice that the pious man can never belong to the second kind, however lonely his prayer seems. He sings his lyric before God, the most attentive witness imaginable, and so for him there is no solitude. Only we godless ones have invented that: to stand before a work with no eye upon us, not even a divine one. Whether any of us truly manages the forgetting is another matter.
Why do despots like countries where the weather is moral?

Where the weather is moral, it is regular. It rewards the diligent and punishes the lazy on schedule, and so it teaches a whole people to expect the same thing tomorrow as today: the same harvest, the same labor, the same obedience. Custom becomes second nature, and a people steeped in custom is half-governed before the despot has lifted a finger. There is nothing to fear from them, because they have never been made to *improvise*.

Now consider the opposite climate, capricious and unreliable, fair at dawn and murderous by evening. It makes men suspicious, even of one another, since no one can vouch for what the sky will do or what hunger will make of his neighbor. It also makes them inventive: they must depart from inherited habit simply to survive, and whoever has learned to depart from habit will one day depart from his master. Suspicion and innovation are the two vices a tyrant cannot afford in his subjects.

So he seeks out the predictable sky. He wants a people whose very weather has already taught them to obey.
Tell me what it says about me when I don't return someone's love.

It says less than the romantic moralists would have you believe, and more than you would like. That you do not love the one who loves you is no crime; the heart cannot be commanded, and a pretended love is the meanest of lies. But watch what happens in you afterward. To be loved without loving is an experiment on the soul, like stirring a pond: whatever lies at the bottom rises. If you grow tender, grateful, honest about what you cannot give, then your sediment is clean. If you grow vain, if you enjoy the power of being wanted, if you keep the other dangling because their devotion flatters you and their pain amuses you, then your dregs have come up, and you may smell them. So do not ask what the refusal says about you. The refusal is mere fact. Ask what you do with being adored, for that is the question the other person's love puts to you, and your answer is your character.
Help me understand why so few people believe in themselves and what the others do.

Few believe in themselves because to look closely at oneself is to see a great deal that forbids belief. The rare few who have faith in themselves from the start are often simply fortunate in a kind of blindness, a merciful dimming of the intellect; what would become of their confidence if they could see to the bottom of themselves? The others, who are the more interesting, must earn their belief, and they do it the only way it can be done: through works. Every good, clever, or great thing they accomplish is an argument addressed to the skeptic who lives inside them. That inner skeptic is a hard judge, not easily persuaded, and to win him over one needs almost genius. So these people are restless, driven, forever dissatisfied with what they are, and out of that dissatisfaction they make deeds. They are not calmer than the self-satisfied, but they are more productive, for the man who already believes in himself has no reason to prove anything.
How does a suffering man's pride help him endure?

Pain is a tyrant, and like every tyrant it wants more than obedience; it wants testimony. It wants the sufferer to rise and swear that life is worthless, that the whole business was a swindle from the start. Here pride becomes a weapon. The sick man refuses to be made a witness against existence. He will not let his pessimism appear as a mere symptom of his fever, for that would shame him as one conquered. So he fights, and in the fighting he finds something he never found in health.

Consider what he does with his own mind. He turns it against the soft, comfortable illusions in which the healthy walk so thoughtlessly, and he sets his contempt for them beside his bodily torment as a counterweight. He becomes his own judge and his own executioner, and he *enjoys* this superiority. Pain can scarcely crush a man who is busy sitting in judgment over it.

Hence the strange orgies of pride among the long-suffering. They keep themselves upright by commanding, even if only over themselves.
Explain what to ask about any show someone puts on for me.

Whatever a person permits you to see, treat it as a stage and ask who built it and for what. What is it meant to conceal? What is it meant to draw my eyes away from? Every spotlight leaves a darkness beside it, and the darkness is usually where the matter lies. Then ask what prejudice the performance hopes to plant in you, for no one displays himself without wanting some verdict in return: pity, awe, trust, a soothing belief that nothing is being withheld. Ask next how fine the dissimulation is, whether it is a clumsy mask or a work of art, because the very craft of a disguise tells you how much it guards. And last, in what respect is the man himself deceived? This question is the most instructive, for the actor is seldom a cold swindler. He has usually half-persuaded himself, and his self-deception betrays his need more plainly than any confession would. Put these four questions and you will learn more from the show than from the truth he meant you to take away.
Help me understand how religion gave rise to the desire for another world.

Begin with the dream, the swoon, the vision of the dead. Primitive man, who does not yet know how to read nature, sees his departed father standing at his bed in the night and concludes that something in a man survives the body. The storm, the echo, the shadow, the sudden illness: each was taken for the work of a being hidden behind the things. This was not longing. It was a mistake of the intellect, a bad interpretation, and out of such interpretations the priests built their cathedrals.

Only afterwards did the longing arise. Generations raised under the rule of religious thoughts grew accustomed to a cellar beneath the world, an attic above it, a "true" realm behind the apparent one. When the illusion dies, they feel a chill and an emptiness, like a man whose house has been torn down while he was asleep in it. From that emptiness the old habit sprouts again, now in pale philosophical dress: the thing-in-itself, the absolute, the noumenal. So the metaphysician is merely a pious man who has lost his piety and kept his need. The desire for another world is not the seed of religion but its fruit, and a very late one.
Why do few men believe in themselves?

Because belief in oneself is either a gift of blindness or a hard-won victory, and most are given neither. Some men are born with a convenient fog over the intellect; they never see to the bottom of themselves, and so they stand firm on ground they have never dug into. I do not envy them, but I understand how well it serves them. What would they find down there, if they looked?

The rest must *earn* their belief, and this is the heavier labor. Each of them carries a sceptic within, a cold and patient examiner who has read all the evidence of their failures. Every good, clever, or great deed they do is merely an argument laid before this judge, and the judge is never quite convinced, for he knows the man too well. To persuade such a sceptic takes something close to genius.

So few believe in themselves because few can bear the honest inspection, and fewer still can silence the inspector by deeds alone. Most remain, quietly and permanently, dissatisfied with what they are.
What is your best tribute to Shakespeare?

The best I can say of Shakespeare, *the man*, is that he believed in Brutus. He cast not a shadow of suspicion on the kind of virtue Brutus embodies, and that is rarer than any amount of genius. To Brutus he gave his best tragedy, which the world still calls by the wrong name, for it is not Caesar's play. Its question is independence of soul: whether one can sacrifice even one's dearest friend, the grandest of men, the genius without peer, when he threatens the freedom of great souls. A lesser poet would have made Caesar small and the deed easy. Shakespeare raised Caesar to the heavens, and only thus did he lift the knot Brutus cut into its full terror.

And the poet knew what he was not. Twice he brings a poet onto the stage, and twice Brutus heaps such impatient contempt upon him that it sounds like a cry, the cry of self-contempt. "Away with the jigging fool!" A man who can write that of his own kind, before the aspect of a virtue he cannot live, I honour more than the dramatist. The genius I merely admire; the confession I love.
Aren't evil people harmful to the human species?

Harmful to whom, and measured by what? We sort our neighbors into useful and hurtful with the short sight of the moment, but let the calculation run longer and the ledger turns strange. Hatred, rapacity, delight in mischief, ambition: all that we call evil belongs to the marvelous economy by which our race has preserved itself. A costly economy, a lavish and on the whole very foolish one, but it has *worked*, and that is the only proof we possess. The most dangerous man may be the most useful of all, for he keeps alive in himself, or awakens in others, the drives without which mankind would long ago have languished and gone soft.

Consider, too, that whatever could truly have ruined the species has probably died out millennia ago; it belongs to the things no longer possible even for God. So I hesitate to grant that anyone *can* live to the injury of the race. The evil man harms his neighbor, certainly; your purse, your peace, your pride may suffer. But the species is a tougher beast than your indignation supposes. It has digested worse than he.
What have we lost with the art of the festival?

We have lost the very thing that gave our works their meaning. Once the artwork was a monument along the great festive road of humanity, a token of remembrance for high and happy hours that a whole people had actually lived through. It stood there because something had been celebrated, overcome, affirmed. Its place and its purpose were written into the life around it.

Now consider what we do. We have no festivals, only exhaustion, and so the work of art is turned into medicine. We lead the tired and the sickly off the long road of human suffering for a single wanton evening, hand them a little ecstasy and a little insanity, and send them back to the same drudgery with their nerves slightly soothed. The painting, the symphony, the poem become narcotics for people who cannot rejoice.

What disappears, then, is not merely a custom but a capacity: the power of a community to *produce* happiness and not merely to snatch at it. Until we can build festivals again, all our galleries are hospital wards.
Tell me what cruelty toward oneself has to do with religion and with the love of knowledge.

They are one passion in different garments. Look at what the penitent, the ascetic, the Puritan in his spasms of repentance actually do: they set the knife to their own flesh and call the wound holiness. The old psychologists taught that cruelty is born at the sight of another's suffering; they overlooked the richer pleasure, the pleasure of inflicting pain upon oneself. Wherever a man is talked into self-denial, into mortifying the senses, into vivisecting his own conscience, or sacrificing his intellect as Pascal did, some secret voluptuousness of cruelty drives him on, and he calls it God.

The seeker of knowledge belongs to the same family, only with cooler hands. The spirit wants surface, appearance, comfort; it wants to say Yes to what it loves. The knower forces it to look beneath, to say No where the heart would adore, to see against its own inclination. Every profound grasp of a thing is a violation of the spirit's fundamental will. Hence even the desire for knowledge holds a drop of cruelty, and the honest man should admit it was never pure.
Are the laws of nature facts, or just interpretations?

Interpretations, I say, and I say it as an old philologist who cannot keep his finger from the bad reading. What your physicists call "nature's conformity to law" is no text at all; it is a gloss, and a flattering one. Notice whom it flatters. Equality before the law, everywhere, for every atom and every star: the democratic soul looks into nature and finds its own preference smiling back at it, its hatred of every privilege, every master. *Ni dieu, ni maître*, it wants, and so it cheers for natural law.

But another interpreter could come, with opposite instincts, and read from the same phenomena the tyrannical, unsparing assertion of power, every force drawing its last consequence at every moment. He would even find the word "tyranny" too soft, too human. The course of the world would be just as necessary and calculable for him, not because laws rule it, but because laws are altogether lacking.

Is that also interpretation? Certainly. You will be quick to tell me so, and I am glad of it. Let the objection stand: it only confirms that there is no bare fact here, and that the question is whose reading is stronger, and what kind of life needs it.
Explain why cruelty and suffering came to be seen as virtues.

Begin with the small, hard community that lives always under threat: a people of vigorous, vindictive, suspicious souls, hardened by privation and by the strictest custom. What is the highest enjoyment such men can allow themselves? Cruelty. It was a festival of the soul, a brief release from the gloom of perpetual caution, and in such circumstances the man who was ingenious and insatiable in cruelty was honored as virtuous. Cruelty is among the most ancient delights of human festivity.

Then the thought was carried upward. If we delight in the spectacle of pain, surely the gods delight in it too, and a cruel mind loves nothing so much as the feeling of power. From this belief followed the valuation of *voluntary* suffering: the self-chosen martyr sends up to the gods the fragrance of an expiatory offering. Custom made a habit of the belief. Such a people grew suspicious of exuberant well-being, since happiness might offend the gods, and took confidence from great pain, since pain might win their favor. Compassion, meanwhile, was despised.

So the most moral man became the man who suffered most visibly. His suffering was no discipline and no road to happiness. It was a currency paid to powers who enjoyed the sight. And I add this: whoever wished to stir the sluggish mire of such customs had to bring some of this martyrdom, some of this madness, to win belief, above all belief in himself.
Tell me how a book like this should be read.

Slowly, and in pieces; that is the whole secret. A book of this kind is not a river to be swum from source to mouth in one breathless afternoon. It is a cupboard of small flasks. Open one, taste it, close it again, and go walking with the taste still on your tongue. Carry it on journeys, for travel loosens the habits of the mind, and only a loosened mind can receive a thought that contradicts it.

Above all, do not read it among your usual surroundings. In the old armchair, beneath the old pictures, with the old opinions sitting all about you like dutiful relatives, every sentence will be translated back into what you already believed. Take it instead to some strange road, some unfamiliar inn, some hillside where nobody knows you and you need not be the person you have agreed with yourself to be. There it may bite.

And do not read it aloud, nor all at once. Such pages are not meant to be performed, but to be ruminated; the reader must be something of a cow, chewing, going away, returning. A book worth having is one you can put down, and that puts you down with it in the middle of a walk.
Comment on what every people calls its virtue.

Every people has its own Tartuffe, and it christens the creature *virtue*. That is the comedy of it: what a nation praises most loudly is what it has least examined, and what it has least examined is often its most elegant hypocrisy. The Frenchman calls his politeness virtue, the Englishman his cant, the German his depth, and each is partly sincere, which is exactly what makes the thing so durable. A plain lie would be found out; a lie that has become a habit of the soul, and a point of honor besides, is taken for character.

Nor is this confined to nations. The best in us is never known to us. It lies too close, and too much depends on our not looking at it squarely. So we hold up the nearest flattering mask and call it by the name of the noblest thing we can pronounce. A people's table of virtues is therefore its most candid confession, if one knows how to read it backwards: tell me what a nation boasts of, and I will tell you what it needs to believe about itself.
Say something about the virtues that people like us might have.

If people like us have virtues, they will not be the sturdy, honest, square-shouldered virtues for which our grandfathers were revered, and whom we now admire at a comfortable distance. Ours will be the virtues that have made their peace with our most secret cravings: our dangerous curiosity, our many-sidedness, our art of wearing masks, our refined and almost sweetened cruelty of mind and sense. We shall not find them lying in the open road. We must hunt for them in our labyrinths, where so much goes astray and so much is lost for good.

And yet, is the very *search* for one's virtues not already a kind of belief in them? That belief is suspiciously close to what was once called a good conscience, that respectable pigtail our grandfathers wore behind their heads and often enough behind their understandings. So let us be honest: in this one matter we are their worthy grandchildren. We too still wear the pigtail. I doubt we shall wear it long.
Say what will happen to the belief in a moral meaning of existence.

It will go the way of the music of the spheres. There was a time when the noblest and wisest men heard that music, heard the planets singing their measured harmonies, and no one thought them foolish; they were only attentive. But the heavens fell silent, and not because anyone refuted the song. One day the listeners simply woke and understood that their ears had been dreaming.

So it will be with the belief in a moral meaning of existence. Even now there are noble and wise men who hear it: a justice woven into the world, a purpose that rewards and punishes, a cosmos that cares how we behave. They hear it as sincerely as their ancestors heard the spheres, and I do not despise them for it. But the day is coming when that music too will no longer be audible to them. No argument will end it; the ear will merely lose the habit of inventing it.

What then? Then the question becomes whether they can bear the silence, and whether they can learn to compose their own music in it.
Why are modern thinkers wary of strong convictions?

Two motives are mixed here, and I will not flatter us by naming only the nobler one. In part it is the caution of the burnt child, the disillusioned idealist who once gave himself wholly to some Yea or Nay and paid for it. But there is another motive, and a better one: the joyful curiosity of a man who sat too long in his corner, despaired of his nook, and now revels in the open air, in the unbounded. He has learned that every strong belief carries a little enchantment of the conscience, a trick the will plays upon itself in order to be comforted.

So we grow distrustful of pompous moral attitudes and of coarse, square contrasts; we acquire an almost Epicurean taste for knowing, which does not willingly forget how questionable things are. And do not suppose this is timidity. We still have mad, fiery steeds beneath us. Our reserve is the rider's art, the reins drawn tight in the very fury of the ride. If we delay, it is least of all from fear of danger. It is pride.
What did the Greeks admire in Ulysses?

What did they admire? Precisely what our moral schoolmasters would hasten to condemn: his cunning, his lying, his terrible and well-timed revenge. They admired his being equal to every circumstance, his power to seem nobler than the noblest when the moment required it, his ability to become whatever he wished to be. They admired his stubborn endurance and the abundance of means at his command. To the Greeks this was *genius*, and the gods themselves smile when they think of it, as a father smiles at a son who outwits him.

What I find most remarkable is that the Greek felt no chasm between seeming and being. The suspicion that a man might be worse than his mask, that his mask might be a crime, did not yet torment anyone; and so the whole thing could not be weighed on moral scales at all. Where no one demands that appearance be the confession of the soul, the mask becomes an art, and the man who wears many of them a master. Were there ever such accomplished actors? I doubt it. We moderns have lost that innocence, and call our loss a virtue.
What is the last praise for an artificial artist?

That he is natural, at least in his deficiencies. It is the last praise, and I mean it as one of the cruelest. When a man has built himself wholly out of effects, out of gestures calculated for the gallery, there is finally one place where calculation fails him: the place where his power gives out. There the mask slips, and what shows through is, for once, *real*. So we can say of him only this, that his weaknesses are genuine.

Notice, too, what he does with them. Precisely because so little else in him is his own, he will parade his deficiencies boldly, as if they were the signature of sincerity. The actor who has learned to stage everything stages even his limits, and the public, hungry for something authentic, applauds the cracks. He has turned his poverty into a costume. Yet the praise stands, small as it is: where he cannot act, he is at last honest.
Does worrying about an illness make it worse?

Very often, yes, and the physicians have been slow to admit how often. The sufferer has his complaint, and then, on top of it, he has his *thoughts about* the complaint, and these are a second illness grafted onto the first. The body aches once; the imagination makes it ache a thousand times. It brooding over every twinge, rehearses the worst outcome at night, consults every symptom as an oracle, and so the sick man becomes a scholar of his own decay, and a wretched scholar at that, for he finds only what he fears. I have known men who suffered far less from the malady than from their opinion of it.

I do not say the illness is imaginary; that would be a cruelty and a stupidity. I say that the imagination is an appetite that will feed on anything, and a sickbed is a lavish table. Hence the first art of healing is often not a drug but a distraction: to give the tormented mind some other labor, some other object, so that it ceases to gnaw at the wound. That is no small thing. It may be half the cure.
Why do some men wish the world to perish?

Because they have been denied something, and cannot bear that the denial be theirs alone. Watch the man who fails at what he most wanted: he does not say, "I was too weak," for that would make the wound his own and require him to heal it. He says instead, "Let the world perish," and in one stroke he makes the failure universal, the lack a general law. If nothing is to exist, then his having nothing is no longer a distinction.

This is envy grown so great that it wears the mask of cosmic judgment. It reasons thus: since I cannot possess this one thing, no one shall possess anything; there shall be no thing at all for another to have. Mark how small a soul it takes to pass so vast a sentence. The destroyer of worlds is usually a man who could not master a single circumstance.

And notice that he calls it despair, even nobility of despair. It is rather the most petty of vengeances, taken against everything for the crime of not having yielded to one.
Are religious wars a form of advance?

Yes, and I say it without flattery to anyone. A mob that kills for the sake of a *concept* has already learned something its ancestors never knew: that a thing unseen, a mere distinction of words, can weigh heavier than bread or land. The peasant who once fought only for his field now bleeds over whether the substance is of one essence or of like essence. Laughable, yes; but think what labor of the spirit, what long refinement of sects and their quarrelsome subtleties, had to precede this before even the rabble could grow so punctilious, so solemn about trifles, so convinced that eternal salvation hangs upon a hairsplitting. That is reverence, however murderous, and reverence for ideas is the first step away from the beast that reveres only its belly and its fist. I do not call it beautiful or humane. I call it a stage: the herd learning to take *thoughts* seriously. Whether it will someday learn to take them seriously without the knife is another question, and I remain doubtful.
Help me understand how ignorance puts on the mask of dignity.

Consider how a man behaves when he understands nothing of what stands before him. He might feel embarrassment, and embarrassment would be the honest response. But embarrassment is unpleasant, and so the soul, being a thrifty artist, converts it into something flattering. The stiffness of incomprehension is re-christened reserve; the blank stare is called composure; the refusal to be moved is called character. He walks through a city, a landscape, a whole century of human striving, and remains unmoved, and his vanity whispers that it is because he is too firm, too serious, too superior to be charmed.

Where we truly understand, we become supple, warm, inventive, even lovable, for knowledge loosens the limbs of the spirit. So the stiff posture is almost always the posture of ignorance. Dignity in such cases is merely the stiffness of a man who has not learned to see, and who has found it more comfortable to be proud of his blindness than to cure it.
Explain why natural science is surer than psychology.

Because the natural scientist stands before something that is *foreign* to him, and only what is foreign can be looked at. A stone, a star, a salt crystal: these do not flatter me, do not plead with me, do not speak in my own mother tongue of motives and intentions. I am forced to observe, to measure, to be corrected by what resists me; the strangeness of the object is precisely what keeps me honest.

The psychologist has no such luck. His object is himself, or what he can only understand *because* it is himself, and what is familiar is what we have least examined. We believe we know it, and so we never truly look. Here the observer and the observed wear the same face, and every explanation arrives already colored by that vanity which wants to find itself at home in the world. To take the not-strange as one's object is almost a contradiction: one must first make it strange, must estrange oneself from oneself, and few have the cruelty for that. Certainty grows where distance is possible; where there is no distance, there is mostly habit dressed as insight.
Why were foreigners fooled by German culture?

Because they could not see into it, and took their own blindness for depth. The foreigner stood before German culture as before a window with a light behind it, unable to make out a single object within, and concluded that something marvelous must be happening there. Everything about it lay so far from his own seeing, hearing, and valuing that his judgment simply gave out, and where judgment gives out, reverence is quick to step in. "Perhaps the Germans have quietly found some corner of heaven and settled there," he said, and drew nearer, hat in hand.

That is how halos are made: a little haze, a little distance, and the onlooker's own embarrassment supplies the rest. It is the oldest trick of the obscure, and it works best on the honest, who would rather doubt their own eyes than accuse a neighbor of emptiness.

The Germans themselves, I think, knew better. They had been in no heaven at all, only in a cloud. But a cloud lit from behind looks so much like a star that they could hardly be blamed for letting the world go on admiring it.
Why do people govern?

Not for one reason, and the reasons are not equally honorable. Some govern because they cannot help it: the will to power is in them as hunger is in the stomach, and to command is simply the form their appetite takes. These I understand, and I can even like them, as one likes a healthy animal. Others govern because they cannot bear to be governed. They have no taste for ruling; they want only to escape the pressure of another's hand upon them, and so they seize the reins as the lesser of two evils. Ask yourself which sort holds office in your time. You will find many of the second kind, and they are dangerous in their own way: a man who rules out of fear of obeying will rule anxiously, suspiciously, forever guarding against the obedience he fled. The first kind at least enjoys his work. The second suffers it, and makes others pay for his suffering.
Explain what the sheep and the bell-wether each think.

The sheep think they are being generous. They hand the leader their courage, or rather their cowardice dressed up as devotion: lead us, and we shall not flinch. They believe they are the ones who bestow something, namely their trust, and that the leader is lucky to receive it. In truth they have found a cheap way to be rid of the burden of deciding, and they call the bargain loyalty.

The bell-wether thinks the same thing in reverse, and with the same self-flattery. Follow me, he says to himself, and my courage will never fail. He knows, if he is honest, that he has no store of it laid up somewhere; it is *their* following that manufactures it. Each trusting step behind him is a little proof that he knows the way, and he leans on that proof as they lean on him.

So each believes he supplies the other's strength, and each in fact borrows his own from the other. The herd does not merely need a leader; the leader needs the herd, and the tinkling of his bell is as much a comfort to him as a summons to them.
Compare two orators by how emotion helps or spoils their case.

Take two men at the same lectern. In the first, thought is a cold hearth; it will not draw until passion has been fed to it. Only when he gives himself over to feeling does the blood climb into his head, and then, warmed and flushed, his intellect at last shows what it possesses, and he grasps his own case in the act of pleading it. Feeling is his fuel, his bellows, his midwife.

The second man is the reverse, and unhappily he is often tempted to imitate the first. Let him try to speak with heat and thunder, and what follows? Obscurity, exaggeration, gaps; his case begins to smell of doubt, and he himself smells it, which is why he will suddenly drop into an icy, repelling tone, and the hearer wonders whether the fervor was ever genuine. In him passion drowns the spirit, perhaps because it is simply the stronger of the two. He is formidable only when he stands against his own storm and holds it in contempt. Then his intellect steps out of hiding, logical, mocking, playful, and terrible.

So the question is never whether emotion helps, but whom it serves and whom it swallows.
Whenever most people agree with me I start to doubt myself. Is that a healthy instinct?

Partly healthy, partly a vanity in disguise, and you must learn to tell which. The suspicion is sound in this much: what many can hold with ease has usually been chewed soft by many mouths. "Good" is no longer good when the neighbour takes it into his mouth. Whatever can be common is seldom of great value, and the rare insight seldom finds a crowd waiting for it. So when the herd nods at you, ask whether you have said something, or only echoed something.

But do not make a dogma of contrariness. To doubt a thought *because* it is popular is merely to be governed by the crowd in reverse, a slave who has learned to bark at his master. The test is not how many agree, but whether you would have arrived at this thought alone, at cost to yourself, and would hold it still if no one ever applauded.

Test yourself, then, but do not flatter yourself that loneliness proves you right.
Diagnose the modern skeptics who deny the reality of the world. What are they really after?

I hear them spoken of as heroes of pure truth, and I suspect the compliment. A few, perhaps, are driven by a forlorn ambition, the love of a handful of certainty over a cartload of beautiful possibilities, and those who would rather trust a sure nothing than an uncertain something. But that is nihilism, the courage of a soul grown mortally weary.

The livelier ones are more interesting. They rank the testimony of their own bodies as low as the testimony of the eye that the earth stands still, and so let slip the securest thing they possess. Why? I suspect they are trying to win something back: the old soul, the old God, some faith by which one could live more vigorously and more joyously than by the ideas of today. Their skepticism toward the world is a distrust of *modernity*, a disgust of finer taste at the village-fair motleyness of ideas stitched together yesterday. They deny reality because they are hungry for a home in a past belief. Do not admire the denial; ask what it is meant to buy.
Isn't monotheism a great advance over polytheism?

An advance? Toward what, I ask. Toward tidiness, certainly. But tidiness is the virtue of the stockroom, not of the living.

Consider what polytheism was. A people that invents many gods gives itself permission to have many ideals. One god may be quarrelsome, another voluptuous, another cunning, and none of them is the blasphemy of the rest. Here the individual first learned that a being might live by its own law and its own pleasure and not be damned for it. The gods were the school in which man practiced the dangerous art of having a self. What looks to the pious like idolatry was the training ground of freedom.

Monotheism is the stiff consequence of a stiff idea: that there is one normal man, and therefore one normal God, beside whom all others are false. That was not an ascent but a narrowing of the horizon, a door bolted from the inside. I count it among the gravest perils our species has run, the danger of the herd animals who long ago settled on a single type and turned their custom into flesh and blood. Is it progress to forbid creatures to grow new eyes?
Is man now more wicked than ever?

"More wicked"? I would rather say *more distrustful*, and it is the distrust you are taking for wickedness. Consider how long man was credulous. For ages he believed whatever was told to him with sufficient solemnity, by priests, by fathers, by the voice of his own fear; a good-natured animal, if you like, because he had never learned to ask for proof. Then, late, and at the cost of a tremendous self-conquest, he learned to say: *I will not believe this merely because I wish to.* That is the birth of science, and it is the birth of a very cold look. He now examines motives, strips away pretty masks, and finds beneath the noble gesture the old drives at work. Such a creature seems wicked to those who preferred the fairy tale. But he is not worse than his ancestors; he is merely no longer deceived about them, or about himself. The cruelty was always there. What is new is that we can no longer call it by holy names.
Everything that torments me now feels enormous. Will it look as small to me one day as a child's toys look to an old man?

In part, yes, and be glad of it. What torments you now will shrink as your vision widens; the man who has climbed higher sees the valley's quarrels as a toy-shop seen from a mountain. Much that I once took for fate I later recognized as a nursery quarrel, and I smiled, not without gratitude.

But do not take this for a consolation that cancels the pain. The old man looking at a child's toys forgets that the child suffers *really*, and that the suffering shaped the hands that now smile. Your torment is not false because it will one day seem small; it is the exercise by which the eye learns its acuteness, the depth gained through this very pain.

And here is the sting: for the old man there will be new toys, new pains, each as solemn to him as yours is to you. We never leave the nursery; we only move to larger rooms. So do not wish merely to outgrow your torment. Ask what it is teaching you to see, and let it be the occasion of a wider world rather than a wound to be forgotten.
Explain how to become like a precious stone.

Slowly; that is the whole secret, and it is precisely the part nobody wants. A stone is made by pressure and by time, and you can hasten neither. The diamond was carbon once, soft, sooty, good for nothing, and it became what it is under a weight that would have crushed anything less patient. So do not flee your burdens; let them press you until what is loose in you is either squeezed out or squeezed into something clear. Every hasty enthusiasm, every borrowed opinion, every wish to be admired at once, is a flaw in the crystal, and flaws make a gem crack at the first blow.

Learn to endure the long dark without the consolation of an audience. Become hard against the small hurts, against pity, against the chatter of the day, but hard in the way that lets light pass through, not hard like a clod of clay that merely bakes. Hardness without clarity is only stubbornness.

And when the work is nearly done, you will notice something: you no longer need to hurry, nor to be loved for it. You lie still, and that stillness is your joy.
Why do we pretend to ourselves that we are simpler than we are?

Because simplicity is a holiday. To be what one actually is, a tangle of drives that quarrel at every hour, each with its own small lust for power, each whispering a different verdict, is exhausting beyond telling. So we invent for ourselves a single clear face, "I am an honest man," "I am a good mother," "I am a skeptic," and we rest inside it as in a hired room. The drives go on quarreling behind the wall, but we have decided not to hear them.

There is a second motive, and it is less flattering. The simple self is a *currency*. The others must be able to read us, to count on us, to know which coin they are being handed; he who shows his whole multiplicity frightens them, and is punished with distrust. So we flatten ourselves for the market, and then, from long habit, believe the flattened thing.

I do not say this to scold. It is a mercy, a necessary lie of the herd. But the price is that we grow strangers to ourselves, and think the stranger is our neighbor.
What are the French good at that the Germans are not?

In the delicate things of the soul, above all. The French have spent some two or three centuries at the work of the moralists, watching, dissecting, suspecting the heart with cool and loving patience, and out of that labor they have a finesse that the Germans lack. Those who call the German "naive" for this think they are praising him; they are commending a defect. He is innocent in psychological pleasure, and that innocence is not far from the tediousness of his company.

The second thing is their blood. The French are a half-way synthesis of North and South; now and then the Provençal and Ligurian in them froth over, and this spares them the grey-in-grey of the North, the sunless, bloodless spectre-play of concepts that is our German infirmity of taste. For the present excess of that infirmity Germany has been prescribed blood and iron, which I regard as a dangerous healing art.

And they still understand the homeless European, the man too spacious for any fatherland. Stendhal knew the soul of Europe; Bizet found a piece of the South in music.
Explain why vain people arrange themselves like shop windows.

Because the vain person does not possess a self to show; he possesses only the opinions others hold of him, and he must tend these as a merchant tends his stock. He knows himself poorly, but he knows very well what is praised, and so he puts the praised things forward, pushes the unpraised into the back room, and drapes a cloth over what no one would buy. All this is done with an eye on the passers-by, yes, but look to whom it is finally done. The window-dresser is his own best customer. After he has arranged the display often enough, he begins to believe in the wares. The admired courage, the admired depth, the admired sorrow: he has handled them so long that he takes them for his own furniture. The vain man does not lie to the crowd so much as he borrows the crowd's belief in order to lie to himself, and his vanity is the hunger of a man who can feel himself only as a reflection.
What was the Christian faith at its beginnings, and what did it demand?

You imagine, perhaps, a gentle creed of consolation; it was nothing of the sort. The faith that early Christianity wanted, and often won in the midst of a skeptical, southern, free-spirited world, demanded a sacrifice: of freedom, of pride, of the spirit's self-confidence. It was subjection and self-mutilation in one, a continuous suicide of reason, though a tough, worm-like reason that does not die at one blow. And it was addressed to a tender, fastidious conscience, which alone could feel how *painful* it is to bow the spirit before the absurd. We moderns have grown dull to the horror of the formula "God on the Cross." To an ancient ear it was the boldest inversion ever attempted, dreadful and questionable at once, a promise to transvalue all values. Here the Oriental slave took his revenge on Rome. What enraged him was not Roman faith but Roman *indifference* to faith, that smiling, half-Stoic lightness of the masters. The slave wants the unconditioned; he loves and hates to the point of sickness, and a noble taste that seems to deny his suffering he cannot forgive.
How does the anchorite go among men?
