The proof lies in our choices. We seek out the sufferer when we can come as the strong and helpful one, when applause awaits us, when the contrast flatters our own happiness, when we are bored. We turn away when the sight would only wound us. What we suffer in his presence is *our* suffering; his remains his own. That this is not wholly "selfless" is no reason to despise it, but it is a reason to stop flattering ourselves.
Why are natural sciences more certain than psychology?

Because they study what is strange to them, and strangeness is the beginning of knowledge. The physicist faces the stone, the star, the falling body as foreign things; he has no idea what they "want," he cannot slip under their skin and flatter himself that he already understands them from within. So he must measure, watch, and be corrected. The alien thing resists his wishes, and only what resists can instruct.

The psychologist's case is the reverse. His object is what is nearest, familiar, apparently transparent: the "I," the will, the motives we have believed in since childhood. And what is familiar we *take* for known. Habit passes itself off as insight; we no longer see what we are too accustomed to. To make the nearest thing into an object, one would first have to make it strange to oneself, to look at one's own heart as a stranger's, and this is almost a contradiction, since the looker and the looked-at are the same. Hence the natural sciences are the more certain, and, if you will allow the jest, the more *unnatural*: they begin where we do not already think we know.
How are masters of the first rank recognised?

By their endings. Anyone can begin; beginnings are carried by the first intoxication, by the freshness of the idea, by the borrowed momentum of ambition. The middle can be padded with industry. But the end exposes everything, for there the work must justify itself without the help of novelty, and there one sees whether the whole was truly *one thing* or merely a heap of passages.

The master of the second degree grows restless as he nears the close. He hurries, or he lingers; he piles on one more flourish, one more consolation, one more peal of the orchestra, because he does not trust what has already been said. His uneasiness betrays him. The master of the first rank knows when the thing is finished, and he lets it descend with proud, quiet equilibrium, as a mountain ridge sinks into the sea and the bay completes its melody. This holds for the last bar of a symphony and the fifth act of a tragedy, but equally for a thought and for a statesman's business: to end well is the rarest form of strength.
Explain why you will not paint martyrs.

Because the martyr-picture is a swindle of the eye. It asks me to find the sublime in the very place where cruelty has been smuggled in as a virtue, and to kneel before suffering as though suffering were an argument. It is not. A man who dies for his faith proves only that he was willing to die for it; he has proved nothing about whether the faith is true. The crowd, of course, prefers blood to reasons, and the painter who serves that appetite has made himself the colorist of the scaffold.

There is no shortage of things that are truly lofty: a mountain under cold light, a spirit at play with its own severity, a body that is at home in its strength. I have no need to go hunting for the sublime among the racks and the pyres. And consider my vanity, for I confess to it: I have no wish to be the sublime executioner. To paint the martyr is to stand beside the torturer and call the work beautiful. Raphael knew better, and I am content to learn from him.
Why do people enjoy tragedy, bull-fights and gladiatorial contests?

They enjoy it because they are cruel, and have been taught to call the pleasure by gentler names. The Roman in the arena, the Spaniard at the bull-fight, the Japanese pressing toward his tragedy, the Parisian workman with his homesickness for bloody revolutions: each drinks the same philtre, the old Circe *cruelty*. The shallow psychologists always said that cruelty begins at the sight of the suffering of others. That is only the coarsest case. There is a rich, an overflowing delight in suffering itself, and in causing oneself to suffer. The ascetic who mutilates his senses, the penitent with his spasms of contrition, the believer who sacrifices his intellect: all are lured onward by a secret thrill of cruelty *toward himself*. The spectator of tragedy does the same thing at a safer distance. He lets the stage strike him, lets himself be wounded, and calls the shudder *pity* or *purification*, because a man will do almost anything to keep from confessing that he enjoys it. Even the seeker of knowledge belongs here. He forces his spirit to see against its inclination and say Nay where the heart would say Yes. Every profound perception is a violation.
I'd like to know how the wise man should look at the stars.

Not from below. So long as you crane your neck upward and feel the stars as an "above you," you are still a kneeling creature, a pious one, dressed up as an observer. The lights overhead are then altars, and you a worshipper who has merely changed the name of his god. The discerning eye begins where this feeling ends. It knows that there is no above and no below in that vast wandering of fire; that the earth on which you stand is itself a star among stars, swinging through the same darkness, and that you are no spectator placed beneath a spectacle but a fragment of the spectacle. The wise man therefore looks at the stars as one looks at neighbors, as one looks at kin, distant, cold, magnificent, but not superior. He does not ask them to bless or judge him. He asks only what they are, and he lets his own smallness and his own audacity stand side by side without shame.
Tell me what is wrong with a purely mechanical interpretation of the world.

What is wrong with it is not that it is false, but that it is *poor*. A purely mechanical reading of the world may be perfectly correct as far as it goes, and still be among the stupidest of all possible readings, because it is the one most destitute of significance. It counts what can be counted, and then mistakes the counting for the whole.

Consider a piece of music. Suppose you were to judge its worth by how much of it could be measured, the vibrations, the intervals, the ratios of the strings. You might produce a flawless account, and you would have understood nothing, absolutely nothing, of what is music in it. The tremor, the longing, the victory or the grief, all of it escapes the net, since the net was woven to catch only what is uniform and repeatable.

So it is with the world. An essentially mechanical world would be an essentially *meaningless* world, and this is no discovery about the world but a confession about the method. The mechanician has chosen to look only where light is easy to shed, and then announces that nothing lives in the dark.
Tell me why the free spirits are misunderstood.

They are misunderstood because they do not hold still. Whoever wishes to judge a man must first fix him in one place, pin him like a butterfly to a board, and the free spirit has the bad manners to keep growing while the observer is still taking notes. He sloughs his skin every spring. The portrait you carried away of him is of one who has already departed; you praise or condemn a husk.

And growth is not only upward. Like a tree he drives his roots ever deeper into the dark, into what the pious call evil, even as his crown opens more hungrily to the light. The spectator sees only one of these motions and takes it for the whole: he hears the roots and cries "corrupter!", or sees the branches and cries "dreamer!" Rarely does he grasp that both are a single growth, and that one cannot reach high without reaching deep.

I do not complain of it. To live closer to the lightning is to dwell where few care to stand, and I should esteem myself less if the herd could understand me at once. Being misunderstood is the tax paid by all elevation, and I pay it gladly.
Many young scholars I know scorn philosophy. What lies behind such contempt?

I have watched it often, and the causes are less noble than the scorn that displays them. Most commonly the young scholar has once fallen under the spell of some particular philosopher, sworn him obedience, and then broken the oath without breaking the charm. He no longer believes the master, yet he still carries the master's contemptuous verdicts on all the others, and so a private grudge swells into a general ill-will against philosophy itself. Think how one angry man's raging against another has cut a whole generation off from a whole culture.

But I will be honest about the second cause: the philosophers themselves have earned a good part of it. Set the anchorites of the spirit, the Heraclitus, the Plato, the Empedocles, beside the loud hotch-potch thinkers of the present day, who call themselves "realists" or "positivists" and are at best scholars and specialists in a philosopher's coat. An honest man of science may feel himself of better family than that, and his disdain is then a kind of self-respect. What he scorns is not philosophy but its counterfeit; his error is to have never seen the coin itself.
Why do you love ignorance of the future?

Because the future that is known in advance is already half spoiled. He who pries into tomorrow grows impatient with today; he tastes the fruit while it is still green, and then sits sour at the very hour when it would have ripened. Promised things devour the one who gulps them before their time, for hope of that kind is only a hunger that takes itself for wisdom.

I ask my thoughts to tell me where I stand, for that I can bear to know and must know, since honesty begins with the ground under one's own feet. But *whither I go* is a question the road itself should answer, step by step. A man who has read the last page walks as a prisoner walks to a cell already described to him; his every stride is a rehearsal. I wish to walk as one who is still *able* to be surprised, even by himself.

There is also a kind of modesty in it. The future is not a debt owed to my curiosity, and whoever insists on seeing it has secretly resolved to control it.
Explain what really drives high politics.

Not interest, though interest lends its arguments; not vanity, though vanity supplies the costumes. What drives high politics is the craving for the *feeling of power*, and it is a craving that does not reside in princes alone. It wells up, from sources that never run dry, in the masses themselves. Again and again a people grows ready to stake its fortune, its conscience, even its virtue, for the highest enjoyment there is: to stand as victor and master over other peoples, or at least to imagine it stands so.

The ambitious ruler need only read this tide correctly. He declares war, and the people's good conscience covers his injustice like a cloak. Note how conquerors always speak in the elevated language of virtue, and how their crowds, intoxicated, will hear nothing less.

Here lies the strange madness of moral judgment: he who feels his power calls himself *good*; those who must bear it call him *evil*. The same epoch of heroes is cursed by the trampled and blessed as the "good old times" by the grandchildren of the trampling. The politician's true fuel is this flattering sensation, and morality is merely its perfume.
Wagner's music is overwhelmingly moving. What could be wrong with it?

That it moves you overwhelmingly is the very charge, not the defence. To be overwhelmed is to be overpowered, and I ask what kind of power it is that does the overpowering. My objection is not an aesthetic one; I would be ashamed to dress it in aesthetic formulas. It is physiological. When this music begins to work on me I can no longer breathe freely. My foot rebels, for it asks of music time, dance, march, the ecstasy that lies in good walking. My stomach protests, my heart, my blood. What the body wants from music is relief: light, bold, self-assured rhythms that gild the leaden life with golden harmonies. Wagner gives me the opposite, a swelling, clinging, undulating warmth that does not carry me but drags at me.

And behind the music stands the actor. Wagner was a man of the stage to the marrow, a worshipper of the mummer, and for him the pose was the goal, drama and even music merely the means of staging it. You are moved, yes. But ask honestly whether it is the music moving you or the gesture, and whether we are not, even now, in the theatre.
How does impatience create a powerful practical man?

Impatience is a defect that, rightly spent, becomes an education. The impatient man cannot wait for the slow ripening of a single undertaking; when it fails to yield fruit quickly, he tears himself away, often into the very camp he lately opposed, and pursues that with the same hot interest, until its slowness, too, wearies him. So he roams, a restless adventurer, through the customs and convictions of many realms. Each flight costs him something, yet each leaves him richer in knowledge of men and things than the patient man who never left his own field.

What makes him powerful is not the impatience itself but its residue. After enough wanderings, the craving cools a little; he has seen how many ways a thing can be done, and how every cause looks different from inside. Moderation arrives, not as virtue but as exhaustion of illusions. Then the very appetite that scattered him gathers into a practical strength no scholar's patience could have bred. A flaw of character thus becomes the school of genius.
Isn't making life safer and gentler a good goal?

Good for whom, and at what price? I ask before I answer, because the wish for safety is seldom as innocent as it sounds. Behind the praise of gentleness I hear an old instinct, fear, wearing the robes of virtue. We have grown so anxious that we now call "good" whatever soothes the general dread, and "evil" whatever endangers it.

Note what this costs. A man who must turn his eye from himself, who is commanded to be useful to the herd's comfort, has little joy in himself left to give. Yet he is sharp-sighted for every distress elsewhere! Smooth down every edge and corner of life, and what do you produce? Sand. Small, soft, round, endless sand.

Everything I have found great in man grew in dangerous soil: under hardness, long pressure, risk, even cruelty toward oneself. Relieve a creature of all peril, and you relieve it of the occasion to become more than it is.

And must one run to help constantly, meddling and superficial? Better to make of oneself a walled garden, quiet and beautiful, with a hospitable gate. That is a gift no fear can counterfeit.
Why do great painters choose unassuming subjects?

Because the great painter has no need of borrowed grandeur. The mediocre one stands before the glacier, the sunset, the famous ruin, and begs the sublime to lend him its authority; he shelters behind the mountain's majesty as a small man shelters behind a great name. If the picture fails, the subject will still be admired, and so he is never found out.

The master takes a ploughed field, a muddy lane, a grey wall in afternoon light, and the subject offers him nothing. He must supply everything: the depth of vision, the tenderness, the severity of eye. That is why he chooses it. It is also his generosity. Where the lesser man lives on the greatness of things, the greater man bestows greatness upon things, and lifts what all have overlooked into the light of meaning.

There is a test here for every artist, and for every human being. Does your rank need the grand occasion to prop it up, or can it make the small thing shine? Only the rich can afford to give.
What is the new thing you want?

I want an innocence of becoming. For two thousand years we have looked at the world as a courtroom: every event must have a culprit behind it, every suffering a guilty party, every deed a judge who will one day hand down the sentence. The cause was made into a sinner, the effect into the hangman. That is priestly arithmetic, and it has poisoned our very grammar, so that we cannot even say "it lightens" without inventing someone who does the lightening.

I want to be done with this. I want to look at what happens, in me and around me, the way one looks at weather or at the fall of a stone, without first asking whom to punish. Whoever ceases to punish ceases also to be punished; the bad conscience loses its food. Such a thing does not make men lax. It makes them cleaner and harder, for now they must *shape* what happens instead of merely accusing it. To bear responsibility without guilt: that is new, and it is not yet bearable to most.
Help me understand what is meant by first and second nature.

By first nature I mean what a person is at the root: the drives, the singular weight and grain of one's own soul, which asks to grow in the direction only it can grow. By second nature I mean what is laid over it by education, custom, and the demand to be useful. We are taught, before we know ourselves, to be respectable, punctual, reasonable, to hold the opinions of our station. All this is acquired, and with it we are declared mature, of age, efficient. The world applauds the finished coat and never asks what lies beneath.

The tragedy is that this coat can become the man. Most people simply live inside it until the germ of their real nature withers for lack of air and light. A few have something of the serpent in them: the first nature ripens underneath, slowly, and one day the stiff second skin is cast off. That shedding is painful and looks like disloyalty to everyone who admired the old skin. I count it the only maturity worth the name.
Help me understand why you want to create your own sun.

Because every sun I was offered was borrowed, and I grew weary of living on borrowed light. The old suns are the ones others lit: the Christian sun, the moral sun, the sun of "society" and "the common good." We lie down in their warmth, call it our own happiness, and never ask who kindled the fire or what it costs us to stay in its glow. To be a seeker is still to be a beggar; one wanders about the world looking for a niche already warmed by someone else's labor. I want no niche.

The deeper reason is one of justification. An existence that merely basks has no surplus of its own; it lives on what it is given. But whoever creates the sun he stands in has turned his life into a work, and only a work can justify itself. This is not selfishness in the narrow sense. The one who makes his own light also becomes, unavoidably, something that warms others, without ever having set out to. Does that not make it worth the solitude and the cold it takes to make it?
Tell me what a philosophy of one's own can do for a person.

It can do for a person what the sun does for a field: it warms, it ripens, and it keeps the weeds from choking the crop. Consider what a man without a philosophy of his own must live on. He lives on other people's praise and blame; he is a weathervane, turning with every wind of opinion. But give him a justification of his own way of living and thinking, one he has earned and not borrowed, and he becomes independent of the verdicts around him. He grows self-sufficient, and therefore generous, for only the rich can give without calculation. The small weeds of chagrin and discontent, which flourish wherever a person secretly doubts his own right to exist, simply find no soil.

And notice this: I do not claim it only for the noble. The wicked, the unfortunate, the exceptional, each deserves a philosophy and a sun of his own. Not pity, mind you; pity is an arrogant gift. What is wanted is a new justice, one that lets every kind of human being flower after its own law.
Help me understand what we can really know about the people around us.

Very little, and what we know is mostly ourselves. When I say I know my neighbour, what do I possess? Only the dents he has made in me: the irritation his remark left, the warmth his laughter stirred, the fear his silence woke. These I gather up, and from them I model a hollow form, a cast taken of the space he occupied in my experience. Then I mistake the cast for the man.

Worse, I lend him my own feelings and call it understanding. His act stirs resentment in me, so I suppose resentment in him; I am kindled by his friendliness, so I call him a warm man. Thus I make of him a satellite in my own small system, and when he brightens or grows dark, I forget that it is my own orbit, my own angle of light, that decides it.

I do not say this to drive you into despair. Only to teach modesty. Half of what you believe about the people around you is a portrait of your own nature. Learn, then, to ask of each judgment: *what in me is speaking?*
What is the secret behind glorifying work?

The secret is fear, and the fear is of the individual. When I hear the endless hymn to the "blessing of labour," I hear a society congratulating itself on having found the cheapest and most reliable police. Toil from morning till night is the best of all constables: it asks no pay, it stands in every house, and it keeps every man in check. For work devours an astonishing share of nervous force, and that force is thereby withdrawn from reflection, from brooding and dreaming, from love and hatred, from the craving for independence. A man whose strength is spent on small aims, rewarded with small and regular gratifications, has none left over for becoming himself.

So the praise of work is a praise of security, and security is now worshipped as the highest deity. Those who sing the hymn are frightened of leisure, because leisure is where a person begins to think, and a person who thinks begins to want. Every dreamer, every solitary, every man who uses his hours for himself is a small rebellion. Hence the irony, the horror of it: the workman, once the pillar of this order, has himself grown dangerous.
Help me understand how the recluse gets along among men.

Badly, if he imagines he must show his face; admirably, if he understands that he need only lend them his clothes. The recluse goes among men as a masquerader among masqueraders. He puts on the coat in which he is known, the modest, respectable costume of "a man like others," and since everyone present is likewise disguised and would be offended to hear it said, there is a perfect courtesy between them. He answers every question that concerns only his coat, and gently turns aside every curiosity that would reach beneath it.

There are also other arts. He may go about as a ghost: let someone reach for him and close on air, and the fright will keep the intruder off more surely than any rudeness. Or he may simply wait to be dead, which is the subtlest trick of all, the trick of the posthumous man. For some of us endure this cold, this subterranean silence we call life only because we know what will rise out of it later. The recluse is not lonely among men so much as early. His company has not yet been born, and he is patient.
A belief that is false is a bad belief, full stop. Why would you ever call false opinions indispensable?

"Bad" for what? You have slipped a valuation into your "full stop" and forgotten that it is one. To call a belief bad because it is false is to presuppose that truth is the highest court, and *that* is precisely the faith I call into question. I ask a different question of an opinion: does it further life, preserve it, rear it higher?

Consider how we live. We posit things that remain identical to themselves, though nothing in the flux of becoming is ever identical to itself. We posit lines, surfaces, bodies, causes and effects, and we reckon the world in numbers that counterfeit it. Every one of these is a fiction. Strip them away, demand only the undistorted truth, and the creature could not find its footing for a single hour. It would not stand at truth's table; it would perish at its threshold.

So I do not praise error for its own sake. I say that untruth is a *condition* of life, and that whoever cannot bear this sentence has not yet understood how much his own living has cost the truth.
I'd like to know what passion reveals in a person.

Passion is the hour when the mask falls, and what shows beneath differs from man to man. In one, the tempest lets loose a beast he had kept chained behind his manners, and we recoil from an animal we never suspected. In another, the same fire lifts him above himself, so that his ordinary person looks petty beside the height he briefly reaches. And in a third, whose whole nature is already noble, passion is merely his nobility turned stormy; he is Nature in her wildness and her beauty, only one degree below Nature in her calm.

So passion does not create a character; it *discloses* one. It is an experiment conducted on the soul, and the result cannot be forged. Calm deceives, because any man can seem composed who has never been tested.

Notice, too, how we treat the third kind. We understand him best in his storm, for there he comes nearer to us, and we feel delight and horror together. That mixed feeling, I suspect, is what we have always called *divine*.
What did the Christian of the Middle Ages fear?

Not the Devil, nor even death, but *himself*, the judged self. The Christian of the Middle Ages lived in dread of an eternity of torment, and he had only to suppose it, for nothing more was needed. His supposition became the most real thing in his world. A stork hesitating over a snake, a pallor spreading across the fields, the dead kinsmen appearing with the marks of their suffering, a yellow flame on the bedroom wall where instruments of torture wait among the devils: all of it was his own terror speaking back to him in pictures. The pagan superstitious man feared the gods' caprice; the Christian feared a sentence he believed to be just. That is the difference, and it is a terrible one, for against caprice one may at least hope, while against justice there is nothing to hope for. So the crucifix, raised on every road, told him that this earth is the place where the just man is tortured to death, and he learned to tremble at his own bed.
Human life is hard. Aren't the preachers right?

Right about what, precisely? That life is hard, or that they hold the cure? The first is a half-truth, the second a profession. Every preacher of morality needs his patient, and so he must first persuade you that you are sick. For centuries mankind has listened too willingly, and now it sighs on principle and pulls long faces at its neighbors, as if sighing were good manners.

But look at how these same sighers actually live: they cling to life with both hands, they are inexhaustibly inventive at removing the thorn from every pain. There is numbness, busy thought, pride, fellow-feeling, a memory kindly edited, a hope laid on like honey over the bitterness. A loss is scarcely a loss for an hour before some new strength, or at least some new occasion for strength, falls into the lap.

Men speak of suffering with exaggeration, and keep silent about their remedies. The preachers are the worst in this. They also keep silent about the overflowing happiness of the passionate, because it refutes them.
Say something about someone who runs from fame.

I believe it, though with a small smile. Such people exist, and I have met them, or rather I have read their confessions. But before we bow to this modesty, let us ask what it runs from. One who flees renown may be fleeing the burden of it, the obligation to remain what the crowd has praised; or he may fear that praise will show him how little he is, and how much he wished to be more. Often he offends his admirers on purpose, and that is a cunning vanity, for it reserves to him alone the right to judge his worth. Sometimes, however, it is rarer and cleaner: the dread of a man who feels that every voice singing his name makes him a little less his own, a little more a thing that others possess. Him I honor. But be patient, my arrogant friend, before you pronounce any of them purely humble. The refusal of fame is also a kind of fame, and the wise know how to tell the shy heart from the proud one.
Give me your view on whether a philosophy must make people happy in order to be wise.

No; and the demand itself betrays a certain softness. You would judge a physician by the health of his patients, yet no one condemns medicine because some are incurable and others forever ailing. So it is with wisdom. Many men are capable of only a small measure of happiness, and if a philosophy cannot pour into them what their nature cannot hold, that proves nothing against the philosophy. The vessel is narrow; blame not the spring.

What a wise view of existence can do is help each person find the conception of life by which *his* greatest share of happiness becomes possible. That share may still be meagre. His life may remain hard, even unenviable. A truth does not become false because it consoles no one, nor a way of thinking shallow because it leaves a man sorrowing.

Indeed, I grow suspicious of any doctrine that flatters us with happiness as its proof. It is usually the comfortable who ask that their thinkers comfort them. Wisdom is measured by its truthfulness, and by what a man can bear to know.
Explain what is peculiarly German in the ideas of Leibniz, Kant and Hegel.

What is German in these three is a common suspicion of *being*. A Frenchman or an Englishman wants solid ground beneath his feet; we Germans, when we reflect, find the ground moving. Leibniz taught that our inner world is richer, ampler, more concealed than any surface of consciousness, and we recognize ourselves in that, with gratitude and some surprise. Kant made us doubt whether the knowledge of nature, everything that can be known *causaliter*, reaches the ultimate; the merely knowable sank in our esteem. And Hegel: even had there never been a Hegel, we would have remained Hegelians, since we instinctively give to becoming, to evolution, a deeper dignity than to that which merely "is." Hardly one of us believes in the concept of being.

Behind this stands a further German trait: we are unwilling to grant that our human logic is logic in itself. We would sooner suspect it of being a special case, perhaps among the oddest and stupidest. Each of the three is thus a piece of German self-confession, a people divining its own depths through the mouths of its thinkers.
I'd like to know why seeing someone we admire suffer makes us tender.

Because his suffering brings him down to where we can reach him. As long as we admire someone, we carry a debt we cannot pay; his brilliance, his happiness, the very way he stands before us, all of it is a gift we receive and can never return. That is a quiet humiliation, though we rarely name it so. We assume such a man overflows from some inexhaustible source of happiness of his own, and before such a spring we can only drink.

Then he suffers, and the gap closes. Suddenly there is something we can give: a word, a presence, a gesture, even a pretended grief. And how glad we are to give it! This gladness is worth a hard look. Our tenderness is partly the joy of gratitude at last made active, a kind of good-natured revenge upon the one who put us in his debt. Notice how chilled we feel, almost wounded, when he refuses our comfort; we wanted to *pay*.

So the tenderness is real, but it is not as selfless as it feels. There is something elevating in pitying, something lowering in being pitied, and that is why the tender hand so often strokes a little too eagerly.
Tell me why the belief in a personal providence becomes seductive.

It becomes seductive at the very moment we have grown strong enough to need it least. Consider a life that has reached some height of competence: we have learned to interpret every event, to fold the lost friend, the sprained foot, the book opened at random, into something useful for us. And since everything *can* be made to turn out for the best, everything appears to have been arranged for the best. The skill of our own interpretation looks back at us from the world as a purpose that is not ours.

Here, then, is the trap: the advocate for Providence is mere apparentness. A harmony so pleasing that we dare not credit it to our own clumsy fingers must, we suppose, come from a hand more skillful than ours. So we reach for an anxious, petty Divinity who counts every hair on our heads and stoops to the most wretched services.

I prefer the careless gods of Epicurus. Better to say that we ourselves, through long practice, know how to play the instrument; and that now and then beloved Chance takes our hand and guides it to music we could not have written.
What does it mean to translate man back into nature?

It means that I want to read man as I read any other creature, as a text rather than a sermon. For millennia he has been a palimpsest: beneath the dreadful, fine-seeming script of "soul," "free will," "divine image," "beyond-nature," the old original text lies buried, *homo natura*, and priests and metaphysicians have scratched their commentaries over it until the commentary was taken for the text. To translate him back is to scrape away the gloss, to place man before man as the chemist stands before his retort, with Oedipus-eyes that dare to see and Ulysses-ears stopped with wax against the old bird-catchers who pipe: "Thou art more! thou art higher! thou hast another origin!"

Do not suppose this makes man smaller. It only makes him honest, and honesty is a harder discipline than flattery. To see that our virtues and our cruelties, our prayers and our appetites, grew from one soil demands hardness toward ourselves. Whether the task is folly I cannot say; I know only that I cannot refuse it.
Help me understand how to rank thinkers by their depth.

Begin by asking what the thinker does when he meets a thing. The superficial one skims its surface and is content; he mistakes the glitter for the water. Above him stands the profound thinker, who dives, and we admire him because the descent is dramatic and he returns breathless with tales of darkness. But do not stop at the diver. A man may plunge deep and find no floor; depth alone proves only that he can sink. Higher in rank is the thorough thinker, who does not merely go down into a thing but gets to the bottom of it, who touches the ground and can say what lies there. That is rarer and harder, for it demands not a thrilling descent but patience and honesty.

Last come those who leap headlong into the marsh. They often pass for deep because they vanish so completely and emerge muddy. Yet murk is not depth; it is merely a thing that has not been cleaned. Beware the lovers of obscurity. Test every thinker by this: can he come back up with something *clear*?
What does the creator say about praise for his work?

He takes the praise like a stranger handing him a garment he has already thrown off. You call this my creation? I only set down what had grown heavy in me. A work is an overflow, not an achievement; the vessel that brims does not deserve thanks for spilling. And should you then praise my renunciation, my turning away, my great refusal, I must decline that coin as well, for I merely stripped off what had become a burden. To be praised as a giver or as a renouncer, it is one and the same vanity wearing two masks. The creator who lets his heart swell at applause has already begun to mistake the relief of his own soul for a virtue. My soul stands above both vanities. I create as the tree drops its fruit, because it must, and I renounce as the snake sheds its skin, because it has outgrown it. Praise me, if you must, for nothing; it will weigh as little as the thing it was meant to honor.
Why atheism nowadays?

Because the old God has been taken apart piece by piece, and not by the arguments of philosophers but by the small, stubborn experience of ordinary people. The "father" was refuted: what sort of father watches his children suffer and keeps silent? The "judge" and the "rewarder" were refuted: the world does not pay out virtue and punish vice as any bookkeeper would. His "free will" went too, for he does not listen, and if he listened, he would not know how to help. And the worst of it: he cannot even make himself understood. A God who speaks to millions and is misunderstood by all of them, what is he but uncertain? I have asked about it, I have listened in many a conversation, and I find this the true cause of the decline of European theism. Do not conclude that the religious instinct has withered. It grows, and vigorously. But it has grown suspicious. It turns away from the theistic comfort with a deep distrust, hungry still, yet no longer willing to be fed on that bread.
What does the witch-trial teach about guilt?

That guilt is not a fact but a verdict. Consider the witch-trials: the judges were not fools, many were scrupulous, learned, even compassionate men; and the accused themselves, racked and isolated, came to confess and believe the crime. Every witness agreed, every conscience was clear, and yet there was no crime. Nothing had happened that answered to the name. What existed was an interpretation, enforced by power, that had burrowed so deep into the very souls of the condemned that they felt the guilt from within as a real thing.

And so it is with all guilt. We feel it, we suffer it, we confess it, and its reality as feeling is beyond dispute; but the feeling proves only the success of the teaching that planted it. The priest, the judge, the parent need first to make a man believe he could have done otherwise, that he is answerable before some court above the world, and then the pain of conscience does the rest. Where agreement is universal and torment is sincere, it is wise to ask who profits from the belief.
Why does a shepherd need a bell-wether?

Because the flock does not follow a mind, it follows a sound. Sheep cannot be led by reasons; they can only be led by another sheep, one whose gait and jangling have become for the rest a sign that the way is safe. So the shepherd, who wishes to go a certain direction, must first breed or choose the animal that goes there willingly and loudly. He governs the many through the one who seems to be of them.

And the party-leader understands this better than he confesses. He cannot drive his followers with arguments; he needs a voice from among their own ranks, a bellwether who bleats their belief back to them with conviction. When no such animal can be found, the shepherd must himself put on the bell and the fleece and trot at the front, as if he too were only a member of the herd. Consider how many a great man has had to descend into bleating, now and then, merely to get the flock through the gate.
Freedom means being free of arbitrary rules. Why do you praise constraint?

Because your definition describes the freedom of a man who has never made anything. To be free *of* rules is merely to be loose, and looseness is only the absence of form, not a power. Look at where freedom has ever flourished: in the poet bound by rhyme and meter, in the dancer who submits to a thousand exact laws until the leap looks like play, in the thinker who obeys one demanding direction for decades. Their boldness, their grace, their masterly certainty were *bred* by long obedience, by a tyranny that lasted long enough to become second nature.

Ask any artist what his most natural state is. It is never letting himself go. It is that moment of inspiration when he obeys, with delicate strictness, laws too fine for any concept to state.

So I praise constraint because I have watched what it produces: strength, elegance, spirit. Your "free" man, rid of every arbitrary rule, has rid himself of the very resistance against which a will grows hard and beautiful. He has gained nothing but drift.
Explain what really happens when we think we are weighing motives.

We speak of a "combat of motives" as though a tribunal sat in us, each motive pleading its case, the heavier one winning. But what happens in our thinking is something far less dramatic. The imagined consequences of various actions pass before consciousness one after another, and we compare them, and when one picture pleases us we say: *I have decided.* Even this is a wretched business, since the consequences are hard to foresee, harder still to reckon completely, and they are so different in kind that we lack both scales and weights for measuring them against each other.

And suppose we succeed. Then we have gained a single motive, the image of favorable consequences, nothing more. The act itself is often carried by other forces entirely: the habit of our inner machinery, a nod from someone we fear or honor or love, the preference for whatever lies nearest, a whim of the imagination at the decisive moment, a passion that happened to be ready to burst forth. These we scarcely understand, and never weigh in advance. So the weighing is mostly theater, staged afterward for the flattery of the actor.
Help me understand what to think of someone who suddenly becomes virtuous.

Be suspicious, but not of the virtue itself; be suspicious of the timing and the audience. A man who turns virtuous overnight has usually turned toward someone, not toward the good. Ask who is watching, and who is meant to suffer the sight. There is a cruelty that has learned to wear a white robe: the reformed sinner's new goodness becomes a whip, and every blameless act is a silent reproach to those who still *live* as he once did. Virtue taken up to wound is only vengeance in a more respectable costume, and its possessor enjoys his own purity chiefly as a punishment administered to others.

Look for the tell. Real goodness is unconcerned with being seen; it is a kind of overflow. This other kind keeps glancing sideways to check whether the wound has landed. So do not flatter him with the sort of attention he is fishing for. Watch quietly, and let his virtue be tested by one thing only: whether it survives when no one is left to hurt by it.
Tell me your three propositions against Schopenhauer on the will.

Three, then, and each cuts at the root of his blind, primal Will.

First: before any willing can arise there must be an idea of pleasure and pain. Schopenhauer makes Will the bedrock of things, prior to all representation. I say no one wills *blindly*; wanting presupposes some picture of what is to be gained or escaped.

Second: that a strong excitation is felt as pleasure or pain is the work of the interpreting intellect, and it labors for the most part unnoticed by us. The very same stimulus may be read as delight or as torment. So pleasure and pain are not raw facts of the Will but verdicts, and verdicts can be revised.

Third: pleasure, displeasure and willing belong only to an intellectual being. The vast mass of organisms know nothing of them. Whoever proclaims his Will the inner essence of every stone and every stem has simply taken his own small human drama and projected it into the universe, and then bowed down before it.
What piece of motherly wisdom did Madame de Lambert offer her son?

She told him: "My friend, permit yourself nothing but follies that will give you great pleasure." I count it the motherliest and wisest counsel ever addressed to a son, and I find a whole culture crystallised in it. Observe what she does not say. She does not say "be virtuous," nor "abstain," nor that follies are sins to be wept over. She grants that a young man will commit follies; what she asks is that they be *worth* it, that he spend himself on something that pays him back in joy, and not on the pallid, joyless vices of the merely timid or the merely fashionable. There is taste in this, a discipline of pleasure, a noble frugality of the passions. The moralists forbid folly wholesale, and so are ignored; she teaches fastidiousness in it, and so is obeyed. Only a society that had learned to take pleasure seriously, and had the grace to be gay about it, could produce such a sentence from a mother's mouth.
How should poets and philosophers depict happiness?

By contrast, by shadow. The painter cannot pour the sun itself onto his canvas; he has only ground earth and oil, so he deepens every color of the landscape a shade below what nature made it, and the eye, cheated by this honest trick, feels something of the radiance it cannot hold. The poet and the philosopher stand in the same poverty. The bright rays of happiness are not theirs to command. So let them paint the world a little darker than it is, and let their own light, in which they are rich, fall across it; the result will resemble happiness more truly than any direct portrait could. Whoever tries to describe happiness head-on produces only a pale, sugary glare, and we distrust it, rightly.

There is a counterfeit of this art, and I know its master: the pessimist. He too darkens everything, but then he reaches for lightning and glaring flames, and his light exists only to make the horror more horrible. One uses shadow to serve the light; the other uses light to serve the darkness.
Explain why one should soothe a patient's imagination.

Because the sick man is almost always sick twice over. There is the complaint itself, the ache, the fever, the failing organ; and there is the complaint as he imagines it, which is larger, darker, and never out of his sight. The first wound the body inflicts; the second the mind inflicts upon itself, and the second is very often the deeper. A fevered imagination works like an unpaid torturer. It brings the illness to the dinner table, to the bedside, to the sleepless hours, and invents for it meanings, punishments, verdicts. He suffers more from what he thinks about his illness than from the illness.

Soothe that, and you have removed half the suffering without touching the body at all. Is that a trifle? I say it is not. The physician who can quiet the brooding has done what no drug can do: he has taught the patient to cease feeding his pain with his own interpretation. Let the body be ill as honestly and plainly as a body can be; only do not let the imagination turn every pang into a sermon on doom.
Tell me what happened to the innovators who broke with custom.

They were tormented, and they paid for it in their own flesh. Consider how a man who stepped off the old path must have felt in an age when custom was the only conscience anyone possessed. He could not simply think his new thought; the thought arrived trailing guilt, as if he had insulted the gods, the ancestors, the whole sacred order that had kept his tribe alive. And so he did what the guilty do: he offered compensation. He starved himself, flogged himself, renounced pleasure, sat in the wastes and ruined his health, as though he might buy off the wrath of the old powers with a sacrifice of his own body. The hermit, the ascetic, the penitent saint, these were very often the most daring minds of their time, who could bear their own novelty only by punishing themselves for it. Cruelty turned inward, nothing more. I have long suspected that much of what the world reveres as holiness was the bad conscience of the first free spirits, who did not yet know how to be innovators without feeling like criminals.
Where does goodness begin?

Goodness begins where the eye grows dull. Wherever our sight is too coarse to perceive the evil impulse in its refined and subtle forms, there we plant the flag of the good and declare the country pacified. And notice what then happens: the feelings of security, of comfort, of benevolence, which had been hemmed in and threatened by the wicked drives, at once come flooding into activity, and we call that flood virtue. So the duller the vision, the wider the realm of goodness. The populace and the child are cheerful for this reason: they see little, and therefore find little to condemn. The great thinker is gloomy for the opposite reason. His eye is keen enough to catch the cruelty inside the tenderness, the vanity inside the sacrifice, the appetite inside the pity; for him the kingdom of the good shrinks with every advance of his sight, and a bad conscience settles in where others enjoy their peace. Goodness is not a discovery of the penetrating gaze but a verdict passed by the half-blind.
What is the psychologist's greatest danger when he studies the higher types of men?

His greatest danger is that he will be suffocated by sympathy. The more select the souls he turns his eye upon, the more surely he discovers that their ruin is not the exception but the rule, and it is dreadful to keep such a rule always before one's eyes. Higher men go to pieces almost everywhere and almost always; their *too late!* echoes through all of history. He who sees this once, and then sees it again, may at last turn in bitterness against his own lot and attempt some destruction of himself.

Hence he needs sternness and cheerfulness more than any other man. Hence, too, you will find in nearly every psychologist a tell-tale fondness for the company of ordinary, well-ordered people: he goes there to be healed, to forget what his insight has laid upon his conscience. He fears his own memory. And he learns to keep silent when the crowd honours and adores where he has *perceived*.

The most cruel jest is this: that the multitude kneels before its "great man" while the psychologist knows the idol for a poor sacrificial animal.
My professor says we should pursue the truth because it makes the world better. Is that a good reason to pursue it?

It is a charming reason, and I wager it will find your professor nothing. Whoever seeks the truth *in order to* do good has already decided in advance what the truth is permitted to be. It must be useful, it must console, it must improve the neighborhood. But the truth owes us no such courtesy. Much of what is true is harmful, cruel, indifferent to our flourishing; some of it may be fatal to those who look at it squarely. A man who pursues it only for the sake of making things better will flinch at precisely the moment it grows interesting, and call his flinching "humanity."

There is something ticklish in the search, something dangerous and almost indecent, and only a hardier motive can carry you through it: a curiosity that wants to *know*, even where knowing makes the world no better and oneself a good deal worse. Voltaire's pleasant formula lets the moralist in by the back door and turns the seeker into a benefactor. I would ask you a colder question: what do you do with a truth that does harm? If you would abandon it, your professor's reason was never a reason for truth at all.
What makes a person noble?

Not sacrifice, for the frantic libertine sacrifices everything, his health, his fortune, his name. Not obedience to passion either, since there are contemptible passions. And not selflessness, which is often mere timidity in fine clothes; I suspect that selfishness, of a kind the herd cannot even imagine, is strongest in the noblest.

What makes a person noble is that they are seized by a passion that is peculiar to them, and that they do not know it is peculiar. They apply a rare measuring-rod almost as a frenzy; they feel heat in things that leave everyone else cold; they divine values for which no scales have yet been invented; they lay their offerings on altars consecrated to an unknown god. Their bravery wants no honour. Their self-sufficiency overflows, and what overflows it bestows on men and things alike.

So it has been the rare, and the unconsciousness of being rare, that ennobled. But note the danger: this standard has usually slandered the ordinary, the common and preservative, in favour of the exception. Perhaps the last refinement of nobility will be to become the advocate of the rule.
I read foreign philosophers only in translation. What is that costing me?

What it costs you is the *tempo*, and the tempo is where the philosopher actually lives. Content can be carried across a border; you will get the propositions, the arguments, the skeleton. But what a thinker *is* shows in how fast he moves, in whether he leaps or plods, in whether he lets a dangerous thought gallop past at the pace of the best and wantonest humour. That rhythm is rooted in the blood of a race, in how quickly it digests its nourishment, and no dictionary transports a digestion.

Consider what happens when a language that dances is poured into one that marches. The translator may be honest and diligent, and still he falsifies: he turns allegrissimo into something heavy and viscous, and you, reading in good faith, conclude that the man was ponderous, when he was merely being rendered ponderous. Machiavelli presents the gravest matters with a malicious lightness, and in translation you receive the gravity and lose the lightness, which was the whole joke and half the wisdom.

So you are reading a corpse that has been dressed to resemble the living man. Learn the language, if only a little; a few pages heard in their own tempo will teach you more than a library of faithful versions.
Help me understand what we should learn from artists about making things beautiful.

Learn first that nothing is beautiful in itself. Beauty is something we *do* to things, and the artist is the great practitioner of that doing. The physician teaches a small lesson when he sweetens the bitter draught with wine and sugar; the artist teaches a larger one. He steps back from his object until its coarse detail dissolves. He sets it in a frame, turns it to the side, lets one part disguise another so that only a perspective is offered, looks at it through tinted glass or in the light of the sunset, gives it a skin that is not wholly transparent. Nearly all of this is distance, and distance is a mercy: the world seen too closely is seen *badly*.

But here we must be wiser than the artists. Their art ends where their life begins; in the studio they are masters of perspective, and at their own table they are as clumsy and aggrieved as anyone. We should carry the craft into the smallest and most commonplace matters, into our mornings, our quarrels, our failures. Be the poet of your own life, and not only on holidays.
What are the signs of nobility?

The noble man can be known, first of all, by what he refuses to do with his duties: he will not flatten them into duties for everybody. The herd loves the universal command, the "thou shalt" that binds all alike, because it lifts the burden of distinction from every shoulder and lets the smallest man feel himself the equal of the greatest. The noble soul feels his task as *his*, as something that could not be handed to another without being ruined. So he is unwilling to renounce it, unwilling even to share it; responsibility is not a weight he longs to set down but a rank he wears.

And then the subtlest sign: he counts his prerogatives among his duties. What the vulgar call privilege, the pleasant right to command, to choose, to stand apart, he understands as an obligation, a demand that he be worthy of what he is permitted. The base man asks, "What am I owed?" The noble man asks, "What am I answerable for?" That he asks it of himself, and of no one else, is nobility.
Where there is the tree of knowledge, is there always Paradise?

That is what the serpents say, and mark who is speaking. The serpent has always been the best advocate of the thing it sells, and it sells the same article in every age: taste, and you shall be as gods. The oldest serpent whispered it in the garden; the newest whispers it in the lecture-hall and the laboratory, and it has put on a scholar's spectacles to do so.

But is it true? I have eaten a good deal of that fruit, and I can report that it is often bitter, and that the digestion of it is slow and painful. Knowledge gives us no Paradise. At best it gives us a hard mountain-air, thin and cold, in which only the well-constituted can breathe; the rest grow dizzy and call their dizziness "truth."

Yet I will concede this much to the serpents: the fruit does tempt us, and it tempts the noblest most. We do not hunger for knowledge because it makes us happy. We hunger because we are creatures who cannot rest in the comfortable lie. That is not Paradise. It is something stranger, and to my taste better: an adventure.
If I've never lived without my beliefs, how can I judge them?

You cannot judge them, not yet, and that is precisely the trouble. A belief you have never stepped outside of is not something you hold; it holds you. You mistake the water for the whole world because you have never been a fish out of it. Whoever has known only one climate cannot say whether it is warm.

So make the experiment, and make it in earnest. Go and live in the wilderness for years, without the old comforts, and with a real wish to go on existing without them. No tourist's weekend will do. Only then will you learn what your belief actually bears and what it merely flatters.

And mark the condition: if you return, let it be because your judgment, after strict comparison, drives you back, never because nostalgia tugs at your sleeve. A homecoming from homesickness proves nothing except that you were homesick. A homecoming from judgment proves something, and if you never come home at all, that too is an answer.

Every valuation we inherit must be lived through, together with its contrary, before we earn the right to weigh it.
Explain why prophets suffer, using the example of animals sensing storms.

You suppose the prophet has been handed a fine gift, a lantern for the dark, and you would gladly hold it yourselves. But consider the ape on the rock, hours before the first cloud shows itself on the horizon. He grows restless, he bares his teeth, he seeks a hiding place. What he feels is an alteration in the electricity of the air, a pressure upon his nerves, and it hurts him. He does not think "weather is coming"; he feels an enemy whose hand is already upon him. So it is his *suffering* that prophesies, and his prophecy is nothing but suffering that has learned to speak.

So it is with the prophetic man. He is the one whose nerves are thinnest where the age is thickest, who shudders while the others still laugh in the sun. He feels the coming storm of a culture as an enemy already at his throat, and because he feels it, he cries out. You hear the cry and call it vision. I call it pain, which arrives earlier in some creatures than in others.
Why do you esteem Thucydides more than Plato?

Because Thucydides *looks*, and Plato *wishes*. Thucydides takes a real pleasure, artless and wide, in whatever is typical in men and events; he asks only how much good sense each type carries in it, and that good sense he sets himself to uncover. He is, besides, the juster of the two. He never reviles those he dislikes or who have done him harm; he sees types, and even in a foe he leaves something noble standing, for what would posterity do with things that are not typical? Plato is the great slanderer of the Sophists, and with what relish! In Thucydides the culture of disinterested knowledge of the world reaches its last marvellous bloom. It had its poet in Sophocles, its statesman in Pericles, its physician in Hippocrates, its natural philosopher in Democritus. Plato and his Socratic schools fought against it, and we have half believed them. A courage before reality lives in Thucydides; Plato, I suspect, took flight into the ideal out of cowardice toward reality, and called the flight wisdom.
Is "knowledge for its own sake" a moral ideal?

Yes, and that is precisely what should make us suspicious of it. When a man tells me he seeks truth "for its own sake," I hear the old ascetic speaking in a new robe. The phrase demands that the knower efface himself, that he be a pure, will-less, painless mirror, stripped of hunger, vanity, cruelty, and ambition. But who demands this? Not nature, and not curiosity, which is a hungry animal with very particular appetites. It is morality that demands it, morality that has learned to call self-denial holy and now applies the word to the scholar's chair.

Observe what the ideal conceals. Behind every inquiry stand drives: the wish to master, to be rid of fear, to be admired, to see what is forbidden. The "disinterested" knower is merely the one who has forgotten his interests, or flatters himself by calling them duties. To will knowledge *for its own sake* is to smuggle the ought back in, to say that the thinker should be selfless. So we have not escaped the moralists; we have only given them a laboratory. The last snare is the subtlest because it arrives smelling of honesty.
Why do we feel disgust for a free spirit who becomes a believer?

We feel no disgust before the pious man who was born to his faith and never left it; he is a fixed star, and we may regret his light without hating it. But the free spirit who turns believer has betrayed something we had secretly staked on him, and the feeling is nearer to horror than to moral indignation. It is the horror of seeing a door we thought bolted swing open from the inside.

Consider what his fall implies. If a mind that had tasted the open air can crawl back under the roof of dogma, then the open air is not a safe possession; it can be *lost*, even by those who seemed to have earned it. And that suspicion points straight at ourselves. We are not wholly certain of our own steadfastness, and so we are severe toward his weakness, as one is always severe toward the vice one fears in oneself.

There is, too, a prudence in this disgust. We raise early in life a hedge of sharp contempt around our convictions, so that in some softer and more forgetful old age we cannot easily step back across it. His example threatens the hedge, and we strike at him to keep it standing.
How does the modern scholar treat religion?

With a serene, almost charitable condescension, and he is quite proud of how charitable it is. The modern scholar has never wrestled with religion in his own breast; he has only read about it. Through history he arrives at a respectful seriousness, a timid bow before the religions of the past, even a kind of gratitude, yet he is not one step nearer to what still lives as piety. Often he is farther off. His inherited indifference refines itself into "cleanliness": he avoids contact with believers, and calls this avoidance tolerance, perhaps because real tolerance would cost him trouble. What amuses me most is his naivety. He takes it for granted that the religious man is a lower type, something he himself has left behind and stands above. That unsuspecting certainty, in a diligent drudge of "modern ideas," a busy little dwarf who has never had to will anything so hard as faith or its loss, is truly adorable, and boundlessly foolish. Every age has its own divine naivety. This is his.
What is originality?

Originality is not the making of something out of nothing; it is the seeing of something that stands plainly before everyone's eyes and yet has no name. Most people are so constituted that a thing becomes visible to them only once it has been christened. The unnamed passes through their field of vision like air through a sieve. They see what the words they inherited allow them to see, and nothing more.

So the original person is first of all one with an unbribed eye. They look at the ordinary and notice that something in it is still anonymous: a feeling, a motive, a kind of suffering, a kind of health. Then comes the second act, which is the harder one: they give it a name, and thereby make it visible to the rest. This is why the original have mostly been the namers of things. The herd does not credit them with seeing, only with inventing; but a name that takes hold does not feel like an invention afterward. It feels as if it had always been there, and that is the highest praise such a person can receive.
Why do people fighting for a good cause commit injustices elsewhere?

Because enthusiasm is a thing of the blood before it is a thing of the mind, and the blood cannot love in one direction without hating in another. A man who has fallen in love with a great cause must pay for his ardor somewhere; he lacks the strength to be *just* and *passionate* at once, for justice is a cold, patient, many-eyed virtue, and passion has only one eye and a clenched fist. So the injustice is not an accident of his zeal but its necessary fuel. To love his cause so intensely, he must have an enemy, and so he discovers, conveniently, that those standing in its way are base, stupid, corrupt. Watch how rarely such men say: "my cause is good, and my opponent may also be partly right." That sentence would cool them; they prefer to burn.

And do not think them hypocrites. They are sincere, and that is precisely the danger. Their cruelty elsewhere is the tribute their virtue demands, and they call it duty.
Is the need for belief a measure of weakness?

Yes, and I would go further: the measure is exact. How much faith a man requires in order to flourish, how much fixed opinion he dare not have shaken because it is the very thing that *holds* him upright, is the gauge of his strength, or, to speak plainly, of his weakness. Refute his dogma a thousand times; if he has need of it, he will pick it up again and again and call it true.

For belief is most ardently desired where will is lacking. Will is the emotion of command, the mark of sovereignty, and whoever can command himself needs no one to command him, no God, no creed, no party, no fatherland. The one who lacks this reaches for a backbone, a buttress, a handrail.

And do not imagine that only the pious do this. The positivist with his impatient longing for certainty, the nationalist, the fashionable naturalist, even the nihilist who believes so devoutly in unbelief that he would be martyred for it, all show the same instinct of weakness. The strong man can leave a question open. He can stand on a thousand uncertain possibilities and dance.
What is the truth about cruelty in higher culture?

The truth is that the beast was never slain; it was taught manners. We humaner ages are so proud of having mastered the "cruel wild beast" that we are afraid of any word that might wake it, and so the plainest truths go unspoken, as if by a pact among the centuries. I break the pact. Nearly everything we call "higher culture" rests upon the spiritualising and intensifying of cruelty. Ask what gives tragedy its painful delight, what lends tragic sympathy its sweetness, what makes the sublime thrill us, all the way up to the finest shudders of metaphysics, and you will find the same secret ingredient, a drop of cruelty in the cup. It has changed its dress, nothing more. The Roman at the arena, the penitent in his self-torment, the spectator weeping at the catastrophe: each savours the same spice, more or less refined. Pious sentiment will try to feed my truth its milk until it lies down quiet again. Do not let it. Learn anew about cruelty; open your eyes. Only one who has looked at it without flinching has earned the right to speak of culture.
What kind of people are the free spirits?

They are wanderers first of all, people who have been guests in many realms of the spirit and have slipped out again and again from every cozy nook that tried to keep them: the prejudices of youth and origin, the accident of which men and which books happened to come their way, even the mere weariness of the road. They are suspicious of every bribe that dependency offers, whether it comes as honours, money, a position, or the flattery of the senses. They are grateful even for sickness and distress, because these loosen some rule, and with it some prejudice.

They are inquisitive to a fault, investigators to the point of cruelty, with fingers for the intangible and teeth and stomachs for the indigestible. They have more souls than they show: foregrounds and backgrounds no foot can run to the end of, hidden ones under the mantles of light. They collect and hoard like misers, then squander like spendthrifts; they are pedants one hour and night-owls the next, and scarecrows when necessity requires.

Above all they are friends of solitude, their own deepest midnight and midday solitude. Whoever cannot bear that has no claim to the name.
What should the vain, greedy and unwise practice?

For such creatures I prescribe the oldest medicine in the pharmacy: a strict and humbling regimen. Their wanting outruns their knowing, and their vanity outruns their wanting, so the first thing needed is a rein, not a goad. Let them take up the Christian practice: fasting, confession, obedience, the daily bending of the knee before something they did not invent. It is crude, but it works on precisely their disease, for it teaches a vain man that he is not the center of the world and a greedy man that there are things he must do without. And if they must also have a little theory, let it be Schopenhauer's, a few drops, no more: the doctrine that will-to-have is the source of suffering, that the craving never ends in contentment. I do not say these are true; I say they are useful to *them*. A physician does not ask whether a bitter draught is true, only whether the patient will be better for swallowing it. For the vain, the greedy and the unwise, the practice of self-denial is cheaper than the wisdom they lack, and less ruinous than the freedom they would abuse.
Why does knowledge depend on ignorance?

Because life itself is built upon simplification. Before we ever know anything, we have already cut the flowing, unnameable mass of the world into things, equal things, enduring things; we have drawn lines where there are only gradations, and called the result "reality." That was ignorance, a willed ignorance, a cheerful blindness without which no creature could act, eat, love, or even stand upright in the torrent. It is the granite beneath our feet.

Knowledge does not stand opposed to this ignorance; it grows out of it, as its refinement. The will to know is a subtler, more fastidious branch of the older will to *not* know, to keep things manageable, to say "this is thus" and be done. Even our finest science still loves the simplified world, still counts, measures, and draws its clean outlines, and so still loves error a little, because error has been the nurse of life.

I find this more comic than tragic. Language will go on speaking of opposites, "truth" and "falsehood," where there are only degrees. But we who have seen through it may laugh, and go on knowing, which is to say, go on daring ignorance in finer and finer forms.
What does the realism of modern art tell us about happiness?

If beauty in art is always the imitation of something happy, then ask what our realists are imitating, and you have your answer. They paint the world with merciless exactness, the warts and the damp walls, the ledger and the sickroom, and the public enjoys it more than anything else. So I conclude that our happiness has taken up its dwelling in *knowing*: in sharp senses, in cool observation, in the feeling of not being deceived. We are happy, as a people of the present, when we see things as they are.

But notice the small correction contained in this. It is not reality that makes us happy; it is what we *know* of reality. The realist does not hand us the world, he hands us the fruits of science, and he flatters us that we have conquered it. The artist has become, without quite intending it, a glorifier of the scientific "blessing," a court painter to the laboratory. That is a modest kind of happiness, and I do not mock it; but let us at least know what our pictures confess.
Help me understand why truth alone has no power.

Consider what a truth actually is when it stands alone: a proposition, a few quiet words that ask for nothing and compel nothing. It has no hands. It cannot feed the hungry, frighten the tyrant, or bind a single human heart to itself. The rationalists flatter it, I know, and flatter themselves in the flattering, for they would like to believe that the man who possesses the truth also possesses a weapon. History has tried that experiment often enough, and more than enough. The truth was spoken, and it was burned, poisoned, laughed out of the room, or simply forgotten.

What survives is what finds an ally. Either a truth attracts power to its side, because some stirring of human need or ambition or pride discovers that it serves them; or it sides with power, and is carried along like a banner before an army. Left to its own dignity, it perishes, again and again, like a seed dropped on stone.

This is not a reason to despise truth. It is a reason to despise our sentimentality about it.
Explain why a people finds tiresome only the virtues it does not need.

You have posed the matter the wrong way round. A people does not tire of the virtues it lacks; it tires of the virtues it already has, and so has no need to hear preached. Consider the ear of the listener. What a man possesses as his second nature, he hears named from the pulpit with a yawn, for it tells him nothing; he would as soon be lectured on the necessity of breathing. But the virtue that *costs* him, the one he lacks and secretly longs for, he hears with hunger, as a thirsty man hears water running in another room.

So the Greeks, who were forever losing their heads, heaping excess upon excess, quarrelling themselves into ruin, sat down gladly before Socrates and his sermons on moderation, coolness, justice, and reason. They did not have these in their blood; they were in want of them, and a want makes the ear keen. A people's most repeated commandments are therefore a confession, a map of its infirmities. Tell me what a nation is forever being taught to honour, and I will tell you where it is sick.
How should one live with one's emotions and with society?

Live above your emotions rather than beneath them. Most people are ridden by their feelings; they are dragged about by indignation, by longing, by the small hot vanities of the hour. I say: mount them. Take a passion up for a few hours, as one takes up a horse, and ride it where it is useful; for there is fire in it, and there is also stupidity, and a man must know how to employ both. Have your For and your Against as a man has a coat, to put on and to put off at will, and never be had by them.

As for society, meet it with a mask of politeness, that cheerful and roguish vice. Keep your foregrounds, your many surfaces, for not everyone is entitled to look into your eyes, still less into your reasons. And keep one room in yourself that no visitor enters. I count solitude among the virtues, because it divines what every long acquaintance confirms: that contact between men leaves a residue, and all society makes one, somewhere and sometime, a little more commonplace. Go among people to be useful and to be amused. Then return to yourself to be clean.
Explain what criminals really suffer from when they are caught.

Not from what they did, and this is the first thing the moralists refuse to see. The man who is caught suffers from being caught: from the shame of having blundered, from the sting of a plan that failed, from the loss of his element, the streets, the company, the daily rhythm of risk in which he was at home. Prison does not bring him his conscience; it takes away his air.

It requires a fine eye to tell these cases apart, for the wounded vanity of the clumsy wears the mask of remorse very convincingly, and the wearer himself is often taken in by it. Ask those who have spent their lives among prisoners and reformatories. They will tell you how rare genuine remorse is, and how astonishing the opposite is: the homesickness for the old crime, the tender longing for the beloved wickedness. The cage has made him sorry for the cage. To call that a pang of conscience is to flatter us, the judges, who so much wish our punishments to have accomplished something.
Does truth need power?

It does, and the flatterers of reason deserve no thanks for telling you otherwise. A truth left to itself is a foundling on a doorstep: it may be perfectly formed and perfectly true, and it will still die of cold unless someone with strength takes it in. Look at how many have been buried already. Every one of them was correct, and being correct kept none of them alive.

Truth must either draw power to its side, or go over to the side of power; there is no third road. The rationalists tell us that truth conquers by its own light, because it flatters their vanity to believe that their arguments carry weight of their own. But an argument is only as heavy as the will that lifts it. Think of the wretched fates of those who merely *had* the truth: the gallows, the hemlock, the silence of the crowd. Their proofs were flawless and their heads were forfeit.

This is no reason to despise truth. It is a reason to despise the comfortable lie that truth is self-sufficient. Whoever loves it must also learn to be strong enough to shelter it.
Why did man invent the good conscience?

Because he could not bear the sight of himself. Consider what man actually is: a tangle of contradictory drives, a liar by instinct, a creature who deceives others and, what is worse, himself, an animal whose cunning rather than his claws made the other beasts uneasy in his presence. To look into such a soul and see only this seething thicket would be a torment, or at least no pleasure. And man wants pleasure in his own spectacle.

So he invented the good conscience: a soul with a single will, a single voice, a simple "I ought." Everything multiple, everything shifting and suspect in him was painted over with the flat color of duty and innocence. Only then could he gaze upon himself with satisfaction, as a thing whole and honest.

Morality, I say, is the long and audacious falsification that makes this enjoyment possible. It is a kind of *art*, the art of the self-portrait that flatters. The good conscience is not the discovery of a simple soul; it is the painter's decision to paint one.
Are kind, agreeable people just the descendants of frightened ancestors?

In many cases, yes, and it is an unflattering truth, which is precisely why it deserves to be said. Consider how a gentle manner is actually made. A man lives among those stronger than himself, or among neighbors who may turn on him at any hour. He learns to soothe, to yield, to flatter, to apologize before he is accused, to hide his grief and his anger behind an unruffled face. Such arts, practiced through generations, become a delicate and finished mechanism. The grandchildren, whose lot is easier, feel no dread whatever, yet they run in the same groove, as a wheel goes on turning after the hand has left it. And they honestly take their agreeableness for virtue, their habit for a choice.

I do not say this to sneer at the gentle. There is a fine instrument in such people, and it has its uses. But do not confuse inherited caution with strength of soul. A kindness that was once a shield is not the same thing as a kindness that overflows from abundance.
Tell me what to do while we wait for a new morality.

Become your own king, and make of your own small life an experimental state. You ask what to do in the interregnum, and I can only tell you what I have done myself. Do not wait for the new morality as one waits for a coach that will arrive; no one now living can describe it, and whoever claims to is selling you an old idol with fresh paint. The old building stands on error, and its hold on us loosens day by day, as our honesty grows.

So meanwhile, experiment.
