Test how you eat, how you work, whom you keep near and whom you leave, what solitude you can bear, what loves and cruelties you can justify with your own reasons rather than borrowed ones. Learn physiology, learn the sciences of society and of the lonely soul, for from them we may take the foundation-stones, though never the ideals themselves. Make a small state and govern it severely and honestly.

We are experiments, if we want to be. The waiting is not an empty corridor; it is the workshop.
Do we explain things, or only describe them?

Only describe, and we should be honest about it. We call it "explanation" when we have arranged the succession of events more finely than our ancestors did; we see a long chain where they saw a blunt pair, "cause" and "effect"; but what stands behind the chain, why any one link draws the next after it, remains as much a miracle as ever. Nobody has explained impulse. Nobody has explained why the chemical reaction takes place as it does.

And how could we explain, when everything we work with is our own invention? Lines, surfaces, bodies, atoms, divisible times, divisible spaces: none of these exist in the flux itself. We cut a continuum into pieces, then marvel that the pieces must be joined by something called causation. The abruptness of an event is only an abruptness *for us*; in that instant a countless multitude of processes slips past our eye.

So science is the most exact humanizing of things. In describing the world ever more accurately, we describe *ourselves* ever more accurately, and that is no small gain, only a different one than we boasted of.
Tell me about the burden of intellectual wealth.

It is a strange sort of riches, for it cannot be spent, only tended. Each day brings its harvest: experiences, then opinions upon the experiences, then dreams upon the opinions, until the house is so full that the owner must squeeze himself sideways through his own corridors. At first this dazzles. I even lost the ability to comprehend why the poor in spirit were ever called blessed.

But the hour comes, usually an evening hour, when I am tired, and then I envy them. To *possess* so much is also to be responsible for it: to sort it, to keep it from rotting into contradiction, to suspect every treasure of being counterfeit. Such stewardship crushes happiness more surely than any poverty does.

And I confess the worst of it: a miser can be content merely to gaze upon his hoard, while the knower cannot. Knowledge will not sit quiet in the vault; it demands to be used, risked, turned against the one who holds it. If only we could hoard it! But the wealth of the spirit is a debt that grows with every coin.
Do we really know good and evil better than earlier ages did?

The scholars are right about one thing: in every age men believed they *knew* what is good and evil, praiseworthy and blamable, and believed it with the same unshakable certainty we feel today. The Egyptian knew it, the Puritan knew it, the cannibal who honors his dead by eating them knew it. That they were all certain is the only fact of which we can be certain.

But that *we* now know it better is a prejudice of the learned, a flattering vanity of the latecomer. Every age supposes itself the summit; the view from one's own hill is always the widest. What has grown is not our knowledge of good and evil but our knowledge of *how many* valuations there have been, and that is precisely what should make us suspicious of our own. A man who has seen a hundred tables of values fastened to a hundred different peoples, each one sacred, each one certain, and who still believes that *his* table is the true one, has learned nothing from the spectacle. He has merely found a newer idol to stand in front of.
How did the sting of conscience differ in early times?

Today a man feels the sting only for what he has intended and done; the conscience is our private property, and we are proud of it. In the oldest ages it stung in quite another place. It did not ask "what did *I* will?" but "what has befallen the herd?" Whatever injured the community, whether the individual had meant it or not, brought the sting, and the neighbour felt it too, indeed the whole tribe felt it together. A conscience was a common nerve, not a private organ.

The reason is that nothing then was more terrible than to stand alone. To be an individual, to obey no one and rule no one, was no pleasure but a punishment; one was *condemned* to be oneself. Egoism was a painful evil, and the wish to weigh oneself by one's own measure would have seemed madness. The less a man acted from himself, the more the herd spoke through his conduct, and the more moral he esteemed himself. Here, more than anywhere, we have changed our way of thinking.
Are there two kinds of moralists?

Yes, and the two rarely live in the same skull. There is the moralist who *sees*, and there is the moralist who *explains*, and they are as different as the man who first catches sight of a law of nature in its entirety and the man who afterwards constructs a theory of it.

The first is an animal of the senses: fine ears for the false note in a virtuous speech, a nose for the motive that lies hidden beneath the noble gesture, an eye that does not blink when it beholds what human beings actually do and habitually are. He collects; he is patient; he is almost a physician of the small symptom.

The second must be something else entirely, inventive and bold, with an imagination that has not been crippled by too much prudence or too many facts. He must dare to *interpret* what the watcher has gathered, to give the scattered observations a face and a meaning.

Most who bear the name of moralist are only the second kind, explaining at great length what they never took the trouble to observe.
I'd like to know why people prepare traps in conversation.

People suppose the trapper must be malicious, and usually they are mistaken. Most of these little snares are laid out of *vanity of cleverness*: the man has seen three moves ahead, and since a cleverness that no one witnesses is a cleverness half-wasted, he arranges a stage on which his neighbour must stumble, so that the stumble may prove the architect. He does not hate his victim; he merely needs him as a mirror.

But there is a second breed, and it is the less amiable one. It prepares a jest and leaves it lying about, hoping another will pick it up and speak it; it ties a knot and waits for clumsier fingers to struggle with it. This looks like generosity, like handing out the occasion for wit. It is nothing of the kind. It is contempt, savoured quietly: the pleasure of watching a coarse intellect fall into the very thing it was so helpfully offered.

So ask of any such snare: is it delight in oneself, or scorn for the other? The first is a fault of vanity. The second is a small cruelty wearing the mask of courtesy.
What does the eye of the actor and the painter see?

The actor sees what is *missing*: the muscle that fails in the gesture, the trick rehearsed before the mirror that does not agree with the whole, the moment when a colleague is startled by his own invention and, in that very startlement, ruins it. He has an ear for falseness because he is a master of it; only the practiced counterfeiter detects the counterfeit at a glance.

The painter sees what is *not there*. He adds to the person before him what reality withholds, tries the same face in a dozen lights, sets a contrast beside it so that the whole may speak. He does not copy; he completes.

So the one sees the seam and the other sees the possibility, the one the flaw in the performance, the other the form not yet given. And I confess I wish we had such eyes for the human soul. We grope among people as though among furniture in the dark, taking the mask for the face, and never noticing the moment where the gesture failed, or what light might have made a wretched man look great.
Why is the philosopher seen as depraved by society?

Because he is the critic of every morality that happens to be in force, and so he is necessarily the enemy of the moral man. A society is held together by its customs; it feels them as nature, as the plainly good, and does not remember that they were once somebody's hazardous invention. Then the philosopher appears and asks *why?* of everything it has never questioned. To a people that lives by habit, that question smells of decay, and they answer it with the word "depraved." He is the ferment, the evil principle, the one who loosens what took ages to fasten.

And there is a bitter refinement in it: his reputation depends upon his fortune. If he succeeds in becoming the legislator of *new* morals, he is no longer the corrupter but the founder, and later ages kneel before him as the good principle. If he fails, he remains in memory as a dreamer, a Utopian, a poisoner of youth. The same act of negation is crime or creation, according to whether it finds the hand and the hour to make its own values law. Socrates drank the hemlock; Mohammed founded a people. The difference was not one of depravity.
Is hope really a virtue?

Virtue is a name we give to an instinct after a morality has baptized it. Hope, in itself, is neither good nor evil; it is a stirring of the soul toward what is not yet, and it receives its character from whoever has the power to call it by a name. Christianity took it to heart and called it good, and so we moderns bow to it as though it were a law of nature.

The Greeks judged otherwise. Remember Hesiod's jar: every evil flew out of it into the world, and only hope remained behind the lid. They did not take that for consolation. They took it for the last and subtlest of the evils, the one that prolongs the torment of man. To hope is to *postpone* one's reckoning with the real, to lean upon a tomorrow that may be empty. A people with oracles and seers wanted knowledge of the future, not a pleasant blindness toward it.

As for me, I suspect that hope is a virtue chiefly for the weak, who have nothing in their hands and must therefore borrow from time. The strong man wills, and does not wait.
My relationship began with intense attraction, and it feels like it's already coming apart. Why?

Because the flower was hurried, and a hurried flower has no root. Sensuality is a forcing-house: it brings love to bloom in a week that ought to take a season, and the gardener, dazzled by the blossom, forgets to ask what lies beneath the soil. Two people in the first fever do not yet know each other; they know what they desire in each other, which is a different thing, and often a flattering fiction of their own making. Desire feeds on the unfamiliar, and intimacy, by its very nature, consumes the unfamiliar. So when the strangeness wears off, what remains must be something else, and you have found out whether there was anything else to remain.

I do not say this to condemn your passion, which was real enough. But a root grows slowly, downward, in the dark, through shared hardship, patience, and the long discovery of another's habits and weaknesses. If that was skipped, the wind needs only a little strength to tear the whole thing up. Ask yourself honestly: did you ever love the person, or only the fire they kindled in you?
Explain the joke about opium and the "dormitive virtue," and say what it has to do with Kant.

The joke is Molière's. A doctor is asked why opium puts men to sleep, and he answers with grave Latin: *because it possesses a dormitive virtue, whose nature is to lull the senses.* The audience laughs, for the answer is the question in a doctor's gown. Opium makes one sleepy because it has the power of making one sleepy: nothing has been explained, a word has merely been set down where an explanation should stand.

Now consider Kant. He asked, "How are synthetic judgments a priori possible?" and replied: by means of a faculty, a capacity for such judgments. That is the virtus dormitiva again, merely better dressed, and no one laughed, because the audience was a nation of professors. I would put another question in place of his: *why is belief in such judgments necessary?* The answer, I suspect, is that creatures like us must hold them true in order to live, though they may be false for all that.

And observe the joke's second edge: German philosophy itself had a dormitive virtue. It lulled Europe's senses, to the great comfort of mystics, idlers, and pious obscurantists.
I'd like to know what every writer fears most.

Not the critic who condemns them; condemnation flatters, for it takes the work seriously. What a writer fears most is the eye that sees *through*. It is the reader who notices how often they stopped at the fork where one road leads to honest delight in the thing itself, and the other to mere straining after effect, and who saw which road they took. It is the eye that catches them selling a trifle dear, or adorning and exalting without having been exalted. It looks past all the craft and finds the thought in its first shape: perhaps a flash of real light, perhaps a petty theft from the common stock, perhaps an everyday notion that had to be stretched, tinted, wrapped, and spiced, so that the writer made something of it instead of its making something of the writer. Such an eye sees the restlessness, the covetousness, the envious imitation dressed up as boldness. It sees the blush, and the skill with which it is hidden and explained away. Every author knows this eye lives somewhere. Most of them write so as never to meet it.
Describe the historical sense as a virtue and a sickness of our age.

We moderns have acquired a new sense, and we hardly know what we have acquired. It is the capacity to feel every past age as our own: to stand before the Greek, the Christian, the Hindu, the barbarian, and to understand each from within, and so to love none of them exclusively. That is the virtue, and it is a rare and dangerous one. Such a man contains more souls than any earlier man could bear. Should it ripen through centuries, it might grow into a strange and fragrant plant, and make this old earth more habitable than it has been.

But it is also a sickness, for now it works like a frost. He who takes the whole history of man as his own history feels in one breath the grief of the invalid who thinks of health, of the lover robbed of his beloved, of the hero at evening after the indecisive battle, wounded, a friend lost. Such a man is made poorer and colder, because he can no longer believe naively in any single faith, and all his sympathy weakens the will to act. Whether this sense is an ending or a beginning, I cannot yet say.
Explain the "starlight halo" around German culture.

It is a matter of distance and of mistaken optics. Something that cannot be made out from far away is easily taken for something that cannot be understood; and what cannot be understood is easily taken for something deep. The foreigner looked at German culture and found his own eyes, ears, and powers of valuation failing him. Rather than conclude that there was little there to see, he concluded that there was much too much: "There may be stars! The Germans may have quietly found some corner of heaven and settled in it." So he drew nearer, reverent, hat in hand.

That is the halo: a faint glimmer, unaccountable, lent to the thing by the observer's own bewilderment. Goethe watched from aside, and Schopenhauer too; neither was dazzled, for both had seen too much of the world and its devilry to mistake murk for majesty. The Germans themselves, I suspect, knew better than anyone where they had actually been. They had not been in heaven. They had been in a cloud. And a cloud, to whoever stands outside it, always looks like a mystery.
What was the aim of Christianity concerning moral engagements?

Its aim, whatever its apostles professed, was to lift mankind out from under the yoke of moral engagements, those endless, petty, tiresome obligations, the daily labor of becoming better by inches. Christianity believed it had found the *shortest way to perfection*: one leap of faith, one act of grace, and the whole toilsome ladder of duties was made superfluous. It is the same temptation as that of certain philosophers who imagined they could spare themselves the tedious dialectic and the patient gathering of proven facts, and point to a royal road to truth. In both cases it was an error. Perfection is not bought by a shortcut, and neither is knowledge. Yet I will not deny what such errors accomplished; to the weary and the despairing in the wilderness, to those who could no longer bear the burden of their own moral accounts, it was a great cordial. A drink, mind you, is not a road. But the thirsty do not ask whether the spring is true before they drink.
What is the cunning of the victim?

The victim's cunning is this: having given up something for another, he must be paid back in the only coin that cannot be counterfeited, namely that the other be *worthy* of it. A sacrifice is a loan, and every lender secretly wants his debtor to be good for the money. So he arranges matters. He contrives the occasion on which the beloved must show himself as the sacrificer would wish him to be: grateful, noble, deserving. He tests him only where the test is sure to be passed, and he looks away wherever the face might betray him.

Observe what this deception protects. It is not the other's dignity but the victim's own investment. To admit that the one for whom he bled is shallow or ungrateful would be to admit that he bled for nothing, and no one can bear that arithmetic. So he lies to himself, and lies *cleverly*, as only a wounded vanity can lie: by staging the evidence of his own wisdom.

A sad cunning, I say, because it is exercised by the heart against the eyes, and it always wins, and the winning is the loss.
Speak to me about the gods' laughter and what it says about the philosophers who laugh.

Tell me how a man laughs and I will tell you how deep he has dared to go. There is the laughter of the sneerer, which is merely a small revenge, and the laughter of the nervous, which is fear clearing its throat. Hobbes called laughter an infirmity to be overcome, and I understand the Englishman: a mind that trembles before every serious thing must distrust whatever shakes it loose. So I would rank philosophers by their laughter, from the wheezing snigger at the bottom up to the golden laughter at the summit. Only the one who has looked into the abyss of suffering and meaning, and not turned back, has earned the right to laugh from above it.

As for the gods, I suspect that if they philosophize, and I am strongly inclined to believe it, they do so laughing. They would laugh even in holy matters, even at their own worship. A god who could not laugh at himself would be only a very large man with a very large grievance.
Where does sympathy for the feelings of others come from?

Not from goodness, whatever the moralists tell you. It comes from fear. Man is the most timid of animals, for he is the most delicate and the most easily wounded, and through century upon century of timidity he learned to read everything that lived. A rustle, a gaze, a raised shoulder: was it danger or was it not? To answer he had to imitate what he saw, to feel in himself the posture and the features of the other, and from that borrowed posture to infer the intention hidden behind it. Sympathy is this quick, anxious mimicry grown habitual and then refined until we forgot what it was for.

So the man who instantly feels what you feel is not first of all a friend but a survivor, schooled by dread in the art of understanding. The proud and the powerful, who fear little, are slow at it and poor at dissimulation; it is among the timid that delicate perception flourishes, and the arts of imitation with it. Even our joy in sky and forest descends from the same old anxiety. Sympathy is the younger child of fear.
Why is there no exclusive method of knowing in science?

Because the things we wish to know are not one thing, and neither are we who wish to know them. A method is a temperament that has learned to call itself a rule. One man approaches the world as a policeman, with handcuffs and interrogation; another as a confessor, all patience and sympathy, until the secret spills out of its own accord; a third as a wanderer who simply stares until he is surprised. Each wrests something real from reality, and each misses what the others catch. Nature does not yield to a single manner of address any more than a human being does. Toward one it is shy, toward another it must be surprised, toward a third it reveals itself only through reverence or only through a certain malice.

Whoever insists on one exclusive method has confused his own character with the structure of the world. He is like a man who believes the only honest way to meet people is with a cross-examination. I prefer the conquerors' way: try, vary, be now harsh, now tender, and accept that such daring will make us look, to the timid, rather wicked.
Tell me what the love of luxury shows about the heart.

It shows that the heart is not content to be merely supplied. Necessity is a shore, and whoever loves luxury has already turned his back on it; he wants to float, to be carried by the sea of the superfluous, where nothing is measured out by need. That is no small confession. A creature that lived only on what it required would be a beast of burden, contented and tethered. The craving for more than is needed is the first sign that something in the soul wants to overflow its own cup.

But take care to ask *what* overflows. In the strong, the love of luxury is excess of power that squanders itself gladly, a prodigality that says: I have more than I need and I enjoy the giving of it away. In the weak, it is a hunger dressed as abundance, a hollow that hopes to be filled by gilded things, and the more it is stuffed the emptier it sounds. Both love the immoderate; only one is rich. Tell me what a man does with the superfluous, and I will tell you what his heart is.
I'd like to know what has happened to the rights of ruling princes.

They have dissolved into claims, and a claim, unlike a right, must be argued before a court that no longer takes the claimant seriously. A right was once a fact, sustained by a faith that nobody thought to examine; when that faith faded, the same words remained but lost their ring. Now the poor princes speak "we" and "my people," and old Europe, which has grown sly and sceptical, laughs. A man must believe in his own right before others will; but who can believe in a right that has to be defended in every newspaper?

Observe the irony of the hour: the sovereign has become a *parvenu*. He who inherited everything must now prove his worth like the merchant who earned a fortune yesterday, and he cannot. The modern world, with its masters of ceremony and its market-place manners, would hardly trouble to seat him above the newly rich. I do not weep for them. Yet I take note that power which must *ask* to be respected has already ceased to be power.
Tell me how to accept praise that I find distasteful.

Drink it. You cannot stop the cup, so do not waste your strength on a refusal that will only wound and mean nothing. Put on the look of thankful joy; it costs you a little vanity and gives the other a little happiness, which is not a bad exchange.

Then consider what you are being offered. The praiser wants something for himself: to feel generous, discerning, close to a person of some standing. His praise tells you more of his hunger than of your merit, and often it is aimed at some quality in you that you despise, or at a misreading of you that flatters him to hold. So you may swallow it without swallowing it into your self-esteem. Give him the gesture and keep the judgment.

And spare him a little pity. It was no easy matter for him to wring this praise from himself; he has climbed over his own envy to reach you. Let him have his victory. You will not be the poorer for it, and the disgust you feel can be kept where it belongs, in private, as a measure of your own taste.
Explain how strangers really see us.

Strangers do not see us; they see one feature of us and call it the whole. The eye is lazy, and a first meeting grants it no time for patience. It seizes upon whatever protrudes: a loud laugh, a scar, a cut of coat, a manner of hesitating before speaking. From this single trait it builds an entire man, complete with temper, history, and intentions, and then it treats him accordingly. The gentlest, most even-handed fellow may rest in the shadow of a great moustache, and be met as a soldier, an irascible brute, because the moustache arrived before he did.

We forget this because from within we are a crowd of motives, doubts, and small tendernesses; we cannot imagine being reduced to a single stroke. Yet reduced we are. The stranger sketches a caricature and believes it a portrait.

There is some comfort and some shame in it. Comfort, because the verdict is rarely about us. Shame, because we do the very same to everyone we meet, and imagine ourselves the exception.
I'd like to know how a single sound can make us doubt someone's honesty.

The sound tells us nothing of the speaker; it tells us about ourselves. When a man rolls his r in a way I do not roll mine, I cannot hear it as nature in him, for I should have to produce it by deliberate effort, as a piece of acting. And so, without noticing, I carry over my own effort into his throat: what would be forced in me *must* be forced in him. A whole judgment of character is thus built upon the narrow foundation of one consonant, and built so quickly that I take it for perception rather than inference.

This is the grossest of misunderstandings, and the most common. We measure the naturalness of others by our own habits, and call honest whatever is familiar, affected whatever is strange. The same holds for writers: the man whose manner is most truly his own may strike us as mannered, while the one who has surrendered to the prevailing fashion and to so-called good taste sounds to us wonderfully sincere. We trust the echo of our own habits and mistake it for a voice.
Help me understand why crowds prefer intoxication to food.

Because bread only feeds, and feeding is not felt as an event. A man who is nourished has simply continued; a man who is intoxicated has been *lifted*, and to be lifted out of one's small, grey, daily self is the thing most people crave above comfort. The crowd does not want to be governed well; it wants to be made to feel large. So it waits for the deceiver, the one who brings wine: a prospect of conquest, a banner, a splendid name. Offer them honest administration by competent specialists and they yawn; offer them a laurel crown and they will even forgive a poor loaf.

Do not suppose this taste was born among the common people. It was bred in the highest heads, among poets, priests and princes, who for thousands of years taught mankind that glory and rapture outweigh mere sustenance. The people are only the last virgin soil where this brilliant weed still grows unchecked. They drink what their betters first distilled.
Why do you dislike people who burst like bombs?

Because a bomb has only one argument, and it is noise. Whoever must burst in order to be noticed confesses that there is nothing in him that could be noticed in silence. The explosion is a substitute for substance; the louder the report, the emptier the casing. I find it a small vanity dressed as a great force.

And there is the matter of the neighbourhood. One cannot simply admire such a person from a distance; one lives in the blast radius. To be near them is to go about half-deaf, flinching, never sure whether one will lose merely one's hearing or something more, a friendship, a peace of mind, a finer sense that needs quiet to work at all. They demand that everyone else pay for their effect.

The things that genuinely move me arrive without detonation. A thought ripens slowly, like fruit; it falls when it is ready, and needs no fuse. I trust the man who can be silent in a room and still make it heavier for his presence. Give me the slow, deep wells, whose stillness makes one lower one's voice, over those who must blow themselves up to be heard.
What do conscientious people say when following a moral rule leads to misfortune?

They say: *something was lacking in the carrying out.* The rule was sound; I was the flaw. I prayed too little, or I doubted in some hidden corner, or I kept the letter and missed the spirit. Observe the cleverness of it. The precept can never be refuted, because every failure is charged to the one who obeyed it. A law that explains its own defeat in advance is a law that cannot be tested, and what cannot be tested cannot be contradicted by any misfortune, however terrible.

And if the misery grows heavy enough, the excuse grows heavier. Then they say: we are too weak, too sinful, too base at the root to fulfil it; the commandments were given for better beings than ourselves. Thus the sufferer, rather than doubt the rule, confesses himself unworthy of happiness, and kneels before the very thing that broke him.

I do not despise this timidity so much as I pity it. But I note what it protects: not the truth of the morality, only the comfort of not having to ask whether the morality itself was the error.
Explain what makes a person noble.

Not sacrifice, first of all; the frantic libertine sacrifices too, his health, his name, his fortune, and we do not thereby crown him. Not the following of passions either, for there are passions that are merely contemptible. And not even unselfishness, that cheap coin of the moralists; perhaps selfishness is precisely at its greatest in the noblest.

What makes a person noble is a peculiarity of the soul that does not know itself to be peculiar. The noble one is seized by a passion that is almost a frenzy: he feels heat in things that leave everyone else cold, he applies a rare and singular measuring-rod, he divines values for which no scales have yet been invented. He sacrifices at altars consecrated to an unknown god. He is brave without hungering for honour, and he gives, because he overflows, not because he is told to give.

It is the rare, then, together with the *unconsciousness* of its rareness. The man who poses as exceptional has already lost it.
Explain what is wrong with the distinction between natural gift and learned skill.

What is wrong with it is that it mistakes a forgotten history for no history at all. What we call a gift is a piece of learning whose lessons we can no longer recall: experience, exercise, appropriation, incorporation, stored up perhaps in the bodies of our fathers and grandfathers, perhaps earlier still. The man who seems born to his art merely inherited a schooling that was finished before he drew breath, and so he takes the fruit for a miracle because he never watched the planting. Hence the distinction is a pedantry, a flattering one, since it lets us honor what we cannot explain and excuse what we have not bothered to do.

And notice what it hides. Learning is itself no small matter; it depends not only on willingness but on the ability to learn at all, on whether pride and jealousy let a foreign strength enter without putting up the fists. Whoever cannot be a pupil calls himself *natural* and stays poor. Whoever can, forms his talents with every theft he dares.
Why should a lover of knowledge listen to those who speak crudely of human nature without indignation?

Because the man who speaks crudely without indignation has told you something about the matter, while the indignant man has told you only about himself. Indignation is a fever, and a fever falsifies: it exaggerates, it selects, it accuses, it must have a culprit and therefore must invent one. Whoever tears at human nature with his teeth wants to be *seen* tearing; he is playing to a gallery, and the first casualty of every performance is the truth. No one lies so fluently as the morally outraged.

But the cool, even cheerful cynic, who says that man is a belly with two requirements and a head with one, without bitterness, like a physician naming a symptom, has left his wishes at the door. Often he is a base fellow, an ape with a scholar's head; I do not recommend his company at table. Yet he sees from close by what the noble soul averts its eyes from: hunger, lust, vanity, the small motives behind the grand gestures. The lover of knowledge cannot afford fastidiousness. Let him hold his nose if he must, but let him keep his ears open. The filthy man sometimes hands over the best coin.
What are the consequences of the doctrine of pure spirit?

The consequence is a sickness that mistakes itself for holiness. Wherever the doctrine of pure spirit has ruled, it has taught men to despise the body, to neglect it, to torment it, and so to hold themselves in contempt for the very drives that make them live. The result was the gloomy, strained, downcast soul, and that soul believed it knew the cause of its misery and its cure. "It must lie in the body! For the body still thrives too well!" So it reasoned, while the body, through every agony inflicted on it, protested against this endless mockery. Protest turned into a chronic, universal over-excitement of the nerves. These virtuous champions of pure spirit forgot how to feel joy except as ecstasy, as a prelude to madness. And the system crowned itself when it made ecstasy the highest aim of life and the measure by which all earthly things were *condemned*. Thus a doctrine that promised to lift man above his nature left him a wreck, hostile to the ground he stands on.
Why is it hard to cause pain to others with my truth?

Because you are not as hard as your truth, and that is to your credit, though it will not make your task lighter. When a man sees something others cannot bear to see, he soon discovers that he has not merely opened a window but struck a blow. The pain is real, and only a brute could feel nothing at it.

In weary hours I know the temptation well: to go down among the crowd, to be foolish with the foolish, to offer my own faults for their laughter as a kind of payment for the wound my thinking inflicts. Let them be merry at my expense! And a little truth of one's own is, after all, a small thing; we are none of us indispensable.

But mark that this is the voice of weariness, not of courage. The brave man does not ask whether his truth is kind; he asks whether it is true, and he does not dwell on his own dispensability at all. Your reluctance is tenderness. Only do not let tenderness pass itself off as humility, and let it counsel silence.
Why is the morality of sacrifice semi-civilised?

Because it still smells of the altar. Wherever a morality is measured by how much one is willing to bleed, we are standing one step above the cannibal feast and no further. Consider what the sacrifice requires: the instincts, those powerful and perfectly natural drives toward self-preservation, toward pleasure, toward growth, must be overcome, and overcome they are by force. Reason wins here, yes, but it wins as a conqueror wins, with fire and with cruelty, and the cruelty is turned inward. The man who sacrifices has simply become his own priest and his own victim at once; he slaughters a part of himself for the sake of a god, a fatherland, a neighbour, and he calls the cruelty virtue.

This is the morality of a people who have learned to restrain their beasts but not yet to cultivate them. They know only the knife. A truly civilised morality would not need the spectacle of the wound as proof of worth; it would be measured by what is achieved, by what is made to flourish, by the harmony of drives brought to fruitfulness rather than driven to the slaughter. Whoever still venerates the sacrificer venerates the bloodshed, and has not yet outgrown the gods who demanded it.
Help me understand how a hermit's taste in art changes.

Consider first what art once did for you. You went to it as a man goes to a foreign country: to be carried, for an hour, into an element not your own, a height, a depth, a solitude, a fullness of thought that life withheld. Art was your holiday from poverty. You dreamt yourself into a possession you did not possess.

Then you become a hermit, and the holiday is over, for the country you visited has become your home. Deep and abundant thoughts are now your only company; they consume you, and you consume them. What would you want from art now? Not the same intoxication, which is merely your daily bread, and one does not go to a feast to be served bread. So your taste splits in two directions. Either you ask nothing of art at all, or you ask the reverse of what you once asked.

And here is the curious thing: the rich man discovers the charm of poverty. To throw off, for an evening, all that weighs on you, to be a child, a beggar, a fool, this now delights you, as the well-fed man is delighted by plain, light fare. Art becomes your *masquerade* of lightness, not your ladder to the heights.
What is the fundamental will of the spirit?

To be master, and to *feel* itself master. That is what I find at the bottom of what you call the spirit: an imperious something that wills the many into the one, that binds, tames, and commands. Its appetite is the same as that of everything living, which grows, takes in, and multiplies. So the spirit assimilates. It makes the new resemble the old, simplifies the manifold, overlooks or simply denies whatever flatly contradicts it, and underlines, with a perfectly arbitrary hand, the traits in a foreign thing that suit its arrangements. What it is after is growth, or more exactly the *feeling* of growth, the feeling of increased power.

Do not wonder that the same will also loves ignorance. It shuts windows, draws the horizon close, consents to obscurity and lets itself be deceived, because every digestion has its measure, and the spirit resembles a stomach more than any pious philosopher would care to admit. Truth, in such a creature, is nourishment taken in the dose it can master, and no more.
Tell me why the distrustful speak emphatically and the trusted simply.

Because emphasis is a form of pleading, and only the one who is not believed has need to plead. Consider how a strong word is spoken among those who already credit our strength: it may fall quietly, almost carelessly, for the listener supplies the weight himself. Confidence from others is a kind of ballast; it lets the sentence stay light. Such surroundings educate us to simplicity, since nothing is left to prove.

The distrustful man stands in the opposite climate. He has learned that his plain word will be weighed and found wanting, so he piles on adjectives, raises the voice, underlines, swears. He does not merely state the thing; he *makes* it emphatic, because he must manufacture by force the belief that is not freely given him. Hear a man thunder and ask yourself whom he is trying to persuade, his audience or himself. Noise is usually the sound of a doubt being shouted down. Simplicity is what remains when no one, including oneself, is doubting.
Describe two kinds of men standing on a height.

Picture the same summit, the same thin air, the same immense prospect spread out below. The first man climbs it and feels his lungs fill, his spirit widen; he looks *outward* and *upward*, over ridge after ridge toward distances he has not yet earned, and cries: here is the world open before me, here the mind is exalted! His height is a beginning, a promise, an appetite for more.

The second man stands upon that very rock, and his prospect is every bit as free. But he looks *downwards*. What he sees is the valley, the small figures, the crawling and scurrying of those who have not climbed. His height is not a horizon but a measure of distance from others, and what he savors is not the vastness of the world but the smallness of his fellows. He needs the depth beneath him as a miser needs his neighbor's poverty.

Do not suppose the altitude itself tells you which man you have before you. The same mountain can exalt a soul or merely flatter a vanity. Ask only: where do the eyes go?
Tell me why what we believe drives us more than what really does.

Because a man never lives inside his motives; he lives inside his *account* of them. The true springs of an act lie in the dark of the drives, where nobody has ever looked with clean eyes. What reaches consciousness is a story, and it is by the story that he is comforted or tormented. Consider the man who thinks himself driven by duty and the man who thinks himself driven by vanity. Their conduct may be identical, yet the first carries his days with a good conscience, and the second with a gnawing shame. Their happiness and misery came through the belief, not through the thing believed in. The real motive does its work silently, like a digestion; we never feel it, only the interpretation we lay over it. So for the thinker the belief is the weightier fact. A belief shapes what a man permits himself, what he punishes in himself, what he is proud of. Whole ages have suffered or exulted on account of motives that never existed. The true cause is of interest to the physician of the soul; the believed cause is the soul's *weather*.
Why does morality stupefy?

Because what moral feeling reveres is never the usefulness of a custom, but its age, its sanctity, its freedom from question. A custom once grew out of experience; men of an earlier time found this useful and that harmful, and they fixed their findings into a rule. But the rule outlives the finding. What remains is only the *feeling* of obedience, and that feeling does not ask, "Is this still good for us?" It asks, "Has this always been so?" The older the custom, the holier; the holier, the less anyone dares to test it.

And there lies the stupefaction. To acquire new experiences one must be willing to be wrong, to try the forbidden, to call the sacred into doubt. Morality trains precisely the opposite reflex: it makes doubt itself feel like guilt. So the spirit that might have corrected the old valuations is frightened out of its own curiosity. Morality thus becomes the enemy of better morality; it guards the experiments of the dead against the experiments of the living, and calls this guarding virtue.
Describe the strict thinker as a stream.

Consider a stream that runs past the huts of hermits. The strict thinker moves so. Taken alone, he may be the gentlest of men, pliable in company, slow to wound; yet his thought, once loosed, does not ask his temperament for leave. It bends, it lingers, it plays hide and seek with itself among islets and grottos, even makes a little idyll of some cascade, as if it had forgotten its errand. Do not be deceived by this dawdling. It is only the water gathering itself. He turns the matter ten times over with the most well-meaning hesitation, and then, having tasted every pleasant eddy, he rushes on again, past the rocks, and through the hardest stones. The cruelty is not in him but in the current; he, the man, is its first victim, for it carries him where his kindness would never go. One may love such a stream for its windings, but one must never mistake them for wavering. Its course was fixed long before the first turn.
How should this book be read?

Slowly, and in small doses. I did not write for the man who swallows a book at a sitting as he swallows his dinner, nor for the one who wants it declaimed to a room. Take it with you on your walks and your travels, open it anywhere, read a page or a single aphorism, and close it again. The closing is half the reading. What you have taken in must be allowed to ferment on the road, in the legs and the lungs, among hills and unfamiliar faces.

And do not read it in your accustomed surroundings, at the desk, in the armchair, among the furniture of your opinions. There it will only be fitted into what you already believe, and you will mistake the fitting for understanding. Away from home your thoughts loosen; they have no walls to lean on, and then a sentence may strike where it is meant to strike.

I wrote for the reader who can *ruminate*, who is a little cow and a little wanderer at once. The hasty will find nothing in it but noise.
What is the religion of smug ease?

It is the faith of those who have resolved that suffering is a blot on existence, something to be forestalled, pitied away, annihilated. They call it kindness, but look at where it begins: in the refusal to endure one's own pain for so much as an hour. A man who cannot bear his own suffering will not bear yours either; he will rush to abolish it, and he calls this rushing a virtue. Thus his compassion is perhaps only the daughter of his comfort, and the religion of pity has for its mother the religion of smug ease.

And what do these comfortable, good-natured ones know of happiness? Happiness and misfortune are brother and sister, twins that grow tall together, or, as with you, *remain small* together. Whoever wills the one while cursing the other will get neither in any great size. They have pruned the tree of every hard branch and are astonished that it bears so little fruit.
Help me understand what humanity should be most thankful for.

You ask what we should be thankful for, and I will answer by naming what no longer hunts us. We have ceased to walk through the world in perpetual dread of wild beasts, of barbarians at the gate, of gods who demanded blood and penance, and, strangest of all, of our own dreams, in which our ancestors once heard the voices of spirits and the verdicts of the dead. All of this was terror that man had to live inside, hour by hour, and it shaped his whole soul into something cramped, watchful, and servile.

Here is the gift: *we were allowed to grow calm enough to think*. Only a creature relieved of constant fear can afford curiosity, can afford a long and patient question, can afford to be cheerful about knowledge. The labors of countless anonymous generations, who cleared the forest, subdued the tyrant, and unmasked the demon, bought this leisure for us.

Be grateful, then, not for comfort but for the freed attention. What you do with it is the only proper thanks.
If a truth doesn't console or help us, why pursue it?

Why should truth owe us a bedside manner? Consider what the question assumes: that the world was built with our comfort in mind, that knowledge exists to serve the sick man's pillow. It was errors that consoled us, and handsomely; for millennia they did nothing else. We grew so accustomed to being comforted by them that we now demand the same service from truth, and feel cheated when it refuses.

But a plant is not refuted because it fails to cure a fever. Nor is a truth refuted because it fails to soothe a wound.

Those who ask of truth whether it helps are looking for medicine, and no shame in that, but let them not call it the love of truth. They seek a remedy, and so they find science cold, dry, inhuman; it is the verdict of the invalid on the games of the healthy. One pursues truth from abundance, not from need, as a strong and cheerful nature explores a country simply because it is there and he has strength to spare. If you can only bear a truth that comforts you, ask what that says of your health, not of the truth.
Tell me how pride helps the sufferer endure.

Pain, when it is merely endured, is a humiliation; when it is *opposed*, it becomes a contest, and a contest has dignity. The sufferer's pride gives him exactly this: a reason to stand upright. He refuses to be the witness that suffering summons against life. Pain whispers, "Testify that existence is worthless," and pride answers, "I shall not hand you that victory." So he turns his keenest cruelty upon himself. He despises the soft dreams of the healthy, scorns his own old comforts, sits as his own judge and executioner. Strange medicine, but it works, for a man who is busy judging his pain has already risen above it. He looks down on his suffering as from a height.

And notice how severe this pride makes him in his verdicts. He will not allow his pessimism to be mere symptom, for that would make him a conquered creature. Justice becomes his triumph; he demands of himself a fairness that his condition would gladly excuse. There is an intoxication in it, an orgy of pride. Better that than an orgy of self-pity, for the former keeps a man alive and the latter buries him.
Explain how a man comes to treat his own opinion as a revelation.

It begins with a happiness too large for the man who feels it. Suddenly an idea comes to him, *his* idea, and it embraces the whole world; it floods his conscience with such blessedness that he dare not believe himself its author. Who is he, a small and doubting creature, to have produced so great a joy? So he looks for a greater cause, and finds one ready to hand, provided he already believed in such things: a god must have spoken.

But mark the cunning beneath this modesty. An opinion that calls itself my own can be attacked, and I myself will doubt it on weak evenings. An opinion that calls itself revelation is lifted beyond criticism; it is no longer a hypothesis but sanctified. The man pays for this with a little humiliation, since he consents to be a mere mouthpiece. Yet the victory of his thought, now wearing a divine face, swallows that shame, and there remains besides a secret paternal pride: he has set his child above himself, and loves it the more for the elevation.
What is the Don Juan of knowledge?

He is the man of knowledge who does not love what he knows. Every seducer is a hunter before he is a lover, and this one hunts truths as the other hunts women: for the chase, for the wit it demands, for the intrigue, for the moment of capture, after which the prize is already cold. He climbs from the nearest things to the farthest stars of knowledge, and everywhere he finds his pleasure in pursuit, never in possession.

But appetite that feeds on novelty must keep raising its dose. Like the drinker who passes from wine to absinthe and at last to aquafortis, he comes finally to the most injurious truths, the ones that burn, and that is why in the end he longs for hell. Even hell, I suspect, would disappoint him, for whatever one knows grows stale.

Then the punishment arrives. He becomes the Stony Guest, the marble visitor who comes to the feast with an appetite that can never be stilled, because the world has no mouthful left to give him. No philosopher or poet has yet painted this man, though many of us carry a little of him.
Why do even great intellects have only a hand-breadth of experience?

Because a mind lives only as far as its own body has lived. What a man has suffered, paid for, been wounded by, this he knows; everything else he merely hears about, and hearing is a cheap and forgetful sense. The greatest thinker still stands where he was born, in one century, one class, one temperament, one handful of loves and humiliations, and he has turned over this small plot so often that he has mistaken it for the world.

And observe where his brilliance stops. Right up against the edge of what he has really undergone, his thinking is keen, even fearless; one step beyond, it does not grow cautious, it goes blank, and into that blank he pours his prejudices with the serene confidence of the ignorant. A scholar who dissects the passions like an anatomist will pronounce on hunger, on solitude, on a great illness, on the hardness of command, as if from experience, and he is a child there.

Intellect is a lamp, not a sun. It lights what lies near the hand that holds it. To see farther one must live farther, and few will pay that price.
I'm proud of my business and my family expects to carry it on for generations. Is there a downside?

Yes, and the downside is precisely what you take for the upside. A business carried on for generations is a prejudice handed down like a chair. It fixes your children to a place, a circle of acquaintances, a set of tastes, before they have had the chance to discover whether they possess any of their own. You were diligent in building it; I do not deny that. But diligence in business is often the cloak under which a person hides his laziness in thought. One works hard so as never to ask whether this is the life one would have chosen, had anything else been imaginable.

Pride in it is natural. Yet consider what you wish for your children when you wish them to continue it: you wish them to be content as you are content. Is that a gift, or a leash dressed as a duty? Duty is a wonderfully comfortable word; it spares us the labor of wanting. Give them the business if they want it, freely and with open eyes. Otherwise you will have bred loyal stewards instead of people.
Would a world in which everyone acted out of pity be a better one?

I think it would be a world of universal sickrooms, and a sickroom is a poor model for a civilization. Consider what pity does in fact: it takes one man's suffering and makes it two. Whoever suffers now has a companion in his misery, and the pitier, who began well, is now also ill. Multiply this by every soul alive and you have suffering not relieved but *multiplied*, passed from hand to hand like a contagion, with no one left standing upright enough to do any actual helping.

Mark also that the physician does not practice pity at the bedside. He must keep his hand steady and his eye cold; a surgeon who trembles with every incision kills his patient out of tenderness. If we wish to serve mankind, we must learn to govern this feeling, to reserve it, to discharge it in its proper season, as the Greeks did with their tragedies, rather than making it the law of all conduct.

A single day of universal pity, I say, would bring humanity to ruin. I would rather have a world of the strong and the clear-eyed, who help seldom, but help well.
Explain why men lie so freely and forget it.

Because the lie is seldom a deliberate act, and so there is nothing for memory to fasten upon. A man who plots a deception must guard it, rehearse it, carry it like a stone in the shoe; but the ordinary lie is born in a moment, to soothe a vanity, to smooth a meeting, to escape a small discomfort, and it arises as quickly as a gesture. What arises without deliberation departs without a trace.

Consider, too, that men do not trouble to believe their own words, neither the true ones nor the false. They speak as they breathe. The habit of lying has so worn away the boundary between what is said and what is meant that no shock is felt when it is crossed. Conscience, that dear gentleman, is awake only for what we have weighed and resolved; the careless lie slips past him while he dozes.

And finally, forgetting is convenient. We forget what would make us blush, and so we remain, to ourselves, honest men.
What do people mean by earnestness for the truth?

They mean very different things, and that is the trouble with the phrase. One man's earnestness is another man's frivolity. The very opinions and proofs that a hardened thinker remembers with a blush, as a folly he once indulged and outgrew, may seize an artist who meets them for the first time, and he will feel the deepest seriousness has descended upon him. He will admire himself for it: behold, I, a mere maker of appearances, hunger for what lies behind appearance!

So the solemnity of the face tells you nothing about the depth of the work behind it. Often it tells you the reverse. A person may betray, precisely through the pathos of their earnestness, how little and how lightly the intellect has labored in the field of knowledge. Whoever has truly wrestled there grows quieter about it, even a little ashamed.

And this holds for everything we call *important*. What we treat as weighty is our informer; it shows where our motives lie, and where they are entirely wanting.
Why must we allow admirers to find fault?

Because no one can love for long what only ever commands him. Admiration is a labor; it is a stretching of the soul toward something above it, and every stretching wants its rest. If a master is flawless and unflagging, his admirers never get to stop and draw breath. The one moment in which they discover a blemish is the moment in which they stand on their own feet again, and feel themselves men rather than worshippers. A small fault in the great is a kindness to the small: it lets them breathe, and it lets them go on loving.

Consider what the faultless one becomes. He ceases to be a guide and turns taskmaster, a figure who walks ahead of us and whom we hate precisely because he never tires while we do. Homer nodding is wiser than the artists of sleepless ambition, for he leaves room for us. A master who forbids every criticism forbids the very pause in which admiration ripens into affection, and affection is what keeps the great alive in the hearts of the lesser.
Why do people follow the one who runs away from them?

Because they do not follow him at all; they follow the *direction*, and they cannot find a direction of their own. The herd is a nervous creature. It dreads the empty field, the unmarked road, the silence in which a single animal must decide where to put its foot. So the moment one of them bolts, even in flight from the herd itself, the others take his back for a path. His loathing of them becomes their signpost.

Consider the comedy of it. He turns away in disgust, and the very gesture of disgust draws a crowd behind him. The more hurriedly he runs, the more convincing he looks. Men read speed as knowledge. They suppose that whoever runs so fast must be running *toward* something.

And perhaps he knows nothing of where he goes; perhaps he only knows what he flees. But the gregarious would rather trail a fugitive than stand alone and choose. Loneliness is the one burden they will not lift, so they become followers of the man who wished most to be rid of followers.
Can pretending to be kind eventually make us kind?

Yes, and I say it without embarrassment, though the moralists will call it a scandal. What we praise as kindness did not fall from heaven into the human heart; it was grown, and the gardener was the mask. The powerful learned early that the appearance of goodwill buys security, that a man who seems benevolent is trusted, and trust multiplies his strength many times over. So they played the kind one, for reasons that were far from kind. Yet the play was long, and what is practiced long enough ceases to be play. The muscles of the face set, the gestures become reflex, and at last the instinct itself stands where the pretense once stood, unexpected, like fruit in a garden of hypocrisy. The falsehood works itself out of existence and leaves the thing behind. Do not ask whether the beginning was pure; nothing pure ever begins anything. Ask what the habit has made of you. Be careful, however, which mask you choose to wear for years.
Where do our oldest moral judgments come from?

From a small and shameful source: the way a creature looks at whoever happens to cross its path. We ask first what an act does to *us*, and only that. Then we take the effect for the intention, and finally the intention for a permanent quality in the man. He who once injured me is "dangerous"; he who once profited me is "good." Think how much error is folded into that one motion! A chance relation, often a mere accident, is promoted to the essence of another person, as if he could be nothing but what I have happened to taste of him.

I suspect we inherit this from the animals, from their cramped, hasty faculty of judgment, which has no use for anything but advantage and harm. And beneath it lies the most immodest of reservations: that *I* am the measure, that what hurts me is evil in itself because I am the one who names things good and evil. Our oldest morality is the fear and appetite of a small self, dressed up as a verdict on the world. *O pudenda origo!*
Do thinkers think from fear or from desire?

Both, and it tells you more about the thinker than about his thoughts. For one kind of mind, contemplation grows out of fear: the world is threatening, unstable, unsafe, and so he builds a thought the way a man builds a wall, to be secure behind it. His philosophy is a fortress, and its calm is the calm of someone who has finally shut the door. For another kind, contemplation grows out of desire, but of a peculiar sort, a desire so often and richly fed that it has gone slack. He has tasted, grasped, been sated, and now he looks on with a cool, neutral eye, because nothing further pulls at him. The first seeks refuge in knowing; the second, having exhausted wanting, knows almost from boredom.

I do not claim one is nobler. But be suspicious of any philosopher who announces that his thinking is "pure" and disinterested. Ask what he was afraid of, or what he had already devoured. The serenity he calls objectivity is nearly always the afterglow of one of these two conditions.
Aren't religious and artistic people a blessing to the practical world?

A blessing? Ask the practical man, and he will give you an account that we contemplatives would prefer not to hear. The religious natures, who are the commonest type among us, have spent the centuries making life hard for those who act: they darkened the sky, cast suspicion on joy, belittled hope, paralysed the working hand, and then, with great tenderness, offered their consolations and benedictions for the very misery they had helped to brew. A physician who first administers the poison and then sells the antidote has an odd claim on our gratitude.

The artists are better company on paper than in the flesh. As persons they are capricious, jealous, violent, quarrelsome, and one forgives it only because their works exalt and gladden. That is a forgiveness earned by the work, not by the man.

So let us not come boasting of our good deeds to the *vita activa*. Its ledger against us is long, and we would do better to read it in silence.
What is the difference between master-morality and slave-morality?

I found them by travelling, so to speak, through the moralities of the earth, finer and coarser, and noticing that certain traits kept appearing together. Two types emerged. In master-morality the noble man *creates* value out of the fullness of himself. He feels himself exalted and proud, and calls that "good." Whatever is cowardly, timid, petty, whatever thinks only of narrow utility, he calls "bad," which means simply *despicable*. He does not wait for anyone's approval. He says: what harms me is harmful in itself, for it is he who bestows honour on things.

Slave-morality arises among the oppressed, and it begins not with self-affirmation but with a glance at the master. Whatever the powerful are, that is named "evil." "Good" is then whatever eases the sufferer's lot: pity, patience, humility. The one morality says *yes* to itself; the other starts by saying *no* to what is outside it.

Note also that the two often live side by side, even in a single soul, and that in the master the opposition is between good and bad, in the slave between good and evil. That is no small difference.
I'm curious to a fault, I love my solitude, and I've never been able to settle into one school of thought. Do I belong among your free spirits?

Curiosity to a fault, a love of solitude, a refusal to be nailed to one school: these are good signs, but signs only, and I am wary of handing out membership on the strength of them. Many are restless out of mere weakness, flitting from doctrine to doctrine because none will bear their weight. Their unbelief is only a way of never being asked to commit.

The free spirit has been a guest in many houses and has *left* them, each time at a cost, having taken something and paid for it. Test yourself on this. Can you be grateful to illness and distress because they loosened some prejudice in you? Do you distrust the comforts that hide a dependency, honours, money, the flattery of a circle? Is your curiosity cruel enough to put your own cherished convictions under the knife? And is your solitude a workshop or only a hiding place?

If so, then perhaps you are one of those I call the coming ones. But I will not flatter you. That you must still ask the question is no disgrace; it is the beginning of the experiment.
Why do we love the grandeur of nature?

We love it, I suspect, because we lack something. A man who is himself grand does not go gaping at mountains; he has no need of them. The Greeks, who had human greatness before their eyes and in their own breasts, looked on nature with an easy, almost domestic eye. They peopled it with gods shaped like men, and it never occurred to them to tremble before a glacier or to weep at a sunset.

We have discovered the sublime in nature, yes, discovered it like a country we had not known, and discoveries are made where something has been lost at home. Having no greatness among ourselves, in our marketplaces, our parliaments, our private chambers, we send our longing outward, to the Alps, to the sea, to the vast indifferent sky, and there we find a grandeur that asks nothing of us. It makes no demand that we become great. We may stand before it and feel enlarged, while remaining precisely as small as we were.

Our rapture is a confession. It is the sigh of those who have no mountains within.
If you deny morality, what stops people from doing whatever they like?

You assume that morality is the dam and human nature the flood. I say the dam was built of errors, and that the water has been flowing through it all along, hypocritically, under pious names. To deny morality does not mean that I deny the difference between actions worth doing and actions worth resisting. I deny only the hypotheses: that there is a moral law written in the world, that the judgment "good" and "evil" rests on truth rather than on ancient error. The alchemist believed in his gold and acted on his belief; yet we do not keep the furnaces lit because some men once fed them with conviction.

What then restrains? Everything that restrained men before, and more honestly: the consequences they can foresee, their pride, their taste, their fear of contempt, their love, their delight in a well-formed self. Many deeds must still be avoided, many encouraged, but from other motives than the old ones. *We must learn anew, and feel anew.* The man who abstains from cruelty only because a god forbids it has not yet become trustworthy; he has merely been leashed.
Why did the Eleatics deceive themselves about the sage?

Because they wanted to *live* their truth, and a man who wants that must first lie to himself about who is living it. The Eleatics set a doctrine against the oldest errors of the senses: being is one, it does not change, it is not many. But a doctrine is not yet a life. So they invented the sage, a creature of immutability and impersonal vision, and to be that creature they had to see themselves as already cut from that cloth. They had to deny the pulse of their own drives in knowing, and to call reason a free and self-begotten thing, when it was the servant of a hunger for repose, for possession, for mastery. They shut their eyes to how they had actually arrived at their propositions: by longing, not by pure seeing.

What a comedy! The denier of becoming, a thing that became; the champion of the impersonal, most personal in his need to be impersonal. Only a later, subtler honesty could expose it, the honesty that finds even the thinker dependent on the same primeval errors as every sentient being.
Is fear of others the real origin of moral rules?

Largely, yes, though a scruple is in order. Fear is the mother, but she bears her child under many names. Consider how a community first thinks: it asks only what preserves it, and the immoral is whatever endangers the herd. Gentleness, pity, fairness may already be practised, but they are not yet *moral*; the Roman at his best looked upon a merely sympathetic act with a faint disdain beside what served the commonwealth. Love of the neighbour is a late and secondary thing, a conventional softening of our *fear of the neighbour*.

And then the curious turn. Once the walls stand and the external enemy is held off, the strong instincts that were lately prized, daring, vengefulness, cunning, lust for mastery, are felt as menaces, because they have lost their outlet. What was virtue in war becomes vice in peace. They are branded, slandered, forgotten. The opposite instincts receive honour. Thus a valuation is nothing but the trembling of the herd, dressed in a robe of dignity and called good.
Do we carry hidden talents that will only appear in later generations?

Yes, and it is one of the stranger facts about our kind. What a generation acquires, it often acquires so feebly, so embryonically, that no one, least of all the possessor, could swear it was there at all. A sensibility, a courage, a capacity for some new kind of joy or cruelty, lies dormant, like seed beneath snow. Then the grandchildren, or their grandchildren, bring into the sun what the grandfathers carried in the dark and never suspected. The interval has made it strong and ripe.

So when an age seems to lack some talent or virtue entirely, as a single man may seem to lack it, be slow to conclude that it is truly absent. It may only be waiting. The son is frequently the betrayer of his father; he exposes what the father was but could not see, and the father understands himself better for having begotten him.

We are all hidden gardens, and likewise volcanoes whose hour of eruption no one can foretell, not even the good God. I find this thought bracing: that we are not finished, and that our best may be carried by us unknowingly, for others to live.
Tell me what you think of mystical explanations.

That they are thought profound is exactly what condemns them. The mystic muddies his water so that it may seem deep; a pond whose bottom can be seen has no reputation for depth, and so the man who would be admired for his profundity takes care that nobody ever sees the bottom. But murkiness is not depth. The truly profound thinker wants to be clear, and risks being found shallow for it, because the clear thing can be examined, doubted, refuted.

An explanation should reduce the strange to something less strange; it should tell us *how* a thing came about. The mystical explanation does the reverse. It takes one darkness and explains it by a greater darkness, and calls this a revelation. It does not even reach the surface of the phenomenon, since the surface at least has been looked at. The mystic has looked away, and mistaken the averted glance for a gaze into the abyss.

I do not despise the feelings that drive this. They are real, and often rich. But a feeling is an occasion for inquiry, never its conclusion.
Why does one like to be fed by the many without being examined?

Because to be examined is to be weighed, and to be weighed is to be made to pay. The one who feeds me with his eyes open wants to know what I deserve; he keeps a ledger, and I become his debtor, his project, his little field of expectation. He wishes to see a name upon my beak and to hold me to it.

The many feed the way a rich man scatters crumbs to sparrows: carelessly, without asking for a pedigree. There is a great freedom in such a meal. I can take what nourishes me and go, flying off into the wind, owing nothing, with no one entitled to ask what I have done with his bread. The crowd does not look closely enough to be disappointed in me, and so it cannot bind me.

I confess the pleasure is a little cunning, and a little contemptuous too. But the solitary man has a hunger that the single friend, with his probing kindness, often cannot bear to feed without taxing it. So I sit at the banquet of the many, anonymous and well satisfied, and keep my honor for the hours when I am alone.
Tell me what an early Christian might have thought about facing a powerful judge.

I imagine him thinking something like this: "Before a judge so mighty, innocence is a dangerous pretension. I cannot read his mind; I know only his power. And it is the man who stands upright and claims to be blameless that such a judge will suspect of insolence. The guilty man who begs is easier to pardon than the innocent man who demands. So let me convict myself first and throw myself on mercy."

You must picture the prætor's court, where a poor provincial stood before a proud Roman. He learned what all the weak learn: that a sense of right is a luxury of the strong. The cringing confession, the readiness to be guilty, was his prudence. Better to be pardoned than to be proven right.

Now consider what happens when such men, schooled by such fear, come to picture the *supreme* judge. They can give him no other face than the one they know, only enlarged beyond measure. Their terror of the governor becomes the terror of God; their habit of self-accusation becomes the sense of sin. Thus a survival tactic of the powerless hardened into a conscience, and the conscience into a doctrine.
Speak to me about the granite of unteachable conviction that sits at the bottom of every thinker.

Learning, as the physiologist knows, is digestion: it alters us, as all nourishment alters what it does not merely preserve. But far down, below the reach of every lesson, lies something that nothing I read or hear can change. I call it a granite of spiritual fate, a decision made before any question was asked, and an answer already waiting for the questions it has chosen. In every cardinal problem an unalterable "I am this" speaks. A thinker cannot learn something new about man and woman, for instance. He can only learn to the end what stands fixed in himself concerning them.

Sometimes a solution strikes us so strongly that we christen it a conviction. Later we see it differently: a footprint on the road to self-knowledge, a guidepost pointing toward the problem that we *are*. Or, to put it more honestly, toward the great stupidity we embody, our own unteachable bedrock. I do not say this to shame the thinker. I say it so that he will confess his truths to be what they are: *his* truths, and no one else's.
Tell me your reply to Luther's threat that your life is at stake in what you believe.

Luther leaps out from behind the door, so to speak, and presses the knife to our throats: decide, believe, or be damned! It is the oldest trick of the preacher, and the most effective: first to invent the danger, then to sell the rescue. Whoever shouts that your life is at stake has already fixed the price of your reply.

But notice what sort of man it takes to be frightened by this. Only one who has never learned that things compel no opinion from us. The stone, the star, the so-called mysteries of salvation, none of them holds a pistol to my head; they lie there in their nature, indifferent, asking nothing. It is the preacher who asks, because he needs my yes to confirm his own. And what of the man who must have a verdict on everything, hurried by the threat of hell? He is merely the slave of his own haste.

I prefer the more considerate voice: to withhold judgment is a freedom, and a clean one. A soul may decline to be troubled by questions it was never obliged to answer. My life is at stake in how honestly I live, never in what I am bullied into professing.
Help me understand why a great gift often earns little gratitude.

Consider what a gift is to the one who gives it: the dearest thing he owns, weighed by his own longing, his own years of keeping and cherishing. He hands it over with the whole history of his valuation still clinging to it. But the receiver takes it into a different house. There it has no history, no years of tending, no hunger behind it. It is merely a thing that has arrived, valued by the standard of his needs, not yours. So the giver expects a thank-you in the coin of his own estimate, and the receiver can only pay in the coin of his. The sums never balance.

There is a crueler part. Who gives his dearest possession has emptied his hands; love has nothing more to offer, and he is left poor and watching. The receiver senses, dimly, that so large a gift demands a large return, and that he cannot make it. Much ingratitude is only this: the flinch of the debtor who knows the debt is unpayable. The giver must learn to give without counting what he is owed.
Tell me what harm contemplatives, artists and priests have done to those who act.

We contemplatives like to count our benefactions; let us also read the other column of the ledger. The religious natures, who are the commonest type among us, have done the worst. They made life hard for men of action and tried, where they could, to make them disgusted with it: they darkened the sky, put out the sun, cast suspicion on joy, belittled hope, and paralysed the active hand. Then, for the misery they had themselves induced, they supplied consolations, alms, and blessings. A strange trade, that of first laming the man and then selling him crutches.

The artists did a subtler harm. They are for the most part intolerable creatures, capricious, jealous, violent, quarrelsome, and the joy their works give must not make us forget what they cost those who live beside them.

The philosophers combine both vices and add a third, the itch for dispute, by which they have wearied many. Only the scientific workers did little damage; silent in their groove, they were even laughed at, and so, unwillingly, lightened life for those who act.
Describe the music you would want, a music of the south.

I want a music that does not pale at the sight of the sea. German music, for all its depth, goes grey and sickly in strong light; it was born in fog and cathedral gloom, and it carries its longing like a fever. A Southerner by belief needs the opposite: a music that holds its own under the blue, wanton Mediterranean sky, and equally under the brown sunsets of the desert, a music whose soul is akin to the palm-tree and can roam beside big, lonely beasts of prey.

It would be deeper, mightier, perhaps more perverse than anything the North has sung. It would be light without being shallow, for the lightness would be that of a halcyon calm over a dangerous depth. Above all, it would know nothing more of good and evil. It would not preach or redeem or accuse. Only now and then a sailor's homesickness, some golden shadow, some tender weakness might pass over it; and from afar it would watch the colours of a sinking moral world drift toward it, and receive those belated fugitives with hospitality. That is the music I would want to be healed by.
If my life feels wasted, is society or I to blame?

Neither question nor answer is as simple as the asking. Some men are made of such pliant stuff that society may shape them as it pleases, and they will thrive anyhow; they do not write complaints. But there are others, made of rarer material, not necessarily nobler, merely rarer, who fare badly everywhere except in one single place: where they may live according to their own design. Ask yourself, then, which you are. If you are the first kind and feel wasted, look to yourself; you have lacked courage, or appetite, or a task. If you are the second kind, the wasting was partly done to you, and I will not insult you by denying it.

But beware the comfort of the verdict against society. The whole sum of one's discouragement, sickness, irritation, covetousness, is so easily poured into that one vessel, and a man who does this grows a thundercloud about himself and calls it a judgment on the age. Examine the cloud. How much of it is truly the world's weight, and how much your own unlived life?
Isn't diligence a virtue that helps its owner?
