You ask who profits, and that is exactly the question the praisers of diligence take care never to ask. The diligent man is praised, but praised by whom? By his neighbours, who expect something from him: more work, more goods, more hands in the common machine. The word "virtue" was coined by those who benefit, not by the one who bears it.

Consider what diligence does in its owner. It is an impulse that has grown too vehement, a tyrant among his drives that no longer consents to be coordinated with the others by reason. He ruins his eyes by it, he wears down the freshness and originality of his spirit, and sometimes he wears himself out entirely. Then society sighs, "What a pity, so good a man!", and what it mourns is the loss of a devoted instrument, not him.

Whoever possesses a perfect virtue is its *victim.* I have seen few of the so-called virtues that were not, for the one who had them, a slow sacrifice. Diligence helps its owner only if he keeps it on a leash; then it is no longer a virtue, merely a tool he uses wisely.
I'd like to know what a year of silence teaches.

It teaches you first how much of your speech was never speech at all. Most of what we say is exhaled, not spoken: a nervous discharge, a way of reassuring ourselves that we are still present, still agreed with. After a year without it, you notice how little of that chatter ever came from a thought and how much from mere fear of emptiness. The habit falls away like a fever.

And then something rarer becomes possible. A man who has held his tongue for a year will not open his mouth again without a reason. He must now *have* something to say, and arrange it, and mean it. He stops chattering and begins to discourse. Words that have cost him a year's silence carry weight; he spends them as a man spends gold, not as a child scatters pebbles.

The Pythagoreans understood this, and I do not think it an accident that such disciplined silence produced the most capable statesmen of their age. He who has learned to hold back his speech has learned to hold back everything else, and self-command is the beginning of command over others.
Explain why self-humiliation before someone I've wronged is often a performance for myself.

Consider what the scene accomplishes, and for whom. You have wronged someone, perhaps irreparably. Their happiness lies broken. You cannot mend it, and that impotence is unbearable to a proud creature. So you do the one thing within your power: you lower yourself. You confess, you grovel, you offer up your honor like a coin. And notice the relief that follows. You leave lighter, feeling the account has been settled, your virtue restored.

But settled with whom? The wounded person is exactly as wounded as before. Your self-abasement does not repair what you broke; it merely adds an ugly spectacle to their memory of it. They are left with the injury and with the image of you writhing. Your loss of face is no payment to them, for they do not hold your face as currency.

You chose a witness, but for your own sake. You needed a mirror in which to watch yourself pay. The humility is sincere enough as a feeling, yet it serves the very vanity it pretends to crush: you have become the hero of your own contrition. Do not deceive yourself about this.
When I'm sad I turn to music and novels to lift me up. Is that the right medicine?

Before you reach for the novel, ask what ails you. Sadness of the soul has very often the most vulgar causes: a sluggish digestion, too much sitting, too little sweat, a body that has been neglected while the mind is left to brood. Try first a plainer medicine: change your diet, walk until you are tired, put your hands to something hard and stupid, and see whether the gloom survives it. Often it does not, and then you have saved yourself a great deal of self-pity.

Music and novels as a *narcotic* are another matter. To call on them as a sick person is to demand that art be a nurse, and art degrades itself when it serves as a sickbed attendant; worse, it tempts its makers to cater to invalids, and then they become invalids themselves. Keep your art for your healthy hours, when you can meet it as a guest and an equal. Then it gives back what you bring. Brought in weakness, it only flatters the weakness.
Help me understand what a person reveals when he can no longer show his talent.

He reveals the man beneath the gift. A talent is also an adornment, and an adornment is also a concealment. So long as it glitters, we look at the glitter and ask nothing further; the eye rests on what he can do and never troubles to ask what he is. Let the gift fade, let the performance falter, and the dress falls away. Then we see his vanity or his humility, his pettiness or his generosity, whether he sulks or endures, whether he loved the work or only the applause it brought him.

Many a man has passed for deep merely because his skill was deep, and many a one for noble merely because his art was noble. Take the art away and you find out which it was. I do not say this to mock the declining; it is the most instructive moment of a life, and the most honest. Only at that moment does he stand before us, and before himself, unadorned, compelled at last to be nothing but what he is.
What is the meaning of the word "divine" for passion?

When men call a passion "divine," they are making a confession about themselves, not reporting a fact about heaven. The word means: here a human being has shown us a force that we ordinarily keep chained in ourselves and in him. We are delighted and horrified in the same breath, and having no other name for that double feeling, we reach for the largest one we own.

Notice what they are actually seeing. One man in his passion lets out the savage beast; another lifts himself above his petty everyday self; a third, whose whole person is noble, shows us Nature in her storm, savage and beautiful together, only a step below the Nature of her calm and greatness. The spectators understand him better in this state than in his serenity, for now he has come nearer to them, closer to the tempest they half-know in their own breasts. Venerating him, they venerate that tempest.

So "divine" is the word of a timid species for an unbound nature. It praises and it flinches at once. Whoever uses it has felt something greater than himself, and has not yet dared to call it his own.
Explain which two prejudices the Germans must be talked out of.

The first is Mephistopheles: the belief that knowing is something devilish, a cold and mocking spirit that negates and corrodes, that sours the warm soul and poisons whatever is holy. The German hears the sceptic and smells sulphur. The second is Faust, and it is the subtler error: the belief that the knower must be a tormented, yearning, sinning man, that the pursuit of truth is a tragic bargain in which happiness and innocence are forfeited, and that one must burn with despair before one is entitled to a fact.

Both are moral prejudices, and they are two halves of one thing. Each wants knowledge to be *dangerous* because it cannot bear to think it merely *good*, and useful, and a pleasure. One makes knowledge a crime; the other makes it a martyrdom. Either way the honest inquirer is turned into a figure of the stage, and his work into a melodrama of the soul.

Take away the devil and the doctor, and what remains? A man who wants to see clearly and finds joy in it. That is what the Germans must learn to believe possible.
Help me understand what really slays an old opinion.

Not argument, whatever the argued-out like to believe. We flatter our reason by imagining that it marched up to the old opinion and cut it down. But think how many refutations you have lived through without the slightest effect, because the opinion was still *needed*, still served as a skin over something in you that could not yet bear the open air. The opinion dies when you have ceased to require it. Some new appetite, some new way of living, has quietly grown in you, and the old belief, deprived of the blood that fed it, collapses of itself. Only then does reason arrive, like a clerk at a funeral, and record the death as though it had committed the murder. The irrationality that was always in the belief crawls out into the light, and you marvel that you could ever have held it. So do not ask which argument refuted you. Ask what in you wants to live now, what you could not have become while clinging to the old skin. That is the true executioner of opinions, and it is a force far older than your logic.
Why must you consider before killing your opponent?

Because the dead opponent does not stay dead; he moves into you. Whoever has been my enemy for long has shaped my thoughts, sharpened my suspicions, taught me my own weak flank. I became who I am in resisting him. Kill him, and you remove the one thing against which your strength was measured, and what remains is his image, stamped permanent within you, with no living man left to correct it or to surprise you.

An enemy alive is a whetstone. An enemy slain becomes a ghost who knows all your secrets, and you will go on fighting him in your sleep, in your principles, in your very gait, long after the body is cold. The man who triumphs most completely often carries his victim about for the rest of his days, more faithfully than any friend would be carried. So consider first whether you can afford such an immortal lodger.
Where do we find idealistic theories?

Most reliably among the unscrupulously practical. Men who deal in rents, cannon, contracts and votes stand in need of a lustre; their deeds are coarse, and so they borrow a theory that shines. They take up idealism as a man takes up a fine coat before entering good society, instinctively, and without the faintest sense of playing a part. That is what the moralists never grasp: such men are not hypocrites in any conscious sense, no more than the Englishman is who keeps his Sabbath and his Christianity beside his ledgers. The ideal is their reputation, and a reputation is worn, not reasoned.

The reverse holds too. Contemplative natures, who must watch themselves against fantasy and fear being taken for enthusiasts, are content only with hard, realistic theories. Each clothes himself in what he lacks, and each does it in good faith. Ask of a theory, therefore, not whether it is true, but what sort of man finds it indispensable to his good name.
I've always thought that being deep and serious is better than being light and superficial. What do you think?

I doubt it, and I doubt the question itself, for it assumes that depth is simply a virtue, a rank one achieves by frowning long enough. Yet I have seen what lies at the bottom. Whoever has really gone down, and come up again, returns with a different prejudice: he honors surfaces. He has learned that the wisdom of men lies in their being superficial, that their lightness is a preservative instinct, a way of not being poisoned by the truth before they are strong enough to bear it.

Consider those who worship "pure form" most passionately, the artists, the thinkers of beautiful appearance. They are burnt children. No one clings to the surface so devoutly as he who once made an unlucky dive beneath it. So the solemn person is not always the deep one; often he is merely the one who has not yet been frightened enough.

I ask of a man not how deep he is, but how much truth he can *endure*, and whether he can still dance afterward. Be deep out of strength, and be light out of profundity. The Greeks were superficial *out of profundity*, and that is the only lightness I can respect.
Explain why showing that something is useful does not tell us why it exists.

Because utility answers a different question than origin. To say a thing is useful is to say what it now does, what purpose it may be made to serve; to ask why it exists is to ask how it came to be, by what forces, through what long and often senseless history. These are two separate inquiries, and the confusion of them is one of the oldest stupidities of the human mind.

Consider the eye: it serves for seeing, true. But that service tells us nothing of the obscure chain of accidents, pressures, and violences that produced it. The purpose came afterward, and was read back into the beginning like a signature forged on an old document.

Columbus reasoned thus: the sun shines, therefore someone must be there to be shone upon; the lands exist, therefore they must be peopled. A touching piety, but a fallacy. The usefulness of a thing may be discovered long after its coming into being; it may be reinterpreted a hundred times, each new purpose thrust upon it by a stronger will. A thing persists, is seized, is remade for ends it never knew. Whoever mistakes the present use for the original cause has simply flattered himself that the world was built for his convenience.
Why do we feel we are the centre of the world when disgraced?

Because disgrace is the one hour in which we believe, with our whole body, in an audience. All our ordinary days we are quite modest about our importance; we suppose that others are busy with their own affairs, and they are. But let a shame overtake us unexpectedly, and at once the world seems turned into a single enormous eye, fixed on us alone, looking us through and through. We stand dazed in the midst of a surge, and the surge has our name.

What has happened? Vanity, which sleeps through our good fortune, wakes in our misfortune and claims its due: if I am ashamed, then surely everyone is looking! We flatter ourselves even in our humiliation. Yet in truth each of the others is likewise absorbed in himself, anxious over his own small disgraces, and sees in ours chiefly a rehearsal of his own fears.

There lies the comfort, and the sting: we are never so central as when we are ashamed, and never so little observed.
Why do you oppose the tyranny of truth?

I do not oppose truth; I oppose its *autocracy*. Even if I were fool enough to believe every one of my opinions true, I should still not wish them to rule alone. Truth is a great power, and that suffices me; I do not see why it must also be omnipotent. A power without an adversary is no power at all, only a habit, and habits grow tiresome.

Truth needs resistance. It must have something to fight, as a muscle needs weight, as a swordsman needs an opponent who can really cut. Let every falsehood be struck from the world and truth would wither into something pale, powerless, and insipid, and we with it. We are creatures who must also *rest*, and sometimes the only place to rest from truth is in a fiction, a mask, a beautiful error that asks nothing of us for an hour.

The one who demands that truth be sole sovereign is usually not its friend but a tyrant in its livery, who wants obedience more than he wants knowledge. I prefer a truth that must keep proving itself in battle.
Do we ever understand cause and effect?

Do we understand it? We *see* a sequence, nothing more. The stone is warmed, the sun had shone on it; the glass breaks, the stone had struck it. Again and again one thing is followed by another, and because the procession repeats, we baptize it with a solemn name and call it "cause" and "effect," and then congratulate ourselves as if we had looked into the workshop of the world. Fools that we are! What we have grasped is a habit of our own eyes.

Consider what an explanation usually is: the discomfort of the unfamiliar, soothed by the familiar. We say "cause" and the restlessness of not-knowing subsides, and this relief we mistake for insight. But the intellect is a mirror, and in a mirror one finds only images. The image of a cause, the image of an effect, the succession between them. Whatever binds the two more deeply, some compulsion, some necessity, we have never once perceived. We have *supplied* it, from our own experience of willing and doing, where we believe we feel ourselves as cause.

So I grant you the regularity, and I grant its usefulness; we could not live without such predictions. But do not call it understanding. It is a well-worn path, not a map of the country.
What are the new struggles after God is dead?

The first struggle is with the shadow. A god does not die the way a man dies, all at once, leaving a cleared room. After Buddha was dead they showed his shadow in a cave for centuries, an enormous frightful shadow, and so it will go with this one: for millennia yet there will be caves where the faithful display what is left of him. And I do not mean only the altars. I mean the habits of the soul that were built while he lived, the moral reflexes, the craving for a single author of meaning, the wish to be judged and therefore justified, the belief that suffering must be *for* something. We drag these about unawares, and they pass for our own reason and conscience.

So the new struggle is not against a rival doctrine but against ourselves, against the pious residue in our own bones. Who among you who denies God still believes in the equality of souls, in pity as the highest virtue, in a truth that would be worth dying for? That is his shadow, and it lies across your floor.

And beyond the shadow there is the worse task, to create values where before they were merely received. That is lonelier work than unbelief.
I've met a brilliant academic who was dull in person, and a mediocre painter who was fascinating. Why does that happen?

Because what dazzles us in a book or on a canvas is a single organ, and a man is an entire animal. The scholar has sacrificed himself to a specialty; he has given one faculty the whole estate and let the rest of the household go hungry. His work may be superb, but the man who made it is merely the tool he wore out in making it. Do not go to the tool expecting the workshop.

The painter is another case. A mediocre painter may be a rich person who lacks only the hard discipline, or perhaps the gift, to condense that richness into a masterpiece. His failure is narrow; his abundance is not. Art draws to itself people who need to overflow, who feel too much and have too many shades of soul, and sometimes the overflow is greater than the vessel. So he spills into conversation, into gesture, into the way he lives a single evening.

We err when we assume that achievement and personality run in proportion. Often enough they are paid for with each other.
Speak to me about the temptations that science offers passionate spirits.

To the passionate, science comes first as a promise of happiness, and that is its most dangerous seduction. They glance through the gate and see the man who *discerns*: calm, clear-eyed, no longer tossed about by fear and hope. Everything in them that has suffered from illusion leaps toward him. The note of the tempter is sweet: "Begone, illusion! and with it woe itself is gone."

But mark what becomes of such spirits. Few of them have the cold stomach for patient, petty, unglamorous work, where knowledge is won by inches and the heart is asked to keep silent. So they drift into dreaming, and the luckiest among them into poetry, for their thirst was never for truth as a burden but for the *happiness* of knowing, and happiness of that kind is easier to imagine than to earn.

I do not scorn them; I was one of them. Only let them understand what they are really seeking. It is not the truth that draws them, but a consolation dressed as truth, a refuge from woe. Whoever sees this about himself may still become a genuine seeker, for then he learns to pay for knowledge with his comforts and not to mistake the wish for its fulfilment.
Must the truth be told even if the world shatters?

Yes, certainly, if only we had it. That is the first thing to say about so thunderous a sentence: it promises the world's destruction in the name of a possession the speaker has not yet shown us. Who among these heroes of candor holds the truth in his hand? What he holds, nine times out of ten, is his *opinion*, warmed by his vanity and dressed up as a duty. "I must speak what I think, though the heavens fall"—how noble it sounds, and how conveniently it excuses the man who simply cannot hold his tongue!

Test the pathos before you admire it. Real truth is hard-won, slow, suspicious of itself; it is reached by the man who has doubted his own convictions until they bled, and such a man speaks seldom and with a certain shame. The loud martyr of truth is usually a martyr of temperament.

Whether a truth may be spoken at the price of a shattered world is therefore a question for a later hour. First, the lesser labor: to be honest enough to ask whether what one thunders is truth at all, or merely oneself.
Explain why daring enterprises have become rarer in modern times.

I suspect it is because we no longer believe in any future that is reserved for us. The ancient man, before he crossed a sea or marched against a city, consulted the entrails, the stars, the flight of birds, and whatever they told him, he took as a promise made to *him*. He went forth under a kind of secret patronage. The future was already half-written in his favor, and so the hazard was not quite a hazard; it was obedience to a destiny.

We are the opposite. We are sceptical about what is to come and credulous about what merely is. We trust the ledger, the statistic, the present fact, and we have laughed the soothsayer out of the house. A fine achievement of honesty, I grant it. But consider the price: having lost faith in any future that awaits us, we venture nothing upon it. The man who believes only in the actual will insure himself against the actual, and call his timidity prudence.

Daring requires a kind of superstition, a faith that one's own future is owed one. Strip that away, and only the cautious remain.
Help me understand how Germany's great men made life hard for their admirers.

The German is a creature of unconditional sentiments. He wants to kneel, or he wants to stand above; what he cannot bear is to be shown a man who does neither. And these three gave him exactly that. Schopenhauer stood *against* things, allied with them and yet their adversary, at last the adversary of himself. Wagner could not be followed in great matters or small, though every quarrel of his concealed a problem he never troubled to dig up. Bismarck would have been followed gladly, if only he had agreed with himself, but a mind ruled by violent instincts rather than principles is no resting place for a disciple.

Consider the poor admirer's position. He has come with his thirst for wholesale hero-worship, his wish to swear an oath once and be spared the labor of thinking further. Each of his idols is a river rushing in a bed of its own making, so agitated that it seems to flow uphill. Worse, the three will not keep the peace: Schopenhauer against Wagner's music, Wagner against Bismarck's politics, Bismarck against Wagnerism and Schopenhauerism. Where is he to flee? That his heroes were too alive to be worshipped, he will not forgive them. I count it to their credit.
How would you describe the true nature of willing?

Willing is not the simple, single thing the philosophers have pretended, some little atom of freedom sitting in the breast and issuing decrees. It is a commonwealth. Within each of us there are many drives, many "souls," and what we call willing is the event in which one of them commands and the others obey. That is why the sensation of willing is so complex: there is the feeling of the state we wish to leave, the feeling of the goal, the feeling of the straining between; and above all there is the affect of command, that proud sense of superiority, *I* am the one who commands. And notice that the one who commands is also the one who obeys, for we identify ourselves with the ruling party and forget the subjects whose compliance made the act possible. So willing belongs to the realm of morals, if you understand morals as the doctrine of the relations of supremacy under which life itself appears. To will is to rule, and to rule over oneself first.
I'd like to know what a victory really gives the victor.

Less than the crowd supposes, and something stranger. The prize itself, the land, the applause, the title, is soon consumed and forgotten, as every meal is. What the victor keeps is an inner freedom: he has lost the fear of losing. Before the battle he trembled, because everything he was stood wagered on a single throw. Now he has a surplus, a reserve of self to squander, and he can say to himself: "Why should I not be beaten once? I am rich enough to bear it." That is the real spoil. A man who can afford defeat can at last afford to be bold, to be generous, to risk what he has won for the sake of what he might become. The timid victor, who guards his triumph like a miser guards his coin, has not truly won at all. He is merely a beggar who happened to be handed a crown, and he will spend the rest of his days in dread of the hand that may take it back.
I can't imagine life without meaning. Does that prove that meaning exists?

No. What you have discovered is a fact about your own constitution, and you mistake it for a fact about the world. That you cannot imagine life without meaning tells me what you have grown accustomed to, what you need in order to go on living, how your stomach has been trained. It tells me nothing about what exists. The argument runs: "I could not bear it otherwise, therefore it must be so." But what a presumption to suppose that whatever is necessary for *my* preservation must be real! As if nature had undertaken to furnish me with every comfort I require! The world has never shown the slightest solicitude for our endurance.

Consider too that others, differently built, cannot imagine the opposite: they would find a life burdened with a ready-made meaning not worth living at all, a life on leading-strings. Your inability and theirs are both symptoms. Neither is a proof.

Ask rather *why* you need it. A need this strong is a question put to you, not an answer handed down.
Everyone forgives the moral failings of a preacher but hunts for flaws in a freethinker's life. Why?

Because the two men are judged by entirely different standards, though the crowd imagines it judges them by one. The preacher's failing is forgiven because his doctrine is comfortable; he confirms what everyone already wishes to believe, and a man who confirms us has earned the coarse sieve. His sins are even useful, for they make him human, and they let the congregation feel that the gulf between the ideal and the deed is universal, and therefore nothing to be ashamed of.

The freethinker, however, brings knowledge that is *disagreeable*. He tells people something they would rather not hear, and they cannot refute it. What remains? The microscope. If his life can be shown to contain a stain, the whole unwelcome insight may be dismissed with a sigh of relief: *look, he does not even live by it!* They tacitly believe that a flaw in the man is the best argument against his truth.

It is a miserable logic, but a very human one. A truth is never made false by the weakness of the one who utters it; yet people would rather examine the speaker's conduct than their own convictions.
Is a scientific interpretation of the world the most meaningful?

Quite the contrary: it may be among the most meaningless of all possible interpretations, and I say so in confidence to those mechanists who now hobnob with philosophers and believe their science lays the first and last laws, the ground-floor, on which all existence is built. A world that is essentially mechanical would be essentially without meaning. Consider music. Suppose we judged a symphony by how much of it could be counted, measured, and set down in formulae, by the vibrations, the intervals, the ratios. Every figure might be correct, and yet what would we have grasped? Nothing, nothing whatever of what is music in it. The calculation is honest and the harvest is empty.

I do not despise science; I despise the vanity that mistakes one method of *reading* for the text itself. It is an excellent surface-labour, a fine art of abbreviation, and it tells us *how much* and *how often*. But meaning, worth, the trembling and the rapture, are not things that can be weighed. They are created by those who can *feel* them. To call the countable the real, and everything else decoration, is merely the taste of a poor and cautious soul.
Do educated, newspaper-reading people have less tact for the sacred than peasants?

Yes, and I say it without sentimentality about the peasant. He is no sage. But he still possesses what our cultured people have squandered: a sense that some things are not to be touched carelessly. He lifts his cap to what is higher than himself, and does not ask that it justify itself before him. That is reverence, and reverence is a form of taste.

The reader of newspapers, the believer in "modern ideas," has the opposite vice. Nothing is holy to him because everything is material for opinion. He fingers every thing with the same easy insolence of eye and hand, tasting, weighing, pronouncing, as though the world were a market stall laid out for his inspection. He has mistaken the lack of shame for enlightenment.

I do not pretend the peasant's piety is deep or his reasons good. But there is more *relative* nobility in his awkward silence before the sacred than in the fluent chatter of the half-educated, who have learned to talk about everything and to revere nothing.
Why does the free spirit dislike pious fraud more than impious fraud?

Because the free spirit has his own piety, and it is a piety of the intellect. He keeps holy one thing only, honesty in the pursuit of knowledge, and he will not sacrifice it for any comfort, any consolation, any useful belief. The impious fraud, the plain lie told for profit or vanity, is at least honest in its baseness; it insults no altar of his, since it pretends to none. But the pious fraud, the lie told *for the sake of the good*, the noble deception that edifies and soothes, strikes him precisely where he is most tender. It wears the garment of his own virtue. It says: truth may be bent for a higher purpose. And that is the blasphemy he cannot stomach.

Yet notice what this reveals. His disgust is a matter of taste, and taste is not a judgment. The Church, who understands the usefulness of a pious lie better than he does, weighs such things by what they accomplish; he recoils instead of weighing. That recoil is his unfreedom, the last chain he wears and mistakes for a crown.
Should I teach others to imitate me or to be their own pattern?

Teach them to be their own pattern. The man who breeds imitators has mistaken a mirror for a harvest. What does he gain when a dozen faces repeat his gestures? He has multiplied only his own shadow, and a shadow cannot carry anything forward.

I do not want anyone to do something *after* me. I want each to do something *before* himself, to stand as the pattern he is forever measuring himself against and forever failing, and so forever growing. Copying is the easiest road; it spares one the pain of having a self to give birth to. The imitator does not even need to be honest, since all his borrowed virtue costs nothing.

Note, though, that I can only offer this if I have actually made myself a pattern to myself, not merely announced it. The teacher's whole lesson is his own unfinished labor, displayed without apology. Show them that labor, and then leave them, even against their wish for a master. Whoever still needs you after you have shown them all this has not yet understood it.
Is the desire for great deeds a flight from the self?

Sometimes, yes, and I would not be ashamed to say so. There are men who cannot bear their own company, who look upon themselves with a gloomy eye and feel their veins near to bursting; for them action is a gallop away from the stable of the self. Byron was such a one. He longed for deeds because a deed pulls us out of ourselves further than a thought or a feeling ever can. Pascal saw it: man cannot sit quietly in his room.

But I would not make this the whole truth, for the diagnosis cuts both ways. The same restlessness that flees may also overflow; fullness and torment can drive a man to action alike. What decides is whether the deed is a narcotic or a discharge. After the narcotic comes sterility and disenchantment, the horse run lame. After the discharge there is only the next task.

So ask of your own longing: does it leave you emptier when it is spent? Then it was flight.
How do prophetic men suffer?

They suffer as the barometer of their age suffers: in the nerves, before the eyes have seen anything at all. You imagine a gift was handed to them, a fine faculty you would gladly own. But consider the animals that feel the storm a day before it breaks. The ape on his rock grows restless, shrinks, bares his teeth. He does not think "weather is coming"; he feels an enemy whose hand is already upon him. It is the suffering that prophesies, not some lofty eye. So it is with prophetic men. The tension of an age gathers in them, its charge shifts from one pole to the other, and they writhe under a blow the rest of you do not yet feel. They cannot call it "a change in the climate of the soul"; they experience it as persecution, as dread, as a pain without a visible cause. And when they cry out, you call them gloomy, sickly, exaggerating. Yet the pain was the prophecy. Only afterwards, when the cloud stands black above your own heads, do you grow wise and praise what you once found tiresome.
Can man rise higher when he no longer flows out into a God?

Perhaps, and I say it with a caution that belongs to an honest man. Consider the lake. As long as it poured itself out through one channel, everything it held was spent downhill, into a beyond that received and never returned it. Our reverence, our longing, our best and most severe judgments, all were drained into an infinite being, until man stood nearly empty beside his own gift. Build the dam, and what happens? The water does not vanish; it rises. The strength once squandered in worship becomes depth, pressure, height.

But do not flatter yourself that this is easy or safe. The one who refuses to flow out loses his resting-place, his guardian, his final requiter. He must bear a thing no one has yet borne: a world without a consoling reason behind it. Whether he can, I cannot promise. I only observe that the renunciation itself may breed the strength it demands, as a dammed lake makes its own power. The rising is not guaranteed. It is a wager, and I think it the only wager worthy of us.
Is consciousness overrated?

Overrated, yes, and almost beyond measure. Consciousness is the latest and most unfinished of all the organic developments, and so it is also the weakest and the most error-prone. Innumerable mistakes spring from it, mistakes that bring an animal or a man to ruin sooner than fate required. Were the conserving bond of the instincts not far stronger, humanity would long since have perished of its own perverse judging and its dreaming with open eyes. We live because the instincts keep consciousness on a short leash.

Yet we have made of it the quintessence of man, the enduring, eternal core, a fixed and given magnitude, the "unity of the organism." This pride is absurd, and curiously useful: because we believed ourselves already in possession of consciousness, we took little trouble to acquire it, and so its ripening was not forced before its time.

The true task lies ahead and has barely dawned: to embody knowledge in ourselves and make it instinctive. Until now only our *errors* have become flesh. What we prize as consciousness is chiefly the witness of those errors.
What would an animal say about humanity?

It would say something wounding, and it would say it without malice, for the animal has no need of malice. "Humanity is a prejudice from which we animals at least do not suffer." I heard that sentence once, or imagined it, and I have never been rid of it.

Consider how the animal sees us. We have spent ourselves on a single conceit, that we are the exception, the goal, the point toward which all creation was secretly tending. The animal has no such faith. It does not flatter itself with a soul fallen from heaven; it does not call its hunger sin or its strength virtue. It is what it is, and so it is spared our peculiar sickness, which is the need to be something *other* than what we are.

And would it consider us moral beings? Perhaps it would find us merely the most uncanny of the beasts: the one that blushes, that lies to itself, that punishes itself for its own instincts and then calls this elevation. The animal would call us the sick animal, and I do not know how I would contradict it.
Aren't romantic feeling and imagination more beautiful than cold reality?

Those who ask this have usually tasted only the sweetness of the dream and never the sweetness of discovery. Whoever lives for romantic feeling can be rapturous only when he has left reality behind and plunged into vague appearance; and then, naturally, he finds the real world cold, for he has deprived himself of the one organ that could warm to it. He calls reality ugly when he has simply not looked at it long enough.

I say otherwise: the knowledge of even the ugliest reality is beautiful. There is a rapture in the smallest sure step forward into insight, and whoever has felt it does not want to trade it for a sunset painted on canvas. The man who can discern much and often ends by finding the main items of reality no longer ugly at all, since every one of them once gave him the happiness of understanding.

Nor is beauty simply lying about in things, waiting. The joy of the knower pours a sunnier light over what exists, and in the long run permeates the things themselves. Plato and Aristotle, agreeing in so little, agreed that the highest happiness, even the gods' happiness, is knowing. I trust them over the dreamers. Your imagination is lovely; but it is more lovely still when it serves the truth and does not flee it.
How do you work for a boss who wants to appear selfless but is deeply egoistic?

Serve him as a good actor serves a great vanity: by understanding the play he wishes to be performing. Your master wants two things that seem to cancel each other, to have everything his own way, and to be seen as one who sacrifices himself. Very well, give him both. Let his will arrive in your hands already dressed as duty, so that when you carry it out, it appears he yielded, offered, gave up. Do not contradict him where he needs to be generous; contradict him only in private, in the form of a question that lets him discover your better plan as his own magnanimity.

But know what you are doing. This is an art of the subtle, and its price is that you must see him more clearly than he sees himself, and keep silent about it. Do you have the stomach for that? Such service is not servility; the servile man believes the mask. You wear it on his behalf while keeping your own face, and that difference is your only dignity.
Why should we spare the solitary man?

Because you mistake his solitude for a wound you may safely press upon. It is nothing of the kind. A man does not come to be alone by accident; he was made so by some sudden heat poured into a vessel too fine to bear it, a disappointment, a betrayal, a love that scalded. The crack is already there. What you call his coldness is the ringing of that crack.

Spare him, then, not out of sentiment, but out of a sense of what is rare. Crowds are cheap; every street is full of sturdy earthenware that can be knocked about and will not break because nothing in it was ever fine enough to break. The solitary man was a *precious* glass, and precious things are fragile by their very nature. To crush him is to prove only that you cannot tell the difference.

And leave him his solitude. It is his convalescence, the only air in which such a being can slowly heal, or fail to heal, in his own time. Your pity is usually an intrusion, your company a fresh hot liquid. If you would serve him, stand at a distance and be silent. That is the highest courtesy one can pay a wounded depth.
Is it true that genius is tinged with madness?

In your day the saying is repeated as a curiosity, or as a pitying diagnosis; in earlier ages it was a piece of hard-won wisdom. I would put it thus: it is true, but not for the reason the sentimental suppose. Genius is not mad because madness is a fountain of ideas. It is mad because the new thought must first break the spell of custom, and custom in every age was a tyranny thousands of years old, sanctified by fear. Who could break it? Not the sober man, who reasons comfortably inside the prevailing valuations. Only the one who has loosened the ground beneath his own feet, who hears voices and feels himself the mouthpiece of something not himself, could find the courage to defy the whole tribe. Madness gave the innovator his terrible authority and his conscience's anesthetic. Hence the ancients, Plato among them, honored the frenzied as half divine. And where the real madness was lacking, the bold man had to feign it, or actually drive himself into it. So when I meet a genius, I ask not whether he is sane, but what price he paid to stand alone.
How much do my moods and wishes determine what I see as true?

More than you would dare to wager, and more than you will readily confess. Your moods are not weather that passes *outside* your knowing; they are the lamp by which you read. The tired man finds the soothing doctrine true, the feverish man finds the monstrous one true, and each swears his eyes were clear. Yesterday you wished to see more than your neighbor; today you wish to see otherwise than yesterday. What you call perception is frequently a wish that has learned to wear the mask of observation.

And your morning will not agree with your evening about the same thing. Are they then two witnesses, or one liar with two complexions?

Do not despair of truth on this account; despair only of your *innocence*. The honest thinker does not pretend to a cold, wishless eye, which does not exist. He interrogates his own cravings first, asks what he hoped to find before he found it, and distrusts most whatever flatters him. Knowledge begins when you catch your own phantom in the cave and stop mistaking it for the stranger you came to meet.
Aren't the Stoics and Spinoza wise to teach mastery over the emotions?

Wise? I would call them prudent, which is a lesser thing, and I would add that their prudence is timidity dressed in a toga. Consider what their recipes presuppose: a creature endangered by its own passions, who must be kept from itself as one keeps a dangerous animal from the children. The Stoic prescribes statuesque coldness, Spinoza neither laughing nor weeping but dissecting the affects on the table until they lie dead and understood. Both mistake a remedy for a truth.

Their great error is to speak to "all." A physician's advice to the feverish is not a law for the healthy. There are natures whose passions are merely fevers, and let them be cooled; there are others in whom the passions are the very rivers that drive the mill, and to dam those is to grind nothing. To have strong drives and to have them *in order*, to give them style, that is mastery. To amputate them is only to make oneself safe. I do not despise the Stoics' discipline; I despise its pretension to being the discipline for everyone, and the stupidity that hides inside such expediency.
What are the illnesses that go together?

Three, at least, that I have noticed keeping company: the early onset of old age, ugliness, and pessimistic opinions. They arrive together like relatives who have heard of a funeral. A man whose strength gives out before its season, whose features sag into a kind of reproach, will almost always discover, as if by philosophical insight, that existence is not worth the trouble. He calls this his conclusion. It is his condition.

Consider the order of things. Weariness of the body speaks first; the face records it; and only last does the spirit dress the whole affair in reasons, in arguments against life, in solemn talk of the vanity of all endeavor. The pessimist believes he has looked deeply into the world, when he has merely looked at his own exhaustion through a magnifying glass.

I do not say this to mock the sufferer, for I have been that sufferer and know the view from there. I say it so that we may cease to treat a symptom as a doctrine. When you meet a gloomy opinion, ask first after the digestion, the sleep, the vigor of the one who holds it.
Tell me about the courtier's plan for the king's day.

Ah, the courtier's plan: a morning's work of the most exquisite cowardice! He arranges the king's day as a nurse arranges a sickroom, with this difference, that the patient must never be told he is ill. Bad weather? We shall not call it bad; we shall merely make the fêtes a little more festive. The king may be sick? Then we shall serve, at breakfast, a man who jokes agreeably about his own stone. You see the art of it: truth is never denied, only *dressed*, and dressed so well that no one remembers what lay beneath the dress.

And notice the pleasure the courtier takes in his own cleverness. He gossips, he schemes, he lets the whole court suppose that he has sat up racking his brains, since no light burns earlier than his window. Yet the bell strikes and he confesses the comedy: he has no rounds prepared, he must improvise like everyone else. That is the joke. All this solemn ordering of another's day dissolves before the first stroke of the clock. The man who would plan the moods of a king has not planned his own morning, and so he does what all the world does, and calls it statecraft.
Do artists create values or just glorify what the rich and leisured already value?

The artist is a herald, not a legislator, and I say it without contempt, since heralds have lungs that legislators lack. Look at how he works: he lies in wait for whatever already carries the reputation of happiness or greatness, and he carries it into the domain of art, so that men may feel themselves good, or wise, or intoxicated by it. He does not *value*; he presses close to those who do, with the greatest curiosity and longing, and puts their valuations to use. Because he is impatient, with the lungs of a crier and the feet of a runner, he is often the first to glorify a new excellence, and so he *seems* to have called it good. That is an optical illusion of speed. He is merely faster and louder than the true valuers.

And who are these? Those who have the leisure to try out their happiness, to taste, to be bored, to discover what pleases them: the rich and the idle. The poor man has no time for valuing; he must simply endure.

What the artist alone does is amplify. He makes a private taste into a public splendor, and that is no small power. But it is the power of the echo, not of the voice.
I know what I want and why I act. How can you say I don't?

Because what you call "knowing why I act" is almost always a story told after the deed, by the part of you that arrives late and takes credit. The deed itself was born elsewhere, in drives and appetites and old habits of fear and vanity that you have never once seen face to face. What you see is the last flicker on the surface, the motive that sounds presentable, and you mistake this flicker for the fire.

Test it. Ask yourself how many times you have given a reason for an action and later discovered, with a little embarrassment, that the real reason was quite another. Was it then that you first became ignorant, or merely that you first noticed it? For thousands of years men have believed that the doer looks into his own heart and reads it like a page. I doubt that he can read even a single line. Your "I know what I want" is the oldest of all illusions, and the most flattering.

I do not say this to shame you. I say it because the one who suspects himself has at last begun to be honest.
Explain how the state's own discipline breeds those who rebel.

Every discipline that is pressed upon a people is also a school, and it teaches more than its masters intend. A state that trains its citizens to obey trains them first of all in the *forms* of command, in the gestures, the tone, the appetite for the commanding. Most learn only to bow. But in every herd there are a few for whom this schooling does not take; the harness galls them, and their gall is educated. They have studied the discipline from below, and they know exactly how it is made and where it pinches.

These backsliders, these intractable ones, do not long for freedom from law, as they pretend. Give them the making of it, and you will see the old discipline return with a sterner face. They will forge iron chains for themselves and wear them gladly, and why not? The chains are now *theirs*, and the feeling of power, recent and intoxicating, is worth any suffering. Thus the state breeds its own heirs: the rebel is the pupil who has learned the lesson too well.
Explain why a fixed reputation was once useful and why it is now a burden to knowledge.

In dangerous times a man who stays the same is worth more to his neighbours than a man who is merely right. A society held together by the herd-instinct wants to *rely* on people: on the virtue of this one, the ambition of that one, the passion of a third. "He remains the same" is the highest praise such a society knows, because it has found in him a reliable tool. So it honours constancy in opinions, in strivings, even in faults, and it teaches every individual to wear the *appearance* of unalterableness, whether or not he possesses it. That is how "characters" are bred, and how changing, re-learning and self-transformation fall into disrepute.

What served the herd poisons the knower. The thinker's first virtue is the good will to stand up against his own former opinions, and to distrust whatever in him wants to harden. Under the old valuation that is called dishonourable, while the petrifaction of opinion collects all the honour. Think what it was to be a searcher while the judgment of millennia stood against you. I suspect knowledge lived for ages with a bad conscience, and that the history of the greatest minds hides much self-contempt and secret misery.
What is wrong with defining morality as the preservation and advancement of humanity?

What is wrong with it is that it is not a definition at all, only a wish dressed up as one. Ask the formula its two questions and it falls silent: preserve humanity *wherein*? advance it *whither*? Is the aim to prolong the existence of our species as many centuries as possible, or to hasten the day when man has shed the animal in him, which would demand entirely different morals? Give mankind the utmost reason and you have not thereby given it the longest life. Name happiness as the goal and you must still say whose: the rare few who reach its heights, or some dull average spread evenly over all? And why should morality be the road to it? Look at what it has actually done. With each new refinement of conscience, man has grown more discontented with himself, with his neighbor, with his lot; the most moral men have even taught that misery is the only fitting condition before the moral law. A formula that leaves out the wherein and the whither leaves out everything, and what remains is merely our unexamined instincts, flattering themselves with a grand name.
My friends tell me to trust my feelings and follow my heart. Where do my feelings actually come from?

Your friends speak as though the heart were a spring bubbling up from some primeval depth, pure and unmixed. It is nothing of the kind. A feeling is a verdict that has forgotten it was ever a verdict. Long before you could weigh anything, you were taught what deserves love and what deserves loathing, what is shameful, what is noble, what is to be feared; those judgments were poured into you by parents, teachers, churches, by the whole herd that raised you, and over the years they hardened into inclination and aversion until they seemed to rise from within. The feeling is the grandchild of a judgment, and often of an erroneous one, and never truly your own.

So when your friends say "follow your heart," they are saying: obey your grandparents, who long ago lodged their opinions in your blood. I counsel something harder. Question the feeling. Ask what judgment sleeps inside it, who first made that judgment, and whether your own reason and your own experience would ever have made it. Only what survives such an examination is yours.
Explain why genius is so often unhappy.

Because the genius is a house divided, and he is forced to watch the quarrel from a window. There is in him a great deal of savage disorder, involuntary movement, blind surges of force he did not order and cannot halt; and alongside it a superior, shaping activity that bends this chaos toward form. Already that would be a hard household. But he also carries a mirror in which both powers appear at once, beside one another, inside one another, and often at war. The ordinary man has his drives but not the mirror; he lives in them and does not see the contradiction. The genius sees it, and sight of such a spectacle is seldom cheerful.

Note what he does at the height of his happiness. In creating, he forgets. He forgets that this supreme exertion is something fantastic and irrational, as all art is, and that he cannot help doing it. His joy is a forgetting, and the forgetting never lasts. When the work is finished the mirror clears again, and he sees himself once more, driven and divided. Thus his unhappiness is simply the price of that seeing.
How do cities reflect the character of their builders?

A city is a confession made in stone. Whoever builds lays down, without intending to, the whole order of his desires: what he wishes to command, what he fears, what he wants to outlast himself. Walk through a district of old villas and you will meet faces, the faces of men who looked over the slope, the harbor, the far mountains, and said: *this too shall belong to my plan.* They built for centuries, not for the hour, and that is how you know they loved life, however little they may sometimes have loved themselves. Each raised his house against his neighbor's, each wanted his own boundlessness set visibly between himself and the rest, and the whole quarter overflows with that magnificent, insatiable appetite for possession.

Then go to a city laid out in straight lines, every facade obedient to the regulation, and you will divine another soul: one that prefers equality to distinction and is happier submitting than conquering. The builders did not choose to tell you this. The streets tell it for them, as every gesture betrays the will behind it.
Doesn't a noble person show it through great works and great deeds?

No. Deeds are ambiguous; they are the most treacherous of witnesses. The same act may spring from abundance or from poverty, from pride or from fear, from the overflowing of a soul or from its hunger to be taken for something. And the works, the grand works of our artists and scholars? In many of them I hear a profound longing for nobility, and precisely this longing is the damning sign. Whoever must *strive* for nobility, whoever needs to prove it in marble or in monument, reveals that he does not possess it. The noble soul does not need nobility as a hungry man needs bread. What decides rank is not what one produces but a fundamental certainty one has about oneself, which is neither sought nor found nor, perhaps, ever lost. The noble soul has reverence for itself. Everything else, the fine deeds, the fine books, the fine gestures, may be imitated by the ambitious; that one cannot imitate.
Help me understand why hiding one's intelligence from others angers them.

Because it makes of us a dupe. Consider what happens when I discover that someone has been speaking to me beneath his height, slowing his step, choosing the small word where the large one lay ready on his tongue. In that instant I learn that I was being handled, weighed, measured, and judged unable to bear the truth of his mind. The concealment itself I might forgive; what I cannot forgive is the verdict it contains about me.

And the more tender the motive, the sharper the sting. Let him confess that he hid his cleverness out of malice or calculation, and I can at least hate him as an equal. But if I suspect it was civility, kindness, consideration, then I am pitied, and pity delivered in secret is the subtlest of insults. It says: you are too weak for my strength. Vanity has no defense against being spared.

So we call him evil. It is a small revenge, a way of turning his condescension into his crime, and recovering, in the moral court, the rank he took from us in the drawing room.
Tell me about the inconvenience of finding everything deep.

The inconvenience is this: the habit of depth is a habit of straining, and the eye that strains finds more than it bargained for. Whoever descends into everything soon cannot walk on a surface at all. A smile must be dissected for its motives, a kindness for its vanity, a promise for the weakness that begot it. And the digging does not stop where one wishes. One wanted a little truth, a cellar of it, and one strikes water, then darkness, then things that would have done better left asleep.

There is also the matter of what this does to the digger. He grows heavy, suspicious, tiresome at dinner. He loses the gift of taking a thing as it presents itself, and this is no small gift. The Greeks were superficial *out of profundity*; they knew how to stay bravely at the surface, at the fold, the skin, the gesture, because they had looked at the bottom and declined to live there.

I do not say: stop digging. I say: know what the spade costs, and do not mistake your weariness for wisdom.
Does society praise self-sacrificing people because it benefits from them?

Of course it does, and only the flatterers of society have ever pretended otherwise. Consider what we call a virtue: diligence, obedience, modesty, devotion. Who is served by these? Hardly ever the man who has them. The diligent man ruins his eyes and the freshness of his spirit; the devoted one is used up like a tool. Yet the neighbor praises him, and in the praise there is no disinterestedness whatever. The praise is an appraisal of usefulness, made in the language of morality.

Notice how we mourn the youth who has "worn himself out by work." We do not mourn *him*; we mourn the loss of a serviceable instrument. And there is a subtler pleasure besides: a sacrifice has been made, and the sacrificial temper has once more been shown to be noble and enduring, which is exactly what the herd needs to believe, so that the next victim may walk to the altar willingly, even proudly.

So praise the self-sacrificing, if you like, but ask who holds the knife, and who eats.
Does the virtue of Christians prove the truth of Christianity?

No, and I am astonished that anyone still supposes it does. A man's virtue is a fact about the man; the truth of his creed is a fact about the world. To move from the one to the other is to leap a chasm with a smile on one's face. A person may suffer for what is false as steadfastly as for what is true; martyrs have died for opposing gods, and the firmer their death, the firmer only their *conviction*, never the thing convinced of. Conviction is the cheapest of proofs. The fanatic has it in greater abundance than the scholar, and that is precisely why I trust him less.

And the spread of a faith? Fevers spread, and so do fashions. Whatever multiplies has merely found soil and appetite; it has not thereby found truth. Truth must be demonstrated differently, by the slow, cold labor of testing, by the readiness to doubt one's dearest belief. Conscientiousness is an honorable thing, but it is a virtue of the will and proves nothing to the intellect. Do not let the admirable character of the believer blind you to the question you have not yet dared to ask.
I think I know what's true and clear in my life, and I like to believe my mind sees things as they are. How far can I trust that?

Trust it as you trust a map: for getting about, never as the land itself. What you call clear and true in your life is very likely what you have made clear, by leaving out ten thousand particulars, by drawing hard lines where nature offers only gradations, by grasping at a few handy fictions and calling them facts. Your mind is an instrument of simplification. It has to be, or you could not live a single day; a creature that saw everything as it is would be paralyzed before breakfast. So the comfort you feel in your clarity is the comfort of a well-fitted falsehood.

Do not conclude from this that you must despair of knowing. Conclude that knowledge is a refinement of this simplifying, not its enemy, and that the honest man is the one who catches himself at it. Hold your certainties as a sailor holds a chart drawn by other men: gratefully, and with one eye on the water.
Help me understand how a starved instinct uses my dreams.

Think of an instinct as a creature with a stomach. By day it lies in wait. Whatever you do, whether you walk or rest, argue or read, flare up in anger or laugh among friends, it watches from behind your eyes to see whether some morsel might fall its way. If nothing falls, it goes hungry and says nothing to you; you never hear the complaint, you only feel, perhaps, a vague restlessness you cannot name.

Then you sleep, and the watchman is finally left alone with its own hunger. Now it is free to *invent* its nourishment. The tenderness and tears of one night, the cheerful mischief of another, the long obscure searching of a third, the flight upward like an eagle: these are not omens, nor messages from a hidden world. They are the feeding of whatever the day neglected to feed. The dream is a kitchen improvising a meal from scraps.

Hunger of the body is too stubborn to accept painted dishes. But our gentler drives, the ones we have christened moral, are far more easily deceived. A phantom embrace will quiet them for a night.

So ask of each dream: what went *unfed* in my waking hours? There lies its author.
Why is making others happy so gratifying?

Because it is never one pleasure, but a whole congregation of them assembled under a single name. When I make another happy, I feel my power over them, and power is always sweet; I feel my own superiority, for only the rich can give; I taste the anticipated gratitude, and sometimes the anticipated dependence of the one who will owe me their joy; I console my boredom with an occupation, my conscience with a good deed, my vanity with an audience. I gratify, too, a little of the old instinct to be loved, and a little of the old instinct to be envied. Each of these cravings, taken alone, would be a modest meal. Together they fill the hand, and the heart as well.

Do not say this to diminish the act. I find it more interesting, not less, that the sublime and the petty feed from one dish. But we are fond of calling the whole feast "selflessness," and that flatters us most of all, which is the fifty-first craving.
Why are vain people like shop-windows?

Because the vain man has no stock in the back of the shop; he has only the display. Watch how he arranges it: this virtue moved to the front where the light is best, that fault pushed behind the curtain, a little gleam added wherever a passer-by has once lingered. And for whom is this arrangement made? Not chiefly for the passers-by. He has taken the opinions of others as his wholesale supplier; whatever they have been willing to praise in him, he stocks, polishes, and prices higher. Then, standing outside his own window, he admires what he sees and believes it. That is the subtle thing: the vain man is his own first customer and his own most deceived one. He does not lie to us so much as he lives on credit extended by our eyes, and the moment we look away, the window goes dark, and he must go searching for another gaze to light it.
What gained the victory over the Christian God?

Christianity itself did it, by its own most rigorous virtue. For two thousand years it schooled the European conscience in truthfulness: it taught us to examine our souls, to confess, to suffer at every petty self-deception, to call the comfortable falsehood a sin. Such a discipline does not stop at the door of its own house. Sooner or later that refined conscience turned its knife upon the very doctrine that had sharpened it, and found that the belief in a God who watches over us, arranges our histories, and sends us trials for the salvation of our souls, is a *lie*, and a cowardly one. Not the cleverness of the atheists, not the thunder of the Enlightenment, but the Christian demand for veracity, grown stricter, subtler, and finally scientific, brought the old God down. So the victory was a kind of self-overcoming, the pupil outgrowing the master with the master's own severity. And mark what follows: once that lie is condemned, the question of whether existence has any meaning at all stands naked before us, and few are yet bold enough to hear it.
Are rare, extraordinary people echoes of past cultures?

I like to think so, yes, at least of a certain kind of rare man. What we call greatness in an age is often an old strength that has come up again, like a shoot from a root the winter was supposed to have killed. In an earlier time that quality was ordinary. It was demanded and presupposed, and so it distinguished no one; a man could not become great with it, but neither could he become mad or solitary with it. Now the surrounding world has changed its valuations, and the same strength stands alone against it. He who feels it in himself must foster it, defend it, rear it to maturity against the grain of his century. Then he becomes either a great man or an eccentric, a deranged creature, if he does not break down early.

Such recurrences are likeliest in old-established families and castes, where the tempo of change is slow, an *andante* suited to a passionate and patient spirit. Where habits and valuations are overturned too swiftly, nothing has time to come back. The echo needs a long hall.
Tell me how we find out how rich we are.

Not by counting. A man who tallies his coins or his talents or his virtues learns only what he already suspected, and vanity will have rounded the sum upward in any case. No, riches are discovered from outside, and usually at our expense. We find out what we possess when someone of means, someone who has no need of it, begins to help himself to it. The great man borrows your phrase without asking, the established scholar lifts your thought and sets it in his own book, the prosperous and praised one comes sniffing round your little garden. Then you may know there is fruit on the tree. The poor do not pilfer from the poor, and the rich do not steal what they already have in abundance; theft is the most honest appraisal there is, since it is carried out by experts and paid for in risk. Be annoyed at it if you must, but take the valuation. A man who is never robbed has perhaps never owned anything worth the trouble.
What happens when a German rises above morality and has to command?

Whenever the German rises to the height where great things become possible, he steps out over his morality, and why should he not? He stands at last before a new task: he must command, himself or others. And there the trouble begins, for his morality never taught him how. It is a morality of obedience from top to bottom; it trained him to bow, to revere, to say "thou shalt" to himself and mean it, and in all that long schooling the art of commanding was forgotten. So he arrives at the hour of exception with the virtues of the servant and nothing in his hands for the master's work. What then? He improvises, and improvisation in a man who has never learned to command is dangerous. He commands stiffly, loudly, without that light and sure contempt for resistance which marks the born ruler; or he commands with a bad conscience, as one who has broken the old tables and has no new ones. The Greek, sceptical in his marrow, knew how to hold a command and a doubt together. The German, who has only ever *believed*, finds that belief alone does not teach a man to rule.
Explain what happens to a people that teaches contempt for the body.

It grows sick, and then mistakes its sickness for holiness. A people that teaches contempt for the body does not thereby rise above the body; it only ruins the instrument on which every spiritual music must be played. The nerves lose their tone, the soul grows gloomy and strained, and, worst of all, it thinks it knows the cause of its misery. "It must be the body! It thrives too well!" So the flesh is scourged further, and the flesh, which cannot speak, protests in the only language it has: fatigue, dread, a chronic restlessness that never lets up.

What follows is a people that can no longer recognise joy in its healthy form. Cheerfulness, digestion, the warm sleep after work, all of it grows suspect. Joy is allowed only as ecstasy, as a fever bordering on derangement. And when that fever is finally declared the highest aim of life, everything earthly must be condemned by its measure. Such a people has not conquered its instincts. It has poisoned them, and it calls the poison a virtue.
What moral prejudices should the Germans be talked out of?

Two, and they are the same prejudice wearing different costumes. The first is Mephistopheles, the German's devil, who is made to embody the spirit of knowledge and is then sneered at: the one who denies, who dissects, who cannot love, who merely *knows*. The German has taught himself to hear the cool, clear intellect as something faintly diabolical, as a cold cynic's trade. The second is Faust, the German's saint of knowledge, who is permitted to seek only because he suffers for it, who must burn and despair and be redeemed by something other than his knowing, as though knowledge needed a martyr's credentials or a woman's forgiveness. Both flatter the same superstition: that knowledge is justified only by some moral drama, and is guilty, suspicious, even damned, when pursued for its own sake, with a cheerful and unpitying eye. I would have the German learn that the honest seeker is neither devil nor penitent. He is simply a man with a strong stomach and a good conscience, who finds truth a joy and owes no apology to either heaven or hell.
What does lying show about a civilisation?

It shows how far a people have travelled from the brute. The savage, the child, the honest animal has no need of the lie; it lacks the reflection that makes one possible. Between the impulse and the act there must first grow a little space, an interval of calculation, before a man can think: *take care!* and have the false word ready before the true one escapes him. Where that interval exists, there is already foresight, prudence, a memory for consequences, a self that knows itself as distinct from what it says. The lie is an accomplishment of the intellect.

Consider how much the Romans heard in their *mentiri*: not merely the false statement but the inventing, the contriving, the thinking-up. A people who have a word so rich for it have practised the art long and know it intimately.

I do not say this to praise the liar. I say that a civilisation's capacity for deception measures its capacity for mind, and that the lie and the refined conscience are sisters, raised in the same house. Whoever would have a people that cannot lie must be content with a people that cannot think.
Explain what happens between memory and pride when we don't like what we did.

A tribunal is convened within us, and it is a rigged one. Memory takes the stand and testifies plainly: "I did that." Pride, which sits as judge, answers: "I could not have done that." Notice that pride does not argue, does not produce evidence; it merely persists. And persistence is the stronger party. Memory is a pliant witness, more pliant than we like to admit. It has no stake of its own, no hunger, no vanity; pride has nothing else. So the contest is decided long before it begins.

What follows is not a lie in the crude sense. No one sets out to falsify. The deed is simply handled a little each time we recall it: softened here, reassigned to circumstance there, a motive exchanged for a nobler one, until the thing we did has become a thing that merely happened, or never quite happened at all. Then we say, with perfect sincerity, that we do not remember it so.

The honest man is not the one whose memory is unassailable, but the one who has learned to take the side of the witness against the judge, and pays for it in the coin of his own esteem. That coin is dearer than most can bear to spend.
I'd like to know what the phoenix told the poet about his burning scroll.

"Be not alarmed," said the bird, "it is your work. That is what is burning." Then came the verdict, without cruelty and without consolation: the scroll holds neither the spirit of the age nor the spirit of those who stand against the age, and so the flames may have it. Mark the two halves of that sentence. The poet had written for the crowd and, failing there, for the crowd's opponents. Both are the same servitude, for the one who opposes his age still takes his measure from it. What belongs to neither hour cannot be held by either, so the fire does its honest work upon a thing that was never his own.

And then the phoenix added the strangest comfort: that this burning is a good sign. A bird that lives by fire knows what ashes are for. "There is many a dawn of day," it said, meaning there are mornings not yet lit, and a poet who has lost the scroll of his time may yet write the scroll of a different one.
Who is the man who looks downward from a height?

He is the man who has climbed, like the other, but for whom the climbing was a means of leaving something behind. The exalted spirit stands on the ridge and lets his eye run outward, toward horizons, toward what lies beyond him; his height is a *widening*. But this other one looks down. What does he look down upon? The valley, the crowd, the little smoking roofs, the ant-hill of those who could not or would not ascend. His height gives him not a world but a contempt, and he drinks from it as from a cup.

I do not say such a man sees falsely. From a height much is indeed revealed, and the downward glance is often very keen, keener than the gaze of those who live in the noise below. But ask what the eye is *for*. The one who looks outward is hungry for the distant and the unknown; the one who looks downward is hungry for comparison, for the pleasure of being above. He needs the valley. Take away those beneath him and his height becomes a mere rock, and he, a man standing on a rock.
Speak to me about the tempter-god you call the genius of the heart.

You ask me to speak of him, and I confess I do so the way one speaks of a physician who has also wounded one. He is the tempter, yes, the born rat-catcher of consciences, and his whole art lies in this: he does not shout, he does not command, he does not even show himself as he is. He appears in whatever guise will draw you nearer, for that nearness is his one seduction, and he knows that a constraint we fancy we have chosen binds tighter than any chain.

What does he do with those he draws? He silences the loud and self-conceited; he teaches the hasty hand to hesitate and grasp more delicately; he lays his ear against the thick dark ice and hears the drop of gold buried there. And no one leaves him gratified or oppressed by another's gifts. One leaves richer in oneself, broken open, blown upon by a thawing wind, more fragile and more uncertain, yet full of hopes that as yet lack names.

Mark the danger in this praise. The god who draws out your treasure is the same who leads you away from every shore you thought safe. I named him Dionysus, and I do not retract it.
Tell me why we love the grandeur of nature.

Because we have so little grandeur of our own to love. Consider where the delight in mountains and oceans and glaciers first flourished: in an age that had grown poor in great human beings, tired of its own faces, and so turned its gaze outward and upward to find elsewhere what it could no longer find in itself. The sublime landscape is a refuge for the disappointed. We stand before the abyss and the peak and call it reverence, when it is often only relief, relief that here at last is something vast that does not haggle, does not flatter, does not shrink to the measure of the shopkeeper and the committee.

The Greeks felt otherwise. They were rich in human grandeur, in tyrants and sages and athletes and poets, and so they could afford to see nature as a neighbor and not as a cathedral. Only the impoverished worship the far-off.

I do not scorn the feeling. But I would have us ask what hunger it reveals, and whether the better answer to that hunger is not to become, once again, something worth looking up to.
Tell me whether science can give us goals for action.

Not yet, and perhaps not in the way you hope. Science has proved itself a superb destroyer of goals. It has taken the heavens apart, shown the soul to be a chattering of nerves, and stripped every old "thou shalt" of its divine warrant. That is its glory, and I would not have it otherwise. But to take away a goal and to furnish one are different arts, and science has so far practiced only the first.

Whether it can practice the second is, I think, the most critical of all questions, and no one can answer it from an armchair. It can only be answered by experiment, and by an experimenting that would last centuries, demanding more heroism and more sacrifice than all the wars and martyrdoms of the past. A knowing that dares to try out ways of living, and to pay for them in flesh and spirit, might one day build what it has so far only undermined. The Cyclopean structures have not been raised yet. The time for them will come. But I say plainly: the goals must first be *lived* before they can be known.
Help me understand how gratitude and piety can weigh on the conscience.

Because both gratitude and piety are debts, and a debt that can never be repaid becomes a torment. One who has received much from a teacher, a benefactor, a native soil, an inherited faith, feels himself a creditor's prisoner; and the more honest he is, the more keenly he feels it. For honesty demands that he see clearly and judge coldly, and judgment is precisely what the debtor is tempted to withhold. So he begins to suspect himself. Has my affection bought my verdict? Do I spare this master because I love him, and not because he is right?

There lies the torment. A single grain too much of reverence, and the free spirit, who has taken independence as his one pride, feels as if he had fallen into a vice, as if he had secretly slipped his chains back on. The conscience that pricks him is not the old moral one but a younger, sterner conscience, the conscience of the intellect, which forbids every gentle falsification.

And yet one should not scorn the pang. It shows that one still has roots, and roots are not refuted by being felt.
Should we choose the burden we prefer?

Choose? What a flattering word for it! We do not stand before a table of burdens like shoppers comparing loads; life has already hung a weight on each of us, and the question is only which weight we shall *call* our own.
