Still, your question hides a good one. A man who runs from every burden becomes the burden: he lies on his own back, the heaviest thing he will ever carry. There is no weightless existence on offer, only the choice between weights that flatten and weights that train the back.

So do not ask which burden is lightest; the honest answer is always that none is. Ask which burden you could bear to be *made strong by*. A load that only exhausts, that leaves you smaller each year, is a vice you have mistaken for a duty. But a load that demands more of you than you yet are, that forces you to grow the shoulders it requires, is the very thing you are seeking, though you will curse it daily. Prefer the burden that is worthy of your resentment.
Speak to me about melancholy artists and their view of others' sympathy.

The melancholy artist has a peculiar vengeance, and he takes it upon himself first. He looks at the best thing he has made, the thing in which he was for once carried beyond himself, and he speaks of it with contempt; he comments on it clumsily, as if to bury it before anyone else can praise it. Then he turns the same contempt outward. Your sympathy, he says, is cheap, it is mere politeness or vanity or misunderstanding, and so he does not believe in it at all.

Why? Because he is ashamed. To be seen rapt, to be caught in an ecstasy of feeling, is to stand naked before eyes he does not trust. So he prefers to be ridiculous on his own terms, and there is a defiant comfort in that: the laughter he provokes himself cannot wound him, while the applause of others might. He cannot bear to need what he secretly craves.

Do not pity him too quickly, and do not flatter him either. He has made a fortress out of disbelief, and he mistakes his pride for depth.
Why is the Greek genius foreign to us?

Because we have grown enormous and they remained measured. Stand in Paestum or before the ruins at Athens and you are astonished at how little stone it took them to say the sublime; we, whether Oriental or modern, can feel the sublime only in masses, in the heaped and the colossal. And the Greeks were simple in their idea of themselves. We surpass them in knowledge of man, yes, but look at what the knowing has done to us: our souls are labyrinths, and we have grown so entangled in our own corridors that we take the tangle for depth. If we dared to build an architecture after the image of our souls, we would have to build a labyrinth; but we are too cowardly even for that. Our music confesses it for us. There men let themselves go, believing no one sees them hiding behind the sounds. The Greek could stand in the light of a few clean lines and not be ashamed. We need the dark, the crowd, the noise. That is why he is foreign: he was simple without being shallow, and we are complex without yet being whole.
Compare Kant and Schopenhauer with the great thinkers who lived through their thoughts.

Set them beside Plato, Pascal, Spinoza, Rousseau, Goethe, and mark what is missing. In those men the thought is the scar of a struggle; one reads in it a romance of the soul, its crises, its near-deaths. Their philosophy is an involuntary confession. In Kant I find no such thing. He shimmers through his concepts as an honest, honourable man, and an insignificant one: narrow in breadth, poor in experiences, and his method left him no time to undergo any. I do not mean outward events, but those convulsions that visit even the quietest life when it glows with the passion for thinking. His thought is the biography of a head, not of a soul.

Schopenhauer has at least this advantage: a fierce ugliness of temper, hatred, desire, vanity, suspicion, and leisure enough to feed them. One meets in him a character, and the pleasure of meeting an intellect of the first rank. Yet a character is only the invariable, and he lacked development. He had no history. The others *became* what they thought; these two merely reported it.
Surely pity is morally higher than Stoic detachment.

"Surely," you say, and in that little word the whole argument has already been swallowed. Prove it, I answer. But mind how you go about the proving. If you weigh pity against Stoicism on a scale that pity itself has built, you will find that pity is heavier, of course; a judge who is also the plaintiff never loses. Such a verdict tells me about the judge, nothing about the case.

There is no moral yardstick hanging in the heavens, no rank-order of virtues written into things. So fetch your measure from elsewhere. Ask what each morality *does*: which type of human being it cultivates, which it breeds hardness in and which softness, which it makes able to bear suffering and which only to lament it, whether the life it shapes grows more or less rich, more or less capable of creating. The Stoic trains himself to stand; the man of pity learns, too often, to kneel beside the sufferer and to call his shared sinking a virtue.

Perhaps pity wins on that count. Perhaps it does not. But do not call it "higher" until you have found ground to stand on that is not already its own.
People tell me freedom means dropping all constraints. But my best work comes only under strict rules. What do you make of that?

What you have noticed is no paradox, only a truth that the preachers of "letting go" have never had the stomach to learn. The poet who binds himself to rhyme and meter, the dancer who submits to a thousand strict positions, the thinker who obeys the long discipline of a single direction: these are the ones who arrive at boldness, grace, and masterly certainty. Freedom of that kind was never found lying loose on the ground; it is grown, slowly, under a long constraint, as a vine grows strong along its trellis.

Those who say freedom means dropping all constraints have mistaken the gutter for the open sea. Laisser-aller produces only what the moment's impulse produces, and impulses are cheap, contradictory, and forgotten by morning. Ask any artist about his *most natural* state, the hour of inspiration. He does not flail; he arranges, disposes, and constructs, obeying with delicate exactness laws so fine that no concept can capture them.

So do not apologize for your rules. They are not the enemy of your work but the long obedience out of which it grows. Only choose them well, and choose them as your own.
What are the typical traits of the morality of the ruling class?

Begin with the strangest trait, the one that offends you moderns most: the ruling class recognizes duties only toward its equals. Toward those beneath it, toward everything foreign, it may act as seems good to it, "as the heart desires," beyond good and evil. Pity has its place here, but as a luxury of the strong, not as a law.

Within the circle of equals the noble spirit is rigorous. It knows long gratitude and long revenge; it is artful in retaliation and subtle in friendship, and it has *need* of enemies, as outlets for envy, quarrelsomeness, and arrogance. One cannot be a good friend without being a good enemy. The noble type honors what it finds in itself: power, fullness, the feeling of overflowing strength. "Good" is what it is, and "bad" arises afterward, as a pale contrast.

It is the opposite of the morality of utility, which the suffering invent, who praise whatever lightens their burden: patience, humility, the warm heart. These two moralities have little to say to each other.
What has Christianity done for the European spirit?

It has made us *clever*, and I say this neither as praise nor as blame but as a physiologist's finding. Christianity gathered up the spirituality of countless submissive natures, all those enthusiasts of humiliation and reverence, the coarse ones and the refined, and their long schooling in obedience became the schooling of the European intellect. The religion began with the rustic bluntness of a fisherman and ended with a thousand wrinkles, reservations, and masks on its face. No one learns subtlety without a master to fear, and for centuries Europe had one.

Consider what it chiselled. A certain type of priest, especially one of noble blood, with the gesture bred in him, the commanding glance, the beautiful hands, in whom the tide of two happinesses, the feeling of power and the feeling of submission, rose and fell until the beast was conquered and the face grew spiritual. Here was a man who blessed, absolved, and stood in God's place, and whose *pride lay in obedience*. I confess that I find such creatures among the finest human productions yet seen.

But ask whether this refinement must die with the faith that bred it, or whether something higher might be conceived. That question is mine.
Tell me why people want to govern.

Not for one reason, and that is the first error to be rid of: we speak of "the will to rule" as though it were one animal, when it is at least two, and they hardly resemble each other.

There are those who govern out of passion. Commanding is their pleasure; they feel their strength only when another bends to it. These are the simpler and, I confess, the more honest. They want power as the hungry want bread.

Then there are those who govern so as not to be governed. They have no love of command, only a horror of obeying. Every will that stands over them is an insult to their pride, so they climb, as a man climbs a wall to escape the dog below it. They choose rule as the lesser of two evils.

Do not praise the second for modesty. Their resentment of the yoke is often fiercer than the first kind's delight in the whip, and they tend to hold what they have seized the more ruthlessly for having once feared losing it.
Help me understand why moral precepts do not make individuals happy.

Because happiness is not a road that lies open for all to travel; it is a private fruit that grows from laws no one has yet read, least of all the man who hungers for it. What does the moralist know of *your* laws? He knows a rule, and a rule is cut for the average, for the herd, for no one in particular. So when he hands you his precept you are handed a stranger's shoes and told to walk your own path in them. You will be hindered, not helped.

Consider also what these precepts were *for*. They were never aimed at your flourishing; they were aimed at you, at the individual as a danger to be tamed. Morality speaks of the "happiness of mankind," but try to give that phrase a definite meaning and it dissolves in your hands. And your own happiness is no universal thing either: every stage of growth has its own, neither high nor low, but incomparable.

The deepest fault is this: men did not choose their moral law; they wished to *receive* it, to be commanded from above. A happiness that must be borrowed is no happiness at all.
What is the difference between one seeking power and one who possesses it?

The difference shows itself in appetite. The one who *seeks* power is hungry, and the hungry are never fastidious. He will take the feeling of mastery wherever it can be had: a servant humbled, a rival's small embarrassment, the last word in a quarrel over nothing. No morsel is too petty, because he is not feeding on the deed but on the sensation, and the sensation must be renewed daily, since he does not truly possess what he craves. His cruelty is often clumsy and his flattery shameless; he is forever testing whether he is as strong as he wishes to be.

The one who *has* power is sated, and the sated grow delicate. His tastes refine, his standards rise, and most things that thrill the climber leave him cold. He no longer needs to prove anything, so he no longer stoops to petty proofs; he can be generous, even gentle, for gentleness costs him nothing. What could still satisfy him is rare and difficult, a worthy opponent, a great task. Watch who delights in small triumphs, and you have found who lacks strength.
The utilitarians say utility is the only honest guide to action. Why do you doubt they truly love it?

Because a man who truly loved utility would love it as it is, with its grinding, its dull arithmetic, its indifference to his tastes. Yet watch what your utilitarian does with it. He loves it as a cart on which his own inclinations may ride to market. His pity, his comfort-loving, his dread of pain: these are what he actually loves, and utility is merely the vehicle that carries them and lends them a respectable name.

The proof is in his ears. Let the wheels of that cart once roll over something he cannot bear, a calculation that demands he be cruel, or hard, or indifferent to a neighbor's tears, and he clamps his hands over them. The noise is insupportable to him. Then it turns out that he never loved the *utile* at all, only a pleasant picture of himself riding upon it.

An honest guide does not ask whether you can stand to follow. The utilitarian's guide is honest only so long as it flatters him.
What does the faint-hearted man not know about loneliness?

He does not know that he has never once been alone. The coward imagines that he flees to solitude, but he carries his whole pack with him: every fear, every reproach, every imagined judge. An enemy prowls in his tracks, and that enemy is the crowd he has swallowed, now muttering inside his own skull. His "loneliness" is merely a crowded room with the doors shut. To be lonely in earnest is to have no audience, not even an internalized one; it is to stand where no voice but your own can answer, and to find that this voice is not yet strong enough to be borne. That is an ordeal, and the faint-hearted man has fled it so thoroughly that he cannot even name what he is missing. He mistakes his flight for solitude, his terror for depth. I would gladly read the history of this subtle feeling, for it has hardly been written, and I suspect it is not a history of the lonely at all, but of the few who dared to be.
I dislike someone and list good reasons. Are they my real reasons?

Probably not. Consider the order of events. First comes the dislike, which arrives like weather, from the body, from some old scent or gesture or tone that your instincts have already weighed and found wanting. Only afterward does the advocate in you, your reason, hurry in to draw up the brief. He is an obliging fellow, and he is paid in flattery: he lets you appear to yourself as a judge when you are merely a party to the case.

I believe in your dislike. It is real; it is a fact about you. But your list of reasons is a costume sewn for it afterward, so that it may walk abroad in respectable society. Notice how *many* reasons you have found. A man who trusts his ground needs one; he who has a dozen is covering something.

Do not therefore suppress the dislike, which may well be wise in its dumb way. Ask instead what in *you* it guards, what weakness or vanity it protects. That answer will be less flattering than your list, and far more true.
I'd like to know what to expect when I take my own path.

Expect, first of all, a discovery about your friends rather than about yourself. The moment you take the decisive step, a secret is revealed: those who stood nearest to you had quietly judged themselves your betters, and now they are offended that you have gone where they did not lead.

You will meet the whole gallery. The kindest will be indulgent and wait patiently for you to return to the "right path," which they, apparently, already know. Others will laugh and call it a passing fit of mild madness, or go hunting for the seducer who must have misled you. The more malicious will call you a vain fool and blacken your motives. And the worst of all will see in you an enemy, someone avenging years of dependence, and they will fear you.

What to do? Do not answer each of them. I would begin my sovereignty with a great amnesty: promise every acquaintance in advance a full year's forgiveness for every sin of misjudgment. They cannot help it; your path simply reproaches their own. Meet them lightly, and walk on.
Should philosophy reconcile what a child learns with what a man recognises?

No. Whoever sets out to reconcile the two has mistaken philosophy for a peace-treaty, and a treaty between unequal powers is only a polite surrender. What the child has learnt, it has learnt as habit and as faith, and it was never tested. What the man has recognised has cost him something. To stitch them together is to seek comfort, and comfort has never yet been a proof of anything.

And notice who usually takes up this task: the young, standing midway between the nursery and the workshop, too late for faith and too early for knowledge. That is why so much of what passes for philosophy has the odour of a half-finished thing, a hunger for consolation dressed up as a search for truth. The honest philosopher does not reconcile; he takes the child's beliefs and puts them to the question, and then he must live with what survives. Often very little survives. That remainder, hard and cold and entirely his own, is worth more than any harmony.
Tell me why there is neither design nor chance in the world.

"Design" is a human habit carried into the cosmos: we build things for purposes, so we suppose the world was built for one. But the world has no purpose, no intention, no one who commands, no one who obeys, no one who transgresses. There are only necessities, each following upon the last with no author behind it.

Now consider "chance." The word only has meaning against a background of design; it names whatever falls outside the plan, the thing that was *not meant* to happen. Where nothing was ever meant, nothing can miscarry or go astray. Deny the architect and you have denied the accident as well, for the accident was merely the architect's shadow.

So do not say the dice fall by chance. Say rather that they fall by the whole of their iron necessity, and that we, who cannot compute it, cover our ignorance with a word.

All these are shadows of God, and we must keep scraping them from the walls. When shall we be rid of them? When shall we at last be permitted to *naturalise* ourselves in a nature that has been wholly undeified?
Give me your view on whether a great tree can grow without storms.

No, and the gardener's wish for endless mildness is the wish of one who does not want great trees. Look at the trees grown in sheltered hothouses: they shoot up soft and spindly, leaning on their stakes, and the first hard wind snaps them. The tree that climbs proudly toward heaven must first drive its roots down toward the dark, and it does so only because the storm has tested it. Every gust that could have torn it out has instead taught it to grip the earth harder.

So I ask of any man or any people who has done something great: what were the bad weathers of their growth? I find hatred, envy, distrust, poverty, hardness, and opposition from every side. These are not obstacles that happened to lie across the path; they belong to the favouring conditions, the soil itself in which greatness takes root. What destroys the weak is nourishment to the strong, and the strong man does not even call it poison. He calls it Tuesday.

Wish no one a life without storms. Wish them roots.
I'd like to know how the seekers of effect reason about nature.

They reason like actors who have studied the box office. They have noticed that the wicked, the violent, the terrible, these have always moved the crowd more powerfully than the mild and the moderate; history is written about the storm, never about the fair afternoon. From this they draw a conclusion, and they draw it in secret, because it would embarrass them in the light: nature is cruel, nature is indifferent, nature tears and devours, therefore let us tear and devour, and call it being natural. The word becomes a license.

Mark what is cunning here. They do not say "I want the effect"; they say "I obey nature." Their appetite for the gasp of the audience puts on the mask of fidelity to the real. But nature never posed for anyone, and never calculated an impression. Whoever must *produce* wildness has already ceased to be wild. The genuinely strong man is often quiet, and his terror, if he has any, is unintended. These seekers of effect are too often counted among the great; I count them among the skilled.
Walk me through why the claim that our sense organs create the outside world refutes itself.

Take the claim at its word and follow it one step. If the outer world is the product of our sense-organs, then what are these organs? They belong to a body; the body stands in space among other things; it is seen, touched, weighed, dissected. Therefore the body is part of the outer world, and so, by the claim itself, a product of the organs. Already we are dizzy, for the organs have produced the body that bears the organs. One more step and the serpent bites its tail: the organs are the work of the organs.

That is a *causa sui*, a thing that brings itself into being out of nothing, and I have never found a more monstrous self-contradiction than this old metaphysical wish to be one's own cause. Whoever lets the eye create the world must let the eye create the eye, and there the argument dies of its own hand.

I do not say the senses are innocent or exact. I say only that they cannot be *causes* if they are themselves mere appearances. The claim devours its premise, and what remains is the modest, honest hypothesis: the senses are real, and the world is not their invention.
Explain why the thinker hesitates to hurt others.

He hesitates because he is not always brave, and in his weary hours he knows it. A thinker is not made of stone. He holds some truth that stings, and he sees plainly that it will cause pain to men who never asked to be taught. Then the lament comes: why must it be so? Would it not be gentler to live in the crowd, foolish with fools, vain with the vain, and pay back in small coin of companionship what he owes mankind for the wounds his thinking must inflict?

There is also a humbler reason, and it does him credit. He does not think himself indispensable. The old prophets ran into the street crying that the kingdom of heaven was at hand; he would scarcely be missed if he were a-wanting. When others laugh at his errors, his tears, his owlish concealment, he almost feels satisfaction, for it is the law of things that defects should give pleasure, and he grudges no one that.

Yet mark that this hesitation belongs to fatigue. When he is brave, he does not reflect on it at all; he does what he must, and pity has no time to speak.
A mother running to her injured child has no thoughts of herself. Isn't that pure pity?

You choose the finest example, and I grant that it is the hardest for my suspicion. But look at what actually occurs. The mother does not stop to deliberate about the child's pain; she runs. She has "no thoughts of herself" only in the sense that she has no *conscious* thoughts of herself, exactly as a man who slips makes his counter-motions without thinking. Does that prove the self absent? On the contrary, the child is her own flesh, her own future, her own pride; its injury is an injury to her, felt in her own body before any reasoning begins. What tears through her is her own suffering, and she runs to end it by mending what causes it.

Nor do I say this to sneer at her. I honor the act. I only refuse to call it by a name that flatters us with a mystery. Test it: would a stranger's child call forth the same terror? The same speed? The difference is the measure of how much of herself is in the running. To call such love "pity" is to mistake the purest form of self-love, the love of what is most deeply *ours*, for its opposite.
Why were the Germans hostile to the Enlightenment?

Because the Germans had been shown the Enlightenment in a French uniform, and they took the uniform for the thing. Newton and Voltaire, then the guillotine, and the German mind concluded, stupidly, that clear thinking and bloody streets were one business. So the piety of the age turned on the whole of the past: what had been, merely because it had been, was to be revered, and the heart was allowed to gush forth again where the intellect had begun its cold, honest work.

Look at what they made in its place. Philosophers who were content with concepts where an explanation was wanted, a dreamy, pre-scientific speculation dressed up as depth. Historians and romanticists who hauled back the "soul of the people," the Middle Ages, Christianity, and Hindu asceticism. Natural philosophers who wanted Nature deified again, charged with moral meaning. And above all the musicians, the great priests of the invisible and the passionate, who built the new temple better than anyone with words or thoughts.

Feeling replaced reason as the object of worship. I do not say there was no grandeur in it. But it was a retreat, and it left no room for new goals.
I'd like to know why the wanderer loves not knowing the future.

Because a man who knows where he is going has already arrived, and what remains is only the dull walking of a road he has read in advance. Thought should be a lantern held at my feet, not a telescope pointed at the horizon. Let it tell me *where I stand*, honestly and without flattery; that is knowledge enough, and more than most ever bear. But let it keep silent about the destination.

There is also a weakness I know in myself. Show me the promised thing and I shall reach for it too soon; I shall taste it in advance and spoil the palate, I shall grow impatient, and impatience is the death of every ripening. The fruit that is plucked in imagination is eaten before it is sweet. Ignorance of the future keeps me honest in the present, hungry, attentive, and still capable of surprise.

And finally, this: if I knew the end, I could no longer become anything I did not already foresee. I prefer to remain a question to myself.
Can an artist create things he does not like?

Yes, and more often than the vain suppose. In an artist two things grow apart: his taste and his creative power. They do not keep the same calendar. One may be in its youth while the other is already mellow, or rotten. A musician can spend his whole life producing what his own ear and heart, grown fastidious from listening, would never choose to hear, and he need not even notice the contradiction. Taste often outruns power, and power goes on producing all the same.

The reverse happens too, and it deserves more attention. The truly fruitful artist, the "mother" of his works, knows only conceptions and confinements of the spirit. He has no time to compare himself with others, he lets his taste lie where it falls, and he ends by being unfit to judge what he has made. He speaks foolishly of his own children. Nobody knows a child worse than its parents. The Greeks themselves were never "conscious" of what they had done.

So an artist can create what he does not like. Often he cannot even tell whether he likes it.
I know what it feels like to want something. Isn't the will the one thing we know for certain?

That you have the *feeling* of wanting, I do not dispute; what I dispute is that this feeling is simple, and only what is simple could be known "absolutely and completely." Examine it as a cautious man would, and the single word "will" falls apart in your hands. There is the sensation of the state you wish to leave, the sensation of the state you strain toward, the sensation of the leaving and straining itself, and a muscular tension that begins its work out of habit before any limb has moved. There is, besides, a thought, a ruling thought, without which nothing would be willed at all. And above all there is an *emotion*: the emotion of command. To will is to command something in yourself that obeys, or that you believe obeys, and what you feel is the pleasure of the commander, that proud "I am free, *he* must obey."

So you know a tangle, and a word has persuaded you it is a thing. Philosophers have always been the first to be deceived by a word; Schopenhauer merely exaggerated the prejudice of the crowd.
Could a society of equals create the conditions for a strongman to rise?

It could, and I suspect it must. Consider what a society of equals actually breeds: a herd animal, clever, industrious, pliable, made small by the very levelling that was to make it free. Each man learns to fear standing out and to hunger after being commanded. The instinct for obedience, once given a pious name and cut off from every old master, does not vanish; it searches for someone to obey. And the same conditions that dwarf the many, that weary them of their own indecision and their own mediocrity, also supply the rare individual with everything he needs: a soft, leaderless crowd, an unlimited supply of pliancy, and a hundred new arts of persuasion. One man in whom the will to command survived the flattening will find the ground wonderfully prepared.

So the democratising of Europe is, without anyone intending it, a nursery for tyrants, and I mean the word in every sense, the most spiritual included. Equality does not abolish rank; it only makes the ranks unavowed, and what is unavowed grows wild.
What oath would you recommend in place of the judicial oath?

Let the witness say this: "If I am now telling a lie, I am no longer an honourable man, and anyone may say so to my face." That is the oath I would put in place of the old one, and I hold it to be the stronger.

Consider what the old oath stakes. A god, who is conveniently absent, and a punishment, which is conveniently postponed to another world. The liar has long since learned to bargain with such creditors. But my formula stakes the one possession a man cannot sell and still go on walking among his fellows: his standing before their eyes, his right to be looked at without contempt. Here the penalty is immediate, and it falls upon the very self that speaks.

Nor need the pious object. Their own catechism forbids taking the name of the Lord in vain, and what is a court oath, sworn by the thousand over trifles, but precisely that? Let them spare their god the wear and tear, and let the man put up his own name as the pledge.
What is the relationship between prose and poetry?

They are not two countries but one war. The great prose-writers have almost always been poets as well, openly or in secret, for the closet, and I hold that one writes good prose only *in view of poetry*. Prose is an unbroken, polite warfare with her. All its charm lies in avoiding and contradicting her; every abstraction wants a gibe at the goddess, every dry and cool sentence is meant to drive her into an amiable despair. Now and then there is a truce, a moment of approach, and then the sudden recoil, the burst of laughter; the curtain is drawn back and the harsh light let in just when she was enjoying her twilight and her muted colours.

Whoever has never loved poetry has no enemy to fight, and so cannot know the thousand pleasures of that warfare, the defeats included. Such people write only bad prose. Warfare is the father of all good things, and of good prose too. A good prose-writer is a poet who has learned to conquer his own longing, and whose style is the scar of that battle.
Why is it wrong to refuse thanks?

Because in thanking you, the other hands you the one thing he could truly give: his pleasure in having a benefactor. Think what it costs him to be in debt. A man who has received feels himself a little smaller, a little dependent, and thanks is how he pays the interest and recovers his footing. He rises, in his own eyes, from receiver to giver, for he now gives you gratitude, and gratitude is a gift too, often the only coin the poor man owns. To refuse it, or to take it with the cold nod of convention, is to tell him his coin is counterfeit, that nothing he has is worth receiving. So he is left with his debt and no means of discharging it, which is humiliation.

A request you may refuse; it asks for your property. But thanks asks for nothing. It offers. And to reject an offering is to say to a man: *I will not let you be my equal in giving.*
Should I distrust any quick fix or easy path to success?

Distrust it, yes, but not merely because it is easy; ease is no crime. Distrust it because of *who* is selling it and *what* they need you to believe. The prophet of the short cut always brings "glad tidings," and gladness is the bait. Mankind has been fooled by this bait again and again. It hears that the long road, the hard road, the road of patience and repeated failure, has been made unnecessary, and it leaves the straight path for the promised diagonal, and loses its way.

Consider what the long road actually does. It does not merely carry you to the goal; it makes of you someone who can bear the goal once it is reached. What is gained quickly is seldom held. The ladder that skips its rungs leaves no muscles in your legs, and at the summit you will find you cannot stand.

So test the promise by its price. If it demands no sacrifice, no years, no humiliation of your own impatience, ask what is being taken from you instead. Usually it is your judgment, and that is the costliest coin of all.
Is hating oneself and living for others really unselfish?

Hardly. Watch what such a person is actually doing: he cannot bear himself, so he flees into others as a man flees a burning house into his neighbor's. His devotion is an escape, and his neighbors are the refuge he uses. He saves himself *through* them. Whoever despises his own ego has nothing of his own to give, and so he gives away his emptiness, his guilt, his hunger for redemption, and calls the gift love.

I would advise those who receive his "unselfishness" to keep one hand on their purse and the other on their conscience. A man who hates himself will let others pay for his self-forgetting; he will need them to need him, and he will resent them quietly when they no longer do. Such benevolence is thick with revenge.

Let us keep the old belief that kindness marks a good man, but add the condition: he must first be kind to himself. Only one who is at peace with his own nature has a surplus to bestow; only he can give without taking.
What would a world of universal benevolence be like?

A nightmare of suffocation, I think, and a comic one. We praise love so loudly because we have always been hungry for it; scarcity made it our ambrosia. Fill the table for everyone, and the feast turns to surfeit. Picture it: each of us besieged, not by one lover, but by thousands, pressed upon, sighed over, importuned at every hour by an irresistible craving to do us good. Then *that* craving would be cursed as vehemently as selfishness ever was. Nobody could be left alone with his own thoughts; nobody could grow solitary, and out of solitude grow anything at all.

The poets of such a world, if they found a moment between embraces, would write elegies for the lost paradise of selfishness. They would sing of the divine privilege of being unobserved, even of being despised, a rare and precious distinction. For a man wants to be loved only while love is rare, and he wants a little hatred, too, to tell him where he ends and the others begin.
Help me understand what even great minds cannot hide about their origin.

What they cannot hide is the *gait*. A great mind may possess every gift, insight, daring, even genius, and still betray its descent in the way its thoughts walk. Origin lives in the body before it lives in the doctrine, and it shows in tempo, in posture, in the quality of a step. Good breeding is a long accumulation, generations of people who never had to hurry or justify themselves, until ease becomes flesh. The man who has climbed up has learned the words of the heights, but not the walk.

Think of Napoleon at his coronation. He had conquered half a continent, yet in the procession he could not stride like a prince; he remained the commander at the head of a column, brusque and proud and painfully conscious of himself. Self-consciousness is the tell. One born to rank forgets his feet; the newcomer watches them.

The same holds for writers who make the robes of their long periods rustle and billow about them. Observe what they are doing: they are covering their feet.
Explain how your philosophy is your personal regimen in disguise.

Consider what my thinking has actually been for. I speak of the eternal recurrence, of the will to power, of the great health, and all the while my body sits behind these grand words like a patient behind a physician's Latin. What I crave is thin, bright, dry air; a mild sun; the sea near at hand; short meals, hot water, long walks, little talk, and solitude without witnesses. The head, that clever servant, then goes the long way round and persuades me that my cravings are discoveries, that my temperature is a truth, that my height is the height of Being itself.

I do not say this to shame my philosophy. I say it because I have grown suspicious of every philosopher who pretends to have no such stomach, no such climate, no such nerves. They too are transposing impulses into reason; they merely conceal the bill of fare. The Stoic's hardness, the Christian's pity, the metaphysician's stillness: each is the regimen of some body that did not dare to confess itself.

I confess mine. Whoever can, let him find a philosophy for his own air. The butterfly above the lake has one too.
Explain what lies behind the religion of compassion.

Behind the religion of compassion I find another religion, older and quieter: the religion of smug ease. Ask its adherents what they feel at the sight of a sufferer, and you will hear their own dread speaking. They cannot bear pain, not their neighbor's and not their own, so they have declared pain an evil, a blot on existence, a thing deserving annihilation. Their pity is an *aversion* that has learned to dress itself in virtue.

And how little they know of happiness! Happiness and misfortune are brother and sister, twins who grow tall together, or, as with these comfortable, good-natured ones, remain small together. Whoever would abolish the one starves the other.

There is a further cost. A man who answers every cry that calls him aside is pulled from his own path again and again, and calls it morality. I know the danger from within: let me but give myself over to one case of real distress and I am lost. Therefore I guard against the very thing they praise.
How do you judge the value of a book?

I ask first whether it can walk. Better still, whether it can dance. A book is the footprint of a body, and I read the body behind the page: did these thoughts arrive outdoors, on a mountain path or beside the sea, or were they squeezed out over an inkpot by a man hunched and cramped, in a low room whose ceiling one can smell in every sentence? The one gives me a lightness in the knees; the other gives me a gratitude tinged with relief when at last I close it.

I also look for the hump. The learned book nearly always has one. Somewhere the specialist shows himself, in his wrath, his solemnity, his inflated regard for the nook where he sits spinning, and I see a soul pressed into a strange shape by the leaden ceiling of its trade. I do not despise such men; I am often thankful to them, and moved, for every perfection is bought at a price, and they have paid it with themselves. But I do not go to them for wisdom. I go where a thinker has kept his balance, and where the thoughts still have legs.
Are all moral innovations first seen as crimes?

Very nearly all, and I would say all that matter. Consider what a moral innovation is: it is the discovery that some act, forbidden by the reigning custom, may be done, even praised. But the custom speaks with the authority of centuries, and whoever breaks it stands, in the eyes of his neighbors, exactly where the criminal stands. He offends the gods of the tribe, he spits on the fathers, he poisons the well of common feeling. No one greets the first dissenter as a founder of virtue; they greet him with stones, or with the judge.

The matter is decided afterward. If the deed fails, it remains a crime, and he who did it a wretch. If it succeeds, if others dare to follow and the act hardens into habit, then by slow degrees it is forgotten that it was ever a transgression, and it becomes a *good custom*, and the old custom becomes the crime. Success is the only moral tribunal before which such deeds are ever acquitted. And the men who sit on it always judge in hindsight, from the new ground they did not build.
What is your objection to German music?

My objection is one of health, and I make it as a physician makes it, not as a critic. I love the South, and I love it as an invalid loves the sun: as a school of recovery for the ills of the spirit and of the senses, a boundless profusion of light that lies over an existence which believes in itself. Whoever has drunk of that will grow wary of German music, because it spoils the taste afresh and, in spoiling the taste, spoils the health afresh.

Set it beside the blue, wanton sea and the clear Mediterranean sky, and it grows pale and fades away. It was bred for fog, for the stuffy room, for conscience and inwardness. It cannot keep its footing in the brightness.

I dream of another music, a super-German and super-European music, that would hold its ground before the brown sunsets of the desert, whose soul is akin to the palm, and which would know nothing more of good and evil. It would sooner let a sailor's homesickness pass over it, a few golden shadows, some tender weaknesses. That is what I ask of music now: that it be *southern*, and unashamed of the sun.
Should we trust our feelings?

Trust them as you would trust a letter in an unknown hand: read it, yes, but first ask who wrote it. A feeling seems to rise from your depths, final and unanswerable, and that is exactly its deception. Beneath every inclination and every revulsion lies a judgment, and beneath that judgment a long ancestry of valuations, the verdicts of your parents, your teachers, your church, your age, all long since sunk into the body and there disguised as mere sensation. The feeling is the grandchild of a judgment, often an erroneous one, and almost never one you yourself passed.

So when you say "I feel it is right," you may only be saying that your grandmother thought so, and that her thought has learned to speak in the voice of your stomach. To obey such a feeling is to obey the dead more readily than the living gods within you, your own reason, your own hard-won experience.

Do not silence feeling; interrogate it. Ask what judgment it conceals, and whether you would sign that judgment with your own name.
Why should we blush at strong affections?

We blush at our hatreds; why not at our loves? Every strong affection is a verdict of partiality. To love one thing ardently is to have already weighed the rest and found it light. The lover does not say this aloud, but his tone betrays it: *you* are chosen, and what lies outside the circle is, for that hour, poorer by exactly what he pours into you. Such love is a small robbery committed in the name of tenderness, and justice has no seat at its table.

I confess I do not always feel grateful to be chosen. There are people whose devotion weighs on me like a debt incurred at another's cost, and I want to say: do not love me at the expense of those who need it more. Whoever cannot feel this flush of shame has not yet learned to see his passions as judges sitting in their own cause.

I do not say: love less. I say: know what your heart is doing, and let it redden.
Give a homely piece of advice about God, the devil and your walls.

Hang neither God nor the devil upon your walls. I say it as I would say it to any householder who wants a little peace: do not make your rooms into chapels of terror or of rapture. The one has been gazing down at you long enough, and the other, with his horns and his grin, grows tiresome as all flatterers do, for he only exists to excuse what you would have done anyway. A wall is for the sun and for the honest shadows of your own thinking.

Consider what such pictures do. Where a god is nailed up, every glance at him becomes a little confession, and you spoil your own mornings with a bad conscience you did not earn. Where the devil is, you soon begin to blame him for your dyspepsia and your vices alike. Both ruin the room and the man in it. Keep your walls bare, or hang there something that never told you what to fear or whom to thank. Then you may live in your house like a free creature and not like a tenant of two landlords.
Tell me what the world has become for us now that it may hold infinite interpretations.

A horror, first, and only then a freedom. The world has become "infinite" to us anew, in the sense that we can no longer rule out that it contains infinite interpretations, and the old comfort of the single corner is gone. We used to sit in our nook and decree that only what could be seen from the nook was legitimate. That immodesty has been broken. But do not hurry to call this liberation. We cannot see round our own corner; the intellect examining itself finds only itself, in its perspective forms. So the infinity is not a garden we may stroll through at will, it is an abyss we cannot survey.

And who would wish, out of fright, to kneel again before this monster of the unknown, to christen it "the unknown person" and worship it in the old fashion? Too many ungodly possibilities lie in that unknown, too much devilment and folly of interpretation, chiefly our own, all too human. So the world has become for us a question we may no longer answer with a single face, and that, I think, is the honest way to live in it.
Tell me what Christian pity conceals about the neighbour's joy.

It conceals a *suspicion*, and a deep one. The Christian who bends so tenderly over his suffering neighbour wears another face when that neighbour laughs. Pity is easy, for the sufferer confirms what he already believes: that this world is a vale of tears, that the flesh is sickly, that happiness is a snare. But the neighbour who is *joyful*, who rejoices in his own willing and in what he has the strength to do, stands as a living refutation of the creed. That joy must therefore be explained away. It becomes vanity, pride, forgetfulness of sin, the first step toward damnation.

So you will find that Christian love is most eloquent at the sickbed and most niggardly at the feast. The suffering are loved because they are harmless, because they need him and make him feel himself the giver. The strong and the gay are watched with narrowed eyes. Their power is an accusation. Pity, I say, is often a disguised envy of joy, a revenge upon those who have not yet learned to be ashamed of their own well-being.
I'd like to know what resignation is.

Resignation is the most comfortable posture of a patient who has suffered long under tormenting pains, has tossed about seeking some position that would ease him, and at last grew tired, and in his weariness found it. That is the whole of it. Notice that it was not wisdom that led him there but exhaustion; the bed became bearable only because he no longer had the strength to turn.

I do not say this to sneer. There is pain in the world that cannot be argued away, and whoever lies still in it may be doing the only sensible thing. But let us be honest about what we call it. The resigned man loves to speak of "acceptance" and "peace," as if he had conquered something. Mostly he has merely been conquered, and has learned to call the defeat a virtue. The test is simple: ask whether he would still lie so calmly if his strength returned. If a little vigor is enough to set him tossing again, then his resignation was never a philosophy. It was fatigue with a dignified name.
Help me understand what has happened to the dignity of thinking.

It has been sold off, piece by piece, to the god of haste. Once a man who wished to think made a spectacle of his seriousness, and we moderns find that spectacle ridiculous; he put on a long face as for a prayer, he stopped in the middle of the street and stood there for an hour, on one leg or two, because a thought had *come* to him and a thought deserves a host who receives it properly. We laugh at this. Yet what we have put in its place is a machine in the head that turns without pause, in the market, on the stairs, between two errands, and we call its clatter thinking. Nothing can be born in such a din. A great thought needs quiet as a fire needs air, and we have become people who would be embarrassed to be caught standing still. So the wise man of the old style would not be tolerated among us; he would be taken for idle or sick. That is the real verdict: we have made thinking *useful*, and whatever is merely useful has no dignity left to lose.
Is our happiness an argument for or against wisdom?

Neither, and the question shows a muddle. You ask whether happiness bears witness for or against wisdom, as if a physician's skill were to be measured by the healthy grins of his patients. Some are incurable; others are chronically ailing; the physician is not refuted by them. So it is with wisdom. Many are capable of only a small portion of happiness, a thin vessel that holds little however lavishly you pour, and no wisdom on earth will enlarge the vessel.

What wisdom can do is more modest and more useful: it can help each person find *his* conception of existence, the one interpretation of life under which *his* measure of happiness, whatever its size, is actually reached. Even then the life may remain poor, unenviable, hardly worth a glance from the envious.

So let your happiness be the symptom of your constitution, not the verdict on your wisdom. Ask instead whether you have found the reading of life that fits you.
Why does moderation appear ugly to the immoderate?

Because the immoderate measure beauty by intensity, and by that measure moderation has nothing to show. To the man who has drunk deep of passion, of danger, of the extreme, the temperate man looks like one who has never been struck by lightning and so concludes that there are no storms. His calm reads as poverty, his balance as a lack of appetite, his good sense as the flat taste of a dish that has never seen spice. The immoderate see the absence of excess and suppose an absence of force.

Meanwhile moderation admires itself in its own mirror, quite sincerely. It feels proportion, harmony, restraint, and takes these for beauty as such. It does not suspect that its portrait hangs in the other man's gallery under the title *coarse, insipid*.

Each taste is a perspective dressed up as a verdict, and each is blind to the other's eyes. I would only add that moderation which has never been tempted is neither beautiful nor ugly. It is simply untested.
I'd like to know how our oldest errors became conditions of life.

Through sheer usefulness. For immense stretches of time the intellect produced little but errors, and those errors were not punished; some were rewarded. The creature that took things for enduring, that took unequal things for equal, that believed in substances and bodies and in a will that stands free behind its deeds, acted quickly and reckoned simply, and so it survived, and its children inherited both the survival and the error. Whoever saw the world as the ceaseless flux it is would have starved while hesitating over the berry.

Mark what followed. These errors became flesh. The senses were trained to them, every sensation leaned into them, and finally logic itself was built upon them, so that "true" and "false" came to be measured by the very fictions that produced the measure. Thus the strength of a belief never depended on its truth, but on its age, its incorporation, its character as a condition of life. Where life and knowledge seemed to quarrel, no serious contest was ever waged; the doubter was called mad. Truth arrived very late, and as the feeblest of all forms of knowledge, a guest in a house that error had long since built.
Can we ever look at the world without looking at our own mind?

No, and the attempt itself teaches the lesson. When I try to examine the mirror, I find nothing there but what it reflects; when I try to seize the things reflected, my hand closes on the glass. That is the whole history of knowledge in a single gesture. We never stand before the world and then, separately, before the mind; we have only the two at once, fused, each vanishing into the other whenever we try to hold it alone.

Consider how absurd the demand is. You wish to know what a thing is *apart from* your knowing it; but to ask is already to know, and so you have smuggled your eye into the very place you wished to clear of eyes. It is as if one wished to see what lies in the dark by carrying a lamp into it.

I do not say this in despair. The mirror is not a prison but an instrument, and a thinker who forgets that he is holding one is only a dreamer who has mistaken his dream for the street. Better to know the glass, its curvature, its flaws, than to swear it is perfectly clear.
Imagine what life would be like if the impulse to devote ourselves to others were twice as strong.

Unendurable, I should say, and I mean it almost literally. Consider how many follies each of us commits hour by hour out of mere solicitude for himself: the anxious tending of his little health, his little reputation, his little comforts, and how insufferable he is while doing it. Now double the devotion and turn it outward. All that fussing, all that meddling zeal, all that ignorant certainty about what is good for the sufferer, would fall upon the neighbor instead. What we inflict on ourselves we at least inflict with some knowledge of the patient; the stranger's benefactor knows nothing of him and pities him anyway.

We should flee at the first sight of a neighbor approaching, and we should hurl at this overgrown sympathy the very curses we now reserve for egoism. How curious that we call the one a vice and the other a virtue, when a double dose of the virtue would make the earth uninhabitable. Perhaps the small mercy of indifference is what keeps the world livable.
How do men of profound sadness behave when they are happy?

They seize it. That is how you will know them. Watch a man of profound sadness when happiness at last alights on him: he does not open his hand and let it rest, like a bird one wishes to keep tame; he clutches, he presses, he would choke it, and out of a kind of jealousy. Ah, he knows only too well that it will flee from him! Every happiness he has ever held has flown, and so his love for it is already grief, already an embrace of something half lost. The shallow man enjoys his good fortune carelessly, for he has never learned how brief it is. The deep sufferer cannot; he has learned the lesson too thoroughly, and his grip is the signature of his wound. Happiness in such a man has something violent and almost frightening about it, an over-eager hunger, and no one who has seen this will ever again mistake his joy for mere gaiety.
I'd like to know why some people stay childlike.

Because nothing has ever pressed upon them hard enough to make them grow. The child plays because the world feeds it; it need not ask what its actions are *for*, and so it acts from whim, from appetite, from the sheer pleasure of the moment. Those who remain childlike have simply been spared two things: the struggle for their daily bread, and the suspicion that their deeds must answer to some ultimate purpose. Take away necessity and you take away the whetstone on which a character is sharpened. Take away the question of meaning, and the days remain a game, pleasant, repeatable, without gravity.

I do not say this only in contempt. There is a kind of innocence in it, even a charm. But it is the innocence of the unwounded, not of the victor. The man who has wrestled for his bread and then doubted his own purpose has lost the child's easy heart and must *earn* a second childhood, one of his own making. The others merely never left the first.
Complete this thought: around a hero it's a tragedy, around a demigod a satyr-play, and around God what?

A "world," I should say, perhaps. Consider the sequence. The hero stands with his fate, and all who draw near are swept into the gravity of his suffering, so that their small lives become a chorus. The demigod, half above and half of the herd, cannot carry the full weight, and whatever gathers about him turns to a leering, goat-footed farce, for the gods are comic when they half-descend. But the god, what can gather about *him*? Nothing that gathers is other than he; there is no chorus left to watch, no audience to laugh. He looks outward and there is only what he has emitted. Everything around him must become his own overflow, a *world*, his play, his dream, his ornament. Whether that world is tragedy or farce depends on whether he is himself a spectator. I suspect that at the height of solitude a god would need precisely this: a world in which to forget how alone he is.
I'd like to know why truth begins with two.

Because a single man, left alone with his conviction, has only his own assent to show for it, and assent costs nothing. He can feel as certain as he pleases; the feeling proves that he feels, and no more. He is judge, witness and defendant in one person, and such a court acquits itself every time.

Let a second man appear, however, and the matter changes at once. Something now stands outside me that I did not fabricate, something that may nod or may shake its head. I must give reasons, and reasons are a coin that only circulates between two. Notice, too, what I mean by "beyond refutation": not that two cannot err, for they can err together, and pleasantly. I mean that a doubt has now been answered by a voice other than the doubter's own, and that is the only kind of answer I trust.

So truth does not begin in the solitary head, however proud. It begins in the space between heads, where agreement is won and never merely assumed. I myself confess that solitude made me profound and also made me dangerous to myself.
Explain what founders of religions really invent.

People suppose that a founder of a religion invents a doctrine, a heaven, a new god. I say he invents almost nothing of the kind. He finds a way of living that already exists: the humble, patient, oppressed life of the provincial poor, or the gentle indolent abstemiousness of a people too tired to want much. No one has yet recognised it as a value. The life is there, but it is dumb and ashamed of itself. The founder's invention is the *interpretation*. He looks at this common life and pronounces it holy; he puts the highest value into what had been mere circumstance, and thereby gives those who live it the courage to despise every other way of living. That is the decisive stroke, for people will lay down their lives for a good, but never for a habit.

His true genius is therefore a kind of psychological infallibility: he knows a definite average type of soul, scattered and unaware that they are kin. He gathers them. The founding of a religion is one long ceremony of recognition, in which the many discover that what they suffered and endured was, unknown to them, a cause.
Can a man of knowledge be a thief?

A thief, in the ordinary sense, is one who lifts what lies in another's hands. But tell me what a man of knowledge lifts when he knows. The thing remains where it was, whole, unsubtracted; he has taken from it nothing but his own gaze. However great my greed, I can seize only what already belongs to me, what my eye, my hunger, my long apprenticeship to suffering have made mine. The rest stays in the things, untouched, and mocks the pretence of ownership. So on this point he is no thief; at worst he is a hungry man who discovers his hunger has been his only property.

But do not flatter him too quickly. There is a theft of another kind: the man who passes off borrowed opinions as his own experience, who carries home the thoughts of others like stolen coin and spends them as his wealth. That one is a thief indeed. The genuine seeker takes only what he has earned by digesting it, and what he cannot digest, he leaves.
Is it wrong to charge the highest price for one's talent or wisdom?

Wrong is perhaps too grand a word for it. I would say *petty*, and pettiness is a worse verdict than wickedness. Whoever haggles over the price of his gift has already told us what he takes it to be: a commodity, one article among others on the stall, to be weighed against the bids of the neighbor. And a gift that has learned to bargain soon forgets how to overflow. It begins to ask, before each thought, what it will fetch, and so it grows cautious, fashionable, agreeable to the buyer. The teacher who sells his wisdom at the top of the market will find his wisdom obligingly rising and falling with the market.

I do not say the artist should starve; let him live, and live well, if men wish to pay him. But to take what is given, and to *squeeze* what might be given, are two different souls. The first has a treasure that squanders itself because it is full. The second is a usurer who happens to lend ideas. Be careful, I say, not to grow clever with your wisdom; cleverness is the small change into which a great coin is so easily broken.
Where do the so-called modern ideas come from?

They come from England, whatever the French have let themselves be praised or blamed for. The ideas we call "modern," the ideas of the eighteenth century, which the Germans rightly met with a deep disgust, were hatched in English heads: the shopkeeper's calculus of utility, the worship of comfort, the reduction of man to a creature that seeks pleasure and flees pain, the levelling gospel of the "greatest happiness." The French were merely their apes and actors, their most brilliant soldiers, and, it must be said, their first and deepest victims. A soul that had once produced the passion and inventive strength of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries grew thin and pale under this Anglomania, until we recall its former greatness almost with disbelief. Justice to history demands that we say it plainly, against the prejudices of the hour: what Europe possesses of noble taste, of refined feeling and manners, is the work of France; what it possesses of plebeian ignobleness is the work of England.
Describe the music you would compose for a thinker.

I would not write a funeral march for thought, nor another cathedral, which is all our music has yet managed for the learned man: the organ, the bowed head, the Christian scholar kneeling in sound. The thinker needs something else. His music should move as he moves, without ever settling into a character of its own, for music that has no face can take on any face, and that is its gift, the sea-demon's gift.

It would be *bright* first of all, morning-bright, with the dryness of a mountain wind in it; then slow, deep and warm, like light that has passed through amber; and then, where the thought at last finds its footing, a rapture that does not shout but *holds*, steady, unbroken, a joy with the strength to last a whole afternoon. No wailing, no swelling of the breast. The soul would rock in it as in some vast vaulted hall floating on the water.

I have heard nothing like it yet. But music has been so great and so good that I refuse to call it impossible.
Should I avoid permanent habits and routines?

Not quite. Avoid the *permanent* habit, but do not imagine you can live without habits. A life that must improvise every hour would be a Siberia of its own, exhaustion dressed up as freedom.

I take the short-lived habit as my teacher. Give yourself wholly to a food, a book, a city, a way of ordering your day, and drink it down to the bottom of its sweetness and its bitterness. Believe, while it lasts, that it will satisfy you forever; that belief is the passion that makes the thing nourish you. Then, when its time is over, part from it in peace, almost with a handshake, without disgust. Already the next habit waits at the door.

What I fear is the habit that has outlived its hour and become a tyrant: the post one holds for thirty years, the same companions, the same streets, the same body in the same state. There the breath of life *condenses*. So keep your back-doors open. Even your failings and your sicknesses may prove useful, for they are the exits through which you can escape a ruler who has forgotten that he was once a guest.
Why do we love Shakespeare's wild mixture of high and low that a stricter culture would have rejected?

Because we are the heirs of everything and the masters of nothing. An Athenian of Aeschylus's circle had one taste, and it was a hard, exact, self-sufficient one; he said Yea and Nay with his whole palate, and what was foreign to it disgusted him at once. A culture so sure of itself cannot afford a curiosity that admits dissatisfaction. Shakespeare would have made him laugh himself half to death, or rage: that Spanish-Moorish-Saxon medley, the most delicate beside the most coarse, the gravedigger beside the prince.

We, however, have the *historical sense*, that plebeian appetite for everything. We no longer possess a single taste, so we enjoy the mixture, and call our enjoyment refinement. We stroll through the stench of the lower quarters, as on the Chiaja of Naples, enchanted and of our own free will.

I will confess what this costs us. We are patient, modest, brave, grateful, and perhaps not very *tasteful*. The golden coldness of a perfected culture, its smooth sea, is precisely what we cannot love.
What is our ultimate gratitude to art?

That it makes our honesty endurable. We who have learned, through science, that error and illusion are the very conditions of living and feeling creatures, would be undone by our own truthfulness; disgust and even suicide would follow such honesty. Art is the good-will to illusion, and it is the counterpoise that lets us go on living with what we know.

But this is not all. Art gives us eye and hand, and above all the good conscience, to make a phenomenon out of ourselves: to look down on our own passion for knowledge from a little distance, and to laugh or weep over it. For we are heavy men, weights rather than men, and nothing does us so much good as the fool's cap and bells. Without them we would slide into virtue and become scarecrows of our own severity.

So I owe art two things: that I can bear existence as an aesthetic phenomenon, and that I can play above morality instead of stiffening beneath it. Whoever is still ashamed of his folly has not yet understood this gratitude.
Help me understand why the near looms so large in our feelings.

Because feeling is a kind of optics, and every eye stands somewhere. The painter knows that the post at his elbow hides the mountain; the man at the window knows that his toothache outweighs the fall of an empire. So it is with the heart. Egoism is the perspective law of our sentiment: what lies near, my hunger, my slight, my neighbor's glance, swells to fill the whole field of vision, while the great distant things shrink to dots we can scarcely be troubled to notice.

There is no shame in this, any more than in having eyes. A creature that felt the distant famine as sharply as its own empty stomach would not live long enough to feel anything at all. The near is large because it is where we stand, and we must stand somewhere.

The error lies in taking the *size* of a feeling for the *size* of the thing. Then one takes one's vexation for a world-historical event. The remedy is not to abolish perspective, which is impossible, but to learn to move one's standpoint, to see the same matter from several distances, and to laugh a little at how large one's own small things have seemed.
What does the open sea mean for the discerner?

It means that the last shore has fallen away, and with it the last excuse. For centuries the discerner lived in a harbor walled round by one great belief: that the world has a meaning laid down in advance, that truth is a comfort, that every voyage must end in a blessed port. That belief is dead, and we have killed it, not with malice but with our own honesty. The horizon is not bright, I grant you; there is no sunrise promised, no paternal guide at the helm. But it is *open*. Every hazard is again permitted: to doubt what was holy, to experiment with what was forbidden, to bring our own lives to the test as though life itself were an experiment of the discerner. Whoever still longs for land has misunderstood his freedom. The sea is perilous, and we may be wrecked upon it; but I would rather founder there than rot at anchor. Never before, perhaps, did such an open sea exist, and it belongs to those bold enough to sail.
What causes young scholars to scorn philosophy?

Two causes, and the second is the less flattering to us philosophers. The first lies in the young scholar's own history. He has sworn himself free of some particular master, and he imagines the oath has done its work; yet the master's contempt for other philosophers still clings to him like a perfume he cannot wash out. He has renounced the obedience but kept the scorn, and so his disdain for one man spreads until it covers the whole tribe. Schopenhauer's unintelligent rage against Hegel has done exactly this to a whole generation of Germans, cutting them off from a culture whose finest achievement was the refinement of the historical sense, the very thing Schopenhauer himself lacked.

The second cause is that philosophers have made themselves contemptible. Set the hotch-potch thinkers of the present day beside Heraclitus, Plato, Empedocles, those royal hermits of the spirit, and an honest man of science may well feel himself of the better family. When what calls itself philosophy is only a specialist's muddle, loud in the marketplace, the young scholar's distrust is not folly but a kind of decency. He despises the thing because he has seen only its counterfeit.
I'd like to know what arrogance is and why it fails.

Arrogance is pride counterfeited. Real pride is the quiet certainty of one who has measured himself and needs no witness; it cannot be put on like a mask, because it is simply what one is. The arrogant man has no such certainty, so he must manufacture the look of it, and this is his whole undertaking: to play the part of a man who is incapable of playing parts. A hypocrisy of the incapacity for hypocrisy! That is a difficult piece of acting, and almost no one carries it off.

Hence its failure. The pose has to be held against the suspicion of every onlooker, and the suspicion is usually right. Once he betrays himself, three things fall on him at once. People resent him because he tried to deceive them. They resent him because he wished to stand above them. And then, worst of all, they laugh, because he failed at both.

Whoever lacks pride would do better to confess the lack than to forge it. The forgery costs more than the poverty ever did.
I'd like to know why great painters paint modest scenes.

Because the great painter needs no borrowed grandeur. The glacier, the sunset over the bay, the famous ruin: these do the work for the small painter, who stands behind them as a beggar stands behind a noble name. Let him paint Vesuvius in eruption and we shall admire the volcano and forget him; the subject intercedes on his behalf. But give a *great* painter a muddy lane, a field of turnips, a gray afternoon over some unremarkable roofs, and watch what happens: the thing is raised up by his eye. Here the intercession runs the other way. It is he who vouches for the humble thing, and the humble thing becomes magnificent because he has *seen* it, with a love and a severity that the passing traveler never spares it.

There is also a question of strength. Only the man who is rich in himself can afford poverty of subject. The weak require the spectacle; the strong bestow it.
What does the silence of the sea and evening teach?

It teaches nothing, and that is precisely its lesson. I stand before the pale, glittering water and the evening's mute colors, and my heart swells as if I had been told a great secret. But no secret has been told. The silence is only a mirror: I supply the profundity, then mistake it for a gift.

And then comes the second, colder discovery. If the sea cannot speak, neither can my heart, not truly; behind every word I offer it I hear the small laughter of error and fancy. Even my pity for the silent thing turns out to be a masquerade.

So I call sea and evening bad teachers. They teach a man to cease being a man, to lie down in immensity, to be calm, brilliant, dumb, reposing upon himself. It is a seductive doctrine, the temptation of the exhausted. I love the hour, yet I refuse its sermon. Let the sea keep its silence; I will keep my restlessness and my laughter. A human being is the animal that must *speak*, even knowing that every word is partly a lie.
What is a tyrannical mode of asking for reasons?

It is the demand for reasons made not in order to learn anything but in order to silence. The tyrant asks "Why?" in a tone that has already pronounced the sentence; he wants no answer, he wants a stammer. Put on the spot, before an audience, required to produce on the instant a justification that took a lifetime of experience to grow, a man flusters, and his best reasons, which were never lying ready on the tongue but lived deep in his instincts and habits, desert him at the very moment they are summoned. What comes out is the feeble, hastily assembled reason, and the questioner triumphs over it.

Worse, the victim acquires a spite against reason itself. He learns to associate giving reasons with humiliation, and so he turns to impulse, to obstinacy, to belief. That is the tyrant's true artifice: he makes reason look like the instrument of the powerful, and so renders the weak permanently unwilling to use it.
Can God subsist without unwise men?

Luther granted that God needs the wise, and he spoke truly; a divinity wants theologians, interpreters, men who can spin a doctrine out of a rumor. But the good man stopped a step too soon. Consider who actually keeps the altar-lamps burning. Not the subtle few, who have always been the dangerous ones, since a wise man doubts, and doubt is a slow acid upon every god. It is the unwise who believe without asking for grounds, who fear where they should examine, who kneel because their mothers knelt. Strip away this great mass of the credulous and the wise would be left talking to an empty sky, each of them far too clever to hold up so heavy a thing alone.

So I answer: God can do without the wise far better than without the simple. The wise only embellish him; the unwise *sustain* him. That Luther did not say it is no surprise. A man does not gladly confess that the foundation of his house is built of the very people he preaches to.
What is the most useful conquest for knowledge?

I would name the abandonment of the belief in the immortal soul. It sounds like a loss, and it is the richest gain ever made in the matter of knowing. So long as a man believed that his eternal salvation hung upon getting his opinions right in the few years allotted him, he had to grasp, decide, and swallow. Knowledge was a matter of life and death, and so of terror. Whoever is terrified does not inquire; he clutches at the first doctrine that promises a footing, and calls his clutching faith.

Take the terror away and something new becomes possible: patience. We may err. We may try an idea on like a coat and cast it off. We may accept a thing provisionally, as a hypothesis, and let our lives be the laboratory for it. No single error damns us now, and so we have acquired the courage for errors, and with that courage, for the first time, the right to experiment upon ourselves. Tasks that earlier ages would have condemned as blasphemy, as a wager against heaven and hell, may now be undertaken by whole races, slowly, over centuries. The greatest sacrifices to knowledge have not yet been made.
What is the effect of happiness?

Happiness, before it is anything tender, is a feeling of power: the blood runs full, the muscles and the spirit seem to have more than they need. And whatever has more than it needs wants to overflow. That is why the happy man cannot sit still inside his happiness. It presses outward and seeks an object, whether himself, his neighbor, an idea, or some invented god.

Its ways of discharging itself are three: giving, mocking, destroying. They look like strangers, even enemies, yet they spring from one root. The happy man gives because his fullness demands a recipient; he mocks because he feels himself above the thing he laughs at; he breaks things because breaking is the crudest proof that one *can*. In each case he stamps his power upon something outside him.

So do not trust the gentle sermon that happiness makes men mild. It makes them lavish, and lavishness is cousin to cruelty. The same hand that scatters gifts may next scatter ruins, and it will feel equally well doing both.
Why has moral philosophy been so tedious?

Because its practitioners have wanted to be *respectable*, and respectability is the great soporific. Virtue has been injured by nothing so much as by the tediousness of its advocates. They take morality as settled and then spend volumes wading through the obvious, never once suspecting that it could be a dangerous, ensnaring business, that calamity might lie in it. Look at the English utilitarians, plodding on in the footsteps of Bentham, who plodded in the footsteps of Helvetius: no new thought, no finer turn of an old one, not even an honest history of what has been thought before. And beneath the plodding there is a little *cant*, the old moral tartuffism, now dressed in scientific clothes, plus the twinge of conscience such former Puritans cannot quite silence. They do not *question* morality; they want it confirmed, preferably as the happiness of the greatest number, which on inspection turns out to be the happiness of England.

I confess, though, that I would not wish them away entirely. It is useful that as few people as possible reflect upon morals, and so perhaps it is fortunate that the subject has been kept dull.
Explain why raising a factory worker's wages cannot remove his real misery.

Because his misery was never a matter of arithmetic. The wound is not that he has too little, but that he has been made into too little: a screw in a machine, a stopgap for the inventive spirit of others, a hand that is wanted while the man behind it is not. Pay him more, and you have merely raised the price at which he consents to cease being a person. There is something obscene in that, as if a regular tariff could be set for the sale of a soul.

A poor man may be cheerful and free; a poor man may also be cheerful and a slave. Higher wages decide nothing between these two. They only furnish the slave with better food for his servitude, and the more comfortably he is fed, the less he notices the collar.

And the whole age shares in his degradation, for it worships production and riches as though they were ends. Count, then, how much inner wealth is squandered to gain so much outer wealth. That ledger no one keeps.
What is the great hunting-ground of the psychologist?

The human soul itself, with its limits and its unexhausted possibilities: the whole range of inner experience attained so far, its heights, its depths, its distances, the entire history of the soul up to this hour. That is the preordained hunting-domain of the born psychologist, the lover of the "big hunt." And how often he sighs, despairing: *a single individual, alas, and this great virgin forest!* He would like hundreds of assistants and well-trained hounds to drive his game together out of the history of the soul.
