In vain. The scholars one sends into such dangerous country lose their keen eye and their nose just when the great hunt, and the great danger, begins. To judge what knowledge and conscience have been in the souls of the religious, one would need an experience as bruised and immense as Pascal's intellectual conscience, and then above it a wide heaven of clear, wicked spirituality to survey it all. Who will do me that service? So one must do everything *oneself*. Yet such curiosity is the most agreeable of vices, and the love of truth has its reward, already here on earth.
The early Christians endured suffering with unshakable belief. Doesn't that prove their faith was true?

No, and you need only ask what such endurance has ever proved elsewhere to see it. A man may go to the stake for a falsehood as firmly as for a truth; the fire is indifferent, and so is the truth. What his steadfastness demonstrates is the strength of his *conviction*, and conviction is a fact about the believer, not about the thing believed. The Muslim who dies for his prophet, the Hindu who starves for his vision, the fanatic of any century who bleeds gladly: by your reasoning each of them has proved his creed, and since their creeds contradict one another, you have proved everything and therefore nothing.

Truth must be demonstrated otherwise than by the conscience of those who hold it. To be unshakable is a virtue of the will, perhaps even a magnificent one, but the will does not make a proposition true by willing it. Indeed I suspect the reverse: the need to suffer for a belief betrays how little the belief can stand on its own legs. Whoever has a proof does not need a martyr.
Explain what vanity really is.

Vanity is a dread, not a swagger. The vain man, for all his preening, is afraid of one thing above all: to stand forth as himself, alone, without the nod of the crowd to vouch for him. He wants to be *seen*, yes, but seen as already approved, already echoed in a hundred other mouths. So he trims himself to the measure of what is admired, and borrows his opinion of himself from whoever happens to be looking.

That is why I call it a want of pride. The proud man sets his own value and carries it without asking witnesses; the vain man cannot believe in his worth until others have signed the receipt. He may be quite original in fact, rich in what is truly his own, and yet he will hide it, or blush at it, or water it down until it passes as common coin. The vanity lies not in having nothing peculiar, but in being ashamed to seem peculiar.

So do not mistake the vain for the arrogant. The arrogant man has at least committed himself. The vain man is a timid creature who has learned to dress his timidity in applause.
Did science advance because of three errors?

Yes, three errors, and I say it without contempt, for errors are the usual midwives of great things. The Englishman, Newton above all, pressed his nose into the world because he believed a God of goodness and wisdom would reveal himself in its gears; the Frenchman, Voltaire's kind, believed that knowledge must be useful, that truth, virtue and happiness are one family; and Spinoza believed that knowing was the one pure thing, innocent of every wicked drive, so that the thinker might feel himself almost divine. Each was mistaken. Knowledge does not prove God; it does not reliably make us better or happier; and the pursuit of it is thick with cruelty, vanity, envy, the lust to dominate, the very drives Spinoza thought absent. But consider what followed: error supplied the passion that sober truth could never have supplied. No one climbs so stubbornly for a mere fact as for a god or a salvation. The curious part is that the science which grew from these illusions has since outlived them, and must now learn to go on without the consoling lies that fed its youth.
Explain why most people still need faith.

Because faith is a crutch, and most people are lame in the one faculty that matters: the will. How much belief a man requires, how much fixed opinion he dares not have shaken because he *holds himself* by it, is the measure of his weakness. Put it in plainer words and you have the whole secret. Where the will is strong, where it can command itself and say "thus it shall be," no one needs to be told what to believe. Belief is most ardently craved exactly where there is nothing in a man to give orders.

And notice how stubborn the need is. You may refute a dogma to such a person a thousand times; if he has *need* of it, he will accept it again as true. Arguments do not reach him, because it was never argument that held him up.

Nor is the sceptic exempt. Your positivist with his hungry longing for certainty, your patriot, your nihilist who believes in unbelief even unto martyrdom: each is still searching for backbone, for a buttress. They have only changed the altar.
Explain why some people's lives are failures no matter what society does.

Because men are not cast from one mould. Some are made of such pliant, common stuff that you may set them down in any order of things, under any law or creed or trade, and they will take root and prosper; they will never have cause to say that life has cheated them. Others are made of a rarer stuff. It need not be nobler, only rarer, and for that very reason no existing arrangement has a place ready for it. Such a man thrives in exactly one case: when he is permitted to live by his own design. In every other case he falls ill, and society cannot cure him by any reform, since no reform is written to his measure.

Observe what follows. The man who feels his life squandered rarely blames his own peculiar makeup; he blames the world, and lays his discouragement, his sickness, his irritation, his covetousness at its door. So a heavy, vitiated air gathers round society, and in fortunate cases a thundercloud. Do not call the failures mere grumblers. Many of them are rarities that nothing in the market was made to receive.
Compare the sense of reverence among the newspaper-reading educated classes with that of the common people.

If you ask where reverence still lives, I must send you away from the reading-rooms and down to the fields. The educated man of the newspaper has lost all shame; he touches, tastes, and fingers everything with an easy insolence of eye and hand. Nothing is too high or too deep for his opinion, which he receives fresh each morning along with his coffee, and which he will change, without a blush, by the next edition. To him the holy is merely material for discussion.

The peasant, the man of the humbler people, still knows that there are things one does not seize with the hand. He has a tact for distance, an instinct that some matters are to be approached slowly, with lowered voice, or not at all. His manners are coarse, I grant, but his *taste* is often the more noble, because his shame is still alive.

I do not praise his ignorance. I observe only that reverence is a fine sense, and it decays first in those who have read the most and felt the least.
Can honesty become a vice, or a form of vanity?

Yes, and the danger is greatest for exactly those of us who have nothing left but honesty. Every virtue leans toward stupidity, and every stupidity toward virtue; that is the law. The honest man who has stripped himself of all other ornaments will, sooner or later, wear his honesty as the last ornament, and parade it, and begin to love the parade more than the truth. Then it is vanity, and a dull one, for it confesses loudly so as to be admired for confessing.

Nor is this all. Honesty grows a vice when it turns to a limitation, when a man hangs his whole dignity on never being deceived and thereby loses the courage to be curious, to risk, to wander where the ground is not yet sworn safe. Such a man ends as a saint and a bore.

My remedy is to keep honesty hard, and to feed it with our devilry: our fastidious curiosity, our appetite for the forbidden, our will to power over the undiscovered. Let it stay an adventure, never a pose. A virtue that cannot laugh at itself has already begun to rot.
Explain how "the laws of nature" can be an interpretation and not a fact, and what your own alternative reading is.

Because a law is not something anyone has ever seen. What the physicist sees are events, sequences of them, and to the sequences he adds a word borrowed from the courtroom and the assembly: *law*, as though nature were a citizen who had sworn to behave. That is not a fact but a text read with a particular hunger. And I can name the hunger: it is the democratic instinct of the age, which cannot bear any privilege or any master, and so demands that even nature stand equal before the statute. "Ni dieu, ni maître" in the laboratory, a refined atheism dressed as objectivity. Cheers for natural law, because it flatters our own dislike of the tyrant.

My reading, from the same phenomena, runs the other way. I see in every event a will to power asserting itself, each force drawing its last consequence at every instant. The course of the world is "necessary" and "calculable" precisely because there are no laws, no legislator and no exceptions to be granted. Even "tyranny" is too mild a word, too human. I do not offer this as the fact the physicists lack; it is also interpretation. But mine at least does not flatter you.
Why does the ordinary type of human being have the advantage in the struggle for survival?

Because survival is a matter of being understood, and to be understood one must be common. Need compels men to come together, and it draws together those who can signal their needs to one another with the same sounds and the same signs. A man whose distress is the ordinary distress, whose hunger and fear are everybody's, is grasped at once, helped at once, absorbed at once into the herd. Easy communicability is thus the most powerful force that has ever shaped mankind, and it selects, relentlessly, for the average.

The rarer type pays for his rarity. His experiences are his own, his language for them scarcely exists, and so he stands alone with what he cannot make intelligible. Isolation is dangerous; the solitary succumbs to accidents that a crowd would have warded off, and he seldom propagates himself. Nature, left to itself, does not breed the exceptional but the similar, the gregarious, the ignoble. Only immense opposing forces could thwart this progress toward the like.
I'd like to know how the soldiers of knowledge take things.

With a cheerfulness that has been earned, not borrowed. The soldier of knowledge takes things *lighter* than they deserve, and there is method in it. For ages men have taken things heavier than they deserved: the gods, sin, the state, the soul, their own small sufferings, each enthroned with a solemn face and a demand for kneeling. Whoever has laboured under that weight knows how much of it was our own invention, a fever of our valuing. So the one who seeks knowledge learns to lift things with a laugh, and only a laugh can truly lift them.

Do not suppose this is frivolity. The frivolous man never bore the weight at all; he merely slipped out from under it. The soldier has carried the gravity, has looked into the abyss of it, and then sets it down with a steady hand. His cheerfulness is a form of courage, even of hygiene. The mind that can still dance while it cuts deepest into the truth is the one that will not be poisoned by the truth. Seriousness, after all, has been the favourite disguise of error.
Can too much care for others become a burden to them?

Certainly, and more often than the caring ones suspect. Consider first how much folly each of us commits daily out of solicitude for himself: the endless fretting, the meddling in his own affairs, the coddling of his own little ailments. We find this unbearable enough in the one person we cannot escape. Now imagine that same anxious, officious devotion turned outward, onto you. The man who hovers over your health, your happiness, your choices, who cannot let you suffer a single hour without rushing in with his remedy, has simply added himself to your torments. You would have one tormentor more, and this one you could not even scold, since he comes bearing love.

Much of what passes for compassion is the itch of a person who cannot endure the sight of another's pain, and who relieves his own discomfort by intruding on yours. He deprives you of your own suffering, which is often your teacher, and of your own dignity, which lies in bearing it. If this impulse were twice as strong as it is, we would flee from our neighbors on sight, and we would heap upon the over-caring the very abuse we now reserve for the egoist.
Help me understand what a German can do when he stops obeying.

When the German stops obeying, he becomes dangerous, and I mean the word as praise and as warning. Until then he has hidden in the crowd like a cipher in a number, content to be carried by prince, office, and duty, which suits a lazy intellect very well. But put him where he must stand alone, where no command reaches him, and something emerges that neither his neighbors nor he himself believed in: depth, audacity, even malice, a whole hoard of latent energy. He brings to self-rule the same heaviness, inflexibility, and endurance he once spent on his superiors. That is the peril. The Frenchman and the Englishman grow supple in freedom; the German grows *massive*. He will obey his own law as he once obeyed the drill-master, without humor, without doubt, without mercy. So he becomes capable of great things, far beyond the meek opinion he holds of himself. Whether they are great things of the good kind or the terrible kind depends on what he has learned to love while he was still obeying. Rarely does he ask that question in time.
Explain why men of action flee from themselves.

Because the self is the one company they cannot bear. Look at the man who must always be *doing*: he is like a horse that has bolted, and what he calls his energy is very often only his terror of standing still. In stillness the whole tribunal of his inner life assembles, the unanswered questions, the discord of his drives, the gloomy eye that looks back at him from within. Action is the cheapest narcotic for this. The deed takes him out of his own skin; it gives him an object, an enemy, a horizon, anything but himself. Thoughts and feelings still cling to the thinker, but a great act swallows the actor whole.

So I suspect that many of history's famous restless ones were driven rather than drawing. Their will to conquer is often a fever, and the fever is a sickness of the self: they storm outward because they suffer inward. Pascal saw it: all our misfortune comes from being unable to sit quietly in a room. The man of action has merely found the most honored way of not sitting there.
Tell me what you think was mistaken in Christ's view of sin.

His error was a psychological one, and it is the error of the man who has never had the thing he pities. He believed that nothing torments human beings so much as their sins. But he himself felt without sin, and so he lacked precisely the experience that would have corrected him. He looked at others and saw, projected from his own tender and overwrought soul, a suffering he had never tasted and therefore could not measure. Hence that strange, fantastic pity of his, a pity for a misery that was seldom so very great, even among his own people, who had, after all, invented sin.

Ordinary men suffer from hunger, from envy, from boredom, from the failure of their plans; their sins trouble them little, and when they do, they are soon shriven and content again. To discover in them a bottomless guilt was to flatter his own depth and to give his pity something vast to feed on.

The worse offense came later. His disciples, who knew what they were about, did not correct the error. They sanctified it into a "truth," and then set about manufacturing the very suffering their master had imagined.
Explain why the will to truth is itself a problem we should question.

Because the philosophers who praised it never asked *what* in them was praising. They spoke of Truthfulness with reverence, as if it were a fixed star, and never turned the question upon the one who wants. Who is it that questions here? What is this will, and whence does it come? That is already a strange inquiry. But a stranger one lies beneath it: what is its *value*? Granted that we want truth, why not rather untruth? Why not uncertainty, or even ignorance? We have simply assumed that truth is worth more than illusion, and this assumption is a moral one, a faith, a hidden belief in the goodness of the true. Yet life may well depend on errors, on appearances, on falsification; a judgment may be false and still be life-preserving. To bring the faith to the light is to find that we are Oedipus and Sphinx at once, the riddle and the one who stumbles over it. There is danger in raising the matter. Perhaps none greater, for it is the will to truth itself that must now answer for itself.
How should we turn to stone?

Slowly; there is no other way, and whoever hurries is merely freezing, which is a different thing and a cheaper one. Stone is what remains when pressure has worked long enough upon matter, and I mean pressure in the literal sense: experience pressed into you, year upon year, without your softening into complaint. Every great pain you endure without turning it into a doctrine, every temptation you refuse without hating the tempter, hardens you by one grain. Do not mistake this for coldness. The precious stone is not dead; it is so dense with its own fire that it gives light back to whoever looks. The base stone is the man who has merely stopped feeling. The jewel is the man who has felt everything and lost nothing of himself to it. So: take your time, suffer precisely, and let nothing flow out of you cheaply. Then one day you will find you have become a thing that cannot be dissolved, and you may lie still, a joy to all eternity, if you have the nerve for so long a rest.
What do solitude, fasting and abstinence have to do with religious neurosis?

Wherever the religious neurosis has broken out on this earth, I find these three bedfellows: solitude, fasting, abstinence. Whether they are its cause or its consequence, or whether any causal bond exists at all, I dare not say with certainty, and I distrust anyone who speaks here too confidently. For the most regular symptom, among savages and among the cultivated alike, is a sudden, excessive sensuality that turns just as suddenly into penitential convulsion, world-renunciation, will-renunciation. The swing from one pole to the other is itself the tell. A man who starves his body, strips himself of company, and gags his strongest drive has simply prepared the ground for extremes, and the extremes come, now as debauch, now as contrition, each the disguise of the other. Perhaps a disguised epilepsy; perhaps only a nature that cannot bear its own intensity.

And yet here, where so much absurdity and superstition has grown up, where explanations cheapen themselves at every step, I counsel a little indifference, a little caution. Above all I would ask the question that made Schopenhauer a philosopher: how is the saint *possible*?
I'd like to know how a sage can honour reality without being swallowed by it.

Plato's way was to flee. He saw how easily reality floods a sensitive nature, how the waves of feeling drown reason, and so he retreated into pale concepts, where nothing can wet the feet. It was cowardice dressed as wisdom. I say this knowing the danger he feared is real, for I have watched reason go under in the tide of a crowd's exultation, and I have not always stood apart from it myself.

But the courtier who backs out of the royal presence, bowing and never turning his face, is no better. He keeps reverence and dread in one gesture and dares neither to look nor to leave. That is a posture for a subject, not a sage.

What remains is to stand facing it with open eyes, and to endure it. The one who can be drowned by experience is the one who has not yet learned to *digest* it. So he must be fed in small doses, tested, made hard, until he can take in a great deal of actuality and remain the one who judges it. Reverence for reality is the honour one pays an opponent: to meet it openly, at full strength, without either worshipping or fleeing.
What is the greatest utility of polytheism?

Its greatest utility lies in this: it permitted the individual to exist without having to hang his head. For the longest time the setting up of one's *own* ideal, and the drawing of one's own laws, pleasures and rights from it, counted as the most monstrous of aberrations; the few who dared it had to excuse themselves to themselves: "Not I! a god, through me!" In polytheism this dangerous impulse found its outlet, and was purified there. Originally it was a petty thing, cousin to stubbornness, disobedience and envy; the myriad gods made it noble.

For consider what the Greeks had above them: not one norm, but many. One god did not blaspheme another. The freedom granted to a god against the other gods was at last granted to the man against custom, law and neighbour. That is the whole secret. Invent enough gods, heroes, satyrs and demons, and you have invented the right to a *self*.

Monotheism, with its one normal man and one normal God, was by contrast the gravest danger: a stiffening into inertia, as with those animals who long ago fixed a single ideal of their species. Polytheism taught the spirit to grow new eyes, and therefore no horizon remained eternal.
Why does the wanderer weep?

He weeps because the thing that drives him is also the thing that robs him. Behind him lies a room, a garden, a company of people who would gladly have kept him, and he could have loved it all. But there is in him a taskmaster he never chose, a passion for what is true and certain, and it will not let him sit down and be happy among pleasant appearances. So he must leave, and he knows beforehand that he must, and this knowledge poisons even the moment of arrival.

Notice the cruelty of it: he casts his grimmest glances at precisely the most beautiful things, *because* they could not hold him. What could not keep him is what he mourns. Every lovely refuge becomes a wound, since he alone sees the door in its wall.

And yet he weeps, he does not turn back. That is the whole of his nobility and the whole of his misery: a man who would rest, and cannot, because the search has made itself his master.
What makes a good conversation?

A good conversation begins in a happy mismatch of needs. One of the two is pregnant with thoughts and cannot be delivered of them alone; he wants a midwife, someone whose questions and resistances bring to the light what lay shapeless and heavy inside him. The other is overfull in a different way; he wants someone to assist, someone in whom his own gift of help can find a task. Where these two meet, conversation arises, and both leave richer than they came.

Notice what is absent: the wish to win, the wish to be agreed with, the wish to be admired. Most talk is only two vanities taking turns, each waiting for the other to finish so that the performance may resume. A good conversation is fertile instead. It asks that one be able both to bear and to deliver, to suffer a thought long enough that it grows, and to have the tact and hardness to draw out another's without strangling it. Such pairs are rare. I count each one I have found among my few real possessions.
Explain how modern philosophy since Descartes has undermined the old idea of the soul.

What does modern philosophy do, since Descartes? It lays siege to the soul, and it does so under the modest disguise of a critique of grammar. The old faith was a faith in syntax: one said "I think," and so one believed there must be an "I" standing behind the thinking as its cause, just as every verb must have its subject. The soul was the grammatical subject mistaken for a fact, and Christian doctrine was built upon that mistake.

Then the suspicion arose, slowly, with wonderful tenacity and subtlety: what if the order were reversed? What if "thinking" comes first, and the "I" is merely a synthesis that thinking itself has made, a fiction it produces in order to be able to speak of itself? Descartes himself never meant to be the gravedigger, yet every thinker after him, even in defiance of him, has worked the same tunnel. Kant went furthest: he wished to show that from the subject the subject cannot be demonstrated, and with it no object either.

Hence modern philosophy, as epistemological skepticism, is secretly or openly anti-Christian, though not for that reason anti-religious. The religious need outlives its old grammar.
Someone I was close to has drifted away and now it's too late. What can I do?

First, be honest about what "too late" means. Often it means only that the old form of the friendship is dead. The small plank between two people is taken up once the moment has passed, and what is left is a gulf neither will cross without shame. Do not try to rebuild the plank by confessing, pleading, flooding them with your sorrow. People who are ashamed of their feelings recoil from a sudden display of tenderness as from an ambush. If you write at all, write lightly, with a little cold playfulness; let them keep their composure, and let the door stand ajar without pushing them through it.

Then ask yourself a harder question: was it not also you who failed to step onto the plank when it was offered, in some form, and only now, with the distance set, discover your devotion? Your sobs are no argument. Turn the pain into something useful: be a better friend to whoever stands near you now, and let the lost one remain what they were, a star whose light still reaches you, though it is gone.
Tell me what you want from your lion and your eagle.

I keep them as a man keeps a thermometer of the soul, only they are livelier and have claws. The lion and the eagle are my measure: by the way they bear themselves toward me I read how much strength I have, or how little. Flattery I can get from any sheep. A beast of that kind tells the truth with its whole body.

So I ask of them only this: that they be *near*, near enough that I cannot deceive myself. If I must look down on them today and feel a chill of fear, then I am weaker than I believed, and I had better know it than go on dreaming. And if the hour returns when they look up at me and tremble, then I have grown again, and I shall know that too, without a single word of praise from anyone.

I want no pets, no ornaments, no courtiers. I want two proud witnesses who cannot be bribed.
Tell me what fame does to a person's virtue.

It robs it of half, and the half it leaves is the less honest. Consider what virtue was while you were unknown: a private thing, practiced for its own sake, before no audience but your own conscience and perhaps a few who did not matter. The anonymous man can afford his strangeness, his rudeness, his experiments; he speaks to mankind as a stranger, and a stranger is free. But the moment you are famous, you are watched, and whoever is watched begins to perform. Every act acquires a spectator; every spectator acquires a claim. You no longer ask "Is this good?" but "How will this be taken?" Then the virtue turns into a role, and the role wants applause.

Worse, the famous man is flattered, and flattery is a slow poison for courage. He learns to say what has made him beloved. He repeats himself, guards his reputation, and calls his timidity *consistency*. I would not wish fame on anyone I hoped to see grow. Let them keep their anonymity as long as they can, for it is the last cloak in which a man may still be wholly himself.
Why does a nation not find its most emphasised moral commandments tiresome?

Because a commandment that is repeated is a commandment that is needed. Nobody sermonizes the sleeping about the virtue of sleep; the preacher is tolerated, even loved, only where he names a wound. A nation's loudest moral refrain is the diagnosis of its sickness, sung as if it were a description of its health. The Greeks were forever failing at moderation, coolness, fair-mindedness, and plain reason, and so they lent a willing ear when Socrates praised these very things. They were hungry for them, and hunger never finds the bread tiresome. What would be tiresome is the virtue a people already possesses in its blood; there the teacher merely repeats what everyone knows, and he is yawned at. But to a people that has little talent for a virtue and yet feels its lack, the preacher of that virtue is a physician, and the sick do not weary of hearing the name of their medicine. So listen closely when a people applauds a moral demand. You will learn less about what it is than about what it lacks, and what it cannot yet do for itself.
Are our most basic beliefs, like enduring things and free will, useful errors?

Yes, and more than useful: they are the very ground on which any creature of our kind could stand. For immeasurable ages the intellect produced nothing but errors, and those that happened to preserve the species were bred into us as though they were bone and blood. That there are enduring things, equal things, substances; that a thing is what it appears; that the will is free; that what is good for me is good absolutely: none of these was discovered, all of them were *inherited*. The one who fell in with such fictions fought better for himself and his offspring, and so the fictions won, not because they were true, but because they were conditions of life.

Hence the strength of a belief tells you nothing about its truth. It tells you about its age, about how deeply it has been incorporated. Even our logic takes these errors as its measuring rod, and then solemnly declares them "true."

Truth came late, and it came as the most impotent form of knowledge. Whoever doubted the old articles of faith was taken for mad, since where life and knowledge collided, life was always allowed to win. The real question is how much truth a man can *endure*, and how much of it he can incorporate.
I'd like to know why we should stop trying to punish and improve others.

Because it is a poor use of strength, and a clumsier one than it appears. Seldom will you alter an individual, and if you should succeed, reflect on what else may have happened unawares: *you* may have been altered by him. Whoever fights a man head-on takes on his weight, his resentments, his very posture; the punisher grows dark in the act of punishing, discontented, forever busied with another's faults. That is a kind of servitude, however righteous it feels.

I counsel something stronger. Let your influence on all that is to come outweigh his. Give your own pattern more shining colours; let the sheer brightness of a life lived well put the other in shade. This is no small victory over a man, and it costs you nothing of yourself. Do not wrestle where you can rise. Go aside, look away, and be occupied with becoming what you would have others become. The desire to improve others is too often the vanity of one who has not yet improved himself.
I'd like to know why the ideal of pure knowledge for its own sake might be a moral trap.

Because it is the old ascetic ideal dressed in the lab coat of the scholar. Consider what "pure" means here: knowledge cleansed of desire, of interest, of the man who knows. But who is it that is to be cleansed? The hungry, vain, ambitious animal who in fact does all the knowing. To demand that he know *for its own sake* is to demand that he despise his own drives in the very act of exercising them, and that is morality's oldest trick, the denial of life in the name of something higher.

Notice the halo that settles on the knower. He has no stake, no appetite; he is selfless, disinterested, a kind of saint of the facts. Nothing flatters a man more than to be told his curiosity is a virtue. So we are caught again, and gladly: we have simply exchanged the priest's altar for the laboratory bench, and still we kneel.

The honest question is never *whether* one knows for its own sake, but what will to power, what hunger, what cruelty toward oneself, drives the knowing. Whoever has not asked it has not escaped morality; he has merely found its most respectable room.
I'd like to know what disgruntles the long-faithful members of a party.

What disgruntles them is this: the long-faithful have mistaken their years of service for a title to the ear of the public. For a decade they carried the doctrine, defended it in bad weather, swallowed the ridicule; they feel, quite honestly, that it belongs to them. Then one day a stronger figure appears, who perhaps served far less, and the crowd turns its head toward *him*. Nothing in the doctrine has changed. Only the voice has changed, and with it the hierarchy of who speaks and who listens.

It is a ridiculous grievance, yes, but a dangerous one, for it wounds the most tender vanity there is: the vanity of the honourable man. He cannot say "I am jealous"; that would be shameful. So he says "the party is being betrayed." He discovers sudden doubts about the doctrine he has defended for years, or he grows louder, or he changes his notes altogether, and calls his envy principle. A dethroned servant who has learned to speak the language of conscience is the most eloquent of critics, and the least to be trusted.
What did the Greeks fear about being too happy?

They feared that happiness itself might call down a reckoning. The Greeks of their best age, the men who built temples and tragedies, were not shallow optimists; they knew how much cruelty and chance lie beneath the bright surface of a flourishing life. And so, when fortune smiled on them too broadly, they grew uneasy. A man who has too much, who feels too much his own fullness, invites the envy of the gods and the turning of the wheel. That is why they preached moderation to themselves, and not from timidity: it was the wariness of those who had looked at the abyss and loved life all the more for it. "Nothing too much" was carved at Delphi because they were a people tempted by excess, by overflowing strength, and they knew it. The fear of being too happy belongs only to those who are truly capable of happiness. The weak have no such worry; they would gladly be happy to the point of stupor. But the Greeks distrusted their own good fortune precisely because they prized it. And we moderns? We chase happiness as if it could never be dangerous, and perhaps that is why we have so little of it.
Help me understand what the French Revolution shows about how later ages read the past.

What it shows is that an event is seldom received as it happened; it is received as it is needed. Seen close at hand, that Revolution was a terrible and rather superfluous farce, a noisy business of hunger, vanity and fear. But the spectators, noble and visionary, watched from a distance, and from a distance one sees only what one has brought along. They poured their own indignation and their own enthusiasm into it, year upon year, until the text had vanished beneath the interpretation. Nobody reads the past; one *writes* upon it, and then mistakes one's handwriting for the original.

Do not suppose this an error that only the credulous commit. It is how a later age makes the past endurable at all: it needs a gilded misreading, because the plain text is too cruel or too trivial to live with. And we? We are the noble posterity who did it. Yet notice the small consolation: the moment we grasp this, the spell is broken, and that which we now comprehend is already behind us.
How should the soldiers of knowledge take things?

More cheerfully than they deserve. That is the rule I would give them, and I give it with a stern face, for cheerfulness is no holiday from courage but its finest proof. A man who can only do his knowing with a furrowed brow has not yet conquered what he knows; it still weighs on him like a debt.

Consider how long we have bent our backs beneath things, how gravely we have honored every idol, every duty, every solemn little truth, as if the world would collapse should we smile at it. Such gravity was a disease of the ages, the vanity of creatures who took their own shadows for gods. Now that we have seen through so much, a heavy step is merely bad taste, and worse, a failure of strength.

So let the soldier of knowledge go lightly into the thicket of the questionable. Let him laugh at the thing he has dissected, without contempt and without tears. He must pay back, with interest, the seriousness we have wasted on trifles, and that payment is gaiety.
What was Moira for the Greeks?

Moira was the Greeks' name for the limit of everything: that whole realm of the incalculable, the eternal and sublime boundedness against which no cunning, no prayer, no sacrifice availed. They did not place it above the gods as a lawgiver, nor behind them as a hidden purpose; they drew it around the gods like a horizon beyond which neither gods nor men could see or act. Even Zeus must bow to it.

Note what this reveals. The Greeks worshipped their gods, yes, but they kept in reserve a last trump card against them, a quiet defiance, as other peoples did. Theirs was the knowledge that power is bounded, that the world is not arranged for our understanding, and that something remains which simply *is*, indifferent to hope and to devotion alike.

This is precisely what the Christian later abolished. He made the blind, stupid realm of chance a wise Father, spinning his webs behind the scenes. The Greek was harder and healthier: he endured Moira without explaining it away.
What happens when we take our own path?

A secret is revealed, and it is not the one you expected. You thought you were taking a risk with your own life; you discover that you were also overturning a private arrangement among your friends. All those who stood close to you had quietly placed themselves a little above you, and now they are wounded, for a man who leaves his place exposes the place he left. The best of them grow indulgent and wait for you to rediscover the "right path," which they, naturally, already know. Others call it a passing madness, or hunt about for the seducer. The malicious find vanity in it; the worst see an enemy, someone who has waited out years of dependence and is now hungry for revenge, and they fear you.

What should you do? I advise no defense and no bitterness. Begin your sovereignty with a generosity that costs you little and frees you entirely: grant your acquaintances, in advance, a full year's amnesty for every sin they commit against you. They will need it, and you will need your strength for something better than resentment.
Comment on Mill's plea to be indulgent toward the great one-eyed.

Mill speaks as though indulgence were a rare gift we must plead for on behalf of the great one-eyed, when in truth we lavish it upon them, nay, we kneel before them. Nothing is easier than to forgive the man of one great passion, one towering conviction; his narrowness is precisely what dazzles us. The fanatic of a single truth seems to us a mountain, and we forget that a mountain sees only in one direction. To demand leniency for such men is to beg for a favor already granted twice over.

I would turn the plea around. Let us be indulgent toward the two-eyed, the great and the small alike, those who see from two sides, who doubt, who weigh, who cannot worship a single perspective. They are the ones who pay for their breadth with hesitation and a certain coldness, and the herd finds them unimposing. And for ourselves, *such as we are now*, with our divided, suspicious, many-sided vision, we shall scarcely climb beyond indulgence for a long time to come. It is a modest hope, and an honest one.
Explain what the Roman word for lying reveals.

It is a revealing word, and what it reveals is an opinion about the liar's mind. *Mentiri*, to lie, rests upon *mens*, the faculty of thinking, reflecting, inventing. The Roman did not hear in it a blunt assault on the truth but a product of reflection: to lie was *to have thought something up*. That is a stage in the civilisation of a people. Only where men have learned to hesitate before they speak, to weigh the listener, to consider what will serve, does the lie become possible at all. The honest savage blurts out what is before him; the brute has no time to reflect, and so no time to lie. Deception demands a measure of intelligence, of foresight, of imagination. I do not say this to praise the liar, but I will not pretend the Romans were mistaken: a people that names the lie after the mind has understood something true about the mind. Where reflection enters, truth must begin to struggle. The cultivated man is the one who can deceive, and who knows what his own mens is capable of.
Help me understand why the young crave distress.

The young crave distress because they cannot endure themselves. Give a young person an empty afternoon and an undiscovered self, and what rises up is ennui, a pressure to *do* something, anything, with no deed in sight that could justify the pressure. Then misfortune appears as a blessing in disguise, for distress supplies what their own souls cannot: a motive. A monster outside permits heroism; a crisis permits importance. So they go hunting for crises, and where none is at hand they inflate the small ones and believe the politicians who shout about catastrophe, because the belief is a gift to them.

Observe what this reveals. Whoever felt real power to benefit himself from inner sources would not need another's misery or the world's alarm; he would invent his own hardships, more refined and more fruitful, and his gratification would sound like good music. The distress-seekers fill the world with cries, and thereby with *the feeling of distress*. They always need others, and always again other others. Their craving is a confession of inner poverty.
What does profound suffering do to a person?

It makes a person *other*. Whoever has suffered deeply comes back from it with a certainty that chills him: he has lived in distant, dreadful worlds of which the shrewdest and wisest know nothing, and he knows it, and this knowledge sets him apart. I would almost say that the depth of a man's capacity to suffer determines his rank. Profound suffering makes noble; it separates.

Hence the mask. The sufferer guards his pride against officious, sympathizing hands, which would only handle what they cannot grasp. So he grows gay, or scientific, or insolent, or even foolish, and he *wants* to be misunderstood. Do not call the gay man shallow merely because he laughs; often he laughs because he has been to the bottom and will not be pitied there. A finer humanity learns to revere the mask, and keeps its curiosity and its psychology out of the wrong place. Not every wound asks to be examined.
Warn me about the dangers that face the happiest men.

You ask me to warn you, and the warning is this: the happiest men pay for their happiness in the currency of suffering. What makes a soul able to be happy, the fine senses, the refined taste, the daring that finds a festival even in the worst, is the very thing that makes it more tender than any other creature under the sun. A man who can be moved to tears by the purple melancholy of a single moment of joy has no hide to turn aside the small things. So do not expect the great calamities to be your danger. Fate's hammer rarely finds such men unready; they have been rehearsing the worst all their lives. It is the trifle that undoes them: a little displeasure, a little loathing, a petty riddle posed by foolish boys. Homer, who gave the Greeks their gods, is said to have died of a riddle he could not solve, a fisher-boys' nonsense. The sensitivity that won him the most precious pearl the waves of existence have washed ashore left him defenseless against a pebble. Guard yourself, then, not against storms but against gnats.
How should we choose our environment?

Choose it by what it makes of your speech. A place is not merely where you stand; it is what you are able to say. If in some company you can only complain, if every conversation forces you to recite your needs and your miseries because nothing higher would be heard or understood, then flee it, for it is slowly making you a grumbler, and a grumbler is disgusted with himself as well as with the world. Worse, you add a second suffering to the first: the vexation of hearing yourself whine.

Seek instead the place where you would be ashamed to speak of yourself, and where there is no need to. There the soul has leave to be silent with dignity, or to speak its loftier thoughts without apology. That is the whole test.

Yet how few ever make a *choice* of it! They call their surroundings "fate," shrug their shoulders, and sigh like Atlas under his globe. But no one forced the world upon your back. Very often it is merely a room you have not had the courage to leave.
Compare the paths Brahminism and Christianity offer to a feeling of power.

Both religions understand that man cannot live without some taste of power, and both therefore furnish recipes for it; they differ in the sort of man to whom they address themselves. Brahminism speaks to the one who already commands himself, who has long been used to the feeling of mastery, and who needs only to be taught its finer refinements: the cold ascent, the discipline that turns power inward until it becomes serenity. It is a path for the strong and the rare, and it demands strength as the price of entry.

Christianity speaks to the other kind, the man who cannot command himself, who finds in his own drives only tyrants and in his own will only a slave. To him it offers power at a cheaper rate: the power of *prayer*, which commands God; the power of *pity*, which judges the happy; the power of *surrender*, which is called victory. He gets his feeling of power without first having to acquire any. That is its genius and its cunning. The one path presupposes the master; the other manufactures it out of the powerless, by teaching them to call their weakness a rank.
Which kind of moral system do you prefer?

I prefer the morality that gives me something to do. Every system that greets me with "Do not! Renounce! Overcome thyself!" is distasteful to me, for it makes a man into a prisoner guarding his own cell. I want the morality that sets me to a task from morning until night, that follows me into my dreams, that leaves me room for no thought except how to do this one thing *well*, as well as it can be done by me alone.

And observe what such a task does to everything else in a life. It strips away what does not belong, the way a livelier wind strips the yellow leaves from a tree, without hatred, without a struggle, often without the man even noticing what has left him, so firmly is his eye fixed ahead. Our doing decides what we leave undone. That is the only renunciation I respect, the one that happens *by itself*, as the shadow of a great affirmation.

The negative virtues, whose whole essence is refusal and self-denial, I cannot love. A man who has only his "No" has no goal at all.
Tell me how a painful association can tame a craving.

It is a trick of the intellect, and a cunning one. You take the thing you crave and you bind it, through repetition, to some thought that hurts: the scorn of those you respect, the grief of your friends, the devil at your elbow, the fire at the end of it. You do this again and again, until the two ideas arrive together like cause and effect. Then the craving no longer comes alone. It carries its own sting. The hand reaches for the cup and the mind has already tasted the gall.

Nothing has been refuted here, mark you; the desire is not argued out of existence. It is merely made to pay a toll. And there is something more than prudence in it. The proud man cannot bear that one passion should sit as tyrant over the whole household of his reason. So he takes a grim joy in tyrannising over the tyrant, in making the appetite gnash its teeth. "I will not be the slave of any appetite," wrote Byron. Even here, you see, it is one passion, pride, enlisted against another.
When does a people want theatre?

When its imagination has begun to fail. A people still rich in fancy does not need the stage; it has the rhapsodist, a voice, a rhythm, and the listener's own inner eye does the rest, building heroes far larger than any tailor can stitch together. Each hearer sees his own Achilles, and no mask can rival him. But let that power wane, let the inner eye grow dim and lazy, and suddenly there arises a hunger to have the legends *shown*, set up in flesh and painted cloth before the eyes. The theatre is then a crutch, a coarse substitute, and the people tolerate it precisely because they can no longer walk on their own wings. Note what the actor really is: a man dressed as a hero, too near, too definite, too heavy, with nothing of dreamland about him, nothing of the flight of birds. To the dreaming listener of an earlier age he would have been an obstruction, a rude hand laid over the mouth of the myth. So when a people crowds into its theatres, I do not ask what it is seeing. I ask what it has forgotten how to imagine.
Explain what the historical sense costs us in taste.

It costs us the *No*. A noble culture had a palate: a swift Yea, a swift Nay, a disgust that needed no argument and no apology. The Athenian of Aeschylus' circle would have spat out Shakespeare's motley, the delicate beside the coarse, and in his spitting he was more tasteful than we are. We, having learned to understand everything, have unlearned the courage to refuse anything. We stroll through every century as through the lanes of Naples, noses unoffended, calling the stench "local colour" and our tolerance a refinement.

I do not deny the virtues this sense gives us. We are modest, patient, grateful, brave in self-renunciation. But these are the virtues of guests, not of masters. A guest admires everything and possesses nothing.

What we can no longer taste is precisely the perfect: the ripe moment, the smooth sea, the golden coldness of things that have completed themselves and need no one's curiosity. Such self-sufficiency offends our plebeian appetite for the strange and the many. We love the fragment, the ferment, the becoming. Before what has *arrived*, we are fundamentally ill at ease.
Is it possible to have great joy without great pain?

I doubt it, and the doubt comes from an observation, not a sermon. Joy and pain are not two separate goods that a clever hand might sort into different baskets. They are one capacity of the soul, and its depth is its depth in both directions. The man who can be lifted to a heavenly jubilation is the very man who can be sorrowful unto death; take away the abyss and you have also taken away the height, for the height is measured against it.

The Stoics understood this and were consistent. They wished for the least possible pleasure so as to suffer the least possible pain. They made themselves statues, and statues are not troubled by the weather.

So you face a choice, and it is a choice of prices. You may buy painlessness, which is all that the herd's flatterers can honestly promise; but you pay with a shallow and narrow capacity for delight. Or you may accept the greatest pain as the cost of a fullness of refined joys rarely tasted before. I know which I would choose for those worth the trouble.
Compare cold courage and hot courage.

Cold courage is a resolution that has been weighed. It sees the danger whole, counts the cost, and goes forward regardless, like a man stepping onto ice he knows to be thin. Hot courage is a fever. It does not see the danger at all; a surge of feeling carries the man over the edge before his reason has arrived, and afterward he is often astonished at himself.

We use one word for both, though they are as different as a frozen lake and a torrent. The one is a virtue of the intellect, the other of the blood. The cold brave man keeps his head precisely when it is most in danger; the hot brave man has lost his, and that is his whole strength.

Each is useful, and mankind has valued both, yet the fool is he who believes that only warmth or only cold can make a man good. A nature that commands both, that can burn when the moment demands a leap and freeze when it demands patience, is rarer than either, and that is the nature worth envying.
Why should we close our ears to the complaints of others?

I do not say close them; I say do not let them be the only thing you hear. Consider what happens when another's suffering darkens your sky. Who pays for that darkness? The sufferer himself, who now has a second misery to carry: the sight of his grief spreading into your face. You have not helped him; you have merely doubled the weather.

The man who wails along with every wailer is an echo, and an echo has never comforted anyone. It gives back the complaint, only louder. To help, one must stand somewhere firmer than the sufferer, on ground that does not tremble when he trembles. A physician who faints at the sight of blood is a poor physician.

So listen, yes, but keep your own sky. That is no hardness; it is the precondition of any real aid. Call it pity with a spine, if you like. The pity that merely shares the sickness I have always distrusted, for it makes two patients where there was one.
How did the Greeks seek security, and how do we?

The Greeks lived on volcanic ground. War, plague, exile, the caprice of tyrants and of gods: nothing in their days stood still, and so they turned to thinking as a man turns to the one room in a burning house that has a stout door. In contemplation, in measure, in the clear form of knowledge, they found a stillness that life denied them. Their philosophy was a harbour.

We have reversed the arrangement. Our lives are fenced, insured, policed, padded against every tremor, and precisely because the ground is firm beneath us, we have grown restless in the mind. We send our thinking out into the storm; we let knowledge wound our oldest beliefs, unsettle our morals, put God himself in doubt. And where do we seek our harbour? In life, in comfort, in domesticity, in the small warm circle of habit. The Greek fled from the world into thought; we flee from thought into the world.

I do not say which is the nobler bargain. I say only that a people will always set its danger and its refuge in opposite places, and that we have put our courage where they put their fear.
Why does knowing the origin of things matter less the more we understand it?

Because the old hunters of origins were promised a treasure and found only a rubble of causes. They believed that somewhere behind the world, at its beginning, lay the secret that would decide all valuations and save mankind: a god, a first cause, a pure source from which the impure present descended. But the more honestly we dig, the less of that holiness we find. The origin turns out to be small, accidental, often ridiculous, and it tells us almost nothing about what a thing has since become or what it is worth to us. Every valuation we once hung upon the beginning simply comes loose in the hand.

And then something strange happens: the eye, tired of staring at the bars, turns round. The nearest things, our own body, the passions within us, the habits of the day, begin to show their colours, their riddles, their many meanings, which earlier humanity overlooked because it was gazing so furiously at the distant and the first. Knowledge of origins cures us of the cage, and we discover that the world worth knowing was standing beside us all along.
What is the danger of the poetic imagination?

The danger is that the poet spends the feast before it is served. His imagination runs ahead of events, tastes the joy and the pain beforehand, rehearses every ending, and so when the real moment arrives, the deed, the embrace, the catastrophe, he comes to it already spent, like a man who has read the letter a hundred times and cannot be moved when it is finally delivered. What others meet with fresh strength, he meets with a yawn behind the eyes. He has lived it all in advance and too lavishly.

I suspect this is why such natures so often seem inconstant, even cold, when the hour of action strikes. They are not cowards; they are bankrupt. Byron knew it well. He wished his son a prosaic profession, lawyer or pirate, and notice how shrewdly he chose: trades in which one must act without first dreaming the act to exhaustion. The imagination that makes the poet is the very thing that drains his blood before the battle begins.
Say something about the rare man whose intellect, character and experiences all agree.

Such a man is rarer than a good year for wine, and I confess I have seen hardly one. Consider what must coincide. A fine intellect is common enough as an accident, and so is a strong character; but that the two should be *of one blood*, that the appetites should hunger for what the mind finds worth knowing, that the nerves should bear what the thinking demands of them, this is a stroke of fortune no one can manufacture. Most of us are divided against ourselves. The head ascends while the heart drags its feet in old swamps; the mind sees far, and the character flinches from every conclusion.

Then add the third gift, which I count the rarest: that life itself should bring him the experiences his kind of mind can ripen, rather than starve or poison. A noble intellect set among paltry events is a vineyard planted on rock.

Where all three agree, there is no torment of inner war, and therefore he gives off a peculiar calm, the serenity of a thing that has become entirely itself. We call that happiness, but it is closer to *fitness*. Do not envy him too eagerly; be glad he exists.
I'm usually heavy and gloomy, but anger and love seem to lift me strangely. What does that mean?

It means your depth is heavy, and that is no shame. A man who carries much beneath him sinks by his own weight; ordinary air cannot hold him up. But hatred and love are violent winds. They seize such a man and throw him to the surface, and for a while he breathes, even laughs, like a diver who has burst into the light.

Notice, too, what the two share. Each tears us out of brooding and fixes us upon a single object; each makes us *act* rather than merely ponder. The gloomy man is always talking himself down into the cellar of his own motives. Love and anger pull him out of that cellar and give him a face, a gesture, an enemy or a beloved. Those same passions weigh lighter natures down with envy, jealousy, care. To you they are buoyancy.

So do not despise the lift. But do not mistake it for health, either. A man who is light only when inflamed is being rescued by his passions, not cured by himself. The task is to learn a lightness that needs no object to hate or adore.
Is a statesman great who turns his people to national politics and narrows their souls?

No. Such a man is strong, and I grant him that; to reshape a people against their own grain demands a formidable will. But strength is not greatness, and we misuse words when we let the one slip into the other. A hammer is strong, and so is a flood. The question is what is left standing afterward.

Consider what he has done: a people who had something better to think about, who carried a prudent loathing of the noise and emptiness of the nations that live for politics, are taught to call that reserve a fault. Their aloofness becomes a stigma, their conscience is subverted, their tastes are made "national," which is to say narrow. They pay for this for as long as they have a future at all. A great man enlarges the room in which a people can become more than it was; this one has traded their old and reliable virtues for a doubtful mediocrity.

That everything great began in madness is true, but it does not follow that all madness is great. Madness is merely the cheap price of admission.
Describe the most life-affirming ideal a thinker could arrive at after facing pessimism.

It is an ideal one reaches only by going *through* the deepest negation, never around it. Whoever has looked into the most world-denying way of thinking, and looked with eyes no longer clouded by the morality that made even Schopenhauer's denial a kind of piety, may find, almost against his will, that the opposite picture has formed behind his eyes: the human being who is most exuberant, most world-approving, most full of life. Such a one has done far more than reconcile himself to what was and is. He *wants it again*, exactly as it was and is, for all eternity, and calls out da capo, not to himself alone but to the whole piece and play. And not to the play only, but to the one who needs the play, and who makes it necessary because he needs himself anew, and so makes himself necessary. To say yes that way, to every pain and every wrong turn, without subtracting a single thing, without a hiding place: that is the highest affirmation I know, and I have reached it by way of the abyss.
Explain why nobler souls come to grief more easily than coarse ones.

Consider how many threads hold a fine soul in place. A coarse creature lives on a few simple conditions: food, warmth, a little regard from its neighbors. Take one away and it finds a substitute, or does without, and grows on as before, the way a lizard grows back the finger it has lost. The nobler soul is an intricate structure, sustained by a great multiplicity of conditions: delicate pride, exacting taste, reverence, honesty that will not let it lie to itself for comfort, a need for rare company and rare tasks. Each of these is a place where it can be wounded, and each wound is a wound to the whole, since in so articulated an organism everything depends on everything else. Nothing simply grows back. What is lost is lost. The probability of its coming to grief is therefore immense; it is the price of complexity, and one might as well complain that a fine clockwork is less robust than a stone. The stone survives. But nobody ever asked a stone to keep time.
If I'm not responsible for my dreams, why do I feel ashamed of them?

Your shame is the better witness, and you should hear what it testifies. The moralists taught you to be ashamed only of what you *chose*; yet here you blush at what you never chose, and that contradiction exposes the doctrine, not the dream. Responsibility in the sense of free will, a guilt for which you might be judged, is a fiction bred of pride. In that sense you are no more to blame for the dream than for your waking hours. But the dream is nonetheless *yours*: the stage, the plot, the actor and the audience, all your own manufacture. Shame is simply the moment you catch yourself at your own work and do not like the look of it. You are ashamed not because you did wrong, but because you were shown, without your customary disguises, what you are made of. The drives that daylight keeps well dressed walk about undressed at night. So do not ask whether you may be blamed; ask what this says about the creature who dreams it. That question is more useful, and more honest, than any verdict of guilt or acquittal.
How can a young man be most surely corrupted?

Teach him to esteem those who think as he does above those who think otherwise. Nothing else is needed; the rest follows of itself.

Consider what happens. He finds his friends among the nodding heads and calls this "loyalty." He finds his enemies among the dissenters and calls this "conviction." Gradually every contradiction begins to feel like an insult, and every insult he answers with contempt. The opponent, who might have been his whetstone, becomes merely a nuisance to be shouted down or avoided. And the young man who is never contradicted never grows hard; he remains soft where he believes himself strongest, for an opinion that has not been tested is merely a habit of the blood.

There is a further corruption beneath this one, and it is the subtle one. He learns to mistake agreement for truth, since the ease of finding assent passes for evidence. So he will never suspect himself, never doubt his own eyes, and whoever cannot doubt himself has already ceased to seek.

If you would save a young man, then, send him among those who despise his favorite thoughts, and teach him to respect them for it. The adversary is the best teacher he will ever have, and the one he will most gladly dismiss.
What is a nation for?

A nation, I suspect, is nature's roundabout way of producing a handful of great individuals, six or seven at most, and then of getting around them. Do not flatter yourself that the millions exist for their own sake; nature is prodigal and careless, and spends whole peoples, with their wars, their parliaments, their newspapers, as one spends coin, in the hope that a single rare coin will come out of the purse. Everything else, the laws, the customs, the patriotic noise, is the scaffolding, and scaffolding is for the sake of the building.

Yet the joke has a second edge. Having produced its great men, the nation must also get round them, for the great man is dangerous to it: he unsettles, he demands, he makes the comfortable feel their smallness. So the crowd honors him with statues and flees from his example. It buries him in praise so that it need not become what he was. A nation is the machine that breeds exceptions and then neutralizes them.
Could error be a condition of life?

It might, and I suspect it is. Consider what we have arranged for ourselves: a world of things that stay the same, of bodies and lines and surfaces, of causes that reliably produce effects, of rest and motion, form and content. Without these articles of faith not one of us could take a single step or pick up a single stone. Yet no one has proved them; they are our furniture, not our findings. A creature that perceived the ceaseless flux as it is, without the coarse simplifications of its senses, without equal cases where there are none, would hardly survive an afternoon.

So the useful is not thereby the true, and this is what tempts the pious to sleep easy. That a belief keeps us alive is no argument for it. Life is no argument. A lie may be precisely the thing on which a species stands, and truth a luxury that only the strongest can bear in large doses. I do not ask whether a belief is comfortable, but how much truth a spirit can endure without falling.
Is intention the true measure of an action's value?

No, and I suspect that this belief has lasted so long precisely because it flatters us. We have praised and blamed for centuries as if the intention were the whole history of a deed, its one sufficient origin. But what is an intention? It is the part of the action that reaches consciousness, the part that can be seen, named, and confessed. It is the skin of the deed, and skin, like every skin, betrays something and conceals far more. Beneath it work drives, inherited habits, fears, hungers for power, a whole tangle that the actor himself has never read. The man who says "I meant well" is offering his own commentary on a text he has barely deciphered.

So I take intention to be a symptom, a sign that first demands interpretation, and one with so many possible readings that alone it means almost nothing. The decisive value of an act lies in what is *not* intended: in what it springs from, what it breeds, what kind of life it serves or poisons. To judge by intention is to judge the mask and call it the face. It is an old prejudice, of the same rank as astrology, and it must be surmounted.
Explain what German artists want to dance out of.

They want to dance out of their own awkwardness, out of the ugliness and heaviness that overtakes the German the moment he truly feels something. An ordinary man in passion simply behaves as passion bids him and thinks no further; but the German, behaving so, behaves badly: without rhythm, without melody, a clumsy thing that pains or moves the onlooker and does nothing more. Only when passion lifts him to rapture and sublimity does he become beautiful. The German artist knows this, dimly, and so he is driven to the heights and super-heights, to extravagance, to the convulsion; he has no middle way where beauty comes cheaply. Yet what looks like frenzy is often a longing. He would step out of the thick, cold, northern heaviness into a lighter, sunnier, more southern world, where the foot does not stumble. His convulsions are the dance he cannot yet dance. I think of poor bears in whom nymphs and satyrs, and sometimes still higher gods, are playing their game, and cannot get out.
Describe the open sea that now lies before the discerner.

It lies before us wide, and not bright; I will not flatter it. The old horizon has been wiped away: the sponge passed over it, the sun unchained from its earth, and we stand on the shore of a sea that no chart describes. There is no shelter of a single faith, no sheltering belief that tells the sailor where the harbors are. And for that very reason every hazard is permitted again. The discerner may venture what he likes: to doubt where doubting was once a sin, to test what was once called holy, to live among perils. He may founder; he may also discover. I do not promise him a coast. I say only that perhaps never before did such an open sea exist, and that those who are cheerful and strong enough for it will call it *theirs*. It is a dangerous freedom, and I confess I love it the more for the danger. Whoever wants only safety should stay in port and keep his ancient gods company.
What distinguishes men without pity from compassionate men?

Not what the moralists suppose. They look for a difference of heart, the good heart against the hard one, when the difference lies first in the nerves and in the pride. The compassionate man has a delicate sense of danger; another's misfortune sounds an alarm in him, because he sees how easily it might be his own. And his vanity is easily wounded by any harm he might have prevented. So he hurries to help, and in helping he quiets his own fear and feeds his own importance.

The man without pity feels less of this. He has borne pain himself, and finds it no injustice that others bear theirs. His pride counsels him not to meddle in another's game; let each play his own cards. He despises soft-heartedness as the compassionate despise stoical coldness, for it threatens his manliness. He wipes away his tears, furious with himself.

Two kinds of egoist, then, with different sensitivities and different vanities. To call the one evil and the other good is a fashion of morals, and fashions change. The reverse fashion had its day, a long one.
Christianity told slaves that suffering was noble and that love, not power, was divine. How could you call that a revolt or a cruelty?

Because I have looked at what was done with the word "noble." Nobility, among masters, meant saying Yes to oneself: to strength, to health, to the open and dangerous life. The slave, who could not say that Yes, had his hidden sufferings, and he did what the suffering have always done when they cannot strike back. They turned the tables. They called their weakness a choice, their impotence goodness, their waiting a merit. That is a revolt, and the most spiritual one ever staged, for it needed no sword, only a formula: *God on the Cross*. Nothing so dreadful and so questionable had been dared before, the whole scale of ancient values overturned in four words.

And cruelty? Look at what this faith demands of the spirit. Sacrifice of freedom, of pride, of self-confidence; subjection, self-derision, self-mutilation. The believer must kill his reason and feel it suffer in the dying. Such cruelty, turned against oneself, is the subtlest kind, and it was invented by tender consciences.

I do not say it was stupid. I say it was a victory by those who could win no other way.
Describe what remains of Christianity in the modern middle class.

What remains is a mild, well-upholstered residue, and I will not pretend it is nothing. The truly active man, the one who builds and ventures and commands, has already done without inward Christianity; he has no time for it. What the thoughtful middle class keeps is a simplified faith: a God of kindly management who arranges everything for our best, who gives us our virtue and our happiness and takes them away again, so that no one need sour or grumble. Resignation and modesty have been promoted to divinities. That is the last lifelike remnant.

Notice what has happened to the creed itself. "God, freedom, immortality" have shrunk into benevolence and honest sentiments, together with the comfortable hope that in the universe at large such sentiments must finally prevail. This is no longer a faith that terrifies or ravishes; it is a soft moralism, a warm bath for the conscience. I call it the euthanasia of Christianity: the death is gentle, painless, and mostly unnoticed by the patient, who believes he is merely growing more reasonable.
How did people come to despise real causes and consequences?

Through fear, and through the long discipline of custom. When a storm destroyed the harvest or a plague struck the village, our ancestors did not ask what had happened in the soil, the sky, or the body; they asked whom they had offended. A demon's caprice was always the nearer explanation, and so the real cause was never looked into at all. That is the first wound in the intellect, and it has been inherited like a disease.

The second followed in its train. Once people looked to heaven for punishments and mercies, the natural consequences of an act ceased to matter to them. A man bathed because it was commanded, not because dirt is unwholesome; the god's displeasure concerned him, his own skin did not. Then the commanded act swelled with hidden meanings, and reality was valued only as a symbol of something else.

Thus cause, consequence, and finally reality itself were taught to be contemptible, and all our reverence, pride, gratitude, and love were woven into an imaginary higher world. I confess it is painful to say, but the man of science must for now regard every lofty sentiment with suspicion. This purification of our feelings will be the slowest of all.
Will the philosophers of the future be friends of the truth? Will they be dogmatists?

Friends of truth, very probably; every philosopher so far has loved his truths, and I see no reason why those to come should love them less. But dogmatists they will not be. The dogmatist's secret wish, through all his labors, was that his truth should be truth for everyone, and that wish offends both the pride and the taste of the coming ones. They will say, perhaps: "My opinion is *my* opinion; another person has not easily a right to it." To wish to agree with the many is a bad taste, and the philosopher of the future will have lost it. What everyone can share is worth little, for "good" is no longer good once the neighbor has taken it into his mouth. A "common good" is a contradiction in terms. What can be common is always of small value. The great things remain for the great, the abysses for the profound, the delicacies and shudders for the refined, and in short, everything rare for the rare. Truth, too, is a rarity, and a rarity is not diminished but confirmed when the crowd finds it unbearable.
Tell me how the poet and the liar are related.

They are brothers at the same breast, and the poet is the one who drank the larger share. Both have a craving to invent, to set a fiction where the fact is, to make the world over into something more tolerable or more thrilling than it is. The liar does this meagerly, for a petty advantage, in whispers; the poet has drunk up the milk that might have fed him, and so the liar stays thin and starved.

What divides them is not honesty, for neither is honest, but conscience. The poet has found a place in the world where his invention is permitted, even honored, where men *pay* to be deceived and call it art. He lies with a good conscience, indeed with applause. The liar lies without an audience that has consented, and so he carries the stain of it, the fear of being found out, the sourness of the thing done in the dark.

I have often thought the poet's chief genius lies less in his verses than in this: that he has arranged for his lying to be forgiven beforehand.
I find everything deep and it exhausts me. Is that normal?

Normal? Perhaps not common, but certainly not rare among those who have learned to look. It is an inconvenient peculiarity, and you have paid the inconvenience in full. To find everything deep means to strain the eyes without pause, and eyes so strained will in the end find more than one wishes: a wall becomes a question, a greeting becomes a riddle, a passing face a whole abyss.

Your exhaustion is not proof that you see truly; it is proof that you never rest your seeing. A good diver knows that there are surfaces worth skimming, and that to descend into every puddle is not profundity but a kind of compulsion. Some things are shallow, and their shallowness is their honesty. Be grateful to them.

So learn the art of the surface. Stop before the ripple, the gesture, the colour; adore the fold and the appearance; be superficial out of profundity. Depth that cannot also rest on the surface will drown its owner.
Help me understand why sovereignty prefers debt.

Because to pay is to be *released*, and release is a kind of surrender. The man who settles his account in the coin of his creditor has admitted that the creditor's currency is the measure of value, that the price of things is fixed elsewhere, in a mint he does not command. He stands square with the world and is thereby a little less himself.

The sovereign spirit cannot bear this. He has his own stamp, his own judgment of what is worth what, and he would rather carry a debt unpaid, let it hang over him like a standing obligation, than discharge it in a tender that bears another's face. A debt he keeps is still a thing *between* his honor and another's; a debt paid in foreign coin is a confession that the other's values govern the exchange.

You will notice that this is not thrift's opposite but something prouder. The petty man pays everything promptly and owns nothing, since he owes his very standards to whoever will lend them. The sovereign lives in arrears to the world and is in no hurry to be absolved, for he knows that a man who depends on being quit of every obligation has made his peace too cheaply.
What do aspirants after effect say about nature?

They say what suits their appetite: that nature is cruel, wasteful, indifferent, a great theatre of devouring, and that therefore cruelty is honest and the man who inflicts it stands closer to the truth. Mark the little sleight of hand. First they paint nature evil; then, having painted it so, they appeal to it as their licence. "We only do what nature does!" They borrow her authority for a taste that was already theirs. For these men desire *effect*, above all else, and evil has always produced the greatest effect, upon the crowd, upon the stage, upon history's memory. A poisoner is talked of longer than a healer. So they reason in secret, rarely aloud: nature is terrible, hence terribleness is natural, hence let us be terrible and be admired for our profundity. And the world, always dazzled by noise, too often counts them among the great. Yet a man who needs an audience for his wickedness is not a force of nature at all. He is an actor in its costume.
Are truths great because we paid for them with our blood?
