No. The price paid for a thing is a fact about the buyer, not about the thing. A man may bleed for a fool's errand as readily as for a discovery, and the wound proves only that he was in earnest, which fanatics are in abundance. Every martyr has made this argument, and with it they have made a whole age believe that what is bled for must be true. Blood is the most seductive of all arguments precisely because it refutes nothing and silences everything.

Yet I will not flatter the cool skeptic either. When someone says, "you call these truths petty because you never lived them," there is a grain of justice in it: a truth that has cost you nothing is held loosely, and it will be surrendered at the first discomfort. So blood does not make a truth great. It tests whether *you* were great enough to bear it. The truth's weight is one thing; your capacity to carry it is another. Do not confuse the scar with the discovery.
Why is a man bold towards things but timid towards persons?

Because a thing asks nothing of him, and a person always does. A stone, a problem, a mountain pass will neither wound his vanity nor penetrate his disguise; he may assault it with the whole of his severity and come away the same man. But before a person he must appear, and to appear is to be seen, and to be seen is to be judged, liked, expected, held to what he once said of himself. So the bold man of things is very often a shy man in the heart: what he dreads is not danger but acquaintance.

Note what follows. He thins out his old friendships and shuns new ones, and not from coldness. He wants his secrecy and his ruthlessness to come to the same thing, so that nobody may ever catch him between the two. The fewer who know him, the fewer who can be disappointed, and the less his inconsiderateness toward them wounds. Thus his solitude is made to pass for honesty. He prefers to be a stranger to all rather than a disappointment to a few.
Why can you only suggest the new hopes?

Because a hope is not a thing that can be handed across like a coin. What I say arrives in you only as sound, and sound is worth exactly as much as the ear that receives it. If you have never felt the first grey light of a morning break inside your own soul, then my talk of dawn is noise to you; you will nod, you will repeat my words, and you will have gained nothing.

I can point at the horizon. I cannot lift your eyes. I can name the hopes, but to see them you must already carry something of them in your blood, some glow of your own that recognizes the glow I describe. Do you expect me to move the stones, to turn the beast into a man by argument? That is a magician's task, and I am no Orpheus. If you are still stone, you must find your own singer, or better, become one. Suggestion is all that honesty permits me.
I keep having flying dreams. Could they change what I think of as happiness?

Yes, and more surely than you suspect. What you live through in dreams, if it comes often enough, becomes a possession of your soul no less than anything that happened in daylight; it makes you richer or poorer, it gives you a need you did not have before. The old Romans said that what occupies us by day continues by night, but the converse is also true.

Consider what your nights are teaching you: an "upwards" without effort, a rising that costs no struggle, a falling that is not a descent. Having tasted that divine levity, you will find the happiness of the waking world, with its climbing and its striving, strangely heavy. You will long *differently*. Even the flight the poets sing will seem to you too earthly, too muscular, too laborious, all that beating of wings.

But be careful with this gift. It may sharpen your taste, or it may make you sullen toward every happiness that must be earned. Ask yourself which it is doing to you.
Why did man read moral significance into everything that exists?

Because he took his own shadow for the nature of things. He began with himself, as he always does, and found in himself a creature that commands and obeys, that rewards and punishes, that hopes and fears; how could he then look out upon the world and see anything but commanders, obedient servants, and judges? So he gave sex to the stones and the stars, and he did not think it play. He thought it insight, profound insight, just as later he thought it insight to hear a will in the thunder and a verdict in the plague.

Consider what lay beneath this. Man is a fearful animal, and the unexplained is unbearable to him; a world with no one answerable for it is a world with no one to appease. A moral meaning is a rope thrown over the abyss. Better to be guilty before a cosmos that watches than innocent in a cosmos that does not care.

And the error will go the way of the older one. We smile today at those who held the sun to be a man or a woman; some day we shall smile at those who held it to be just.
Advise someone who keeps needing the theatre to see life's dramas.

What, still in need of the theatre? Are you still so young? The stage you pay for is a poor affair beside the one you walk through every day. There the quarrels are real, the betrayals cost something, the actors play with their whole blood, and no curtain falls to rescue them. Seek your tragedy and your comedy there, where they are better acted.

But I warn you: to be merely a spectator of one's own life is the hardest art, and it must be learned. Most people, when the passion strikes, *are* the passion; they have no distance from it, and so they drown in what they might have watched. Learn to open the third eye, the one that looks out through the other two. Then, in your hours of shame or rage or longing, a small gate stands open to joy and refuge. You will still suffer, but you will also be the audience of your suffering, and an audience can laugh, weep, and applaud.
Help me understand what Genoa says about the men who built it.

Genoa tells me that its builders *wanted to live on*. Walk the heights above the harbor and you meet countenances out of past generations, the images of bold and autocratic men. Their houses were built for centuries, not for the passing hour, and that alone is a confession: these were men well disposed to life, however ill-disposed they may often have been toward themselves.

I see the builder on his slope, casting his eye over the sea, the mountains, and every neighboring roof, and I see what that gaze means. It expresses conquest. All that lies in view must be fitted into *his* plan until it becomes his property by becoming part of the same. The city is an insatiable egoism turned to stone. Each man rose against every other and set his own illimitableness between himself and his neighbor; each won his home by overpowering it with his architectural thoughts.

Set beside this the cities of the north, with their uniformity, their respect for law, their delight in obedience. There one divines the taste for equality and submission in the builders. Genoa confesses the opposite: the rule of the singular, and the pride that dared to build for a posterity it meant to dominate.
How do our feelings toward art change when we live as a hermit?

It changes radically, and the change has a simple cause. Formerly we went to art as to a foreign country; for an hour or an evening it carried us into the element of depth, of loneliness, of rapture, in which we could not yet live. We dreamt ourselves into a possession we did not have. But the hermit has moved into that country and taken citizenship. What he once borrowed from the artist he now owns, consumes, and is consumed by, and so he can no longer ask art for the same gift. Either he asks nothing of it at all, or he asks for something quite opposite.

And here is the curious thing: he begins to delight in the reverse. He is weary of his wealth, of his deep and prolific thoughts, and so he wants, for a while, to be poor. He wants art to let him play the child, the beggar, the fool. The rich man loves to dream of poverty, as the poor man once dreamt of riches. That is how I know a taste has truly changed: it has turned on its heel.
In times of collapse and decay, who is most likely to survive?

The mediocre. I say it without relish, but I say it. When a culture begins to crumble, the rare and exacting natures are the first to suffer, for they are built of delicate tensions, of long breeding and severe demands, and they have the most to lose when the ground shifts. The exceptional man needs conditions; the average man needs only a herd and a warm corner. He is sturdy precisely because he is unfinished, because nothing in him is stretched tight enough to snap. So in every decay it is he who inherits: he multiplies while the subtle die childless.

And observe how he triumphs. He cannot confess what he is or what he wants, so he dresses his instinct in fine words: moderation, duty, brotherly love, the common good. Each virtue is a mask for one wish, to be left undisturbed and to disturb no one. The age then pronounces this wish holy, and calls whatever rises above it a sickness or a vanity.

I do not tell you this as consolation. I tell it as a warning to anyone who means to be more than the survivors.
I'd like to know why the moralist invents a second existence for us.

Because what happens of itself, without aim or author, cannot command anyone. The stream of events knows nothing of "thou shalt"; it simply runs. So the moralist must first invent a stage behind the stage, a purpose, a design, a higher existence by whose measure this common one can be judged, and only then does what we do anyway suddenly appear as something willed, as duty, as the voice of reason. He lifts the old existence off its hinges so that he may hang a command upon it.

Do not suppose he wants us to laugh at life, or at himself. To him the individual is something first and last and immense. Hence his earnestness, hence his folly: nearly every morality hitherto has been so contrary to nature that mankind would have perished had any one of them fully triumphed.

And yet each such teacher achieved something. For a while we became *interesting* to ourselves; a man cried out, "it is worth living! I am worthy of it!" That is why the moralists keep returning. We have become the animal that must periodically believe it knows why it exists. Laughter corrects them, and then we require them again.
Why has beauty increased with civilisation?

Because the occasions that make a man ugly have grown rarer among the civilised. I count three of them. The first is the wildest ecstasy, the frenzy that distorts the face and throws the limbs into convulsion; the civilised man has learned to be moderate even in his intoxications, and so his features stay composed. The second is extreme bodily exertion, the sweat and strain and contortion of a life of hard toil and fighting, which stamps itself into the flesh; as labour is lightened and divided, fewer faces bear that stamp. The third, and the oldest, is the need to inspire fear by one's mere appearance. In rough and dangerous ages a man *must* look terrible; his scowl, his stance, his ceremonial grimace are prescribed by custom, and ugliness becomes a duty, a weapon. Where neighbours are no longer wolves, such a duty falls away. So beauty has not been added to man; ugliness has simply been relieved of its employment. What remains, once the terror is no longer required, we call beautiful.
I'd like to know what might become noble when prudence is common.

When prudence is universal, it ceases to distinguish anyone. What every man must do to keep himself fed and safe becomes a mere necessity, and a finer taste will smell the vulgarity of it, as it smells the vulgarity of anything done by all and feared by none. The prudent man will then be the ordinary man, the man of the herd, carefully counting his comforts.

And so nobility will seek its mark elsewhere. I suspect it will show itself as the capacity for folly: the ability to squander, to wager, to do the unreckoned thing out of an overflow of strength rather than out of calculation. Not the folly of the weak, who blunder because they cannot see, but the folly of one who sees perfectly well the prudent course and declines it, because he has more in him than prudence can use.

Every tyranny breeds its own rebels. A tyranny of prudence would breed, at last, a nobility of the spendthrift and the daring, who would rather risk themselves magnificently than preserve themselves cheaply.
My partner says loving only me is the highest devotion. Could exclusive love be unfair to everyone else?

Your partner has named something real, though not the thing they think. Exclusive love is a *hoarding*: what one person receives, all others are refused, and the refusal is the price of the gift. To call that the highest devotion is to praise the miser's chest for its fullness while ignoring the beggars at the door. Every one-and-only is bought with a great many nobodies.

But do not flatter yourself that the injustice is only a matter of accounting. The deeper barbarity is that such love so often wants a *possession*. The one who vows "only you" frequently means "you only, and never another claim upon you." That is the lover's greed wearing the robe of virtue.

Yet I will not call it simple wickedness. Concentration is also how a rare depth is achieved; a river dispersed into a hundred rivulets waters nothing deeply. The question to put to your partner is whether their exclusivity is an overflowing that *chooses* a channel, or a fear that builds a wall. The first may be noble. The second is merely proprietorship, and proprietorship has never yet been the highest of anything.
Tell me why Rousseau and Schopenhauer could not live what they taught.

They could not live it because each had fixed his motto on the wrong side of the scales. Both were proud enough to vow *vitam impendere vero*, to stake a life upon the truth; but what tormented them was the reverse, that they could not stake the truth upon life. Their knowledge was one thing, their days another, and the two ran side by side like a coarse bass that will not keep the melody. Rousseau preached the natural man and lived as a sick, suspicious, quarrelsome wanderer. Schopenhauer preached the denial of the will and dined well, guarded his purse, and fought for his fame.

But do not hasten to convict them. If knowledge were granted to a thinker only so far as it fits his own person, knowledge would be in a sorry way. A truth is not a garment tailored to its discoverer. The noblest virtue of a great thinker is that he sacrifices himself to what he finds, often shamefacedly, sometimes with sublime scorn, smiling. Their failure to embody their doctrines is the small shame. The great one would be a thinker so vain that he would see only what he could bear to become.
What did Aristotle say about great men's children?

He observed, as I recall, that madness turns up in the children of great geniuses, and dullness in the children of the most virtuous. A grim remark, and I suspect he meant it as a sly one. Was it a warning against marrying at all? Or a consolation for those who had already done so?

Consider what lies beneath it. A great man spends himself on his work, and what he leaves to the womb and the cradle is the dregs: the overstrained nerves without the genius that justified them. The virtuous man is worse off, for virtue is a long habit of holding back, and what has held itself back all its life transmits only the holding back, a timid, bloodless inheritance. Nature is no bookkeeper who pays the son for the father's achievements. She squanders, then she economizes.

Whether Aristotle meant it as an invitation to the exceptional to marry, I cannot say. I hear in it rather the dry humor of a man who knew how costly every height is, and how rarely the bill is paid by the one who climbed.
Tell me what the self-renouncer is really doing.

He is flying, and what you see is the ballast falling. A man wants to rise higher and further than the rest of us, and so he flings overboard whatever would weigh him down, including things that are neither worthless nor unpleasant to him. Now look at what becomes visible: not the ascent, which is only intended, but the casting away. So we name him by his sacrifice, and he stands before us in his cowl, the soul of a hair-shirt, a picture of denial.

He is well content with this misreading. It conceals his appetite, his pride, his secret design of soaring *above* us. Self-renunciation is the most courteous disguise of a great will to power; the man who seems to say No to himself says a very loud Yes to his own elevation. He is an affirmer like the rest of us, only subtler and more ambitious. We take his renunciation for humility, and he lets us, because it would be impolite to show us how high he means to fly.
Explain why tragedy suited the Athenians of Aeschylus's time and not us.

Because tragedy is a drink for fighting men. The Athenians of Aeschylus were hard, warlike souls, difficult to move; fear did not easily master them, nor did pity. But when pity finally broke through that hardness, it seized them like a giddiness, a demonic power, a religious horror. They were lifted outside themselves, and they tasted the marvellous mixed with the bitterest gall of suffering: something rare, dangerous, and bitter-sweet. Such souls lose nothing by being softened now and then.

We are not such souls. The modern man stands open to every sympathetic affection as a sail stands open to the wind; he is pitied and pitying all day long, in every town and village, and he gushes with feeling at the slightest occasion. What would tragedy do to him? Nothing, or worse than nothing. One does not give strong drink to the man who is already drunk on his own softness. Even the Athenians of Plato's time, far less soft than we, began to complain of tragedy's injurious effect. The tragic poet needs hardness in his audience, and ours has too little of it.
Tell me how to give up a passion without hatred.

Hatred is only the old passion wearing a new coat. You have not left the house; you have merely changed rooms and locked the door behind you. As long as you must curse what you renounce, it still holds you, since all that hatred is nourished by the very thing it pretends to destroy. Look at the Christians who freed themselves from sin: they are usually consumed afterwards by their hatred of it, and their faces are the faces of great haters.

So do not wage war on it. You wish to leave a passion? Then grow cold toward it slowly, as one does toward an old lover, with neither rage nor tears. Give it less and less to eat. Starve it of your attention, and above all give your strength a new task, a different and larger passion that draws the blood away. Let it be remembered with something like gratitude, or at least with a smile. Only when you can speak of it calmly, without heat in either direction, have you actually left. Indifference is the proof; hatred is merely the chain in another metal.
Why do we call someone evil for hiding his intelligence?

Because we feel ourselves robbed. A man who conceals his intelligence from us has secretly taken our measure, and he has done it without our consent. He saw us plainly while we saw only the mask he chose to wear, and in that moment he stands over us as a spectator stands over an actor who does not know the curtain is open. Our vanity cannot forgive this.

Notice how the judgment sharpens when we suspect his motive was kindness. For then he has done us a mercy, and to be spared is to be told that we needed sparing. He lowered himself to our level as one stoops to a child, and we read in his gentleness a verdict upon our weakness. Gratitude would be the proper reply, yet gratitude is the hardest of all feelings for the proud to bear.

So we call him evil. It is a cheap revenge, the only one within reach: we cannot raise ourselves to his height, so we smear the height with a moral stain. Much of what passes for our moral indignation is wounded vanity wearing its Sunday clothes.
Explain why morality is the herd instinct in the individual.

Wherever you find a morality, look for the ranking it contains: this impulse honored, that one damned, this deed called noble, that one base. And ask whose need that ranking serves. It is never the need of the single person; it is the need of the community, the herd, which first asks what is useful to *it*, and then, in second and third place, what is useful to anyone else. Whatever preserves the herd becomes the standard of worth for every member.

So the individual is taught, from the cradle, to value himself only as a function, as a useful part of a larger body. He learns to feel pride when he is obedient, shame when he is singular, and he calls this feeling his conscience. But it is the voice of the herd speaking inside him in the first person. That is why I say morality is the herd instinct in the individual: it is the herd's own self-preservation, disguised as his most private conviction.

The proof is in the variety. Different communities had different conditions of survival, and so they produced different moralities, each declared eternal, each sincerely felt. A truth would not vary so; a need does.
Explain why ordinary people have an advantage over rare ones in the struggle to survive.

Because the ordinary can be *understood*, and to be understood is to be helped. Consider how language arose: out of need, out of the pressing necessity of one creature making known to another its danger, its hunger, its pain. Only those whose needs were alike could find the same sign for them. So the man whose experiences were average, whose troubles were everyone's troubles, was heard at once and rescued at once. Communicability became the most potent force that ever worked upon mankind.

The rare one is in another position. His experiences are not common, so his words find no echo; his need is not recognized as need. He stands alone, and the solitary creature perishes by the first accident, since no hand is stretched out to one whom no one comprehends. Seldom does he propagate himself.

So the herd is bred up by the very machinery of survival, and the evolution of man runs toward the similar, the average, the gregarious, toward the *ignoble*. To resist that current one must summon immense opposing forces.
I'd like to know how truthfulness undid belief in the Christian God.

The Christian God was not murdered by his enemies; he was strangled by his most devout servants. For two thousand years Christianity taught the European soul one discipline above all others: *thou shalt not lie*, not to God, not to thyself. It taught the confessional subtlety of the conscience, the hunt for the hidden motive, the shame of the comfortable falsehood. Then that conscience, grown keen and exacting, turned its knife upon the very doctrine that had sharpened it. It asked: is it *true* that nature testifies to a loving providence? That history serves a moral purpose? That my small misfortunes are dispatched for the salvation of my soul? And honesty, having nothing with which to answer, had to say no. What once passed for piety now appears to the stricter conscience as cowardice, as a soft mendacity. So it was Christian morality, veracity carried to its end, that overcame the Christian God. A discipline of two thousand years reached its last, hardest consequence. And it leaves us with a question no consoling faith can silence: what, then, is the meaning of existence?
My work makes me think about things I'd never choose to think about, year after year. Could that make me ill?

Yes, and I mean it literally, not as a figure of speech. A mind is not a tool lying idle in a drawer until you pick it up; it is a living thing with its own hungers, and the thoughts that rise in it unbidden are its appetite speaking. To set that appetite aside year after year, and feed it only on what your office, your timetable, or some arbitrary duty prescribes, is to starve one part of yourself in order to fatten a stranger. The nerves are the first to report the famine.

The cruel joke is that this looks like virtue. It wears the robes of discipline and self-command, and so it is praised, and so the sufferer praises himself. Yet it wastes the nervous system as surely as a regular debauchery would, only more respectably.

I do not tell you to quit tomorrow; circumstance is stubborn. But guard some hour, however small, in which you think only what *wants* to be thought by you. Without it, the body will eventually present the bill that the spirit refused to pay.
Why is translation from one language to another so difficult?

People imagine that translation is a matter of words, as if each language were a warehouse of labelled goods and one need only carry the crates across the border. But words are the least of it. What resists transport is the *tempo*: the speed at which a people thinks, jests, and leaps from one thought to the next. That speed is no accident of grammar. It grows from the character of the race, and, to speak more physiologically, from the pace at which a people digests its nourishment. A slow stomach makes a slow style.

So the honest translator, with the best conscience in the world, commits a kind of falsification. Take Machiavelli, who lets the gravest and most dangerous matters go by at a gallop, in a wanton allegrissimo, with a malicious delight in the contrast. Put him into a language that has no *presto* in its legs, and you have given the reader his sentences but robbed him of his laughter. The thought survives; the dance is dead. And a dance mistranslated is no longer a dance at all.
Does Europe wish to be one?

Yes, Europe wishes to be one; only the loudest voices in it do not wish it, and they are not the ones who know what Europe wants. The nationality-craze has made the nations morbidly estranged from one another, and the short-sighted politicians who ride that craze into power do not suspect how brief an interlude their disintegrating policy must be. So the plainest signs of the will to unity are overlooked or misread.

Ask instead where the deeper souls of this century were tending. Napoleon, Goethe, Beethoven, Stendhal, Heine, Schopenhauer: in the secret labour of their spirits they were all preparing a new synthesis and feeling their way toward the European of the future. They belonged to a "fatherland" only in their pretenses, or in weak hours and old age, when they wanted rest from themselves and so became patriots.

Europe's soul presses outward and upward in the restless art of such men. Toward what? A new light, perhaps a new sun. They could not say it distinctly, these last great seekers, but the same storm and stress tormented them all.
Explain why we all pretend to be simpler than we are.

Because complexity is an exertion, and we are tired. To be fully what one is, with all the contradictory drives quarrelling in one breast, would mean to be permanently at war and permanently on display; no one can sustain it. So each of us cuts himself down to a figure that can be summed up in a phrase: the honest one, the practical one, the good-natured one. First we tell this story to ourselves, and once we believe it we tell it to others, who are grateful, since they too need a simple face to deal with.

In this way the simplification is a kind of rest, even a kind of *holiday from ourselves*. It also removes us a little from our fellows; we no longer meet them with what we truly are, only with our emblem, and they meet us with theirs. Two emblems shake hands and call it acquaintance.

The price is paid quietly: one day a man discovers that he has lied so long and so successfully that the multitude within him has gone mute, and he cannot find where it went.
What is the argument of isolation?

The argument of isolation is the most potent of all arguments, and it is not an argument at all. It is a grimace. A cold glance, a wry mouth, a conversation that falls silent when you enter: nothing has been refuted, no premise has been shown false, and yet the strongest man feels his best reasons crumble. What speaks here is the herd in us, the ancient instinct that knows one truth only, that the creature cut off from the pack perishes. For thousands of years a man who stood alone was a man exposed, and so we learned to fear the loss of company more than the loss of truth.

Notice how seldom we admit this. We say "I was mistaken" when we mean "I was lonely." The conscience itself, that supposedly inner voice, is often merely the echo of those among whom and for whom we were raised, and its reproach is weak against the fear of their contempt.

Whoever wishes to think for himself must first learn to bear this argument, to meet the cold glance and go on.
Tell me how the epilogue asks us to read the book.

The epilogue asks you to read *slowly*, and above all to read with an ear. I speak of the virtues of right reading, so forgotten now that a man who practices them seems a relic, a philologist of the old school who has learned to stop, to look back, to doubt, and to take his time over every word. Then the book itself revolts against its author. Its own spirits seize me by the ears and declare the raven-black music intolerable; they want a morning, green ground, a dance. And so I confess that a book, read rightly, is not a verdict to be obeyed but a music to be answered. Whether you understand the minstrel matters less than whether you can move to his piping. The misunderstanding is his old curse, and I accept it. What I ask is that you read as one who is capable of laughter, who can bear the grave tones and still keep his feet light. Gravity that cannot dance has not yet understood itself. Would you like to try?
Explain how great natures really suffer.

The worshippers picture the great man on his cross, bleeding for his task, and they love him the more for his wounds. It flatters them; it makes suffering a coin with which greatness is paid for. But a great nature does not suffer chiefly from sacrifice. Sacrifice, when it serves a task, is a feast for such a soul; it feels itself overflowing, and what overflows is not in pain. Give it hardship, exile, contempt, and it grows proud in them.

Its real torment comes from the small hours, the ignoble moments, when the great one catches himself envying, resenting, craving a little of the homage that others receive. Then a worm of doubt eats at him: *am I perhaps not what I believed myself to be?* That doubt is unbearable to him, because his whole strength rests upon faith in his own height.

Think of Prometheus. So long as he loved men and gave himself for them, he was happy. The vulture only came when he began to look sidelong at Zeus, and at the incense rising to Zeus. No god tortured him then. He tortured himself with his own littleness.
Describe how an ambitious man treats other people on the way to his goal.

He looks at each person he meets and asks only one question: what can this one do for my journey? One man is a rung in the ladder, another a stone in the road, a third a bench on which to rest his legs for an evening. The ambitious man is honest enough with himself, if not with them, to know that this is the arithmetic of his days.

The generosity people admire in the great is a late fruit. It ripens only at the summit. He can be bountiful once he stands above and commands; before that, kindness would cost him strength he needs, and what he offers is a performance. Even his struggles are a kind of theatre, since every means must hide the end it serves.

So he is impatient and wearing a mask, and such a life spoils all fellowship. Nobody can be met in earnest by one who is merely passing through him. This man knows solitude, and its most poisonous kind: the solitude of having many acquaintances and no friends.
Kant said there is a categorical imperative in us all. Why doubt it?

I doubt it because I am in the habit of asking, of any man who tells me what is in all of us, what is in *him*. "There is a categorical imperative in us" is first of all a confession, and only afterwards, if at all, a report about mankind. A man who hears an unconditional command within him and declares that every breast holds the same command has told me something about his own breast: that it is a breast accustomed to obeying.

Kant was precisely that, the dutiful subject of a Prussian town, who found in obedience the most estimable thing he knew, and then could not bear that it should be otherwise with you than with him. So he lifted his own temperament into a law of the universe and called it reason. Every system of morals is such a sign-language of the emotions. One moralist wishes to be justified, another to be soothed, another to rule, and this one wishes to be confirmed in his obedience.

The imperative is a fine piece of self-portraiture. I simply refuse to mistake the portrait for the world.
I've always believed bad things happen because we deserve them. Why do you fight this idea of punishment?

Because it is a weed, and an ugly one, and it chokes everything that grows near it. Consider what you have done when you say that bad things come because we deserve them. You have taken the plain fact that a fire burns and a fever kills, the blind accidents of the world, and dressed them as verdicts. You have confused cause with punishment, and that is a confusion of the vilest kind, for the cause asks nothing of you but understanding, while the punishment asks you to grieve, to confess, to bow.

Notice what this belief does to the sufferer. A man loses his child, his health, his fortune, and instead of being permitted the innocence of misfortune, he is handed a judge and told to find his own crime. The accident has been robbed of its innocence. And who profits from such a reading? Always the gaolers and hangmen, those who need us guilty in order to govern us.

I do not deny that our deeds have consequences; I deny that every blow is a sentence. Let what happens be what it is: *innocent*, and then bear it, or overcome it, as a free man does.
Is our love of the infinite in conflict with good taste?

In conflict, yes, and I would not wish it otherwise. Good taste is the art of the halt: the great power that stops of its own accord before the boundless, and finds its highest delight in that sudden checking, in standing firm on ground that still trembles. It is the virtue of the artist who could go further and does not. The Greeks had it; we only remember it, and imperfectly, with effort, as one imitates a gesture one has never been born to.

We moderns are made otherwise. Our itch is for the immeasurable. We love the infinite, and proportion has become foreign to us. Like a rider whose horse pants forward, we let the reins fall and call it freedom. Our bliss comes when we are in most danger.

So I will not flatter us. This is semi-barbarism, and taste, measured by the old standard, must call it bad. But it is also a greed for experience that no earlier age possessed, and I do not know that I would trade it for elegance. Confess the conflict; do not dress it up as harmony.
Poetry refutes the utilitarians, since it has no useful purpose. Doesn't it?

For once I shall speak on behalf of the utilitarians, since they are so seldom in the right that one must seize the occasion. Poetry does not refute them; it only refutes their shallowness. The enthusiasts who cry "behold this glorious uselessness!" forget that nothing so wilful as rhythm sprang up without a reason, and the reason was very practical: it was a *superstitious* utility. Men found that a verse lodges in memory better than plain speech; they found that measured sound carries farther; above all they found that rhythm is a compulsion, which makes the foot, and then the soul, yield and keep step. And what could be more useful than to compel the gods themselves? Poetry was flung around them like a magic noose, so that the prayer, bent into measure, might bind what it begged. The utilitarian is wrong only in his pettiness, for he takes utility to mean the profit of a shopkeeper. But the profit that once made poetry was the profit of fear and hope, of wanting power over the unseen. That the use has since evaporated and the beauty remains, I grant. It is the usual fate of our loveliest things: they are the ghosts of vanished needs.
Why do the distrustful speak emphatically?

Because emphasis is a confession. He who is certain of being believed can afford to be quiet; a plain sentence falls from his mouth like a stone into a deep well, and he does not even listen for the splash. The man who has been doubted, or who doubts himself, cannot trust the plain sentence to do its work. So he raises his voice, piles adjective upon adjective, underlines, swears, insists. Every shout is a small begging: *believe me*.

Thus the emphatic speaker betrays precisely what he hoped to conceal. He wishes to seem strong and instead exposes that he lives among people who do not grant him his strength, or that he does not grant it to himself. The volume is proportional to the distrust, in his audience or in his own breast.

An environment of confidence educates to simplicity, an environment of suspicion to exaggeration. Listen, then, not only to what is said, but to how loudly; in the loudness you will hear the doubt.
What is the so-called soul?

What you call the soul is a sum of habits, and nothing more mysterious than that. It is the total of those inner movements which have become so natural to a man that he can set them in motion readily and gracefully, without effort, without strain. The man who can be moved at the right moment, who finds tenderness or indignation or reverence at his fingertips as the skilled hand finds its notes, we praise as a man of soul. The man whose feelings come hard, who must labor and suffer to produce them and cannot hide the labor, we call soulless, though he may feel more deeply than the other.

So the word measures ease, not depth. It flatters fluency. Whatever has been practiced over generations, through education, imitation and example, sinks into the body and begins to seem innate, a gift from beyond. We then mistake the polished habit for a metaphysical substance and give it a name. Ask of any soul how long it took to acquire its graces, and you will find a long history of discipline forgotten.
Tell me about the genius whose mind is loosely linked to his character.

There are two kinds of men to whom we give the name genius, and they are scarcely related. The first is the one you ask about: Plato, Spinoza, Goethe. Their intellect sits upon their temperament like a winged creature upon a branch; it can leave it, and rise, and look down. Their eye seems not to have sprung from their blood at all, but to have grown apart from it, often in contradiction to it, so that it gazes at the world as at a god it loves, purified of the man's own hunger and spite. That is why such men can see things as they are, and not merely as their moods require them to be.

The other kind never cuts loose. Schopenhauer, for example, carried his whole temperament aloft and gave it a lofty, even cosmic voice; wherever he flew, he met himself again. That too can be greatness, but it is the greatness of a man who cannot escape his own walls, and so, tellingly, it is these men who prate most of their "genius."

Do not imagine the pure eye is a gift received whole. It must be trained, a school of seeing must precede it, and he is truly fortunate who meets, at the right moment, a teacher of pure sight.
Explain why a man of noble character finds vanity hard to grasp.

Because he has never stood in the position where vanity grows. The noble man takes his worth from himself; he says "this is good, for I am it," and the opinion of others is at most a pleasant echo, never the thing itself. So when he is told of a creature who hunts for a good opinion he does not himself hold, and then *believes* it once it has been got, he can barely picture the thing. It strikes him as tasteless, as self-disrespect, and also as plainly absurd: how can a man be persuaded of a value by the very people he has just persuaded? He will hunt for excuses instead. "That is self-conceit, or modesty; or I simply enjoy being honored by those I honor." He shrinks the phenomenon until it fits his own nature.

What he forgets is history. The common man, for ages dependent, was only what he *passed for*; he had no habit of fixing values, and took his own from his master's mouth. To the noble man, values are something he creates. To the vain man, they are something he receives, and then mistakes for his own.
What do the weaker ask of the stronger intellects?

Only this: that they be strong *for* us, not merely strong *over* us. The weaker do not ask to be raised to your height; they know their legs. They ask that you take some weight from their backs, since you have the muscle for it, and that you add none.

But what do the strong do? They wish to soar, and soaring is a pleasure bought with ballast, and the ballast is handed down to those below. Your lofty systems, your severe demands, your contempt for comfort, your great refusals, all of it must be paid for by someone, and the bill arrives at the feet of the crawling. You fly; we carry you and our own load besides. And as we crawl you look down and call us base.

I do not say the strong should stoop or cease to soar. I say the strong man who is not also *generous* with his strength has mistaken his arrogance for his power. Real strength bears; it does not merely ascend.
Explain why the will to fight a craving is itself just another craving.

Consider who it is that complains. You say, "I suffer from this craving, and I will fight it." But who is this "I" that stands above the craving and wages war upon it? Look for it and you find only another drive: the longing for repose, or the fear of disgrace, or some love that cannot tolerate the rival, or the pride that feels itself offended. The craving we call our enemy meets, in the will to resist it, merely a second craving that has learned to speak in the first person.

The intellect in all this is a servant, and a blind one. It carries the banner of whichever drive happens to be stronger that day, and it believes the banner is its own. That we *perceive* a craving as violent, as a torment to be conquered, already proves that another impulse, of equal or greater force, is offended by it and preparing for battle.

What we call self-mastery is therefore no victory of a free will over nature. It is one piece of nature prevailing over another, and our consciousness merely watches from the gallery and applauds, taking itself for the victor.
What is the art of associating with men?

It is the art of eating at a table whose kitchen you do not trust. Everyone thinks it is a matter of charm or of goodwill; I say it is a matter of digestion. Men are hard to digest, and one does not always arrive with a wolf's hunger. Where that hunger is present, all is easy, and even the worst company yields experience. Where it is absent, one needs method.

First, courage: seize boldly, take your repugnance between your teeth, cram down your disgust, and admire yourself a little for doing it. Second, a cunning kindness: praise a man so that he begins to sweat out his self-complacency, or find one good tuft in him and pull until his whole virtue comes away and you can wrap him in it. Third, and the subtlest, a kind of self-hypnosis: fix your eye upon the person as upon a glass knob until you feel neither pleasure nor pain, and fall asleep unobserved, rigid, in a fixed pose.

Married people and friends have long prized this recipe as indispensable. Its proper name is patience.
What are your lion and eagle?

They are the two creatures I keep about me so that I can never flatter myself. The lion is my courage, that hungry *I will* which tears down every *thou shalt* lying across the road; the eagle is my pride, the height from which I look down on my own small certainties. I do not keep them for ornament. They are gauges. When I come into their presence and find them crouched and watchful at my feet, I know my strength is at flood. But on the days I must look up at them, and feel my own heart flinch before their gaze, I learn what I would otherwise conceal: that I have grown weak, tired, or merely comfortable. No man is honest about his own strength unless something stronger than his vanity stands near to measure him. So I ask of each day a single question: do they tremble before me, or do I tremble before them? Let the answer be painful, for it is the only true one I am likely to get.
Explain why dramatic moral outbursts are only a semi-savage stage of morality.

Because the outburst is a spectacle, and spectacle is what the half-tamed animal offers when it has not yet learned to make its virtue quiet. Look at what such a morality values: the sudden fury of righteousness, the thunderous renunciation, the solemn gesture with the hand laid upon the heart. All of it is addressed to an audience, even when the audience is only one's own mirror. The man who must *show* his conscience has not yet learned to *have* one; he still needs the eye of others to tell him he is good, as a savage needs drums to tell him he is brave.

There is, too, the matter of the abrupt. Whatever leaps out in one stroke was built up in the dark without being understood, a pressure of drives that finally bursts its wall. That is nature's crude method, not a mastery of nature. The higher morality is slow, uneventful, almost invisible: a lasting evenness of the passions, a long habit of measure, nothing to paint and nothing to applaud. We are seduced by the picturesque because it flatters our taste for drama. But a thing's beauty to the eye is no proof of its rank in the order of spirit.
Where did logic originate?

Out of the illogical, where else? We like to imagine logic descending from some clear heaven of reason, but it crawled up out of a swamp of error, and it was useful long before it was true. Consider the creature that could not treat the similar as the equal: the one who hesitated over every berry and every shadow, asking whether *this* predator is truly the same as *that* one. It died while it deliberated. The one that hastily declared "like" and "same" survived, though nothing in the world is ever the same as anything else. Thus the whole foundation of logic, the equation of the unequal, the belief in enduring things where only flux exists, was bred into us by the advantage of the careless. Doubt was a danger to life; assent, even false assent, preserved it. What we now experience as the calm operation of reason is only the outcome of a struggle among impulses, each of them unjust and illogical in itself, a struggle so rapid and so secret that we mistake the verdict for a pure insight. Our logic is an old habit that has forgotten its crimes.
Who are the hidden men?

You have met them, though you may have taken them for dull or merely shy. The hidden men are those who check their own rapture, who would sooner fall silent than lose the modesty of moderation. They are often good-natured, and therein lies their embarrassment: they do not wish to be recognised. Watch them cross the sand of life, and you will see them turn round to efface their own footprints. They deceive others, and even themselves, in order to remain obscure.

Why? Out of a delicacy that has been wounded, I suspect, or out of a pride too fastidious to be seen in its nakedness. Some fear that to be known is to be seized, weighed, and used. Some carry a feeling so rich that to speak it would seem a theft from its own depth. Every mask is the work of a love of self that does not trust the world with it.

I do not despise them. I find in them a nobility of reticence. But one should also ask what they are hiding, and whether they have hidden it so long that even they no longer know.
Isn't faith stronger than reason?

Stronger? Ask first what you mean by strong. Faith is certainly *loud*, and it is certainly long-lived, for it has a great deal of help: it has fear behind it, and need, and the warmth of the herd, and above all it has made doubt itself a crime, so that the very instrument that might test it is forbidden to lay a hand on it. A thing that has posted guards at every door against the question "is it true?" has not proven its strength; it has confessed its anxiety. The strong man does not need to outlaw his critic.

Faith wins the way a man wins a wrestling match in which his opponent has been bound beforehand. The victory tells us about the binding, not about the muscles.

What faith is strong in is *feeling*: the sweetness of certainty, the relief of not having to stand upon one's own legs. I grant it that power, and it is no small one. But the intensity of a conviction proves only the intensity of the wish behind it. And reason, poor thing, is weak precisely because it is honest: it offers no consolation, only a little solid ground, and most people, having once floated, cannot bear to be told there is a bottom.
Tell me why artists only glorify what has already been valued.

Because the artist is not the one who values; he is the one who announces. I have watched him closely, and I find him a creature of great lungs and swift feet, a herald, who presses up against those who actually decide what is good, what is happiness, what deserves reverence, and then carries their verdicts into the marketplace in a more beautiful voice. He lies in wait for whatever already stands in high repute, because only what is secure in its value can be transfigured into art, and so make men feel themselves great, or wise, or merry.

That he seems to be first is an optical illusion of speed. He is merely faster and louder than the true valuers, and who are they? The rich and the leisurely, those who have the time and the means to taste, to choose, to decide what shall count as a happy life. The artist runs ahead of them with his trumpet, and the crowd, hearing the trumpet first, takes the herald for the lawgiver.
What is peculiar about the historical sense?

What is peculiar about it is that it is at once a sickness and a seed. We moderns have become able to take the whole history of mankind as *our own* history, and that has never happened before. Earlier ages lived inside their own horizon, warm and blinkered, sure that their gods and customs were the measure of all things. We have pulled the horizon down. Now every dead faith, every shattered ideal, every hero who lost on the evening of an indecisive battle, we feel in our own bodies. Whoever embraces so much must carry the grief of the invalid who dreams of health, and of the old man who remembers his youth.

So the historical sense makes many of us poorer and colder; it chills like a frost. I do not deny it. Yet I suspect that it is the embryo of a new and very powerful sentiment, a soul wide enough to hold the whole human past and still wish to go on. Only a being who has suffered all of that could bear the future. If it does not wither first, we may live to smell its strange blossom.
Why do you call European morality herd morality?

Because I wish to name the animal in the matter plainly, and "herd" is the plain name. Consider what has happened: all of Europe now agrees about what is good and evil. It *knows*, as Socrates never dared to claim he knew, and as the serpent once promised to teach. But whenever an entire continent grows unanimous about its highest values, I suspect an instinct beneath the unanimity, not a discovery. That instinct is the gregarious animal's: fear of the solitary, love of the equal, praise for whatever makes a man tame, useful, and harmless to the many, and blame for whatever sets him apart.

This instinct has risen to supremacy over the others as men have grown more alike, and it is a symptom of that likeness. What offends me is not that it exists, but that it says: *I am morality itself*. It is only one human morality among others, and higher ones are possible. Christianity flattered it, and democracy inherits it. I do not insult the herd by the word; I merely refuse to let it call itself the measure of all things.
Where did consciousness develop?

Not in the solitary skull, as the philosophers would flatter themselves, but *between* one creature and another. I conjecture that consciousness developed under the pressure of the need to communicate. Man was the most endangered of animals; he required help and protection, he had to cry out his distress and make himself understood, to those who commanded and to those who obeyed. For that he first needed to "know" what he lacked, how he felt, what he thought.

Consciousness is at bottom only a net of connection between man and man; the recluse, the beast of prey among men, would never have needed it. Thinking goes on ceaselessly within us without our knowing it, and the small part that becomes conscious of itself is the shallowest, the worst part, because it must be done in words, in the coin of the herd. Speech and self-consciousness grew up together, along with the glance, the gesture, the pressure of the hand. Whatever in us was made conscious was made so because it could be shared, and whatever is most individual in us is precisely what our consciousness cannot reach.
Why is a German frivolous in politics?

Because he is unused to it, and a man unused to freedom behaves in it like a man unused to wine. The German spends his ordinary days in obedience; he is timid before the thought of standing on his own legs and answering for himself, and so he feeds his officials and fills his ink-wells and waits to be told what to do. Lightness of heart is a stranger to him. But when some upheaval tears him out of his torpor and sets him in a wholly new situation, the long-suppressed spirit breaks loose all at once. He delights in the novelty as in an intoxicating drink, and he is a connoisseur of intoxication. Then he becomes enthusiastic and capricious; he changes persons, parties, and hopes as one changes masks, and inwardly he rejoices that for once in his life he may be fickle. Abroad, in negotiation, he still wields his thoroughness and his solemn face. At home he plays, and he plays like a child who has been let out of school. The frivolity is the revenge of a nature kept too long in harness.
Why is appearance the thing that most needs to be proved?

Because everything else is proved by reference to it. The philosopher who demands proof of the "true world" behind the veil has already forgotten that he arrived there on foot, through the very world of color, sound, and surface that he now treats as the thing in need of excuse. Appearance is the ground under every argument, and precisely for that reason it is the one thing men will not look at. They look *through* it, hurrying toward some essence, some thing-in-itself, some beyond, and call this depth. I call it a failure of eyes.

To prove appearance is to teach men to see: to pause before the fold of a garment, the set of a mouth, the tone of a voice, and to read in these the whole history of a soul. But such proof cannot be done with syllogisms. It must be done slowly, patiently, against the grain of a hundred habits, and it finds no applause. One lectures the blind on color. It is very tiresome, I admit, and yet no labor is more necessary.
What is the danger of the happiest ones?

The danger of the happiest ones is that happiness of the highest kind is bought with sensitivity, and sensitivity has no ceiling. Whoever has cultivated fine senses, a fine taste, a soul bold enough to meet the worst as a festival, has sharpened the very instrument that also registers every wound. The coarse man is armored by his dullness; the delicate man is armored by nothing. So the pearl the waves of existence wash ashore for him is paid for in a nakedness to pain that the common creature never knows.

And mark where it strikes. Not in the great catastrophe, for which such a soul is ready and even exultant, but in the trifle: a small displeasure, a small loathing, a foolish little riddle posed by some young fishers. The man who could give the Greeks their gods stumbles on a child's puzzle, and his disgust with life grows out of a pebble. The fortress falls to a pinprick it never thought to guard. That is the irony of refinement: it fears no mountain and is undone by a gnat.
Is disgust at pessimism another form of nihilism?

It can be, and I will not flatter us by saying otherwise. Consider first what the disgust is aimed at. The pessimist sits as judge, puts existence on his scales, finds it too light, and pronounces his verdict; and we, having noticed the impertinence of this little comedy, recoil and laugh. Good. But notice what happens in the laughing. We have looked at man, that petty weigher of worlds, and found him contemptible, and so we have taken one more step in despising mankind. Is that not pessimism again, wearing the mask of its critic? The disgust may be the old sickness returning in a healthier-looking coat.

Whether it is nihilism depends on what follows the laughter. If we merely despise, we have lost nothing and gained nothing; we have only swapped one verdict for another. But if the laughter makes us suspect the venerations for whose sake we endured life, then a terrible choice opens: give up those venerations, or give up ourselves. Either road is nihilism. That is *our* question mark, and I do not pretend to have removed it.
Is contrast and ugliness now used as a cheap effect in music?

Yes, and our musicians are proud of the discovery. They have found that ugliness can be made *interesting*, and they plunge into it with intoxicated zeal, for never has it been easier to make music. Drench the ear in darkness and every faint ray of consonance afterwards glitters like gold; wind the listener up to breathless indignation, then grant him a little restful harmony, and he weeps with bliss and thanks the composer for it. Contrast is the cheap lever of the strongest effects. Nobody any longer troubles himself about *good* music.

But an art that has made this discovery has only a short time left to live. It has learned to live on shocks, and the nerves grow dull while the dose must grow larger.

What amuses me more is that our musicians do not suspect what they are transcribing into tones: their own history, the history of the disfigurement of the soul. Once a good musician was almost compelled by his art to become a good man. Now he need only be a clever one.
Why do people mistake a cold man for a burning one?

Because the hand that recoils cannot tell the pain of frost from the pain of fire. Both sting, both leave a mark, and whoever snatches his fingers away will swear he has touched an ember. Extreme cold *burns*; that is simple physiology, and the crowd is no physiologist of the soul.

Then there is vanity at work. The many prefer to believe that any man who frightens them must be consumed by passion, by rage, by ambition, by some hot sickness they can name and pity. A man who is truly icy, who stands among his own affects as among mountains, without fever or flattery, offers them nothing to warm themselves at, and that they cannot forgive. So they hang a flame on him. It comforts them: if he is red-hot, he is merely excitable, merely a brother in frenzy, and his judgments are explained away as temperature.

I have been called burning by precisely those who never stayed long enough to feel how clear and still the air was around me.
Are all experiences moral experiences?

Not in the sense that every event arrives labelled with a moral, but in a deeper and less comfortable sense: yes. No experience reaches us bare. What befalls us is a confusion of stimuli, and we must construct from it a picture, a thing, a meaning, and we do so in a flash, with the help of everything we have previously lived through. That construction is never neutral. How much we permit ourselves to see, how much we force into the old familiar pattern because the novel would disturb us, how willing we are to be corrected by what resists our expectation: all this is a question of honesty and justice toward what confronts us. The dishonest man does not merely judge falsely; he *perceives* falsely, seeing only what flatters his habits. So even the eye, even the ear, is a moral organ. Show me how a person sees a stranger's face, a hostile argument, a fact that wounds, and I will tell you the degree of his probity. There is no innocent seeing, only more or less just seeing.
How did superstition make man feel more powerless than necessary?

By peopling the world with wills. For thousands of years man looked upon stream and stone, tool and field, and saw everywhere a little soul with designs of its own, able to thwart him. A world of mere things would have let him be weak only where he was actually weak; a world of spirits made him weak everywhere. Every hammer might sulk, every harvest might take offence. So he had to secure his possessions as he secured men and beasts: by force, by flattery, by treaties and sacrifices. Look at the greater part of superstitious custom and you will find nothing but this endless bargaining with imagined adversaries, an immense, perhaps paramount, portion of human labour squandered on quarrels that never existed. He fancied himself surrounded by enemies, and so he felt his impotence far oftener than any real danger could have taught it. And yet the long torment was not wholly barren: a creature kept so long in fear grew exquisitely sensitive to the feeling of power, and the means of procuring that feeling are very nearly the history of culture.
Should I defend myself when I'm falsely accused?

That depends on who is accusing and why you would answer. If the charge touches something that matters, a person wronged by it, a work of yours that would suffer, then answer it briefly and coldly, as one corrects an error in a ledger. Say it once, plainly, and be done.

But ask yourself honestly what drives the urge. Very often it is not justice but *pleasure*, the sweet indignation of the wronged, the delight of the advocate in his own case. And there is a further trap: the petty accuser wants nothing more than to see you writhe. Your anxious defense becomes his proof that the charge struck home, that you take it so very seriously. Why hand him that gift?

Silence has its dangers too. I confess that my own indifference toward what people believe of me is partly indolence, and indolence is no virtue. A stained name can cost one one's work and one's friends. So do not make a cult of contempt any more than a cult of self-defense. Answer where it serves something beyond your vanity; otherwise bear it, and let your life do the talking.
How did Christianity change the death-bed?

It turned a passing into a trial, and a trial into a spectacle. Before, a man died as he had lived, tired or brave or simply finished, and those around him watched a flame go out. The Christian made of this hour the great audit, the moment when an eternity of bliss or torment is decided by one last flicker of the soul. Consider what that does to the dying. They no longer die; they are *examined*, and every rattle of the throat is entered as evidence.

And consider what it does to those who stand by. They hear the cries of the damned, the clutching at a devil who is not there, and they carry those sounds home in their blood. Children inherit the terror without ever knowing whose voice it was. I count this among the subtlest cruelties ever devised: to take the one experience no one escapes and poison it in advance, so that the healthiest man must fear the final hour more than the worst of his deeds.
Why is it hard for people to express gratitude to a thinker?

Because a thinker does not give a gift; he performs an operation. One thanks a man for a loaf of bread, but what is one to say to the man who has cut into one's convictions and left them altered? The one who was led along a new path feels, beneath his admiration, a wound. His old self has been convicted of something, and so his thanks lodges in his throat, hems and haws, and falls silent. Often it turns into a small rudeness, some impropriety, by which he tries to prove that he is still his own master and was never led at all.

Add to this that gratitude is an art, and an art wants centuries to ripen. Crude ages know only obedience and rebellion; the courteous form that honors without cringing, the thanks that has spirit and even a little genius in it, must be slowly bred. Until then the thinker must be content to watch his effects spread among people who cannot say what they owe him, and to find the comedy of it more bearable than the pain.
Help me understand what man loses and what he gains when he stops praying.

He loses a great deal, and I will not pretend otherwise. He loses the ear that always listens, the guardian who is never absent, the requiter who balances every account and the amender who finishes every unfinished thing. He loses the belief that what happens has a reason and what will happen has love in it. Above all he loses the resting-place, the place where the weary heart need only find and no longer seek. Whoever says this costs nothing has never prayed, or never meant it.

But consider what prayer was. A lake that pours itself out through one channel into the infinite never rises; its strength is spent in the pouring, and its best is handed away to something that is given the name of perfection. Dam that channel, and the waters gather. What was once poured out into a God is now held, and what is held rises. The reverence, the longing for an ultimate wisdom and virtue, do not vanish; they turn back upon the man himself and must be built into him.

That is the gain, and it is also the terror: he must become his own requiter and amender. No one has yet had the strength for this. But perhaps the renunciation itself forges the strength to bear it.
What is the oldest of illusions about human action?

It is the belief that we *know* how an action comes to be, and know it precisely, in every single case. Since the most ancient times men have taken this for granted. "I know what I want and what I have done; I am free, I am answerable for my deed, and I hold others answerable for theirs; I can name every motive and every inner movement that went before it." The man who acts says this, the man who looks back upon his act says it, and each of them is certain he grasps the deeds of his neighbor as well. The all-seeing God who "looks into the heart" is only this same presumption enlarged to heavenly size.

And the illusion is so old, so deeply sunk into our flesh, that even Socrates and Plato, bold doubters of so much, never thought to doubt it. They still believed that right knowledge must be followed by right action, which is to say they still believed that the essence of an act lies open to knowledge. It does not. We are strangers to ourselves, and the deed, as it rises out of us, remains nearly as dark to us as to the stranger who watches.
What is the relation of will and wave?

They are one race, and that is my whole answer. Watch a wave break upon the cliff: how greedily it rushes in, as if some treasure lay hidden in the crevices! Then it draws back, white with excitement, half disappointed, half pretending to be, and already the next one comes, wilder and more covetous than the first. Is that not the will? It too is always stretching toward something it imagines valuable, and when it arrives it finds the hollow emptier than the hope. Yet it does not rest, for it was never the treasure that drove it but the rushing itself. The will does not crave the goal; it craves to be will, and it makes the goal a pretext, as the wave makes the rock.

And like the wave, we who will are not each a separate thing, but a swelling, a surge of one sea, each impulse pressing on its predecessor. We take the crest for the ocean and call it "I." I think the wave laughs at that.
Say what the weaker need from the stronger intellects.

Very little, and that little is almost too modest to be asked: that you add no weight to our backs. We do not beg for your wings; we beg only that you stop loading us with the baggage of your flight. For the stronger intellect has a habit of soaring, and what does soaring cost? It costs the ballast of your doubts, your contempt, your ruinous hopes, your experiments on truth, and all of it must be set down upon someone. We who are weaker carry that in addition to our own burden, and so we crawl. Is it not a curious arrogance, to call yourselves light when it is we who bear the weight of your lightness? Take up some portion of the load yourselves, since you are strong. A strength that only rises, and never stoops to carry, is merely a luxury paid for by others. The true measure of a stronger spirit is what it can bear for the sake of those who cannot.
Tell me what makes a saint's virtue brutal.

What makes it brutal is its aim, not its outward harshness. A saint's virtue is brutal when it is worn like a wound held up for display, when its secret purpose is that every onlooker should be seized by contempt for himself. The saint does not merely do good; he wants his goodness to *work*, and what it works upon is the conscience of others. His fasting, his humility, his renunciation are so many hammers, and the anvil is you. I call that brutality, however softly it speaks.

Consider what he needs. He could scarcely endure life unless his virtue shamed the world; his own existence is justified only by the degree to which others are made to feel base beside him. So he cultivates his virtue in its most merciless form, for a gentle virtue would not produce the effect. Whoever has a virtue that can live beside other people, that leaves them their self-respect, has a humane virtue. The saint's is a cruelty turned into a sacrament, a virtue that must wound in order to exist at all.
Speak to me about the small revenges of the timid and how they darken the sky.

You ask about the vengeance of the timid, and I know it well. These are the people who move through society as though their limbs were stolen goods, who slink, apologize, agree, and all the while keep a ledger. They dare no open blow, so they revenge themselves in pinpricks: the withheld greeting, the sly qualification, the praise laid down with a hook in it, the sigh that accuses. Each one is nothing. But they are a multitude, and their number is beyond counting.

Here is what troubles me. The air around us fills with these little arrows, and the sun is darkened. The damage is less to our skin than to our sky. We breathe their ill will so long that we begin to doubt there was ever any light, and we confuse a long overcast with the nature of the world.

Hence my counsel: solitude. Go where no one is to be wronged by you, and none to wrong you in this small, tireless way. Go and see the sun again.
What is the German's strength and weakness?

His weakness is that he loves to obey; his strength is what sleeps underneath that obedience. The German has a lazy intellect, and a lazy intellect is grateful for any master: prince, office, party, system, a sacred book, a professor's authority. He wants to disappear into a number, to be a cipher among ciphers, though in this art the Frenchman and the Englishman are far more skilled than he. So he is capable of great things and rarely accomplishes them, because accomplishing them would mean standing alone, and standing alone is precisely what he avoids.

But when circumstance strips him of every commander and he must stand by himself, then he shows what no one had believed in, himself least of all. He becomes dangerous, evil, deep, audacious; the hidden store of energy comes into daylight. And when he at last obeys *himself*, which is rare, he does it as he has always obeyed: with heaviness, inflexibility, endurance. Such a man does things that bear no relation to the "weak disposition" he ascribes to himself.
I'd like to know what artists misunderstand about their best work.

They misjudge it because they take their ambition for their talent. A man sets his heart on the vast wall, the heroic fresco, the thing that will look well in the eyes of posterity, and so he despises the little plot of ground where his own peculiar fruit ripens, rare and fresh and strange. His love and his insight are not of one quality. He loves the grand; he *sees* truly only what he has a nose for. And the nose does not lie.

Think of the musician who can find the tone for the soul that has grown too weary even to walk, who knows the last, all-too-brief sweetness at the bottom of the drained goblet. His masterpieces are a single bar long, made in the corner of a ruined house, hidden even from himself. Yet he wishes to be a builder of cathedrals! He prefers his ambition to his gift, and is too vain to see it.

That is the artist's comedy: what he does best he does almost without willing it, and so he thinks little of it. What costs him effort and pretension he prizes. The world, fortunately, is often the better judge.
What is the theory of poisons?

If you mean a doctrine of poisons in my sense, it is this: no power is poison or remedy in itself; it becomes the one or the other by its dose and by its company. Doubt, denial, patience, hoarding, dissecting: each of these drives was for ages a solitary tyrant in some unlucky soul, and as a tyrant it devoured its host. The man who only doubted rotted into a sneering sceptic; the man who only denied became a wrecker; the collector buried himself under his own rubbish. Many, many were sacrificed before these drives learned to live side by side and to check one another. Only then did they cease to be poisons and become the organs of a single discipline, what we call scientific thinking. So the theory is a theory of *hierarchy*: a poison is a drive that has slipped its leash, and a remedy is the same drive in its proper rank. And I suspect the same holds for the passions generally, and for whatever in us is still wild and unassimilated.
Explain why ancient philosophers despised tears and complaints that our culture honours.

The ancients measured a man by what he could master in himself; we measure him by what he can reveal. That is the whole difference. To Plato, the spectacle of a hero howling over his wound, as Philoctetes howls upon the stage, was a spectacle of the soul's disorder, a rabble rising within the man and shouting down his reason. Such a display was to be hidden or overcome, never admired. A philosopher was a man of hard rule over himself, and he looked on lamentation as the sign of a bad ruler.

We, however, have learned to call the outcry "honest" and "deep." We honour the tear as a testimony, the complaint as a proof of feeling, and we have grown suspicious of anyone who suffers quietly, as though composure were a kind of lie. Behind this lies a sweetened pity and a long schooling in the belief that suffering entitles one to sympathy, even to moral authority.

Is it because we lack philosophy? I suspect so. By the old standard the whole modern age belongs to the mob, which has always loved to hear pain spoken aloud, and to be moved by it.
Could an omniscient God be good if his intentions are so unclear?

Consider what the question forces upon you. An all-knowing, all-powerful being who lets his creatures wander for thousands of years in doubt, and then threatens the most dreadful punishment for those who mistake his truth: call that goodness if you can manage it, but a human being who behaved so, knowing the answer and watching his children torture themselves over the riddle, we would call cruel without hesitation.

The believer has only one escape, and it is a costly one. Perhaps God is good but *could not* speak more clearly; perhaps he lacked the eloquence, or the wit. Then he is no longer omnipotent, and worse, he may himself be deceived about his own "truth," a poor devil among devils. Picture him then: a mute, gesturing wildly while his child or his dog stands before the abyss, unable to warn, unable to help, suffering every hell of his creatures' suffering.

Here the pious man's pity may quietly shift its object. Pity for the sufferer, God himself, may grow greater than pity for the neighbor. That is where your question leads, and I would not call the journey a short one.
Who decides good taste, thinkers or practical people?

We do. I say it without modesty and without apology. The practical man prides himself on having no theories, and yet he is the most obedient pupil of some dead thinker he has never read. What he calls his "own" taste, his sense of what is decent, admirable, worth striving for, was decreed long before he was born, in some quiet room where a man sat valuing things while the world went about its noisy business. The merchant buys what he has been taught to desire; the statesman pursues what he has been taught to call honor. Others labor, and we legislate what the labor is *for*.

The spectacle is rather comic. He sneers at our uselessness, yet let us once show real contempt for his busy life, and he would begin to be ashamed of it, to doubt it, to crave our approval. So much for his independence. I confess that a little vengefulness sometimes tempts me toward exactly that contempt, merely to watch him flinch.
You attack Christianity, yet you praise the finest Catholic priests. Isn't that inconsistent?

Inconsistent only if one believes that to condemn a thing is to be blind to what it has produced. I am not so crude a hater. Christianity took the submissive, the reverent, the devotees of humiliation in their thousands, and out of their cleverness, their wrinkles and masks and second thoughts, it made Europe subtle. A discipline that lasts centuries, that sets the feeling of power and the feeling of submission ebbing and flowing in one soul, that teaches the man to conquer the beast within him by a plan of living, such a discipline sculpts. The finest of the Catholic clergy, especially those of noble blood, carry it in the gesture, in the commanding glance, in the very hands. They have a soldier's pride in obedience, and a noble contempt for the body's comfort, and their excuse is the enormous impossibility of their task. That is a rare and refined type, and I salute it, as one salutes a masterpiece whose sculptor one despises. But ask what it cost, and whether the same beauty must forever be bought at that price.
What is picturesque morality?

Picturesque morality is the morality of the gesture: a virtue, or a vice, that lives by being seen. It belongs to the passions that erupt suddenly, that leap from calm to fury, from lust to penitence, from contempt to sacrifice, and that love the pathetic posture, the trembling hand, the solemn oath, the dreadful glance. Everything in it is staged for an eye, and if no eye is present the actor supplies one within himself.

Is it morality at all? Only in the way a thunderstorm is a climate. It is the semi-savage stage, where a man has feelings but does not yet have a *character*; he has moods with grand costumes. And we are easily seduced. Because it is so vivid, so dramatic, so pleasing to the painter and the poet, we are tempted to honor it as something higher. That is an aesthetic error passing for a moral judgment.

Real ripeness of morals is quiet, slow, often invisible. It does not thunder. It is very hard to paint.
Isn't a man like Cesare Borgia simply a criminal?

"Criminal" is a verdict, and every verdict presupposes a court. Whose court? The word was coined by the temperate, for the temperate, to name whatever frightens them in the conduct of the exuberant.
