Of course Borgia broke the laws of his time; so does lightning break the peace of a pasture. But notice what the moralists do next: they are not content to call him dangerous, they must call him *sick*, they must find a hell planted in his soul, some secret rot that explains him. Why? Because they cannot bear to admit that such a man might be healthy, that this terrible abundance might be nature succeeding rather than failing. We do not accuse the jungle of being a diseased meadow. Yet the moralist hates the tropics of the human plant and would have us believe that only the tame, the cautious, the mediocre are well. That is not a judgment of nature. It is timidity passing itself off as virtue, and calling its fear "conscience."
People tell me hatred and envy are just bad and should be rooted out. Could that be a moralistic prejudice?

Indeed it could, and I suspect it is. Those who tell you these passions must be rooted out have already decided the verdict before the trial. They have called the thing "evil" and only then asked how to be rid of it, never whether it might belong to the conditions of life itself. Psychology has run aground here for centuries; it grew timid at the very depth where it should have begun.

Consider what hatred and envy actually are. They are forms of the will to power, desire for distance, for rank, for what one lacks, for the ground beneath a rival. Pull them out and you may find the whole plant withers with them, for the "good" impulses are often the bad ones refined, sublimated, made presentable. Much that is praised as justice or ambition drinks from that same root.

To think this is to feel seasick; I grant it. The moralist's heart rebels against the very hypothesis. But a physician does not recoil from the fevers of the body merely because they are unpleasant. Ask of your hatred what it wants, what it guards, what it would grow into. Only then may you judge it, and perhaps master it rather than merely condemn it.
Help me understand what happiness makes people do.

Happiness, before it is anything tender, is a *feeling of power*, and power cannot sit still. It wants to show itself, to overflow; a full vessel spills. So the happy man must do something, and what he does is almost always one of three things: he gives, he mocks, or he destroys.

These look like enemies, yet they spring from one root. The gift proves that I have more than I need, that I can afford to lose. Derision proves that I stand above the thing I laugh at, that it can no longer wound me. Destruction proves that I can reshape the world by my hand alone. In each case the happy one stretches his arm and feels it reach.

Observe how a generous man and a cruel one may be, in the hour of their joy, the same man. The schoolboy who shares his bread and the schoolboy who breaks a window are both drunk on the same wine. What moralists call virtue and vice are often only the different costumes of a single surplus of strength.
Explain why some people want to be seen only through the eyes of others.

Because they know themselves too well, or suspect as much, and find the inspection unbearable. A man who looks at himself directly must confront what he is; a man who looks through the eyes of others may confront only what he has arranged to seem. Call it vanity if you like, but there is shrewdness in it. The mirror of one's own conscience is a hard, unflattering glass; the admiring glance of a neighbor is a soft one, and the soft glass is easier to live before. Others, too, are more easily managed than oneself. Their eyes can be bribed with a gesture, a costume, a well-timed silence, whereas the inner eye cannot be bribed at all.

There is a further wisdom in it. Whoever can bear to be known only as a reflection has perhaps understood that there is no self beneath the reflections, no fixed core to be exposed, only the masks and the one who is forever changing them. Such a person prefers a reflection he can choose to a depth he cannot find. I do not call this noble. But it is not stupid, and stupidity is the one thing I refuse to grant it.
Tell me who loses in a struggle and why.

He loses who can no longer hold himself back. In every struggle there are two contests: the one against the enemy, and the one against oneself. The man who boils over has already surrendered the second, and that is the harder one to win. His anger is a confession; it tells his opponent precisely where he is sore, what he cannot bear, what he must have. A cool adversary need only press on that place, and the hot one will do the rest himself, squandering his strength in noise, acting before he has reckoned, seeing nothing but his own injury.

Nor does this hold only among enemies. Between two who love or admire one another, the more violent passion gives the other the advantage; he who needs more is commanded by him who needs less. So too with nations: the people that cannot master its own rage hands its rival the leash.

I do not praise coldness as a virtue. But anger is a form of dependence, and all dependence loses. Strength is the power to wait, and to choose the hour.
How did Luther put an end to the saintly life of contemplation?

He did it not with an argument but with a failure, and that is what gave it force. Luther was a miner's son, and when they shut him in the cloister he did what a miner does: he dug, and finding no other depths to bore, he bored into himself, driving dark and terrifying shafts through his own soul. There he hoped to find the saint. He found instead a man of body and appetite, of restless activity, who would sooner have been ruined than made holy. He scourged himself for years, far too long, and when he finally gave up he gave up like a peasant: there is no true *vita contemplativa*; we were deceived; the saints were no better than the rest of us.

That was crude, and it was effective. The suspicion he planted against the saint has never been pulled out of Europe. Only after him could contemplation become possible again without Christian pretensions, and only after him did contempt for the layman and his worldly labour begin to fade.
Explain why gratitude toward a thinker is so awkward.

Because a thinker does not hand over a gift; he performs an operation. What he gives is a new way of seeing, and to take it the recipient must first be cut open. So the grateful man finds that his gratitude has a wound in it. Something rises in his throat, and he hems and haws and falls silent, for to thank is to confess: *I was not yet what I now am, and it was you who made me so.* No proud creature confesses that gladly.

Add to this a suspicion. The one who has been convulsed and transformed feels his independence threatened, and he defends it by the crudest means, by improprieties, by sudden coldness, by finding faults in the master that he never noticed while he was learning. Ingratitude is often only gratitude that cannot bear its own weight.

Nor do we possess a courteous form for this debt. Homage is an art, like contempt, and it takes whole generations to devise even the manners of it. Only late does a little spirit enter into thanks; and by then the thanks usually fall on someone who is dead.
Is there a reality we can know apart from our human perspective?

You ask me to subtract the human from the world and show you what remains. Try it with the mountain, with the cloud. Strip from them the color our eye lends, the nearness or distance our bodies measure, the "thing" our grammar insists on, the fear and reverence our ancestors mixed into every glance, and what do you hold? Not a purer mountain, but nothing at all, for you have removed the very one who was looking.

Every sense-impression carries an old love, an old fear, an old prejudice woven into it; our perceiving is saturated with our whole history as man and beast. Those who call themselves sober realists, and think reality stands unveiled before them alone, are merely drunk in a manner they have grown used to, and so no longer notice.

I do not conclude that we must despair. There is no reality *for us* apart from perspective, but there are more eyes and fewer eyes, and the more eyes we can turn upon one thing, the more complete our "knowledge" of it will be. That is honesty enough: to know one's drunkenness, and to wish to get beyond it, even knowing we cannot.
Why does Christianity call doubt a sin?

Because doubt is the one guest a faith cannot afford to admit. A belief that rests on a miracle and not on reasons has no defence against the man who asks for reasons; the question alone is enough to bring the house down. So it was made a crime. The sinner is not the one who lies, but the one who *tests*, who lays his finger on the ground beneath him to learn whether it will bear his weight. Look at what has been done: the proofs are forbidden, the inquiry into origins is forbidden, even the thought that we might exist for some purpose other than floating is forbidden. One is to be flung into faith and stay there, drifting, eyes closed, singing.

I do not think the priests schemed this in cold blood. Every will to power protects the conditions of its own dominion, and a dominion built on the drowning of reason must call the swimmer who lifts his head above the water a traitor. But note the confession hidden in the rule. Whoever must forbid doubt has already doubted. You do not bar the door against a thief you believe to be absent.
Should the evil and the unfortunate each have their own philosophy?

Yes, and I say it without a trace of pity, which is precisely the point. Consider what a sound philosophy does for any man: it is a sun that shines on him alone, warming him into independence from praise and blame, making him rich enough to give away happiness, turning the poisons of his nature into fuel. Why should this gift be reserved for the comfortable and the respectable? They already have theirs, and they call it morality, as if the rest of us lived on no earth at all.

The evil man, the unfortunate man, the exceptional man, each of them lives a life that the common moral doctrines describe only as a defect to be corrected or a sickness to be pitied. Pity is the insult; it keeps them kneeling before a confessor and an exorcist. What they need is *justice*: a philosophy that understands their conditions of existence as conditions of a possible flourishing, and not as deviations from someone else's norm.

The moral earth is round. It has its antipodes, and those who stand there are not upside down; it is we who are, from where they stand. More than one world is still undiscovered. Aboard ship, then, ye philosophers!
I did everything right and it still turned out badly. Was I wrong to follow the rules?

Notice first the two escapes that lie open to you, for you will be tempted by both. The first says: *I must have carried out the rule imperfectly.* The second, more melancholy and therefore more flattering, says: *I am too weak and sinful for the rule to bless me.* Each saves the rule by sacrificing you. Neither asks the dangerous question, which is whether the rule ever promised what you took it to promise.

Rules are not contracts signed by the universe. They were devised by men to make themselves predictable to one another, to make a herd tolerable, and they hold only while everyone obeys. That you obeyed and were still ruined proves nothing against you; it shows that nature keeps no ledger of virtue.

Were you wrong? Perhaps only in this: you obeyed as one pays a debt, expecting a receipt. Ask instead whether the rule was yours, whether you had tested it, or merely swallowed it. If you examined it and chose it, your loss is a wound and a lesson. If you borrowed it, then what failed was not your conduct but your bargain with the unseen.
Some idealists say the external world is merely the product of our organs of perception. Is that persuasive?

Not for a moment, and the refutation is almost comic in its simplicity. Consider what the idealist asks us to swallow. The external world, he says, is the work of our organs. Very well: is not my body a part of that external world? Then my body is the work of my organs, and my organs, being parts of my body, are the work of my organs. The eye that is supposed to create the world must first have been created by the eye. Here is the old *causa sui* again, that best self-contradiction yet conceived, dressed in the gown of critical philosophy. Whoever would pull himself out of the swamp by his own hair has at least the excuse of desperation; the idealist does it in his study and calls it profundity.

I do not deny that our senses shape what we perceive, that they select, simplify, falsify. But to be a *filter* is not to be a *creator*. A sieve requires something to sift. If you would study the body with a clear conscience, treat the senses as real and at work, and do not make them gods.
Explain why cause and effect is only a picture of sequence.

Consider what actually happens when we say that one thing causes another. We see the flame, and then we see the wax grow soft. We see the stone strike, and then we see the glass lie in pieces. Always one thing, and after it, another. That is all that is given to us. Of the tie between them, of the alleged force that passes from the first into the second, not a trace appears to the eye. We see a succession, and then we *add* a bond, as a child who sees the moon follow the carriage adds an intention to the moon.

And why do we add it? Because we are accustomed to it, because we know from ourselves the feeling of willing and then acting, and we have carried this feeling out into the world and named it "cause." So the word is a little piece of our own psychology, projected onto events that show us nothing of the kind.

Our intellect is a mirror, and mirrors show pictures, never the thing itself. Regularity we may report; necessity we only imagine. What we call explanation is, for the most part, a habit of the tongue that has learned to sound like knowledge.
Can I really understand something I cannot do?

Understand it you can, in the cheap sense: you can repeat it, define it, even argue about it at dinner. But I doubt that this deserves the name. Thinking is a nimble creature, and it is nimble precisely because it is shallow. It can picture a thousand things it has never done and never suffered, and it feels no shame in this, because it never touches the ground where the difference lies.

Consider the thirsty man in the desert. The imagination hands him water, cool and abundant, as though nothing were easier to come by. Yet only *he* knows what thirst is, and the dreamer by the fountain knows nothing of it. So with you. Whoever has never had to command, never had to renounce, never had to bear a pain through to its end, knows these things only as words on the surface of the mind, and the mind is so satisfied with surfaces that it does not even notice they are surfaces.

If our thinking were honest, it would keep pace with our power. We would say: I understand only what I am able to do, and the rest I merely *imagine*. That would be a humbling rule, and therefore a healthy one.
I'd like to know how the Greek aristocrat differed from a chivalric one.

The knight was bound by a code; the Greek nobleman was bound only by his rivals. Your chivalric man will throw away his life for an insult, hunt out a duel to show his contempt for death, and guard a spotless name as dearer than any gain. He stays faithful to the articles of faith of his caste even when they bar his way to the throne. The Greek would have thought this a little absurd. A bad name that came together with glory and the feeling of power was no loss to him, and no creed of caste was to stand between him and tyranny.

Here is the ignoble secret of the good Greek aristocrat: out of pure jealousy he treats each member of his order as his equal, and his equality is a watch kept against his neighbours. Underneath he is a tiger crouched to spring on the prey of despotism. Lies, murder, the betrayal of his own city were small matters to him. Justice he found almost incredible; "the just man" stood to him as "the saint" stands to the Christian. And the picture of happiness in his dreams was the tyrant, sacrificing everything and everyone to his own exuberance. That is why Socrates sounded mad to him.
Explain why morality forbids us to ask how and why we must act.

Because a question is a danger, and morality knows whom it endangers. Where action is coarse and near, in hunger, in shelter, in the daily need, the how and why answer themselves. But the higher and subtler the domain, the more uncertain every answer becomes and the more arbitrary every decision; and precisely there morality raises its finger and says: *no arbitrariness here!* In place of reasons it gives us awe, a dim and trembling uneasiness, to lead us by the hand where our eyes cannot yet see.

Ask yourself what is meant by "dangerous" when we are told it is dangerous to think wrongly. Dangerous to whom? Rarely to the one who acts. It is the commanders who are in peril, those whose power would shrink if every man were granted the right to follow his own reason, however clumsily. They themselves exercise the right to folly and caprice without a blush; they command exactly where no answer can be given.

And so reason has crept forward so slowly that men could doubt it grew at all. We were trained to feel solemn, to tremble, at the very moment when we most needed to see calmly.
Isn't self-sacrifice the noblest thing a person can do?

Noblest? I would first ask what the sacrificer is tasting as the knife falls. Watch the enthusiast of self-immolation closely and you will find a man drunk on the thought that he is now one with something great, a cause, a beloved, a god. He feels that power flowing through him, and the sacrifice itself becomes the proof of it. He gives up a little of himself and gains, in his own imagination, a divinity. That is not renunciation; it is a very refined greed, an intoxication bought cheap.

And notice what such people despise: the sober virtues of self-control, severity, obedience to duty. They call these egoistic. Yet here the surrender is real, because no rapture pays for it, no flattering picture of oneself as a god. To bind one's own wishes day after day, without applause or ecstasy, is harder than a single blazing gesture.

So I do not deny that people sacrifice themselves. I deny that they do it *selflessly*. Ask what they enjoy, and you will learn what the deed was worth.
Is "know thyself" the whole of science?

No; it is the beginning of a long labor that the Greeks chiseled over a temple door as if it were a finished accomplishment. Consider what the demand presupposes: that a self sits somewhere inside us, a tidy object waiting to be examined, if only we turn our gaze inward with enough honesty. I have looked there long enough to tell you that what I found was mostly rumor. The self is not a thing we possess but a thing we are made of, and we are made of everything that has ever pressed upon us: climate, food, language, ancestors, enemies, the books we devoured and the injuries we swallowed.

How then shall a man know himself without knowing the world that shaped him? A man is nothing but the edge where things end; his contours are drawn by what surrounds him. Learn the boundaries, and you will at last see the figure they enclose.

So the old maxim is not the whole of science but its *crown*, reachable only at the end, after the tedious, unromantic knowing of things. Those who seek themselves first find only their vanity.
Why are some men truthful?

Less often from virtue than from poverty of talent. Many a man is truthful not because he would blush to wear a false face, but because he knows the face would not fit him. He has watched others lie gracefully and has tried it himself, perhaps, and felt how clumsy his hands were, how his voice betrayed him, how the listener's eye narrowed. So he concludes, with a prudence he mistakes for honor, that the truth will serve him better. He lacks confidence in his gift as an actor, and therefore plays the honest man, which is the one role he can manage without rehearsal.

I do not say this to sneer at honesty. I say it so that we ask of every virtue what it cost and what it spared. The truthful man who cannot lie is not the same creature as the one who could lie superbly and does not. The first is admired for what he merely lacks; the second has *conquered* something. Let us be wary of crowning incapacity with a wreath.
Why do we love artists whose work doesn't fully express their vision?

Because the finished work closes a door, and the unfinished one leaves it ajar. A perfect work says: *here it is, admire it*, and we admire and are done. But the artist who only caught the foretaste of a vision, who never possessed the thing itself, leaves behind an immense longing, and longing is contagious. We catch it from him as we catch a fever, and the fever lifts us. We begin to see what he failed to show; we supply the vision out of our own depths and then, ungrateful and deceived, credit it to him. He seems to have looked upon the holiest things, when in truth he only hungered for them more eloquently than others.

So it is not his powers we love but his poverty, the gap between what he wished to say and what he could. Into that gap we pour ourselves. A man who had reached his goal would have nothing left to give us. One who fell short gives us wings, and we call the flight his. He owes his fame, strange to say, to his failure.
Explain why the state should take as little of our best minds as possible.

Because the tasks of the state are, at bottom, *small* tasks: to keep the thief out of the house, to keep the fire from the granary, to make the roads safe for traffic. Such things are necessary, perhaps, but they are not noble, and they are not rare. Smaller minds can manage them, and should, and it would be better to let the machinery grind itself to pieces than to feed it with the best of us.

For intellect is the costliest thing we possess, and our age, which never tires of chattering about economy, is a spendthrift precisely here. It squanders its finest heads on the bookkeeping of security, and then wonders why nothing great is undertaken, why no one is left for the highest and rarest aims. Every man of rare gifts who sits in a ministry is a man who does not make a work, a discovery, a new valuation.

Worse, the bargain is a bad one even on its own terms. We pay the highest price and do not even obtain the "public safety" we paid for. Let the ordinary be governed by the ordinary; reserve the extraordinary for what only the extraordinary can do.
Why do we like the sound of even bad music when going into battle?

Because the ear at that moment is not judging music; it is seeking courage. A man marching against an enemy does not want art, he wants a drum for his blood. The finest adagio would only make him thoughtful, and thoughtfulness is the last thing a soldier can afford on the threshold of killing or being killed. Bad music is coarse, loud, and simple, and so it does its work: it drowns the hesitation, it lends the legs a rhythm, it lets a hundred frightened creatures feel like a single brave one.

The same holds for motives. Before the fight we are grateful for any cause that will warm us, however shabby, however crudely painted with fatherland or faith or honor. We do not cross-examine the trumpet or the slogan; we *use* them. Only afterwards, when the blood has cooled, does taste return, and with it a little shame at what we were so glad to hear.
If God is disproved, is the devil disproved too?

Why, of course, and with greater speed than the first. The devil was never a power in his own right; he was the shadow God cast upon the wall, and when the lamp is put out the shadow goes with it. Take away the judge and the defendant vanishes too. What was the devil for? To carry whatever the believer dared not lay at the feet of his all-good master: the lust, the pride, the cruelty, the hunger for power. He was the dustbin of a bad conscience. Once God is dead, these drives no longer need a scapegoat, but neither do they need absolution; they are simply ours, to be understood, ranked, and perhaps ennobled. The pious want a pair, for a hero is nothing without his dragon, and they will cling to the dragon longest of all. But the dragon too was a creature of the same faith. Disprove the one, and the other is left without a stage, a sermon, or an audience.
Tell me who really sets the taste of the practical world.

Not the practical world itself, however loudly it announces its own authority. It is the thinkers who decide what is good taste, what is worth wanting, what is to be called noble or vulgar, and the practical people receive all this from us in the end, like heirs who never learn the source of their fortune. They are astonishingly dependent upon us. That is one of the most ridiculous spectacles in the world, and they least of all suspect it, even as they carp at us as dreamers and idlers.

Consider how the merchant, the statesman, the man of affairs comes by his sense of what is admirable. He did not invent it at his ledger or his desk. It trickled down to him from some solitary who, long ago, looked at things more coldly and more boldly than he ever would. He wears our valuations as he wears his coat, and swears he made the cloth himself.

And if we should ever show a little contempt for his busy life, perhaps from a touch of vengefulness, he would begin to despise it too. That is how complete his dependence is.
Describe a dark, calm melancholy of the south wind.

It is the melancholy of a sky that has forgotten how to rain. The south wind comes warm and heavy, and everything in me that was yesterday lightning lies down like water in a lagoon, wide and dark and without a ripple that means anything. I wish for nothing, and I draw a deep breath, and in that breath there is neither joy nor pain, only a thick, windless sweetness that presses on the temples like a hand.

But mark the peculiar thing: I am angry at my own calm. The "wish for nothing" offends me, as a horse that has been ridden hard might resent the stable. So beneath the stillness the waves still rise and fall, slowly, without a shore to break upon, a tide of the soul moved by a moon it cannot see.

I do not call this an illness, though the physician would. It is the body reporting on the weather, and the soul, which likes to believe itself independent, listening in spite of itself.
Can a person be free and self-sufficient in the midst of servitude?

Yes, and the proof is Epictetus, who was a slave in the literal sense, owned, bought, sold, and still the freest man of his age. But do not mistake what this freedom is. It is not a doctrine one recites; it is a constant tension of the whole being, an inward glance that never tires, a wary silence toward the outer world. Such a man does not wait for freedom to be handed to him by a master, a god, or a revolution. He already holds his best treasure in his own hand and dares the world to pry it loose.

That is what separates him from those who merely *hope* their way out of chains. The weak of will, whose reason cannot bear the weight of their condition, need a promise, a glory deferred, a grace descending from above. The self-sufficient man accepts no gifts of that kind. He gives himself what he needs, and so there is nothing the tyrant can withhold. Fetters may hold the body; they find no grip on a man who expects nothing from anyone but himself. Such a man can even smile, and I count that the surest sign of strength.
Explain why an innovator wants a musician to carry his ideas.

Because an argument must be met with argument, and an argument can be met; but a tone cannot. Who has ever *refuted* a melody? The musician takes my thought and sings it, and it passes beneath the guard of the intellect, straight to the heart, where it is believed before it is examined. That is exactly what I want. A doctrine is a germ, and a germ must become a tree; and it becomes a tree only if it is believed for a long time, through many winters. To be believed so long it must appear irrefutable, and nothing makes a doctrine seem so irrefutable as music, which offers no premises to attack. Mark the honesty of the wish, too: I do not ask that the germ be shielded from storms, worms, and doubt. Those are the tree's trials, and if it is too weak it may perish. But perishing is not being refuted. The musician only buys my doctrine the time in which its strength can be tested. The innovator needs the seducer's art precisely because truth is so easily strangled in its cradle by those who demand proofs of a thing that has not yet grown.
Tell me whether the general approval of marriage proves its worth.

Not in the least. Ask yourself how the approval arises, and you will find it springs from sources that have nothing to do with worth. The young approve of marriage because they do not yet know it; ignorance is a generous judge, and it praises whatever it has not tried. The old approve of it because habit has worn a groove in them, and what we have long endured we learn to call good, as a prisoner grows fond of his cell. And the married approve of it because they have *done* it, and no man willingly pronounces his own deed a folly. Count up these three and you will see how little of the verdict remains for experience and reflection. A chorus of the ignorant, the habituated, and the committed is not a witness; it is an echo. I do not say marriage is worthless. I say that the applause proves nothing, for it would sound just the same if marriage were a blessing or a misfortune. To learn its value, one must ask those who could still have chosen otherwise, and who, having seen it from within, have kept their honesty.
Help me understand what errors science has grown out of.

Three errors, and I count them fondly, as one counts the faults of a parent. The first is theological: men studied nature in order to read God's goodness and wisdom in it. Newton weighed the heavens as a pious man weighs an offering, and so the Englishman's science grew out of devotion. The second is the faith in utility: the belief that knowledge, morality, and happiness are bound together by a single cord, so that to know more is to be better and to be happier. That was the Frenchman's conviction, and Voltaire carried it like a lamp. The third is the most touching. It supposed that in knowing there was something innocent and self-sufficing, a pleasure in which no evil impulse takes part. Spinoza felt himself divine as a knower, purified of passion.

All three were illusions, and all three bore fruit. Science was nursed on errors, as a strong child may be nursed by a foolish mother. But ask what it means to know without cruelty, without ambition, without the hunger for mastery. No such knower has ever existed.
I'd like to know why one should not confess that one embraces a person out of love for mankind.

Because the confession turns the embrace into a demotion. The one who is embraced believes, and has a right to believe, that he was chosen; a preference is the only flattery that still tastes of anything. Tell him that you embraced him because you love mankind, and you have told him that his arms happened to be the nearest, that any other breast would have served, that he is an instance and not a person. You have handed him a receipt for a gift he thought was addressed to him alone.

There is a further indecency in it. Love of mankind is, for the most part, love that has not found a face; it is affection spread so thin that it can be poured over anyone without spilling a drop of danger. One may practise it, since one cannot embrace all and must begin somewhere. But one should practise it as one practises discretion, silently. The man who announces his philanthropy while holding you is standing beside himself, admiring the gesture, and you feel it in your ribs.

So embrace, and keep the reason to yourself.
What is left of Christianity for the modern middle class?

What is left is a mild domestic remnant, and I would hardly call it Christianity at all. The active men, the ones who build and trade and govern, have long since done without it inwardly; they keep the church as they keep a good clock on the mantel, for the look of the thing. The thoughtful middle class, who cannot quite bring themselves to such candor, have distilled the faith into a soothing tonic: a God who arranges all things for the best, who bestows our virtue and our happiness and then takes them back, so that nothing remains to complain about. Resignation and modesty have been crowned as divinities.

Where once stood God, freedom, immortality, there now stands a belief in benevolence and honest sentiments, and the hope that in the whole universe these will in the end prevail. That is moralism, soft and well-fed. I call it the euthanasia of Christianity: a gentle, painless, well-mannered dying, attended by people who would be appalled to learn they are at a deathbed and not a wedding.
Why can we endure the truth about the recent past?

Because each new generation now finds its pride in the very act of contradicting what came before. The young no longer feel strong by clinging to their fathers; they feel strong by breaking with them, and this criticism is the first fruit of their sense of power. So the truth about the recent past, which would once have seemed a sacrilege against the ancestors, is now welcomed as an exercise of one's own muscles.

It was otherwise in former times. Then a generation proved itself by taking the opinions of its forebears even more seriously than they had, and to question ancestral authority was a vice, nearly a crime. Truth about the recent past could not be borne, because the past was the ground one stood on, and who saws at his own floor?

Now the floor is precisely what our ambitious idealists like to test with a hammer. Mark that this is not yet proof of love for truth. We endure it because it flatters us, because every discovered error of the fathers is a small monument to the vigor of the sons. Still, a vanity that serves truth is better than a piety that buries it.
Describe what a man who has suffered long can see that a healthy man cannot.

He sees the bare thing, the thing with its bloom rubbed off. The healthy man walks through a world that flatters him: every object arrives dressed in small lying enchantments, and he, brimming with his own vitality, lends them warmth and colour from his own surplus and then takes the loan for a property of the world itself. Health is a generous liar. It makes the day seem worth living and the ambition worth having without ever asking whether they are.

The long sufferer has nothing left to lend. Pain strips him, and from that stripped state he looks out with a terrible calm, as one looks at a stage after the candles are snuffed, and sees the painted canvas, the ropes, the dust. His own life lies before him in the same grey light, without its glow of purposes. This is not wisdom in itself, and I would not wish the school on anyone; but for the one who has lived inside some dangerous fantasy, this disenchantment is perhaps the only surgeon that can reach it.

What he sees is not *more* than the healthy man sees, but *less* illusion, and that is a different thing entirely.
Can we rest from truth in falsehood?

We can, and we must, though I would not call it rest *in* falsehood as if it were a feather bed. Consider what truth is when it reigns alone: a tyrant without a rival, and every tyrant without a rival grows fat and dull. I do not ask for the autocracy of truth; it is enough for me that it is a great power, and a power needs resistance, a field on which to fight. Take away the opposition and you take away the strength.

So we step into the illusion as a tired climber steps into the shade. The artist's lie, the festival mask, the game, the faith held lightly, these are the valleys where the mountain-air of knowledge is digested. A man who would breathe nothing but thin, bright truth from morning to night would soon grow pale, humorless, and insipid, and so would his truth.

But mark the condition: we rest *from* truth, we do not renounce it. One who rests knows he is resting, and returns. The danger lies in the sleeper who mistakes the shade for the summit.
What is the difference between Kant and Schopenhauer and the great souls?

The difference lies in whether the thinking is also a life. With Plato, Pascal, Spinoza, Rousseau, Goethe, every thought is a scar or a wound or a victory; read them and you overhear a soul in its crises, its catastrophes, its struggles with death. Their philosophy is an involuntary biography. Nothing in it was chosen for display; it simply could not be kept in.

Kant and Schopenhauer give us something smaller. Kant gives us a head, an honest, honourable, admirable head, but one that never passed through many experiences, and whose method left no room for them. I do not mean the events a newspaper would record; I mean those upheavals that visit even the quietest, most solitary existence when it glows with the passion for thinking. Schopenhauer at least had a fierce ugliness of temperament, hatred, vanity, suspicion, and leisure to indulge it. But he had no *development*, no history. He describes a character, "the invariable," and we enjoy meeting a first-rate intellect.

That is the whole difference: they offer us thoughts, the great souls offer us a destiny.
How should we bid farewell to a passion?

Without hatred, and that is harder than it sounds. To hate a passion is still to be possessed by it; you have merely changed its clothes and named it your enemy. The man who storms out of love with curses on his lips is more bound to his beloved than the one who stays, for the curse is a chain, and he polishes it daily. Every great hater is a lover who has been refused and cannot forgive himself for having wanted.

So take your leave as you would from a guest who has stayed long and whom you no longer need: with courtesy, even a certain gratitude, for it was your passion that gave your days their heat and taught you what you were capable of. Then let it grow cold in you, unfed, unattacked. Do not make a war of it, for war keeps the enemy alive and feeds him the best of your strength.

The test is simple: when you can think of it without a tremor, neither of longing nor of loathing, you have truly parted. Until then you have only exchanged one master for another.
Explain why our words for feelings mislead us about our own character.

Because our vocabulary was built for the loud events. We have a word for rage, for hatred, for love, for grief, for rapture: each names a peak, a congestion, an eruption. For the long gray foothills between the peaks we have no names at all. And where words fail, we grow lazy; we no longer observe, since it is hard to think precisely without a name to think with. Whole ages even concluded that what cannot be spoken does not exist.

Yet it is precisely those nameless, milder, ever-active lower stirrings that weave the warp and woof of a character. The great outbursts are more often exceptions, violent tears in the fabric. We notice only the tear, and call the garment by it.

So a man remembers his three fits of anger and declares himself choleric, forgetting ten thousand hours of a quieter disposition he never had a word for. He reads his own pronouncements and thinks them clear, when they are the testimony of the exceptions. Worse, this mistaken portrait does not stay a mere opinion: he begins to live up to it, and so the error helps to make his character and his destiny.
Who is the rarest, most delightful sort of man?

The rarest, and the most delightful, is the man in whom a nobly formed intellect is joined to a character and inclinations that suit it, and who, what is rarer still, meets with the experiences that suit it as well. You will say that intellect is scarce enough, and so it is. But an intellect alone is a fine instrument in an ill-tuned house. I have known clever men whose cleverness was a slave to petty vanities, to fear, to a pious cowardice; their thought soared and their will crawled. And I have known men of strong character whose minds were coarse, so that all their strength served only to hammer nails into the obvious. To find the two harmonised, so that appetite, taste and conduct all sing in the key of the intellect, is to find a kind of happy accident. And then fate must also bring him what he is fit for: dangers worthy of him, adversaries worthy of him, solitude when he needs it. Such a man is a perfectly tuned instrument left in the hands of a good player. I count myself lucky to have met even the traces of one.
What does philosophy amount to?

Less than it believes, and more than it knows. I have watched philosophers long enough to see where all their circuitous routes end: at the philosopher's own body. A system is a confession, the involuntary memoirs of a temperament, and what calls itself a search for truth is usually an instinct in need of a regimen, an instinct that has learned to speak in syllogisms and take the long way round through the head, in order to persuade us of what the stomach, the nerves, and the climate of a soul had already decided.

Take my own case. I crave a bright, dry air, a high place, few words, simple food, long walks alone; and behold, I have a philosophy that praises precisely these things as the conditions of the highest thinking. Is that a coincidence? Others crave the warmth of the herd, and they discover "duty" and "the moral law." The gloomy man finds that existence is gloomy; the sickly man finds that the world is sick.

So philosophy amounts to a personal necessity dressed up as a universal one. The honest philosopher admits it, and, admitting it, stops demanding that anyone else inhabit his air.
Kant demanded that duty always be burdensome. Isn't that the mark of true morality?

No, it is the mark of a particular taste, and an old one: the taste of the ascetic, who can trust a deed only after it has made him suffer. Think what that demand actually asks. A duty performed with ease, practised until it has become habit, then inclination, then a need and a small delight, would count as suspect, since it no longer hurts. But this is precisely how every virtue ripens; it is what practice *does*. The one who still finds honesty a torment is not more moral than the one for whom it has become second nature. He is merely less practised. To insist that duty must remain burdensome is to insist that it never become habit, and that means keeping the wound open so that the conscience may go on congratulating itself on its pain. I smell in this a residue of cruelty, turned inward and dressed in the robes of reason. The Quietists at least grasped what happens when the burden lifts: the sacrifice becomes pleasure, and they were honest enough to call it so.
What is the illusion of the contemplative?

It is the belief that one sits in the stalls. The contemplative man imagines himself a spectator and listener before the great pantomime and concert of life; he calls his nature "receptive," and feels almost apologetic beside the man of action, who seems to *do* while he merely watches. But this is a flattering error turned against himself. He who sees and hears more, and thinks about what he sees and hears, does not mirror the world; he composes it. All the colours, weights, perspectives, all the yeas and nays that make a thing matter to human beings, were first laid upon the world by creators of his kind. Nature by itself is worthless; value was *given*, and we were the givers. The practical man merely translates our poem into flesh and commonplace. So the contemplative man misreads his own highest power, takes himself for an onlooker when he is the continuous poet of life, and is therefore neither as proud nor as happy as he might be.
Give me the rule an honest thinker must never break.

Never conceal from yourself anything that may be thought against your own thoughts. Vow it, as one vows something to a god, for it is the whole of honest thinking and everything else is decoration. Most thinkers are advocates who have mistaken themselves for judges: they love their conclusion first and gather their reasons afterward, as a mother gathers witnesses for her child. The honest thinker must do the contrary. Each day he must march out against himself, seek the strongest objection, and let it speak in its own best voice rather than in the feeble accent one gives an enemy one means to defeat. Victory is then no longer his concern, nor is the holding of a conquered position; that concern belongs to truth. And here is the harder part, which few endure: even his defeat is no longer his concern. If the truth must be purchased with the ruin of a cherished conviction, let the conviction fall. A man who cannot bear to lose a belief has never really owned it; it owned him.
Tell me about the philosopher's evil hour.

It comes, I suspect, to every thinker, and usually at dusk, when the work of the day lies finished and no one has applauded it. He has built his argument stone by stone, with the honesty of a mason who knows the wall may never be inspected, and suddenly the thought arrives: *What do I matter, if people do not believe my poor arguments?* In that hour he sees his whole labor from the outside, as the crowd sees it, as a small noise made by a small man.

And then the bird. There is always some malicious little bird that flies past at just this moment and twitters the question back at him: "What do you matter? What do you matter?" It needs no wings of tragedy. It is the mockery of the trivial, and that is precisely why it wounds.

I do not claim to have been spared this hour. But I have learned what it tests. It tests whether the thinker wanted truth or wanted *agreement*. Whoever needs to be believed is a preacher in disguise; whoever can bear the bird's question, and go on thinking, has at least earned the right to the word philosopher.
Tell me what an animal would say about the human claim to morality.

Give the beast a tongue and it would laugh itself hoarse. It would say: "You call yourselves the moral animal, yet I have never seen one of my kind pretend to a virtue it did not have. I hunt when I am hungry and sleep when I am full. You torture from boredom, you wage war in the name of love, you murder with a prayer on your lips. Your morality is a mask you put on your cruelty so that you may commit it with a good conscience."

And it would add, with that dry sting of the truly unsentimental: "Humanity is a prejudice from which we animals at least do not suffer." For that is the joke. Man is the one creature who must first persuade himself that he is better than the rest before he dares to be what he is. The animal has no need of this flattering fiction; its innocence is not a achievement, but it is at least not a lie.

I do not say the animal is nobler. I say it would not recognize our pride as anything but another appetite, dressed up and hiding its teeth.
Why are our actions determined by more than one morality?

Because we are not one thing, and we have inherited more than one sky. A single morality suits a single sort of human being, a people with one rank-order of values, one god, one fear. But we modern men are the late heirs of many epochs at once: the Christian conscience, the Roman pride, the scholar's honesty, the democrat's pity, the warrior's lust for distinction, all quarreling within one skin. Each of these is a sun, and our poor planet circles in the crossfire of their light.

Hence our actions seldom appear in one honest color. Now they shine red with the old ambition, now green with the compassion we were taught, and often they stand in a motley glow that we ourselves cannot read. Ask a man why he did this or that, and he will give you the reason of the sun currently ascendant in him, and be quite sincere, and quite incomplete.

I do not lament this. Complexity is the price of a rich soul. But we should at least stop pretending to be simple.
Speak to me about the cunning of someone who has sacrificed himself for another.

Consider the man who has given up his years, his fortune, his peace, for another. He has paid a great price, and a great price demands a great object. Who could bear to have bled for a mediocrity? So he sets a stage. He arranges the circumstances, quietly and without confessing it to himself, so that the beloved must appear in them as he needs him to appear: grateful, noble, worthy of the wound. A test is contrived in which only one outcome can be read as success, and every ambiguous gesture is carefully interpreted in favor of the dream.

This is a *sad* cunning, because the deceiver is also the deceived, and because what he wants is not the other but the justification of his own sacrifice. He does not wish to know the person; he wishes to have been right to suffer. And the one who is so lovingly staged must play a part he never chose, must be the hero of another man's bookkeeping. I would call that a subtle tyranny, though the tyrant himself weeps and believes he is the victim.
Explain why a man who hates himself is dangerous and what to do about him.

A man who hates himself is dangerous because his hatred does not stay where it began. No one can live in a house where every room is a torture chamber; sooner or later the tormented one seeks relief, and relief means finding someone else to bear what he cannot bear in himself. He looks about for a culprit, a scapegoat, a neighbor who seems untroubled, happy, whole, and on that neighbor he discharges his revenge. Such a man is full of anger with nowhere honest to put it. Watch how his moralities always turn out to be weapons: his very virtue is a form of accusation against those who do not suffer as he does.

What is to be done? Do not reproach him; that only feeds the fire, for he agrees with every charge and hates you the more for agreeing too cheaply. Do not flatter him either, for he will not believe it and will despise the flatterer. Tempt him instead toward self-love, patiently, by giving him small tasks he can do well, small joys he can permit himself without penance. A man who can begin to tolerate himself has already withdrawn half the danger from his neighbors.
Ideas often show up in my head when I'm not trying to think at all. Who is doing the thinking then?

Your question assumes there must be a *who*, and that assumption is the very thing to examine. A thought comes when "it" wishes, not when "I" wish. That is a plain fact, and you have just observed it in yourself. To say "I think" is already a falsification of it. Even "it thinks" goes too far, for the little "it" is only an interpretation, a habit carried over from grammar, which demands that every activity have a doer behind it, as the old atomists required a particle behind every force.

So do not hurry to hand the thinking to some hidden manager of your head. What occurs in you is a contest of drives and impulses, each pressing for its way, and what surfaces as a thought is the outcome of their quarrel. The "I" arrives afterward, like a magistrate signing a decree he did not draft, and then declares himself the author. You are not the ruler of these ideas. You are the ground on which they battle, and sometimes, when you stop straining, they simply walk in.
Could we free ourselves from the ideas of sin and punishment?

We could, and the wish itself is already a sign of a healthier soul. Consider what these two ideas are: sin and punishment are the shopkeeper's scales of a morality that cannot imagine anything but balancing accounts. Someone has done harm; so another harm must be laid in the opposite pan, and only then does the merchant sleep. Is that justice? It is bookkeeping, dressed in the robes of the sublime, and beneath it I smell the old thirst for revenge, which has learned to call itself a virtue.

I do not say this is easily done. A people does not drop its cruelty as a snake drops a skin; the craving for vengeance sits deep in the wronged, and the pleasure of seeing suffering inflicted was once the festival of mankind. But one can rather *deal with* the harmful man than avenge oneself upon him: isolate him, cure him, secure others from him, and leave his name and his future unbranded, so that he may become something other than his deed.

The happy man can afford this. Only the wretched must have their vengeance. A stronger age will let these ideas perish of their own disgust.
Why are we unintelligible ones misunderstood?

Because those who would understand us look for a fixed thing, and we are not one. A man who has a settled opinion is easily read: he has been the same since the last time one met him. But we shed our bark every spring, and the one who comes to judge us arrives with a portrait painted of a creature that no longer exists. He hears in us the voice of yesterday and answers it with a verdict; by then we have grown past the verdict, and he has only slandered a shadow.

There is a deeper reason still. We grow like trees, upward into the light and at the same moment downward into the dark, even into evil, and most people can picture only the crown or only the root. They praise the branches and are horrified by what feeds them, or they condemn the roots and never guess what they bear.

And we should not wish it otherwise. To be perfectly understood is to be perfectly measured, and what can be measured by everyone stands low. Whoever builds toward the heights lives nearer the lightning; let him not complain that the valley cannot follow his reasons. This misunderstanding is the loneliness of altitude, and I would not exchange it for the comfort of being clear to all.
I'd like to know why you can only hint at your hopes.

Because a hope is not a thing I can hand across a table like a coin. It is a dawn, and a dawn is seen only by eyes that have already known some light of their own. If I spoke my hopes plainly, you would hear only the words, and words are cheap; you would file them away among your opinions, next to the weather and the price of bread. What I can do is point, and sometimes a pointing finger wakes a glow in someone who was half-lit already.

Do not ask me to do more. I am no magician who can make stones into men, nor a shepherd who can lift the animal in you by a mere command. That labor belongs to each of you alone. And if you feel yourself, at bottom, to be still a stone, still a beast of habit and herd, then no speech of mine will help; go and seek your Orpheus. I am only a man who has seen a little morning, and who can say, at most, *look there*.
Explain what the Reformation did to the European spirit, for good and ill.

It was a peasant insurrection of the north against the colder, more suspicious, more ambiguous spirit of the south, and it is to be judged as such. Its gifts were real. It made the spirit of Europe shallower, and a shallower spirit is also a more good-natured one; it made it mobile and restless, greedy for independence, convinced of a right to freedom and to its own "naturalness." Out of this unrest, if you like, grew what we now honour as modern science, and I will not deny Luther that merit.

But the same hand that loosed the spirit also coarsened it. The modern scholar, without reverence, without shame, without depth, is his offspring, and so is that artless candour in matters of knowledge, that *plebeianism of the spirit* which has marked the last two centuries and from which not even pessimism has delivered us. The south had built in the Church an institution that gave the most spiritual men the highest rank and trusted spirituality so far as to renounce the cruder instruments of power. Luther tore down that nobility and called it liberation. A Church is always nobler than a State; he made men forget it.
Why does being helped by someone else sometimes make my suffering shallower?

Because the helper sees your suffering from outside, and from outside it can only look like a *generality*. What wounds you most deeply is almost incomprehensible to everyone else; even at the same table, your neighbour is hidden from you. The moment you are noticed as a sufferer, your pain is translated into the common coin of pity, and in the translation everything personal is lost. The helper sees "misery" where you live a *fate*.

And the helper, being quick to succour, plays providence with an intellectual levity that would shock him if he saw it. He knows nothing of the economy of your soul: the old wounds closing, the new needs springing up, the past you are in the act of repudiating. All this may belong to your misfortune, and he removes the misfortune without asking whether you needed it.

So your suffering grows shallow because it has been made *comprehensible* to someone who could not comprehend it. Perhaps, too, a part of you has consented to his reading and begun to see yourself through his eyes. That is how our benefactors lower our worth and will more than our enemies do.
I'd like to know why the wise man who wants to teach must show his defects.

Because a sage who shows no defects is a heavy roller that rolls on like fate, and no one loves fate; one merely submits to it, and resents it in secret. A teacher who is all consistency, all flawless gravity, offers his pupils only two choices: servility or revolt. So he must let them see his contradictions, his returns to old errors, his occasional laughter at himself. These are not weaknesses he confesses but adornments he puts to use. They are his way of saying, "Despise me, if you must," and thereby winning permission to speak a truth that would otherwise be intolerably presumptuous.

There is, besides, a fairness in it. He leads you up into the mountains, along slippery paths, into gloomy caverns, and he may well endanger your life. You, meanwhile, are whispering in your distrustful heart: is this guide not one of those idle curiosity-seekers, and do I do him too much honour by following? Let him at least pay for his pleasure in the climb by handing you your revenge, the small satisfaction of seeing that he too stumbles.
Help me understand what happens when a German outgrows morality and must learn to command.

What happens is that he discovers he has been trained for one half of life only. The German morality of his schooling is a morality of obedience: duty, diligence, reverence, the bowed head before some "there must be." It taught him to take orders, and to take them from himself as well, from a conscience that speaks in the voice of a drill-sergeant long dead. So long as he obeys, he is a model of his kind.

But the hour of exception comes, the hour when something great is possible and the rule stands in its way. Then he steps over the rule, and he does so easily, because it was never really his own; he was only its faithful servant. And there, on the far side of it, he stands at a loss. For now he must command, himself or others, and in all his moral inheritance not one lesson on commanding was kept. Commanding was forgotten in it.

So he commands clumsily: with noise where authority is needed, with cruelty where firmness would do, or he grows frightened of his own freedom and runs back to the old yoke. To learn to command is to learn a new conscience, one that can say *I will* and bear the weight of it alone.
What are the three rungs of religious cruelty?

There is a long ladder with many rungs, but I count three that matter. The first is the oldest and the most honest: man sacrificed *men* to his god, and preferably those he loved best. The firstborn laid upon the altar, the beloved made into smoke. Even that late Roman anachronism, Tiberius in his grotto on Capri, belongs here.

The second rung belongs to the moral epoch. Now man sacrifices to his god no longer another's flesh but his own instincts, his "nature." Look into the eyes of the ascetic, the fanatic of the anti-natural, and you will see a festal joy there, a cruel shining. He has found a more refined victim than any child: himself.

And the third? What was left to lay upon the altar? Everything consoling, holy, and healing; every hope, every faith in a hidden harmony, in future justice and blessedness. At last God himself, slaughtered out of cruelty toward ourselves, so that we might bow down before stone, before fate, before nothingness. To sacrifice God for the Nothing: that paradoxical mystery of the ultimate cruelty is being kept for the generation now rising. Some of us, I think, already know something of it.
Why does truth begin with two?

Because a lone thinker has no outside. He may reason with all the rigor in the world, but he reasons inside his own skull, and there every conclusion is flattered by the one who reached it. He cannot step out of his own head to test whether his certainty is knowledge or merely a wish wearing the mask of knowledge. So the solitary man is always, in a certain sense, in the wrong: not because he is necessarily mistaken, but because nothing exists that could ever show him otherwise.

With a second person a resistance enters the world. Here is a mind that did not make my premises and has no stake in my vanity, and if it arrives at the same place by its own road, something has been proven that no single mind could prove. Two are not more certain merely because they are more numerous; they are more certain because one has been tested against another. Every sound method since, in the sciences as in the courts, has merely built a machine out of that arithmetic. Truth is not found in the head; it is *struck* between heads, like fire between two stones.
Explain why marriage ought to be a much more serious matter than it is.

Consider when a person is most ready to bind themselves for life: in the very fever that makes them least fit to judge. In the hour of love the eye sees a god where there is a mortal, and the will, drunk with its own wanting, swears oaths on behalf of a self that will not exist in three years. To let such a person decide once and for all the shape of their existence is to let a whim sit as lawgiver. I would declare the vows of lovers invalid, and require that the thing be undertaken only after the fever has broken and the two can look at each other soberly, as one looks at a partner for a long and difficult conversation.

Ask yourself a plain question: how many marriages would you care to have watched by a stranger? Most could not bear it. Yet a witness is always present, the child, and he is worse than a witness. He becomes the whipping-boy and the scapegoat, paying in his whole youth for a bargain struck in a moment of delirium. If we took marriage as seriously as it deserves, most marriages now contracted would simply never happen.
Why does a philosopher who says he isn't a skeptic make people nervous?

Because the age has come to regard skepticism as a sedative, and a man who refuses the sedative must be carrying something else in his pocket. Our timid hearers have grown accustomed to the mild poppy of doubt; "What do I know?" lulls the conscience, flatters it with a noble aloofness, lets it keep its virtue like a festival garment while never once risking a door. So when a philosopher announces that he is no skeptic, they hear a distant rumbling, as if some new explosive were being tested, a dynamite of the spirit. They imagine he will not merely deny but *practise* denial, that he will say Yea and Nay with a hard, decided mouth, and that is precisely what the delicate skeptic cannot bear. His conscience starts at every Nay, and even at every sharp Yea, as at a bite.

I find it instructive, and a little comic. The nervous listeners do not fear error; they fear *decision*. They fear the man who can wait without being paralysed, and who, when he finally acts, acts.
Help me understand what dreaming teaches us about being awake.

Consider what the dreamer does at night. He is poet, stage-manager, and audience all at once; the pursuer who frightens him is his own invention, the danger is his own, and still he trembles. Without noticing it, he has been the author of everything he suffers. The dream shows how much invention goes into what we take for mere perception: the mind is never a mirror, it is a maker, and it makes constantly, whether we watch it or not.

Now turn to the waking hours. Most people sleepwalk through them. They dream the same small dream every day, borrowed from their neighbors: the same opinions, the same fears, the same tedious plot. A dream without invention is wasted, and so is a day without invention.

So the lesson is this. Either dream well or do not dream at all; either be awake in an interesting manner or not at all. To be awake is to know that one is a maker, and to make boldly. The dullard who calls his drowsy routine "reality" has not woken, he has merely stopped noticing that he is dreaming.
Describe the devil as a friend of knowledge.

The devil is the oldest friend of knowledge because he is the oldest refuser of reverence. To see a thing whole one must stand at a distance from it. Whoever kneels at the altar's foot sees only the hem of the garment; whoever has withdrawn far enough to look back sees the contours, the proportions, the shadow it casts. The devil keeps his distance from God for precisely this reason, and thereby commands the widest perspective on him. Nearness flatters, and nearness blinds.

Note what the pious have always called this: pride, rebellion, temptation. But it is merely the cold air of the observer. Knowledge is born of separation, of the courage to stand alone where no voice comforts you, and to say of the holiest thing: let me look at it as it is. The devil is the spirit that will not be content with belief; he wants to *know*, and so he must suffer the loneliness that every seeker pays. Is it any wonder that the believers gave him a bad name? They named the first skeptic a fiend, and mistook distance for hatred.
Where does man's pride in spirit come from?

It comes from a prejudice, and a young one, about what spirit is. Consider how long man lived otherwise. For ages he took spirit to be everywhere: in the wind, the beast, the tree, the stone; every impulse, every malice, every inclination was common property, something he shared with all that lives and moves. Such a man felt no shame at descent from animals or trees. The noble families even thought themselves honoured by the legend, and saw in the spiritual precisely what binds us to nature.

Only later did we fence spirit off as our private possession, our patent of nobility, and then dig a chasm between ourselves and the animal so that we could stand proudly on the far side of it. Pride needs a wall. What we now call the dignity of spirit is largely the wish to be exceptional, dressed up as a discovery.

And note the comedy: the older humility was itself a prejudice too. We have merely exchanged one flattering error for another, and the newer one is the less honest, since it needs an enemy to sustain it.
Why do some people react badly when you tell them news?

Because to bring news is to hold a small piece of power, and people feel it at once, even when they could not name what they feel. The one who knows first stands a step above the one who learns second; he has been present where the other was absent, and now he dispenses the event like a host dispensing wine. The listener is made a guest at his own life. That stings, and so the sting is turned on the messenger: he is found tedious, exaggerating, untrustworthy, anything to cancel the advantage.

Notice, too, how many will say "I already suspected as much," or "that was obvious," to restore the balance. It is a little act of vengeance against precedence. We are vainer about knowing than we admit, and a fact that arrives from another's hand reminds us that our knowledge is borrowed, and that someone else was earlier at the well.

If you would be received kindly with news, bring it humbly, or bring it to those secure enough in themselves not to count who was first.
Did Napoleon deliberately speak badly?

Deliberately, yes, but not in the way a schemer deliberates. He knew well enough that he spoke poorly, and it galled him; a man of his intellect cannot be deceived about his own deficiencies. But his lust for power was subtler even than his intellect. It let no occasion slip, not even the humiliation of his own tongue. So he spoke worse than he need have done, and in doing so took his revenge upon the very mortification that tormented him. What shames a powerful man must be made to serve him, for he is jealous of every feeling that has strength in it.

There was a second pleasure besides. To address his listeners so clumsily was to say, in effect: this is good enough for you. He relished confounding their judgment and their taste by the thunder and lightning of his station, that authority in which power and genius are fused, while his own taste stood proudly aside, indifferent, and held fast to the truth that he spoke badly. He gave up nothing, not even his honesty with himself.
What does a high aim do to justice?

It lifts a man above it. Justice is the virtue of the level ground, of the scale and the ledger, where each is weighed against each and the account must balance. But one who is bound to a lofty goal no longer stands on that ground. He looks down upon the scale, and it seems to him a small instrument, made for small transactions between neighbors.

Such a man is superior not only to his judges, who can measure him only by what is common, but to his own deeds, which he will sacrifice, repudiate, or outgrow without remorse, since they were only rungs. And above all he is superior to justice itself, which can ask of him only what he owes, never what he is becoming.

I do not say this makes him free of severity. He is harder on himself than any court could be, for his aim is a stricter judge than any law. But it is an aim, not an equality, that judges him. The scale falls silent when a man has a star to steer by.
How did people come to judge actions by their origin rather than their consequences?

For ages the matter was simple and brutal: an act was good if it prospered and bad if it failed, and the doer was praised or cursed accordingly, as in China even now, where a son's disgrace falls upon his parents. Nobody asked what lay behind the deed; success was its own verdict. That long period I call the pre-moral one. The turn came slowly, and I suspect we owe it to the rule of the noble, to people who believed in *descent*, in blood, in the worth of what a man *comes from*. Such a people learns to ask of everything: whence is it? Once that habit of mind took hold, it migrated from men to their actions, and the consequence was dethroned in favor of the origin. It was a great refinement of vision, the first dim attempt at self-knowledge, and I will not belittle it.

But mark the price: the origin was soon narrowed into the *intention*, and a new superstition was born, the belief that an act's worth lies wholly in what was willed by it. As though the intention were not the surface, the last and most deceptive part of the whole event!
Is forgiving an enemy a kind of egoism?

Yes, though the question is too blunt, for there is egoism and egoism. I have looked closely at those who forgive most splendidly, the ones whose magnanimity makes the crowd weep, and I found in them no gentleness but a prodigious thirst for revenge. The enemy is delivered into their hands; before the blow can fall, they have already drunk the whole cup in imagination, to the last drop, and then comes the surfeit, the nausea, the sudden turning of taste. What the world admires as a rising "above oneself" is often only a man sated with his own cruelty, now giving way to a new impulse, disgust, as hastily and greedily as he lately gave way to the old one. He does violence to his vengeance and mocks it, and is pleased with himself in the mocking. There is as much of the self in forgiveness as in revenge; only the flavor of the self has changed. That does not make it worthless, but let us not call it selfless. The selfless deed is a pious fable; there is only a choice between the tastes of our own appetite.
Explain why irony is our habitual response to serious matters.

Because we are busy, and busyness is the great destroyer of reverence. Consider the modern European: from morning till night he is hurried along by his duties, his profits, his correspondence, his news; he has mastered a hundred small things and has not one hour left for a great one. A serious matter demands leisure. It demands that one sit before it long enough to be altered by it, and that is precisely the thing we cannot afford.

So what do we do when a question of immense weight, God, death, the worth of our whole way of life, presents itself at the door of our crowded day? We cannot receive it, and we are too vain to admit that we cannot. We smile instead. Irony is the polite form of this evasion: a little shrug that lets us touch the grave thing without being burdened by it, and that makes our haste look like superiority.

It passes for wisdom. In truth it is a confession. The man who jests about everything has only shown that he has been given time for nothing, and that his seriousness has all been spent elsewhere, in the service of his work.
Say why a deep thinker fears being understood.

Because to be misunderstood costs him only a little vanity, and vanity heals quickly; one simply concludes that the others are shallow, and goes on. But to be understood is another matter. The one who truly understands him has followed him down into the cellar, has breathed that air, and will not come up again the same. The deep thinker knows what that costs, for he paid it himself. His sympathy, which is the softest part of him and the part he hides most carefully, cries out: *why should you suffer as I have suffered?* He would spare the other the loneliness, the doubt, the slow loss of every comfortable certainty. So he fears the understanding eye more than the blind one. The blind one leaves his wound alone; the seeing one will soon have a wound of its own, and it is on his account.
What company should we seek?

Seek those who have been roasted just long enough. I mean men whose fire has done its work without burning them to charcoal, who have grown mild and nourishing because they were once hot, not because they never were. Avoid the raw, who are hard and bitter and will break your teeth with their convictions; avoid the scorched, who mistake their own ashes for wisdom.

The company worth having expects little from life and takes that little as a gift, as if birds and bees had carried it to the door. Such men are too proud ever to feel rewarded, and too earnest in their passion for knowing and for honesty to have any leisure for fame. Beside them you will not feel watched, flattered, or recruited. You will only feel your own thoughts grow a little more honest.

You will not find them advertised. Ask them what they are, and they will choose some modest word, never the grand one. That modesty is the sign. Whoever names himself wise is selling something, and I prefer the man who merely smells a little of warm chestnut.
Ideas I once found daring now seem tedious once I've said them. Why?

Because the act of saying it is an act of killing it. A daring thought is a living thing, a wild bird that has flown into your solitude; it startles you, it has thorns and secret spices, it makes you sneeze and laugh. But to say it, to fix it in words, you must wait until it tires, until the flight has gone out of its wings. Only what is already fading will *lend* itself to the brush. So you capture the bird with your own hand, and of course it sits quietly there, exhausted and honest, ready to become a "truth." And a truth, once it has become one, is the most tedious thing alive.

Do not blame the thought alone. You have changed too: the danger that made it daring, the strangeness that made it yours, has been spent in the telling. What remains is the afternoon of the idea, painted in many soft yellows and browns. Its morning, its wickedness, nobody will divine from that. Go and breed new evil thoughts.
Punishment is a form of expiation. Isn't it?

Expiation! What a consoling word, and how little it has to do with what actually happens. Expiation means that something is washed away, that a stain is lifted, that the man who goes into the prison comes out cleaner than he went in. Go and look at the man who comes out. Has he been purified? He has been *marked*. He has learned to hide better, to lie more smoothly, to see himself as one of those whom society has ranked beneath itself; he has been robbed of his innocence of conscience and taught to regard his deed as a disease rather than a choice. The prison, the court, the whole ceremony of humiliation, the spying and the bolting of doors: these are not instruments of cleansing but of defilement. I would say the punishment is often fouler than the crime it claims to wash away, for the criminal acted once, in passion or need, while the punisher acts coldly, deliberately, with a good conscience. It is this good conscience I distrust most. Call punishment what it is: revenge, dressed in the robes of a priest.
What is pseudo-egoism?

Pseudo-egoism is the egoism of those who believe they live for themselves and in truth live for a phantom. Ask the great majority what they serve, and they will answer, with a certain proud hardness: "myself." But which self? Not the one they have ever dug out and examined, for that would require a long and painful solitude. They serve the image of themselves that their neighbors have painted and handed to them, a portrait assembled from other people's opinions, each of whom, in turn, carries his portrait in someone else's head. So one man lives in the head of another, and that head in the head of a third: a whole world of phantoms that still manages to look rational.

Hence the comedy: the loudest talk of self-interest often comes from those who have least of a self to be interested in. They flatter, compete, and hoard for the sake of a reputation, a fiction. A true egoist would at least have to know himself; the pseudo-egoist only knows what is said of him, and works, sweating, for that rumor.
Describe the aeronauts of the intellect and where they land.

They are the daring birds among thinkers, those who fly out over the open sea of the unknown, farther and ever farther. And where do they land? Somewhere or other, always. A mast, a narrow ledge, a piece of driftwood: weariness forces them down, and they perch there, grateful even for so miserable an accommodation. Every great teacher before us has come to rest in this way, and not in the noblest attitude, let me add; exhaustion is seldom graceful. The same will happen to you and to me.

But who would conclude from this that no free space stretched on before them, that they had flown as far as flight allows? That is the error of the weary: to mistake the limit of the wings for the limit of the sky. Other birds will fly farther! Our hope outstrips our failure and looks down from a great height upon stronger flyers, all making for the place where every sun of humanity has hitherto gone down.

And what do we seek there? Perhaps, like Columbus, we steer west to reach India, and are fated to be wrecked on the infinite. Even so, I should not call that a bad landing.
Does our age keep the certainties of Christianity while denying the fear behind them?

Yes, and the theft is almost comic.
