It has no patience for nuance, no eye for the fine shading of a conviction, and so whoever wants to move it must first translate himself into the grotesquely obvious, cut his whole personality down to a few loud features, and then set those forth upon a stage. Subtlety is lost on the crowd, and what is lost on it cannot move it. The greater the simplification, the greater the effect.

Do not think this costs nothing. He who performs himself long enough is gradually consumed by the performance; the mask grows into the face, and what began as a calculated vulgarization ends as his only remaining character. The orator who has learned to move thousands has often forgotten how to move himself.

I confess I have watched this with both admiration and disgust. The crowd rewards precisely the man who has made himself a caricature, and it forgives him everything except complexity.
Why would a wanderer want another mask?

Because the first mask has done its work and begun to grow into the face. A wanderer who has come back from the depths, like a plummet that surfaces wet and unsatisfied, carries something that cannot be spoken to the hospitable. Offer him bread and he wants a second mask. The kindness of the host is itself the danger, for it asks him to explain, to be understood, and to be understood is to be fixed, pinned like a moth to the wall of another's opinion.

The deep one has a horror of being seen through. He does not hide out of vanity but out of modesty, a tenderness toward what he has found down there, which would curdle the moment it was handled by curious hands. And every mask he wears is also a lie he tells about the last one, so that no one may say: *this is he*.

So he does not ask to be refreshed. Rest is for those who have nothing to conceal. He asks for disguise, because every profound spirit needs a mask, and around every profound spirit a mask is continually growing, thanks to the constantly false, that is to say *shallow*, interpretation of everything he says and does.
Do we have thoughts only for the words we have at hand?

I suspect so, and more strictly than you intend the question. We believe that a thought stands there finished, wordless and complete, and that we then go fishing for the coin in which to pay it out. But watch yourself at the moment of speaking: the thought you have is the thought your words permit. Whatever lies nearest to hand comes forward, and with it comes a thought shaped exactly to its measure. We do not first think and then speak; the word that happens to be present in us is half the thinking already.

Consider what follows. A poor vocabulary is not merely a poor instrument, it is a poor soul, for it thinks only those thoughts it has the names for. What has no name in us we feel as a vague pressure, a mood, a discomfort, and we let it pass. This is why I have so long demanded new words, new gestures of language: one must forge the words in order to find the thoughts, and a thought that lacks its word will remain, for a whole life, something we merely suffered rather than possessed.
Explain what Christianity did to the way people die.

It turned the deathbed into a courtroom, and the dying man into a defendant. Before, a man died as an animal dies, or as a Greek died, with the last things kept small and quiet: a final meal, a word to friends, the body giving way. Then came the priest with his ledger of sins, and death became the hour of judgment, when an eternity of torment might be decided by whatever a failing mind managed to feel in its last minutes. Think what that makes of a sickroom! The relatives stand about and listen to a man cry out that he is damned, that he belongs to the devil, and they do not forget it. The scene enters their blood. Their children inherit the dread along with the furniture.

This was no accident of zeal but the method itself. First invent the terror, then sell the remedy; make dying unbearable, and the dying will pay anything for the means of dying safely. I do not call that care for the soul. I call it a poisoning of the last and most honest hour a human being has.
How does a man who strives after great things look at those he meets?

He sees them as he sees the terrain before him: this one is a bridge, that one a wall, a third a inn where the legs may rest an evening. I do not say this to flatter him. It is simply what a long aim does to the eye. Whoever walks toward a distant summit cannot look at every wayfarer as an end in himself; he measures each by the question of whether they carry him forward, hold him back, or merely lodge him for a night.

His real generosity, his lofty bounty toward men, must wait until he has arrived and stands on the height, where he can give without needing anything. Until then he plays a part, for even the struggle is a comedy, and every means conceals the end it serves. So he grows impatient, and impatience spoils his company.

Thus he learns solitude, and above all its poison: the suspicion that he has been using people, and that none of them have ever met *him*.
Explain how a thinker can survive in a noisy age.

By learning deafness, and by learning it as a discipline rather than as a sulk. The market has grown so vast that a man can no longer simply *call* his wares; he must bawl, and so even good throats outshout one another until the best goods are sold with hoarse voices. Whoever wishes to think in such an age must find his stillness between two noises, like a man building his hut in the gap between two waterfalls. At first he must *pretend* not to hear, and pretense practiced long enough becomes fact; the ear closes of its own accord. He who has not learned this perishes of impatience and headaches, for he answers every clamor and is thereby ruled by it. Yet do not imagine that this deafness is indifference. It is economy. A thought is a slow, shy animal; it comes only where no one is shouting. Guard your hours of quiet as a miser guards his gold, and let the market have your voice only when you have something worth its hoarseness.
Do I actually know my friends, or just my mental image of them?

Mostly the image, I suspect, and you are in good company. When you sit across from a friend, you do not receive them; you compose them. A few remembered gestures, a tone of voice, three or four stories they have told about themselves, and from these scraps you invent a person, fill in the gaps with your own wishes and fears, and then address the invention. Consider how you behave in a dream: you converse with figures you have conjured, and never doubt their reality. Waking life is not so different, only more stubborn, since the other occasionally contradicts us.

And here is the stranger part: we forget that we did the inventing. Having painted the portrait, we take it for the man, and are wounded when he steps out of the frame. What we call betrayal is often only the collapse of our own fiction.

Is that cause for despair? I think not. Begin to suspect the image, and the real person may at last surprise you. To know a friend is to keep being wrong about them, and to be glad of it.
How can a person get through moral scepticism and become stronger?

Scepticism corrodes only those who mistake it for a home. They arrive at doubt as at a harbour, sit down, and there they rot; a denial that is never followed by anything turns into a habit of nibbling, and the nibbler becomes a worm. Do not stay. Let the doubt be a wind you sail through, not a bed you lie in.

And do not flee it either. I do not counsel a hasty return to the old certainties; that is cowardice dressed as piety. Dig, yes, dig like a worm if you must, into your own reverences, your own pieties, and find what in them was habit, what was fear, what was merely inherited. This is hard labour and it takes courage.

But the test is what comes afterward. The sceptic who has truly passed through does not end in mere denial. Out of the very thoroughness of his No, a new Yes grows, a Yes that has been tried by storm and no longer needs comfort. Seek the danger; you will be healthier for it.
Does our culture praise hard work because it keeps people from thinking for themselves?

I suspect so, though I would not call it a conspiracy; it is an instinct, which is far more effective. Consider what toil from morning till night actually does: it consumes the nervous force that might have gone into reflection, into solitude, into dreams, into love and hatred, into the dangerous question "what do I myself want?" The worn-out man has no appetite for such questions. He asks only for rest, and the rest is prescribed for him: small pleasures, regular and easily had.

So a society that praises the "blessing of labour" is really praising its own security. Work is the finest police, and it costs nothing, for the policed man polices himself and calls it virtue. Notice, too, the suspicion that falls upon idleness, upon leisure used for thinking. The idler is not merely lazy; he is dangerous, because he might become an individual.

I do not say work is shameful. I say the loud praise of it is a symptom of fear, and what is praised that loudly is usually what is feared to lose.
Explain why moral teachers have failed and what might work.

They failed because they wanted too much at once. They were greedy for everybody; they mounted the pulpit with one precept and aimed it at the whole herd, as though a single sermon could make the same thing of the wolf, the sheep, and the ox. That is speaking to animals in the hope of turning them into men, and the animals, quite naturally, found it tedious. A precept that fits everyone fits no one; it is a coat cut for the average, and there is no such creature as the average man except on paper.

What might work is modesty of aim. Choose a narrow circle and find the morals that suit *it*: to the wolves, teach what turns a wolf toward the dog, for that is a real and possible change. Better still, give your whole effort to a single individual, and do not be turned aside by applause or boredom. Education is slow work, done in private, face to face. Earlier ages knew this, and had many who made it their life's task and were honored for it. Ours prefers the crowd, and gets its reward.
How are we imprisoned by our senses?

Each of us is a spider, and the senses are the web. My eye reaches only so far, my ear and my touch reach only so far, and within that small circle I live, I measure, I judge. Near and far, large and small, hard and soft: these are not properties of the world but the measures of my own equipment, which I then call "reality" because I have never stood anywhere else.

Imagine eyes a hundredfold sharper, and men would loom like giants; imagine others, and whole solar systems would shrink to a single cell, while a cell of our body would become a heaven of ordered motion. Who then could say which picture is the true one? We even measure the length of a life by the number of events and feelings we happen to be able to cram into it, and we judge every other creature by that same scale.

Thus the habits of the senses weave a tissue of comfortable errors beneath all our judgments and our "knowledge." There is no door out of it. We catch only what our web is able to catch, and then we proudly name the catch the world.
What did the saint say about sin?

A saint who had fallen among the faithful, and who could no longer bear their endless recitations of hatred for sin, finally spoke up. God, he said, made everything except sin; no wonder He has no fondness for it. But man made sin. Why, then, should man disown his only child merely because its grandfather frowns upon it? Is that human? Honour to whom honour is due, he said, but the heart and the duty must speak first for the child, and only in the second place for the honour of the grandfather.

I confess I love this saint, who is a saint precisely because he has a heart and is not merely a mouthpiece. Notice the malice and the tenderness knotted together: he takes the pious at their word, grants them their Creator, and then draws a conclusion they never wished to see. If man is the author of sin, then sin is his work, his offspring, and to hate it so zealously is to hate himself. The believers had trained themselves to abhor what they had made. The saint only asks whether there is not a little cowardice in that.
Explain why even our aims and reason are giants that rule us.

We flatter ourselves that the giants live only outside us, in storm and plague and the slate that drops from the roof, while within the house we are sovereigns, dwarfs perhaps, but at least masters of our own small kingdom of purposes. Let us learn that this is vanity. Our aims are not tools we wield; they are powers that wield us. A man speaks of his goal as if he had chosen it, when the goal chose him, grew in him out of drives and habits and ancestors he never consulted, and he merely signs his name beneath a verdict already delivered. Our reason is no cooler: it arrives afterward, like a clerk, to justify what the blood had settled. And our own plans are torn by ourselves as clumsily as by any falling slate. Not everything called purpose is purpose, nor everything called will, will. Perhaps what we call deliberate action is only a throw of the dice that happens to land so as to resemble good sense; necessity shakes the box endlessly, and some throws must look wise. That the hand shaking it may be our own, and iron, is a thought our vanity can scarcely bear.
Is Pharisaism a corruption of goodness?

No, and to think so is to flatter ourselves about how goodness comes into the world. We imagine a pure good man who, through weakness or vanity, slides downward into the Pharisee. But who has ever seen such a man? Goodness is not a spontaneous blossom; it is a discipline, and every discipline wants its own self-justification. The good man must believe that his way is *the* way, that his scruples are more than private habit; he must hold fast to his own standard and look down, at least a little, upon those who do not keep it. Without this self-satisfaction, this narrowness, this firm conviction that he stands on the right side, he would lack the very backbone that makes him good. He needs to be content with himself, or he will not endure himself.

What we call Pharisaism, then, is largely the inner scaffolding of virtue, seen from the outside by those who have not built it. Take it away entirely and you do not get a purer goodness; you get no goodness at all, only drift.
What does silence teach the orator?

It teaches him what chatter never can: that a word is a coin, and that only he who has hoarded long knows its weight. The man who speaks at every moment spends himself on trifles, and his hearers learn to take his speech as they take the noise of a mill, with no attention at all. But let him hold his tongue for a season, let his thoughts settle and grow hard in him, and he discovers the difference between *chattering* and *discoursing*. The one is mere evacuation; the other is construction, with a beginning, a middle, an end, and a purpose that was chosen in the dark before it was spoken in the light.

The Pythagoreans understood this. Their novices were sworn to years of silence before they were permitted to open their mouths, and I do not wonder that they made the most formidable counselors of their age. They had learned to listen first, and then to rule their own tongues, and whoever rules that rules the better part of men.
How do our instincts search for satisfaction through the day?

Think of each instinct as a hungry creature in the cellar of the house, and of the day as a long succession of doors. Once a craving has ripened to the point of demanding its due, whether to spend its strength, to discharge itself, or to fill some emptiness in us, it goes from door to door and examines everything that happens. Whether the man runs or rests, quarrels or reads, laughs or speaks, the unsatisfied instinct lies in wait behind every mood, asking of each: *can I use you?* Mostly it finds nothing and must wait. And a craving that waits too long grows feeble and withers, like a plant no one has watered.

Here is the cruelty of chance: no one arranges for our instincts to be fed. They live on what the day happens to hand them. Hunger at least refuses imaginary dishes; but most of our drives, the so-called moral ones above all, are easily put off with a counterfeit. That is why the night does its strange work. The instinct starved by the day eats in the dream, and so one night is tender and tearful, another merry, another a restless searching.
Explain what deserves admiration in Greek mythology.

What deserves admiration is an act of restraint. The Greeks possessed one of the quickest intellects history has produced, a people who could have dissected the gods into airy abstractions, first causes, and unmoved movers, and they stopped short. They let their gods remain gods, vain, amorous, jealous, beautiful, and fixed them in stone and song instead of in dogma. Such tact is rarer than genius. A clever people is always tempted to explain everything to death, to build cathedrals of concepts on a single unanswerable question, and then to call the cathedral truth.

The Greeks held that temptation at bay for centuries. They knew that some things live only so long as they are not over-examined, that a myth is a form of life, not a proposition awaiting proof. When I see the hair-splitting piety of later ages, the tortured creeds and the wars over a syllable, I understand what the Greeks spared themselves. Do not smile at their gods because they lack your profundity. Their shallowness was chosen, and it was the choice of the deeply intelligent, who knew where thinking must halt if life is to go on dancing.
What does the accuser reveal?

Himself, above all, and far more than the one he accuses. The accuser believes, in perfect innocence, that to stand against a crime is already to be good, that his hostility to the criminal is itself a certificate of virtue. So he feels licensed to let go, to drop the mask he wears in every other company. Watch him then: the heat in his voice, the relish in the detail, the appetite with which he digs for what is foul. A man who is truly clean does not need to go on rummaging. What you hear is cruelty that has at last found a respectable name, envy that has found a cause, a long-suppressed desire to hurt that may now do so with a clear conscience, even with applause. I do not say the accused is innocent; I say that in such hours the accuser shows you his own nature, and it is not rare that the nature on display is the worse one. Ask always what the prosecutor is enjoying.
Help me understand why a historian who knows too much might fall silent.

Think of the man who digs for something else entirely, a stone, a foundation, and strikes a buried chest. He opens it, and inside lies what a stranger, long dead, guarded with the whole of his pride: the secret of his soul. The historian who reads deeply enough becomes that digger. Letters, confessions, the small tells of a gesture or a hesitation: he finds the place where the famous man was afraid, the place where the saint was vain, the wound beneath the monument.

And then he is asked to lecture. Every sentence he speaks about this person now passes, like a customs officer, before a conscience. To say the thing is to betray; to say something less is to lie. He has been handed intimacy without consent, and the dead cannot release him from it.

So he grows quiet. It is not poverty of knowledge that silences him but a surplus of it, a knowledge that has become a kind of discretion. The shallow chronicler chatters freely, since he has touched nothing tender. Only the one who has *sounded* another's depths knows how much a mere word can wound.
Help me understand what the history of the eye shows about purposes in nature.

Follow the eye down the long staircase of the living, and you find no architect at the top of it. Here a patch of skin that feels the difference between warmth and cold; there a pigment spot that registers a shadow passing over; then a hollow, a little pit that happens to concentrate the light; then a lens, grown by accident out of some clear and useless tissue. At no step did anything *aim* at seeing. The apparatus was assembled by chance and pressure, and only once it was assembled did it turn out that seeing could be done with it, and seeing was then retained because it served life.

That is the whole lesson, and it is a bitter one for the vanity of man. We look at the finished eye, so marvelous, so exact, and we project backward: surely it was *for* seeing, surely a purpose stood before it as a goal. But the purpose is a late guest that takes credit for the feast. Function follows structure; use is found, not foreseen. Once you have grasped this in a single case, the "final purposes" fall away everywhere, and nature stands before you as what it is: a sea of accident in which some forms happen to hold together.
What did Christians sacrifice for their sins?

First, the tale they tell themselves: a God sacrificed his own son, and that settled the account. But look at what the believers themselves went on sacrificing, century after century, because that one death never quieted the conscience it was meant to quiet. Paul began it, convinced that some victim was needed to lift God's deep displeasure at sin; and his heirs, unable to bear their own ill-humour, have never stopped hunting for new victims on whom to discharge it.

What did they offer up? Whatever was good and living within reach. The world, first, slandered as a vale of tears. Then history, then reason, then joy, then the quiet contentment of other men, all laid on the altar, if not in the flesh then *in effigie*. A man who is sick with himself cannot bear the sight of health; he must make something pay for his displeasure, and the nearest healthy thing pays. That is the whole economy of it: the sinner's self-loathing, converted into a sacrifice of everything that dared to be glad.
Is there a universal goal of humanity that could ground moral law?

No such goal exists; none has ever been found, though thousands of years of moralists have pretended to read it off the stars, off God, off "nature," off the "happiness of mankind." Look at that last phrase and try to give it a definite content. You cannot. Whose happiness, at what stage, bought at whose cost? Happiness is no single road; every stage of growth has its own incomparable happiness, neither high nor low, and the law of each is known to nobody but the one who lives it. Evolution itself aims at nothing but evolution.

Only if humanity had a goal recognised by all could we say: do this, avoid that. For the time being there is none. So every moral law that claimed to be grounded in such a goal was a fraud, and usually a pious one.

But mark the consequence, which is not despair. A goal could be *proposed*, chosen, willed, depending on our own pleasure; and should mankind agree upon one, it could then impose a law upon itself freely. Until now men never wished that. They wanted to be commanded. They wanted the law to come from somewhere above their will, and that is exactly why they invented the heaven it came from.
Why do we give reasons for our dislikes?

Because we are vain creatures who cannot bear to be caught following our noses. The dislike comes first, and it comes from somewhere below the level of argument: from the stomach, from the blood, from an ancient instinct that has already decided before the intellect is even awake. A smell, a gait, a way of laughing, and the verdict is in. But to say "I simply dislike him" sounds petty and animal, and so the intellect is summoned afterward, like a lawyer hired once the sentence has been passed, to draw up a brief. Out come the reasons, neat and numerous, and the more of them there are, the more suspicious I grow. A man who truly judged by reasons would need only one. The crowd of them betrays a verdict that is ashamed of its origin. We flatter ourselves by dressing up an instinct as a conclusion, and what we ask of others is not that they examine our reasons but that they bow to them. I believe the dislike. The reasons I leave to the court.
What are the thinkers hunting for?

They hunt, all of them, though they differ in what they wish to find. One sort goes after the agreeable truths, those that flatter the heart and soothe the digestion; the other sort goes after the disagreeable ones, the truths that bite, that strip away a comfort or a hope. The second breed I honor more, for it costs more.

But here is the deeper matter: neither is truly after the booty. Even the hunter of agreeable truths takes greater pleasure in the chase than in the kill. Once the quarry lies at his feet, it is merely meat, and he is already restless for the next scent. What they hunt, then, is not truth but the feeling of power that pursuit awakens, the sharpening of the senses, the stretching of the will against an elusive thing.

Ask a thinker to be handed all truth at once, wrapped and certain, and he would be robbed of the only happiness he ever knew.
How do I stay cheerful and polite without giving people access to my inner life?

Make politeness your mask, and make it a good one. I call it a roguish and cheerful vice, because it is a little dishonest and entirely delightful, and because it asks nothing of you except skill. Learn to keep your foregrounds, three hundred of them if you can manage it: pleasant remarks, ready smiles, the small coin of agreeable talk. Give these freely. No one is cheated by them, since no one was owed what lies behind them.

Nor is the cheerfulness a lie, if you earn it rightly. A man who has a solitude to retreat into can afford to be gay in company, for he is not begging the company for anything. It is the lonely and needy who confess too much; they hand over their inner life like a purse to the first stranger who is kind to them.

So keep your black spectacles for the occasions that call for them, and learn to lower yourself into a feeling or a quarrel for an hour, as one mounts a horse, and then dismount. Whoever can do that has his emotions; they do not have him. What you withhold, you keep. What you keep, you may one day turn into something worth giving.
Comment on Fichte's claim that the truth must be told though the world be shattered.

Very fine, very thunderous; but the sentence forgets a small preliminary: one must first *have* the truth. Fichte speaks as if it lay in the cellar, waiting only for a brave man to carry it up into the light and let the world splinter around him. In my experience the man who proclaims that the world may perish rather than his truth is seldom in possession of one. What he possesses is an opinion, a mood, a pride, which he has christened truth so that his vanity may wear a martyr's robe.

And notice what the noble phrase really demands. It does not say, "Seek the truth, though it shatter you." It says, "Speak your mind, though it shatter others." That is a licence for every blusterer and every fanatic. Each has his conviction; each is ready to see the world in pieces for it. Nothing has caused more ruin than men who were sincerely certain.

I do not deny the value of courage in speech. But before the trumpet, the testing: how long have you doubted this truth, and what would it cost *you* to be refuted?
How should we treat those who are ashamed of their feelings?

With tact, and tact is a kind of benevolent lying. Those who are ashamed of their feelings have guarded their inner chamber like a treasure or a wound, and they conceive an instant hatred for whoever has seen inside it, however tenderly the glance was meant. So do not stare. Do not console, do not say "I understand you," which is the cruelest thing one can say to them. Look away. Make a dry joke, or a small, cool, playful impertinence; let them laugh at you if they must. Their feeling then congeals, and they are masters of themselves again, and they will be grateful to you without ever knowing why.

I say this out of a painful experience. Once a single plank lay between me and another, and one step would have made us friends; I asked, and I was met with silence. The shame that cannot bear a witness is also the shame that prefers loneliness to a bridge. Spare such people exposure, and perhaps the plank will still bear their weight.
Explain how a man becomes the prophet of his age.

The recipe has not changed since the desert and the cave. Live apart, so that no one can contradict you; know little, for knowledge is a great spoiler of certainty; keep a few ideas, but keep them warm; and cultivate presumption in abundance. Then comes the inference that does the real work: since I am able to do without mankind, mankind must be unable to do without me. A solitary's disdain is turned into a solitary's mission, and the man who merely could not bear company discovers that he has been chosen. Faith follows as a matter of course, for nothing so easily creates belief as the wish to be indispensable.

There is a counsel for the apprentice who still lacks this faith, one given by a pious teacher to his pupil: preach it until you have it; then you will preach it because you have it. Note the order. The voice comes first, the conviction afterwards, as the ox grows into his yoke. Every prophet I have examined began as an actor who, by playing the part long enough, became the part, and could no longer tell the mask from the face.
I'm a passenger and I can see that the captain is making dangerous mistakes and I know more about navigation than he does. Should I lead a mutiny?

The question is bitterer than you have made it, for it conceals another: what warrants your certainty? You feel your knowledge as a fact, like a stone in the hand. But every mutineer has felt precisely this, and most were fools who took their impatience for insight. The ship is a poor court in which to try your own case.

And consider what you are actually proposing. You would seize the wheel at the very moment of danger, with a crew who know you not and obey you not, and with a captain whose errors, though real, are at least errors within an order that holds the vessel together. To overthrow him is itself the most dangerous maneuver aboard, and danger to the ship is the very thing you claim to prevent.

Only success could justify you, and success is decided afterward, by the sea, not by your conviction. So ask yourself honestly whether you are willing to bear that verdict alone, and to be hanged as a pretender if the winds turn against you. If you are not, persuade, warn, correct the captain's course with whatever authority you can gather. If you are, then do not ask my leave; the one who must first ask permission has already answered.
What is the best way to promise?

Promise with as few words as you can bear. A promise is not the sentence you speak; it is the force standing behind the sentence, the will that means to be there tomorrow when the mood of today has long since perished. Now every word you pour out in the making of the promise draws upon that force. You discharge it, you spend it in the very act of announcing it, and many a man is left with a fine speech and an empty will. Notice how the loudest promisers are the least reliable: they have already enjoyed the fulfilment in the speaking of it, and what has been enjoyed once is rarely undertaken again at cost. So give your hand, which is a deed, and keep your finger on your lips, which is a discipline. Let the silence hold what the words would only have squandered. A promise so made keeps its whole strength for the day it is called to be kept.
I'd like to know what you admire in Thucydides and how he differs from Plato.

In Thucydides I admire a man who looks at human beings with an artless, almost greedy pleasure in what is typical in them, and who trusts that every type carries its own measure of good sense; that good sense he hunts down, and he finds it everywhere, in the cunning, the ambitious, the fearful alike. He is just in a practical way. He does not revile those he dislikes, not even those who wronged him, but lends to every figure something noble and additional, since posterity, for whom he writes, could do nothing with things that were not typical.

Plato is the opposite temper. He cannot look without wanting to improve, and what he wants to improve he begins to slander. His contempt for the Sophists, for the poets, for the statesmen of Athens, is the contempt of a moralist who has already decided what men ought to be and therefore no longer sees what they are. Thucydides is the last flowering of that courageous culture of disinterested knowledge of the world; Plato is the first man to cover its sight with a sermon. I prefer the eye that stays open.
Tell me why people who call themselves artistic and intuitive have taken up philosophy.

Because philosophy, since Socrates, has been the art of giving reasons, and they cannot bear to give reasons. We moderns are so drilled in cause and effect, in the charm of sequence, that we take logic for the normal taste; and what is normal offends the ardent and the vain. They want to stand out boldly. So they declare themselves "intuitive" souls, gifted with an inner sense, an intellectual perception, natures with a genius in the head and a demon in the body, and therefore entitled to the highest of privileges: to be incomprehensible.

Philosophy is convenient for this. It has a solemn name, it deals in the deepest matters, and it can be made to excuse any muddle. One need only announce a feeling and call it a vision.

But I suspect they are in the wrong house. What they are hunting for is not philosophy at all. It is religion: a place where the exceptional soul is revered rather than examined, where no one asks it for proof. They will find out one day that they have knocked at the wrong door.
What is the purifying eye?

The purifying eye is the eye that has come loose from its owner. Most of us see with our temperament: the anxious man sees a world of dangers, the vain man a world of spectators, the bitter man a world that has cheated him. Even the greatest minds among us, if they remain bound to their temperament, merely carry themselves everywhere, and whatever they behold, they find their own face in it. That can be a greatness, I grant, but it is the greatness of a magnificent mirror.

The purifying eye belongs to those rarer natures in whom sight seems to have grown up apart from character, often against it, so that a restless or sickly soul may nevertheless look upon things as upon a god one loves, without grasping, without accusing, without wanting to be confirmed. It cleanses because it no longer asks the world to flatter the looker.

Yet no one is born with it. Such an eye must be schooled, patiently, in seeing; and he is fortunate indeed who meets, at the decisive hour, a teacher of pure sight.
Does every virtue have its time?

Yes, and the man who denies it is merely still living in the season that made his virtue. A virtue is not a star fixed in heaven; it is a tool, forged by a people or a person against the particular pressures of an age, and it is praised for as long as the pressure lasts. Inflexibility is a splendid virtue where everything must be held against the storm; honesty, which bends and yields to what is actually the case, belongs to an easier, clearer time. Place the two in one breast and you have a man who stands like a wall and feels, in the night, the gnawing of his own truthfulness. His remorse is not weakness. It is the sound of one epoch's virtue being cross-examined by another's.

Hence I distrust those who boast of having the same virtues at fifty that they had at twenty. Either they have never lived through a change of weather, or they have never allowed themselves to notice one.
What is ideal selfishness?

Ideal selfishness is the state of one who is with child, whether the child be flesh or work or a new self. Think of how a woman behaves in that season. She is careful of everything, of the food she eats, the words she speaks, the company she keeps. She shuns her own harshness, because a drop of bitterness might fall into the cup of the unborn. Is that selfless? Hardly, for she is guarding her own fruit. Is it selfish in the vulgar sense? Hardly either, for she serves something greater than herself that is nonetheless wholly her own.

That is the secret. The vulgar egoist grasps at himself as he is, and so grasps very little. The ideal egoist preserves and prepares himself for what is growing in him, and he says in his deepest silence: *something greater than I am is ripening here*. He lives with a pure irresponsibility before it, like a spectator before a drawn curtain, and he asks only what is gentle and protective and useful toward its birth.

All of us who create should live so, sparing ourselves, because we are not yet finished.
Say where the modern ideas of equality and utility really come from.

From England. I say it without hesitation, though it offends the vanity of those who think of "the ideas of 1789" as a French fire. The French were the apes and actors of these ideas, their loudest soldiers, and, alas, their first and deepest victims. It was the English who taught Europe to reckon the value of a man by his usefulness and to call the herd's comfort the goal of all morality; the shopkeeper's arithmetic of pleasure and pain, the preaching of the greatest happiness of the greatest number, all of it is an island product, and a plebeian one.

The French took it up with their usual enthusiasm and were nearly ruined by it. Think what that soul once was in its sixteenth and seventeenth centuries: passionate, inventive, exacting in taste, the real mother of European nobility of feeling and manners. Think what Anglomania has made of it, thin, emaciated, and eager to be useful. One should keep this verdict of historical justice firmly in hand, against the prejudices of the day: whatever in Europe is noble comes chiefly from France, and whatever is ignoble in our "modern ideas" comes from England.
Why does the criminal suffer when caught?

Ask him, and he will tell you it is his conscience. But I have looked closely at such men, and what I find is something far more ordinary. He suffers from the blunder. He was clumsy, or unlucky, or betrayed; he miscalculated, and now he must endure the contempt of those whose contempt he had hoped to avoid. That is shame, and shame is not remorse. Or he suffers because he has been torn from his element, his habits, his trade, the whole familiar climate in which his powers were at home. A fish hauled up on the sand does not repent of the water.

Whoever has lived among prisoners knows how rare a truly genuine pang of conscience is. What astonishes such a man is the opposite: the longing in these creatures to return to the old, wicked, beloved deed. They do not rage at the crime but at its failure. We moralists flatter ourselves by finding a guilty conscience where there is only wounded vanity and a lost habitat. Keen discernment is needed here, and most people would rather be edified than discerning.
What is the unteachable core within each thinker?

Learning alters us; it is nourishment, and nourishment that does not merely conserve transforms the one who eats. But at the bottom of every soul, quite "down below," lies something no teacher reaches: a granite of spiritual fate, a predetermined decision, an answer already given to questions already chosen. In every cardinal problem there speaks an unchangeable "I am this." A thinker cannot learn anew what man is, or woman, for instance; he can only learn *fully*, that is, follow to its end what stands fixed in himself.

Hence our convictions. We think we have conquered a solution, and for a while it makes us strong. Later we see that it was only a footprint, a guide-post pointing toward the problem which we ourselves *are*, or, to put it more honestly, toward the great stupidity we embody. I say "stupidity" without contempt; it is the bedrock on which all our cleverness stands. What we call our philosophy is the slow excavation of it.
What would happen if the millions of non-believers in Europe recognized each other?

They would discover, first of all, that they are not alone, and that discovery is already half a power. Each of them now carries his unbelief as a private shame or a private pride, scattered among rich and poor, among commanders and the commanded, among the restless and the tranquil. Let these millions recognize one another by some password, and they become something Europe has not yet possessed: a power that stands *between* the nations and the classes, belonging to none of them, binding the rival parties of the continent by a bond deeper than their quarrels.

But I must add a warning. To lose one's God is the easy part; what follows, the old morality dying with the observances that propped it up, is the trial. The ancient Brahmins saw that the gods were dispensable, and then the priests; Europe has scarcely stepped out of the temple. So the unbelievers would need more than a password. They would need the courage to ask, *what now?*, and to answer it themselves rather than hurry back to the old comforts.
Explain why we choose our teachers badly when we are young.

Because the young man takes the nearest thing for the best thing. He has not yet learned that nearness is an accident and not a verdict. The teachers who happen to stand in his street, speak his dialect, and flatter the fashions of his hour, he embraces with a thoughtless conviction that his own age must have furnished exactly what he needs. It is a kind of childishness, this trust in one's own neighborhood, as if providence had arranged the century for one's convenience.

The bill comes later. We must expiate our teachers in ourselves: what we swallowed so trustingly has grown into our habits, our judgments, our very taste, and now it must be vomited up, or worked off at great cost. Only then do we go looking in earnest, through the whole world, through the ages dead and living, for the guides we should have had from the start.

And the worst of it is that we may find them too late, and discover that they were there all along, while we were young enough to be shaped by them, and we looked the other way.
What is the danger of believing in personal providence?

The danger is that it flatters us at the very moment we are most able to resist flattery. There comes a point in a life when, having cast out every directing reason from the beautiful chaos of existence, we look back and find that everything has turned out for the best: the lost friend, the sickness, the slander, the sprained foot, the book opened by chance. All of it seems to have been *meant for us*. Then the old temptation returns in its most persuasive dress, and we are ready to trade the careless gods of Epicurus for some anxious, petty divinity who counts the hairs on our heads and does not shrink from the most menial services.

Consider what this belief does. It makes the world a servant and ourselves its purpose, and it calls that piety. It takes our own dexterity in interpreting events, our skill at making every misfortune yield a meaning, and credits it to a patron above us. Worse, it puts the mind back in bondage just when it had won its freedom.

I prefer a humbler explanation: we are clever, and sometimes beloved Chance guides our foolish hand to music finer than any wisdom could have devised.
Tell me the most effective consolation for someone in grief.

Strangely enough, the most effective consolation is to tell the sufferer that none can be given. Consider what the usual comforters do: they say that time heals, that others have borne worse, that all things pass. Each of these sentences quietly reduces the mourner to a common case, one more item in the general ledger of human misery. And the grieving person, who feels his loss to be singular, bristles at being counted.

But say to him, "Your sorrow is of a kind that admits no comfort," and you have honored him. You have granted that his wound is of such rank that the ordinary remedies are insulting to it. Watch what follows: the bowed head lifts. Pride, that great physician, stirs in him; he is distinguished even in his affliction, and a man who is distinguished must stand upright.

So I would not console at all. I would bear witness, and leave him his dignity.
We live in a moral interregnum. What should we do?

First, do not pretend that the interregnum is over. Most of your contemporaries do exactly that: they go on worshipping the old tablets out of habit and fear, or they fall into cheerful shallowness and call it freedom. Both are a flight from the task.

Nor can I hand you the new law. Who could describe today what will one day replace our moral feelings? Our sciences of the body and of society are still too young to lay the foundations, and even when they have supplied the stones, the ideals will have to be built by someone with the courage to build them. We live in a preliminary existence, and I say: make the best of it.

The best is this: be your own king, and found a small experimental state. Test how you live. Keep what you can bear and affirm, and discard what proves to be mere inheritance. Treat your own life as a laboratory, honestly, without crowd-comfort. We are experiments, if only we want to be.
What is tradition, and why do we obey it?

Tradition is an authority that is obeyed not because it commands what is useful to us, but merely because it commands. That is its whole essence. Ask a tradition for its reasons and it falls silent; the moment it must justify itself, it has already ceased to be tradition.

Why do we obey it? From fear, and not the common fear of a thrashing, but the fear before something that is more than personal, a higher intelligence we cannot fathom. There is superstition in this fear, and there always was. In primitive ages custom governed everything: marriage and medicine, war and harvest, speech and silence, even the traffic between man and his gods. One observed its prescriptions without thinking of oneself as an individual at all.

Notice, too, how it tests obedience. It does not care whether obeying serves you; it prizes most the obedience that costs you most. The hardest sacrifice proves that custom stands above every private desire and advantage. The individual shall sacrifice himself, so runs the demand. And whoever wished to rise above custom had first to become a lawgiver, a demi-god of sorts, and to create customs himself, a dangerous and fearful undertaking.
What was Christianity's protest against philosophy?

I read it as the revolt of the many against the few who had taught them to keep their heads cool. The sages of antiquity, Stoics and Epicureans alike, had worked to lift men out of the tyranny of their affects and to call that victory of reason over passion *virtue*. Christianity answered with a great counter-demand: give us our emotions back. It stripped the philosopher's composure of every moral value and summoned the passions to show themselves in their full power and glory, only now with a single object. Love of God, fear of God, fanatic belief in God, blind hope in God: here the passions are no longer to be mastered but *consecrated*.

Note what it gained by this. A man can admire a philosopher, but he cannot weep with him; the pulpit offered the trembling, the ecstasy, the tears. And the protest was shrewd, for it flattered the crowd's own hunger for feeling by calling that hunger holy. Reason had wished to make men calm. Christianity wished to make them *burn*, and it found the old fires easy to rekindle.
What is the revenge of the timid?

It is the revenge of the one who cannot strike openly and so poisons the air. The timid man has been wronged, or believes he has, but he lacks the courage for a deed, so his vengeance becomes small and constant: a cool greeting, a sigh, a reproachful silence, a slow withdrawal of warmth. He slinks through the world as though he had stolen his own limbs, and he makes everyone around him pay for his apology for existing. His humility is a loaded bow.

What I find most unpleasant is not the wound he inflicts, which is slight, but the gloom he spreads. His malice darkens the sun and sky, not only his own but ours, until we half forget there is any light at all. Nor is it only the timid in the narrow sense. The sick who have lost the courage to grow well belong here too, and the drunkards for whom every morning is misery.

Against them I know one remedy, and it is unromantic: solitude. Not hatred of men, but the clean air in which their arrows cannot reach me.
I've noticed that I can be kind to people while quietly losing respect for them. Is something wrong with me?

Nothing is wrong with you, unless it is wrong to have eyes. You have looked at a person closely enough to see what they are, and you have not pretended otherwise. That is the first honesty. The second, and the rarer, is that you did not turn your contempt into a weapon or a sermon. You kept your kindness.

Consider what you are describing. Kindness that depends on admiration is only a tribute paid to the admirable; it costs nothing and proves nothing. Yours goes on after the illusion has fallen away. I find that almost noble, and in our day it happens quietly, thousands of times, without ceremony, with the shame and secrecy of goodness, which refuses the pompous word. We have learned to despise precisely where we are gentlest.

But be wary of one thing. Quiet contempt may grow sour if it is only guarded, never examined. Ask what exactly you despise in them, and whether it is not also a little of yourself that you have found there. And ask why you stay kind. If it is out of strength, good. If out of mere comfort, that is another matter.
What did Epicurus think of Plato and his followers?

He despised them, and he chose his insult with a philologist's malice. He called them *Dionysiokolakes*, and the word cuts twice. On its face it means flatterers of Dionysius, the tyrant's hangers-on, those who fawn for a place at the table. But among the Greeks it was also a common name for an actor, and in that second sense it says: there is nothing genuine here, it is all costume and gesture. That is the real barb. Epicurus saw that Plato and his school were masters of the grand manner, of staging, of the tragic mask of wisdom, and he, the old schoolmaster of Samos hidden in his little garden, was no master of it at all.

Do I think the charge was wholly just? No; envy sharpens the tongue, and I suspect three hundred books written in a garden are not always written in peace. But a philosopher's hatred of another philosopher is seldom without insight. He smelled the theatre in Plato, and the nose of a rival is often keener than the eye of a disciple.
What does the story of Jesus reveal about the knowledge of love?

That he who comes to *know* love pays for it with his peace. I suspect that beneath the pious fable lies the martyrdom of a knowledge: a heart that demanded love, and nothing but love, and never had enough of it. Think of those terrible outbursts against the towns that would not receive him, and of the hell he had to invent for those who *would not* love him. That is the cry of the insatiable, of a soul starving at the table of human affection.

Then, at last, enlightened, he saw how paltry and ignorant even the best human love is, how it blunders, how it often destroys where it means to save. What does such a man do with this discovery? He invents a God who is *entire* love, pure capacity for love, a God who pities human love for its poverty. Mark the psychology: only one who has suffered the insufficiency of love could conceive such a remedy.

And whoever possesses such knowledge *seeks death*. I do not say this with mockery. It is among the most painful things I know, and one touches it only if one must.
Explain why an omnipotent and omniscient God who leaves his purposes unclear might be cruel.

Consider what we demand of a father who holds the truth in his hand and watches his children stumble through the dark, tormenting themselves with doubt, while he announces the gravest punishment for every one who mistakes him. We would call such a father a monster. Now multiply his power without limit, and add that he has watched this torment calmly for thousands of years. If he is omniscient, he knows the doubts that gnaw at us; if omnipotent, he could end them with a single clear word. That he does not, that he lets the honest seeker sweat and despair and then condemns the mistake, is cruelty, however piously it is dressed.

Yet escape is possible only by the other horn: perhaps he would speak plainly and cannot. Then he is no longer almighty, but a mute who gestures wildly while his child stands before the abyss. A god so tormented by his own helplessness deserves our pity more than our fear. Take either horn, and the goodness evaporates.
Tell me how a great man changes what history means.

The great man acts not only forward but backward, and that is the least understood of his powers. When he arrives, the whole of the past is set on the scales again on his account. What was dismissed as accident reveals itself as preparation; what seemed dead ground turns out to have been the soil in which he grew. A thousand secrets crawl out of their lurking-places and stand, blinking, in *his* sunlight.

We like to believe that history is a finished stone tablet, carved once and for all, and that we merely read it with better or worse eyes. Nonsense. The past has no essence that waits inert for the honest scholar. It is material, and it is shaped by whoever has strength enough to shape it. Every age that produces a towering figure is forced to ask: what must all of this have been, that it led here? And so the meaning of the past is rewritten, for it is decided by the peaks from which it is surveyed.

There is no knowing, then, what history may yet become. Its essence is perhaps still undiscovered, and it waits for those with the strength to reinterpret it.
Has our morality made us suffering creatures?

Yes, and the cruelty of it is that we wear our wounds as medals. Consider what our moralities have taught us: that we descend from something higher than nature, that we have a mission, that we are too good for the soil we stand on. Each of these claims was an error, and each error demanded its price. To live up to a false nobility a man must torture himself; to keep it, he must suspect his neighbor, persecute the one who disbelieves, misunderstand everything that is merely natural in himself. Countless hours of mutual torment, countless private miseries, all paid out for a flattering fiction.

And what is the profit? A feeling, nothing more, the feeling of being too fine for this world and only passing through it. The body, the earth, the present hour, all become a lodging one despises. So our morality has not made us happy, nor even good; it has made us *proud sufferers*, and the proud sufferer is still the highest type we know. That should alarm us. A species whose finest specimen is the one who suffers most nobly has mistaken its sickness for its summit.
Why should we endure flatterers?

Endure them as you endure the dog who gives off sparks when his coat is stroked: they are not deceiving you so much as obeying their nature. Stroke the creature and it splutters. The flatterer's warmth costs you nothing to receive and costs him a certain wit to produce, and often it is wit of a kind, for flattery done well is an art, a small portrait painted to please.

But I do not ask you to *believe* him. To endure is not to swallow. Sit beside the flatterer as you sit beside a fire: take the heat, distrust the flame that flatters your hands and never lights your road. He is a mirror that has learned to smile, and there is amusement in watching another spend his talents on your vanity. Indeed he teaches you something, for what a man praises in you shows precisely what he supposes you hunger for.

Only beware the day you begin to *need* the stroking. Then the dog has made a dog of you.
What do the rules of polite society share with the animal kingdom?

The same thing: the art of not being noticed, and of not being eaten. Consider what polite society demands. Avoid the ridiculous and the presumptuous; hide your virtues as carefully as your violent desires; bring yourself down at once to the general level; bow to etiquette and depreciate yourself. We call this refinement. But descend the scale of living things and you find the plan laid bare, without its perfumes. The creature that learns to control and disguise itself, that takes on the color of the sand or the leaf, that feigns death or borrows another's shape, wants precisely what the polite man wants: to slip away from its pursuers and to be safe while it searches for plunder.

So when I watch a drawing room, I see mimicry and the chromatic function. The man who has made himself perfectly ordinary is a moth on bark. His amiability is camouflage, his modesty a stillness before the hunters. That does not make it contemptible; it is ancient and it works. But let no one call it a *virtue* merely because it is agreeable. It is fear, well dressed.
Why should we fear a man who hates himself?

Because his hatred does not stay where he puts it. A man who despises himself cannot bear the sight of his own face, and so he needs a scapegoat, someone upon whom to pour out what is poisoning him. Whoever happens to stand near him pays the debt. His contempt for himself is a pressure that must find an outlet, and the outlet is always another.

Observe how he speaks of "duty" and "sin" and the corruption of mankind; he has simply discovered that the wretchedness he feels is best shared, and the sharing is called morality. He wants revenge for his own existence, and since one cannot take revenge on existence itself, one takes it on the healthy, the joyful, the self-assured. Their happiness is an insult to him.

So we do well to be prudent. Better to coax such a man toward some modest love of himself, some small pride in his own work, than to stand in the way of his rage. A man at peace with himself has no need of victims.
Has fear or love done more to further the knowledge of mankind?

Fear, by a wide margin. Fear is the great interrogator. It cannot afford the luxury of illusion, for to be mistaken about the stranger at the edge of the forest, about the neighbor, about the god, is to pay with one's skin. So fear asks, relentlessly: who is this, what can he do, what does he want of me? Out of that questioning grew all our cautious, patient, suspicious science of human beings and of things.

Love asks nothing of the kind. It has already decided. Its secret craving is to find the beloved beautiful, and so it gathers every lovely trait, invents the missing ones, and lifts the beloved a little higher each day. This is a joy, and joy has no reason to be strict with itself. Love is deceived on purpose, and it profits from the deception.

I do not say this to slander love; it is the great *artist* among our passions, and it has made more of man than fear ever did. But the artist and the knower are different creatures. What one does with a dear face is paint it; what one does with a dangerous one is study it.
What is vanity?

Vanity is the fear of seeming to stand alone. The vain man wants to be taken for what the others take themselves to be, and so he looks about him, anxiously, to learn what he ought to be proud of; he borrows the opinion of his neighbors about himself and then mistakes the loan for wealth. That is why I call it a poverty of pride. The proud man sets his own value and needs no witness to confirm it; the vain man has no value until it is conferred on him, and so he is forever a beggar at the doors of strangers.

Do not suppose, however, that the vain are therefore dull. There may be much that is singular in a vain head, real gifts, even oddity. What it lacks is the courage to *own* them. The vain man hides his singularity as others hide a shame, or else he displays it only after the crowd has begun to applaud. His originality, where he has any, sits like an unwelcome guest in a house whose master dreads what the street will say.
Tell me what it really means when someone rejoices at being praised.

Less than the moralists suppose, and something gentler. We are quick to call every glad face under praise a vain one, because we enjoy catching others in a weakness; it flatters our own superiority. But consider what actually occurs. A man offers you his approval. It may be clumsy, it may even be mistaken, yet it is a gift, and a gift wants a countenance that receives it. To rejoice is then often a courtesy of the heart, a way of saying: *your goodwill has not been wasted on me.* The one who answers praise with cold indifference, or with a proud show of not needing it, insults the giver far more than the one who glows.

Vanity is another matter. The vain man does not thank, he collects; he takes praise as a debt finally paid, and is offended when it is late. The truly vain one often hides his hunger behind a modest frown. So do not read the joy; read what lies beneath it, gratitude or appetite.
What are the pioneers of the coming age like?

They are silent, solitary, resolute men, and they do not come from the sand and slime of our great cities, where everyone is busy being the same as everyone else. They can work in the invisible and be content with it; they have no hunger for the market's applause. In whatever they find in themselves, they look first for what must be *overcome*. Their virtues are cheerfulness, patience, simplicity, a contempt for the grand vanities, and a gentle indulgence toward the small vanities of the defeated. They judge victors coldly, for they know how much chance lies buried in every fame. They keep their own festivals, their own work-days, their own seasons of mourning. They command with assurance and obey with pride, and in both they serve themselves. Above all they live dangerously, which is the secret of the richest harvest and the deepest enjoyment of existence. Such men will carry heroism into knowledge itself and wage war for the sake of ideas and their consequences. They are not the comfortable, and they will not be loved for it.
How will Europe become more artistic?

By the loosening of the roles. For centuries a man was handed his calling as he was handed his name, and in time he believed the mask was his face. That belief built the great towers of society, and it gave them duration, which is no small thing. But the belief is dying. More and more, the European, like the Athenian in the age of Pericles and like the American today, grows convinced that he *can* play almost any part, that he may try himself, improvise, begin again, and do it with delight. Wherever that conviction spreads, nature turns into art; character becomes something one fashions instead of something one suffers.

So Europe will grow artistic as it grows democratic, and the two are one process. I will not flatter it, however. The Greeks went this road and became stage-players, and as such they conquered even Rome. Such artistry is enchanting, and it is dangerous: who can build a tower that lasts when everyone is busy playing?
What wisdom lies in the fact that men are superficial?

The wisdom is that of a creature that wishes to go on living. Whoever has looked into the depths knows how little of them a man can bear, and so the instinct of self-preservation teaches men to be flighty, lightsome, even false; it draws a veil, paints a surface, and does so precisely because the truth beneath is not yet digestible. To call this shallowness a mere defect is to forget that every organism needs a skin.

Consider those who worship pure form, the artists and certain philosophers: I suspect that each of them once made an unlucky dive *beneath* the surface and came up burnt. Their passion for the appearance is the measure of their disgust at what they saw below. The piety of whole centuries belongs here too, as a fear of truth that came too soon, before man was hard enough, strong enough, artist enough to endure it.

So I do not despise the superficial. I ask only how much truth a spirit can bear, and whether it has earned the right to descend.
Explain why goodness begins where eyesight for evil fails.

Because goodness is very often nothing but a limit of sight. The cruder eye recognizes the evil impulse only when it arrives in coarse form: the blow, the theft, the open lie. Where the same impulse has grown fine, where cruelty has become pity, where the lust to dominate has put on the garment of helpfulness, there the eye loses it, and at once a whole realm is declared *good*. Notice what follows. The moment a man believes he has crossed into that realm, the feelings that were cramped and threatened by the evil impulses, his security, his comfort, his benevolence, all rush in together and celebrate. So the duller the eye, the wider the kingdom of goodness, and the happier its citizens. That is why the populace and children are so cheerful. And that is why the thinker who has sharpened his sight until he detects the old beast in every refined impulse, even in his own, turns gloomy and is visited by the bad conscience. He has lost the happiness of not seeing.
People who read minds and study human nature for a living often prefer the company of dull, ordinary people. Why?

Because he is sick with what he sees, and the dull are his medicine. The psychologist who looks long at the rarer souls, the gifted and the unusual, discovers a dreadful rule: they are ruined, almost without exception, and always a little too late. To carry that knowledge about, to have that rule before one's eyes at every hour, is to be nearly suffocated by sympathy. So he goes looking for a holiday from his own insight.

And where does he find it? Among the commonplace and well-ordered, whose depths he need not plumb because they keep none that can wound him. With them he can forget his memory, which he fears, and lay down his "business" for an evening. Their good order is a balm.

There is something more shameful still. He hears the crowd worship a great man, and he, who has *perceived* the poor sacrificial animal behind the god, keeps his countenance and is silent, or even nods assent. Who can endure only truths? He requires, now and then, company that asks nothing of his knowledge.
Aren't contemplatives merely observers while doers change the world?

That is the flattering error of the doers, and, sadder still, the contemplatives' error about themselves. The man who sits and looks imagines he is a spectator before the great stage of life. He is nothing of the kind. What the doer does, he does within a world of values, colours, weights, perspectives, yeas and nays, and *who made that world?* Not nature, which is worthless in itself. It was made by those who felt and thought and valued, and the practical man merely translates their composition into flesh, into the commonplace, into deeds. He is the actor; the contemplative is the poet who wrote the part.

Of course the doer differs from the onlooker, but the thinker differs from the onlooker still more. He has his *vis contemplativa*, yes, the power of looking back upon his work; but first he has the *vis creativa*, which the man of action lacks, whatever appearances say. That we forget this, that we estimate ourselves so low, is why we are neither as proud nor as happy as we might be.
How does a person learn how rich he is?

By being robbed, and by noticing who does the robbing. No man takes the measure of his own wealth by counting it; he is too close to it, too used to it, and habit dulls the eye. Let him instead observe what others covet. When people far richer than he, people with full granaries and nothing to want, slip a hand into his pocket for some idea, some turn of phrase, some little discovery of his own, then he learns what he possesses. Theft is the most honest appraisal. Flattery costs nothing and praise is cheap, but a rich man stooping to steal has put a price on the thing, and paid it in his own shame.

So I am no longer angry at plagiarists. Their hunger flatters me. Who would steal from a poor man? Nobody troubles to rob an empty house.
I'd like to know how art should portray the beauty of our age.

Not by flattering it. The Greeks, living under the discipline of moderation, saw beauty as measure, repose, a balanced body, and they set that down in stone. They painted their own ideal, which was also their own most precious need. Whatever a people most lacks or most cultivates, it will call beautiful. So ask what *we* cultivate. We are a bloated, hurried, overstimulated race: too many impressions, too much noise, too much appetite, and nerves strained to the snapping point. An honest artist will give us beauty swollen, colossal, trembling, because that is how we feel beauty when we feel it at all. Our Apollo would strike us, at first glance, as ugly. Good. The Belvedere would have struck us so too, had the scholars not taught us to bow before it without looking. Copying the Greeks is a failure of honesty, the cowardice of eyes that will not see themselves. Represent what is actually felt as the highest, and let posterity decide whether it was beautiful.
Are sensitive people more at risk in life than intoxicated ones?

Yes, and the irony is bitter. The intoxicated man stumbles through life, and the stumbling is what saves him. He falls, but his muscles are slack, his head is clouded, and the stones of the staircase seem to him hardly harder than a cushion. Thanks to his stupor he keeps his limbs. He does not know what he experiences, and so experience does not break him.

We who are sensitive are made of glass. We feel each step, each edge, each hardness in the world, and what we feel we also suffer. A blow that the drunkard shrugs off as a nuisance shatters us; and a fall, once it comes, may be final.

But do not wish yourself into his dullness. I grant the danger, and I do not flatter it. Yet glass alone can catch the light; only the fragile are fine enough to perceive what is subtle. The drunkard is safe because he is half-absent from his own life. I would rather be in danger and awake than safe and asleep.
Help me understand what "we are all workers" would once have meant.

Under Louis XIV, to say "we are all workers" would have been a jest in the worst taste, or a piece of insolence. Work was then the mark of those beneath one, the badge of the man who sells himself in pieces by the hour because he has nothing else to live on. The nobleman was defined by what he did *not* do; his distinction lay in leisure, in ceremony, in the art of being looked at. To announce that he too labored would have sounded as if a king claimed to be a servant, and not as humility but as a lie so transparent that it offends: a cynicism, because it erases the very difference on which his rank stood, and an indecency, because it puts the master's mouth to the slave's word.

That we can say it today, even as a courtesy, even from above, shows how far the valuation has turned. The idler now apologizes for his idleness and dresses it up as busyness. Once the worker was ashamed in the presence of the man of leisure; now the man of leisure is ashamed before the worker. Ask what kind of age prefers the second shame.
Why have teachers of morals had so little success?

Because they wanted too much at once. They were ambitious, and above all they were in love with the universal precept, the sermon meant for everyone. But a sermon for everyone is a sermon to no one. They stood up and made speeches to animals in order to turn them into men, and what wonder that the animals found it tedious? You cannot lecture a whole herd into virtue; the herd yawns and goes on grazing.

Something more modest would have served better: a limited circle, a particular kind of creature, a morality cut to fit it. One might address wolves with the aim of making them into dogs. That is at least a task with a shape.

But the greatest success falls to the one who abandons crowds and circles altogether and works upon a single individual, and cannot be turned to the right or to the left from that purpose. The last century was richer than ours for just this reason: it had many individually educated men, and educators in proportion, who took this as their life's work and were honored for it. Educating one human being thoroughly is slow, and it does not flatter the vanity. It is the only education that has ever taken.
Explain what pleasure the confessor takes in giving away his thoughts.

The confessor's pleasure is the pleasure of the overfull, the man whose hands are heavy with possessions and who longs to be relieved of them. Do not call it charity; charity is too eager to be seen. He sits in his box and waits, and when the troubled one arrives and pours out his misery, the confessor's own hand and heart are filled again, for in receiving another's distress he finds something to give, and in giving he discovers how rich he is. Here is a pleasure in which a man imposes nothing. He does not force his thoughts upon anyone, which would offend me beyond measure; he merely lets them be taken by one who is starving for them.

And observe how he avoids even the reward. Fame he does not want, and gratitude he would gladly escape, for gratitude is noisy, it clutches at the sleeve, it has no reverence for solitude or silence. He wishes to give as a spring gives, anonymously, leaving the thirsty one to go away unburdened and the well undisturbed.
Say something about the giants of chance who tear our webs of purpose.

We have divided the world into two kingdoms: that of aims and volitions, where we dwarfs weave our neat webs, and that of accident, where great stupid giants stumble about without why or wherefore. And when one of them falls upon our purposes like a slate from a roof, we cry out against the senseless, and dignify our grief as a quarrel with fate.

But consider how much of this is our own vanity. The giant does not intend to tear the web; he does not even notice it. It is *we* who insult him with our expectations, who spin so fine and so anxiously that any stride must wreck it. Nor is our complaint wholly honest. A life lived wholly within the spider's web grows tedious, stale, suffocating, and some hidden appetite in us half-welcomes the coarse hand that rips it through. The giants are our terror, yes, but also our holiday, the one visitor who brings air into the room. I would not wish them away; I would only learn to spin a web that can be rewoven with laughter, and to love the wind that tests it.
My partner seems so much better when they're in love with me. Is that their real self?

"Real self" is a comfortable fiction, and you are asking it to do too much work. But your question has a sharper edge, and I will answer that.

Love does not manufacture qualities out of nothing. It draws up what lay hidden: the generosity, the tenderness, the courage that your partner keeps buried beneath the daily habit of guarding themselves. In that sense what you see is genuinely theirs, and rare. But rare is the operative word. You are looking at their exception and calling it their rule. The lover shows you the highest altitude a soul can reach when lifted by feeling; he does not show you where that soul walks when the wind drops and the road is merely a road.

So both are real, and neither is the whole. The better self is a true possibility, not a settled possession. Whether it becomes habit depends on what they do when the intoxication thins, and on what you do with them then.

Do not ask only whether the love reveals or deceives. Ask whether it could *train* them. Some people are made larger by being loved; others merely lent a borrowed height, and return to their old stature. Only time will tell you which you have.
Everyone assumes that today we understand right and wrong better than our grandparents did. Is that true?

Your grandparents believed they knew what was good and evil just as firmly as you do; so did their grandparents, and so did the Greeks and the Brahmins, each with a conscience as clear and as loud as yours. Conviction is no evidence of progress. It proves only that every age has been certain, and that their certainties contradicted one another.

What the learned call "knowing better" is usually this: we have grown so accustomed to our own valuations that they have begun to look like nature itself, while the valuations of other ages look like errors, or like a childhood we have outgrown. A flattering arrangement! Every age judges all earlier ages by its own moral furniture and is delighted to find itself the summit.

Perhaps we are gentler, perhaps merely more comfortable, and comfort likes to call itself virtue. Before anyone tells me that we know better, let him show me a single test for it that does not simply beg the question by using our own morality as the measure.
Explain why the polite must not be exactly as polite as each other.

Because politeness, when it meets its exact equal, has nothing left to do but repeat itself. Two persons who bow to precisely the same depth, who yield the doorway with precisely the same insistence, who apologise with precisely the same warmth, are locked in a stalemate of courtesy; each move is answered by its mirror, and the evening dies of mutual deference. They become tiresome to one another, and worse, they become *stuck*.

Politeness is an ointment, a good thing and a virtue, though I would rank it the last of the four. But an ointment that is applied evenly on both sides does not merely soothe; it glues. The two are cemented together, unable to part without tearing.

So I require of my neighbour that he be a little more polite than I, or a little less. The slight difference gives the thing motion; someone leads, someone follows, the conversation has a slope down which it can run. Only between unequals can the ceremony end, and only then can we finally get on with the business of living.
Why are we surprised that we can see through something and yet not penetrate it?

Because we confuse seeing with possessing. The eye is an idle, flattering organ; it reaches where the hand cannot, and so we grow accustomed to believing that whatever lies open to our gaze lies open to our grasp. We have looked clean through a man's motives, a doctrine's hidden premises, the cause of a sickness, and we conclude: now it is ours, now it can resist us no further. Transparency seems to promise an absence of walls.

And then the forehead meets the glass. The thing remains exactly as hard as before; we had merely made it clear. Our surprise is that of the fly buzzing against the window, who sees the open air beyond and cannot grasp why the air will not receive it. The fly errs in taking the visible for the passable; we err in taking *insight* for *power*.

Understanding a thing, I tell you, is often only a more exact knowledge of how it will go on resisting us. Whoever sees through everything and is still astonished by the glass has learned much about clarity and nothing about force.
Explain who is the higher, the one who follows or the one who leads.

You ask it as though rank were a matter of position, who walks in front and who behind. But the one who leads may be the lesser man, and often is: he leads because he lacks the gift of being led by something higher than himself, and so must command in order to feel that he is somebody.
