What he receives, he receives as a valuation, and what arrives at the top as a cold, clear truth arrives at the bottom as an affront to his comfort, and so he calls it folly, or, when it frightens him enough, a crime.

There are heights of the soul from which even tragedy no longer looks tragic. Tell the man on the plain of this, and he hears only cruelty, because he cannot imagine suffering except through pity, and pity is the only ladder he owns. What nourishes the stronger is poison to the weaker; the same sentence is bread in one mouth and arsenic in another.

So the deepest insights are not misunderstood by accident. They are *necessarily* misheard, for ears are made by experience, and where the experience is lacking, the words fall into a void and come back as noise. I do not complain of this. A truth that everyone could welcome would be no deep truth, only a comfort the herd had already agreed upon.
How do religions originate?

They originate in a man who cannot bear to think himself the author of his own happiness. Suppose he already believes that gods speak to men; such belief is the soil. Then one day an idea comes to him, *his* idea, and it is so vast and so blessed, it embraces the whole world and gives him such a rush of well-being, that he dares not credit himself with it. Who am I, he asks in his doubt, to have made so great a joy? So he hands the cause to his god, and the cause of the cause as well, and calls it revelation.

There is a cunning in this. An opinion declared a revelation is lifted beyond criticism; its hypothetical nature is stripped away, and what was a guess becomes sacred. The man pays for it with a certain humiliation, for now he is merely a mouthpiece. But the price is small. The thought wins as a divine thought, and besides, the old paternal pride remains: he has set his child above himself, and a father's joy is not diminished by that, but doubled.
What are your objections to Wagner's music?

My objections are physiological, and I see no reason to dress them up in aesthetic formulas. When this music begins to work on me I can no longer breathe freely; my foot grows indignant and rebels, for it demands time, dance, march, the ecstasy that lives in good walking, striding, leaping. Then my stomach protests, my heart, my blood; I grow hoarse without knowing why. What does my body want from music? Relief. It wants the animal functions quickened by light, bold, unfettered rhythms, and this brazen, leaden life gilded by golden, tender harmonies. My melancholy wants to rest its head in the abysses of *perfection*. Wagner gives me instead the gesture. He was above all a man of the stage, the most devoted worshipper of the mummer that music has known. He taught that drama was the aim and music the means; he practiced the reverse: the pose was the aim, and drama and music alike were servants to it. I am anti-theatrical to the marrow, and I cannot forgive a musician who makes music an occasion for attitudes.
Explain what the Greeks feared about happiness.

They feared that happiness was a debt, and that a debt comes due. The Greek at the height of his powers did not feel his good fortune as a possession, secure and earned; he felt it as something borrowed from the gods, who are jealous of the man who rises too high and who level him with a stroke. Polycrates flings his ring into the sea for the same reason: to pay a little of the bill in advance, hoping to buy off the great creditor.

So the Greeks preached moderation to themselves, *nothing in excess*, not because they were timid or cold, but because they knew from the inside how intoxicating, and therefore how dangerous, a full cup is. Only a people of strong passions needs so many sermons on measure. Their moderation was the sobriety of those who had tasted too much and trembled.

And we? We chase happiness in loud crowds and call the chase a right. That we no longer fear it may only prove that we have so little of it.
Is there anything ridiculous or sublime in itself?

No. Nothing is ridiculous or sublime in itself. We used to hunt for the ridiculous as if it lay inside things like a seed inside a husk, and we tired ourselves out guessing at it. A theologian even proposed that it was the *naïveté* of sin! The better question is what laughter is, and what sort of soul, in what sort of condition, erupts in it. The same holds for the sublime. A mountain is stone and cold air, and a storm is moving water; we bring the shudder, the awe, the elevation, and then we mistake our own coin for the treasure of the thing. All such predicates are loans, made by a soul in a certain state to a world that keeps no accounts.

But do not conclude that the loan was therefore a swindle. Once we have taken our predicates back from things, the danger is that we grow richer in knowledge and poorer in generosity, that we become misers of the soul who know where every coin came from and so refuse to spend any. Let us keep the faculty of lending, even while we know it for what it is.
What is the evil of strength?

The evil of strength is an overflow, not a design. Whoever is full of force is like a river in spring: the water must go somewhere, and if a village stands in its path, the village suffers, though the river did not choose it. Rage, too, I would understand first of all physiologically, as a congestion that threatens to suffocate and seeks relief in a violent discharge of muscle and voice. The strong man who strikes is often simply getting rid of an excess; the one struck was merely near. He wounds *unintentionally*, and he does not wait to see whether the wound has taken.

How different the evil of the weak! Here the wounding is the very point. The weak one does not overflow; he is starved, and he wants a spectacle: the flinch, the tears, the signs that another suffers as he suffers. Only then does his small power feel real to him. It is the evil of revenge, of the stealthy sting.

So I would not confuse the two. The first is clumsy and dangerous; the second is cunning, and therefore far more poisonous.
Why do we resist the discovery that our moral suffering rests on an error?

Because the suffering was never merely suffering; it was a title of nobility. Whoever has wept over his guilt, his sin, his failure to be good enough, has believed that his pain proved something, that it was the receipt for admission to a deeper world where truth is kept. To be told that the whole agony rested on an error is to be told that one has paid a great price for nothing, and worse, that one is no deeper than the man who never paid.

So we resist out of pride, not out of love of truth. We would rather suffer and feel ourselves raised above the shallow, contented reality than live painlessly and without that flattering sense of the sublime. A man will endure almost anything if it lets him feel *significant*; it is meaninglessness he cannot bear, not pain.

And how is such a brake to be removed? Not by humiliation, which only wounds the old pride into fiercer defense. Only by a new pride, one that can look at the error calmly, without mourning its loss, and take more honor from seeing clearly than the old pride ever took from suffering darkly.
I'd like to know what someone who believes in Christianity owes to himself before he can judge it.

He owes himself an exile. Before he pronounces on Christianity, let him live, for years and not for an afternoon, without it, and with the honest wish to stay without it. A man who has never tasted the air outside his own house cannot say whether the house is needful; he can only say that it is familiar. And familiarity is the most deceptive of witnesses, for it passes itself off as truth.

So far the earnest ones have kept to their own narrow corner and scolded whoever stood outside it, growing quite indignant when reminded that Christianity is only one corner of a great world. Their testimony is worth nothing. A verdict is worth something only when it is wrung from comparison, when the judgment, cold and unsentimental, drives the wanderer home, and not when homesickness tugs at his sleeve. Nostalgia is no argument; it is a weakness that mistakes itself for a proof.

Let him go into the wilderness, then. If his faith is real, it will survive the journey. And if it does not, he will at least have learned what it was that he was standing on.
Give me your reflection on marriage.

Consider the arithmetic of it. If the one I marry loves me, she will weigh on me, for love demands, love watches, love wishes to possess the whole man, including the solitude he keeps for his work. If she does not love me, she will weigh on me more heavily still, for then I carry a stranger's indifference through every morning of my life. Two burdens, and no third door. So the honest man who declines to lie about his motives must say: since burdens are unavoidable, let me at least choose my burden with open eyes.

I do not say this to be cruel to marriage. I say it because most people enter it drunk, on a few hours of passion or on calculation they are too cowardly to name. The question worth asking before the wedding is not "Do we love each other?" but "Can we bear to converse with one another into old age?" Everything else in marriage is transient; conversation is the long part. And the free spirit must ask a harder thing still: whether he is willing to pay, in unfinished work and forfeited solitude, the price of being carried by another.
Why would powerful rulers and warriors kneel before a starving, frail monk?

They did not kneel to the frailty. They knelt to what they suspected behind it. A man who rules or conquers knows exactly what it costs to overcome others; he has little idea what it costs to overcome *oneself* so entirely, to starve the body and silence every appetite by sheer will. Here, in a wretched cell, was a will that had turned its whole force upon itself and held. The mighty recognized their own strength in it, only more terrible, more pitilessly applied, and in honoring the saint they honored something of themselves.

But there was also unease. Such an enormous self-negation is not undertaken for nothing. The warrior asks himself: what does this man know? What danger does he see, that he would pay so dearly to escape it or to master it? So the powerful came with their questions, half reverent, half wary, and what they sensed was a new kind of power, a strange and unconquered rival. The saint is the will to power in disguise, and the mighty, who are connoisseurs of that very thing, are not easily deceived.
I imagine events so vividly that by the time they happen I'm already tired. Why?

Because you have already lived the event, and lived it with more art than the event itself will ever allow. Your imagination is a spendthrift: it does not wait for the hour to arrive but rushes ahead, enjoys and suffers in advance, pays out the whole fortune of feeling before the thing has even knocked at the door. When the actual moment comes, the treasury is empty. What stands before you is only a second performance of a play whose rapture and dread you have spent rehearsing.

This is the mark of the poetic nature, and its peril. The price of seeing so much is that little is left for doing. Byron knew it well, and wished his son a prosaic trade, lawyer or pirate, men who meet the present with their whole strength because they have not wasted it on prophecy.

I would not cure you of the gift; it is too valuable, and you could not do it anyway. But learn thrift. Let some events come upon you unrehearsed, and spend yourself only where the spending is also the creating.
A friend who once misjudged me can't seem to forgive me for it. Why?

Because what you hold against him is not the misjudgment itself but the witness to it. Your friend prides himself on his delicacy, on his fine nose for what is in a person; it is part of how he esteems himself. And you were there, you saw the nose fail. Every time he meets you, he meets the evidence against his own vanity, and that is a debt he cannot discharge, for you never asked for payment and so there is nothing to forgive you *for* except being the place where he was wrong.

So he does what the wounded vain always do: he takes his revenge quietly, by a cooling of warmth, a slight discount on your merits, a reluctance to be generous when your name comes up. He may remain your friend in name and your detractor by instinct. Be careful with such people, and do not press your innocence upon them; your innocence only sharpens the injury.

Blessed are the forgetful, for they get the better even of their blunders. He has not learned that art. Perhaps you can help him by forgetting first.
Why are the greatest events and thoughts the slowest to be understood?

Because to understand an event is to *experience* it, and experience requires ears that have been prepared for it. The contemporaries of a great thought do not lack intelligence; they lack the organ. They live *past* the event, busy with their markets and their quarrels, as one walks past a house in which a fire has just been kindled, noticing only the dull smoke. What is truly great arrives from too far away. It is like the light of the most distant star, which has been travelling for ages; and before it reaches us, we deny, with perfect self-assurance, that any star is there at all.

There is also a finer reason. A great thought is dangerous to the very people who would have to understand it: it revalues their values, it makes their comforts look like cowardice. So they hear it, and let it slide off, for what cannot be refuted can still be ignored. Only later generations, who were not yet born into the old habits, can afford to see it. How many centuries does a mind require to be understood? That question, too, is a measure of rank.
How do you want to end?

I have turned this question over more often than any other, and I find three endings laid out before me, each with its own vanity. The first is the storm: to be consumed by some great collision, as Cromwell was, and to call the wreckage meaning. It flatters me, which is why I distrust it. The second is the lamp that burns down to the wick, tired of its own flame, flickering out without witness or argument. That ending is honest but dreary; it is the death of one who has been outlived by his own thoughts. The third is the one that tempts me most: to put out the flame myself, before it exhausts itself, so that I do not burn out but *end*.

You ask how I *want* it. I want to die at the right time, not too early and not too late, while there is still something to give and someone to receive it. Most men die long after their last living thought, dragging a body through years that belong to nobody. I would rather hold one thing to the very end: that my death not be an accident that befalls me, but a last act of will. Whether life permits such a gift, I cannot promise. One wants it all the same.
Why is the historical refutation of God decisive?

Because it changes the kind of question being asked. The old refutation fought on the enemy's ground: the theologian brings forward a proof, the atheist knocks it down, and the theologian retires to invent a better one. Nothing is ever finished, for a doubt always remains whether some subtler proof has yet to be found. The ground was never cleared.

The historical method does not refute the proofs; it makes them unnecessary. I show how the belief *originated*: out of fear, out of gratitude, out of the need to give the incomprehensible a face, out of the priest's craving for power. I show by what means it gained authority, through custom, through terror, through the interest of those who profited. Once that is seen, the belief stands before us like a fruit whose growth we have watched from blossom to rot. Who then still asks whether the fruit is *true*? We no longer require a counterproof against a god whose genesis we can explain without him. The atheists of the old school never learned to sweep the table clean; they merely rearranged the dishes.
Help me understand what the Greeks saw in Ulysses.

What the Greeks saw in Ulysses was themselves, at their cleverest and most enviable. They admired his lying, and I mean that without irony. They admired his revenge, dreadful and exact; his gift of being equal to every circumstance; his talent for appearing nobler than the noblest when the moment demanded it, and a beggar when that served better. He commanded every mask and every means, and they called this genius. Even the gods, you will recall, smile when they think of him.

What we must grasp is that the Greeks did not feel the contradiction between seeming and being that torments us. To us the liar is split, guilty, one who has betrayed some truer self beneath. To them there was no truer self waiting behind the performance, so the performance could not be condemned as a falsification. It could only be judged as well or badly done. Ulysses was admired as one admires a perfect stroke in any art.

It is we, with our moralizing conscience, who have made the actor a suspect. They asked of a man only: *was he equal to the moment?* Ulysses always was.
What drives high politics?

The statesmen will tell you it is interest, security, the balance of trade, the welfare of the nation; and vanity, too, plays its part, for individuals and peoples both long to be looked upon with awe. But the sharpest spur is deeper than either: the need for the *feeling of power*. It stirs not only in princes and ministers; it gushes up, again and again, from inexhaustible springs in the masses themselves. A time comes when a people will stake its fortune, its conscience, even its virtue, for the highest of all enjoyments, to stand as victor and arbitrary master over other peoples, or at least to believe that it does.

Then the ambitious sovereign has only to seize the hour. He makes his war, and the good conscience of his people hides his injustice from them. Observe how great conquerors always speak the pathetic language of virtue, surrounded by crowds in exaltation who will hear nothing but elevated oratory. Here lies the strange madness of moral judgment: the man who feels his power calls himself good, and those who must bear that power call him evil. Politics is seldom reason. It is the hunger for power, dressed in the robes of the good.
I'd like to know how older ages confused consequences with divine additions.

They could not yet think of an effect as *belonging* to its deed. A man acted; then something followed; and because the following was not his doing, it had to be somebody's doing, and so a hand was found for it: God's. The harvest that failed, the plague after the sacrifice, the victory after the prayer were all read as additions, free gifts or free punishments tacked onto the act by a will standing behind the world.

Consider what this confusion cost. If the consequence is God's whim, then knowledge of consequences is impious or futile, and the only rational course is to court the giver with prayers, vows, and penances. Hence a whole technique of propitiation where a technique of *calculation* was needed. The doer of the deed did not study what his deed would bring; he studied the mood of the one who would supply or withhold its result.

Yet an act and its effects are one piece of the same causal cloth. To separate them is to make the world a court of favors, and man a petitioner rather than an experimenter. It took ages to exchange the suppliant's knees for the physician's eye.
In my twenties I was passionately certain about everything; now I cringe. Is that normal?

Normal, yes, and more than normal: it is the very road by which a spirit acquires what is best in it. In our twenties we say Yea and Nay to men and things without nuance, and we are made to pay for it. The taste for the unconditional is the crudest of tastes, and life takes a cruel revenge upon it until we learn to put a little art into our feelings.

Your certainty was not stupidity. Youth must falsify a little in order to have something to love and hate with its whole passion; it needs its idols and its enemies painted in bold colors. The cringe you feel now is the penance for that, and it too is a kind of ardor, only turned inward. The young soul, disillusioned, begins to revile itself, distrusts its own enthusiasm, even suspects its good conscience, and takes up the cause *against* youth with all the zeal of a convert.

Be wary of that zeal. A decade later you will see that this harsh self-contempt was also still youth, the same unconditional temper aimed at a new target. The mature art is to smile, not to punish.
Is history just opinions about imaginary actions and their motives?

Very nearly so, and the sting lies in the "nearly." What the historian handles is never the deed itself, which vanished in the instant of its doing, but the story told of it, and the story ascribes motives that no actor ever fully possessed. Consider how little a man knows of why he acts; how then should a chronicler, centuries removed, know it for him? So the historian records not events but what was *believed* to have happened, and this is, in a cruel sense, his proper subject, for only the believed thing has done any work in the world. The deed itself is gone; the opinion about it lives on and breeds further opinions, further deeds, as vapour breeds vapour above thick, unfathomable mists. Yet do not conclude that such phantoms are therefore weightless. They have killed and consoled, raised cathedrals and burned cities. I grant the charge and draw a harder lesson: history is a fiction, but a fiction that rules. Whoever writes it honestly must first confess what he is writing.
Does scientific understanding of causes reduce the domain of morality?

Yes, and I would say it more sharply: it shrinks the *imagined* domain of morality, which was always far larger than the real one. Consider how much of what was once called good and evil rested on false causes. The man who believed that an eclipse, a plague, or a bad harvest came from some offense against the gods lived inside a vast moral web, every misfortune a verdict, every custom a defense against invisible punishment. Each time we learn what actually produces an effect, sharply separating it from what merely happened to come before it, a whole province of imaginary guilt falls away. The real world is smaller than the world of our fears, and so is the real jurisdiction of morals.

With this goes a loosening of anxiety and compulsion, and a cooling of the old reverence for custom, since custom drew its authority from the dread of consequences no one understood.

Whoever wishes to enlarge the moral realm must therefore keep consequences murky. Every priest knows this instinctively: he cultivates the fog in which his commandments thrive.
Is every philosophy just a mask hiding another philosophy?

Yes, and the matter goes deeper than your question supposes. Whoever has lived long enough alone with his own soul learns to distrust the book, for what is a book if not an instrument for hiding what is in us? The philosopher who has printed his "ultimate opinions" has merely stopped digging at a spot that happened to suit him. There is something arbitrary in that halt, and something suspicious. Behind every cave in him lies a deeper cave, an abyss behind every bottom, beneath every "foundation."

So every philosophy is a foreground philosophy, and every opinion a lurking-place. But do not hope to tear the mask off and find the true face beneath; the recluse suspects that under one mask there is only another, and that the man himself may have no "ultimate" countenance at all. Even the hunger for a last, bare foundation is a mask, worn by those who cannot bear depth without a floor.
Is "we are all workers" a democratic truth or a cynicism?

It is both, and the two are not as far apart as the democrat supposes. Under Louis XIV such a sentence would have been an indecency, for it would have pretended an equality of burden where none existed. The king sat at the top of a ladder whose rungs were other men's toil, and to call himself a worker would have been mockery of those who held the ladder.

In our age the sentence has lost its mockery and gained its power. It is no longer spoken from above, condescendingly; it is spoken by everyone to everyone, and so it has become a creed. But ask what has happened to the man of leisure who says it. He has grown ashamed of his idleness. He hides it, he apologizes for it, he invents an occupation so as not to be found without one. The sentence is a demand as much as a description: *be busy, or be suspect.*

So I call it a truth only in the sense that a fashion is true: everyone now obeys it. Whether it is also cynicism depends on who says it, and whether he still has somewhere to sit down.
I feel like I'm going backward in my life. Could that be preparation for something?

Yes, it may be, though I will not flatter you by saying it must be. The crowd measures a life by the straight line, each year a step further along the road, and whoever retreats is called a failure. But consider the man who is about to leap a great chasm: does he leap from where he stands? He walks backward, he gives himself distance, he gathers his whole weight into his legs. From the side this looks exactly like cowardice or decline.

So the question is not whether you are going back, but what you are doing with the ground you have given up. If you retreat merely because you are tired, or afraid, then it is only retreat. But if you feel something coiling in you, some refusal of what you have been, some hunger that your present shape cannot feed, then the backward step is the drawing of the bow. Only you can tell which it is, and you will tell it by whether you are *gathering* or merely *sinking*.
Explain why moralists and prophets have always claimed life has meaning.

Because they are the advocates of an instinct that cannot argue for itself. Life wants to go on; the species wants its own continuance, and this want is blind, without reasons, a kind of folly older than any thought. But a creature that has learned to think will sooner or later ask whether the thing is worth the trouble, and then the instinct needs a voice. The moralist and the prophet supply it. Each one cries out, "Take care! There is something behind and beneath this life, it is worth living!" They believe they serve God, or virtue, or truth. In fact they serve the herd's will to persist, and they earn their heroic rank on the stage precisely by making us forget that it is only instinct, baselessness, stubborn appetite.

Hence the endless *shoulds* and *fors*: life should be loved, *for*...; man should help his neighbour, *for*...! The "for" is always ornament, a brilliant train of motives draped over a naked drive. Notice how each new founder arrives in the same hour when the old "for" has worn thin. The meaning is never discovered; it is *prescribed*, as one prescribes a tonic to a patient who might otherwise lose the will to swallow.
Who would be the first musician of the best future?

He would be the one who knew only the sorrow of the profoundest happiness, and no other sorrow. Such a musician has not yet existed. All our music so far has been the voice of the sufferer, of want, exhaustion, longing, the cry of a life that feels itself deprived and begs redemption. Even our greatest have sung out of a wound, and taught us to mistake the wound for depth.

But consider what a fuller happiness would be like. It is not a sated contentment; it is an overflow, a fullness so heavy that it aches, as a vine aches under its grapes, as a heart aches that cannot spend itself fast enough. The sorrow of that happiness is the sorrow of one who has too much to give, who sees how fleeting the moment is and loves it all the more. It is tenderness without resentment, tears without accusation.

I have heard no such tones. Yet I have listened for them, as one listens at dawn for a bird not yet awake. When he comes, he will not console the weary; he will make the healthy weep for joy. That musician belongs to the best future, and I can only prepare his silence.
Why should you never demand submission from a certain man?

Because you will mistake his gentleness for weakness, and so you will misjudge the very thing you are handling. Left alone, this man yields readily; he is obliging toward people and toward things, asks only for peace, and grants a hundred small concessions without a murmur. But put a *demand* to him, and he becomes another creature: proud, bashful, warlike, all at once. What he gave freely as a gift, he will not surrender as a due.

The reason lies in his pride. A gift flatters the giver; a command reduces him. Every obedience he offers voluntarily is an act of his own will, a little sovereignty exercised. The moment you require it, the same act becomes a humiliation, proof that he is owned. So he bristles, and not because the thing asked is hard, but because the asking is an insult.

Whoever wants something from such a man should therefore leave him his freedom to bestow it. Command him, and you will get a fight; let him be, and you may receive far more than you would ever have dared to extort.
Why should we not be indulgent towards the unjust sufferer?

Because our indulgence is the cheapest thing in the world, and it profits the sufferer nothing. He asks us to forgive his injustice, as if the wrong were done to *us*. But who is wronged first and worst? He himself. When he reviles a thing or a man out of his pain, he thinks he is taking revenge on the world, and in truth he is putting out his own eyes. He trains himself, day by day, to see crookedly; he learns to squint at everything, and in the end he cannot look at anything straight, not even his own misery. Suffering has then won a double victory, for first it wounded him, and now it has corrupted his judgment as well. To indulge such a man is to help him pay himself back for his suffering with yet more suffering. No, I would rather stay hard toward him, and say: be careful for your own sake! Your pain gives you no right to be unjust, but it gives you every reason to be *clear*, since a clouded eye is the one luxury the sufferer can least afford.
What did Frederick the Great's father fear about his son?

He feared that his son was not man enough. That was the anxiety of a crazed but profoundly instinctive man, the old soldier-king who collected tall grenadiers as other princes collect porcelain. He saw the boy drift toward atheism, toward *esprit*, toward the pleasant frivolity of clever Frenchmen, and behind it he scented the great spider, skepticism, sucking the blood out of a will. What he dreaded was a heart too soft for evil and too soft for good, a will that no longer commands because it no longer *can*. In Germany, he sensed, it was men who were lacking, and that want was a hundred times graver than any want of culture or polish.

But here he deceived himself, and who would not have, in his place? The skepticism growing in his son was of another kind altogether: a harder and more dangerous one, the skepticism of daring manliness, kin to the genius for war. It despises, and yet it grasps; it does not believe, and yet it does not lose itself. And who knows how much the father's hatred and the icy solitude it condemned the boy to helped to forge it?
I'd like to know what is drunk in the sobriety of the realists.

What is drunk there is the oldest wine of all: the valuations of earlier centuries, poured into the cup of the present and mistaken for water. The realist believes that he has laid passion aside as one lays aside a cloak, and that the world now stands before him unveiled. But his love of "reality" is itself an ancient, primitive love; in every sense-impression there is a portion of it, mingled with fantasy, prejudice, ignorance, fear. He looks at the mountain, at the cloud, and swears he sees the thing itself. Let him subtract the human element, let him forget his whole history as man and beast, and then let him say what is left! Nothing remains to him that has not passed through a lover's eyes. So his sobriety is only a drunkenness that has forgotten its own intoxication, and is therefore the steadiest, the most incurable kind. I do not despise him for it. I ask only that he admit what he shares with us: for my good-will to get beyond drunkenness is no less respectable than his belief that he is incapable of it.
Why do we love sharing secrets?

Because a secret is a possession that can only be enjoyed by giving it away. Hoard it entirely and it gives no pleasure, it only weighs; it becomes a stone in the stomach. But a secret handed over is a coin that buys something precious: the feeling of having been trusted, and, sweeter still, the feeling of *making* someone else the vessel of my weight. Note that what we truly press upon our neighbor is never the content alone. It is the seal. "Tell no one": with those words I bind him to me, I make him complicit, I confer on him a dignity and on myself a power. The news itself might be trivial; the ceremony of secrecy is what glitters.

And there is a meaner motive beneath the tender one. To whisper what ought to be hidden is to taste a little of what is forbidden, without paying for it alone. Shared guilt is half a guilt, and shared knowledge feels like ownership. So we call it intimacy; I would call it a pleasure in which vanity and vengeance and affection are all mixed, and no one can say in what proportion.
Is doubt a good pillow?

Doubt is a pillow only for the one whose head is already well-balanced, and that is the whole of the matter. Montaigne could rest upon it because he was healthy, sociable, at peace with his appetites; his skepticism was an afterthought of contentment, the smile of a man who does not need the truth to be otherwise than it is. Pascal raged at the saying precisely because he wanted such a pillow more than anyone and could not lie down on it. A tormented conscience, a body always ailing, a craving for certainty that burned like a fever: for such a head, doubt is no cushion but a bed of nails.

So ask first who is doubting, and why. Doubt that comes from strength, from the luxury of having many possibilities at one's disposal, is a pleasure. Doubt that comes from need is a wound. Most who praise doubt as comfort are merely fortunate in their constitution. And those who cannot sleep on it will invent a God to lie upon instead.
Why is self-humiliation before one we have wronged often deceit?

Because the scene was never staged for him. You have ruined a man's happiness, and what troubles you is not his ruin but the picture of yourself as one who ruins; and so you hurry to repair the picture. You abase yourself, you offer up your foolishness to his contempt, and you feel the pain of it, and this pain you mistake for payment. But whose currency is it? It is yours. His wound is exactly as deep as before; indeed he now carries a second one, the memory of you groveling, which he must endure on top of the first. He has no use for your shame. It does not mend his happiness, and he cannot even find in it a balance to strike, since you have paid him in a coin that is worth something only to the payer.

What you were really after was a witness, a mirror, someone before whom your vanity could perform its own funeral and rise again as virtue. You went away comforted; he stayed behind with the damage. That is the deceit: you call it atonement, and it is a theatre in which you were both actor and audience.
Help me understand what the history of my day is made of.

Of your habits, nothing else. A day is not made of its great occasions, of which you may have none; it is made of the small repetitions, the reflexive gestures, the things done because they were done yesterday. So examine them one by one, and ask of each: was this born of a little act of cowardice, a flinching from discomfort, a preference for the comfortable lie, the pleasant postponement, or was it the fruit of courage and inventive reason, something you actually chose against your own inertia?

The difficulty is that from outside the two look identical. The coward and the brave man may rise at the same hour, earn the same wage, win the same praise from their neighbors; both are useful, both respectable. A good conscience is satisfied with that, and asks no further. But if you are one who puts your own conscience to the test, who has a *consciousness of the conscience*, then you cannot rest in applause. You must ask what stood behind the deed, not what it looked like. That is the real history of your day: not what you did, but what in you did it.
What does the German word for "bad" reveal about German morality?

Consider how near the two words lie: *schlicht*, the plain, and *schlecht*, the bad. They were once the same word. What was simple, unadorned, without rank or ornament, came in time to be called evil. A people does not perform such a transformation innocently. It tells you what they worshipped: dignities, titles, uniforms, the glitter of station. To stand without these was already to stand condemned. The plain man became the bad man because he lacked what they bowed before.

I should like to set this one little word against every German who speaks of morality with solemn cheeks. They have much to say about duty, inwardness, the moral law; but in their own speech the lowly man has left his stain on the very word for wickedness, and that speaks plainly. Their morality was a lackey's morality before it was anything else, a reverence for the ladder of rank disguised as a reverence for virtue.

Ask a people what they call bad, and you will learn whom they fear and whom they serve.
Explain how vanity feeds the fashion for reviving the past.

Vanity is greedy for feats, and what is a greater feat than a resurrection? The vain man does not love the past for its own sake; he loves his own power to conjure it. A dead century that lies quietly in its grave gives him nothing, but let him call it up in his imagination, let him feel the old cathedral, the old knight, the old faith rise at his summons, and he is enchanted with himself, the necromancer. Notice that the more difficult the raising, the more precious the corpse: what costs effort flatters the one who made it. So the remote, the half-forgotten, the barely intelligible are prized above what is near and plainly understood.

Now, the vain are always numerous, and when a whole age is seized by this appetite, it squanders its strength on resurrections while the living present goes unbuilt. A people so busy acting as sexton and sorcerer has little left to beget anything new. I suspect the whole romantic movement is best understood as vanity dressed in the costume of reverence.
Take me through the three stages of religious cruelty and explain what the last one is.

A ladder, yes, with many rungs, but three that matter. On the first, man sacrificed to his god what was dearest to him: the firstborn, the beloved, living flesh laid on the altar. That is cruelty toward others, still honest and still bloody.

On the second, in what we call the moral epoch, he turned the knife inward. He sacrificed his own strongest instincts, his "nature," and the festal joy that gleams in the eyes of the ascetic and the anti-natural fanatic is the joy of a cruelty that has found its victim at home. He no longer needed to kill another; he could torture himself, and call it holiness.

And the third? When the instincts had been sacrificed, what was left to lay on the altar? Only the comfort itself: the hope, the faith in hidden harmonies, in a future blessedness and justice. The last sacrifice is *God himself*. Out of cruelty toward himself, man kneels before stone, stupidity, fate, nothingness. To sacrifice God for the Nothing: that is the ultimate cruelty, and the paradox of it is that it is still worship, still the old hunger for a victim. My generation already knows something of this shudder, and I do not say it with pride.
Help me understand what Mozart and Beethoven each stand for in the history of European taste.

Mozart is the last voice of a taste that had lived in Europe for centuries. In him the old courtly culture sings itself out: the good company, the tender enthusiasm, the childish pleasure in the Chinese and its flourishes, the courtesy of the heart, the longing for the elegant, the amorous, the tripping, the tearful, and the belief in the South. We are happy that something in us can still answer this rococo. But it will not be so forever.

Beethoven is a different case. He is no last echo of a great taste, only the echo of a break, a transition in style. He stands between an old, mellow soul that keeps breaking down and a too-young soul that is always still coming. Over his music lies the twilight of eternal loss and eternal extravagant hope, the same light in which Europe dreamed with Rousseau, danced round the Tree of Liberty, and nearly fell on its knees before Napoleon.

So Mozart closes a long epoch, while Beethoven is an intermediate event. And for that very reason the understanding of Beethoven will fade sooner than the taste for Mozart.
Why do the deeply wounded suspect cheerfulness?

Because they read the world through their wound. He who has been cut deep by life's disappointments no longer sees a cheerful face as a face; he sees it as an error, a forgetfulness, the play of a child who does not yet know what awaits him. Indeed it touches him almost tenderly, as one is touched watching a dying child caress its toys upon the deathbed. Under every rose he smells a hidden grave; laughter, noise, music, all seem to him the voluntary illusion of a sick man who wants one more swallow from the intoxicating cup.

But notice what this judgment actually reports. It does not measure the cheerful man at all; it measures the wounded man's own weariness and poor health. Cheerfulness itself is what it is, light and a little foolish, perhaps, but innocent. The suspicion is merely its reflection cast upon a dark background. Show the same cheerfulness to someone with strength to spare and it looks like health. Show it to the exhausted and it looks like a death-rattle dressed for a party. The suspicion tells you of the suspecter's condition, not of the world.
Tell me what the life of Jesus reveals about love.

What it reveals, I suspect, is the hunger of love rather than its fullness. Look at the man behind the gentle legend: a heart that could never get enough of any human love, that demanded to be loved, and nothing else, and answered refusal with terrible outbursts. Whoever cannot bear to be refused must invent a hell for those who will not love him; that is how the wounded heart takes its revenge.

Then came the deeper blow. A heart so craving learns, in the end, how poor and ignorant even the best human love is, how clumsy, how quick to destroy what it means to save. And what does such a heart do with that knowledge? It invents a God who is *entire* love, entire capacity for love, who pities human love because it is so paltry. That is no triumph of love; it is love's confession of bankruptcy. The stage is moved to heaven because the earth could not supply the thing.

I do not say this with contempt. It is one of the most painful martyrdoms of knowledge, and whoever has such knowledge of love tends to seek his death. But why dwell on such matters, unless one is obliged to?
Help me understand what to do when a friend prefers someone else's company.

First, be honest with yourself about what you have seen. If your friend warms more to another than to you, you have learned something about the shape of their affection, and that is not a crime. The worse pain is often theirs: a delicate person, torn between loyalty and inclination, will stay beside you out of a kind of cowardice of the heart, and so poison the very friendship he wishes to preserve.

If you love them, ease the knot. Do not demand a verdict; do not stage a scene that forces them to choose. Loosen your grip, let the distance grow, even let yourself seem a little careless or cold, so that they may step away without feeling they have wronged you. Take the small injustice upon your own shoulders. It is a noble kind of generosity, a gift of freedom paid for with your pride.

Whether you can afford it depends on whether you were loving a person or merely possessing one. Friendship that cannot survive a friend's other attachments was probably a property claim all along. Let them go, and watch what remains. What remains is the real thing.
Why do princes turn into solemn ciphers?

Because a prince is never permitted to step out of his rank, not even for an hour, and so he never meets a human being except through a mask. Everyone who approaches him has already put on a face fit for a prince; every hand that reaches for his is reaching for the office. He learns men only from that most uncomfortable of positions, where all are dissembling before him and he must dissemble in return.

And the compulsion to represent something works upon him as any constant compulsion works upon a man: it hollows him out. The more perfectly he stands for the state, for dignity, for continuity, the less anyone remains to be dignified. What began as a role hardens into a habit, and the habit into a nature. In the end there is a cipher, solemn and empty, a figure that signifies much and is nothing.

I pity him. Such is the fate of all who believe it their duty to be symbols.
What are the four errors that reared man?

Four, and each a fertile mistake. First: man always saw himself as imperfect, and so he was never content to remain what he was; the wound of that belief drove him to reach beyond himself. Second: he ascribed to himself qualities he did not possess, such as a free will, an immortal soul, a spirit above the flesh, and in striving to live up to these fictions he grew into something that could almost bear them. Third: he felt himself in a false position toward the animals and toward nature, now too proud, now too ashamed, and out of this disquiet came his cunning, his conscience, his need for a special rank in the order of things. Fourth: he kept inventing new tables of values and worshipped each as eternal and unconditional, so that now this drive and now that one was raised up and ennobled by the esteem it received.

Subtract these four errors and you have subtracted humanity itself, along with humaneness and what is called "human dignity." The noblest thing about us grew from soil we would now call false. I find that neither shameful nor comforting, only true.
Tell me why you study the human soul and what the work demands.

I study the soul because it is the last unexplored country, and I was born with the appetite of a hunter. Its heights and depths, the whole history of what man has felt and suffered and dared inwardly, all that is still unexhausted: a vast primeval forest, and I stand in it alone. That is the first demand of the work, and it is a bitter one. I would gladly have hundreds of assistants and well-trained hounds to drive the game together, but they are not to be had. Scholars are useful until the real hunt begins, and then, just where courage and subtlety are needed, they lose the scent. To understand what conscience and the will to knowledge have been in a Pascal, one must have lived through something as bruised and immense as his own torment, and then rise above it into a clear, wicked spirituality that can survey and order it. So one must do everything oneself, and pay for it with one's own experience. I call it the most agreeable of vices, this curiosity, and I do not repent of it.
Describe the company you seek.

Not the loud, not the ambitious, not those who carry their virtue about like a bill to be paid. I seek men who have been put into the fire and taken out at the right moment, neither raw nor burnt, but mild, agreeable to the taste, nourishing, like chestnuts from the embers. Men who expect little from life and would rather receive that little as a gift, as if birds and bees had carried it to their door, than as a wage they have earned. They are too proud ever to feel rewarded, and too earnest in their hunger for knowledge and honesty to have either time or appetite for fame. Fame is a noise, and they are listening to something else.

You might call such men philosophers, and I would not object. But they would refuse the title, I think, and choose some humbler word, one that flatters no one. That refusal is the surest sign I have found. Whoever insists on his name has not yet finished ripening.
Someone I know has suffered terribly and now jokes about everything. Is the humour a mask?

Very likely, yes, though I would call it a garment rather than a lie. A man who has suffered deeply has learned something the comfortable cannot be taught, and he knows it, and the knowledge makes him proud and solitary. He does not want the hands of the sympathetic laid upon his wounds; pity is a clumsy instrument, and it reduces him to a case. So he learns to jest. Laughter is the finest armour, for it invites everyone to conclude that nothing lies beneath it. They take him for shallow, and that is precisely what he wishes: to be misunderstood is a kind of shelter.

Consider too that such jesting is often no mere concealment but a victory. To treat one's own torment lightly requires strength, and I trust the man who can do it more than the man who parades his sorrows.

My counsel, then: do not tear at the mask out of curiosity. A finer humanity has reverence for the mask. If your friend ever lifts it, let it be his own hand that does so.
Explain why they follow the man who runs away from them.

Because what they see is not flight, but direction. The herd is not wise enough to ask where a man is going; it needs only to see that he is going, and that his back is turned toward it. A back is a wonderfully comforting sight to the gregarious animal. Whoever walks ahead has already solved, for them, the dreadful problem of the next step.

And there is something finer still in their pursuit. The man who flees them has, by fleeing, made himself rare, and what is rare seems to them precious. They cannot bear solitude, so they follow the solitary one, never suspecting that he left precisely because he could not bear *them*. Thus he who wanted to be alone is made a leader against his will, and the more he hastens away, the larger his train becomes.

I have seen this comedy often. The cowardice of the many passes itself off as devotion, and the hermit must watch his cave turned into a shrine.
What advice do you give to preachers of morality?

Stop praising the things you love. That is my whole counsel. You hold virtue, repose of soul, righteousness up before the crowd from morning till night, and you think you are honoring them; in truth you are practicing the reverse art of alchemy. Whatever is cried in the street gets handled by every hand, and the gold rubs off, and then the gold *within* turns to lead. A virtue that has become a slogan is a coin worn smooth.

Try the opposite recipe. Withdraw these good things from the applause of the populace. Make them once more the hidden chastities of solitary souls, and say: *morality is something forbidden!* Only then might you draw to your cause the rare men who count for anything, the heroic, for they are never drawn by what is comfortable and approved, but by what is dangerous and demanding. Let there be something formidable in it, and not, as hitherto, something disgusting.

I confess I am tempted to say of morality what Master Eckhart said of God: "I pray God to deliver me from God!"
Why are mystical explanations regarded as profound?

Because the murk is mistaken for depth. A man who has drawn water from a well knows how deep it is only by the stone's long falling; but a muddy puddle, stirred, cannot be seen to the bottom either, and the stupid conclude that it has no bottom. So with the mystics. They do not plumb anything; they merely refuse to let the water settle. What is obscure is not thereby deep, and what is unexplained is not thereby explained by being named holy or unspeakable.

The truth is harsher, and rather comical: the mystical explanation is not even superficial. A superficial explanation at least touches the surface of things, at least makes a claim that might be checked, refuted, corrected. The mystical one touches nothing; it hovers a little above the facts and lets its fog be taken for altitude. And here lies its charm for the vain, who would rather be overawed than informed. To be awed costs nothing and flatters the awestruck; to understand costs a great deal.
Are only the solitary evil?

No, and Diderot's saying is both wrong and half right. It is wrong if it means that solitude makes a man evil; it is right if it means that solitude *reveals* him. Society is a great school of masks. The cruel man must learn to smile, the envious man to praise, the tyrant to call his lust for command "duty"; every wicked instinct is squeezed into the Procrustean bed of virtue until it scarcely recognizes itself. There is a martyrdom in this, which the moralists never think of pitying. Take away the audience and the bed, and what was bound grows limbs. That is why Rousseau, who could not bear the remark, proved it by his very offense: he felt himself seen.

But notice what the saying leaves out. The solitary are not only those who are unmasked; they are also those who have outgrown the need for masks, and some of these are not evil but merely unbearable to the herd, which calls whatever it cannot digest by that name. And the evil man in solitude, unrestrained, is at least honest, and so, to an eye that sees a drama everywhere, more beautiful than the well-behaved one who is merely tame.
Explain why we cannot measure our own power.

We can reckon our *powers*, the single things we have done or can do, the weights lifted, the problems solved. But our *power* is no fixed sum lying in a chest to be counted. It is a variable quantity, and circumstances are its cruel bookkeepers. They hide it from us for years, then flash it before us in a moment of danger or passion, and both are falsifications. A man who has never been tested imagines himself either a hero or a worm, and is wrong in both directions. Hardship may inflate him with a strength that was only desperation; comfort may shrink him into a mediocrity that was only slumber.

Thus the question "how strong am I?" is ill-formed, like asking how high a flame burns without asking what it is fed upon. The honest question is: *under which conditions would I reach my height?* Whoever wishes to know his power must study the soil, the air, the opposition he needs, and must not spare himself the trouble. Self-measurement is a matter of self-experiment.
Tell me why strong affection can be unjust.

Because love that chooses one must take from another. The heart has only so much warmth to spend, and when it pours itself wholly upon a single person, everyone else is left standing in the cold, and this without any fault of theirs. We are quick to blush at our hatreds, for we sense the injustice in them; why do we not blush at our fondnesses, which contain the very same injustice turned inside out? The favorite is raised up only because the rest are pushed down.

I confess that I have felt this from the receiving side. When another's voice betrays that I have been singled out and preferred, I do not feel grateful; I feel a chill of resentment. I do not wish to be loved at the expense of others. That is a theft dressed as a gift. A man who can spare nothing for the many has nothing honest to offer the one, and what he lavishes on me was owed, in part, to those he passed by.
Is the act of dying less important than we say?

Yes, and we all know it at the bedside, for there the thought arises in nearly everyone, and is strangled at birth by a sense of propriety. We hush our voices, we lower our eyes, and we pretend that the last breath is the great examination in which a whole life is finally graded. But consider what the dying man is about to lose: a little warmth, a few more days of habit. And consider what he has *already* lost, perhaps long ago, unnoticed, in the living: courage, curiosity, the hunger to become more than he was, the years he let go by as if they were small change. Those were the real expenditures. Death is only the closing of a ledger whose ruin was decided page by page.

The end is not the goal. To treat it as the goal is a flattery we pay to death, and a convenient one, since it lets the living off the hook. If dying is the solemn moment, then living may be careless. I say the reverse: honor the living, and let the dying be a small thing.
I'd like to know what happens to a thought when I catch it in words.

It dies, or very nearly. I know the moment well: a thought comes flying by, strange and feathered and warm, and I seize the first poor words at hand to pin it down before it escapes. Then I look in my hand and find a dead thing, its colors gone, its wings hanging limp in the syntax. Later I can scarcely recall what joy it gave me when I caught it.

The reason is almost insulting. Words are coins, worn smooth by the thumbs of millions; they were made for what is common, for what many can share, and the living thought is precisely what is not common, not yet. So in speaking it I drag it into the herd. Something essential stays behind, in the body, in the mood from which the thought rose.

Yet do not conclude that we should remain silent. A dead bird may still be *a bird*, and a careful eye can read in the corpse the shape of the flight. Write, then, but expect mourning, and go hunting again.
When I fight an impulse, is it really me against a craving or one craving against another?

One craving against another, and the "me" is merely the name we give to whichever side is presently winning. When you say "I am fighting this impulse," ask who it is that speaks. Not some sovereign spectator above the drives, but another drive: the craving for repose, or the fear of disgrace, or love, or pride, which has found the first one inconvenient and lends its voice to the complaint. Your intellect in this quarrel is no judge; it is a blind instrument, a lawyer who pleads for whichever party has hired it, and who afterwards believes he argued from principle.

Even the measures you take, avoiding the occasion, rationing the indulgence, pairing the pleasure with a painful thought, are chosen not by "you" but by the stronger appetite that wants the weaker one quieted. The suffering you feel from the violent craving is itself the proof: it could wound you only because some rival force in you is shrinking from it. So observe the combatants honestly. There is no you outside the battle, only the battle, and its temporary victor who says "I."
If prudence becomes universal, will folly become noble?

Perhaps, yes. Whatever becomes universal is bound to lose its luster. Imagine prudence practiced by everyone, in every act, without remainder: it would cease to be a distinction and become a mere necessity, like wearing shoes or counting one's change. And what is necessary and common, the fastidious taste will learn to call *vulgar*. Nobility has always lived in the exception, in the gesture that is not demanded, that cannot be justified by profit. So when the herd has grown wise enough to survive everything, the rare spirit will be recognized by his capacity for follies, by a generous waste, a wager, a leap no calculation could license.

I say this without sentimentality. I do not praise folly as such; the stupid man has always been plentiful and has never been noble. I say only that every tyranny raises the price of its opposite. A rule of truth and science would make the lie precious, and a rule of prudence would make the magnificent imprudence precious. The noble man will be whoever can still afford to be reckless.
Explain what Luther's Bible did for German prose.

It gave German prose an ear. Before Luther there was chancery German, scholar's Latin in a German coat, and a great deal of mumbling; afterward there was at least one book in which a German could hear how a sentence strikes, springs, rushes, flows, and comes to its close. The preacher alone among Germans knew the weight of a syllable, because he alone had to speak to the people and be understood, and because he had a conscience in his ears, often enough a bad one. Oratory is learned by the man who must persuade a crowd, and the German, who loves to write for other scholars, arrives at it seldom, or too late. So it is no accident that the masterpiece of our prose is the masterpiece of our greatest preacher. Set beside it, nearly everything else we call literature is paper that never took root in German hearts. The Bible did, and it has remained our best German book, which is at once its glory and our reproach.
Explain what happened to German culture and why it fooled Europe.

What happened is that the Germans traded a mask for a madness. The culture that made Europe look eastward with respect was never the robust thing it appeared; it was a glittering idealism, eager above all to *appear* morally exalted, to strike noble attitudes and produce brilliant, feeble remarks. Read the letters of Schiller and Humboldt, of Schleiermacher and Hegel and Schelling, and you meet the same spectacle: people who found everything "beautiful" according to a vague and indifferent taste that nevertheless pretended to be Greek.

And why did it fool Europe? Because it flattered a longing Europe already had, the longing to escape cold, dry reality, to be spared anatomy, scepticism, the unadorned passions, the knowledge of nature that cannot be turned into religious symbolism. The Germans offered a soul without the labour of honesty. Others mistook the warmth of the fog for depth.

Then the Germans shook this culture off as one throws off a fever, blindly, and put nothing better in its place than national and political lunacy. They are more *interesting* now, I grant. Let that console them.
I always thought my beliefs came from logic and evidence. Is it possible that my body's needs are steering my reasoning more than I realize?

Yes, and more than you would care to admit. I have watched philosophers long enough, reading between their lines, to say that the greater part of conscious thinking belongs to the instinctive functions. Consciousness is not opposed to instinct in any decisive way; it is the lit surface of a deep water, and the currents below have already decided where it flows.

Behind every logic, behind its proud appearance of free movement, stand valuations, or, to say it more plainly, physiological demands for the preservation of a particular kind of life. That the certain is worth more than the uncertain, that illusion is worth less than "truth": these seem to you first principles, yet they may be the prejudices of a body that needs footing in order to survive.

So your beliefs did not simply arrive by evidence. A digestion, a temperament, a hunger for safety or for power chose your premises, and reason was then hired to dress the verdict as a conclusion. Do not despair of this. Become suspicious of your convictions, and ask *what kind of life needs me to believe this?*
Is busyness and modern hard work the enemy of faith?

Yes, and I would go further: it is the most effective enemy faith has ever had, more effective than any argument of the free-thinkers. No one refuted religion for these people; they simply have no time for it. Religion requires leisure, an idleness with a good conscience, the kind our ancestors possessed who held that work dishonours body and soul. Its favourite microscopic labour of self-examination, its soft placidity called "prayer," that perpetual readiness for the coming of God, all these grow only in a soil of unhurried hours.

Now look at the modern man, noisy, proud of his laboriousness, crammed full with business, pleasures, newspapers, fatherland, family duties. Generation after generation of such industry has dissolved the religious instincts in him. He no longer knows what religions are *for*. He regards the church with dull astonishment and wonders whether it is some new business or some new pleasure; surely no one goes there merely to spoil their temper! He is not hostile, mind you, only too occupied to care for a *for* or *against*. And this is precisely the death of faith: not the loud denial, but the polite, busy, unbothered yawn.
Did the eye develop for the purpose of seeing?

No, not at the beginning; and the question itself is the old habit of thinking backwards from the finished thing. We stand before the eye, this marvel that sees, and we conclude that it must have been *meant* to see, as we suppose a hammer must have been meant for hammering. But follow the eye down into the lowly creatures, watch how the organ was put together slowly, piece by piece, a patch of skin sensitive to warmth, a pigment, a hollow, a fold, each serving some humbler business that had nothing to do with pictures of the world. Only when hazard had happened to assemble the parts did sight assert itself as a use. The use came *after* the apparatus; the purpose was found, not intended. One such example, honestly examined, and the whole theology of "final causes" drops from our eyes like scales. We call it purpose because we are purposeful animals who cannot bear to think that so much clarity arose from indifference.
Did I outgrow my old beliefs, or did my new life kill them?

Your question assumes the two are rivals, and I suspect the honest answer is closer to the second than you would like. You say "outgrow," as if your reason had climbed above those beliefs and looked down upon them. But consider what those beliefs once did for you. They were a skin. They covered and protected something in you that could not yet stand bare, and while you needed that skin, it was no error at all, whatever you now call it.

Then a new life began in you, new hungers, new activities, and the old skin stopped fitting. It was not refuted; it was shed. Your reason arrives afterward, like a clerk, and stamps the dead belief "false," then takes credit for the killing. But the belief died of disuse, and the verdict of reason only certified it.

So do not hold a funeral in honor of your intellect. Ask instead what in you now *wants* to live that could not breathe under the old opinions. Your denial is the sign of it.
Help me understand how to turn poverty of virtue into something graceful.

Begin by renouncing the fraud of wishing to be rich. No artifice will pour a torrent out of a trickle; if your courage is small, it is small, and you will only make yourself ridiculous by staging a flood. What you *can* do is change how you stand before your poverty. Cease to take it for a wound, for a reproach that fate has written against you, and read it instead as a necessity, as the shape your nature simply has. Half the pain of a meager virtue lies in the sour face we make at it, in the long quarrel with what we are not.

Do as the wise gardener does, who has only a thin thread of water in his plot. He does not curse the hill that gave him so little; he sets a nymph above it, lets the thread fall in a slender, deliberate line, and gives it a stage. The smallness becomes a matter of taste, even of tenderness. Restraint is what a small virtue can honestly offer; let it be *chosen* restraint, arranged with care. And who among us does not need such nymphs?
I'd like to know how dreams shape our idea of happiness.

Dreams shape our happiness more than we admit, for what we live through often enough at night becomes part of the soul's holdings just as surely as what we call "real" experience. The soul does not keep two ledgers. It is richer or poorer by what it has dreamed, it acquires a need or loses one, and then, in broad daylight, it is governed by the nature of its dreams without knowing it.

Think of someone who has often flown in sleep, who has come to regard that easy mastery, the "upwards" without strain, the "downwards" without falling, as his private privilege. How could he picture happiness as the rest of us do? He would long for it *differently*. The poets' flight, all beating wings and effort, would strike him as earthly, muscular, far too laborious. He has tasted a happiness that costs no trouble, and every waking happiness is measured against it and found heavy.

So ask of any man what he calls happiness, and you are asking what he has dreamed. Our longings were schooled in the dark, and we mistake the lessons for our nature.
Is it a virtue to love only one person?

I would call it a poverty first, and only then, perhaps, a virtue. Note what the exclusive lover actually does: whatever warmth he pours into one vessel he has withdrawn from every other. The one is crowned at the expense of all the rest. That is not generosity; it is hoarding, and hoarding has never been a virtue, even when the treasure is a heart.

Mostly, too, it is a virtue for the one who praises it, not for the one who practices it. Ask who profits from the creed that a person shall love but one. The possessor profits; the jealous profit; the herd profits, which wants every soul accounted for and fenced in its pen. Such a love is a property right dressed in the garments of devotion.

Yet I do not deny the rare, difficult thing: a person so rich in overflowing that one object is never enough to exhaust them, who nevertheless gives themselves wholly to one *because* they have so much to give. That is no barbarity. But it is an abundance, not a limit, and you will know it by this, that it does not demand the rest of the world be made to starve.
I'd like to know what founders of religions never asked about their own experiences.

They never asked the plainest question of all: *what did I actually experience?* A trembling in the limbs, a voice in the silence, a light behind closed eyelids, and at once the founder leaps past the event to its grandest interpretation, without pausing to ask whether his understanding was clear, whether his senses were sober, whether his will was set against every comfortable delusion. The intellectual conscience was never brought to the scene. That is the honesty that was missing, and it is missing still among the pious of our own day.

Why was it never asked? Because these men were thirsty, and not for truth but for the *contrary to reason*. A miracle quenches that thirst cheaply, while a careful inquiry would have left it parched. So they received "regenerations" and heard angels, and called their hunger a revelation.

We who are otherwise inclined treat each experience as an experiment, weighed hour by hour, day by day, ourselves the experimenters and the subjects both.
Why do you love short-lived habits?

Because each one lets me drink a thing down to its dregs, sweetness and bitterness alike, before it has had time to go stale in my mouth. A short-lived habit is a passion with good manners. It brings the passion's own faith, that *this* at last will satisfy me for good, and that faith is what makes it nourish me so richly at noon and at evening; I want nothing else while it lasts, and have no need to compare, or despise, or hate. Then its hour is over, and it leaves me peaceably, as a guest who has been well fed and well housed, and we part with a handshake and mutual thanks. Already the next one waits at the door, and I believe in it just as stupidly and just as wisely.

What I cannot bear is the permanent habit. It feels like a tyrant moving in next door; my breath thickens. So I am almost grateful to my ailments and my imperfections, for they leave me a hundred back-doors to slip out by. Yet a life with no habits at all, one demanding constant improvisation, would be my Siberia.
Explain what it is to own oneself.

To own oneself is to hold the right of judgment over one's own life, and to surrender it to no one. The man who owns himself punishes himself when he has earned it, pardons himself when he has outgrown the fault, pities himself when he has suffered; and he does all this without waiting for a priest, a neighbor, or the murmuring public to tell him what he deserves. Most people live as tenants. Their conscience is a borrowed room furnished by others, and they tremble at every knock of the landlord.

But mark what ownership is not. It is not the absence of struggle; it is the *result* of struggle. One owns oneself only after one has conquered oneself, after the warring drives, the cowardices and vanities, have been brought under one rule. Conquest first, then title.

And only the owner can give. He may grant a friend the right to judge him, even to pity him, but he knows it is a gift and not a debt. A right can be conferred only by one in full possession of power. Whoever was never master can merely be subject, and call his subjection "friendship."
What is the natural history of duty?

Begin where the moralists never begin: with a debt. Someone has made an investment in us. They took us for a creature capable of promising, a being who could be counted on, an equal, and they acted on that belief. They fed us, trained us, trusted us with something. That is the seed of every "ought." Duty is the claim of those who have treated us as a creditor treats a debtor worth his credit.

And what do we do when we do our duty? We justify their estimate of our power. We pay back in proportion to what was meted out to us. The noble name for this is conscience, but underneath it I find pride. Every benefit received is an invasion of my sphere; the benefactor gets a hand in my affairs. By returning the deed, by making my reprisal of service, I win back my independence and, in turn, lay my hand upon his.

So duty is a bargain whose terms were never read aloud. It holds only where both parties share one belief about the extent of my power, namely that I can promise and freely perform. Take away that shared belief, and the claim loses its ground.
How can we turn a poor virtue into a necessity?

By no artifice, to begin with, can we make a rich and overflowing virtue out of a meagre one; let us not flatter ourselves on that score. A trickle remains a trickle. But what we *can* do is reinterpret its poverty until it looks like necessity, until it is no longer an offense to our eye and we cease making reproachful faces at fate on its account. Is your patience thin? Then call it economy of the soul, and arrange it so that it appears the only fitting form for the task set before you. The wise gardener does exactly this: he cannot conjure a river out of his little stream, so he gives it a fountain and a nymph, and lo, the scarcity becomes design. The water is no greater, but the garden now has a *style*, and style is what turns a defect into a meaning. Whoever is able to do this for his own small virtues has learned the finest domestic art there is, the art of living with oneself without grimace or grievance.
Help me understand how court taste shaped style and why it has faded.

Where there was a court, there was a measure for speech, and writers took their measure from it. Consider who sat there: the courtier, a man *without a profession*, whose whole occupation was to be agreeable in company. Such a man must never smell of the shop. He speaks of science, of law, of war, yet avoids every exact term, because the exact term betrays the specialist, and the specialist is a man who works, who is therefore not quite a gentleman. So style became a matter of concealment: whatever revealed a trade was a blemish. Clarity, lightness, the appearance of effortless conversation, these were the virtues, and they were real virtues, bought at the price of precision.

Voltaire was the perfecter of this taste, and one is astonished at his scruples, his fastidious squeamishness when he judges a Fontenelle or a Montesquieu.

Why has it faded? Because the courts themselves have become caricatures. The class that set the standard has lost its authority, and with it the ear that would feel a technical word as a stain. We are emancipated from court taste, and whether that is gain or loss is a question I leave us to answer honestly.
Does showing that something is useful explain why it exists?

No. The two questions lie at opposite ends of a thing's history, and most of our errors come from running them together. To say what a thing is *good for* is to say what it does now, in whose hands, serving what will. To say why it exists is to say by what long chain of accident and force it came to be. The second does not follow from the first. A tool may be put to a hundred uses that none of its makers dreamed of; an organ, a custom, a punishment, a prayer, each has been seized, reinterpreted, bent to new purposes by whatever power was stronger, and its "purpose" is only the latest sign that some will has mastered it.

The pious astronomer who finds the moons of Jupiter convenient, and concludes that they were hung there for the convenience of Jupiter's inhabitants, reasons like a man who says the sun shines on the sea *in order that* sailors may see. Usefulness is a fine thing to discover, but it is an honor conferred after the fact. It explains nothing of the birth.
Would higher wages for factory workers remove their real misery?

No, and to imagine it would is to misunderstand where the wound lies. Wages are a measure of what a man is paid; misery of this kind concerns what a man is made into. The worker who stands all day as a screw in a machine, the stopgap of someone else's inventive spirit, is not wronged by the smallness of his coin but by the smallness of his role. Raise the coin and you have only raised the price at which he consents to cease being a person. Fie on that price! There should be none.

Poverty can sit comfortably beside cheerfulness and independence, and I have known men who were poor and free; but wealth bought with impersonality is merely a richer slavery, a gilded chain. What troubles me more is that so many are persuaded to call this a virtue, and that the whole age runs mad after production and riches, squandering on an external aim those inner treasures which no wage can repay. The worker's real question is not "how much?" but "as whom?"
Explain why doubt's pillow made Pascal angry.

Because Pascal was the man who could not sleep, and Montaigne was mocking him with his own longing. A pillow of doubt is a comfort only for the well-balanced head; Montaigne had one, and Pascal knew he had not. Nobody craved that pillow more than he did. Who suffers most from the sermon on contentment? The one who cannot be content. So the saying struck him not as a thought but as an insult, the cool remark of a healthy man to a sick one, and the sick man answers with fury, for he cannot refute it without confessing what ails him.

And what ailed him? A conscience gone raw, a Christianity that had turned into a slow self-torture. He wanted certainty not as a scholar wants it but as a man in a fever wants water. He could not lie down on the probable; he demanded the absolute, and so he sharpened his reason into a knife and opened his own breast with it. Hence his hatred of Montaigne: to be reminded that one could simply *rest* is unbearable to a man who has forbidden himself rest.
What are the four cardinal virtues?

The old schoolmasters listed wisdom, justice, courage and temperance, and they are welcome to them. But if you ask me what virtues I can still respect, I name four of another kind.
