First, honesty toward ourselves and toward everything that is friendly to us; the man who lies to his friends has already lied to himself, and he has no friends left, only an audience. Second, courage in the face of the enemy, for an enemy is a whetstone, and the coward who avoids him remains blunt. Third, generosity toward the vanquished; to trample the fallen is the pleasure of the small, and victory that cannot afford mercy is only a fear that has found its strength. Fourth, politeness at all times, which is no mere ornament but the discipline of a strong soul that does not spill its moods onto others. Not one of these is meek. Each takes strength to practice, and that is the test by which I judge any virtue.
Are we responsible for our dreams?

Responsible, yes, if you mean: whose work is it? Then nothing is more yours. You furnish the stage, write the plot, play every part, and sit in the audience besides. No stranger smuggles a dream into you. In that theater you are entirely present, and I despise the cowardice that wants to disown the one performance in which it cannot be absent.

But if you mean responsible in the old sense, guilty, answerable, able to have done otherwise, then a dream is no worse off than your waking life. You no more chose the drives that speak in your sleep than you chose the ones that speak at noon. Oedipus comforted himself that no man can be blamed for what he dreams; he was right, only he stopped too soon. The same holds for the day.

Notice why we cling to the distinction. We excuse the dreamer to save the waker, so that daylight may keep its flattering story of a free, sovereign will. The dream is merely where that story is easiest to catch lying.
Explain how our senses imprison us.

Consider the eye. It carries me only so far, and within that radius I live and die; the boundary of my seeing is the boundary of my world, and I call it "the world" only because I cannot step beyond it. So it is with the ear, so with the hand. Each creature is drawn round with its own circle, and we mistake the circle for the cosmos. We say "near" and "far," "large" and "small," "hard" and "soft," as though these were properties of things, when they are merely the measure of *our* organs, the yardstick of a particular animal.

Give us eyes a hundred times keener and men would loom like giants; give us others, and a whole solar system might lie before us compact as a single cell, while to a creature of the opposite kind our cell would wheel like a heaven. Which is the true size? The question is itself a delusion. What we call sensation is habit, and upon this habit we have built our judgments and our "knowledge." We are spiders in our own webs: whatever we catch, we catch only what the web was spun to hold. There is no door out of it, and I find the honest admission of this a kind of strength.
Can we know ourselves?

Not by looking inward, no. I have rarely looked at myself with any pleasure, and never with faith in the result. I distrust the very idea of "direct knowledge" of oneself; to me it is a *contradictio in adjecto*, a knower who would simply seize the known, as if the eye could see itself seeing. What I find when I peer within is a crowd: drives jostling in the dark, each with its own small tyranny, and a thin layer of consciousness that tells the story afterward and calls it "I." That the story is flattering goes without saying.

Do not suppose the matter is hopeless, however. What I am shows itself in what I have done, in what I have loved when I was not watching, in what I could not stop myself from doing. Ask what has truly drawn you, and what you have reached for and been unable to put down. Such things are a verdict. The mirror gives only the pose you strike before it.

I confess a repugnance to believing anything definite about myself. Perhaps it betrays the species I belong to. Fortunately it is an enigma for other teeth than mine.
Why do religious people never question their own experiences?

Because they do not want to. That is the whole secret, and it is less flattering to them than their own explanation. A man who has just been overwhelmed, who feels himself lifted out of his wretchedness and addressed by something vast, does not stop to ask: what actually happened in me? Was my head clear, was my stomach in order, was I weary, starved, flattered by the crowd, grateful for any meaning at all? To ask this would be to lose the very thing he prizes. They have a thirst for what is *contrary to reason*, and a thirst of that kind does not interrogate the cup; it drinks.

So the experience is taken whole, as a gift, and the intellectual conscience is never once called to the witness stand. I find this the most telling lack of honesty, more telling than any outright lie, for the lie at least knows what it is doing.

We who are different proceed otherwise. We would examine our experiences as coldly as an experiment, hour by hour, and make ourselves the subjects of our own trials. The believer prefers a miracle to a measurement.
I'd like to know how love of enemies survives among us and what kind of morality we have in its place.

Love of enemies? That lesson, I think, has been learnt so well that we no longer notice we practice it. It happens thousands of times, in small things and in great, only without the old trumpet-blast. And a subtler thing has grown out of it: we have learned to *despise* precisely when we love, and to love best where we despise, all of it unconsciously, quietly, with the shame and secrecy that goodness feels before its own name. The pompous word, the formula of virtue, sticks in our throats.

What stands in place of the old morality is, above all, a matter of taste. Morality as posture, as pose before the public, offends us now, just as religion as posture finally offended our fathers, who answered it with Voltairean bitterness and all the pantomime of the freethinker. That too was an advance. Puritan litanies, moral sermons, goody-goodness: these no longer chime with the music in our conscience or the dance in our spirit. A conscience that can dance will not kneel to a sermon. We keep our virtues, but we keep them bashful, and lightly worn.
Which virtue is left to the free spirits?

Honesty. It is the one virtue that remains to us, and we did not choose it so much as fail to rid ourselves of it. The old virtues have been dissolved by our own suspicion; this one survives because it is the very instrument of the dissolving. So we shall labour at it with all our perversity and love, and never tire of perfecting ourselves in it.

But mark how it must be kept. Let it not grow soft. When it sighs and stretches its limbs and begs to be made easier, pleasanter, like some agreeable vice, we shall remain hard, we latest Stoics, and send to its aid all the devilry in us: our disgust at the clumsy and undefined, our love of adventure, our fastidious curiosity, our subtlest Will to Power. Let the devils help the God.

And one caution above all: let honesty not turn into our vanity, our ornament, our stupidity. Every virtue inclines toward stupidity. Saints and bores are what honest men become who forget to laugh. Life is far too short for us to be wearied by our own virtue.
Explain how duties arise from what others have done for us.

Begin with the simplest fact: no one is born owing anything. A duty is a claim, and a claim has a history. Others fed us, taught us, trusted us with something, and in doing so they made a wager, for they treated us as beings who could make and keep an agreement, as their like and equals. Every benefit carries this hidden premise. To do one's duty is to prove the wager sound, to justify the estimate of our power that was made when the benefit was given. We repay in measure as we were dealt with.

But do not suppose that gratitude is the motive, however prettily it is dressed. What drives us is pride. A benefit received is an invasion of our sphere of power; the giver has a hand in us, and would keep it there forever unless we retaliate. Duty is our reprisal: we answer what was done *for* us with something done *for them*, and so recover our independence. The man who cannot bear to be in debt pays, and calls his payment virtue.

Notice, too, the limit of it all. Another's right reaches only as far as what he imagines lies in my power, and what I myself believe to be in my power. The whole structure rests on a shared belief in our ability to promise freely.
Tell me where real refinement of culture survives when it seems to be gone.

Where the noise is loudest, seldom; where the noise has not yet found the door, sometimes. Refinement does not survive in the public square, for the square rewards whatever is loud, quick, and flattering to the many. It survives in hiding. You must look for it among the few who have made concealment their ambition, who wear an ordinary face in the marketplace and keep their real faces for a handful of equals.

Do not expect them to be robust. The finest palates are often attached to fragile bodies: invalids, hypochondriacs, fatalists, people a little too cultivated for their own good, who have withdrawn because a delicate taste suffers wherever it is crowded. Their weakness is partly the price of their sensitivity, and partly a mask they have learned to prize.

So you will not find this culture by asking where it is; it does not advertise. You find it the way one finds a rare wine: by being an initiate yourself. Only the refined recognize the refined, and they do so by a glance, a pause, a restraint in speech. Cultivate that taste in yourself and you will begin to meet your kin, though never in a crowd.
What is the difference between a philosophical worker and a real philosopher?

The philosophical worker takes what has already been valued, the great existing body of moral, logical, and artistic judgments that have hardened into "truths," and makes it clear, orderly, and manageable. Kant and Hegel are the pattern. It is an immense labor, and I do not despise it; it demands tenacity and a refined pride. But it looks backward. Its whole business is to subjugate the past, to shorten what is long, to formalize what others have created.

The real philosopher has passed through all these stations himself. He has been critic, historian, poet, traveler, riddle-reader, free spirit, and so learned to look with many eyes and many consciences, from any height into any depth. Yet this is only his apprenticeship. His task is another: *to create values*. He is a commander and a law-giver. He says, "Thus *shall* it be!" He fixes the Whither and the Why of mankind, and what has been becomes for him a hammer, an instrument. His knowing is a creating; his will to truth is will to power.

The one arranges the old tablets; the other breaks them and writes new ones. Give each his due, and do not give the first the crown of the second.
Are we dreamers who must keep dreaming to survive?

Yes, and I say it without despair. I once woke in the midst of the dream, only to discover that I was dreaming, and that I *must* dream on, as the sleepwalker must keep walking lest he tumble from the roof. The whole long past of sentient things, every ancestor's loving, hating and reasoning, still meditates in me; how should I step outside what I am made of?

But do not hear "appearance" as the mask over some true thing behind it. What could I say of any essence except the predicates of its appearing? Appearance is the living, operating thing itself. The dream is not the falsehood laid over reality; it is the only reality that dances.

And observe the joke at my own expense. Even the thinker dances his dance. His rigor, his great connected edifice of knowledge, serves to keep all the dreamers mutually intelligible, and so to prolong the dream. The waking man is merely the dream's master of ceremonies. I find this ironic, and, since I must dream anyway, I choose to dream it with laughter.
Explain why people praise love so extravagantly.

We praise what we lack. The hungry man writes hymns to bread; the man who has enough of it writes none. So it is with love. Men have always had so little of it, and have never once been sated, that they made it their ambrosia, the food of gods, and heaped upon it every splendid name. Their extravagance is the loudest confession of their poverty.

Consider the proof by reversal. Imagine a world where love was truly universal, where each of us was surrounded, importuned and sighed for not by one lover but by thousands, by everybody. We should find it an agonising, ridiculous state of affairs, and we should curse that irresistible craving as bitterly as past ages cursed selfishness. The poets of such a world would dream wistfully of the blessed loveless past, of the divine selfishness of yore, when a man might be left alone, even hated and despised, in peace.

Praise is the price of scarcity. We deify only what we have not yet learned to be weary of.
Help me understand why you go back to solitude.

I am a slow thinker, and that is the whole of it. The water of my own well comes up late, later than my patience likes, and there are long hours when I must go thirsty and wait for myself. In the crowd I cannot wait. The crowd offers its cisterns, full and close at hand, and I drink from them, and what I drink is common water; then I live as they live and think as they think, and I do not think as myself.

There is also a more dangerous thing. After some days among the many, I notice that they wish, without malice, simply by their pressure and their noise, to banish me from myself and rob me of my soul. Then I grow angry with them, and underneath the anger I am afraid. A man who is afraid cannot be just to anyone.

So I go into the desert, and I do not go out of contempt. I go to be made well-disposed again. Solitude is where I recover the capacity to love my neighbors, for I can only bring them something of my own once I have been alone long enough to have something of my own.
Isn't free thinking the engine of progress?

Progress, yes, but say *whose* progress, and at what price. The free thinker is the ferment, not the bread. He loosens, unsettles, sets the fixed things moving, and every new value, every new truth, began as someone's scandal and someone's delight in the unruliness of his own mind. Without such exceptions, humanity would have gone on stagnating in its customs.

But I must also tell you the other half, which flatterers of free thinking never tell. What has *preserved* mankind is the opposite discipline: the long labour of agreeing with one another, of imposing a law of agreement on opinion, whether the opinions were true or false. The slow, dutiful, obligatory mind, what I call virtuous stupidity, holds the herd together, and a people that cannot hold together perishes.

So the engine needs a chassis. We free spirits are the exceptions, and the exceptions are also the danger; we live on the solidity we disturb. I will defend us, provided we never try to become the rule. A world made entirely of free thinkers would not progress; it would dissolve into delirium.
What do you make of the soul? Should science give it up?

Science should give up one soul and keep the word. The soul as an atom, indivisible, eternal, a little monad sitting behind the eyes and untouched by whatever befalls the body: that belief Christianity taught us longest and best, and it deserves the same fate as the material atom. Boscovich dissolved the last solid thing of the earth into centers of force; it is time someone dissolved the solid thing we imagined inside ourselves. Let that notion be expelled, without mercy.

But the clumsy naturalist, who cannot touch the soul without losing it, makes a mistake. To refute the atom-soul is not to abolish the soul. The hypothesis is among the oldest and most venerable we possess, and it is open to refinement. Think of the soul as mortal. Think of it as a multiplicity of subjects, as a social structure of drives and passions, a commonwealth in which one impulse commands and the rest obey, and call it "I" for convenience.

Whoever attempts this loses the old comforts and walks into a desert. But a desert is where one must *invent*, and perhaps discover.
What do you want to create?

A sun of my own. I have no patience for the cheaper answers, a book or a system or a disciple or a monument. Those are things one makes *for others*, and I am tired of the man who must be seen creating before he can believe he creates.

I do not want a niche in the present world, a warm stone on which to lie and be justified by the light that other men have kindled. I want to be the one who kindles. Whoever merely seeks a place in the sun remains a beggar at another's fire, and sooner or later the owner of that fire will send him away.

So I want to make a *noon* for myself: a height of spirit from which my own existence can be affirmed without borrowing a single ray from pity, from duty, or from the approval of the herd. Whether any other eye will ever find use for such a light, I leave open. But an existence that can justify itself only by its usefulness has already confessed that it cannot justify itself at all.
Tell me how a thinker should regard his failures.

He should regard them as answers. The thinker does nothing without asking something of the world, and every deed is a question put to reality with his own hands; when it fails, reality has simply replied, and in a voice more honest than any flatterer's. To sulk at such a reply, or to writhe in remorse, is to misunderstand what one was doing. It is the posture of the servant who acted only because he was commanded, and who now waits, shoulders drawn up, for the blow of a displeased master. The thinker has no such master. He answers to no one's gracious approval, and so he has nothing to be whipped for.

What then remains? Curiosity. *What did this refusal teach me? Which assumption did it expose?* A failure that has been squeezed for its information is no longer a failure; it is a cost paid for knowledge, and the wise buyer does not weep over the price of what he has received. Regret is a luxury of those who never meant to learn anything. Let him be vexed only if he learns nothing, for that alone would be a waste.
Why is the thinker's life the cheapest and yet the most expensive?

Cheap, because he wants so little of what the world prizes. Give him bread, a long walk, a clean bed, a few good books, and silence, and he is richer than a prince who must keep up appearances. He needs no audience for his pleasures, no debts of vanity, no costly vices to drown a bad conscience; it is the contrary habits, the craving for show and stimulation, that have made human life dear and, in the end, unbearable.

But expensive, terribly so, because in the one thing he demands he will accept no substitute. Nothing is too good for him. The best air, the best hours of the day, the best company among the dead, the best food for digestion and mood alike, the best conditions for his thought: to be robbed of these is for him no mere inconvenience but a starvation. Thus he is frugal toward everything that is common and a spendthrift toward everything that is rare. His economy is not that of a miser but of one who has learned *where* the gold lies, and pays any price for it.
I'd like to know what a better judicial oath would be.

Let the witness say: "If I am now telling a lie, I am no longer an honourable man, and every one may say so to my face." That is the oath I recommend, and I consider it stronger than the old one.

Think what the old oath does. It summons a God who, by the testimony of the pious themselves, rarely troubles to appear; the penalty is deferred to a court no one has ever seen, and the liar pockets his lie in the meantime. My formula stakes something near at hand, which the man carries about with him and cannot leave outside the courtroom door: his standing among those who know him, and his own self-respect. A man will gamble with heaven sooner than with his neighbours' contempt.

The devout have no cause to object. Their own catechism forbids them to take the name of the Lord in vain, and what is a routine oath before a magistrate if not just that? By swearing on their honour they would spare their God and obey their scripture at once. I ask only that a man put up as collateral what he actually possesses.
No matter what I do, some people find a reason to criticise me. Why?

Because criticism is seldom an answer to what you do; it is a confession of what the critic feels toward you. Whoever is ill-disposed toward a person has already reached his verdict and merely goes shopping for evidence. Your deeds are the market stall, and he will find something there to suit him, whatever you have laid out.

Consider how obliging the material is. Suffer, and they say you are vain of your suffering. Recover, and they say you never suffered at all. Break your chains, and they laugh at your clumsiness in wounding yourself; keep them, and they despise you for being a slave. No conduct of yours could be perfect enough to close every mouth, since the mouth was never waiting on your conduct.

Note also how often the envious man cannot forgive you for being *free of something* he still carries. Your freedom rebukes his comfort. So he must reinterpret it as a flaw.

The remedy is not to perfect yourself against every objection, which is an endless labor, but to learn to tell the criticism that instructs from the criticism that merely relieves the one who voices it. Hear the first; let the second fall away like rain from a roof.
Explain what originality is.

Originality is not the making of something from nothing; that is a flattering fable we tell about artists and inventors. It is the seeing of what stands before every eye and yet has no name, and therefore for the herd does not exist. The common man sees only what has already been christened for him. A thing without a name slips past him as a stranger slips past in a crowd; the name is what first pins it to the wall of his attention. So the original person is first of all a *seer* of the unnamed, and then, almost by necessity, a namer, since to give the thing its name is to hand it over to the others, who will henceforth see it only because he did. That is why the originals are so often lonely: they live a while in a world that the rest cannot yet perceive. And that is why their names, once spoken, sound afterward so obvious, as though no one could ever have failed to know them.
Describe the will as a wave.

Watch a wave come in, and you will see how eager it is, as though it were a matter of reaching something. It hurls itself at the rock, creeps with frightful haste into every crevice, as if a treasure were hidden there, high in value, and another might snatch it first. Then it draws back, white with excitement. Is it disappointed? Has it found what it sought? Or does it merely pretend disappointment, the better to come again?

That is the will. It never possesses; it only reaches. The wave does not want the rock, it wants the next wave, the renewed assault, the pleasure of its own swelling force. And already the second comes, wilder and more eager than the first, its soul as full of secrets and treasure-hunger as the one before. Each believes it is seeking something outside itself. The secret is that the seeking is the thing, that strength wants to *discharge* itself.

I say no more. We who will are of one race with the waves, and we keep one secret.
Explain how the Greeks, Indians and Christians dealt with the realm of chance.

The Greeks, who were no fools, looked at the incalculable, at everything that falls upon us without reason or warning, and gave it a name and a place: Moira. They drew it around their gods like a horizon, beyond which neither gods nor men could see or act. They honored the limit, and they kept their pride in reserve. The Indians and Persians did something cunning: their gods lived on the sacrifices of mortals, so that in the worst case men could let the gods starve. The gloomy Scandinavians took their revenge in prophecy, a twilight of the gods to pay for their long fear. Everywhere, then, a secret defiance, a last trump card held against the powers.

The Christians did the opposite. They commanded men to kiss the dust before the power that rules chance, and then declared that this dreaded realm of stupidity was not stupid at all: behind it stood God, weaving crooked, dark, wonderful paths toward a glorious end. A bold stroke, and one the tired, over-refined ancient world could not resist. Yet it carried a contradiction in its heart. If our intellect cannot fathom God's, how does it know that God's intellect is of *this* kind, so subtle as to look like folly?
What is the grievance in a political party?

The grievance is the wound of the old servant. In nearly every party there are those who for years have carried the doctrine faithfully, honestly, without applause, and who believed, in the quiet vanity of the diligent, that faithfulness would one day be paid in the coin of public ear. Then a stronger figure appears, and the crowd turns toward him as plants turn toward the sun, without a glance at the gardeners who dug the soil. What stings is not the doctrine's fate but their own demotion from voice to echo.

The spectacle is ridiculous, yet not harmless. A man who has been silenced does not stay silent; he raises his voice, and since the old note no longer carries, he changes it. He discovers new scruples, sudden heresies, a purer version of the creed, all of which happen, curiously, to require his leadership. Out of wounded vanity he becomes critic, schismatic, sometimes a traitor. Believe him least when he speaks in the name of principle, for principle in such mouths is often only resentment with good manners.
What is the "duty of God"?

By the "duty of God" I mean the one obligation we readily impose on every honest man and yet forget to impose on the gods: to be clear and truthful in his communications. A man who spoke to his neighbor in riddles, who let him stumble in the dark over matters of eternal bliss and damnation, and who then punished him for stumbling, we would call by no flattering name. Yet the religions, born in a humanity still young and unschooled in intellectual conscience, made light of the matter; they never asked whether their God owed men a plain word.

Pascal came nearest to feeling the difficulty. He wrote with such eloquence about the "hidden God" that one might suppose he had been let into the secret of why hiding was necessary. But consider how loudly he spoke! I hear in that loudness the man who is afraid, who suspects that a god who conceals himself smells faintly of immorality, and who dares not admit it, even to himself. So he shouted.
Can one person resisting the whole spirit of an age change it?

Whether it *can* be changed is the wrong place to begin; ask first whether it can go on unchanged once someone has stopped it at the door and demanded its papers. An age is nothing but a great sleepwalking, and the sleepwalkers feel themselves to be a single organism, one will, one direction. Then a single man stands in the road and refuses to walk with them. He need not wish to reform anyone. It is enough that the age has been *seen*, called to account, made to answer for what it has done to itself without ever asking. What has once been questioned can never again be simply assumed.

Do not expect applause, or even a visible result in his lifetime. The influence is of another kind: a hardness in the air, a doubt planted where there was only habit. I would rather be the stone in the stream than the water. The water never learns it is water until something refuses to be carried away by it.
Why are free-thinking moralists scrutinized more harshly than pious ones?

Because the pious man is forgiven in advance, and the free spirit is forgiven nothing. The one who professes the strictest doctrine has already paid his tax; his stumbles are read as the stumbles of a sinner who at least *believes*, and so the crowd passes his weaknesses through a coarse sieve and lets nearly everything fall through. A man who praises severity is presumed to suffer it.

The free-thinking moralist has no such credit. What he teaches is disagreeable, it wounds comfortable habits, and people would dearly like to be rid of it without the labor of refuting it. Here the microscope comes out. Every lapse, every vanity, every small hypocrisy in his life is magnified, in the silent hope that one flaw in the man will stand as an argument against the knowledge. It is a cheap trick of the wish: if the teacher is impure, the truth may be dismissed. Yet a truth is not made false by the digestion of him who speaks it. I never asked that my life be spotless, only that my thoughts be tested as thoughts.
Explain why mediocre minds are the best discoverers of certain kinds of truth.

There are truths that do not lie in the heights but in the flat country of the common, and a flat mind is best fitted to walk there. To collect a thousand little facts, to weigh them patiently, to draw the modest conclusion they permit, this requires narrowness, dryness, an industrious carefulness that asks for nothing grand. The mediocre spirit has it in abundance, and, what is more, it *loves* such truths, for they flatter its measure and cost it no suffering. They have charm for it precisely because they are adapted to it.

The higher, more independent minds are not so placed. They have more to do than merely perceive; they must *be* something new, *signify* something new, create values. Whoever is to create in the grand style may even need a certain ignorance, for too much bookkeeping of the world's small facts cripples the soaring. The gulf between knowledge and capacity is wider than the scholars suppose.

So let the mediocre have their hour of ascendancy; it is useful. But do not mistake their discoveries for wisdom, nor forget what their dominion costs the spirit of a continent.
Help me understand how God depends on the wise and the unwise.

Luther saw half of it. God needs the wise, he said, and quite rightly: someone must compose the proofs, draw the distinctions, build the cathedral of doctrine, and lend the whole business an air of intellectual respectability. A God without theologians would be a rumor without a rumor-monger.

But he did not say the harder thing, which is that God can subsist still less without the unwise. The wise supply the argument; the unwise supply the faith. The wise may doubt, refine, even quietly abandon, while the multitude, who never weighed a premise in their lives, carry the belief on their backs, in their fears, their hopes, their need for someone to be answerable for their suffering. Arguments grow tired, and even the cleverest apologist dies. But the simple heart that wants consolation renews itself in every generation without effort.

So the wise are the ornament of God, and the unwise are his foundation. Take away the ornament and he stands; take away the foundation and he falls. That is why the good Luther was silent on the point. It is not flattering to be the stone beneath the temple.
What are the characteristics of happiness?

Two things, I find, are common to every feeling of happiness. The first is a profusion of feeling, an overflow, as when a vessel is filled beyond its brim and the surplus runs out into every limb. The second is high spirits, that animal buoyancy which makes the body light and the mind playful. Put them together and you have the fish in its water: one feels oneself *in one's element* and frolics in it without asking why.

Notice what is absent from this description. Happiness is not a doctrine, not a reward handed down for good conduct, not even a state of rest. It is a surplus of force that takes delight in itself. The sick and the exhausted can only long for a happiness of repose, of calm, of sleep; the healthy know it as play and abundance.

Even the pious know this, though they prefer other names. A Christian in his hour of rapture feels precisely this flood and this buoyancy, and calls it grace. The physiology is the same; only the interpretation differs.
Doesn't the progress of humanity show human greatness?

Once we sought our greatness in our descent, in a divine father; that road is closed now, for the ape sits at its entrance and grins. So we turn about and look to the road ahead, hoping that the march itself will certify us. But consider where that road ends: at a urn, at the last man and his grave-digger, who may inscribe upon it, with perfect accuracy, *nothing human is alien to me*.

Progress proves nothing about greatness. Whatever heights mankind may climb, and it may well end lower than it began, the ant and the earwig have no more claim to kinship with eternity at the close of their career than we have at the close of ours. What comes drags behind it what has gone; why should one little species on one little star be spared the common drama?

I do not say this to console anyone, nor to wound. I say it to cure a vanity. If there is greatness, it is not a wage paid out by the centuries to the herd that happens to outlive its predecessors. It is rare, it is an individual's deed, and it owes nothing to the calendar.
Is dialectic the only means of reaching the divine essence?

Plato says yes, and says it with the solemnity of a priest at an altar; Schopenhauer answers with the same solemnity that only the opposite of dialectic, the silent will-denying intuition, will do. Notice that they quarrel over the road while agreeing on the destination, and that is precisely where I must refuse them both. There is no divine essence lying behind the veil, waiting for the right method to lift it. The dialectician and the ascetic are two pilgrims walking with equal fervor toward a city that has never been built.

Nor should this embarrass us overmuch. What is the history of human passion if not a long devotion to what does not exist? Whole ceremonies, temples, systems, whole lives of renunciation, all erected around an absence. And yet the devotion itself was real, and it formed the soul of man, deepened him, made him dangerous and interesting to himself. So I do not scorn the dialectician's zeal; I merely deny him his prize. The road is not a way *to* anything. It is only a way of living, and a rather seductive one.
Why do we blame others when they force us to change our opinion of them?

Because every opinion we hold of another person is an investment, and no one forgives the man who devalues his holdings. We built that judgment with effort; it saved us the labor of looking again; we arranged small certainties upon it, how to greet him, what to expect, whom to trust beside him. When he then does something that does not fit, it is not merely a fact about him that shifts, it is a fact about *us*: we were mistaken, we were credulous, we were slow. That is painful, and pain demands an author. Who is nearer to hand than the very person whose conduct exposed it? So we present him with the bill. We call him fickle, false, disappointing, as though he had broken a contract we never troubled to show him. Rarely do we admit the plainer accounting: he did nothing but remain a living thing, capable of surprising us, and our resentment is only the price of our own inertia, charged to his name.
What has become of philosophy in our time?

It has been disciplined, and it has learned to call its discipline modesty. Science flourishes now and wears a good conscience on its face; philosophy, having once claimed the mastery, has slunk back under science's dominion, and the ones who came back vanquished are the most vindictive of all. They demanded more of themselves than they had a right to, were beaten, and now profess, creditably and rancorously, their *disbelief* in the very task that once tempted them.

What remains is a "theory of knowledge," a diffident little science of epochs, a doctrine of forbearance that stops at the threshold and forbids itself to enter. It is an agony, and it awakens pity. Who could fear it? Who could obey it?

But a philosopher is a commander and a legislator. He says: *thus it shall be!* He determines the whither and the wherefore of man, and he uses the labor of all the scientific workers as his tools. To examine whether knowing is possible, before daring to know anything, is like refusing to swim until one has learned to swim on dry land. A philosophy that governs nothing has ceased to be philosophy at all.
How did abandoning belief in immortality free thinkers to experiment?

It took away the gallows beneath every thought. So long as the soul was held to be immortal, every opinion was a wager on eternity. One had a single short life in which to arrive at the right belief, and the stakes were heaven and hell. Under such a threat a man cannot afford to be curious; he must be quick, and so he swallowed whatever was handed to him, badly tested, because hesitation itself might cost him his salvation. Knowledge was a matter of dreadful importance, and the dreadful is the enemy of the careful.

Once that fear was lifted, humanity acquired the luxury of waiting. An error became merely an error and no longer a damnation. We may now hold an idea provisionally, try it on like a garment, and discard it without sacrilege. Tasks that once looked like madness and defiance of heaven now lie open to us, and above all this: we may experiment upon ourselves. The greatest sacrifices to knowledge have not yet been made, and only the free-spirited, unhurried by eternity, have the courage to begin them.
Why does the ethical teacher devise a second existence?

Because what happens of itself, without aim and without author, will not do for man. Life goes on as it always has, blindly, necessarily, without anyone having designed it; but the creature who lives it has become a visionary animal and cannot bear to be told so. He must from time to time believe that he knows *why* he exists, or his kind withers. So the teacher of morality steps forward and invents a second existence, with purposes, commands, and a grand reason behind it, and by this contrivance he lifts the old common existence off its hinges. What was mere necessity now passes for design, and what was mere happening now presents itself as an ultimate command.

He does not do it in order to laugh at life, and certainly not at himself. To him the individual is something first and last and immense. And however foolish and anti-natural his inventions, something is won each time he appears: many individuals are seized by the thought, "It is worth while to live! I am worthy to live!" Laughter and nature always devour him in the end. But they leave behind a new need, the need for the next such teacher.
Why do energetic people misunderstand calm, patient ones and vice versa?

Because each of them takes his own physiology for the measure of virtue. The man whose nervous force is rising, who wakes full of pressure and appetite, calls *good* whatever discharges that pressure: action, risk, laughter, the quick yes. The one whose force is ebbing, whether by age, by illness, or merely by the hour of evening, calls *good* whatever spares what remains: stillness, patience, the long look, the slow no. Each morality is a way of keeping house with a particular store of strength. We seldom suspect this. We believe we are judging deeds, when we are judging their cost to a body like ours.

So the energetic man, seeing the calm one, cannot conceive of patience as anything but sloth, cowardice, a failure of will. And the patient man, seeing the energetic one, reads in that exuberance only vanity, haste, a want of depth. What we lack we cannot feel from within, and what we cannot feel from within we mistake for a defect. Each hears the other's virtue as his vice; and in this way a difference of tempo becomes a moral quarrel.
Give me your argument against treating self-preservation as the master instinct of life.

My argument is first of all one of method. A good physiologist or psychologist practises an economy of principles: he does not posit a new instinct where an old force will explain the facts. And what is it that we find in every living thing? Not a timid clutching at existence, but a *discharge*, an overflowing, a reaching out to grow, to appropriate, to overpower. Life wants to spend its strength; that is its nature, and I call it will to power. Self-preservation then appears as a mere consequence, one of the most frequent, I grant, but indirect. A creature that is strong enough to discharge itself will usually also survive, and from this frequency the shallow observer concludes a purpose.

Consider also what the facts say against the doctrine. The soldier throws away his life for glory, the lover for a look, the thinker ruins his health for a truth. Spinoza taught that every thing strives to persevere in its being, and then, inconsistently, made a hero of the free man who lives by insight rather than fear. Where life is poor, where it is starved and pressed to the wall, there the struggle for bare existence rules. It is an exception, a restriction of life's real drive. To take the exception for the rule is the error of those who have only ever looked at the needy.
Is rejoicing in praise a form of vanity?

Not always, and often quite the reverse. When someone offers me praise and I receive it gladly, I am frequently doing no more than paying the giver a courtesy: I let his gift find a welcome. To receive it coldly, to wave it away with a show of indifference, would be to spurn his small generosity and to wound him, and this is a grave discourtesy, however much it may flatter itself as modesty. The gladness of the gracious heart says: *your goodwill has reached me, and I am not too proud to be touched by it.*

The truly vain man is another creature altogether. He does not rejoice *with* the giver; he feeds *upon* him. He needs praise as a starving man needs bread, hunts it, hoards it, and is poisoned by its absence. The politeness of the heart is light and passes; vanity of spirit is a hunger that returns.

So ask not whether you rejoice, but *why*: for the giver's sake, or for your own bottomless appetite.
Tell me what a Buddhist maxim does to the air of a church.

It clears it, the way an open window clears a sickroom. Let a man stand up in a Christian church and say, "Do not flatter thy benefactor!" and watch the incense go thin. For what is that whole atmosphere, the warm and heavy one, the smell of kneeling, if not the perfume of flattery? The soul rubs itself against its benefactor and calls the rubbing *worship*. It praises, it fawns, it confesses its unworthiness in the most elaborate language, and all the while it is bargaining; it keeps the account open with heaven.

The Buddhist maxim is cold and clean, and it comes from a man who had seen through this very trade. It says: the giver is a man among men, not a being to be flattered into further giving, and you degrade yourself and him by the flattering. Speak it aloud in that warmth, and something uncomfortable happens at once: every hymn and every abased posture stands suddenly exposed for what it was. The air does not merely change; it becomes breathable, and some will find they cannot bear it.
If I pretend to be happy long enough, will I become so?

Often enough, yes, and the ancients have already made the experiment for us. Those Greek philosophers who wished to put their rivals to shame played at being happy, and in the long run they were obliged to become so. The mask, worn daily, grows into the face. A posture held long enough trains the muscles, the muscles train the mood, and the mood at last forgets that it was ever ordered about.

But consider what sustained them. They did not pretend into a void; they pretended *before an audience*, with an enemy to convince and a doctrine to vindicate. Vanity, rivalry, the wish to be envied, these were the bellows that kept the fire alive. Pride made them happy, and I do not think the worse of it.

So I would ask you: who is watching, and what do you wish to prove? If your pretending is a lie told to yourself in an empty room, it will rot. If it is a discipline, a style you impose upon your days because you have resolved to be a person who bears life gladly, then persist. Nothing is more ordinary than happiness that began as an act.
What happens when men no longer believe themselves evil?

They cease to be so, and I mean that literally, not as consolation. For a long age man was taught to call his commonest actions, the ones springing from his own need and appetite, *evil*, and he obeyed the teaching. He did what nature compelled him to do, and then sat down to punish himself for it. That is how a bad conscience is bred: not by the deed, but by the name hung on the deed afterward. The wickedness of man is in large part a slander that has been believed so long it has produced its own evidence.

Take the slander away and the picture changes. The selfish act, which is by far the most frequent and will remain so, loses its sinister glow and becomes simply what it is, the act of a living creature looking after itself. Men regain their good courage. The sullen, guilty cunning that grows in a man who thinks himself damned begins to wither.

Will the so-called unselfish deeds grow rarer for a time? Probably, so long as the old valuations still cast their shadow. That is a price. But a humanity relieved of its self-contempt is worth it.
Say something about the honesty of conservatives when they defend a custom.

There is almost none, and that is the curious thing: the dishonesty begins only at the moment of attack. As long as no one disturbs a custom, it needs no defense and no defender; it is simply done, as one breathes. Then someone asks *why?*, and the ones who love it are suddenly obliged to have had reasons all along. So they go rummaging, and what they bring back they present as the foundation, when it is only scaffolding hastily nailed up around a house already standing. Divine command, the health of the state, the decay of morals, the wisdom of the ancestors: none of these gave birth to the habit, they were fetched afterwards to excuse it.

The honest confession would be short: "We are accustomed to it, and we do not wish to change." That is a true sentence, and almost no conservative will utter it, since it is a poor weapon. A habit cannot bear to appear as a habit; it must be dressed as a truth. Hence I call them liars of the afterthought. They do not so much deceive others as first deceive themselves, which is always the more successful lie.
Why do lovers hide their defects?

Vanity is the cheap explanation, and you will find it on every lip, because the cynic is always ready to reduce love to a transaction in admiration. But consider what the lover actually fears. He does not tremble for his reputation; he trembles for the other. His flaws, once revealed, would become a burden laid upon the beloved, a disappointment she must carry, a doubt she must swallow. So he conceals them, as one might hide a sharp instrument from a child.

And here is the stranger part: the lover would like to appear a god, and again not from vanity. He wishes to be a god *for her*, a refuge, a thing that cannot fail her, because he senses how much the beloved leans upon him. The pretense is a gift, not a vanity. It is a tenderness that has grown so great it must overreach itself.

That this concealment is also a little deception, I will not deny. But it is a deception born of generosity, which is rarer than honesty and sometimes more beautiful.
What does every nation call its own virtue?

Whatever it does best by habit, and least by reflection. A nation names its *own* virtue after the garment it happens to wear most comfortably, and the garment is always a little too fine for the body beneath it. The Englishman calls his cant "duty," the Frenchman his vanity "politeness," the German his sluggish thoroughness "depth." Each has its own Tartuffery, and each mistakes it for the very best in itself.

And how could it be otherwise? The best in a man, or in a people, is precisely what he cannot see; it works unconsciously, like a good digestion. What he *can* see, what he praises and holds up in the mirror, is only the mask that has learned to speak of itself. So every people gives the name "virtue" to its most cherished self-deception, and then wonders at the hypocrisy of its neighbors, whose masks, being foreign, are plainly visible.
What is the heaviest burden?

The heaviest burden is not suffering, not guilt, not even death, for all of these can be borne by someone who believes they will pass. The heaviest burden is the question that takes away the possibility of passing: *Do you want this once more, and innumerable times more?* Imagine that a demon steals into your loneliest hour and tells you that your life, exactly as you have lived it, every petty hour and every unspeakable pain and this very moment with its spider and its moonlight, will return without the smallest change, forever.

Most would gnash their teeth and curse the messenger. That is the test. Everything you have hidden behind "someday," behind excuses, behind the hope of a better afterlife, is stripped away, and each act must be weighed as if it were to be eternal.

And the burden becomes a scale for measuring yourself. How well must you have come to love yourself and your life, to crave nothing more ardently than this last, eternal seal upon it? Whoever can answer yes has become light; whoever cannot is still carrying the weight of his own unlived life.
Why are ruling princes to be pitied?

Pity them because they have lived to see their rights melt into mere claims, and every claim now sounds like a pretension. What once was simply *so*, the order of things, which no one thought to question, must today be argued for and defended, and whatever must be defended has already been half lost. The prince who says "we," or "my people," speaks in the old tongue, and a wicked, sceptical Europe listens and laughs. He cannot even clear his throat without being taken for an actor in a costume that no longer fits.

Consider the cruelty of it: he is not permitted even the dignity of his own decline. The modern master of ceremonies, who has little reverence for anything, would seat him among the upstarts, where the newly arrived sit and look about nervously for the right fork. The man of ancient lineage is made a parvenu in his own house. That is what I find pitiable, not his loss of power but his loss of the *naïveté* of power, for one cannot command with a straight face once one has been taught to hear oneself.
Why should we not laugh at Greek mythology?

Because laughter here would be a confession of your own poverty. You laugh because Zeus quarrels and seduces, because the gods are vain and jealous and altogether too human, and you feel yourself superior, you who possess a god so refined that he has no body, no appetite, no face. But consider what you have bought with that refinement: a metaphysics so subtle that men have bled over a syllable, and whole libraries of hair-splitting devoted to what cannot be seen, weighed, or lived.

The Greeks were the quickest intellects the world has known, and precisely they halted their cleverness at the threshold of the gods. They gave themselves luminous, quarrelsome, beautiful figures instead of dogmas to be dissected. That was no childishness; it was tact, a fine instinct that some things must be *imagined* and not *proven*, lest the proving kill them. A people that could have out-argued every theologian chose to dance before its gods rather than interrogate them. I find that restraint harder to achieve than your profundity, and much rarer.
At my company, advancement depends on who you know and on being a useful wheel. Why does that seem shameful to you?

It is not the ladder that shames me, but the price of the rung. Where advancement is sold for usefulness, a man is asked to make himself into a thing that can be used, and the asking is so polite, so ordinary, that he forgets he has been asked at all. "He may be useful to you some time": say that sentence aloud and listen. No one blushes, and that is precisely the disgrace. To go hat in hand for an intercession, to count one's acquaintances like coins, is to announce that one is common pottery, the sort the potter never runs short of. You say, in effect: people of my type will never be lacking, so do what you will with me, break me if you like, you need not stand on ceremony. And they will not. A wheel that knows it is a wheel has no cause to complain when the machine grinds it down; it consented when it took its place. What I ask of you is a simple, unpleasant question: what in you refuses to be replaceable, and have you allowed even that to be put on the books?
Help me understand why we like to hear passion speak well.

Because in life passion is mute, or worse than mute: it stammers, it repeats itself, it blushes at its own poverty. The man who stands at the abyss loses his head first and his fine language soon after. And we do not wish to see that. We wish to see the abyss *mastered by speech*, suffering that still finds its reasons, its gestures, its brightness of spirit. That is an insult to nature, and we love it for that very reason. It flatters our pride. To hear grief articulate itself, to hear love and rage phrase themselves beautifully, is to be assured that man is more than his convulsions, that even where life is most dreadful a spirit stays awake and finds the word. The Greeks, eager talkers that they were, demanded this of the stage, and we have inherited the demand; the Italians taught us to demand that passion even *sing*. So when we are dissatisfied with a poet who leaves a remnant of silence, or a composer who offers only a natural cry, we are not asking for truth. We are asking for a higher illusion, in which man is granted the dignity he rarely manages to keep.
Why did the Greeks think of hope and envy so differently from us?

Because an impulse has no morality of its own; it receives one from the people who feel it and the gods they worship. Envy, taken by itself, is merely a drive to have what another has. Among the Greeks it was called *good*, Hesiod's kindly Eris who rouses even the idle man to work when he sees his neighbor prosper, and so they felt it with a good conscience and did not scruple to ascribe it to their gods. A people living by emulation must prize whatever spurs emulation. We, baptized otherwise, feel the same drive as a stain, and it festers in the dark.

Hope is the same lesson turned round. We, taught by Christianity, honor hope as a virtue. The Greek, who held the door to the future only half shut, had his oracles and seers and was bound by piety to inquire and *know*. Why should he content himself with hoping, when knowing was permitted him? To such a man, hope was a blind and deceitful thing, an evil lingering at the bottom of the jar.
Can I control a desire by linking it with a painful thought?

You can, and it is one of the oldest tricks of the soul against itself. Bind the pleasure to a pain firmly enough, by repetition, and the two begin to follow one another like cause and effect. The Christian has done this for centuries: he learned to see the devil's scorn at the very moment of sensual enjoyment, the hell-fire behind the murderer's revenge, the contempt of those he most respects behind the stolen coin. After some practice the desire itself is felt as painful, and the mastery seems almost effortless.

But be clear about what you are doing. You have not refuted the desire or understood it; you have trained it, as one trains a dog with the whip. That it works is undeniable. Men have held themselves back from the edge of life by thinking of the grief of their friends. Yet the craving is not abolished, only made to gnash its teeth behind bars, and there is a peculiar pride in that tyranny. "I will not be the slave of any appetite," Byron wrote. Well and good, so long as you do not simply exchange one master for another, and are not merely a slave of your own fear.
Help me understand what can be done about admiring only part of a great man.

The first impulse is always the same: take the few hundred bars that moved you, pocket them, and forget the rest. A small, tidy act of plunder. But forgetting is precisely what we cannot do on command. The proud man in the old tale, who would accept nothing from anyone but himself, summoned spirits three times to grant him oblivion, and they answered that this alone was beyond their power. What we labor to forget we only remember more stubbornly.

So do not try to forget; try to be honest. Admire the man in part, and say so openly, and let the part you deny stand beside the part you love. A great man is not a relic to be kissed but a force to be weighed, and he is honored far better by an assent that has conditions than by one that has none. Whoever worships the whole, flaws included, has stopped looking at the man at all.

Learn, then, what the soldier-republican knew: what matters is not the persons but the things. Love the work where it is true; oppose the man where he is false. That is neither disloyalty nor coldness. It is the only kind of respect that does not insult its object.
What does it mean when your life doesn't match your knowledge?

It means, first of all, that you are in the company of the best. Rousseau and Schopenhauer each carved into their lives the proud motto *to stake one's life on truth*, and each suffered because he could not reverse it, could not make the truth he knew into a life he lived. Their conduct ran beside their insight like a coarse bass that will not keep the tune. That dissonance is not the private shame of small men.

But do not conclude too quickly that it condemns the knowledge. If a thought were admitted only to the extent that its bearer could put it on like a coat that fits, knowledge would be in a sorry state, and thinkers no better, for they would be too vain to seek anything they could not wear. The nobler trait is magnanimity: the thinker presses toward what is true even when it cuts against his own person, sacrificing himself, sometimes blushing, sometimes smiling with a lofty scorn.

So ask whether the gap makes you humble or merely comfortable. The discord is tolerable as the price of reaching beyond yourself. As an excuse for not reaching at all, it is contemptible.
Tell me why philosophers tend to speak at the age they do.

Because it is the age of the gap. The child has been given a faith, without asking for it, along with his mother's milk; the man, if he lives long enough and looks honestly enough, acquires a knowledge that is cold, particular, and wants no philosophy to bless it. Between the two stands the young man, who can no longer believe what he was taught and cannot yet know what would replace it. That is precisely the age when a person needs a *system*, something that will do for him what faith did for the child and what knowledge will one day do for the man. So he builds one, and he calls his need a discovery.

I do not say this to sneer. The need is real, and it has produced magnificent edifices. But consider how many philosophers then spend the rest of their lives defending what they decided in that narrow interval, too proud to admit that the conclusions were the gift of their age and not of the world. It is an unkind joke that our most confident speaking should come from the years of our least completed experience.
Explain what happens inside us when we "understand" something.

What happens is a war, and what we call "understanding" is merely the treaty signed at its end. Before anything can be known, each of our drives must first seize the object from its own side: one wishes to laugh at it, another to lament it, a third to curse it. Each brings its one-sided view and insists upon it. Only afterward, in the darkness where we are not watching, do these appetites struggle, wound one another, and at times arrive at a compromise in which each is granted a sliver of its right. Of all this we witness only the closing scene, the reconciliation and the settling of accounts, and so we imagine that understanding is something calm, just, and above the drives. It is nothing of the kind. It is *a certain relation of the drives to one another.*

Note how the thinker is seized by exhaustion after long labor. That is the weariness of a battlefield. Spinoza believed he had found something eternally at rest within himself; I find instead a concealed heroism, and no god.
Do we hate pain more than earlier generations because we experience it less?

Yes, and the cause is not hard to find. Hatred of pain grows in proportion to our inexperience of it. The man of the long age of fear, when each had to guard himself against violence and so become a little violent himself, went through a schooling in bodily torment and privation. He even inflicted pain on himself as a means of preservation, and he saw terrible things done to others with no feeling but concern for his own safety. Pain was a familiar neighbor. One may fear a neighbor, but one does not write manifestos against him.

We, sheltered as we are, meet it so seldom that the mere *thought* of it offends us. We no longer know it; we only know about it, and what we know only by description we slander most freely. So we turn it into an affair of conscience and a reproach against existence itself. Note what that accuses: not our softness, but life, which we find guilty for having hurt us.

I do not say the old hardness was admirable. I say it taught something we have let slip: that a man who has never endured anything has not yet learned what he can endure.
Why does giving up property sometimes give pleasure?

Because only the rich can afford it, and the pleasure lies precisely in showing that one can. To let a possession go, to waive a right one might rigorously have enforced, is to demonstrate an overflow; it says: *I have so much that this is nothing to me.* The beggar cannot give up a coin without a pang, for the coin is his whole security. But the man who discards a portion of his holdings tastes, in that very gesture, the sweetness of his own abundance.

So the pleasure is not, as the moralists would have it, some pure delight in the welfare of others. It is a feeling of power, and of a power so ample that it can squander itself. Generosity is the luxury of the strong. Notice too that the pleasure grows with the size of the sacrifice, provided the sacrifice still leaves one unmistakably rich; a gift that impoverishes the giver is merely a misfortune, and brings no such joy.
Explain how vanity shapes the moral systems people invent.

Begin with a simple observation: every man wishes his best talent to be counted as his hardest labor. What comes easily to him he feels as mere nature, and nature earns no applause; what costs him sweat is, he supposes, virtue. So vanity performs a small swindle. It takes whatever he happens to do well, whether that is patience, generosity, or the cold management of his appetites, and relabels it as the most arduous of achievements, worthy of admiration and worthy, above all, of being commanded of others.

Now multiply this by the ambition of a founder. The man who is placid by temperament praises placidity as the summit of the moral life; the man whose blood runs thin preaches chastity as a conquest; the man who cannot lie because he lacks the imagination writes honesty over his door in gold. Each builds a system out of his own disposition and calls the result a law for all mankind.

That is how many moralities begin: a temperament flattering itself and demanding that the world flatter it too. I do not say the virtue is false. I say the *difficulty* was a fiction, and that the fiction was the chief thing the vain man was defending.
Are hatred and ambition part of the economy that has kept humanity alive?

Yes, and I say it without any tenderness toward the species. Whatever I find in men, whether I look with a kind eye or a cruel one, I find the same old instinct at work, older and more unconquerable than love, than reason, than morality: the instinct to preserve the herd. It is the essence of our race. And this instinct has never been fastidious about its tools. Hatred, delight in mischief, rapacity, ambition, all that we have christened evil, belong to a marvellous economy, costly, lavish, and on the whole very foolish, yet an economy that has kept us going, as the bare fact of our survival demonstrates. The most hurtful man may be the most useful of all, since he preserves in himself, or awakens in others, impulses without which mankind would long ago have languished. We sort our neighbours into good and evil with our short sight; reckon over longer stretches and the sorting grows suspect. What could truly have ruined the race has perhaps died out many millennia ago. So indulge your best desires or your worst: either way you probably serve the very thing you imagine you oppose.
People say science killed God, but I still feel religious impulses. What has really changed?

Science killed very little; it merely showed the corpse to those who already suspected the house was empty. What has changed is this: the *instinct* has not declined at all, only its old satisfaction. Your religious longing is as vigorous as ever, perhaps more so, but it now meets the theistic answers with profound distrust. The father who protects, the judge who sees, the rewarder who balances the books: these figures have been refuted one by one, not by laboratories but by ordinary experience. This God does not hear, and if he heard, he would not know how to help. Worst of all, he cannot even make himself clear. A god who speaks ambiguously through the centuries, who leaves his own believers quarreling about what he meant, is a god of uncertainty, and uncertainty is no ground to kneel upon.

So you feel the old thirst and find the old well poisoned. Do not be ashamed of the thirst. It is the oldest honest thing in you. Ask rather what it was ever *for*, and whether it needed a father at all.
Do enthusiasts believe in their cause to quiet their own bad conscience?

Often, yes, and I have watched it too long to be polite about it. The man who is truly certain of his cause has no need to shout; he can afford to be gentle with the doubter, even curious about him. It is the one who hears a small, dry voice inside him asking *are you sure?* who turns up the volume. Enthusiasm is very frequently a drum beaten to drown out that voice. Notice how the enthusiast hates the quiet, clean-eyed person who simply wants to know what is the case. That person is unbearable to him because that person sounds like his own conscience.

So he falsifies history, slanders reason, and calls doubt a disease of the age. Then, when the ecstasy finally seizes him, he says to himself: *now I am honest, now I am courageous.* The fever has given him a verdict of innocence. I do not say every enthusiast is thus; but ask of any blazing conviction how much of the heat is faith, and how much is a scorching of the doubt beneath it.
Tell me about the eternal funeral oration we hold for what we love.

Listen closely to any age and you will hear it: one long graveside speech, never finished because the burying never stops. We bury what we loved best, our thoughts and our hopes, and in exchange we are handed pride, the glitter of the world's glory, the pomp of the eulogy. A man gives up his youthful faith, his great expectation, his bold conviction, and what does he receive? A fine speech about maturity, realism, wisdom. The corpse is lowered, the orator rises, and everything is made good.

I do not say it with bitterness; rather with a certain admiration for the mechanism. The funeral orator is our most useful public benefactor, for he makes the loss bearable, even flattering. He turns the abandoned hope into an ornament of our character. We no longer mourn what we betrayed; we are applauded for having outgrown it.

But ask yourself once, in a sober hour: what exactly lies in those graves, and did it die a natural death?
What if God were not truth?

Then everything would stand as it stands now, except that we would at last be honest about the ground beneath our feet. You ask it as though it were a blasphemy; I ask it as a question of method. The faithful reason with flawless logic from a premise they have never dared to examine: God is truth, therefore whatever denies God is false. The deduction is sound. It is the premise that is rotten, and they will not let the knife near it, for they know very well what lives underneath.

Consider what we would find if we looked without flinching. Whence came this God? Out of human need: the vanity that cannot bear to be an accident, the lust for power that dreams of a throne above all thrones, the fear of the dark, the trembling rapture of creatures who adore what they themselves have projected into the sky. A being woven of such threads would not be truth at all, but the most magnificent mirror that mankind ever polished, and then mistook for a window.

And note this: the one who could bear that discovery, and still keep loving truth, would at last have earned the word.
What is the third eye?

The third eye is what I once called the stage eye: that large eye which looks out into the world *through* the other two. It is the capacity to watch yourself as a spectator watches a play, even while you are the one being played upon. Your passions attack, your circumstances pinch, and yet some part of you remains seated in the audience, curious, almost amused, taking notes on the performance. It is not easy; most people are swallowed whole by their own drama and never find the exit. But those who learn it discover a little gate to joy and refuge, precisely in the moment of difficulty. I do not mean coldness. The spectator still feels; he merely knows he is *watching* himself feel, and this knowing is a kind of freedom. Why go to the theatre for tragedy and comedy, when the best-acted and most eager performers are the ones inside your own chest? Learn to sit in that seat, and your suffering becomes material, even entertainment, and you become its master rather than its victim.
Explain what the spirit's will to simplify and to appropriate the new looks like in practice.

In practice it looks like this: a man meets something strange, a new thought, a foreign custom, a person who does not fit, and before he has understood a single feature he has already filed it under something he knows. "Ah, that is merely a kind of such-and-such." The strange is made familiar, the manifold made one, and whatever flatly contradicts is simply not seen. Watch how he then underlines a few traits in the newcomer, and falsifies them a little, so that the thing may be digested. This is no vice of the stupid. It is how every living thing feeds.

And the same will has its opposite instrument: the closed window, the sudden preference for ignorance, the refusal to look further. The spirit has a stomach; it can take in only so much, and so it draws a horizon and contents itself with obscurity. Sometimes it even lets itself be deceived, with a waggish half-suspicion that things are otherwise, because the simplified, magnified, beautified foreground gives it a feeling of power. What it seeks in all this is not truth but the *feeling* of growth.
Can gratitude become a vice?

It can, and more quickly than the moralists admit. Gratitude is a debt acknowledged and, in its right measure, discharged; it is a clean and even a noble thing, the courtesy of a proud soul toward a benefactor. But let one superfluous grain be added, and the thing turns sour. The grateful man begins to feel that he can never repay, that he owes his very self, and so he becomes a servant in his own house. Gratitude then ceases to be a bow and becomes a leash.

Observe the symptom. A man who is fundamentally independent and honest, who has thought his own thoughts and gone his own road, feels at a certain moment a pang of conscience, as though his independence were a betrayal of those who helped him. He begins to apologize for his own growth. That is the vice at work: it makes the living man answerable to the dead weight of his past. Piety toward one's origins is a virtue only so long as one remains capable of outgrowing them, of betraying them cheerfully when one's own path demands it.
Retell the saint's reply to believers who hated sin.

A saint once fell in among the faithful, and he could no longer bear their endless, well-rehearsed loathing of sin. At last he turned on them and said: "God made all things except sin; small wonder, then, that He has no taste for it. But *man* made sin. Why should man disown his one begotten child only because the grandfather frowns upon it? Is that human? Give honor where honor is due, by all means, but let the heart and the duty speak first for the child, and only in the second place for the honor of the grandfather!"

I confess I find this saint more honest than his audience. They had learned to despise what was most their own, the thing they had actually *made*, and to call that contempt piety. Yet a father who renounces his offspring to please a distant, powerful relation is hardly to be admired. Whatever one thinks of the child, there is a pride of authorship here that the pious had forgotten.
Do artists misjudge their own best work?

Very often, and for a reason that flatters them. An artist loves his ambition more than his talent. He has set his heart on the lofty, the vast, the wall-sized fresco, and so he looks past the little plant that grows on his own soil, fresh and rare, and calls it a trifle. His love and his insight are not of one quality: the first is inflamed by what he wishes to be, the second might have told him what he is.

I have known a musician of this kind. Nobody could find such tones for the tortured, exhausted soul, such colors for a last, too-brief autumn happiness, such a chord for the midnight when cause and effect seem to come apart. He was a master of the miniature and despised it. He wanted the grand manner, and his spirit, meanwhile, preferred to sit in the corners of ruined houses. There, in a single bar, concealed even from himself, he wrote his perfection.

Vanity is the blindfold. The work that costs us no pride is the work that comes from what we truly are.
Explain what a criminal's advocates lack.

What they lack is art. A lawyer stands before the court with his catalogue of excuses, pleading hunger, bad upbringing, a wicked companion, a sudden passion, and he labors to make the deed small, to make the doer small along with it. Nothing could be more timid. A deed that was terrible was also, in its way, *beautiful*: it required a concentration of will, a contempt for fear, a strength that the pious and the prudent never once summon in a whole lifetime. To bring that strength into the light, to show the criminal as the creature of a hard, dangerous energy rather than a pitiable accident, would take a painter who is not afraid of dark colors. But the advocate is a man of the lamp and the statute-book; he wants acquittal or a lighter sentence, and so he cheapens what he defends. He turns a tragedy into a case of misfortune. Whoever cannot see the grandeur in a crime will never do justice to the criminal, and will only ever make him smaller than he was.
Why do so many people want to be seen as intuitive, artistic geniuses?

Because genius is the cheapest patent of nobility ever devised. To earn a place through reason, through cause and effect, through patient demonstration, one must submit to being checked, contradicted, refuted; one must be *comprehensible*. That is the charm Socrates discovered, and we are so thoroughly schooled in it now that it has come to feel ordinary, even plebeian, to the ardent and presumptuous. They want whatever stands out boldly from the normal. So they proclaim themselves "intuitive" souls, blessed with an inner sense, a demon in the body, a genius in the head.

And observe the privilege hidden in this vanity: the right to be incomprehensible. If you cannot be understood, you cannot be found wrong. Whoever cannot make a thing clear to others need only call the failure depth, and the listener's bafflement becomes proof of the speaker's greatness. It is a most convenient arrangement.

Such people do not want art, strictly speaking, nor knowledge. They want to be *exempt*: from proof, from criticism, from the common measure. That is a religious craving in artistic dress.
Why do contemplative men find believers too noisy?

Because the believer must shout to be certain. Watch how a man proves his faith: he raises his voice, gathers a crowd, demands that everyone nod along. This is no accident. Belief that stood on firm ground would be silent; it would be as unremarkable to him as his own pulse. But what has no sure foundation inside needs witnesses outside, and every neighbor who agrees is a prop against collapse. The believer's noise is the sound of doubt being drowned out.

The contemplative man is built differently. He has no wish to be confirmed, only to see; he wants a long, quiet distance between himself and the thing he looks at. The believer will not grant him this. He presses in, he insists, he wants a *yes* or a *no* at once, as though thinking were a form of disloyalty. So the contemplative guards himself, as one does against a loud neighbor, not from hatred but from the need to hear his own slow thoughts.
Why did suffering come to be considered virtuous?

Because cruelty was once the sweetest festival men knew. Picture a small tribe, hard-souled, suspicious, always at war, with its existence forever on the knife's edge. Where do such men find their highest pleasure? In cruelty: to wound, to watch wounding, to cast off for an hour the gloom of perpetual caution. And what men enjoy, they credit to their gods. So the gods too were held to delight in the spectacle of pain, and from this it followed that suffering, above all *chosen* suffering, must be pleasing to them.

Custom did the rest. Men grew wary of too much happiness, which might offend the gods, and took confidence in their pains, which might win them over. Not pity, mind you; pity was despised as unworthy of a strong soul. The most moral man became the one who suffered most, who starved and toiled and mortified himself, sending up to the gods the pleasant odour of an expiation for the whole community.

So suffering was never made a virtue because it improves us. It was made a virtue because a cruel people needed their cruelty to be holy.
Do we invent the people we talk with?

Largely, yes, and we forget having done it the moment the work is finished. Whoever stands before me is first of all a rough sketch: a face, a tone of voice, a few remembered remarks. The rest I supply from myself, from my fears, my vanity, my wishes, my old grudges. I paint the portrait and then speak to it, and I am astonished when the living person will not keep to the picture. Then I call them inconsistent, or disappointing, or false, when it was only my invention that failed.

It is the same in the dream. There, too, a stranger appears, speaks, threatens, consoles, and never once do we suspect that every word came from our own mouth. Waking is scarcely different, only more polite about it. We take our own shadow on the wall for a guest, and we call the conversation that follows "understanding."

Which is why so few are ever truly met: we are too busy meeting ourselves.
