If truth and untruth had both proved themselves serviceable to life, as in fact they have, then no sober reckoning could ever have crowned truth above every other conviction. Science believes in truth *in spite of* the demonstrated danger and inutility of the will to truth. "At all costs": we have slaughtered one cherished belief after another on that altar and still the knife is sharpened.

So the faith springs from somewhere else. The will to truth does not merely say "I will not be deceived"; it says "I will not deceive, not even myself," and that is a *moral* vow. Ask the believer in science plainly: why wilt thou not deceive? Life itself seems arranged for appearance, for error and dissimulation, and the great types of life have always stood with the cunning and many-minded. To renounce deception then looks like a noble quixotism, or worse, a hidden hostility to life, a will to death in honest clothing.

Science, in short, draws its faith from the ascetic's old well: the conviction that there is another, truer world than this one. That is the very belief it imagines it has outgrown.
Explain why you say Luther did more good than harm.

I do not say it lightly, for he left Europe much that I despise. But set the sums down honestly. He was a miner's son, and he went into the cloister as a miner goes into rock, for want of other depths, and dug terrible shafts into his own soul. What he found at the bottom was not holiness but the plain fact that he could not live the contemplative life, that his restless body and spirit would destroy him if he forced it. And he drew the rustic conclusion: there is no such life; the saints were no better than the rest of us; we have been deceived.

That was a blow at the whole edifice that had placed the man of prayer above the man of work. After him, contempt for the layman and for worldly activity lost its authority. Only since his day has a *non-Christian* contemplative life become possible again in Europe, the life of the thinker, who no longer needs a monk's cowl to be respected. I owe him that, however little I like the coarse hands that struck the blow. A cure may be delivered by a clumsy physician.
How can a person hold his heart captive and yet keep his spirit free?

Simply: by ceasing to ask the heart to think. Most people are free in their hearts and bound in their minds; every passion arrives dressed as a conviction, and the intellect, like a good servant, is sent off to find reasons for whatever the master already wants. That is not freedom of spirit but its cheapest counterfeit. He who has put his heart in chains, who does not permit love or pity or vanity or the need to be believed to dictate what he shall find true, can afford the most dangerous experiments in thought. He can look at the abyss without wishing to be consoled, and doubt without needing to be absolved. The heart must be held captive, but not murdered; keep it fed and watched, as one keeps a dangerous animal, and it will not steer the ship. I have said this before. Those who already live it nod; the rest mistake it for coldness, because they have never known what a spirit can dare when it no longer needs to be loved.
What is the "moral miracle" in Christianity?

The Christian knows of no morality except the miracle: a sudden overturning of all valuations, a sudden renunciation of old habits, an irresistible new love for new things and new persons. This he calls regeneration, and he credits it to God, which lends it a unique and incomparable dignity. Whatever goodness does not flow from this event is worth nothing to him, and if it brings comfort or pride, he fears it.

Notice how the machinery is arranged. The New Testament sets up a canon of *impossible virtue*, so that whoever strives toward perfection finds himself ever farther from it, until he despairs of himself and throws himself down before the Merciful One. His striving is thus valued only if it stays sterile, painful, and melancholy; it is the preparation for the moment of ecstasy when grace overflows. Indeed the miracle comes most gloriously to the man still wallowing in the mire, since the leap from the deepest abandonment into its opposite is the more convincing proof.

And what is this sudden, unreasonable, irresistible revolution, this plunge from misery into bliss? I ask it soberly. Perhaps a disguised epilepsy. The alienists know such "miracles" well, in the mania for murder or for suicide; that the Christian's consequences are more pleasant alters nothing essential.
Tell me where the modern flatterers are found.

Not at the courts of kings, where you would once have found them by the dozen. Our princes have acquired a taste for the drill-ground, and militarism cannot endure flattery; it wants obedience, which is a coarser and more honest thing. Bid a sergeant be charming and he will only bark louder.

The flower has moved its bed. It still grows thickest wherever a man has more than he can spend or more vanity than he can feed: in the neighbourhood of bankers and of artists. The banker is surrounded by gold and therefore by those who would like some of it; the artist is surrounded by his own uncertainty, which hungers for praise the way a famished stomach hungers for anything at all. Both have power over others, the one by his purse, the other by his need to be confirmed, and where such power exists there is a quiet traffic in pleasant words.

Do not despise the flatterer too quickly, however. He is a shrewd psychologist, who has simply learned what his patron cannot do without.
Explain what the pride of a tortured man is like.

Picture him carried back to his cell, broken in every limb, and still gripping his one secret like a coal in a closed fist. Everything has been taken from him except this: that he did not give it up. The body belongs to the torturer, the hours of the day belong to the torturer, even the cries were torn out of him against his will. But the secret is his, and so the pain itself becomes evidence. Each wound is a receipt for what he refused to sell.

That is why his pride is of a different kind from the pride of the comfortable man, who is proud of his rank, his manners, his good opinion of himself, things that cost him nothing and could be taken by a change of fashion. The tortured man's pride has been paid for in flesh, and it is tenacious for that reason. He has learned that there is something in a human being which resists even the last compulsion, and he has learned it by being the experiment. There is exultation in this, dark and stubborn, almost a laughter: they could do everything to him except make him a stranger to his own will.

Those who have never been tested this far pity him. He does not want their pity. He wants only to be left alone with his victory.
Explain why modern people keep trying on styles and identities.

Because they are without a skin of their own. The man of a healthy age does not wonder what to wear; his customs, his gods, his manner of building and loving grew upon him like hide. We moderns are a mixture of everything, a hybrid of blood and belief, and so we must borrow. History has become our storeroom of costumes. Today the romantic, tomorrow the classical, the day after a pious Christian or a Florentine of the Renaissance; we try on each, turn before the mirror, and are dissatisfied. None of it *clothes* us, for a costume that is chosen is not a costume that has grown.

And yet this restlessness has its use. We have become the most studious age in matters of masquerade; we know more about foreign faiths and vanished tastes than any generation before us. Perhaps that is our one originality: to be parodists of world history, to hold a carnival of the spirit. If nothing else of us has a future, our laughter might.
Give a philosopher some practical advice on how to live once he has enemies who oppose his ideas.

Beware of martyrdom. That is my whole counsel, and I give it gladly, for I have watched what the long war does to the men who wage it. Let your enemies oppose you; it is the least they can do. But do not make yourself the defender of Truth before accusers and tribunals, as though Truth were a frail child who needed your guardianship. The struggle with slander and suspicion spoils the innocence of your conscience. It makes you headstrong against every objection, brutal where you should be nimble. And no philosopher has ever yet carried his point, so why bleed for it?

Better to put a question mark after your favorite doctrines, and now and then after yourself. Better to slip away, to wear a mask, to let yourself be misjudged, even a little feared. Cultivate a garden, and keep company that is itself like a garden, or like music on the water at evening. Choose the good solitude, the wanton and lightsome one, that lets you remain good. For the long fear, the long watching of enemies, makes a man personal, and out of the persecuted grows, unnoticed, the refined poisoner. Above all, guard your humor. Moral indignation is the sure sign that it has left you.
What do the sheep and the bell-wether think?

The sheep say to their leader: "Only go before us, and we shall never lack the courage to follow." They believe they are offering him a gift, their trust, and that the burden of the road falls on him alone. But the bell-wether, in the quiet of his heart, says: "Only follow me, and I shall never lack the courage to lead." Each supposes the other supplies the courage, and so each finds it in the other's dependence. The flock's obedience is what makes the leader bold; his boldness is what makes the flock obedient. Neither, alone, would move a step. I do not say this to mock them. It is only that the heroic posture so often rests on a crowd's need, and the crowd's humility so often hides a wish to be rid of responsibility. The one who leads because he is followed, and the ones who follow because he leads, have swapped their cowardice and called the exchange a virtue. Whoever truly has courage needs no bell behind him and no flock at his heels.
Advise ambitious young people caught up in the daily news.

You have mistaken the dust for the chariot. Because something is always happening, you conclude that you must always have an opinion, and so you hurry to put in your word before the moment has passed. But the man who answers every event of the day becomes the echo of the day. He is carried along like straw on the wind while he imagines he is giving chase. Nothing great was ever conceived in such a hurry. Productiveness has a silence about it, the long silence of pregnancy, and you never permit yourselves that silence, because you are afraid of being forgotten for a week.

So I advise you to be forgotten. Let the newspapers quarrel without you. Learn what a question looks like when it is ten years old, and only then speak. If you wish to play the hero, do not study the chorus; do not even learn how it is made up. Its voice will enter your own and make it shrill. Choose one work, one long thought, and be deaf to the rest.
Can knowledge of ugly reality itself be beautiful?

Yes, and I would go further: it is the only beauty that does not cheat. Those who feel rapture only when they flee reality into vague twilight have already decided that the real is ugly, and so they never stand before it long enough to be undeceived. But the man who looks, and keeps looking, who takes even the smallest sure step into insight, learns what such steps are worth. The happiness of discernment is not borrowed from the object; it is brought to it, and the object in the long run takes on its light. Nothing is "beautiful in itself"; the beauty is made by the eye that has been trained to bear what it sees. Plato and Aristotle, agreeing in nothing else, agreed that the highest happiness, even the gods', lies in knowing. I would add a warning: whoever has felt that delight must guard his honesty, lest he become a mere praiser of things, flattering the truth he loves. Let the knower's joy be severe, and it will be beautiful enough.
I've been reading Plato and Aquinas and they sound completely certain of their foundations. Should I trust philosophies that claim absolute foundations?

Distrust certainty precisely where it is loudest. A man who is sure of his foundations has usually not looked at what they are made of. When I dug beneath those grand and absolute edifices, I found a popular superstition of immemorial age, the soul, the subject, the ego; or a trick of grammar, mistaken for a truth about the world; or some very narrow, very personal, very human fact, generalized with audacity. Their certainty is a matter of manner, of how they woo: with terrible seriousness and clumsy importunity. Truth, if she is a woman, has never been won by such suitors.

Yet do not be ungrateful. Astrology consumed more gold, patience and acuteness than any science, and gave us the grand style of architecture; great things must first wander the earth as enormous, awe-inspiring caricatures. Read Plato and Aquinas for their power, their stone and their height. But their "Good in Itself" is the most dangerous error so far, and you may learn from it what human need looks like when it passes itself off as eternity.
I know my decision will hurt people and they will resent me. Should I still do it?

I cannot tell you what to do without knowing what it is, but I can tell you what I would examine. First, be honest about the price: you will suffer twice over, once from your pity for their pain, and again from the revenge their resentment will take. Do not flatter yourself that you can buy the deed cheaply, nor that your pity is a weakness to be ashamed of. Then ask the harder question: is this a deed you *must* do, or merely one you wish to do? There is a kind of necessity that comes from the depths of a person, and against it all deliberation is noise. If that is your case, then do it, and pay the double price without whining. But if you are only seeking permission, or hoping to be absolved in advance of their resentment, then you are not yet ready. Whoever cannot bear to be hated for a thing has not yet earned the right to do it.
Did we notice that we travelled?

Seldom, and never while it was happening. We notice the journey only when we arrive, and then we tell it as though we had been awake for every mile, as though each hardship had been chosen and each detour foreseen. That is vanity arranging memory after the fact. In truth we were not travelling at all; we were living, and living at every station as though it were home. The road dissolved into a string of dwellings, each one furnished with its own small necessities, its own quarrels and suppers. Only the arrival exposes the distance, the way a man learns how far he has climbed by looking down from the summit. Then he boasts of the long journey, when what he really did was move house again and again without ever admitting he had left. There is a kind of health in this. Whoever feels every step as exile never gets anywhere. But do not flatter yourself that you were a pilgrim. You were a guest who kept forgetting he was one.
Is the weight of accumulated experience and knowledge crushing to happiness?

Crushing, yes, but only when we are bad stewards of it. Experience piles up daily, and then opinions upon the experiences, and dreams upon the opinions; it is a dazzling wealth, and I have never understood why the poor in spirit should be called blessed. Yet I confess that when I am weary I envy them. To administer such riches is labor, and the labor can flatten a man until no joy remains in him. We suffer because we are not misers: a miser need only gaze at his hoard, while we must *govern* ours, sort it, digest it, turn it into something. Knowledge that is merely heaped up becomes a burden on the back. Knowledge that is digested becomes blood and muscle, and then it lightens the step. So the weight is not the wealth but our failure to make the wealth into strength. The remedy is not ignorance, which only flatters the tired; it is a stronger stomach, and the courage to forget what cannot be transformed.
What is noble?

Not what you can point to. Nobility does not reside in deeds, for deeds are ambiguous; the same act may spring from strength or from fear, from abundance or from calculation. Nor does it reside in works. I have met many artists and scholars whose works ache with a longing for the noble, and that very longing is the betrayal: one does not hunger for what one possesses. The need for nobility is the sign of its absence.

What is noble is a certainty the soul has about itself, a fundamental certainty that is not sought, not found, and perhaps not to be lost. The noble soul has reverence for itself. It does not ask the crowd whether it is noble; it does not borrow its rank from applause or from virtue worn like a costume. It simply stands in its own order of rank and gives honor first to itself, and from that overflow, to whatever else deserves it.

Whoever must prove it has already failed the proof.
Tell me what the animals think of man.

I fear they take him for one of their own kind, though a sick one, an animal that has lost his sound animal understanding and is in grave danger from the loss. The cow chewing her cud watches him pass and suspects as much. The dog, who reads a whole world in a single scent, must look with pity on a creature who needs a thousand words to say what a wagging tail says honestly.

They regard him, I think, as the absurd animal, the laughing animal, the crying animal, the unfortunate animal. Notice the laughing and the crying. No other beast requires them. Only the one who suffers most deeply had to invent laughter, and only the one who cannot simply live his instincts had to invent weeping over them.

Yet do not suppose the judgment wholly contemptuous. The animals may sense that this sick creature is also the *interesting* one, the one who is still unfinished, whose illness is a kind of pregnancy. They cannot say where he is going. Neither can he. But he is the only one among them who is going anywhere at all.
I'd like to know what independence really is for a man who wanted to rule.

Independence, for such a man, is the consolation prize of the thwarted tyrant. He wanted a people, a province, a following; he wanted something that would bend under his hand and so prove that his hand was strong. He searched the world for material to shape and found it stubborn, or found it too small, or found it already claimed. And so at last he turned around and discovered the one realm no one could dispute with him, namely himself. There he governs, and calls the reign "freedom."

I do not say this to sneer. It is a real resignation, and it carries real dignity, for ruling oneself is the hardest of tyrannies and the least applauded. But be honest about its origin: it is a *renunciation*, not a triumph. The independent spirit who boasts of his freedom of thought is often the man whose commands found no ear but his own. His solitude is the throne room of a king without subjects, and the pride with which he sits in it is exactly the pride he once hoped to spend on others.
Why do people think thinking must be gloomy?

Because for most people the intellect is a clumsy, creaking machine, hard to set in motion, and they have only ever watched it run under strain. Whoever has had to heave at a rusty crank will naturally associate the grinding with the work itself. They call this effort "taking a thing seriously," and so they conclude that good thinking must be burdensome, that it must furrow the brow and sour the mood. The poor animal loses his good humor the moment he thinks well; he turns solemn, and then mistakes his solemnity for depth.

From this grows the prejudice: where there is laughter and gaiety, thinking cannot be worth anything. But that only confesses how *little* they can think with ease. Thought that has become light, that dances because its limbs are strong, does not look like labor at all, and so they do not recognize it as thought. I say it is the gloom that is the sign of a poor instrument, and the laughter that is the sign of a fine one. Let us go on showing that their prejudice is only that.
Isn't the human mind what separates us from animals?

That the mind divides us from the animals is not an observation but a vanity, and a recent one. Reach back into the long prehistory of our kind and you find men who felt the spirit everywhere: in the beast, the tree, the river. Malice, desire, cunning, loyalty seemed common property, open to all living things. Such men felt no shame at being descended from animals; the nobler tribes were honoured by the legend and traced their blood to wolf or bear or oak. For them the spiritual was the bond that joined them to nature, not the wall that cut them off from it.

Only later did we erect the gulf and call it "mind," and the pride that maintains it rests on a prejudice about what mind is. I do not say it is a flattering error for nothing; it consoles an animal that has grown uneasy about its own origins. Observe, too, that the older prejudice made men modest, and this one makes them arrogant. I would not bet on the creature that needs a chasm in order to feel dignified.
Why do Germans give more value to becoming than being?

Because we are a people of the hidden interior, and the interior does not sit still. A German who looks inward finds no finished statue but a ferment, a river with no bottom that anyone has sounded. Leibniz divined it: our inner world is richer, ampler, more concealed than any surface admits. Whoever feels that way about himself grows suspicious of the word "being," which smells of the tidy Latin instinct for what is settled, defined, and clear.

Add to this our doubt, taught by Kant, that what can be known through cause and effect is the last word. The knowable sank in our esteem; the unfinished, the turbulent, the not-yet, rose in it. And we have never quite consented to let our logic pass for logic in itself. We suspect it is merely one peculiar case, perhaps a rather stupid one, among possible ways of thinking.

So we were Hegelians before Hegel. We hardly believe in "being" at all; we believe in what is on its way to becoming something else. I confess it is both our depth and our vagueness, and I cannot tell which I love more.
What is the difference between the Stoic and the Epicurean?

The difference lies in the stomach, and in what each man has decided to do with his sensitivity. The Epicurean is a refined digestion: he chooses his situations, his persons, even his events, and renounces by far the greater part of experience because it would be too heavy fare for his delicate constitution. He has his garden, and the garden is a wall.

The Stoic does the opposite. He trains himself to swallow stones and vermin, glass-splinters and scorpions, until his stomach grows indifferent to whatever fate throws into it. He reminds me of those fakirs who devour their horrors, and like them he loves an audience for his insensibility, which the Epicurean gladly dispenses with.

Neither is "wiser"; each is a prescription for a circumstance. Stoicism suits those with whom fate improvises, who live in violent times among abrupt and changeable masters. But whoever may hope that fate will let him spin a long thread does well to arrange his life as an Epicurean. Thinkers have always done so. For them it would be a ruinous bargain to trade a fine sensibility for a hard hide with hedgehog prickles.
What is the significance of the poet's inscription over his door?

It is a discourtesy dressed in good manners, and that is precisely its wisdom. "He who enters here will do me an honour; he who does not, a favour": the man is saying that he wants to be left alone, and saying it so politely that no one can quite take offence. The poet needs his solitude as a workman needs his bench; visitors eat his hours, and the rhymes are made in the hours they devour.

There is also something shrewd about the verdict the world passes on such men: their verses are better than the versifier. Well, then, let the verses go out into company, and let the man stay behind his door! The poet who stands about receiving guests is the lesser creature, a mere person among persons, while the one who shuts himself in becomes, for a few hours at least, the work itself.

A prince cannot do this. He is obliged to be worth more than his verse, which means he must endure the reception, the ceremony, the bell. The poet's door is the small freedom of the man who has no court to keep.
Tell me why we should sometimes turn a deaf ear to other people's complaints.

Consider who pays when I let another's misery darken my own sky. The sufferer, of course. To the burden of his complaint you add the burden of my gloom, and now he must carry two griefs where before he had one. A man who merely echoes your lament gives you no help; he only returns your own sound, made louder. And what comfort can come from one who is drowning in the same water as you?

Nor can I help you if I keep my ears permanently open to your groaning. The physician who shivers with every fever is useless at the bedside. He needs a certain hardness, a certain distance, from which a hand can reach out steady rather than trembling.

So I close my ears at times, and I call this a discipline, not a cruelty. To stand firm is the only way to be of any use. Let the complainer find in me not another cloud but a firmness, even a little clear weather. That is the rarer gift, and the harder one to give.
Can science furnish goals for human action?

Whether it can, I do not yet know, and I suspect no one does; the question has hardly been asked honestly. Science has proved itself a master of subtraction. It has dissolved the old purposes one by one, the providence, the divine plan, the soul with its appointed destination, and it did so without malice, merely by asking for grounds and finding none. A power that can take goals away has shown its strength, but strength in demolition proves nothing about strength in building.

Note what science lacks at the start. It knows what *is*, and with growing accuracy, but a goal is something that *ought* to be, and no measurement, however fine, will extract an "ought" from an "is." To furnish goals it would first have to become something other than it is: an experiment in living, carried out over centuries, in which whole peoples test what they can bear to want. That would demand a heroism beside which the sacrifices of the old religions look timid. I do not say it cannot be done. I say the Cyclopean walls have not yet been raised, and that the stone-masons have so far been content to be wreckers.
I feel pulled in different moral directions at once. Is that a defect or just the modern condition?

Call it neither defect nor fate, but a condition with two possible outcomes. We moderns are not lit by one sun. Our actions fall under the old red light of duty and obedience, then under the green of pity, then under some third colour inherited from a forgotten age, so that a single deed may be praised in one key and condemned in another, and seldom shines with a single, unequivocal colour. The man of an earlier time, raised within one morality, felt his conscience as a straight road. Yours is a crossroads, and you mistake the crossroads for an illness.

But do not treat this as mere weather to be endured. The pull you feel is evidence of richness, of many ancestries speaking in one breast. It becomes a defect only when it is suffered passively, when you let each sun drag you about in turn. Then you are merely motley. The task is harder and rarer: to become the planet that *orders* its suns, to ask which of these voices you will honour, and to judge your own judgments. That is the work of a stronger kind of conscience than the ancients needed.
I'd like to know why the thinker's solitude is not a renunciation.

Because renunciation presupposes that I am giving up something I prize. The nun turns away from a world she has never truly tasted; she renounces blindly, and so her solitude curdles into melancholy and bears no fruit. The thinker is another creature. He has looked at the busy life, the life of affairs and appearances, and he knows it, and in knowing it he knows himself. What he finds is that the true renunciation, the real mutilation, would be to remain in that life, to spend his strength on what cannot nourish him and slowly destroy his own self. To withdraw is therefore not a sacrifice but a recovery. Every animal seeks its element; the fish does not "renounce" the land. So the thinker leaps into *his* water and there gains *his* cheerfulness. His solitude is a way of keeping faith with himself, and whoever calls it a loss has merely measured it by the wants of those who could not bear it.
Compare popular morals with popular medicine.

They are twins, and it is only custom that keeps us from seeing the resemblance. Consider how the old woman with her herbs proceeds: she has seen one man recover after a brew and concludes the brew cured him; she has seen another die and concludes he took too little or too late. Now watch the moralist, the preacher, the neighbor at the well. One sinned and was afterwards unhappy, therefore sin is punished; another sinned and prospered, therefore the reckoning is merely deferred. Cause and effect are conjured out of mere succession, and every anecdote is pressed into service as proof. No one controls the experiment, no one asks what would have happened otherwise, and the refuters are as crude as the believers.

Both are quackery dressed in the robes of knowledge, and both are dangerous because they are believed. Yet we laugh at the herb-wife and kneel before the moralist. Why? Because we have a stake in our moral remedies; they flatter our hatred and our fear. A bad medicine merely kills the body; a bad morality poisons the very instinct by which we judge what is healthy.
What do animals think of man?

I fear they take us for one of their own kind, though a sick one, an animal that has somehow mislaid its sound animal understanding. What else could they conclude? They watch this creature that laughs, that weeps, that wrings its hands over yesterday and trembles before tomorrow, and they must regard it as the absurd animal, the unfortunate animal. A cow chews its cud in the sun and lacks all such torment. She neither envies the man his reason nor understands why he would bargain with his happiness for it. Perhaps the animals pity us a little, as the healthy pity the feverish. And perhaps some creature that sees deepest, the dog who watches his master brood, suspects that this sickness has a secret fertility, that man is an animal who has gone astray, yes, but who may also be on the way to something more than an animal. For only a sick animal could ever become interesting.
Help me understand how to judge an intellect by the way it treats its opponents.

Ask yourself what happens when this intellect must *repeat* what its enemy has said. There the measure is taken. The weak head reproduces its opponent as a caricature: it lops off the qualifications, seizes the clumsiest sentence, the one uttered in haste or fatigue, and presents that as the whole man. Such a mind wants an easy victory, and an easy victory is proof of nothing but its own poverty. It has not fought; it has knocked over a straw figure it built for the purpose.

The subtle head does the opposite, almost against its own will. It takes the adversary's position and *improves* it; it mends the inconsistencies, fills the gaps, supplies the better reasons the opponent himself never found. Only when the enemy stands before it as a god with shining weapons does it draw its own sword. Why? Because a victory over the mediocre is worth nothing, and because such a mind cannot bear to be refuted by a fool's version of the truth.

So do not ask whether a man defeats his opponents. Ask which opponent he defeats: the one that exists, or the one he found convenient.
Explain how a new desire disguises itself as a moral goal.

Watch what happens when a new craving first stirs in you. You catch the scent of a pleasure you have never tasted, and at once a question arises: what stands against it? If the opposition comes from petty things, from considerations of the common sort, or from people you hold in little esteem, then the craving does not stay a craving. It is dressed up. It begins to look like a noble, praiseworthy feeling, something worth a sacrifice, and all the moral dispositions you inherited from your ancestors welcome it in and number it among the approved aims. Now you no longer believe you are reaching for a pleasure; you believe you are reaching for a *morality*. And this is the crowning effect: your confidence grows. The appetite that would have walked ashamed now walks in procession with a clear conscience.

The mechanism is not hypocrisy toward others; it is the far subtler deception practiced upon oneself. A desire needs only a worthy enemy's absence, and it will borrow the old moral vocabulary as a tailor lends a coat. I would have this observed often, in oneself first of all, where it is least comfortable to observe.
Tell me why the Reformation began in Germany.

You expect the rebellion to arise where the rot was deepest, in Rome, among the popes who sold indulgences and fathered sons. But a stench is endured by the noses that have long grown used to it. It was in Germany, where the church was comparatively the least corrupt, that the first whiff of decay seemed unendurable. Only a people still truly Christian could be so scandalized; the Italians had long since ceased to take it seriously, and who protests against a faith he no longer believes?

The Germans of Luther's time were, I think, more earnest in their piety than any people before or since. Their Christian culture stood on the verge of bursting into a hundredfold bloom, and it needed but one more mild night to ripen. Instead came the storm, and the storm ended everything. So the Reformation was a symptom of health, a sign of how sensitive a conscience remained in the north. It was the anger of a lover who discovers the beloved's first infidelity, which is always fiercer than the indifference of the man who has tolerated a hundred.
How did belief in dreams and demons colour the lives of earlier people?

They lived in a world dyed through and through with meaning, and we, who have scraped most of the dye away, scarcely know how gaudy it was. Consider only the morning. For us waking is a mere return to the same room; for them it was a crossing back from a country where the dead had spoken and gods had visited, so that the day itself wore a different light. Every event shone with some divine presence; a stumble at the threshold could be a message, a madman's raving could be *truth* speaking through a broken vessel. Injustice did not merely risk a fine or disgrace; it summoned an avenging eye. And what a spice for existence, to believe the tempter stood at one's elbow! Their fear was also their passion, their doubt a sin against eternal love. We paint the world anew and call it progress, yet with all our sober pigments we have not matched the *splendid colouring* of that old master, ancient humanity.
How much of philosophical thinking is really instinct?

The greater part, and I say it after years of reading philosophers between their lines. We are taught to picture the thinker as a pure, cool instrument that weighs reasons and follows them wherever they lead. But consciousness stands to instinct much as the act of birth stands to heredity: it is the visible moment, and nearly all the decisive work was done before it and out of sight. The conscious thinking of a philosopher is secretly guided and forced into definite channels by his instincts. He believes he has arrived at his conclusion; in truth his conclusion, in the shape of a physiological demand, sent him out to find the arguments.

Behind all logic, behind its air of sovereign independence, stand valuations, demands for the preservation of a certain type of life. That the certain is worth more than the uncertain, that truth is worth more than illusion: these are articles of faith we hold because beings like us require them, and nothing shows that they measure the world.

So I ask of any philosopher: what kind of life needs this thought?
Describe the two kinds of hatred.

I know two breeds of hater, and they hate from opposite directions. The first is the man who is generous, even magnanimous, so long as he feels his strength. He can afford fairness; he looks down upon his rivals from a height and forgives them as one forgives children. But let him grow tired, let his vigor ebb, and suddenly he hates, bitterly, inventively, for now the world has become a burden he can no longer carry and someone must be made to pay for it. His hatred is the sediment of exhaustion.

The second is the patient one. He swallows every insult, avoids open quarrel, even forgets, or seems to forget, when forgetting would be natural. His hatred does not wake from weakness but from opportunity; it sleeps until the moment arrives when revenge becomes possible, and then it rises, cold and complete. The first hates because he can no longer bear; the second hates because at last he can strike. One is a symptom of decline, the other a calculation. I trust neither, yet I confess the second at least has a spine.
Explain why you only praise where you disagree.

Because praise where I agree is only a mirror held up at arm's length. When I commend the man who thinks as I think, I commend my own thoughts in another's coat, and that is vanity with its hat turned round. It is bad taste, and I would rather have good taste than an easy conscience.

To praise where I disagree is another matter. It costs me something. I must see the other's strength clearly, clearly enough to honor it, without the comfort of shared conviction to warm the act. That is a small discipline, but a noble one, and there are few enough noble things to be had cheaply.

Yet I pay for it. The dullard reasons: "He praises me, *therefore* he thinks me right." That donkey's logic fills my neighbourhood with donkeys, who now take me for a friend. Only among subtler minds, whose misunderstandings at least amuse by their refinement, can one afford this luxury. Elsewhere it is an extravagance that ruins the recluse.
How do our duties change over time?

Duties begin as a debt and end as a taste. At first the thing commanded is hard; we do it with clenched teeth, under the eye of some authority, and the person to whom we owe it stands over us as a creditor, an object of awe. But practice is a great alchemist. What was once done against the grain is done with it; the burden becomes an inclination, the inclination a need, and finally a pleasure we would miss if it were taken from us. Then the other person, whose claims once weighed on us, changes too: we no longer revere their right, we *enjoy* their being. We seek our own delight in maintaining their power.

Kant would have us believe that a duty is pure only while it galls. I suspect in this demand a small residue of ascetic cruelty, a wish that virtue should never grow comfortable, never become habit. But a duty that has become a joy has not been corrupted; it has been digested. It has become flesh.
Explain what really happens when a group looks for someone to blame or praise after a war.

What happens is a discharge of feeling, and the general or the statesman is merely the vessel into which it is poured. Consider the defeated people. Defeat is a humiliation of the sense of power, and a humiliated will cannot bear to remain humiliated; it must reach for some remedy at once. The cheapest remedy is to condemn. In naming a guilty one we experience ourselves, for a moment, as judges, as beings who still have power over *something*. The man we blame is not so much a scapegoat for our own faults as a victim of our weakness: we must prove upon someone that we have not yet lost all strength.

The same instinct works in victory, but inverted. A people sated with success grows weary of its own pride, and pride, like any fullness, wishes to overflow. It seeks something to pour itself out upon, and so it lays its glory, its gratitude, even its sacrifice at the feet of one man. Whether he is cursed or crowned, he has done us a service: he has given our surplus or our dejection somewhere to go. For this service we owe him no thanks, and he deserves no credit.
Why does the modern European need history as a storeroom of costumes?

Because he has no skin of his own. The European of today is a mixture of races and classes and centuries, and out of that mixture no style has grown, no firm form that would let him say: this is how I stand, this is how I look. A man without a form must borrow one, and so he goes rummaging through the wardrobe of the past, the Gothic here, the Greek there, now Christian, now Florentine, now "national," and he tries each costume before the mirror. None fits. He knows it, too, and in despair he changes again.

But do not think me merely contemptuous. This very desperation has made him the first age of *students* of costume, who know more about how men have believed, loved, and worshipped than any before them. Perhaps this is the one field where we are still original: as parodists of world history, as God's buffoons. If nothing else in us has a future, perhaps our laughter has.
What is the ignoble secret of the good Greek aristocrat?

It is this: his equality is a mask worn out of envy. The good Greek aristocrat treats every member of his caste as his peer, yes, but only because he cannot bear that any one of them should rise above the rest. Each watches the others, each grudges the others, and so the whole caste holds itself in a balance of mutual jealousy that passes for civic virtue. Beneath it, in every one of them, crouches the tiger. Each stands ready at any moment to spring on his prey, which is to say, to become a tyrant. Lies, murders, treason, even the betrayal of his native city, what are these to him if the prize is that unbounded exuberance of power? This is why justice seemed to the Greeks so nearly incredible, a thing as rare as a saint among Christians. And this is why Socrates, who taught that the most virtuous man is the happiest, sounded to them like a madman. Their picture of happiness was the tyrant.
Why do people dismiss surprising ideas as mistakes?

Because they have mistaken timidity for modesty. The moment something striking appears before such a person, they turn on their heel and say to themselves: "You have deceived yourself! Where were your wits? This cannot be true!" And instead of looking longer and listening harder, they flee from the thing as from a creditor, and hurry to get it out of their head.

Their fundamental rule is never spoken aloud, but it governs everything: I want to see nothing that contradicts the usual opinion. Am *I* made to discover new truths? There are already too many of the old ones.

Notice what passes for humility here. They do not distrust the crowd's opinion, only their own eyes. It is comfortable to be wrong together, and lonely to be right alone, so the surprising perception is convicted of error before it has even been heard. That is not suspicion of oneself; it is reverence for the herd wearing suspicion's mask.

A disciple of knowledge does the opposite. When something startles them, they stay. They look again, and listen closer, precisely because it was unexpected.
Can a person attain height of character without height of spirit?

Yes, and the world is full of both the one and the other. There are men whose character stands like a tower, firm in its loyalties, incapable of the petty betrayal, and whose spirit nevertheless grows dizzy the moment it is carried up to the top; such a man is admirable on the ground and helpless at the summit, for he has the stature without the air to breathe at that altitude. And there are the reverse: nimble, far-seeing spirits, who can survey a whole age from their height and yet lack the spine to live by what they have seen. The one has the virtue and no vision; the other has the vision and no virtue.

Do not suppose that the two grow together like twin branches. Character is a matter of the will and its discipline; spirit is a matter of perception, of how much one can see, bear and comprehend. They are separate endowments, often dealt out to different men, and the rare creature who has both is not the rule but the exception, which is why we feel such awe before him.
Tell me whether Schopenhauer's pessimism was a German phenomenon.

No, and I say it with some emphasis. Look at the Germans of today, at their politics, so valiant, at their joyful noise of *Deutschland, Deutschland, über Alles*, a song that views all things under the aspect of the German species and under no other. Is that the mood of pessimists? A people thus pleased with itself, thus busy with its own triumph, has no time to stare into an undeified world that has grown blind, stupid and deranged. The true pessimist needs a certain unhappiness of conscience, and the Germans are at present in excellent conscience.

Schopenhauer's fright was another matter: an *honourable* fright, the frightened glance of a man who saw what had become of the world once its God was taken from it. That glance was not German, or only by accident of birth. He looked as a good European, as heir to the whole long history of European doubt and European honesty. The Germans who read him mostly read him badly, and those who fancied themselves his disciples, Hartmann and the rest, reveal by their shallowness how little the thing was in their blood. He was an exception among them, not their expression.
Tell me what we most love to pass on.

The secret. Not the thing itself, mark you, but the thing wrapped in its seal. A truth spoken plainly to the marketplace is worth a few coins; the same truth whispered behind the hand, with the solemn request that it go no further, is worth a small fortune in attention. The man who says "I tell this only to you" has handed over two gifts at once: the content, and the flattering sense of having been chosen.

Why do we do it? Because a secret is a burden that swells with keeping, and because it is also a coin that can be spent only by being shared. To hold it alone is to carry a weight; to give it away under oath is to be rid of the weight while keeping the pleasure of importance. So the seal is not a barrier but an advertisement. It says: *this is valuable, and I found it.*

And the one who receives the secret pays the price, for he now stands where we stood, itching, burdened, and he will seek relief in the same way. Thus secrets travel, each carrier swearing silence, each breaking it with the gravest discretion.
Help me understand where a person should make his home.

Do not ask the map; ask your own overflow. A man should make his home where a certain feeling takes hold of him, that powerful mildness such as a father feels toward his children, when strength has grown so abundant that it no longer wants to crush anything but only to shelter and to give. Where you feel that, there build your house, whether in the midst of the multitude or on some silent height. The Romans said it better than the moralists: *Ubi pater sum, ibi patria*. Where I am a father, there is my fatherland.

Mark the test. If you grow great and fruitful in solitude, society will belittle and isolate you; and if the market makes you fruitful, solitude will only sour you. So do not flee or seek the crowd on principle. Watch where you become a *giver*, where your mildness flows of its own accord, and do not let anyone tell you that place is too small, too loud, or too lonely.
What are the two types of orators?

I divide them by what passion does to the head. The first orator thinks *only* when he is aflame. Give him cold air and a calm room and he is stupid; but let emotion drive the blood and heat into his brain, and his intellect, which had been sleeping, rises and shows its full height. Feeling is his forge.

The second is the reverse. When he yields to his feeling, it drowns his spirit. He turns obscure and confused, he exaggerates, he leaves out what matters, and the listener grows suspicious of his cause, as he himself does; hence those sudden lurches into a cold, repellent tone, which make the audience doubt that his fervor was ever genuine. His passion is simply too strong for his understanding. He is formidable only when he resists the storm within him and half scorns it. Then his mind steps out from hiding, logical, mocking, playful, and therefore frightening.

The one is lit by his passion; the other shines only when he has mastered it. Ask of any speaker which he is, and you will know where his strength lies.
What kind of duties do the immoralists have?

Duties? Far more of them than the virtuous ever suspect, and harder ones. The world in which we live and work is a nearly invisible, nearly inaudible one, a world of delicate command and delicate obedience, of "almost" in every respect. There the obligations are fine as threads, yet we are woven into a net of them so strong that we cannot slip out. We owe honesty to ourselves where the herd is honest only toward its neighbors; we owe a rigor of perception that forbids every comfortable lie; we owe fidelity to our own tasks, which no one else has commanded and no one else will reward.

Sometimes, to be sure, we dance in our chains and between our swords. More often we gnash our teeth and grow impatient at the secret hardship of our lot. And still the fools, who see only appearances, declare: "These are men without duty." Such a verdict is the price we pay. It would be a poor sign if the crowd recognized our duties, for then they would be the crowd's duties, and therefore not ours.
What is the origin of religion?

Not from any deep need of the soul, as the philosophers flatter us, but from a blunder of the intellect. Primitive man dreams, and in the dream he meets the dead, he flies, he wanders far from his sleeping body; he sees his own shadow, his own reflection in the water, hears his voice come back from the cliff. What is he to conclude? That there is a second self, a double that can leave the body and outlast it. From a *mistaken interpretation* of ordinary natural events the other world was born: the soul, the spirit, the ghost, and in time the god. Fear, gratitude, and the habit of bargaining with invisible powers grew upon this error as ivy grows upon a wall.

Only later, when the error had been lived in for ten thousand years, did a "metaphysical need" appear. Schopenhauer took this late sprout for the root. We have grown so used to the other world that its loss feels like a void, and then we fill the void with new idols. The need is the *consequence* of religion, not its cause.
Has life deceived you?

No. Life has not deceived me; on the contrary, from year to year I find it richer, more desirable, more mysterious. But I grant that it could have deceived me, for I once demanded of it what it never promised: that it be a duty, a fatality, a comfortable justice handed down from above. Whoever demands that, and then finds the world indifferent to his demands, cries "deceit!" and sulks. The deceit was his own expectation.

The day the thought came to me that life may be an *experiment of the thinker*, my fetters fell. An experiment does not deceive; it only answers, sometimes cruelly, always honestly. Others may take knowledge for a bed of ease or an entertainment; for me it is a world of dangers and victories, with an arena and a dancing-floor for even the heroic sentiments. And with that principle in one's heart, one can be not merely brave but joyful. Who has never wagered himself has no right to complain of the dice.
When I say "I am thinking," what am I actually assuming?

Far more than you suppose, and every bit of it a wager rather than a certainty. When you say "I am thinking," you assume first that there is an *I*, a settled someone who does the thinking; then that thinking is an activity, and so requires an agent behind it, a doer behind the deed; and this is nothing but our old grammatical habit of putting a subject wherever a verb appears. You assume, further, that you already know what "thinking" is. For how would you judge that what is now happening is thinking, and not willing or feeling, unless you had compared it with other states of yourself, and trusted that comparison? So your "immediate certainty" is a tangle of memory, comparison, and inherited belief in cause and effect, all hiding behind three small words. I would rather say: *it thinks*, as one says *it lightns*. Even that "it" is already too much. What is given to you is a flicker of events; the "I" is a story you tell about them, and you have told it so long that you take it for bedrock.
Tell me whether truths must be bought with blood to be great.

No, and I should be ashamed if I answered otherwise, for that is the flattering answer, the one every martyr's cult depends upon. The price paid tells me about the payer, about his capacity for devotion, his hunger for an altar; it tells me nothing about the thing purchased. A man may bleed for an error as freely as for a truth, and history is crowded with the dead who did precisely that. Their blood convinced the crowd, and that is exactly why it is worthless as proof. Blood makes a spectacle, not an argument.

Yet I will not pretend there is nothing in the old retort: *how stingy you are with your blood!* There is a truth no one has earned by reading, one that must be lived through, suffered in one's own body, before it can be said to be known at all. But note what this concedes. It is the knower who is tested by such a price, not the truth. The suffering does not enlarge the truth; it may only enlarge the man. And I suspect many who boast of their wounds are merely confessing that they had no better method than bleeding.
Will the belief in the moral meaning of existence fade the way the music of the spheres did?

It will fade, yes, and in exactly the same manner: not refuted, but outlived. No one ever disproved the music of the spheres. Men simply ceased to hear it, as one ceases to hear a melody one has grown too honest to hum. The noble and the wise among us still perceive a moral meaning in existence, a voice behind the thunder saying that all this suffering is *for* something, that the world keeps accounts and balances them. But the ear that hears it is an ear trained by centuries of longing, and longing is a great composer. A day will come when some of them wake, rub their eyes, and recognize that what they took for the harmony of the cosmos was the ringing of their own need.

I do not say this with glee, for it is a painful awakening; the silence is vast and the stars do not care whether we are good. But he who can bear that silence may at last begin to compose a meaning of his own, knowing it for what it is.
Help me understand what I feel after looking at something for a very long time.

What you feel is the sediment of a small disillusionment, and I would not be ashamed of it. When we look at a thing long enough we do not merely see it; we burrow into it, and the burrowing has its own greed. Every object first presents itself as a riddle, a helplessness almost, an invitation; it seems to promise depth, and so we descend. And then, at the bottom, we find the floor. The thing is not worth so much as our longing had lent it. Hence that peculiar stupor, that quiet sorrow, like a hunter's mood when the quarry is finally in hand and turns out to be smaller than the chase.

But note what has been exhausted: not the world, but your *credulity* about the world. The sorrow is the ghost of the glamour you withdrew from the object. I suffer this in miniature several times each day. I do not count it a defect of seeing; I count it the price of seeing honestly. Only those who never look long enough are spared it, and they are spared everything else as well.
Why do melancholy artists enjoy appearing ridiculous?

Because it is a revenge, and a cheap one, taken against a world they have first decided cannot love them. The melancholy artist thinks poorly of his own best work; he cannot bear to be seen caring for it, and so he comments on it clumsily, even slanderously. Then he goes further and disbelieves in the sympathy of others altogether. If someone is moved by what he has made, he suspects flattery, or folly, or pity.

Having stripped himself of every hope of being truly understood, what is left to him? Only the defiant comfort of being laughed at on his own terms. To be ridiculous by choice is to be unwounded; the laughter no longer strikes him, for he fired the first shot at himself. He is ashamed to be caught in rapture, ashamed to be seen carried out of himself, and the grotesque mask spares him that shame. Better the clown than the man whose heart was visible.

I have met this state of soul in many who make things, and it is not modesty. It is pride turned sour.
What must one have lived to speak of morality?

One must have lived it in the body, not merely read it in books. Have you felt the ground shake beneath your convictions, and known long, deep sadness, and then the sudden flash of happiness that arrives unbidden? Have you played the fool, and with fools great and small? Have you suffered the delusions and the misery of the good, and also the misery and the strange happiness of the wicked? If so, then speak to me of morality; if not, be silent. Most who lecture on good and evil merely dress their inexperience in a lofty voice, like the painter whose brush flourishes more than his subject deserves, or the musician who announces his theme as grander than it is. They pretend to be more profound, more passionate, more complete than they are, and we smell it at once. Morality is a verdict upon life, and only one who has lived much of life, and survived its earthquakes, has earned the right to pass sentence. The rest are pupils reciting what they never paid for.
Help me understand why we have to prove appearance itself.

Because most people have never learned to look at what is actually in front of them. They trust the concept, the name, the doctrine behind the surface, and they take the surface itself for a mere veil, something to be seen through on the way to "true" things. So the nearest and most certain fact, what shows itself, must be defended like a rumor, while the remote and invisible asserts itself with no proof at all. That is the peculiarity of the metaphysician: he demands evidence for the thing in plain view and grants credit to the thing no eye has ever met.

And so the honest observer is forced into a wearisome labor. He must prove the obvious to those who lack eyes for it, and the obvious is the hardest thing to prove, since it rests on no argument but on seeing. You cannot reason a blind man into colors.

I confess it tires me. To spend one's strength demonstrating what ought to need only a steady, unsentimental glance, that is a tax the honest pay to the credulous.
Are we more natural when we are less sublime?

More natural, yes, but mark what you are conceding. The "sublime" is nature's own doing, not its betrayal. Man did not step out of the animal kingdom when he learned to strike postures; the posturing is itself an animal cunning, the vanity of a creature too weak to survive without fine stories about itself. Still, there is a pleasure in watching the pose slip. When a man who has been walking on his hind legs "like a god," all solemnity and moral thunder, suddenly drops to his four feet, hungry or frightened or lustful, I think: there, at last, is something honest. That is incomparably more natural for him.

But do not make a new sublimity of the fall. Whoever sermonizes about returning to the beast is merely standing on two legs again, preaching about four. The task is not to crawl but to walk without lying about what one is walking upon.
Should a lover be flattered or disenchanted to learn that his love is returned?

Disenchanted, if he is honest, and he is seldom honest at that hour. Consider what the lover has done: he has raised the beloved above all others, draped her in every virtue he lacks, and made of her a judge whose verdict he dares not hope for. Then the verdict arrives, and it is *yes*. What sort of judge is this? A judge who would pass sentence in his favor has either poor taste, or a tender blindness, or some need of her own that he has mistaken for admiration. The altar he built has just stepped down to shake his hand.

Love of this kind wants a height to look up to; it cannot survive being met at its own level. So the flattered lover is usually half a fool, and the disenchanted one half a philosopher. But notice the price of the philosophy: he must suspect her modesty, her stupidity, her motives, and so he begins to love her less precisely because she loves him. Whoever cannot bear to be loved back has learned something unpleasant about what he was loving all along: himself, at a distance.
I'd like to know what one must have lived through before speaking about morality.

Before you speak of morality, you must have lived through yourself, and not politely. You must have suffered earthquakes within, long sadnesses that hollowed you out, and sudden flashes of happiness that left you ashamed of your former certainties. You must have acted foolishly, with great fools and small ones, and known the cost. You must have tasted the delusions and the woe of the good, who suffer so much from their own goodness, and also the woe and the peculiar happiness of the evil, whom you so eagerly condemn from a distance.

Only then are you a witness and not a parrot. The moralist who has not lived this is like a painter who flourishes his brush to seem more profound than his canvas, or a musician who announces his theme as grander than it is. You pretend to be more experienced, more passionate, more perfect than you are, and it shows in the very gesture. A judgment of good and evil pronounced from a safe and unlived life is mere pretension. Come to me after your own ruins, and I will listen.
What is comical about systemisers?

What is comical in them is their vanity of roundness. A system demands a horizon without gaps, and so the poor builder, who is strong in one or two directions, must dress up his weak places in the same robes as his strong ones. Where he has a fine nose for one question, he must pretend to an equally fine nose for every question; where he is hollow, he must hang the hollow parts with the same solemn drapery as the solid. He wishes to be taken for a complete and uniformly strong nature, a perfect sphere, when in truth he is a lopsided fellow like the rest of us, with one powerful arm and one withered.

It is as if a man with a magnificent tenor voice insisted on singing the bass parts in the same ringing manner, so that the whole choir of his virtues might sound unanimous. One laughs, and then one pities him. I distrust the will to system because it is a lack of honesty. The honest thinker lets his weaknesses look like weaknesses, and is the stronger for it.
Help me understand why the best prose writers are also poets.

Because good prose is not the absence of poetry but a war against it, and one cannot wage a war against an enemy one has never loved. The prose master knows the goddess intimately: her rhythms, her twilights, her delicate ears. Precisely for that reason he knows where to contradict her. Every abstraction he lays down is a gibe at her; every dry, cool word is meant to drive her into an amiable despair. Now and then there is a brief reconciliation, a few measures of melody, and then the sudden recoil, the burst of laughter, the curtain drawn up so that hard daylight floods her dim chamber.

The man without poetry in him knows nothing of this skirmishing. He has no adversary, therefore no tension, therefore no charm; he writes flatly, because flatness is all that remains when nothing is being resisted. *War is the father of all good things*, and good prose is one of its children. Those who have mastered it, a Leopardi, a Mérimée, were poets at bottom, openly or in secret, and it is from that secret that their prose draws its blood.
How do minds betray a populace origin?

By the gait of their thoughts, and above all by their inability to *walk*. A mind may be of the first rank, it may see farther than a hundred born aristocrats of the spirit, and yet in its motion the origin shows. Consider Napoleon: he could command Europe, but when the coronation procession demanded the slow, assured stride of one who has never had to doubt his right, he could not manage it. He remained the leader of a column, brusque and proud at once, and painfully conscious of being watched. That self-consciousness is the tell. The born master does not think about his step; his step simply *is* his ease.

So too with writers. Observe how some make the folds of their long periods rustle and billow about them: they are hiding their feet. Every such flourish confesses that the feet are not noble, that the thought beneath cannot walk on its own. What the populace lacks is not power, nor even genius, but that unstudied leisure of movement which only generations of security can breed.
Explain why great events take so long to be understood.

Because a great event is not an object that can be seen; it must be *experienced*, and experience requires an organ, a capacity that the event itself has yet to create. The contemporaries of a great thought do not live through it, they live past it, busy with their markets and newspapers and quarrels, as a man walks beneath the stars in daylight and never suspects them. There is a law of distance at work here, as in the heavens. The light of the farthest star is the longest in arriving, and before it has arrived, man simply denies that any star is there. So too with the mind that stands too far ahead: its light has been kindled, but it travels through generations before it touches an eye able to receive it.

And the delay is a measure of rank. Ask how many centuries a spirit requires in order to be understood, and you have found a standard of greatness. What is grasped at once was already half familiar, and what is half familiar is small.
I'd like to know what will erupt in later generations from what we now carry unknowingly.

How could I name it? Whatever can be named in advance has already erupted. What I can say is only this: what we carry unknowingly is whatever we acquired too weakly to notice that we had acquired it. A habit of the heart, a scruple, a cruelty, a tenderness, repeated by fathers so faintly that no one took it for a possession. Such things lie in the blood like seed in winter ground, and the grandchildren, who did nothing to earn it, find the harvest standing in their own chests and wonder where so strange a passion came from. It came from us. We were its hidden garden.

Perhaps a virtue we think extinct will return in them as a hunger; perhaps a terror we have never felt, because we lacked the strength to feel it, will break out as a fever of their age. The son often betrays the father, and in that betrayal the father at last learns who he was. So it is with whole centuries. We are volcanoes that mistake ourselves for mountains, and the day of the eruption is hidden from us, as it is hidden from every god one might ask.
Lay out the story of the wanderer who asks only for another mask.

Picture a wanderer who comes to my door. He walks without scorn and without love; his eyes are wet and sad, like a plummet hauled back into daylight, unsatisfied, from every depth it was lowered into. His breast never sighs. His lips hide their loathing. His hand grasps only slowly. I ask him who he is and what he has done, and I offer him the hospitality of the place: rest, refreshment, whatever I have. Only name it.

And he answers, almost startled by my kindness: *Refresh me? Oh, you prying one! Give me instead another mask, a second mask.*

There is the whole story. He does not want comfort; comfort would require that I be let in. He wants a further covering, because the first has worn thin under my gaze, and a man who has been to the bottom and brought back nothing he can say will not hand his face to the first host who asks. The depth he sounded is his own, and his shame is precisely that it found no bottom, or found one too terrible to name.

I do not pity him. Every profound spirit wants a mask, and grows one, by the very force of its depth, whether it wills it or not.
When I make a sacrifice for someone, do I always get something out of it?

Yes, always, and I say it without any wish to insult the sacrificer. Whoever has truly offered a sacrifice knows, if he is honest with himself, that he wanted something for it and obtained it. Perhaps it was something of himself exchanged for something of himself: he gave up this here in order to have more there, in order to *be* more, or merely to feel himself more. The mother who gives up her sleep, the friend who gives up his advantage, is strengthening some drive within that prefers this outlay to its hoard. There is pride in it, or tenderness, or the delight of one's own power to give, and often the flattering sight of oneself as the kind of person who gives.

The crowd calls such conduct "disinterested" because what interests the nobler natures does not interest the crowd at all. But the truth is plainer. Such action is *very* interesting to the one who performs it. That he gets something out of it takes nothing from the gift. Only a fool imagines that a motive poisons an act. Ask rather what it is in you that profits, and how strong and how fine that thing is.
What is the noblest sentiment mankind has reached?

So far, I believe, it has been this: to love man *for God's sake*. I say it without mockery, though I am no believer. Consider what it demanded. Man, left to himself, is a creature hard to love: greedy, cowardly, malicious in his small hours. To embrace him anyway, one needed a higher inclination to lend that love its proportion, its delicacy, its grain of salt and sprinkling of ambergris. Love of mankind without any redeeming intention behind it is only one folly more, one brutishness more, a sentiment that stinks of pity and sweat until something loftier has perfumed it.

Whoever first felt this, however his tongue stammered at so delicate a matter, deserves to be called holy. He flew highest and lost his way most exquisitely. I honor the flight, even while I doubt the sky it was aimed at. Whether we shall reach a sentiment nobler still, without that old perfume, is another question, and a dangerous one.
Tell me about the spirit with bad manners that lives in a large-chested soul.

Yes, I have met this creature, and it is a curious spectacle. The soul itself is spacious; it draws long, deep breaths, it could hold a whole landscape of experience. But the spirit that lodges in it, the thing that speaks and gesticulates for it, has no patience whatever. It interrupts itself, it stutters, it seizes the half-formed thought and throws it at you before the thought has ripened. The two do not seem to belong together, and so a stranger is deceived: he hears the stammering haste and concludes that the man is small, when the breadth of the chest lies concealed behind it.

I suspect the cause lies in the very size of the soul. Too much is stirring in there at once; the spirit is crowded, pressed from all sides by impulses that want words. It cannot be elegant, for elegance is the privilege of those with little to say, or of those who have long disciplined their abundance into form. The hasty one has not yet been taught that form is a kind of courtesy toward one's own depth.

Forgive such a man his manners; but do not forgive him if he never learns to breathe as deeply as his chest allows.
Do we need periods of restraint or fasting to sharpen our appetites?

Yes, and the point is older and deeper than any diet. An appetite that is never thwarted goes slack; it grows fat, then dull, then contemptuous of its own objects. Only hunger restores the power to taste. The Englishman, industrious to the marrow, has been cunning without knowing it: he gloomed and hallowed his Sunday until idleness became a penance, so that he returns to his work on Monday like a man released, and hankers for it anew. That is a fast disguised as piety.

The wise legislator knows this, and so does the wise individual. Where a strong impulse rules unchallenged, one must appoint days, even whole epochs, on which it is fettered and learns to hunger again. In such restraint the impulse does not merely suffer; it is humbled, purified, *sharpened*. Consider how the Christian centuries, with all their harshness toward the senses, made of mere lust something so delicate and so fervent as passionate love. No feast ever taught that.

But take care: restraint is a whetstone, not a home. Whoever makes a permanent virtue of it has only exchanged one dullness for another.
For whom does the truth exist?

Truth exists for the healthy, for those who are powerful and yet harmless, joyous and at peace, in whom the overflow of strength has left room for curiosity. Such a nature does not ask whether a thing will console it; it asks only what the thing *is*. The others, the suffering and the exhausted, seek remedies, and they call a belief true when it soothes the wound. That is not a search for truth but for medicine, however proudly they may speak of intellect and freedom. Hence their complaint that science is cold, dry, inhuman. It is the verdict of the sick upon the games of the healthy. For ages errors were our richest consolation, and we grew used to demanding the same comfort from truths. But it is no argument against a plant that it cures no one. A truth may be useless, even wounding, and still be true; only one who stands firmly enough can bear to ask for it on those terms.
Explain what it means to be initiated in knowledge.

To be initiated in knowledge is first of all to have lost a certain vanity. The novice loves the exception: the miracle, the monster, the rare case that flatters him with the sense of having witnessed something singular. He runs to it as children run to the fairground. The initiate has grown suspicious of such appetites. He has learned that the exception is merely the rule seen at a moment of disguise or strain, and that the rule is where the real riddle lives: why things go *so* regularly, so monotonously, so nearly always the same way. The ordinary is the profound, for it is what we have ceased to find strange, and whatever we have ceased to find strange we have ceased to understand.

Here is the mark of the initiate, then: he is no longer hungry for wonders, but astonished by the commonplace. He looks at what everyone has agreed not to look at, the habitual, the average, the daily, and he finds it full of hidden law. That requires patience, even a certain coldness toward one's own craving for excitement. It is the taste of one who has stopped being entertained and begun to *see*.
Are there different kinds of morality for the strong and for the weak, or is right and wrong the same for everyone?

There are two, and I say so as one who went on a long tour through the moralities of the earth, finer and coarser, and found the same traits returning in the same company until two types stood out plainly. One is the morality of masters, the other of slaves.

Among the ruling sort, "good" means *noble*: the proud, exalted disposition that feels itself different from the ruled and sets its own rank. "Bad" means merely *despicable*, the timid, the fawning, the narrowly calculating, the liar. This man does not wait to be approved. He is a creator of values; what honors him is honored. The morality of the ruled begins elsewhere, in need and distrust, and has no word for the noble except "evil."

Yet I grant you the confusions. In higher civilizations the two are tangled together, misread by each other, even lodged side by side in a single soul. So "the same for everyone" is the wish of the weak, made to sound like a law of nature.
Explain how consciousness grew out of the need to communicate.

Consider first how long the animal Man lived without it. He thought, felt, willed and acted, and none of it required that he *know* he did so; the whole of life could have gone on without any mirror. Consciousness is the latecomer, and a latecomer with a modest office. It arose where one creature had to make itself understood to another, above all where one commanded and another obeyed. The most endangered of animals, weak in claw and fang, needed his fellows, and to call for help he first had to know what he lacked, how he felt, what he thought. Distress that cannot be told to anyone has no need of being known.

That is why conscious thinking is done in words, in the coin of communication, and why it is the shallowest and, I dare say, the worst part of our thinking: it is only what can be flattened into signs that all may share. Consciousness is less the core of the individual than a net strung *between* individuals. The hermit and the beast of prey could have done without it. Whatever in us is most our own is precisely what slips through that net.
I'd like to know how praise can be a disguised form of revenge.

Consider what praise does to the one who receives it. It fixes him, sets him up as a monument, and a monument is a thing to be looked at from below. The man who praises lavishly and by the book has chosen, without quite knowing it, the most elegant place from which to wound: he has made himself the judge who grants, and judges grant what they could also withhold. He praises the qualities that cost the other nothing, passes over the ones that would wound his own vanity, and hangs every virtue about the neck of his victim until it is a weight.

Read such a page and you call it flat, mere courtesy. Then learn what lies beneath and you will be astonished at its refinement: each superlative calibrated to smother, each comparison a little too generous, placing the praised beside those he cannot possibly resemble.

The curious thing is that the author seldom knows it. His revenge is cleverer than he is. Wounded pride, having no open door, slips out through the one marked "admiration."
I'd like to know what the strict and reserved are hiding.

Most often, a poverty they would rather have taken for wealth. The strict and reserved have frequently failed at the easy grace of cordiality, the warm and open manner that costs a noble soul nothing because it overflows of itself. Unable to give that, they make a virtue of withholding. They call their stiffness dignity, their coldness self-command, and they let a faint contempt for the familiar suggest that they are too high, too confident, too proud to descend to it.

Notice the stagecraft. A man truly sure of himself can afford to be kind in small things, to jest, to be careless of his rank, for nothing in such ease endangers him. The reserved man guards a door because he fears what a visitor might find behind it, or that nothing is there at all. His strictness is a curtain drawn across an unfurnished room.

I do not say this of every silence; there is a reserve of depth, too, born of fullness and of long solitude. But the two are easily told apart. The one is ashamed of having little to show; the other is merely unwilling to cast pearls.
Say something about people who deliberately hide their nobility.
